The game is paced really well, it has a great variety of amazing looking locations, and I found myself actually wanting to explore and unlock and discover everything I could. The game does a good job at not making you feel like an invisible action hero, which is a good thing. Laura is supposed to be a rookie. I never felt like I was unecessarily violent or that it was straying into action hero territory.
The downside I think is that the game tends to be too easy, even on hard. There werent very many times I had to retry anything and the puzzles are not much in terms of mind benders. I get they want everyone to be able to solve the puzzles but I wish there was at least one that had me thinking for a day. And the DLC isnt really worth the price, it has the usual optional clothes but the temple you can get is a big puzzle that can be solved within 30min. But the game is worth the GOTY edition so you'll get all that DLC anyways for the same $20. Worth it if you ask me.

Deep within the depths of Steam.  Buried underneath thousands and thousands of Steam games lies a game called Cloney which was apparently released March 15, 2014 yet just now has come to the attention of achievement hunters.  Is it a legendary treasure that hunters are seeking?   From my understanding, this "attention boom" comes from recently gaining achievements.  As someone who's unearthed this treasure chest, I can verify it's more like a container that holds a monster rather than a treasure.  Pandora's box holds a monster who should have stayed buried.
is just as it sounds.  It's a clone game.  Now, I've seen reviews calling this a rip-off of something called "Flappy Birds", a game I've never played but have heard about many times.  After looking it up, it looks exactly like it with the exception of being able to pick up coins (which will count as your score rather than distance).  If this isn't bad enough, the developer itself confirms that this is a clone of
.  For a game that was made in 24 hours, it's a decent attempt, but there are horrors to this game that make it one that should have stayed buried.  And as far as the title is concerned, "A tapped out adventure"?  You'll find yourself p*ssed off and your hand either spazzing out (like mine) when you need to concentrate or you'll find yourself tapping-out (quitting).
The model of the main character (which seems to have been a screamer from the trailer of the game) looks familiar....too familiar....have I seen this model before?  Yes.  In Orion: Prelude.  Cloney the character is just a copy of the dragon model from Orion: Prelude, which is most likely some open-source model developers either pay for or nab for free.  Without a credits page, I can only confirm that the usage of this model is PLAGIARISM!
Aside from the character, the music is.....pretty bad.  But we'll get back to this in a bit.  I will say that the only redeeming factor physically would be the backgrounds which are well-done, but I don't know if the developer itself actually made the backgrounds or nabbed them from somewhere else.
Now, for the gameplay.  You may think "Easy 100%" and if you're someone who has good rhythem and patience, you'd be right.  But even then, the price is one's sanity. You'll find yourself losing easilly and in a matter of seconds.   The two final trials to test your mettle are "Gather 40 coins" and "Live for 15 minutes"....simple enough, yes?   No....wrong.   Dead wrong.  Gather 8 coins and your speed increases.  When your speed increases, you are less able to have time to analyze and dodge.
As for the "15 minute" achievement challenge, had to redo this about 7-10 times...got close 3 times only to lose within the last 2 minutes or (on one occassion), the last 24 seconds.  To gauge my time, I had to have the TV on in the background (one half episode and an entire commercial break is long enough to help out...listen to it to gauge to your time).   My experience each time is similar to what I've seen
was like...except I admit it was all in my head.  The repetitive music....became demonic as my sanity slipped away.  I could swear I saw pentagrams on the ground and burning red fire where the branches that kill were.  I saw the dragon turn into a red ball, which didn't work well as a hitbox (hitbox appears to be somewhat larger than your character.  It was a terrible experience.
There is only one endless level...one mode.  It's basically plug-n-play.  Easy to boot up and just play without a story or forced tutorial.  So at least it has that going for it.
PROS:
Nice looking backgrounds
Was made in 24 hours
Free
Achievements
No forced tutorial  (In fact, no tutorial at all)
CONS:
Nightmarish achievements (40 coins and Live for 15 minutes.  Edit: Now a little more tolerable with an active pause function)
Game breaks on some occassions (Dragon will stay on the ground, go under water....cannot reset game)
Poor music choices
PLAGIARISM  (Devs put credits on a website, but still need IN-GAME credits.  People who do not visit the website will come to the same conclusion)
I'll be honest, this game made me sick to my stomach.  It was easilly one of the worst Steam experiences I've had on Steam.  If you like free games or want to try getting some easy achievements (100% won't be so easy though), then go ahead and try, but don't say I didn't warn you.

Now; I don't have much experience with our friendly neighborhood priestess Denira, but from the little experience I do have I can guarantee to you, she is in fact not weak at all. Her powerful healing and ability to res your heroes helps a lot, trust me. I highly suggest you check this game out and add it to your library; it's not so often a game makes me want to come back for something that isn't just a daily reward. La-Mulana is an absolutely fantastic game. Personally, I've lost count of how many times I've played through it. I've even beaten Hell Temple once, though that was on the Playism version. Yes, this game was good enough that I bought it twice. Anyway.
La-Mulana is an open-world platformer that sends you, an archaeologist, delving into the eponymous ruins of La-Mulana. At first, you're only in it for the treasure, but the plot slowly unfolds into something much bigger than that. The controls, once you know why they are how they are, are fantastic. When I first played it, I was confused why the jumping was so strange, but after I learned that they were done like that to harken back to the MSX game Maze of Galious, it all made sense to me. The enemies, somewhat uniquely for a game like this, are purposefully only annoyances. The real challenge of the game is in its puzzles. While they are completely ingenius, I'm not ashamed to admit I used a guide for a lot of them. Even with that, however, the game was still an awesome experience, and I'd highly recommend it to anyone looking for a game that wants you to think.

Challenging, puzzling, and amazing. La-Mulana throws you into a massive world, with no sense of direction. You're introduced to three huts, one open, and you're told to explore, but how deep can those ruins go? At times, is may get frustrating due to the fact you may forget something important, or get stumped by a hard boss fight. No matter what though, do not loose hope, and explore what the ruins have in store for you!

Do you remember back in the NES days when games were hard as hell? Making progress from one level to the next was a monumental task. You couldn't just sit down, turn your mind off and breeze through any task; games required you to memorize and adapt. It made even the most awesome of ideas sometimes horrid.
La-Mulana harkens back to that exact idea. If the game isn't kicking your♥♥♥♥♥ you must be Jesus. While I appreciate a game that doesn't hand hold me, I'm torn on exactly how La-Mulana goes about torturing the player. Sometimes, it can feel really unfair; other times, your objective is clouded in obscurity that nearly necessitates a guide.
The basic breakdown of the game is akin to Super Metroid or any more recent Castlevania. You explore dungeons on a 2-D plane, acquire weapons that will help in different rooms and proceed to tackle bosses and enemies as they come to you. It's all about exploration, puzzle solving and some tight jumps.
The difficulty comes from a lot of cheap tactics and some staggering hits from your foes. The developers philosophy was that a normal person placed in a hidden cavern wouldn't have the know how to get out. You normally wouldn't jump down a black hole and expect to land softly.
That does make sense, realistically, but it kind of hurts the game in some parts. Puzzles end up following their own logic and you often are required to walk through hazards to make any progress. It can lead to you being unsure, backtracking a lot to find some different route and then giving up and just saying, "♥♥♥♥ it!"
It's cool to see a cavern designed in a way that should facilitate logical thinking, but to hide so many core solutions behind layers of riddles and abstract thought stinks. I just want to be able to evaluate the situation and move on, not have to constantly refer to a guide to figure out what I'm doing.
The game makes up for this with extremely tight controls and some incredible music and graphics. The artwork comes to life in all it's 32-bit glory. The soundtrack is immediately nostalgic while being modern and energetic. The boss fights are intimidating and demand you to master your skillsets.
It makes for some climactic and exhilirating encounters, but getting to those points is often frustrating beyond reason. That I somehow managed to finish the game in around 20 hours is a testament to how determined I was, but most players won't have that resolve.
La-Mulana asks a tremendous amount from you. You are only going to get from it what you put it. Nothing about the game will coddle you until you succeed. If you cannot adapt, you will fail; time and time again.
So while I think the game is good, I can't recommend it to a lot of people. It's just going to put off more casual players or gamers who like not relying on walkthroughs. If you can muster up the courage for the challenge, it's definitely a worthwhile investment.

It explores a few bits of dystopian scifi future moral quandry type issues that wouldn't be out of place in the Outer Limits or the Twilight Zone, and this is when the game truly shines. It would have been good to continue down this route offering additional "cases" as the main character progresses, but this is limited to two or three side "quests".

In all, this game is absolutely worth it, and in my mind very underrated. It's beautiful to look at, listen to, and to read. Please check it out, give it some love, and enjoy it. I sure as hell did. These stories and characters will stick with me for a while. #Jana

Players not used to pinball in general may find The Pinball Arcade somewhat frustrating at first. It's just one of those things you have to persevere with. If you do, you will be rewarded with an experience that hones your instincts like a sport. There is strategy to it, patience, luck, and the need for twitch reflexes. Basically, everything's a target and you are constantly scoring points and bonuses, so it has a highly addictive effect on the reward system of your brain.
A great deal of production time was invested in making the original pinball machines, and that finds its way into the game. Buying all of the tables in The Pinball Arcade may seem expensive to some people, but compared to the cost of owning dozens of actual pinball tables, it is extremely cheap. You can even play the table Tales of the Arabian Nights for free. Some of the tables are works of art in game form, and most people will not encounter pinball machines in their local area the way they used to up until the late 1990s.
The tables in The Pinball Arcade are replicas of ones from the stables of Williams, Gottlieb, Bally, Stern, Data East, and Sega. Farsight Studios (the company behind Pinball Arcade) have produced a string of previous games that attempt to achieve authenticity and pay homage to the history and culture of pinball. They now own the licenses to many of the best tables of all time.
The Pinball Arcade plays quite a lot like real pinball, although the physics are never going to be 100% accurate on any pinball video game, and nudging is particularly easy on The Pinball Arcade. The game manages to look fantastic without adding a layer of graphical effects that couldn't be incorporated into real tables. The tables appear mechanical, although they are of course simulated.
Like most other pinball games, there is a lot crammed into an area that's a different shape to a landscape orientation monitor. Thankfully, in Pinball Arcade, you can swivel the monitor 90° into portrait mode if you have that kind of monitor. Even without this, the game is highly enjoyable and one of the best pinball video games ever made. In my opinion it is much better than Pinball FX2.

After playing this game since V1 at launch to V1.2 now, I can surely say that this is a great game and very impressed with the dev support.
TL;DR. It's a simple addictive game, but can be quite daunting to start with. Overall worth the £15 (or $20 I think)
Basically you land in a little ship, set up the absolute basics to maintain a self sufficient colony then grow it from there balancing resources, population and productivity. You can trade with traders who will come and go, allow visitors to have a rest stop for a fee (Which is determined by the game) and defend yourselves from bandits who will in effect try to kill everyone so they can take over your base.
Graphically the game is excellent, it's not ground breaking photo realism but it certainly isn't terrible at all either. The sound work is also very good too. the UI can be a little confusing to start with but once you have a decent size base, you'll know the UI back to front. The gameplay is very simple but that is part of what makes the game so addictive, you build, manage and once you have the resources, you build even more, to which it carries on like that until you fill out the entire map. From there you move on to a more challenging planet.
But of course the game does have its flaws. as mentioned in a lot of reviews the AI isn't fantastic. I have never had a terrible problem with that, like I said, it is about striking a good balance.
It also taps into the whole design of the base itself, place similar parts near each other, not at other ends of the base. Follow this and the AI problem is a thing of the past, if anything it's quite reqarding being able to sit back and watch the base actively run itself. The only other issue new players would have is that it is quite unforgiving to begin with, your first base will not survive, you will have to run a couple of bases into the ground to learn and understand the game fully but stick with it and it does become quite simple after that.
Overall, the game is well worth its price tag, if its your kind of game you can sink lots and lots of time into it, at the time of writing this review, I have over 60 hours and I haven't finished the last planet yet. It still has a lot of untapped potential but it is still great in its current state.

My first review was negative, I've later decided to have another go at this game. If I could I'd leave a neutral review, but seeing I've spent over 40 hours on this game there's no denying it has something worthwile.
The game offers 4 difficulties (represented by planets), the first planet is the easiest one, and by easy I mean 20+ hours of grinding with at least as many retries as hours spent. All this grinding is to familiarize yourself with the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ way the citizens behave, and to determine the uselessness of all facilities you have at your disposal. The second planet only required two tries.
There's different "jobs" and every citizen is assigned one upon arrival to the planet, this can be customized by adjusting the percentage of all jobs, by far the most useful tool you have.
The citizens will do their jobs, and not surprisingly, only that. This makes starting of a colony a bit tedious. Say that your colony happens to starve a bit, every single person will refuse to do any work effectively halting any remedy to the starvation. The only hope for you to come out of it is if the job responsible for food (it's a job, so 7 of 10 citizens will look at the plant thinking 'wow, wish I had the mental capacity to water this thing so I wouldn't die') is not sleeping or watching TV. Another solution is that half the population dies out, and hopefully not the biologists.
But, after a while you get a bit more stable colony with more citizens assigned to jobs so the workload is divided and you can finally breathe a little.
This is not viable in the long run though, because the game is setup in a way that you always have a shortage of something. It's annoyingly well calculated, and it forces you to always expand until you simply run out of planet (you don't, but you will hit invisible borders making further construction/expansion impossible).
For every need there's a special room, or dome, let's go through this headache step by step:
* Oxygen - requires power and water
* Power - Comes in two forms: wind and solar. Both are incredibly unreliable and a mix of both is recommended (on the first planet anyway, the other planets restricts the use of them). Since both forms can stop producing you need to store excess power in a special building dedicated to that.
* Water - Straigt forward, it pumps up water up to a specific capacity but can also just... not pump at times. Unreliable so you need more of these than actually necessary. Of course they require power.
* Food - Biodomes produce veggies. It needs a ton of water and constant care of a biologist. Diversity among the veggies is important to fight malnutrition. Different veggies grow at different speeds and you just don't have any way to track what grows how fast so it's all guesswork to make "balanced" meals. Also, power.
* Sleep - Dorms is where you put beds for the citizend to sleep in. Nothing fancy about this, it's just beds. The largest dorm with maximum amount of beds will suffocate the citizens inside if it's full though. Power.
* Morale - Citizens need their morale to be up or they refuse to work, even if it means death for them and all of mankind. If they're not having fun then what's the point, eh? Morale is boosted by any of three means: better beds, alcohol (a new room weirdly enough called 'bar'. Uses up all your veggies so they'll starve but will be drunk doing it) and working out in a gym. Everything needs power of course.
All these needs are required to be met for a citizen to keep on working, and, all these needs need their own room which in turn needs power and water. None of which would be possible without materials, which comes from mining the planet and growing starch in the biodome. These raw materials are then grinded into useful materials in another room requiring more power and water.
Now you're thinking "that's it? Just build one of each and have just the right surplus of power and water to keep going" am I right? Well! The vicious cycle completes with the dreaded 'SPARE PARTS'. The power-generators will break down, and they do it often. They need to be repaired so you need to produce spare parts, requiring another room requiring more power and a constant flow of materials. If you produce spare parts too slow the generators will stop working and everyone suffocates and/or starves. You need a bigger workforce to handle the load, bigger workforce means more food, beds and recreation. All of which requires more power and water, which requires more 'SPARE PARTS'.
There you have it, the cycle that makes sure you're always one step away from disaster.
Oh, and the AI which at first was THE worst thing I ever experienced is something you get to live with. The pathing is horrible, the citizens make sure to take the longest route to everything which means they can pass 2-3 restaurants on the way to the last one and starve before reaching it. It also makes sure your facilities is not used to their full capacity. A worker can stand idle right next to something that needs attention, but a second worker a minute away has already been assigned that particular station so the first one mustn't touch it.
Some say it's intentional, and if it is it's bad design. It's not the proper way to increase difficulty in a game. I want to think it's lazy developers and it will be fixed if they every come back and patch the game.
***** CONCLUSION *****
- horrible AI
- the unbalance is way too balanced. I'd like a sweetspot where I could just relax with the game.
+ the balanced unbalance. I'm really impressed by it at the same time as I don't like it, good job devs to get it to that perfect point of desperation.
I do enjoy this game, but the amount of grind required before you learn it is unreasonable.
The milestones for every planet (self-sustainability, X population, X robots etc) is a challenge to get for every planet. I've so far only completed the two first planets (all milestones on the same playthrough, a milestone of my own). After you've completed a planet there's really nothing for you left to do on that difficulty. You don't play Planetbase because of the endless fun, no, you do it because you must see if you can handle the pressure and complete all the goals.
Don't get it thinking 'a nice slow-paced RTS, perfect to relax after a hard days work' NO! It's an extension to your hard days work.
But, if you like a challenge (deliberate or from poor development) then this is absolutely worth it. Seriously, I've spent over a workweek on this and just got the hang of it... that's what you call bang for your buck.

I enjoyed Tomb Raider with one unusual, really big caveat that I will mention at the very beginning: This game has very significant, perpetual camera sway that is largely independent from your in-game movement and there is no way to turn it off. If you are susceptible to motion sickness (even just slightly), I am almost sure that this game will knock you sick if you play it for extended periods of time, it sure did for me.
Apart from that I think this is a very worthy addition to the modern Tomb Raider series. It shows the very beginnings of Lara Croft's career as an action hero-archaeologist and as such the game starts out with her being little more than a young student on an expedition. Naturally, something really bad happens and the team ends up stranded on an island somewhere in the pacific where they have to fight for their survival. The progression from student to action hero is drawn pretty nicely, with story events having a visible impact on Lara's equipment, clothing and even scars. In contrast to the Legend-trilogy there is less of an emphasis on solving environmental puzzles and more on moving across the island, exploring the areas for collectibles and progressing the story. When you do have to climb it feels nice and fluid, but the levels admittedly don't pose very big challenges to your navigation-skills.
You find out very soon that there is something not quite right about the island, a weird cult inhabits it and you fight them all over the place. Some combat sections end up so bombastic that it really ends up clashing a bit with the exploration and a few times it took me out of the experience a bit because the hordes of enemies and dozens of explosions just felt so exaggerated and out of place. Nevertheless, the combat is simple but fun, allows for some limited variation by giving you some silent options in addition to guns and it gets more fun the further you are in the game since your equipment and abilities open up more possibilities to dispose of enemies.
While some of the scenes where Lara gets hurt and thrown around the place seem a bit laboured with all the pained moaning and crying, it surprised me how grim the game got and how often it didn't shy away from showing some grueling stuff. Personally, I think it definitely adds to the game and gives it some heft and weight that the very flat characters and dialogue just don't provide. However, if you're especially squeamish or easily grossed out, you might not like it.
I'm not a big fan of the way the story is presented or the characters, but the environmental and enemy design deserves praise for creating detailed, intriguing backdrops and enemies to fight. To a layman like me, the artifacts you collect and the armor some of the enemies wear may as well be real archaeological finds.
All in all, there is a lot of attention to detail that went into this game and it provides a good amount of things to do with some optional content off the beaten path. The camera sway is a crying shame and the gameplay could have been a bit deeper and more varied, but as it stands Tomb Raider still provides a worthwhile package that I enjoyed playing (with breaks).

This is a game that I find it hard to recommend, but don't want to discourage either. I gave it a "recommend" rating, but that's only because I couldn't choose a neutral answer. It's one of those weird in between games that, while not necessarily a bad game, it's just not good either. I got this one on sale for $4.99, and really I can't say I wasted my money, but I can't possibly say that I would have paid full price of $20 for it.
Let me get the negative stuff out of the way first. Largely, the story. It's largely forgettable. It features your standard 'fighting for survival against a crazed cult on a deserted island' story line that is meant to serve in large part as a prolouge for the future Tomb Raider titles. The game even ends with the tagline of "A Survivor is Born." I really couldn't remember some of the characters names outside of Lara's, Sams, and Reyes', and that's only because the latter two are shouted every 10 minutes.
Even some of the "plot twists" that were 'revealed' at the end I was able to see coming from a mile away (I won't spoil it though). It made me scratch my head thinking "Huh, these guys are just NOW figureing this out? I thought this was the whole point the entire time." Plus, just some of the choices made by a few of the characters were a bit weird.
Now, for the gameplay, this is where I'm ultimately on the fence on. I understand that the Tomb Raider series sorta revolutionized the platforming genre to include scaling walls, cliffs, and using the room to up and across mixed with some cool gunplay. I'm going to admit however, that I enjoyed the Uncharted series for this repect far more, despite it coming in much later. This game wasn't bad at all in it's platforming, and I really liked the bow and arrow mechanic, but I feel like it saw how Uncharted perfected the game Tomb Raider started, and just tried to mimic it.
My biggest gripe however was it's use of the Quick Time Events, or QTE's. This annoyed the heck outta me. It was a poor game mechanic on consoles and I feel like it's even worse on PC. The final boss is literally nothing but a QTE a battle after a semi-QTE boss battle. It may as well not even be counted as a boss battle.
Now, for what I liked. I DID in fact like the fact that it was a reboot that starts with Lara Crofts "origin story." I know I griped about it being just a glorified prolouge but I WILL admit, it felt good to finally see her beginnings from an innocent to a survivor, even is it was just against your steriotypical bad guys in a steriotypical setting. Instead of just hearing about her surviving some crazy even that turned her into a hardened treasure hunter, we see it unfold ourselves. I just thought the story could have been much more fleshed out and some of the supporting cast been less like cardboard cutouts
Plus, I can't say I entirely hated it's gameplay, I DID like Uncharted for a reason, and because of those games it definitely helped this series get to where it needed to be. It had fluid controls (for the most part, despite the camera acting a little wonky at times like snapping behind Lara unexpectedly at random times), and the guns handled fine. If it weren't for those darned QTE's. I might have enjoyed it a bit more.
Plus, I also very much enjoyed it's visual design. I loved the drab colors and washed out grays. I'm not being facetious in saying it, but it really did help set the mood for this game.
So in closing, I'm not going to give it a "recommend" rating as I don't see it as a "must play" game, but I won't give it a "don't recommend" rating as it's not so bad that it's unenjoyable. It's just there, take it or leave it. If you feel like you need to play it, or want to play it before diving into Rise of the Tomb Raider like I did, then wait for it to go on sale before buying it, but don't pay full price for it.

*Review for v1.3.209*
For a free Flappy Bird style game where you dodge trees, collect coins and unlock achievements, I thought this would be interesting and fun. However, upon playing it, it seems as though it was made for one platform and then rushed out onto Steam as fast as possible. Therefore, read below to find out my pros and cons.
Pros:
♦ Good Graphics and Sounds (Sound is relaxing; trees/backgrounds/our character are well detailed)
♦ Controls just work (This is because pressing any button on the keyboard, works as “Tap” to make your character move)
♦ Well made for a 24hour game
♦ Easy Steam Achievements (Just by playing the game you easily unlock them)
♦ Steam Leaderboards (This is awesome as they just seem to work)
Cons:
♦ Cross-Platform that hasn't fully been tested on all platforms released for (The game itself works, however everything from buttons, in game icons, menu's etc are all mobile styled. Plus, the game tells you to tap to play even though I'm on a computer without a touchscreen. Also as the game is cross-platformed it looks as though it was built for Mobile and the devs just hoped it worked for other platforms without actually fully changing everything and testing it on the other platforms than Mobile)
♦ No Full Ingame Options Menu only a Unit Options Menu outside the game which tends to be broken  (This is annoying as you can't change resolution, graphics etc only Sound within the game and have to use the Unity Option Menu outside of the game which tends not to work most of the time and has control options when the game has no controls as every button works as a "Tap")
♦ Resolution and Fullscreen Problems (I had to play windowed because the game auto started in fullscreen and the menu was pushed far right and I couldn't get it back without hitting alt+enter)
♦ No distance and time counters in game (This is weird as your total distance and time is shown on the death score screen)
♦ Makes you check it's website for cross platform leaderboards (This is nifty as it tells you who got what score and what platform they were using... but on PC with Steam, it should have a built in mechanism in the game to check these leaderboards without automatically opening an external Steam Browser window and loading the game devs website to view the leaderboards)
♦ Sometimes coins are few and far between (This is annoying as some rounds you can have more coins than others making it extremely hard to get anywhere in the game and even register a score)
♦ Hitbox sometimes can be off (It's jerked me into branches above me that I should never have been able to hit with the jump I made)
♦ 3 star rating system isn't calculated properly (I keep getting random amounts of stars each time I finish. Also, I got 2 stars on 10 coins which took me 31 seconds to do. Hence, stars seem pointless, too easy to get and not calculated properly)
♦ No actual tutorial (This is bad as there is nothing to tell you that collecting x number of coins increases your speed regen. Plus there is nothing to tell you how time, x number of coins and distance works together to give you a score. There is only a splash screen explaining minimal things)
♦ Time and Distance seems pointless (This is the case because it seems like collecting coins is the only factor for score)
♦ Can't get back to Main Menu from within the game after you click play (This is annoying as you have no way of going back to the main menu to click either of the leaderboards buttons to view them)

Overall, even though the game is playable, it has a lot of areas that could be improved especially for a PC version/ Non-Greenlight Steam version of the game as shown by the numerous cons and few pros. Therefore, even though it is a free game and you get what you get, I still can't recommend this unless you like 100% cross-platformed games that are made in 24hours and look 100% as though it was made for a mobile device and mobile UI with minimal to no changes it. Drawful is a Jackbox Party Pack game. This slightly updated sequel is sold as a stand-alone.
All players must be able to see the host's display, by being in the same place or streaming online. Each player is given a prompt to draw a picture based on, then false prompts are written by your opponents and everyone tries to guess what the real one was. This is all faithful to the first game.
New features:
- You have a light and dark colour to draw with. You still don't get an eraser, though.
- Writing your own clues adds a whole new dimension to the game, since the same sense of humour that goes into the false answers may have been involved in writing the real ones, and players might recognize a prompt they wrote. You can also "publish" sets of prompts and share the seven character code with others on the game's discussion boards if you wish.
- Get extra points for finding the true prompt multiple times in a row.
- You can set the game to extend the drawing timers, and adjust several other settings through an options menu.
These additions are welcome, the presentation is updated, and Drawful 2 is a game that can stand up on its own merit. However, the similarity to the original Drawful may make it redundant if you already have the former, unless you really want the ability to write custom prompts.

But it isn't.
I've put about 22 hours into this game. It can be fun, challenging and
rewarding. But most of the time, the game relies on trial and error rather than good strategy, and that's a major problem.
This is an older game, and I'm sure EIDOS set out to make a game that forced people to think and strategize, but really, thinking about your strategy is only about a quarterof the game. The rest of the game is going and trying to make it work, saving when you make a modicum of progress (and you had better make absolutely certain that you do), and then dying because you couldn't time the move right, or dying because the controls are bad, or dying because what you thought was a clear, unseen corner by a guard is actually seen ...
.
One area in particular I succeeded by sneaking all of my guys through a gate and saving immediately, but the problem wasn't that I had finally devised a plan to get them through the gate; rather I had finally succeeded at doing the same thing over and over a few hours and it finally just happened to work to this time. Strategy never changed, I just happened to not be noticed this one time.
There have also been instances where I needed to run up to a guard, kill him silently, grab his body and move away from the area before I was noticed, and then deposit the body in some unseen corner. It takes multiple attempts to get the stealth kill right, because sometimes when I click on the body the game just doesn't register the click and I'm just standing behind the guard, costing me seconds, which leads to me being noticed, or sometimes I click on the guard to stab him, but my cursor was off by just a fraction of a millimeter and I ran past the guard into his line of site, or I made a noise by running that
is fine, but a quarter of the time the other patrolling guard hears it, so I have to reload, or I finally was able to make the kill and carry the body,  so I deposit him in the unseen corner, but now his foot is hanging out so it gets noticed and the alarm sounds, so I try again and turn his body a different direction, but this time my footsteps in the snow were noticed, so I have to take a different route, but the different route is populated by guards, so now I have to kill them, but I absolutely cannot simply sneak all my guys past the guards, etc.
The game can be fun when you FINALLY get through a mission, but you're really just running experiments to see what works and what doesn't for long stretches of time. This game doesn't punish incompetence; it punishes impatience because it takes an inordinate amount of time to complete anything.
Being a fan of games like Dark Souls and Bloodborne, I am not afraid of games with a high degree of difficulty. I've put about 80 hours into Dark Souls III and I highly enjoy it - may replay it with a different character at some point. That game is less trial and error, and more about exploring and fighting with a high proficiency, and using your items and resources (souls) to your advantage.  That, friends, rewards strategy, timing and execution.
This game ...
... because no matter how good your plan is, no matter what resources at your disposal you use, no matter how foolproof a way feels, something will always set you back.
With DS you get better as you play, thus making you feel like you've accomplished something. This game does not provide the same. You can know that you know how to play this game, and it just doesn't matter. This simply isn't always fun.
So ... as a review ... if this game is on sale it'll only be a little more than a dollar. Buy it then, and only then,
. I don't regret buying this game, but it can feel like work more than fun. And for that, at full price, I will not recommend this game. Video games have come a loooong way since this was released, and if you want your strategy and high degree of difficulty fix, there are plenty of other options out there.

I greatly enjoy city builders, resource management, and survival games; so I tried out Planetbase. It is a fun game and I enjoyed my first few hours with it immensely. It looks polished with storms blowing dust clouds and snow, lightning striking on some planets, lasers shooting down asteroids, and it has a great UI.
However, after the first few hours, some issues did stand out to me. The AI are not the smartest, and the lack of ability to control individual units gets frustrating as your base grows. Even with the ability to prioritize tasks, I still found ai not responding dynamically to updates I made to the base. This leads to annoying inefficiencies such as a unit carrying a resource to a building you canceled construction on, only for that unit to then leave the resource outside and return in, requiring yet another unit to repeat the route to retrieve it. This wastes resources(as the units get hungry/tired) and time. It wouldn't be a big issue if it didn't happen so frequently. After a base gets above 30 population, you see the AI start to do the most inefficient routes and tasks very often. I also found that in the mid to late game, after having successfully built a sustainable base, I would want to fast forward time to accrue some resources needed to continue my base expansion, but even the fastest setting left me sitting for many minutes wishing there was an even faster button to get on to what I wanted to do next.
My biggest critique though is the lack of content and game mechanics for the price. I constructed all the buildings in 4 to 5 hours and figured out a basic rule to expanding the base. Once I had done that, the game became pretty monotonous. Once you figure out your economies of scale, it becomes an exercie of repeating that design over and over until you've maxed out your population and achieved all of the milestones. It is essentially the same process and base design on all planets with a minor twist here and there.
For example, you do the same process on Enceladus that you did on Mars, except with a different mixture of power sources and more frequent storms. This does add a new challenge, but for me it just wasn't enough. It took me a little bit longer to figure out how to deal with the new wind and sun condiditons but then was the same rinse and repeat base layout once it was solved.
The most enjoyable planet is the last one, which is the Titan analog (no spoilers), and I argue that it was due to the addition of a new building and with limited building space, and thus an increase in strategy and the game's power management mechanics. In summary, I had fun, but just wanted more. I wanted more strategies available to me, more buildings, more ways to expand my base and have my units and structures interact. More control over my units and more things to trade in the economy.
I've played 14 hours of Planetbase and am pretty much done with all of the content this game has to offer. I've unlocked all planets, and achieved most, if not all, of the milestones on them, have played a few challenges (which also get repetitive in strategy and leave me wanting a faster speed button), and am done with the game for now. When I compare its price to the content and the hours of play, I feel that it falls short compared to others. For example, Factorio is in the same genre, same price tag, and I have over 50 hours of very enjoyable gameplay and haven't even scratched the surface of that game's content.
In summary, Planetbase is a pretty game that is fun for a few hours, but soon devolves into repetition due to a lack of diversity in strategies and challenges, and just not enough content that makes it not quite worth the price.

The game looks good and has serious promise but runs into several problems that hold it back.
The first problem I encountered was specifically the game options and how limited it is. You cannot adjust the individual volumes from within a game. You have to go to the main menu for that. You cannot mute the notifications or control when they appear or even remain. You cannot control exactly the number of colonists you want or need, merely set quotas with a rather clunky interface that constantly changes values to things that you don't want.
The second problem I encountered was the AI. There is no way to control the AI in any way. You can disable individual rooms, or disable individual stations, but you cannot force a worker to work on a specific station or work a specific room. You cannot control what buildings are built and in what order beyond placing each individual building one at a time, waiting for them to complete it, and then place your next one. In addition, the AI really is not optimised as colonists will wander off to places that are not only inefficient but also hazardous to their health.
The final problem that seals it for me is how restrictive the building system is. You have to build your buildings close to other buildings and connect them. However, should a building not actively have a connection, you cannot build there at all. If you are too close to any number of buildings or objects and you cannot build there at all. You cannot separate your base into sections as the entire thing must be connected to each other, no exceptions. This can be extremely problematic when you connect buildings in such a way that the colonists actually trap themselves within impassable walls.
I have no idea what kind of update would be needed to fix all the problems listed. It would have to be a substantial one as ALL of these problems were found completely within the FIRST LEVEL. In the end, playing the game simply didn't feel fun anymore. Not because I couldn't advance to other levels. No, the other levels unlock as you reach milestones. It stopped being fun because the further you go, the more noticible the problems become. I stopped paying attention to the notifications when they popped up every few seconds. I quickly got sick of the unskippable cutscenes when first starting the game or seeing an event. I just can't...

Pros:
- Some nice set pieces
- Interesting scenery
- fluid control reminescent of the best the old Tomb Raider series
- good length for $5-$10 range (10-30 hours to 100%)
Cons:
- gameplay is fundamentally different from the classic series; exploration is largely missing
- SHAKE CAM
- puzzles are too few, and not very challenging
- numerous QTEs, though not as egregious as some games
- writing is meh
I'm not much of a one for multiplayer, so I didn't check that out. It's possible there's something revolutionary there, but I somehow doubt it.
My biggest beef with the game comes in level design. There's a fair amount of verticality in many areas, but unfortunately it's much more linear than its predecessors. You will follow one line through the game, and the inclusion of the "survivor sense" (analogous to the Arkham series's "detective vision") means that there's not much mystery as to where to go next, which was arguably the strong suit of the early games. Gone are the days of going around in circles checking all the nooks and crannies for that tiny tunnel that will lead you to the next key or switch (maybe a good thing), but gone also is the pay-off when you do finally crack the riddle. I think this is a trade-off for the set piece design, visuals and story pacing, which thankfully are all well-executed, but it does stretch its Tomb Raider bona fides.
I got this for a fiver during a sale, and I feel I got more than my money's worth out of it. It's not the most immersive gaming experience I've ever had, but I found it engaging enough to get 100%, which is something. Just go in expecting a pretty, B-movie-level entertainment rather than the pitiless explore-a-thons of the old PS1 era.
Oh, and pass this one by if you're easily prone to seasickness. It took me a while to get used to the constant shaking of the camera.

Given the poor survival chance of everyone, this really makes the story more upsetting when your favourite characters get killed off because they're going to be your favourite because you actually spent game time on them as opposed to other characters. You choose who your prominent characters are outside of the main story. Some of them actually foreshadow later events really well and in my replay I just started I'm picking up on things I hadn't noticed before.
That's the other thing I like about it - the game is more than just solving increasingly more elaborate crimes. In between the murders you have members of the cast who are actually looking for a way out and/or trying to figure out how on Earth they got into this situation. All round good story telling, the cast interact very well (Though most of them aren't as good as the cast from the second game), and the postgame is a way of leaving nice memories in what was really quite a distressing series of events.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Wow, Damned well this game has a special place in my diaphram. The jumpscares that this game produced have not yet been matched for a long time. While this game is not necessarily the scariest game around, I will say if you play against someone who is GOOD at the monster then you will have a time of your life.
While there are newer games that fall into this genre now, this game was one of the first that I remember and was the first that I played. I have put more than 100 hours into playing this game with all of my friends, and even to this day we still give it a shot every now and then. However there are a few things that have kept us away. One major flaw in this game was the constant bugs that seemed to plague everyone anytime we would play. One such bug was that I suffer from is 50% of the time I will be stuck below 15fps throughout the whole game. The only way for me to fix this issue is to do a full system restart. Some of my friends have had issues in the past as well such as crashing, frozen characters, keys not spawning, unpassable doors/boards and others.
TLDR:
Scare Factor 7/10: (If you play with a decent monster you can have a great experience in this game, however playing with people who do not know what they are doing can lead to a boring game filled with lots of hiding. WHEN IT WORKS IT WORKS GOOD)
Optimization 4/10: (While the game does run at 60fps on my current system, before I upgraded my video card the game had a hard time keeping the fps above 40. While this could have been a bug I'm placing it here anyway.)
Gameplay 6/10: (The "Finding Keys to unlock doors to Find More Keys" gameplay is rather interesting and I actually enjoy it. In some other similar games you simply are looking for a number of objectives such as "Finding so many items to win". I think having the goal to escape is a great gameplay element and something I enjoy versus other game strategies.)
OVERALL
I have always liked this game, and will continue to recommend this game to anyone who loved Async 1v4 horror games.

The game plays over an isometric field where enemies like bandits, cannibals and stray mutts are all out to steal your lunch money and kill your face. You can see enemies on the map and can sometimes manoeuvre around them unperturbed with your party. Alert them, and you’ll find yourself embroiled in an awkwardly slow and painfully boring turn based battle dictated by a stingy allocation of action points. It’s hilarious to watch; you and your pals are running around the map like gazelles, then BANG, a scary bandit stops you and now you can only move a few inches at a time. It’s incredibly frustrating to get within a centimetre of a bandits smelly unwashed face only to find you’ve run out of action points, allowing your foe the first strike with a splintery bat upside your generic, unnamed face.
Literally everything is dictated by your action points; attacking, moving, using items, changing items, reloading items – just everything. I know that’s how a lot of turn-based games work and some people may actually like it but I just felt strangled by them and how they never allowed any wiggle room for a battle to go in a different direction. If you’re mercilessly slaughtering a bunch of enemies for example, you have to ride out the boring regulations that only allow you to kill one at a time because you have to spend tonnes of points reloading your firearms and moving from one to another. Wait a minute? Can’t I just sit in one area and shoot all the baddies from miles away? Nope. Don’t be stupid, this is the apocalypse, and your cable-tied guns aren’t worth jack. You’d be better off throwing dog♥♥♥♥♥♥at your targets as it would probably go farther and possibly do more damage if you got them in the eye.
Luckily, Krai Mira isn’t exactly a visual car crash, and effectively conveys an adequate, albeit unexceptional, atmosphere of post civilisation. It kind of reminds me of one time I got my eyes tested and had to endure a drop of dye that made everything look as if it were steeped in cold tea. That’s it, Krai Mira has been liberally swabbed with an old soggy teabag to give it that exquisitely browny brownness. Do not adjust your colour calibration folks, you’ve just been teabagged.

I am a brand new player of MtG, and I found this game very helpful in learning the rules and tactics of the game. I'm glad to say that it isn't as complicated as I had thought it would be, and I'm really looking forward to diving in to the world of tabeltop MtG now that I understand a bit more about how certain themes and decks operate, and that is largely thanks to Magic 2014 - Duels of the Planeswalkers.
However, I'm sad to report that this game only gave me the briefest taste of the action, and fell well short of leaving me satisfied. As a brand new player feeling this way, I can only imagine that veteran MtG fans will be left disappointed. Once I had beaten the shot campaign (which is comprised of a series of duels against static enemies who always draw the same cards, in the same order), and felt I had a pretty good grasp of how certain cards could synergize with each other, I was disappointed to see that there wasn't much of an option to build my own deck and experiment. The only exception to this is the sealed deck mode, where you are given a small number of random cards, and can earn up to three booster decks to craft your own deck. However, this feels almost completely pointless, as once you have unlocked the three booster packs (For a total of 9 packs, I believe), there is no way to unlock any more. You're stuck with what you have. Like it or not. Your only options after that point are to continue fighting the same battles you already fought, but without the rewards.
Overall, I'd say that Magic 2014 is a decent purchase if you're brand new to the game, and just looking for a stage to learn the rules of the game, and have a chance to play around with premade decks to learn a few possible tactics. If you were hoping for the possibility of actually building your own decks, though, then you should probably stable your expectations.

La-Mulana is a side-scrolling platformer game that pits you against a sprawling, convoluted temple filled with monsters, traps, and puzzles. This game requires patience, determination, memory, and puzzle-solving skills above all else.
The combat is simple but solid; Initially, you are only provided with a whip with which to dispatch a vast array of enemies and bosses, but later you unlock many different sub-weapons and main weapons with different attack styles.
The way you learn to move your character, Lemeza, over the course of the game becomes a refined art. It feels odd at first, but once you get used to the quirks, you learn how to use them to your benefit and further explore the ruins.
Solving puzzles in this game feels incredibly rewarding, because often the solutions are only presented to you if you are paying very close attention to everything you encounter. It pays to have a pen and paper available to jot down every little thing you see.
A word of warning: Throughout the course of this game, you may very well find yourself stuck and in need of guidance - and that's okay. It's happened to me, plenty. If you find yourself in this situation, rather than find a complete walkthrough, it's best if you use it to find the solution to one or two major puzzles which will hopefully then point you in the right direction to continue your adventuring unaided. You can always backtrack later, once you've gotten well and truly stuck again.
If you purchase La-Mulana then you should keep in mind that it can be very frustrating, especially at the beginning, but if you persevere you will find that this is actually a beautifully constructed game with plenty of love and attention to detail poured into it.
Definitely worth getting.

I'm very on the fence about this one but I'll just barely give it a recommend.
La Mulana's an interesting game which feels a lot like Legend of Zelda and Castlevania: Symphony of the Night. The game's good points do really shine and make it at least worth a look - for one the game is massive with over 20 different areas to explore, and each of them filled with lots of truly unique puzzles and secrets. The game's soundtrack and art design is also very good, and while I'm not a huge fan of the cartoony style in favor of the more realistic look of games like Castlevania and Metroid, I can overlook this.
As many others have said though the extremely cryptic nature of the puzzles can be a big turn-off, as well as the fact that the game gives you almost no information about what to do or where to go next. This means that most players won't be able to progress withoutt using a guide. There are also a few cheap instances in which the player can simply become stuck due to running out of certan items, or due to getting caught in certain traps which they'd have no way of knowing about in advance - and if you haven't collected a special item then your only option is to reset the game and lose your progress.
However the most flat-out annoying flaw for me is the controls. The jumping mechanics in the game are unnecessarily stiff and clunky and make the boss fights especially frustrating and not all that fun.
Still I have to give this game crops for its creativity and making an effort to be challenging unlike many commercial games. I probably will never devote the time to finishing it but overall I still enjoyed what little of it I played.

First, if you have played Banishment and like it. Then, this is the game for you. It's a space version of almost the same game with a few twists.
It took me roughly 54 hours to get all the acheivements. When you play a game for over 50 hours in a short time you can easliy pick out the cons and pros of a game. I'm only going to name a couple though. Here they are:
Pros:
- Challenging yet easily managable at the same time. For example: If you are starting to notice you are going through food faster than you can produce, then just stop the incoming flow of colonist so it won't go down faster.
- Pretty well thought out. Needing chains of resources to make things like robots took some thought, lol.
- The Challenges is a refreshing change from your normal building a base.
Cons:
- There needs to be more challenges.
- The AI really sucks. My carrier bots should not be sitting idle while my engineers are taking food to the warehouse instead of making spares....
Tips:
- When building for the long haul, add plenty of airlocks around starports and mines or your colonist/bots will have to wait a while to get in and out.
- Don't just add O2 generators for the amount of people you have. Be sure to add them every couple buildings. If not, once you get a high quantity of people in one area a single generator can't keep up.
- Start trading early. I found that if you build addition mines and drill bots you can trade metal for a decent price compared to other stuff.
Anyways, I found this to be a great game. I'm looking forward to see if they add anything in on patches or DLC.

If you like relaxing games where you can just turn your brain off, listen to some music, while you just do some stuff, then this game MAY be for you. Note the "MAY". Now, I only have eight hours in-game, but I can definitely tell you that there are a few points in this game that are kind of enraging. I can compare this with the game "Rymdkapsel", released a few years back. In that the goal is simple, expand your space-station to get to the four monoliths, while at the same time defending yourself from intruders. The game was minimalistic, a bit overpriced, but enjoyable for a quick buck, though you probably get bored of it sooner or later. In that game, the just of it is to expand your base to be able to support more people, to expand your base to support more people... and so on, much like in Planetbase, although it's more defined. As in, now the expanding part and the people part are more complicated! Hurray. Another comparison to make is the fact that the AI is god-awful. In Rymdkapsel, you could expect it, since the people are literally just rectangles, so you expect them not to have a brain, which makes it a fair challenge. In this, where the people are actual 'people' (and robots), it just makes the game much less realistic as a whole if one of your colonists decides to go out of the base to take a♥♥♥♥♥♥or something in the middle of a god damn thunderstorm. Sure, there is a room you can make with which you can sound the alarm which forces the colonists to stay inside, but for ♥♥♥♥'s sake, it isn't that hard to look outside the bloody window and see that there is death waiting outside, is it. For the robots, maybe, to go outside is fairly logical, but for the colonists? No. Another irritating thing is that the airlock cycle can only support one colonist (or robot) at a time, going in AND out, and the AI would stack up on the door in an orderly fashion and would go in order of the first one to arrive at the airlock to the last one. So, let's say you have a colonist outside that is almost out of oxygen, and desperately needs to go inside, but the airlock is stacked up with people and/or robots going in/out to do construction or some other♥♥♥♥♥♥ The AI doesn't re-order itself to let the person desperate for air in first, and there is no way at all to do it manually either. If you are in this situation, the colonist is most likely to die. Next to that, there is a priority system in this game, as in, you can choose which construction has the general priority over the others. You can't make a queue, which I would have liked, and half of the time the construction prioritized gets ignored anyway.
So, basically, the only challenge in this game is either the retardation of the AI, the occasional intruder that comes in and probably kills everyone in your base because the AI doesn't understand that the thing that person's holding kills people, and the unfortunate event of a meteor crashing straight into your base. Next to that, the game is shallow. Like I said, the only part of the game is to expand your base, to be able to support more colonists, to expand your base more, to support more colonists, and so on. That's it. You do that until you achieve your goals, like "build 10 robots", or "get a total of 100 colonists". And when you get enough goals gone, you move to the next planet, where there are even more intruders and meteorites. The grand total of planets is 4. 4 Planets with slightly different color schemes and varying difficulty. Oh boy.
Of course, there is the Steam Workshop with custom challenges, which are basically just the same as the normal game only often easier or harder.
Unless you are the sort of type that just likes to replay old games a ♥♥♥♥-ton, or just likes to relax and play, I honestly can't find it to recommend this game. If you like this sort of game, then you are free to buy it (although do it in sale, since the 20 euro pricetag is imo way too high for a game this shallow).

Be aware that this game has several awful symptoms of "Consolitis", and depending on your preference, may render it virtually unplayable. Sadly this is the case for me, and I've passed the refund window trying to hack the Unreal Engine to make it work.
1.) Inverted mouse acceleration - Yep, there's such a thing as inverse mouse acceleration and apparently, it cannot be disabled here. What this means is, the slower you move your mouse, the faster the player actually turns. On the other hand, quick snap motions cause the player to move only very slightly. This makes it incredibly frustrating to actually move in the game.
2.) Awful, AWFUL field of view - You thought Deadspace was bad? Wait till you see this. If you have a modern monitor you are going to find the FOV extremely narrow. This coupled with the mouse acceleration makes it difficult to actually move around in, or even see your surroundings. Furthermore, the effect is very unsettling and I've not been able to play the game for more than 30 minutes without eye strain. There is a "hack" to "fix" the FOV, but this just renders a nasty fishbowl effect instead.
Sadly, these two issues simply make the game unplayable for me, and so despite all of the effort that clearly went into it, I have to review this as a hard pass. If you are put off by terrible mouse mechanics, and zoomed in FOV that seem to be "in fashion" amongst games these days: Stay the ♥♥♥♥ away from this one.

Particularly, the scoring system is great. EVEN IF YOU CAN'T DRAW, YOU CAN COMPETE! Selecting the correct drawing prompt outside of your turn gives you as many points as having players guess your drawing prompt correctly (1000 points). Other players selecting your given fake prompts will score you 500 points. It keeps the game on-track but doesn't outright DISCOURAGE silliness.
I wish the line width was a lot smaller, and this is a complaint a LOT of people had--we managed to draw very clearly anyway, but it was more of a frustrating hassle than a "hahahaha" feature (such as there being no eraser, which I think is a good choice).

===
> Essential purchase
> Recommended purchase
> Purchase if on a sale

===
Krai Mira is a post-apocalyptic role playing game, set in the near future where the world has been devastated by nuclear warfare. The title is set in some baltic region, possibly Crimea since the GPS system used to navigate the map is called Crimea Sat, but this is not certain. You are one of the many survivors of the apocalypse, trying to make it through the day in the small settlement of Quiet Bay, but suddenly rumors of a savage cannibal tribe approaching the area endangers everyone living there, and so your struggle to survive begins.
===
+ The world to explore is fairly large, there are many types of random encounters and optional places to visit
+ Option to select between Real-Time and Turn-Based combat
+ Decently made locations and environments
+ Possibility to explore the whole world from the start
+ Decent amount of equipments, loot and perks to unlock as you level up
===
- Uninspired and quite dull main storyline.
- Written dialogues and descriptions of events are of sub-par quality and often contain many errors and incosistencies.
- Very limited possibility of choice in dialogues, or even no choice at all, even in important ones.
- Unexplainable events in the main quest seem to force it to progress in one way, and show no logic at all. Example:
.
- Clunky movement system, user interface and animations.
- Terrible weapon and characters 3D models.
- Many quests will be poorly explained and it will be very hard to understand what is to be done.
- Many graphical glitches and artifacts.
- Simplistic economy system and too high win rate of certain games of chance found in places make the player far too rich in a very little time.
- All NPCs have very limited interaction, or no interaction at all, not even a line, they will just stand idle doing nothing.
- Party system is poor: you cannot command your companions, you cannot change their equipment, you cannot see how much health they have outside combat, you can't even talk with them.
- "Stealth" system is poorly made and often will not work as intended. There are mandatory stealth sections. Add 2 and 2.
- Problems with loot balance can make the game either too easy or too hard at times.
- Lack of general gameplay depth: only basic attributes and passive perks as character development, no gear modification / repairing, very simple combat system with only basic attacks and passive skills.
===
Krai Mira, even in its Extended Cut edition, does not deliver what is to be expcted from a good post-apocalyptic RPG. It inspires itself to some similar games, mostly Fallout 2 and Wasteland 2, but it does not succeed in delivering a quality gameplay most of all, other than also a hooking story and a decent progression and exploration system. Ultimately, this is a sub-par, medium-low quality generic RPG that is not worth the price it is sold at, has many problems and debateable game design choices, and is definitely not worth your time. Move on to better titles of this type if you are looking for a RPG.

Year Walk is an enticingly atmospheric game. It does a wonderful job of building tension as you're wandering through the woods with the beautiful soundtrack. The puzzles are all satisfyingly challenging (though that does not extend to the achievements; a couple are strangely obtuse for no reason but are at least easy to obtain with a guide).
Most of all, I appreciate the in-game encyclopedia of the folklore inspiring the game. Read through it as soon as I started up the game, and I felt like it really added to the experience, knowing a bit about the creatures I would run into. Also did a good job of really setting the tone for the game.
The two endings do leave something to be desired, but (for what feels like the first time ever) I wasn't too put off by this. For me, Year Walk was very much about the journey rather than the destination. The story, when we get down to it, is frustratingly heartbreaking. But if you're able to put that aside, it's a great little game.
Ultimately, a short but worthwhile adventure.

In short, Year Walk is the mobile port of a game you never played (but should), and about folklore you never knew about (but should).
In long, Year Walk is based on the pagan ritual of Årsgång, and the Swedish folklore behind it. In theory, if the participant survived or passed certain tests during the Walk, he would be able to see into the future.

Done on nights that were believed to be more magically and spiritually charged than others, such as new years eve, Christmas eve, and solstices, the participant was required to deprive himself of food, rest, and light for a day before making his way through the woods to the nearest churchyard. It was there, if he was deemed worthy enough, he could learn his fate and the fates of others in the year to come.
In the game, you are one such individual, and making your way to the churchyard is your task.
But you are not alone in the woods.
The demons, sprites, and figments of folklore surround you and test you on your journey. They do not wish you well, and they will make you prove your worth in the woods. There are light puzzles you must solve, usually revolving around backtracking and fetching...things...which can get very dull. Fortunately they are short, save one, which I highly recommend using headphones for, otherwise you will more than likely have difficulty. You’ll know it when you get to it. I almost wish this one wasn’t in the game, though the conclusion of it will stick with you for quite some time.
In fact, most of the game will likely stick with you. The spirits of the woods are subtle yet terrifying to the core. The sounds of the woods are quiet and haunting. The color palate is soft, yet foreboding. The in game encyclopedia is a wonderful, and for one of the puzzles, required, read. Or at least a quick scroll through. I won’t spoil for what here, but let’s just say it’s one of the best uses of an in game encyclopedia I have ever seen. Though nobody may say so directly, Year Walk is an often subtle, a few times not so subtle, short, horror adventure.
If you can get past the odd, mobile-friendly navigation of practically strafing through the world instead of walking through it, as well as the aforementioned backtracking, you should definitely play this, especially if it’s on sale. It’s not long at all, a couple hours at most, but very meaty and entertaining for those couple hours. There are incentives to replay, too, through some mysterious achievements. Year Walk will frighten you, scare you at times, and chill you almost constantly. Maybe even frustrate you, or stump you. But yes, you should definitely give it a go.
Why?
Well, I think we all, at one point or another in our lives, have wished we could know some of what our futures hold for us. Though debates could rage at what the idea of seeing the future means to us. Some would want to know it all; some would not want to know anything about what is to come. Some could say the future can be changed; some would say everything is written in stone. Some would say if they knew their future they would try to change it; others would say they would leave it alone, come what may. Year Walk offers a glimpse into a world where such discussions would have merit beyond character studies and musings. Where such a privilege would have to be earned in a dangerous world, in a snowy evening, in a churchyard.

Just a quick note from a few of the more recent reviews regarding developer updates being slow.
Once upon a time games were made, optimised, tested, bugs fixed, tested again and then rolled out to Gold and released to the public.
Sending thousands of 5 1/4 inch floppy drives out for patches was expensive and slow.
With the advent of the internet games are generally sold in a bug ridden partially finished state and then patched for a couple fo years, sometimes extra content is added.
Apparently this Dev hasnt done much in the way of bug fixes or DLC, perhaps it's because they finished the game properly and squashed the majority of known bugs before release due to a proper testing cycle, perhaps there is little extra DLC because the game shipped with what appeared to be enough content to fil lthe game.

It would be a really nice and awesome game, but unfortunately the AI is incredibly stupid. =(

Planetbase bears the qualities of a solid space-colony simulator. It has a respectable variety of structures, resources, characters, and natural threats to accommodate a varied, challenging economic system. Building your colony, piece by piece, and watching its population and resources proliferate is satisfying. And once you reach the milestones set by the game, such as achieving self-sufficiency and galactic renown, you're overwhelmed with pride, seeing fireworks sparkle in your otherwise-empty mental trophy cabinet.
The above would have enticed a recommendation out of me had the AI not been so damn obtuse (which is a euphemism for a much harsher word) throughout the experience.
What ruins Planetbase is how utterly incompetent your colonists can be. The slightest imbalance in workload, colonist needs, or stock can devastate your colony, causing starvation, dehydration, asphyxiation, radiation poisoning, and, in some cases, death by meteors. This is because it is so simple for several crucial parts of your workforce to stop working.
Are your biologists too hungry to harvest the next batch of food that will satisfy their hunger? Too bad. They won't do it.
Are your workers too thirsty to erect the water fountains that will douse their parched throats? Too bad. They won't do it.
Are your medics too radiation-addled to go to the sickbay and prescribe themselves the medication they need? Too bad. They won’t do it.
Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ A solar flare is incoming, and half of your workers are exposed! You need to activate a yellow alert and get them back inside! Oh, but wait. Your guard hasn’t been to the gym lately so he’s feeling too glum to go to his workstation and issue the alert to save his fellow colonists. Too bad.
It’s annoying. I don’t mind needs or injuries affecting the performance of your colonists, but to render them entirely inoperable, to the point where they won’t even carry out the duties that would satisfy their grievances? Utter retardation. For the first two planets, this didn’t bother me, but come the third one I was tearing my hair out. Sadly, difficulty is tied to the planets you visit, and there are no sliders you can adjust to ease the onerous part of establishing a colony that could be doomed to destruction within a matter of minutes.
Which sucks, because the planets have different environments, which unlock new challenges and structures. There's so much more to this game that I can't experience because of the damn AI and its capricious sensitivities.
Perhaps I could go back, ‘get gud’, and try my hand at building my eighth colony on that one damn planet. Or maybe I won’t, because the colonist AI is ridiculous and will turn idle for the most illogical of reasons.
Unless you’re willing to dedicate yourself to mastering every facet of this game, making meticulous use of every resource and second by the time you reach the third planet, I would give Planetbase a miss until they fix the arbitrary problems with the AI. With its current level of frustration, I can’t recommend Planetbase to anyone bar the most patient of players.
4/10, but it should be an 8.

Planetbase is entertaining. Let me just get that off first. The concept of making a base on different planets and managing them is a good concept that works. Also the basic game is well done. Production, energy, food, water and resource management is smooth and logical, same with base expansion. The game looks decent as well.
So what is the flaw? The problem with Planetbase, and the reason I cannot recommend it at 20 euro, is that while it is a good game it lacks content and depth. You have four planets with slightly different looks and modifiers but still very much the same. Within the first couple of hours and after your first base you have seen everything, unless you want to do everything again in a slightly different environment. The only real challenge is early game to get the base rolling and then it is just a matter of you not messing up any balance in the resources as you expand.
While it can be enjoyable, specially the first few times, it just feels a bit hollow. If you can find it for less than 20 euro, then you should consider it.

+ The voice acting is pretty good for a non-AAA title

+ It's not too short
Cons:
- It may very well be too long. It started to REALLY drag for me in the last few hours.
- The actual gameplay is very limited. This is more of a visual novel than a game.
- The game really can't decide if it wants to be cyberpunk or horror. You'd think it'd be a great combination of the two, but for me it just made it feel muddled.
- The story is, as I said, "pretty good". But it's just not *great*.
