What starts of as a masterpiece in cyberpunk art, quickly turns into a headache for which you need Panadol. Although this game was fun initially, it becomes very monotonous and repetitive after a while. The horror elements begin to get annoying and very grindy, soon you begin to wonder why this plot is still dragging on. Everything is more or less locked down, there are bits and pieces in the game which allow you to make a choices, but it’s all very much controlled. It really reminded me of playing Portal - you have to overcome one puzzle only to be thrown onto the next. You never really get to explore the world of Observer, aside from wondering around inside the hotel. Why make such an effort to create a visual masterpiece, only to entrap the entire game in one location? And that’s the grand plot summary of Observer - one giant trap from which you are trying to escape from.
The lack of save options further hurts the game, as I would've loved to been able to replay certain parts and see the end results. There are also several major bugs, especially during the ‘flying television baby’ part - I kept having to restart due to glitches. The ambience in the game is great, and part of the sound track is nice too, however tracks and sounds are often overused and they become like an annoying motif. Visually this game is like a double edged sword, it provides something unique, but it also feels like an artist severely vomited all over this game. Art is literally shoved down your throat, and so are horror elements, they are consistent and unrelenting. Eventually there is so much going on that you can no longer take it, at that point your head hurts and you feel motion sickness.
To conclude, I would recommend this game if you have Panadol nearby - moreover, I would recommend this game if it went on discount. For the current price, I don’t think I could recommend it at all. The entire experience took 10 hours to finish (which for this game is long), and at the very end it didn’t leave me with a pleasant feeling. As it stands it’s a bit too ‘artsy fartsy’, the atmosphere and world of Observer was cool, but I feel like it drags on for far too long. The presence and execution of some parts were lack lustre, unnecessary or outright annoying. Everything felt too confined and forced. I feel like this Observer game could've gone to so many places, but in the end, it’s stuck in the misery of an old hotel.

I had the opportunity to play this game as intended yesterday, at an afterparty.
There were five of us, and even though I'm completely artistically ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, and got clumsy fingers, it was very amusing.
The way it works, is you start the game om your computer (preferably connected to a TV that all players can see)
A 4 letter code is displayed on screen, and all the players just navigate to
on their handhelds (computer works too, but this game is designed with handhelds in mind)
Once you start the game, every player gets a word or a sentence that you're supposed to draw.
And not stuff mortals can actually draw within the timer limit, without eraser and only two colors...
"Blood bank robbery", "a car that runs on love", "beef night" and "pie gun" was a couple that I got.
When everyone's done, each players drawing appears, and the other players get to type in what they think it is.
the idea here is not to guess the real word, in fact, if you do, it will say you were too close to the real - or someone else's answer - and you'll have to come up with something else.
But on the next screen all the participants suggestions are listed, including the one that the drawer was told to draw.
If you guess the right one, you and the drawer get points. If you guess wrong, the one who came up with the description gets point, but not you.
I recommend this game as an ice breaker on parties, or just when you're 4+ bored friends and only 1 computer.

Danganronpa is a visual novel cut up by intense trial and investigation segments. For most of the game you're reading along with the plot to follow the story with few game-like interactions, but the meat of the game is building on that knowledge to solve murders. You collect evidence to discover how a murder was committed, and shoot down or confirm theories at the trial to catch the individual responsible. It's a lot of slow buildup for a few segments of intense payoff, and you have to enjoy the writing style and conventions of the visual novel genre, but the mysteries it presents the player are excellent.

Krai Mira falls flat quickly largely because it fails at even basic game design principles. The story does not flow at all. The game feels like a pile of disjointed pieces, and the dialog is often poorly translated. Regardless, the game has a ton of potential for sure.
So why does the game fail at even some of the most basic rules of game design? The answer is for a number of reasons. For example, the game doesn't help the player at all. You're just dropped into the world and the game doesn't even tell the player about basic controls. There have been posts from people not realising they had some special abilities until hours into the game. It is common to be in the middle of a quest and not know what the developers want you to do as the game doesn't have any subtle hints in the levels like it should. You have only the dialog to guide you, which would be fine if it was clearer. Sometimes the objective is clear, but its completely unclear how they want you to do it.
The game world has a number of major locations. Each is a small, square map. Each map generally is pretty well detailed with many details in it like buildings and trash and a few npcs. The buildings and terrains are pretty nice on some maps, though you can see some assets being reused too much at times. Most npcs are stationary and tend to have nothing to say at all except for quest givers. This makes the world feel a bit empty in a way. In short, the game world does not come alive because of all of the immersion breaking flaws. There is no auto saving as saving is up to the player. That's fine, but you have 10 save slots that have cryptic time stamps for labels, making the save/load screen rather poorly designed.
It is painfully obvious that very little thought went into the game design in many areas. As a game designer you are crafting an experience for players and therefore you must look at your game through the eyes of your players and think about how things will work and how they will affect the player. This game shows no sign that much of that was done at all. Many aspects of the game are much more of a chore/annoying than fun. The combat system, and the overworld map are examples (as is the fact that the game is often confusing). The random encounters on the world map are excessively frequent and obnoxious, and this is compounded by the fact that some of them are gratuitously unskippable.
Another example is how its common to see dialog options that jump you back to a previous topic in the dialog tree in an unrealistic manner. Or the fact that non quest-giver npcs often never have anything to say at all and just go straight to a little interaction menu. When you get a quest to ask people about your dog, you can explore the whole island. There is only one npc you'll find to talk to. But at first he starts talking about something completely different. His mention of the dog is buried a little deeper in the dialog tree. This is poor design. The conversation should've started with the dog as that's what the player is looking for! The guy has his own quest to give you and he talks about that first, which can easily make the player think "Oh this isn't the right NPC". The player is then likely to stop talking to him and continue searching the world in vain. So as you can see, there are a lot of places where seemingly little thought was given to the actual design of things. Also, when you get that quest mentioned above while searching for info on your dog, that quest takes you to an irradiated area. When you get there, you discover you're underpowered and the game seems to transition gratuitously into a suddenly much more grindy experience. In the realm of gaming, grinding is all too often used as a lazy way to increase a game's total play time. It certainly isn't there because players think its fun, because they generally don't.
Posts from people saying they're lost and don't know what to do next in the game seem to be a bit common for Krai Mira. The only reason you don't see more of that is because this game is not getting many new players. It is ridiculous and misleading that Krai Mira sits here on the Steam Store pretending to be a complete game, when in reality it should still be early access. It still has a long way to go to rise above the quality level of a Beta. Gameplay is king in video games, and its the biggest shortcoming of this game. Krai Mira simply does not play well. It's unfortunate, but the graphics make the game look a lot better than it really is.

Should've stuck to my gut reaction to the hype this game received: that it was a pretentious hunk of crap with a lame gimmick, made more difficult than it needs to be by not giving you any instructions.
But the sale made me decide to go for it, and initially I was glad I had as I absolutely loved the first few hours of the game. It was immersive, interesting, and the puzzles were engaging in how they changed things up a little bit each time.
After that, however, the game gives you no direction at all, not even telling you what the symbols mean or how to use them. When I thought I had the right idea as to how to pursue the next batch of puzzles, suddenly the game would slap me in the face and poke me in the eye, chiming in with: "No, you dirty pig♥♥♥♥er, you are wrong! You thought you knew the rules? Well, ha-ha-♥♥♥♥ing-ha. You only got that previous puzzle via some sort of supernatural fluke! Try again, dickwad!"
And so on and so forth.
Is there any good reason for the game to not properly train you? Not really. The Talos Principle—by far one of my favourite games, both in recent memory and of all time—did this far better. It started you off with the basics and made sure you knew what you were doing, then it gradually added more tools to your disposal and eased you into harder puzzles. And it also had a story.
Go play that game instead.

I love this game, but it's also the most pretentious piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥ever made.
It's like having the best confectionery of your life in a high class establishment, only to stop and choke on a hard object hidden within it, and after coughing it up and struggling to breathe with a punctured trachea, you see what appears as pieces of an intricately designed small shattered glass bottle, several pieces of tinsel, and red streamers in front of you with a note sprawled upon the blood spattered glass saying "I created this dessert and I am a genius, please refer to the server if you would like to congratulate me, Sincerely, the chef" in cursive.
It just ruins the whole experience...
The developer is repugnantly self-absorbant, and lacks the self-perception to understand that with any genius and good craftsmanship, there's a responsibility and diligence to respect the user of whatever item you have crafted.
This game makes you feel like a goddamn genius sometimes with expertly created consistently designed puzzles that are perpetually difficult using a finely tuned game world that requires information from other parts of the map to continue, and the game explains this with little to no direct communication to the player, and its AWESOME... but then it shatters the perception by also being stupid as ♥♥♥♥, using the ugliest puzzle mechanics ever that you will never guess in a million years where to even start solving them (I'm looking at you bird\jungle noises), and don't even get me started on the mechanics of traversing the game world... I'll sum it up in brief; prepare to spend the equivalent time of a trans-continental flight on crossing a damn puddle in this game... This game has carefully made a wonderful world with carefully placed oddities and intricacies, only to severely ruin the experience with some dumb ideas here and there, a super pretentious over-tone, and a logistical nightmare in some areas just to manoever around small spaces.
Even though I slammed this game like nobodies business, I oddly recommend this game for what it does right, but it wastes a lot of your time, and I can't decide whether the bad outweighs the good, but the good is pretty damn good I must say.

The Witness is about aha moments.
Did you play Braid? Remember how you felt when you solved that one puzzle after staring at it for an hour? The Witness wants you to feel that a hundred times.
I lost count of the number of times I decided a puzzle was impossible. First I learned when I should come back to it later. Then I learned to pay attention. Then I learned to patiently sit and think. Slowly, I beat the game without spoilers.
So should you. Beating the game doesn't matter. What matters is the moment you finally solve that puzzle you're stuck on and feel like the smartest person who ever lived. But you have to hunger for that moment, because if you don't, bad news: the only reward is more puzzles. They only get harder. That's also the good news: another aha moment is coming.
My biggest complaint was the lack of guidance in the early game. I was uncomfortable with not knowing whether I should be able to solve a puzzle or not. I've never done well at Myst-style games so some aspects didn't come naturally to me. A lot of early hours were frustrating as I wandered aimlessly, making zero progress.
It was worth it.

Somehow this beautiful, atmospheiric cyberpunk-acid-trip of a game ended up being boring. There are a few puzzles, stealth segments, and story impacting  choices to make, but, at least for me, the 'horror' seems to be held at arms length. Sure there are plenty of dark, even Cronenbergian themes, but, more often than not, these are only hinted at in dialog or by props and sets.
LIke layers of fear, this game seems to take many cues from horror films (particularly supernatural horror), but this doesn't translate into an interactive game very well. Maybe scripted jump scares are more effective when the director can control the camera, soundtrack and actors... the liberties provided to the player actually work against them. What's more, most of these scares pose no threat at all to the player, so you are quickly condition to expect and ignore them.
Pros:
- Stealth segments
- Graphics
- Story and themes
- Voice acting
Cons:
- Puzzles
- Noneuclidian (or at least apparently so) mazes
- Limited opponent AI
- Ineffective jump scares
- Limited threats to the player
Overall, it was worth a play-through for the story and but I don't really feel it was worth $30US, nor any additional attempts at further completion.

Observer, stylized as >observer_, is an atmospheric horror/mystery game, in which you take the role of Detective Lazarsky to investigate a murder. The victim might possibly be your son, and you will do whatever it takes to uncover the truth. The interesting point is that you are not just any detective: You can connect directly to a person's mind to see what really happened.
By the time of this review, Observer costs 27,99€ or your local equivalent, and it takes between 6-10 hours to complete, depending on how long you take, how much time you spend with optional objectives and if you desire to do a re-run with possibly different outcomes.
Observer shines through its worldbuilding and atmosphere, but not through the gameplay. Most of the time, you will be walking through an apartment complex or the surreal landscapes of a subject's subconcious. Occassionally, the game adds a few puzzles or stealth sections, which I greatly enjoyed. To me, they were not particularly challenging, and despite my ego telling me otherwise, I am not very good at puzzles or stealth games. As such, I believe they should not pose too much of a threat.
This is arguably the meat of the game. Observer plays with the idea of your senses not telling you what is true and what is not. Afterall, what greater horror is there than going insane and not noticing it? The game heavily relies on visuals and sound design to build a terrifying atmosphere, which at a few points results in an actual, intense scare as a pay-off. This doesn't mean that the game relies solely on jump-scares, which are very rare in this game, aside from the occassional washing machine tuning on when you pass it.
Of course, Horror is subjective, just as almost everything else, but I would consider this to be a good attempt of a horror game.
While 6-10 hours for 27,99€ is not a cheap price, I have to say I enjoyed every moment of it. Is it a good bang for the buck? Ehh, maybe? I dislike bringing this up as a criticism, because I'd rather spend 30€ on a 10 hour game, of which I enjoyed every moment, than spending 10€ on a 100 hour game which never got better than "Ehh, it was alright, I guess?".
So yes, if you like the idea of an atmospheric horror game and have 27,99€ to spare, I highly recommend you to buy Observer.

I really don't know where to begin with this review.
I'll try to segment this into three core categories:
-Graphics and Gameplay
-Narrative
-Reccomendation
Graphics and Gameplay:
Gameplay is extremely simple. This is a heavily narrative driven game (A Noir/Puzzle/Horror game). You mostly walk around looking for and connecting information, with the option of running, crouching, interacting with specific elements which will be highlighted when looked directly at, administering "medicine" from the minimalist status menu, talking to various npcs and switching between 3 "UI overlays" (Bio-sensor-vision to analyze organic material, Mechanics-sensor to identify electronics and augmentations and nightvision) which are nicely implemented in terms of believability, as the entire experience is told through the eyes of Dan Lazarski (Voiced by and Designed to look like Actor Rutger Hauer, who acted in Bladerunner), who is a heavily augmented cyberpunk police detective, who is dependant on the before mentioned medicine, apptly named synchrozine, to keep our character synchronized, or "sane". If you do not consume this medication, several glitch effects and view-distortions begin to accur, which brings me to graphics.
This game delivers on graphics, big-time. Not only are all locations crafted beautifully, but the textures and mindblowing SFX help to immerse the player into the slums of a cyberpunk distopian future. Right in the middle of a small appartment complex. Due to the compact design, of what I'll refer to as the hub (The Appartmentbuilding, in which you will be exploring), everything you can explore is loaded with detail, which really emphasizes the cluttered, messy lifestyle portrayed within this environment. This is a good point to talk about the narrative.
Narrative:
Everything in this game is directed towards one goal, and this, surprisingly, isn't horror. Far from it. Everything in this game works towards fleshing out the very few characters you meet and giving you, the player, the agency to look into what you want to know. Very few decisions are a must. You play Dan Lazarski, the way you choose is correct, which delivers a fun little element of role-playing, when investigating mysterious or criminal ongoings. You choose which of the optional stories you unravel and how far you do. At most any point in the game, you can choose, which path to take, although the overarching journey never changes. This has helped in telling incredibly fleshed out stories, within dialogue, e-mails and content found strewn throughout the hub, while letting the player decide how these stories end, or if they end at all. I felt completely immersed for the first 9 hour plathrough, as I believed in the character and his circumstances within the universe I was presented with. Which now of course, brings me to the horror elements. They do not feel cheap and this is immensely important, to me, when horror wants to do it right. All horror elements felt spot-on and believable. These occurances were all tied heavily to the protagonist, his state of mind, the universe and the world (hub) you are exploring.  No cheap, "here's some horror for horrors sake".
Reccomendation:
I heavily reccomend this game for it's narrative and its delivery alone. However, I do believe, that a fondness for cyberpunk, lovecraftian and cronenbergian horror, as well as story-driven puzzle solving (in this case, case solving) are a greater insurance of the enjoyment of this title. Great game for halloween, or any other occasion, on which you would like to be scared sh*tless and unbelievably endeared in a story, all at once.

This game is incredible. It's a few years old, but still looks amazing! If having 95% positive reviews on Steam wasn't enough to convince you already, perhaps I can help tip you.
The game has the old Tomb Raider badass feel, but in a much better and more enjoyable format. As far as I know, this is the first game in the Tomb Raider series that is open world. All the other TR games I've played before this have just moved you from level to level, especially the PS1/2 games I know best. Tomb Raider has a surprisingly impressive open world. The world is lively, and quite a nice place to explore. You are rewarded for exploring, with animals you can hunt, salvage that can be used to upgrade weapons, and other cool things, like Secret Tombs, quick side quests that award you with a lot of extra salvage.
The game has a fairly short story mode, I've played 14 hours as of writing this review, and I believe I'm roughly 80% through. Some may consider this a bad thing, but personally, I think this is good play time. I wouldn't want it to be any shorter, but it is beginning to drag out a bit now. I find that nearer the end of the game, while new mechanics are still being added, I feel they aren't as engaging or exciting as the earlier mechanic unlocks.
As every Tomb Raider game, this game has a lot of Quick Time Events (QTEs), but damn, some of them are hard. Granted,  the difficult ones aren't too common, but still a pain when you experience them. Also, perhaps I missed a tutorial somewhere, but some QTEs don't seem to be very well explained, but you can solve them fairly easily but searching online.
Crystal Dynamics has done an incredible job with level design in this game. Certainly there will be times when you find yourself screaming at your monitor asking yourself how Lara could do something that dumb, but for the most part, it's done well. A shocking amount of things can be climbed and interacted with. I'm actually not sure how they managed to make so many paths and climbable objects in such a large game. The game does well at making you play dynamically, whether it's a heavy machine gun destroying the cover you're behind, or an enemy throwing dynamite at you, or even noticing you're taking cover behind an explosive barrel, you will find you will often have to scramble to another cover and quickly. This is a good way to prevent the player just camping behind a metal wall, sometimes peaking out to execute a well positioned headshot, and in my opinion, this is a really great way to keep the player engaged and on their toes.
Talking of headshots, all the weapons are great to use, even at the late stages, they are always being replaced with better, stronger versions with more features, and, as I mentioned earlier, you can upgrade your weapons too.
Most of the problems I've found with this game can probably be explained by saying I'm just bad, like when Lara fails to grab onto a rock face she was RIGHT NEXT TO, and falls to her death.
I can't speak for the multiplayer, as I haven't played it yet. Apparently player numbers aren't very high. Regardless, I think this game is worth it for the story alone.
Overall, I think this is a very good game. I bought the Game of the Year Edition while it was on sale for £6, and while most of the DLC is cosmetic or a map pack, I'm pretty glad I bought it. I would suggest you buy the GOTY Edition too, if it's on sale and/or you think it's cheap enough

Story is fantastic. 15 kids are trapped in a school where one must kill to escape..if they don't get found out. Every chapter leads to unexpected turns. If you pay attention you can find out certain things, which is all the more fun! You can feel like you're learning with the characters as they go. While every chapter is basically set up the same, they are unique enough in how it presents itself that it never feels repetitive. It does have a slightly slow start, but the train quickly picks up steam as it launches you into the insane world of Danganronpa. While there ARE insane stuff, the game also does a nice job of staying relatively down-to-earth. Expect insanity, but also not be afraid to think logically on some things.
Characters are all amazingly fleshed out. Everyone has their own quirks and backstory. Everyone has a reason to live and act the way they do. You will get connected with everyone, and that makes the story as you go all the more intense. Everyone's interactions come off as very natural (plus the expected anime quirks).
Gameplay is actually quite large compared to most VNs. It's highly interactive. When you aren't spending time talking to the other characters, you're exploring the school in a 3D space, with a cute cardboard-esque charm. you interact with objects to find clues, coins, and useful things that can be used to increase your friendship with the others (this is good for aquiring skills that help in the core gameplay). At the end of each chapter you undergo a trial to investigate the culprit, and the music along with how fast the gameplay is add an air of intensity that make you go on the edge of your seat to get the correct answers! Even if you're not the best at logic and putting the pieces together, the game is very nice to you on its "Kind (easy)" difficulty so that you may enjoy the story!
Lastly, the music and art are superb. Danganronpa's art style really stands out and adds a charming mix of light-heartedness and the grim despair of the atmosphere the game shrouds upon the cast. The music (especially in the later chapters) will keep you attentive and in the mood through the game perfectly.
Highly recommend it even if you have never touched a VN before. Especially if you like a good mystery story.

A game for all skill levels.
Not good at games? Go the bulk up route. This game does not strictly require you to fight any bosses until you're roughly 90% done the game. You can get most of the items, including health upgrades, without fighting any bosses. It feels like sequence breaking but it's (usually) completely intended. The bosses all have roughly the same difficulty, meaning you can fight them in whatever order you feel like.
Average at games? Play through the normal way. When you're done an area, fight the boss, and move on. None of the bosses are particularly harder than any others, they just take some getting used to.
Good at games? Set it to hard mode. More enemies, harder enemies, bosses have more health and do more damage. Accidentally went to hard mode, but can't do it? Don't reset. You can still explore the ruins to get more items, just like you would do during a bulk up run. With enough health, anyone can win.

Play Length: Pretty long.  Although I still need to play the Steam version more, I've played the original extensively.
Positives: This is an excellent nod to classic MSX games, particularly the Maze of Galious.  But I think it's better designed than those games in many ways.  The graphics in the original look right out of a MSX game and are lovingly crafted.  You might fear that the updated graphics for the Steam version would lose some of their charm, but luckily the original creator worked on them and they still look great.  Now they look more like a Super Nintendo game, which works perfectly well.  The same is also true for the music, a lot of care was taken to make sure it retains the charm of the original soundtrack.
The game itself is excellent.  Having played both versions, I have to say that the Steam versions smoothes over a few problems with the original version and makes it even better.  One excellent addition is the ability to save all the notes you've read in an in game journal; while I kind of enjoyed keeping a written journal of notes when I played the original game, it's certainly easier this way.  The puzzles themselves have been smoothed over a bit, to be a bit more fair and a little easier to figure out.  But they are still by no means easy.  The puzzle design is very good, with a lot of clever puzzles.
Although they toned down the puzzles a bit, they compensated for this by increasing the game's skill based difficulty.  This is a good change.  In the original game, it often felt like health didn't matter, and bosses were a bit too easy to steamroll through.  Now your health meter matters a bit more.  The difficulty is still not a big deal, as the ability to warp renders many of the challenges moot, but it's a welcome change none the less.
Negatives: Although I like the updated graphics and music, it does lose a bit of it's MSX feel that the original version had.  So, if you are a big fan of the MSX, I would encourage you to check out the original version, which is still available and free.  Also, while I think that all the puzzles are fair and solvable, some of them are very devious and a bit vague.  And you will likely need to do a lot of wandering around, and trial and error.  Many people will probably need to resort to a guide to finish this game.
Overall: This game does a great job of making you feel like an archeologist.  The ruins you are exploring feel mysterious, the puzzles are clever and memorable.  The music really sets a great tone for the game and will stay with you after you've played.  This is not only one of the best love letters to classic games ever made, but it's one of the best indie games ever made.  Even if you're not a fan of the kind of games it's referencing, this game absolutely must be tried by anyone who likes independant games.
About my rating system: I have two things I rate on.  The first is the overall score, and the second is soundtrack.  The reason why is because I feel like soundtrack is tremendously undervalued; to me, it's a tremendously important factor in whether I like a game.  For the score, I grade on a scale of 1-10, and I try to grade in such a way that each number has a meaning and each has equal importance.  The numbers have the following meanings:
0: Garbage, 1: Awful, 2: Poor, 3: Underwhelming, 4: Mediocre, 5: Decent, 6: Good, 7: Great, 8: Excellent, 9: Phenomenal, 10: Masterpiece
La Mulana's score:
Game Rating: 9 (Phenomenal)
Soundtrack Rating: 8 (Excellent)

Fun! Scary! Rich in lore! Beautiful to look at! I enjoyed almost 100% of Year Walk.
Positives:
There is something extremely delicious about a game that encourages you to have a notebook handy to keep track of clues and write down hints. And it's doubly good in a snowy icy world, for the same reasons I love mysteries set in a snowed-in cabin or the remote northern woods in winter. You become the cold but determined detective and the sheer joy of solving clues is enough to pull you forward. Year Walk really delivers on the atmosphere, you can tell it is lovingly crafted with a deep interest in Swedish lore in mind. Maybe because I typically get through games slower than most people, my natural tendency to take my time and enjoy the view helped me become quite immersed in the game.
The horror of Year Walk is very beautiful, some jump scares but also subtle reveals, eerie atmosphere, and the game likes to mess around with the fourth wall a tiny bit. There are parts that are scary, parts that are sad, and some parts are just lovely to see play out. The sound design helps add to the scariness and is very, very well done. It is all very memorable and you will surely have a favorite moment or two by the end that will stick in your head for a while. The eerie atmosphere never gets old, and I loved that it never relied on gore or violence to frighten me, but well crafted visual cues, dark implications, and building tension. You truly feel you are on the precipice between the real world and some strange spirit world, and there is an increasing sense of dread as you progress that maybe the spirit world really isn't a place for humans, much less one lonely human in the middle of the night on new years eve.
Negatives:
The gosh darn singing puzzle really got my knickers in a twist.I would recommend trying this puzzle for a little while to be properly immersed in the game, because being hopelessly lost in the woods with bizarre singing and your life on the line is part of the story, and hell if this puzzle doesn't perfectly put you in that mindset. But just have a guide ready, scribble the solution out on your notebook ahead of time so you have it, because it relies ENTIRELY on your quality of hearing and you will be one step closer to madness with each failed attempt. You might still have to try it a couple times with the guide, even. It's one of the most frustrating puzzles I've run up against in a game.
Other things I didn't like where very minor. For the most part this was a very smooth experience. Every once in a while I got stumped because the next action you take is to click and drag something, and you can tell in these moments this game was made for an iPad. There is one area near the end of the game I was excited to uncover but there was surprisingly little to discover there and we never had a reason to go back to it, at least in the first playthrough (I only played through once), so that was a smidge disappointing.
In closing:
Year Walk is memorable, well made, and throughly spooky. There are some replayability incentives, though I can imagine it getting a little tedious playing through the game back to back. It will be a game I pick up again once I've forgotten enough of the scares and I'm ready to be frightened alone in the snowy woods again. For anyone who loves horror games it's a must, and even those who typically aren't fond of the genre will find a genuinely interesting narrative and enjoyable game.
Tldr/; Great game. Some minor bumps with one really frustrating puzzle (get a guide for the singing puzzle ahead of time). Take your time, it's beautiful and scary and worth it. Definitely recommended.

It offers a variety of matchup options that range from 1v1, 2v2 up to modes that support 12 Players at once.
The Experience is very smooth and apart from a few UI elements which look a little clunky and outdated (some font choices are a bit odd too) The Sound design too doesn't feel entirely finished yet.
However, both the Ship and the Environmental design are gorgeous and really bring out the best of the underwater setting and so far I haven't stumbled over significant balancing issues.
If you're looking for a fast to pick up fun to Play game to start up for some quick play sessions and you want to feel like Captain Nemo waging war I can wholeheartedly recommend this game.

It is a real trip... A completely different reality to experience, jammed full of plot and a well written story. I played it from start to finish in one sitting. I couldn't put it down.
Lasted about 10 hours, plus another 10-12 to find all the collectibles and write a scratchpad guide to uncover all the plot and squeeze everything out of the game that I could.

Uses the same fright tactics as films such as Final Destination or unexpectedly bumping into an ex, who makes you feel the urge to shower, shave all your body hair and burn your clothes.
Less a game as an interactive movie. The majority of "puzzles" are figuring out how to progress along the plot-line (and a mini-game that is probably the only real puzzle/game in the game), similar to old Ubisoft CSI games.
The game has such impact that it is not easily forgotten and so limits replay value, however - there are collectibles that are "locked out" through progression and require a restart. This got me. Only flaw.
Beautiful art-style, excellent score, thought provoking, tense and - in some strange way - psychologically disturbing, with some comic interludes.
While not an entirely original premise, I have not encountered a game that explores the subject matter in such a way before. A good job at translating what would be a great sci-fi novel into a computer game, without losing any of the content. Perhaps even adding to it.

Yes/No/
You and 3-8 friends draw a randomly assigned and silly prompts and take turns guessing what your friends' topics are.
+Chill music that doesn't get annoying
+Easy to pick up. Literally anyone can play this as long as they have a smart phone.
+Really great ice breaker at a LAN party or Christmas party or whatever.
+Prompts that you're assigned are generally pretty funny
+It can be played over skype or a stream or any service that lets you share your screen to an audience
+Fun to watch as well with the audience mode.
+Allows up to 8 players.
+You can make your own prompts.
-You can't play without 3 or more people.
-The game only runs at 30FPS as far as I know.
-You either play full screen or windowed and you can't change the resolution of the game.
-You can't erase when you're drawing. This can lead to funny moments but it can also be frustrating.
-No custom rules like number of rounds, how long the turns last, etc.
Drawful 2 doesn't deviate far from Drawful 1 so if you liked Drawful 1, chances are you'll like this game. The premise is you create a lobby online, you and all your players go to Jackbox's site, log into the lobby and start playing your game based on whatever appears on the host's screen. Lower numbers of players will do 2 rounds, a large group does 1. All in all, the game is really fun when playing with friends and is an easy way to break the ice with people you don't really know, like if you were to have people over and they bring friends/relatives/whatever. Rounds feel like they're just the right amount of length with the only real issue in my opinion  is how long it CAN take but that's more of an issue when playing online and with people who are playing for the first time. After a round or two, it's pretty easy to grasp how to play and rounds are faster.
Overall, if you play games with a lot of people pretty often via parties, streaming, whatever, this game is worth picking up. If you play games alone a lot, this might not be as good of a purchase since you need 3 players minimum to play.

TL;DR: It has some flaws, but overall I really like it!
This postapoc world somehow makes more sense to me than those of Fallouts and Wastelands. The game is nicely paced, some quests are quite difficult to figure out and pull off, which I enjoy. The storytelling is good, though the English is a bit broken sometimes, but who has times for dictionaries in a radiated world anyway. Random encounters are many and varied, though the terrains they occur on become a bit repetitive after a while.
I enjoy the battle mechanics, but it would be nice if the player had some control over his companions (now the AI controls them all), as usually they tend to just blindly charge the enemy and you have to constantly keep saving them from certain death, by taking the hits meant for them. Makes the tactic of sniping safely from afar rather useless. This is particularly annoying when you're escorting (and protecting) traders, as they're weak, unarmoured, but still charge ahead and get killed after only a few hits. Basically all combat AI does is zero in on the closest enemy and gets in range to shoot or club them. No flanking, no keeping distance for shooters, no tactics.
I like the fact that barter prices aren't the usual "10 when selling, 100 when buying" like in most RPGs, but with just a bit of a margin for the trader, so you can make some decent profits selling loot you've risked your life for. A storage locker somewhere in the world (or at least a trunk in your vehicle) would be nice for stowing away the items you wish to keep but are not currently using. As it is now, you want to convert any heavy object into weightless ammo asap by bartering it away, as the carry limit is quite low, particularly if you put on any armour.
The music is very nice and fitting to the atmosphere of the game and the graphics are what I'd expect from this sort of a game.
I do hope the devs keep working on the game, upgrade and improve it, because it is an unpolished gem with a lot of potential to become a classic of this genre.
Overall I give this game a:
10/10 for awesome post-apocalyptic atmosphere
9/10 for music (the bar track with the shredding guitar also shreds your nerves after a while)
7/10 for storytelling
8/10 for combat mechanics concept but only
1/10 for extremely stupid and completely brainless combat AI

I wish I could pick something beyond the binary of "yes" or "no." This game has incredible animation, visuals, atmosphere, and sound design, but the game mechanics are incredibly cryptic. Even with a guide, I found traversing the world very tedious and frustrating. However, I do wish I could pick something closer to "nuetral" on my stance, since this type of game isn't typically my favorite (despite loving the art style), and it may be better suited for those that enjoy cryptically difficult puzzle/adventure games.

There isn't much positive to say about this game, except for the visuals. The visuals are really beautiful, and sometimes eerie, and will definitely give you a short fix of novelty, if that's something you deeply desire. You will also learn a little bit about Swedish folklore, which to me is unfairly overlooked. It's much cooler than Greek mythology, which seems to be more popular in creative works of art.
But aside from that:
It's very short (1.5 hours on average), the puzzles are meh, it's sometimes unclear how the game mechanics work, the sidescrolling format and simplified interaction mechanics never let you forget that this is in fact a game, so it's hard to get immersed in the experience, and the whole thing feels like some interactive presentation about Swedish folklore.
Get this game if you want to spend an hour looking at some beautiful visuals. If you are looking for a good game, or even an immersive experience, look somewhere else.

Play Length: Pretty long.  Although I still need to play the Steam version more, I've played the original extensively.
Positives: This is an excellent nod to classic MSX games, particularly the Maze of Galious.  But I think it's better designed than those games in many ways.  The graphics in the original look right out of a MSX game and are lovingly crafted.  You might fear that the updated graphics for the Steam version would lose some of their charm, but luckily the original creator worked on them and they still look great.  Now they look more like a Super Nintendo game, which works perfectly well.  The same is also true for the music, a lot of care was taken to make sure it retains the charm of the original soundtrack.
The game itself is excellent.  Having played both versions, I have to say that the Steam versions smoothes over a few problems with the original version and makes it even better.  One excellent addition is the ability to save all the notes you've read in an in game journal; while I kind of enjoyed keeping a written journal of notes when I played the original game, it's certainly easier this way.  The puzzles themselves have been smoothed over a bit, to be a bit more fair and a little easier to figure out.  But they are still by no means easy.  The puzzle design is very good, with a lot of clever puzzles.
Although they toned down the puzzles a bit, they compensated for this by increasing the game's skill based difficulty.  This is a good change.  In the original game, it often felt like health didn't matter, and bosses were a bit too easy to steamroll through.  Now your health meter matters a bit more.  The difficulty is still not a big deal, as the ability to warp renders many of the challenges moot, but it's a welcome change none the less.
Negatives: Although I like the updated graphics and music, it does lose a bit of it's MSX feel that the original version had.  So, if you are a big fan of the MSX, I would encourage you to check out the original version, which is still available and free.  Also, while I think that all the puzzles are fair and solvable, some of them are very devious and a bit vague.  And you will likely need to do a lot of wandering around, and trial and error.  Many people will probably need to resort to a guide to finish this game.
Overall: This game does a great job of making you feel like an archeologist.  The ruins you are exploring feel mysterious, the puzzles are clever and memorable.  The music really sets a great tone for the game and will stay with you after you've played.  This is not only one of the best love letters to classic games ever made, but it's one of the best indie games ever made.  Even if you're not a fan of the kind of games it's referencing, this game absolutely must be tried by anyone who likes independant games.
About my rating system: I have two things I rate on.  The first is the overall score, and the second is soundtrack.  The reason why is because I feel like soundtrack is tremendously undervalued; to me, it's a tremendously important factor in whether I like a game.  For the score, I grade on a scale of 1-10, and I try to grade in such a way that each number has a meaning and each has equal importance.  The numbers have the following meanings:
0: Garbage, 1: Awful, 2: Poor, 3: Underwhelming, 4: Mediocre, 5: Decent, 6: Good, 7: Great, 8: Excellent, 9: Phenomenal, 10: Masterpiece
La Mulana's score:
Game Rating: 9 (Phenomenal)
Soundtrack Rating: 8 (Excellent)

This game is not well-liked by a lot of people, but it is because they do not understand how the intricacies of this game make the true experience. Every boss has a true strategy (or a few), but some require such deep knowledge that they appear unknowable foes. Perhaps, the same could be said for all of La-MULANA.....
By the way, the valley in which the game starts out in is based upon Bahrun Valley of Nepal, where it is believed that an immortal race of humans lived. Now, it is uninhabitable, being to high in the mountains to remain in that place for long.
There are many things to examine in this game which will deepen your appreciation for mythology. Without this game, mythology was almost impossible for me to grasp. It still is pretty hard to grasp, though.....

This has been my favorite game ever since the Japanese Wii release. When I first ever played this game, I couldn’t figure what the heck I was supposed to do. That was until I learned you can use the challis to teleport out of the temple and back to the surface, and that’s where the rea fun begins.
The basic idea of the game is for players to transverse through a very large and difficult temple, filled with items that make your more powerful, traps that cause massive amounts of damage, monsters who try to get in your way, and gigantic boss who try to kill you quickly. Once a player gets into a dire state, they are teleport out of the temple to heal themselves and then return back to the temple to try to get even deeper into La-Mulana.
This game is not for everyone, it can be extremely frustrating and will most likely cause you to run around in circles for hours trying to figure out what the heck to do next. What makes it fun to me is the fact that it is extremely challenging and each puzzle’s solution is hidden in a mystery; they don’t hold your hand like most games do these days.
I grew up in a video game era were video games would just throw you into the action and it was up to you to you figure it out yourself. This game takes me back to that time and every time I solved a puzzle on my own, I feel happily rewarded as I progress even deeper through LA-Mulana.

This is a game for masochists.
I mean, really, who wants to spend 50+ hours running around a dungeon, frustrated and confused by where to go, failing to make the same jump because a stupid bat flew in your way, retreading steps to find that hidden entrance you missed so you could get that item you need to summon the boss, and then getting blown up by said boss over and over again. You will die in this game. A lot.
...and yet there's something magical about it still. The freedom of exploration, the amount of depth to the level design, the satisfaction of finally killing that stupid Lizard monster from the minecart, and the hope just maybe if you make it far enough into the lava you'll find an item worth the struggle. This is one of the best crafted, charming, unforgivingly brutal Metroidvania-style games out there. From time to time you may need to take a break, and the temptation to use a guide is extremely real, but the enjoyment you'll find in the surprisingly deep story, settings, and gameplay is what makes this game worth playing - as long as you're ready for a challenge ;)

- Slot machine
- Pet sanctuary

If exploring vast landscapes and coming across mysterious secrets is one of your favorite things to do in video games then this will be one of your favorite video games of the year -- as long as you're ok with solving puzzles, too. Lots of puzzles.

The line puzzles, for what they are, are fairly inventive despite the limitations. Each area of the game introduces new concepts into the maze puzzles, and many of the harder puzzles merge a variety of these concepts together. Over the course of the game you will gradually learn this language so you will be able to intuitively understand these puzzles, although they will always remain a challenge. Some of the later puzzles are fiendishly challenging, which will leave you reaching for a guide.
After the tutorial area of the game, you can wonder across the Myst-esque island at your leisure, and some areas of the island are clearly meant for you to complete after you've finished some of the easier areas. However, the game never tells you "you don't know how to complete this puzzle yet", which can lead to frustration if you attempt a series of puzzles you haven't mastered the rules of.
Furthermore, some of the puzzle design can be counter-intuitive; certain puzzles are able to be brute forced by process of elimination, and if you’ve missed environmental clues or other hints, or simply don’t understand what you’re supposed to be doing, these do not feel very fun. Indeed, a lot of the game can feel deliberately un-fun. The game doesn’t have any kind of traditional reward structure; by completing puzzles you simply unlock more puzzles, but don’t get any kind of feedback other than that. You get your enjoyment through the act of solving the puzzles themselves, instead of any external validation. There are also a lot of optional puzzles that essentially do “nothing”, and completing them is not required to “finish” the game.
Visually the game is without fault, with a gorgeously lush and colourful world with various biomes including a swamp, a town and a desert. Each area feels nicely distinct, while nonetheless integrating into the rest of the world. However, the island is most of the time completely disconnected from the puzzles you’re actually solving, meaning it functions mostly as a pretty backdrop. There are only a couple of areas where the environment is used in conjunction with the puzzles (such as the mazes in the castle) and these are definite highlights. While there are some ambient noises, the game is completely lacking any soundtrack or music, something I think is a great shame considering the excellent use of music in the lead developer's previous game, Braid.
I liked certain things about The Witness; its gorgeous visuals and the fairly interesting puzzles. But what makes me feel so infuriated by it is that philosophically and intellectually the game is a mess, and it does not have its own voice at all. Instead, it simply borrows from other philosophical traditions and introduces them without any preamble in an attempt to appear “deep”. It also has essentially no story or in-universe justification to speak of at all; any story must be inferred from a secret ending that occurs after you finish the game the first time.
Rather than advancing or suggesting some themes, The Witness cribs wholesale from the work of others. If you go to the trouble of hunting them down, there are several videos that you can watch in the underground cinema. These videos are from third-party sources and suggest several different philosophical viewpoints, but there is no analysis of their validity, or exploration of their content. One goes on for over an hour and is a complete waste of your time. You’re just presented the videos and left to work out how you feel about them on your own.
The audio logs, which are the other main collectible, are just out of context quotes from a variety of philosophers, scientists and theologians, stuffed into the game seemingly without rhyme or reason. They’re clearly designed to show you different “viewpoints” and to show how different people see things differently, but that is a theme that can be summarized in a single sentence. The Witness doesn’t have a clue what it’s trying to say apart from “people see things in different ways”; it honestly feels like these audio logs were put into the game simply to give the player something to find when they’re not solving puzzles, and to pepper the sometimes unnervingly quiet island with sounds. The Witness wants you to think there is some deeper meaning here; it wants you to think about the stone figures and the island and question it all, but there are no answers and it’s completely pointless.
The Witness is a bit like a dolls house. It's beautiful but it’s lacking any kind of soul, and beneath the surface you can see the fake wallpaper and the plastic furniture. Emotionally, The Witness is cold as ice and the island, despite its beauty and colour, feels uniformly lifeless, artificial and empty. I came away from The Witness actively disliking it; scorning it for its blasé, meaningless attitude actively wishing it had had “something” interesting to say. The Witness desperately wants you to think it’s clever and that it has hidden depth, but ultimately it’s a lie. It’s just a pretty game with some line puzzles in it, and nothing stringing those two elements together. That’s fine, but it should come clean rather than hiding itself behind obfuscating layers of pretension.
The Steam store page for The Witness says
This is just one of several blatant lies that pepper the store page, which you will discover as you play. The Witness downright revels in wasting your time, sometimes in infuriating ways. I can only recommend The Witness to people who enjoy solving line maze puzzles for the sake of solving line maze puzzles, but I cannot recommend it to anyone looking to intuit any greater meaning, purpose or enjoyment from it other than that.

Imagine meeting another culture and trying to learn each other's languages, but you point to an apple, they have never seen an apple, so they do not have a world for it to relate, what do you do?
So, you might have to resort to its color, shape, texture, TASTE, or maybe even the sound it makes when you bite it, the basic elements...
That is what you can expect from this amazing puzzle world/adventure!
The puzzles in this Myst-like world are a kind of language...You must observe by looking, listening and thinking about your surroundings.
The developers have done a great job of creating a kind of learning mechanism for the mechanics, then helping the player see when and how to apply each of the mechanics to the puzzle at hand.  I would say that for a puzzling adventure, it is far more intuitive than MOST.
I will admit that at first I was feeling a kind of disappointment, until I started to see the depth of their accomplishment.  I was afraid that I would be doing mundane maze puzzles all throughout, but I was so very wrong with that early impression.
As one of the original fans of Myst, this game really does embrace the spirit of a mythical world, left to ruin and you come along to discover its mysteries and purpose (if any).  This is a strange, yet intriguing formula of discovery, where you feel compelled to move along and take in more, only to understand the strange world you find yourself in.
As a puzzler they have done a nice job of slowly introducing simple examples of puzzle mechanics, that are later used in a more complex way.  You will find yourself amongst a group of similar puzzles that are solved collectively, using similar mechanics, allow you the opportunity to fully grasp the underlining logic.

ACHIEVEMENTS:  There is one for completing and another secret ;)
ISSUES:
1.) Treehouse gets tedious :(
2.) I am guessing, to prevent simple guessing, failing most puzzles, causes power off of the active puzzle and you have to repetitively finish the previous :(

With 50+ hours of gameplay and all acheivements unlocked, I think I can provide a decent insight to Magic 2014 - Dules of the Planeswalkers. If you're a new player to M:tG, this is a great place to learn the very basic gameplay and mechanics of the game. You'll be exposed to cards from the very first sets all the way up to now. The game will have you unlock decks and stronger cards by facing other Planeswalkers. Deck construction is a bit limited, but with a pool of about
cards per deck, you should be able to come up with a few strategies for each of them. It's a great place to start if you don't want to pour money into the physical card game or Wizards of the Coast's Magic Online. Diehard fans may be a bit dissappointed with the game on the whole considering how broad and intense Magic can be outside of DoTP, but this game balances out the power curves you'll see in standard Magic: the Gathering play. You can add your own creativity in the Sealed Deck mode which enables you to build a 40-card deck from semi-radomized packs. You may have to switch your strategy as you play this mode, as you'll face different opponents who have different strategies. You won't get blown out by Pro decks, but watch out for the DLC decks as they are more powerful. You can join forces with your friends to face other AI Planeswalkers (which you can higher or lower in difficulty) or other human players. Overall, it's a great way to scratch the surface of a very in-depth game, hone your skills, and discover cards that could change the way your physical decks operate.

I punched out of And Yet It Moves after about 20 minutes the first time I played it, and that was so many years ago I couldn't remember why. I started it up again recently and spent some time getting re-adjusted to the jumping and spinning, but it didn't take long to refresh my memory on its failings. AYIM feels like a platformer built to be the antithesis of platformers, a game that embodies everything that platformers aren't. It works at what it does, mind you, it's just that what it does isn't at all fun.
I don't think there's a plot to And Yet It Moves, you're just trying to get your mop-haired avatar to the exit of each level. The terrain of each cave or forest or wherever you find yourself is impossible to navigate with just his plodding gait and weak jump so you are empowered to rotate the world around him to proceed. Using this power you'll saunter up the walls and ceilings of caverns, bend around the edges of cliffs, and navigate boulders and planks through mazes of ledges. You'll encounter a few new gimmicks as you progress as well, including animals that must be fed to pass and breakaway platforms to watch out for.
This sort of puzzling is bare-bones for 2017 but it was a clever twist on a tired genre back in 2009 when it came out. AYIM certainly helped pave the way for other world-bending puzzlers that came after it, but that doesn't necessarily mean it's the best example of it. You can only rotate the world 90 degrees at a time, for example, which can make some slopes and complex cliffs hard to navigate. You'll also be doing a lot of flipping from the top to the bottom of platforms and the interplay of momentum and stiff rotation complicates your maneuvers. And I know I mentioned other gimmicks but they're honestly pretty sparse, leaving the majority of the gameplay to just making the same jumps and flips over and over.
What really kills this game, though, is the fall damage. There's a lot of circling around and doubling back in AYIM's level design, so to prevent players from taking shortcuts or coming up with their own routes through levels, anything longer than about a six-foot drop kills you stone dead. Actually it's not even the drop that kills you, it's the momentum, so if you get going too fast on a moving platform or stay airborne while rotating for too long, you'll also splatter. It's so bad that on some platforms you have to flip onto the backside of, if you jump too high you'll explode when you land where you're supposed to.
This is what I was talking about when I said And Yet It Moves is the antithesis of platformers. Fall damage is easily the worst part of any game that includes it, going all the way back to the original Donkey Kong. It adds nothing as a game element, it only serves to limit players in how they can navigate a level. The same end can be accomplished with walls without having to kill your player, or with pits or spikes so that incidental jumps aren't deadly if they happen to go too high. AYIM is doubly terrible in this regard because speed, not distance, is lethal, enforcing a slow and plodding pace to a game in a genre where some of its best games are high-speed romps.
And Yet It Moves works fine as the puzzle game it is designed to be. My problem is how that design prevents AYIM from utilizing the best parts of its genre and turns them into frustrating punishments. It gives you large, sprawling levels of caves and trees and whatever the hell the third world is because I didn't get that far, and then murders you if you try to hop around it or experience it too fast. Outside of the puzzles though there's very little to the game, with no secrets or unlockables to chase. The collage artstyle is fine but underutilized with only three environments and the soundtrack is so minimal and ambient that it makes the game feel even emptier. I doubt I could have seen anything to recommend about AYIM back when it released, and I definitely can't at present.

I'd been on the fence about this game for weeks but finally decided to go ahead and buy it. I should have bought this game sooner because it is a great little game.
While mostly simplistic in scope, ZombieParty's only 'mistake' seems to be the title as I've found myself shooting more strange monsters, aliens and other oddities than zombies, which given the name is a bit silly.
At it's core, it feels to me like a very relaxed and casual top down shooter that is more about having fun than being truly difficult. However, it is pretty addicting and has what I think are some pretty clever calls from the creator.
Don't let the simple pixelated art style put you off from what this game really has to offer, which is more than I expected.
For more about what I think makes it truly shine, read on.
-----------------------------------------------
- There are multiple ways to play this game.
I've spent most of my time in dungeon mode, which is what it sounds like. You search the map for loot, money, enemies and the staircase to proceed down to the next level. There are also shops that spawn every floor or two to buy specific items from if you want to. Every 5 floors, there is a boss before a change of environment happens. Each boss is progressively harder. The floor styles will repeat but the dungeon continues to get harder with every boss beaten.
Adventure mode is basically a wave-shooter. You are dropped into a wider, more open arena and face off against waves of enemies. The enemies drop random loot and money. Inbetween each wave you are given a small reprieve to buy from the shop, use any stat points you have and equip your guns with any runes or artifacts you may have found before the next wave begins. After 5 waves, a boss will appear to challenge you. The bosses in this mode are entirely different from the dungeon mode bosses.
There is also a 4way I believe death match with either other players or bots. And an arcade mode that is purely kill / high score orientated but I haven't tried either of those, honestly so I'm not positive there.
So one thing this game does is offer you several ways to play it and that is really smart. Offering a slower, more progressive pace with dungeon and then a wave shooter alternative, too.
- There's lots of fun ways to modify weapons.
You will find many [Runes] that grant your weapons new traits. Spread Shot, Split Shot, Homing, Piercing, Ricochet to name a few. You can have up to 3 runes on each of your base gun slots. There are also [Artifacts], which change your weapon in pretty crazy and fun ways. Yes, you can spread shot, pierce and have homing bullets -- but what about having a machine gun that fires ROCKETS? Or Grenades? Or Sawblades? Or Skulls, or Eyeballs? Or LASERS? That's what Artifacts do. You can have one per weapon and it changes what the gun shoots and how it behaves. It's freaking amazing to have a machine gun spewing out waves of rockets or firing lasers everywhere.
You can also equip or unequip runes and artifacts at ANY TIME during play that you have a moment to open your equipment screen. They do not slot permanently and are not destroyed if replaced. You just add or remove them whenever you feel like it.
- There are a ton of unlockables.
Whenever you give up or die during a run, you are awarded gold at the end of the run based on how far you got. This amount has NOTHING to do with what your character has on them or has spent during the run, so do not keep gold unless it is to buy specific items you want from later shops.
The gold you are awarded at the end of each run becomes a kind of "out of game" currency, which is spent entirely on unlockable things, of which there are many. There is a huge roster of characters ranging from different looking, to outright weird. For instance, there are several different human characters -- but there's also an unlockable character who's a Fish -- and there's a Slime -- and I think a Snow Man, an Alien, etc. Each have different gold costs to unlock permanently.
You can also improve your characters' base starting statistics like damage, health, etc in return for gold you're willing to invest in it.
And perhaps the most interesting decision with gold is that every character has access to some basic weapons in addition to anything else they may have. A basic gun slot, with unlimited ammo and then an assault rifle, machine gun, shotgun and grenade launcher, all of which have limited ammo. Each [slot] / weapon has many different variations. The basic gun slot for instance starts with a basic handgun, but you'll find at shops you can buy a bow and arrow, or twin pistol combo, or a laser blaster and this is true for all of the above listed weapon slots.
You can use gold out-of-game to permanently unlock any variation of any of the original slots. So if you want to always have the twin pistol combo like I wanted? Cool, you can use gold to permanently unlock that. Same goes for the Assault Rifles, Shotguns, SMGs and Grenade Launchers.
You cannot however unlock runes, or artifacts. Those you will always find randomly or buy from shops.
I think the way gold is set up strikes a really nice balance between permanently unlocking things and still finding exciting things you want during your actual gameplay, since this game has it's roots in randomization.
It offers some stability to go with the randomness.
- Pets.
I'll go ahead and mention these too. There are random pets you will save by shooting them free from their cages and these appear randomly in adventure mode and dungeon mode. There's also a pet paradise where you can go and visit them. In my experience so far, the pets don't appear to do anything meaningful but maybe I just haven't realized what they're for yet. All the pets are unlocked permanently just by finding and freeing them. So even if they do nothing else, they are another little added surprise / unlockable that you can only get through gameplay.
-----------------------------------------------
While I doubt many people will read through my entire review, I wanted to elaborate on all of these features because I think they are all smart calls on the developer's part and they make the game stand out from it's "competition".
ZombieParty has simple and enjoyable gameplay but for me, it was deceptively more fun and elaborate than I gave it credit for. So the developer deserves recognition for his many great ideas, wrapped in a charmingly cute looking little game.

I like this one. A bizzare cyberpunk noir detective story with some philosophical and moral implications here an there. Hell, that was an interesting ride! I only hope I got this game right.
The job description of the detective with the voice and looks of Rutger Hauer (yes, the same Rutger Hauer who played the role of the batshit crazy Nexus 8 replicant in Blade Runner) is simple: look for clues and leads, interrogate suspects, victims and perps, and if necessary jack yourself into their crazy minds - and all of this while maintaining your own precious sanity. Sounds easy, right? Scary, though, yeah. Well, wading through shattered subconscious minds of killers and junkies isn't the scariest part, because, you know, none of this is actually real, and you're a professional observer after all, right? The poopy pants part starts when you're not pretty sure anymore if you're still inside someone else's head or if those guys are hunting you for real. Yeah, the paranoia is freakin real. When the actual reality starts literaly break down to pieces in front of your eyes and mess with your head and stomach. There is no logic to decide which door to open and which turn to take. When to look back and when to run for your last bit of sanity. Only observation, intuition and guts are your guides. It's intented to be confusing. Hell, we grow up being all confused the hole time, unsure what's wrong and what's right, what's real and what's fantasy. What do you expect to find jacking into other people's heads? Answers? lol Good luck with that. In this insane plot *you* are the one who's supposed to make sense of it all. No one is going to deliver it to you on a silver platter.

This... is a tough review to write.
The game has hundreds of points of exceeding brilliance.
The game is frequently a battle with the level layout and the UI, trying to figure what's desired of the player next. (especially in the "dream" bits)
The game explores topics in ways that haven't been adequately covered in years. (think: puree Ghost in the Shell, Blade Runner, and William Gibson books; add salt and rat poison to taste)
The game has an autosave system, and at least one point-of-no-return w/o a clear warning of the same.
If you're looking to feel like you've mainlined Noir and cyberpunk-based drain cleaner.  If you're looking to feel confused and bewildered most of the time.  If you want to wade neck-deep in poverty, despair, and black humor.  Then get it. (on sale, natch)
Otherwise, just wait for some poor b@stard to make a Let's Play, and laugh as they proceed to lose their minds.
TL;DR: I have no way to reduce this one to a number which will do my feelings justice.  I really liked it, but I'm still not sure if I hate it too.

I wandered the woods looking for spirits in seemingly random locations. I noted pagan patterns and reproduced them elsewhere. I read and reenacted obscure Scandinavian legends described in the encyclopedia. I manipulated polygonal floating shapes in the Beyond.
The game's excellent mythological source material is unjustly wasted on flat design and unintuitive mechanics. Despite several promising base ideas, as a whole it just isn't very entertaining.
The first puzzle you encounter, a wooden box with strange symbols arranged in a circular pattern, is one you literally can't solve until after you first complete the game. It acts as a sort of epilogue to reveal the true ending, which is fine except it highlights one of the game's main problems: elements are presented in an order that feels wrong.
Figuring out how to perform simple actions due to awkward controls turns out to be unnecessarily convoluted and my main gripe with the game. Many times I knew what to do (wind the doll, carry an object to the next scene, etc) but failed in the execution. That's not innovation, that's bad UX design.

I do not know if this game was unique in its concept at the time, but it's must certainly one of the few puzzle strategy games out there. I've not seen many like it. Only the Desperado games, set in the Wild West, as far as I know.
Commandos: Behind Enemy Lines follows bunch of special missions in WWII where you as an officer use the skills of a couple specialised commandos, specially trained British soldiers. Each commando has his own set of tools to help you to complete each mission. And it's up to you to decide when and how to utilise each commando to overcome certain obstacles. If any of your commandos dies, you'll fail the mission. You'll have to pay attention not to alert any of the German soldiers or officers, as they're always alert and on the lookout. They watch and listen to anything suspicious. Some garrison buildings with the swastika flying will contain soldiers that will come out and patrol when the alarm is sounded. This will make your missions far more difficult, so stealth is key. Each new mission is an ever bigger puzzle you have to try to complete. You have 20 to complete.
The game has, despite being from 1998 and sometimes in need of workarounds to get it working properly, a great atmosphere, supported by actual WWII film footage and little background stories, and a unique aesthetic.

This is a bad game. Don't buy it.
Let me articulate: the game is extremely simple, repetitive, and any variation in gameplay comes from poor UI and artificial limits.
This would have been an acceptable computer game in the mid '90s, or a browser or mobile game. It's not an acceptable game in the 2010s.
As in most games in its genre, it's about optimizing resources. The totality of the gameplay is micromanagement of trade and productive structures. If you could set autotrades (whenever a trader comes, buy metal, until a maximum of 10. Wheneber a trader comes, sell ore, until a minimum of 30), set priorities to workers (produce spare parts, until you have a mximum of 10), or just see resources projections (at current consumption rates, you will run out of ore in 4 days), the game could be set to run on its own, and the challenge would be how fast you reach your goals.
Unfortunately, none of this is possible, so you have to grind for hours waiting fro traders, switching structures on and off, and setting tresholds for production.
Let me summarize: the game exists only because of a poor UI. With a better UI, there would be no game. This is unacceptably poor game design.

I have never played Magic the card game, nor any of the inspired video games. I've always had some interest in it, but the cost of getting the cards and having to learn how to actually play the game was always a deterrent.
Then came along a Steam sale, and I bought this game having read that this is one of the best places to learn how to play the game for beginners. And I'm glad I did. At the moment I am over 20 hours into Magic 2014 and enjoying it inmensely. This while not even having tried online gaming, nor the expansion which I bought in the bundle, or a "closed deck' game. As a matter of fact I don't even know what a "closed deck" game means, since I'm re-playing the campaign trying to unlock cards for the different sets. Again, this while being over 20 hours in the game.
To concur with the other reviews: this is a fantastic place to learn how to play the game for beginners. The tutorial explains everything perfectly. As you go further into the campaign you will have cards with certain attributes which weren't explained in the tutorial, and with a simple mouse-click on the card you can see what it does. I'm surprised how easily it was to learn how to play Magic to be honest.
Replayability is necessary to unlock most of the cards. Considering the enemies in the campaign play the same way every time, one might think this becomes boring. For me this couldn't be further from the truth. I am actually enjoying replaying the campaign with different sets. Since you play with different cards, you'll have to rethink your strategy and despite the AI playing the same order of cards every time (I don't think this is the case for bosses though) it still becomes a new experience with every set.
As I said, I have never played Magic nor it's videogames, as such I can not judge this game by looking at other offerings and seeing what the 2014 version does worse (or better) than other versions. I can only tell that my experience with this game has been a very good one, and I would easily recommend it to anybody.
If you like magic or card games or wanna try them, great choice. Sealed play is excellent add on to the game.
