Okay..  There are moments we've almost all had as gamers where we get frustrated in a game, overthink everything and spend a ton of time looking for what we need to move on to the next level or progress the story.  - And then when we discover how simple it was we feel like a complete dope.  ..That's what happened with me in my initial review of this game, and it resulted in a negative score because I was so frustrated at the time.
After a little bit of time however, I started realizing that there is actually a lot of this game that I really like.  So I reached out to one of the developers and decided to give the game another chance, realizing that this might all be on ME.
And in this video, a much more in-depth look at this game Krai Mira, you'll see exactly how foolish I was.  I MADE A MISTAKE AND MISSED SOMETHING SO OBVIOUS THAT EVEN A COMPLETE NON-GAMING NOOB WOULD SHAKE THEIR HEAD AT!   ...There, I said it.  It was all 100% on me.. and not this game.
I have left my intial review and video at the bottom of this review, just so you all can see how drastic my overall first review is now that I discovered what a goober I was in my first play.  It might give someone a good laugh anyhow.
So what is Krai Mira?
It's a pretty damn good looking turn based RPG adventure game made in the shadows of the original Fallout PC games.  ..I mean the original old school Fallout games from the 90s, don't be thinking Fallout 3 or Fallout Vegas or you might be left disappointed by the isometric perspective and graphics.
It offers stats, special skills which can be upgraded as you choose as you level up.  It offers an inventory system and plenty of people willing to trade with you, as long as you give them enough items to suit their desires.  You can pretty much barter with any NPC and you'll see lots of them, and each one carries different items for trade.
Most NPCs will also offer you the ability to play a game of Dice where you take turns rolling 5 dice to score the results in a very Farkle scoring system.  Don't worry if you are not familiar with the dice game of Farkle, as the dice rolling screen shows you a clear dice scoring chart.  This is a game of double or nothing as the winner takes all at whatever score point you decide to play to.  And this game is where my biggest suggestion goes out to the developers...  You have your dice rolling system in place.  You have the scoring in.  Now just make it a small game of "Farkle" where dice can be rolled and you can choose to gamble further for more points or risk losing all your turn points to roll again.  Basically my suggestion is to change the current single dice rolls and 100% luck game to a game of Farkle where strategy and skll will be part of your dice game gamble.  I think that this upgrade alone would take this game from a "good game" to a "fantastic game" that would also be much more addicting!
The turn based combat system is a lot of fun already and I love how while it shows your entire move area when you in a battle, it doesn't show you the move grids like so many of these games do.  Please watch my video for a better idea of how it all work.
Mature Content Warning: You'll see a lot of curse words in the text dialogues and options of how to respond, especially the F-bomb.  You'll also see naked women and lots of sexual innuendo!  - This may be a positive for some people however!  ;-)
So now this game has taken a huge turn after more time playing, and I actually scored this game at an 84%  (Value: 34/40, Fun 25/30, Controls & Bugs 17/20, Graphics and Sound 8/10)
An 84% is a VERY high and respectable score for a game like this that is still in early access right after the EA launch!
Definitely recommended especially to any RPG game, Fallout, or apocolyptic style games!

I remember playing this game throughout the mid 2000's and beating the game around 3 times on both XBox and PS2 and was very glad to see the game remastered for the PC where I am working on my 4th playthrough. - The controls in this game are ported over from XBox and are not the easiest to use on PC which can make the game irritating at times. I would strongly advise bookmarking a page online that has the controls aswell considering there are no real ways to determine what button does what in game.On a side note if you have a controller you will likely have an easier time.

- There are bugs in this game however most of them have been fixed however I will post 2 that I encountered for the sake of awareness:
+ Left eyes of sarcophagi are invisible
+ A rare bug where conversation is inescapable and uninteracable with the NPC that runs the Heliopolis obstacle course.
- Voice acting is pretty much non-existant outside of incomprehensable noises made by the characters in cutscenes.
Despite the game's buggy behavior It has solid replay value and is a great fit for anyone that liked to play older action-adventure platformer games.

Hello everybody, End World Gaming here to share an excerpt from my review for Sphinx and the Cursed Mummy HD by Eurocom and THQNordic.
Sphinx and the Cursed Mummy HD is a remaster of an action adventure game from 2003. As of writing this review the game has only been released on PC but I hope that the game will receive a console release (Again) in the future so more people can enjoy the game.
The game is based on Ancient Egyptian mythology and it features many of the gods and heroes from the time period, like Imhotep and Anubis.
The story follows two characters, the first is named Sphinx and he’s used mostly for combat, while Tutankhamen is used to solve intricate puzzles. The game frequently alternate’s between the two of them and in doing so it makes the game a lot less boring.
Each area of the game is beautifully designed and the HD enhancements look great considering the game’s age. Most of the areas are quite large as well and often have side quests for you to complete. Doing side quests also has benefits to the game itself but there are some that aren’t required to complete the game, like capturing monsters for the museum, as an example.
As you progress through the game the puzzles that you encounter with Tutankhamen become increasingly more intricate and complex. Since he’s a mummy for the majority of the game, he’s immune to death and this fact is utilized in each of the game’s puzzles. He can be set on fire, electrocuted, split into 3, and flattened. Each of these unique states lasts only for a short period of time so you must move quickly to solve each of the game’s puzzles. If he’s on fire or electrified, falling into the water will get rid of the effect and you’ll need to go reacquire it again. Getting any of the effects will also automatically replace the existing effect too.
When you’re in control of sphinx you’ll be able to use the Sword of Osiris to battle enemies. Enemies come in many shapes and sizes and each have their own unique abilities to them. They’re pretty limited in skills though, so you can easily learn their moves without much effort.
At the start of the game, Sphinx’s skills are pretty limited but as you complete major points in the story, he’ll acquire items that grant bonus abilities such as fast swimming and double jumping.
Overall, Sphinx and the Cursed Mummy HD is a very entertaining game and the developers did a great job on the remastering of it. There are some minor issues that I ran into like the usage of items being rather cumbersome and until recently the font being too small (Which has now been fixed thankfully). Outside of those, I’ve been having a lot of fun with the game and I look forward to finishing up my video playthrough of the game. If you’re a fan of action adventure games and want something that’ll take up a lot of your time then Sphinx and the Cursed Mummy HD is a great choice.

I like the style and music, but the gameplay is tedious. The game introduces a lot of gimmicks to keep you interested, but none of them ever really come together or develop. There are no real puzzles in the game, just sort of prodding at the game's physics engine until it works. I would never want to play it again, which, for a game that was only 2 hours long, is disappointing.

Some warnings up-front: this game can be hard to get into.  The controls aren't explained well initially, and it takes time to get a feel for the platforming mechanics, which are fairly idiosyncratic.  It's not an easy game either; it pulls very few punches and is much stingier than most modern games about checkpoint placement and health recovery.  There are also several fairly tough puzzles that require some creative interpretation of the sometimes-badly-translated hints strewn throughout the game.
Despite all of the above, this is quite simply one of the largest and most satisfying Metroidvania games I've ever played.  The maps are massive, the backstory is interesting and integrated into the puzzles.  The power-ups are fun, and the weapons provide enough variety to be satisfying without being numerous enough that any of them feel like afterthoughts.  In terms of content for the price, this game is an absolute steal.  If you have the chops for it, bring your action-platformer and adventure-game-puzzler A-games and take this one on right away.

Note: I just finished the story for the first time, and my opinion is unchanged from when I wrote this.
Even during early access, Layers of Fear was immediately one of my favorite horror games ever. Jump scares aside, the game was creepy, disturbing, nightmarish, and completely gripping. Layers of Fear sinked its hooks into me with the fantastic visuals. They nailed the biggest challenges of two genres at once: making a horror game that focuses on the use of atmosphere/environment, and making a "walking simulator" that was exciting and interesting to play the entire way through.
With >observer_, Bloober Team has solidifed themselves as one of my favorite developers out there right now. Everything good about Layers of Fear is here tenfold. They've added interactivity and side content to the world to elevate it from feeling like a "walking simulator" to feeling more like a point-and-click adventure of old mixed with the first person control of modern games.
They've completely nailed the Cyberpunk genre in every way. Classic cyberpunk tropes and aesthetics are abundant in >observer_, and even though it may seem somewhat cliched on paper, the developers' raw talent at making a visually stunning game and mastery of atmospheric horror make it feel like no other Cyberpunk game around. Their skill lends itself to the Cyberpunk genre. Bloober Team has, yet again, created a world filled with endless detail and character.
Jumpscares are toned down in >observer_ from the levels in Layers, which is a very good thing. There are still a few you'll run across, but you'll quickly forget about them as you navigate your way through the claustrophobic hallways of the Stacks. The team's talent with visuals adds to their ability to create a great horror game. Very few horror games do as good of a job at making you feel like you're losing your mind by disorienting you and forcing you to make sense of something you're not meant to comprehend.
There's a lot about this game that you can praise, and not much that you can objectively criticize. If you're open to the idea of a cyberpunk horror/thriller that focuses on telling you an interesting story and showing you an interesting world instead of having you shoot endless waves of identical enemies, >observer_ is for you. If you liked Layers of Fear and are curious to see more of what this developer can do, >observer_ is for you.

Zombie Party is an overall solid roguelike experience, studded with a variety of weapons, characters, pets and enemies. It has permanent progression elements and enjoyable coop (online and offline with splitscreen). As of this review, the game is still in early access and it will show from time to time. This hasn't deterred me from enjoying the experience alone and with friends. It supports controller, but I find it is best played with a mouse. If you like top-down rouguelikes, especially ones with permanent character progression, I would recommend this game at its current price. It's a no brainer at $5 or less.
I'm a huge fan of Crimsonland, and it has been difficult to find a game that harnesses the chaos of that game. Zombie Party scratches that itch for me. There are waves of enemies that constantly spawn in various places in the map, causing you to run, kite, and jump to control the masses. The jump mechanic adds an interesting feature to the top-down experience that I've come to enjoy. At first I largely ignored it, but it becomes necessary at tougher difficulties.
It provides 4 game types that are different enough to add some replayability. Game modes will resonate with you depending on the type of experience you are looking for. Personally, I enjoy the dungeon and arcade modes as they have a sense of game progression (as opposed to survival mode or deathmatch).
The leveling system is simple but effective. You have several different attributes (damage, hp, speed, magic dmg, fire rate, and luck) that you can increase either permanently on the character screen, or temporarily as you level up during a run. It seems to cap fairly quickly though. There is a variety of loot and plenty of drops. There are modifiers for your weapons, spells/equipment, potions, and special weapons that you can only acquire through drops. Arcade mode also has power-ups that give you temporary boosts. Overall, the modifiers and spells are the bread and butter of the combat. It's entertaining finding the perfect combination of modifiers for your favorite weapon to ravage the masses while spamming your favorite spell.
If you are a completionist, there are a ton of characters to unlock and max out. There are also several pets that you can collect and level up.
The content is a little sparse. If you're a veteran at top-down rougelikes, you'll breeze through Dungeon mode within an hour or two. Arcade mode has some variety but you'll see repetition with added difficulty. The game never seems to get more difficult in terms of bullet-hell, they just add more health to the enemies, causing everything to be bullet spongey. I'm not a huge fan of bullet sponge games, so this was a minor deterrent. If you enjoy survival modes there may be more replayability for you.
Another con for me was, although there are plenty of spells/equipment, I find most spells overshadowed by the mines and grenades. They seem to have the lowest cooldowns and lowest mana cost which is vital for spamming at all the goons chasing you. The stats on spells are pretty random, but you can always attain the same spell with better stats. However, when the game increases difficulty, the loot doesn't seem to scale. Overtime, spells tend to lose their value and you are better off just selling everything you pick up to buy more skill points.
One last thing that may bother some is any gold acquired, whether spent or saved during a run, will be retained when you die. This eliminates one aspect of roguelikes with permanent progression that I enjoy: balancing your choices. You don't have to worry about saving gold, so you can spend it on skill points or other items in the shop without any consequence. This makes it pretty easy to blow through the content in a single playthrough.
There are some serious frame rate issues with this game. In Dungeon mode, for reasons I can't explain, the frame rate gets progressively slower. It feels like you are constantly using a slow motion power-up. There are also spells that cause fps drops for all players. Here's a
to give an example. Since this game is still in early access, I give them the benefit of the doubt and assume this will be fixed eventually.

As a big fan of Prison Architect I decided to try out Planetbase when it was included in the latest Humble Bundle. Sounded like a similar concept but in space. While visually impressive and well optimized, Planetbase is missing one key component from other similar games that allow them to function. That is the ability to restrict different groups of people to certain areas. Without this the AI will often do incredibly stupid things. For example I've seen an AI walk around the entirety of my colony to pick up a lone resource, in the process nearly dying of both starvation and asphyxiation. When your base is small towards the start of the game the problem is not really noticeable, but when you need to have certain character in certain locations at certain times to make a massive colony run smoothly, the lack of any sort of system for controlling AI behavior just ruins this game's potential.
All told there are a couple key systems that could be added that I think would fix almost all of the problems with the game.
Firstly, a system where certain areas can be designated as the work places or living places for a certain group of colonists. Even if the system just broke colonists down by profession that would still help a ton as you could instruct all your medics, for example, to use the beds and canteens near the medical centers and labs, so they would never be far from where they needed to go.
Secondly, a more granular system for controlling who is allowed to go outside and when. Again splitting this even just by profession would be a big help as it would allow me to keep certain people doing their job. Also, a setting that allows only  robots outdoors would be very helpful in a lot of situations.
Lastly, and I think this could come afterwards, I think a logic system for doors and airlocks that let's me program who can pass through any door would be a big help as well. Being able to evacuate and then seal off a portion of the colony would be great in case of an emergency, plus it would allow the developers to build a more accurate system for simulating oxygen needs. Plus other hazards like fires or nuclear radiation could be added and dealt with using door systems that let in and our the atmosphere.
What is here is a nice start, and I have to give kudos to the developer for creating a very in depth tutorial which many of these games don't have. Plus visually this is a step above a lot of similar titles. That said, the lack of control makes the late game simply not fun.
I guess as a final suggestion for the future, adding the ability to create secondary bases away from your main colony would also be really nice eventually.

I've seen this some time ago and I was skeptical about grabbing it for 20 euros. So I grabbed recently as part of the Humble Bundle pack. And it was well worth it - I would say it's even worth the 20 euros if you're into city building games.
The game itself is not overly complicated. But that doesn't mean it's an easy game. While the construction options become universally available very early in the game, you have to constantly balance each type of colonist you have with the resources you are producing/using.
This is more difficult then it sounds. Run out of food ? Colonists start dying pretty quickly. No electricity ? They start dying very quickly since there's no oxygen.
You didn't start building spares to repare the solar panels and the wind turbines ? They stop generating electricity and your oxygen goes out.
And this is on the first available planet - which is also the easiest. The other planets get unlocked over time and they each have their own peculiarities and disasters.
Overall an addictive, simple game that's not necessarily easy.
10/10 recommend (and it's a must-grab if you find it on sale/humble bundle).

DISCLAIMER: First of all, I am going to write this ignoring all contraversy regarding Ubisoft and
their actions and focus on purely the game and almost ALL it's features and mini-games. :D
GAMEPLAY:
I have completed the story on medium/hard difficulty and it is quite challenging, but quite easy if you understand its mechanics. It is likely you will die quite a lot at some later levels, as you quite litterally get swarmed unless you escape by boat, as both police, criminals and other enemies can only use cars and boats which means you just need to outrun a helicopter which is way to easy, even without a certain perk. The hacks aren't really flawed in any obvious way, and you do get help telling you when to click your hack button. The hacks also work well in combat and kill people very stealthily or enable you to stop reenfocements/distract them. When intruding into places, you have to do hacking puzzles, which are very easy.
The cars also drive quite well, and you can tell whether it is a sports car or muscle car, and the engine sounds are accurate. When yu crash, it feels more arcade-like as the damage seems to get worse based on how many times you crash, not how bad the crash is, which means you can basically drive full speed at a wall and not even recieve a scratch. The motorbikes are so fast that if you fly off the bike and almost die.
Guns have quite nice recoil - as in it is a bit realistic (you can't spray with an LMG or a Sniper) - and enemies die with 3+ bullets depending on the gun. If it is silenced, enemies are clueless as to how their friend died, but if you go in guns blazing you may get overrun and die without hacks. Snipers do lots of damage but are marshmellows when you get to them and enforcers require 2 IEDs to kill them or multiple clipswhich means you must pay smart or get destroyed by them. Headshots are very effective against all enemies and so are explosions, which can get you multiple kills. Sometimes it is easier to run away when the option to kill everyone left or escape is given, but it doesn't make much of a difference to the result.
Side-missions play out just like story missions, except usually you have to collect things from certain locations before doing the actual mission. Mini-missions such as 'Criminal convoys' and 'Fixer contracts' in which you have to complete a task such as take out a gang in a certain area or chase a vehicle to gain data and then take the vehicle out. They are quite fun to play if you need money, skill points or XP.
Money is a bit too easy to get, as somehow - I have no clue how - I have over $750,000 and have almost every weapon and car. Their isn't much to buy except weapons and cars, as well as crafting items, and there its no point to buying cars on the 'Cars on demand' app as you can fins supercars on street corners. The perks are solid and there aren't any overpowered perks, although I recommend you prioritise the hacking, combat and crafting skills first, and don't care about the car perks much.
The vigilanty random crime prevention is amazing, and very entertaining. I sometimes just roam around the city doing them and other side-missions. Preventing crimes give you good karma, meaning the public are less likely to call police upon seeing you, and actually take pictures of you cand cheer you on. Shooting a criminal gives you a boost of karma, but not as much as talking them down, and if the victim is killed, you get even less of a boost. Killing police, civilians, robbing stores and injuring civilians wild seroiusly hurt your karma. If you get bad karma, civilians call the cops on you more, people run away from you, and the police are more aggresive. Karma doesn't affect the story, which could have been a thing.
STORY (NO SPOILERS):
I have completed the whole story and can say anyone that tells you the characters are bland and the story is boring are wrong amd the story is quite solid, but the shortness of the story does affect the quality of it. Someone called Jordi that you meet within the first 5 minutes of the game is barely even met or talked to for more than 5 minutes, yet he when he is met he seems so intressting and satirical character and the character  are not presented in too much depth, yet what you do get to know forms such a good basis for more. The main character has a good backstory yet he has no personality. It is clear that Ubisoft either did't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about making good characters or a good story or where too busy trying to add other features or just  didn't have enough  time. This game had such potential to have a great story but didn't which is one reason why many people♥♥♥♥♥♥on this game or don't rate it highly. In addition, of course the end is kind of a sequel bait if you don't skip the credits.
ONLINE:
This is going to be short as I wasn't that intrested in this when I played the game. You can disable it in the options menu and it'll reset your online profile (points and online XP). The game modes all revolve around either hacking or the normal activities that you would find in GTA:V or other multiplayer games of this genre. You can  hack other players in their game and steal 'data', go as teams and compete to get 'data', decrype other people/team's 'data', racing, tailing other players and of course free roam. To me, I didn't like them as the invader can maipulate the world too much, as thjey can cause blackout after blackout to stop you getting to them, and hide in places almost
impossibe to guess someone would be. Multiplayer free roam is ok, it might have the trypical trolls but the basic mechanics are simple and fun. Races are just general but you can also use hacks to stop others. Another thing about them that annoyes me is that the most common time for me to get intruded is when I am about to start a mission, which is incrediblly annoying. The only gain from doing these missions is to gain points to unlock perks, weapons and cars, as well as fun.
PERFORMANCE, OPTIONS AND GRAPHICS:
The graphics options are quite ordinary, nothing out of the ordinary, nothing really missing. You can change SFX, dialogue, music, etc. You can stop music auto playing in cars, turn off motion blur (recommended), all good. But even since they they patched some performace issures, the game still runs liek♥♥♥♥♥♥for a triple-A game. I know i only own a MSI GTX 960 2GB, but even people with 980s get stuttering, sudden dips in frame rate and other graphical problems. I got this on sale, hoping that the only issue was that gamers were just dissapointed that the graphics in the actual game are nowhere near as good as demonstrated at E3.  Sadly, this game as a number of serious flaws.
Issues:
- Worst driving 'physics' of any game I have ever played.  I though people were exagerating when they said it was like bumper cars on ice.  High-performance cars are almost completely uncontrolable.  I don't think anyone at Ubisoft has ever driven a car.  This makes even the simplist of driving missions impossibly difficult.  This, coupled by the cop's ability to stick to you like glue, and you're in for the most frustrating experience of your life.
- Uplay.  Yes, even though it's a Steam game, it launches through Uplay.  Not only that, but you have to register your game key with uplay, and if you have DLC, register those keys as well.  It's a very cumbersome and unnecessary process.  To make matters worse, the Uplay overlay causes the game to crash on loading.  The result is that Uplay makes the game completely unplayable.
- Bug with key remaping.  It's shocking that in this day and age, something as simple and obvious as this is broken.  Rebinding the keys (I use ESDF) causes the game to think that there are unbound actions, even if everything is bound.  This means that in order to rebind your keys, you have to accept the bindings, when it warns you that keys are unbound, you have to go back.  Thankfully, going back saves your kemaps, so you have to Alt-F4 OUT OF THE GAME in order to save you keybindings.  This means that you CANNOT rebind your keys while playing (for example, if a key binding turns out to be inconvenient)
- Performance is absolutally abismal.  I have an i7-3770k with 2x7970 in crossfire.  I can easly play Shadow of Morrdor in my Eyefinity resoution of 5880x1080.  I was forced to go back down to 1080p in order to get this game to run at even remotely playable framerates without constant hitching and stuttering.  Of course, this would be understandible if the graphics were amazing, but they are not.  GTA 4 (not 5, but 4) looks better than this game, and has much better performance.
Pros:
- Didn't kill my cat
- Was on sale, so I didn't waste $60 on this thing.
To sum things up, it seems that Ubisoft is riding on it's name alone at this point.  They haven't even attempted to optimise this game for the PC, and have critical, game-breaking issues unaddressed.  The overall concept is good, but it needs a LOT of work in order to go from the garbage it is now to an amazing franchise.

Group of 4 really enjoyed this game. It was hard to for some to understand how the strategy of the game goes so maybe this will help
-First phase: Everyone draws a picture of the Titles provided
-Second phase: A players picture is selected at random, all other players observe the drawn picture and create convincing titles for the drawing to be added to the title guessing phase based on what they think the image looks like.
-Third phase: Players now get a shot at guessing which Title amongst the player created ones is the Original Title given to the drawer. If you guess the correct Title YOU will be awarded 1000 points.. If another player guesses your "false" created title as the original YOU get awarded 500 points. For each CORRECT guess of the Original Title the drawer of the real title will be awarded 1000 points.
In closing. You want to guess the correct titles when its your turn to guess... You want to do the best you can to draw a cohesive picture when you are in the drawing phase, because the fastest way to get points is when your Original title is guessed by all other players. 1000 points each...  and lastly when you are in the title creation phase you want to do the best you can to create clever titles for the image to trick other players into thinking your made up title was the drawing title provided.. each player that guesses your false title you will be awarded 500 points.
I hope this helps, if its seems strange at first just play a couple rounds. If youre on the fence about this game for a party or gathering dont be...its very fun. def worth the inexpensive price...

A great visual novel/investigation game in the same vein as Phoenix Wright. The basic premise is 15 students get trapped in a school and the only way to escape is to murder a fellow student AND get away with it. This is all antagonized by Monokuma, a mascot for the series who has a personality that clashes with the game's circumstance and his appearance. There's an overarching mystery as well and a colorful cast of characters to participate in the trials that get you invested in the story. Every character is an "ultimate" being the absolute best at something which adds a lot to their personalities from the beginning.
Most of the game is exploring the school and developing relationships until a murder takes place. The exploration then becomes more focused and directed in looking for clues at the crime scene and related areas. The trials themselves play out as various minigames involving using clues from your investigation and matching the right clues to the right statements to prove logical inconsistencies and slowly corner the killer. The trial has a certain style to it that many fans appreciate and get attached to. And every trial is lenghty with plenty of twists to keep you off balance, it's certainly the meat of the gameplay.
The game is very anime (and has an actual anime which is a consice version of the game without the relationship building), so as long as you don't have any major issues with the style, I highly recommend this game. Also the music is boss. And I would consider a playthrough of this game mandatory is you're considering playing the sequel as there are significant links.

Boom Town is a fairly simple simulation game where you build a mining town and go mining using explosives.  You essentially pick out the spots on the map where you think there is gold set explosives then drive around the map with your truck to pick up the gold.  You then take your profits improve your truck, the town, and your explosives.
The concept is pretty simple and as well as the gameplay.  There isn't much of a fail state, it is more of just trying to complete the scenario as quickly as possible.  The games mechanics all seem to work properly together and it is a fun relaxing game.  There are some issues however, notably that it is a grindy game and the core gameplay isn't that good to keep you wanting to come back to it time after time.
I would say it is a 3/5 but I won't pay more than a $0.50 for the title.  It is enjoyable for what it is, but don't be expecting great things out of it.

Year Walk is a dark and mature adventure game based on Swedish folklore. You play as Daniel Svensson, a young man who on the New Year's Eve 1893 decides to undergo the ancient rite of årsgång (i.e. year walk). During your årsgång you encounter various mythical beasts and creatures as you wander around the small village and solve puzzles.
The 2D visuals are fairly basic but they are also quite stylish and atmospheric. The mythical creatures are well realized too. Overall the visuals are well done and fit the grim theme extremely well.
The game has a great moody soundtrack and the sound effecs are well done too. There's no voice acting.
Most of your time in Year Walk will be spent wandering around the map and looking for puzzles to solve to progress the story. The game doesn't give you too many directions and often the puzzles are rather obtuse. On a more positive note the PC version has an extensive hint system, so getting completely stuck is rare.
There's very little dialogue in the game and almost no items to use. The puzzles have some variety at least, although personally I thought they were bit of a hit and miss.
Year Walk also uses a rather curious movement system. While exploring a location you are always facing the same way and can only move sideways. At specific spots you can follow a path up or down and move to a different area. This system is slightly confusing at first, but on a positive note the game does feature a solid map system.
While the puzzles are not terribly complex, many of them are rather obtuse and it's fairly easy to get stuck for a while.
Year Walk was originally made for iOS and it certainly shows to some extent. The controls are passable enough with mouse and keyboard too, but some actions are slightly tricky to perform.
Much of the game is based on research by Swedish folklore expert Theodor Almsten and it certainly shows. The setting and the characters feel authentic and overall the writing is very solid.
The narrative itself is quite interesting too, although I would have liked to see more of the story told in the game itself instead of the encyclopedia and the journal.
Without spoiling too much the game also has two separate endings. Finishing the game the first time around will give you some hints that will help you reach a second alternate ending. It's by no means a happy ending, but in many ways it's a more satisfying one.
I didn't encounter any major bugs and overall the game was quite polished.
Overall I found Year Walk a pretty solid adventure game. It is extremely atmospheric and the story is quite interesting too. Unfortunately the gameplay isn't particularly interesting and the puzzles can be bit too obtuse. Still, I would recommend the game, especially if you are interested in ancient folklore.
It took me 1.5 hours to reach both the endings.

This game is simply amazing! I was not sure what to expect when I first got it. I thought that it was a puzzle game similar to Myst, but then, as I started playing, it looked more like series of puzzles from a smartphone app. I was skeptical.
But as I continued playing, I realized that it was way much more than that. It reminded me of Rhem, of its huge maze world where you can freely roam around with no other goal in mind than solving its puzzles to unlock new areas and move forward.
Like Rhem, the Witness is a pure puzzle game, there is no apparent story, no background music to distract you. But it is also not just a collection of grid puzzles as I thought first. No, the whole world in the game is in fact an intricate web of puzzles. The game is about exploration, search and discovery.
I would say that if you mix together Rhem, the Talos Principle, a line puzzle app with an hint of Tetris, some 3D hidden objects game with very well studied landscape designs with tons of art and cultural references, what you obtain is the Witness.
The game offers two types of puzzles for the player to solve:
- First, the grid puzzles, which consists of figuring out the correct line pattern on a square or rectangular grid. Solving a puzzle will either unlock another puzzle to solve, open a door or activate some mechanism (laser, elevator…). The learning curve is gradual, starting with overly easy puzzles to much more difficult ones.
Some puzzles are only going to take you a few seconds to solve while others will require 10 or 15 minutes, maybe more…
I would also say that there are two subtypes of line puzzles in the game. One type where special symbols are included on the grid, giving silent instructions of how the line should be drawn, and another type where the correct pattern solution is hidden and has to be found in the immediate surrounding. The first challenges our logical thinking, while the second appeals to our observation skills and intuition.
And if you are stuck, it either means two things: you don’t know the significance of one of the symbols on the puzzle, and you might need to explore somewhere else first to find some tutorial grid to teach you the meaning of the symbol, or you haven’t checked yet all possible angles of your immediate surrounding where a solution could be found and you need to take a break and come back later to look more.
To note, a few puzzles (about 10) are solved using a sound pattern which will be difficult to figure out for tone-deaf people. In fact, it was a sound puzzle, the one found in the shipwreck, that was definitely the most difficult puzzle in the game for me.
Similarely, there are some puzzles with various color symbols that might be difficult to solve for color blind people.
- Then, you have the black hexagonal towers puzzles, which consist of finding and activating line patterns that are hidden into the island landscape. I was already several hours in the game when I discovered this second set of puzzles.
And this is when the game started to be really fun, because I started looking at everything with new eyes. The grid puzzles became secondary, it was not anymore just solving grid puzzles after grid puzzles, but everywhere I went, I was looking all around me, trying to find some hidden patterns, and then figuring out how to activate them, sometimes it was easy, and sometimes really hard…
The least we can say is that the game is gorgeous. You could spend hours exploring around all sides of the island. In fact, I would recommend starting the game by exploring the island to get a good feel of its design instead of trying to solve all puzzles right away.
This is also a good way to find some tutorials grids that can teach you about symbols.
There is a boat that allows you to tour the island following a predefined circuit. I found that part really cool! It has 4 speeds and one stop button, and you can backtrack anytime if you need to.
So if you are tired of puzzles and walking around, just take a boat tour, admire the view and relax!
It is also a good way to see some aspects of the island you would have missed otherwise.
Audiologs can also be found everywhere on the island, but are tiny and easy to miss. They play excerpts of writings from famous people like Albert Einstein or Richard Feynman (ok, those were the only famous names I knew from the recordings I found…), and after some time, I realised that they actually provide some thinkings or stories (sometimes hints!) directly related to some design or object in your immediate surroundings.
As you can guess, I absolutely loved this game. But now, can I recommend this game to you? Ask yourself: are you a curious person? Would you like walking freely around on a island, alone, without any directive of what to do? Would you enjoy finding hidden patterns in your surroundings? Would you not mind solving a lot of the most diverse line pattern grid puzzles possibly imaginable? I will let you figure this out for yourself…

If you ever played any games like Myst or its spiritual successors, this game will appeal to you. It has a very intuitive control system that plays like Myst, but you can switch to a more free-form method of controlling the game with the WASD keys.
This game is absolutely fantastic. I can't stress that enough. The only thing it lacked for me is the music, but only because it's overshadowed by other gameplay elements. The visuals are stunning and gorgeous, and there's a wide variety of scenic themes so you never get bored of trudging through the earthy hues of an autumn forest or the sandy savannah. However, where The Witness REALLY gets most of its appeal from, is its method of puzzle-solving. It's one thing to create a puzzle game with puzzles that actually demand your attention and are just the right degree of challenging, but something beautiful happens when you've looked at lines and dots for so long, puzzles start to leak out into the surrounding world. I won't reveal much about this, but I've gotta say the revelation moment is incredible.
I would definitely recommend this game. The price might seem a little steep for a lot of people, so I would suggest getting it on sale, but even for the price I got it at, I'd say that I got my money's worth.
There is a sort of half-plot to the game. You're dropped into this new and exciting world with a very good intro sequence, and you basically sort of wander around and do things as you will. There are multiple 'zones' to explore, and the zones don't lock each other off based on what you've completed, so you can already access most of the world. There are some secrets you can discover, and doing so will unlock films you can watch. For the most part they're nothing special - something you might see an arts graduate directing, but there are some golden nuggets in there.
Oh, and don't aim for a 'true ending'. DON'T. If you want to finish it, you can finish it and then get right back into playing the game from where you left off, but if you complete all the puzzles, I would highly suggest not triggering the ending, because the 'true ending' is awfully frustrating and you'll wish you hadn't done it.
Other than that, it's a superb game. Thekla did a great job and should be proud of this creation.

The story of Dax Stewart is a sad one; he left his home and everything he knew to do his part in thrusting mankind forward amongst the stars.
Initially everything was great for Dax and even though sometimes he felt a deep ache in his heart for the things he left behind he tried to find solace by feeling pride in his work and finding a sense of fulfillment in working with his fellow colonists to make something for themselves, in fact sometimes he even likened himself to a pioneer in ancient America that he would read about in books by a dim bunk light as the alien wind relentlessly howled an eery sound that would bombard the dorm walls.
Eventually as some time had went by new colonists started arriving at Base Alpha and that is when Dax started to swell with pride in his heart knowing that he could now share his hard work with others who also dared to live among the stars but unbeknown to Dax and his fellows a harsh reality was soon to arrive with the new colonists.
As the colony rapidly grew resources increasingly became scarce and though initially the colonists had resolved to work together the dwindling supply of food caused their bellies to grumble causing that unknown harsh reality begin to bring out the true animals inside each colonist that was as brutally savage as the unrelenting howling outside that Dax had listened to on many sleepless nights.
People Dax had considered his closest friends had quickly turned on each other as they lashed out in violence even going so far as to kill one another for so much as a half-eaten chocolate bar and Dax was afraid as he held himself hiding in the dark with the screams of those suffering at the hands of their fellow man and the laughs of the hungry animals that now occupied this colony echoed throughout the corridors.
Dax did everything he could to survive holding back the tears because he knew he would likely never see his loved ones from across the immense expanse of space who waited ever patiently to see him again, and he spent each night hiding and trying his best to keep out of sight as the screams and sounds of violence echoed throughout the colony making his imagination run wild as to what horrors must have lay beyond his hiding place.
As Dax grew ever weaker he hoped beyond all odds that a new colony ship would arrive with supplies and men to help restore order to the colony that Dax once felt so much pride for but alas as each night passed those sounds that would echo through the corridores became fewer and fewer until Dax was sure he was the last one left and still no one ever came to his rescue.
As the colony began to fail from neglect Dax could hear the various systems begin to fail and shutdown and with each clatter of various machines and systems failing Dax felt his impending doom as his eyes grew ever wearier and his weak body felt ever colder until the time came when Dax could no longer hold his eyes open only to slowly fade away and never open them again...
tl;dr: In space no one can hear you starve.

When I can finally play the game, it's pretty fun stuff. The stealth is the best part. Even though it is easy, it is engaging and enjoyable simply because of the freedom of movement and the number of angles you can explore.
When stealth fails, the game can be a bit rough. Aiden melts in a blink. The player needs to be able to shoot and scoot, like Splinter Cell: Conviction. When that's not possible, they will need to use the focus abilities effectively.
Of course, the gorilla in the room is the hacking mechanics. Effectively, point at thing, press Q, hack thing. It is that simple. There are some Pipe Dreamish puzzles, but they are a notch above placing a square block in a square hole. Ubisoft could have do a bit more at least with the deeper hacks.
Main thing that remains is the driving, which ain't bad. You need to use the handbrake is all I'll say. You'll need to use it a quite bit really. The driving escapes are pretty cool, by the way, once you get a handle on them. Just hack the city to lose pursuers. I will warn the the CTOS scans are bullcrap and you shouldn't waste jammers on them.
One more thing, if you do end up getting this game, make sure to explore the mini-games. The creators put a huge amount of effort into some of these, especially the digital trips.

I very rarely review games, but this one does in fact deserve it.
Pros:
- Hacking is simple yet fun. It's also pretty freaking effective.
- The story and characters are great. I found myself emersing myself in the world and emphasizing more with Aiden "The Fox" Pearce than ANYONE in GTA V. I love that ubisoft chose a vigilante storyline as opposed to generic criminal one.
- The city is very immersive and looks good, even on medium settings. On ultra it does not quite compete with GTA V, but watch_dogs is older and has a FAR lower budget, so I'll cut it some slack.
- With the exception of driving (I'll get back to that...) gameplay in this game is very enjoyable.
- The game runs and scales well across my $500 laptop with a i5-5200u 2.2gHz dual core, 8gb ram, and gt 940m (playable at custom medium settings w/ fxaa @ 720p easy) as well as my $850 desktop with an i5-4440 3.1gHz quad core, 8gb ram, and a gtx 970 (playable at ultra settings 1080p).
- Side missions add a lot of extra content and fun to the game.
- While the multiplayer is not as good as GTA Online. (Not even close) this game's story mode absolutely takes GTA V's story out into a parking lot, beats the hell out of it with a baton, and leaves it for the police.
Cons:
- While the graphics are quite good, the physics are... questionable. Some of the destruction (particularily larger objects) is aquard and looks like it came from a source game circa 2004.
- Driving is terrible. It's like the whole game is the ice level. Argh.
- Uplay. No. Just... no. For watch_dogs 2, PLEASE remove uplay integration. If steam is everybodies' favorite DRM, uplay is everyone's least favorite.
- Multiplayer not as good as it could or should be.
All in all, watch_dogs is one of my favorite games. It is a game that everyone interested in good stories, vigilantes, and sci-fi should pick up, in my opinion. I payed the full $60 for this game (which I rarely do) and have not regretted it once.

is a surprising title to see remastered but it is a welcome surprise. Its strong 3D puzzle platforming and sense of nostalgia will endear it to a niche audience. Remnants of old game designs may frustrate those looking for a modern experience. Poor keyboard controls are hopefully only a temporary flaw in this otherwise good quality port.
Even as a newcomer to
I felt pangs of nostalgia from playing it. Not because I recognized anything but because its designs and features felt so familiar. It is a puzzle action platformer that draws obvious inspiration from the
series. Coming from an era predating physics based puzzles (
would be released a year later) means you'll be solving puzzles with good old switches, buttons and an ever growing selection of equipment and environmental factors.
As the title suggests you'll be splitting your time between playing as Sphinx, the lion tailed hero, and Tutankhamen, the cursed mummy. The pacing is excellent as you swap between the two at predetermined times in the story. Sphinx plays like a hero should. He swings a sword, double jumps like a champ and knows how to use the tools he finds. And he does it all with a confident air and swagger in his step.
Meanwhile Tutankhamen, once called "the Misfortunate Mummy" in the title, plays the slapstick comic relief. He is imprisoned from early on and his mission is one of stealth and thievery. There is no combat in his sections and item use is limited. Instead he uses his undead body as a tool. Among other things, he can be lit on fire, smashed flat and sawed into pieces. For all his misfortune he keeps a cheery demeanor.
With a launch price of 14.99$ and a run time averaging around 16 hours I'd call this a solid value for a niche audience. It took me just over 18 hours to 100% complete it. It will primarily appeal to those of us that were gaming back in 2003. Those looking for more 3D puzzle dungeon delving outside of the Zelda series should also find enjoyment in it.

All right, let's start with negatives:
1st things first if your not a fan of the Japanese visual novel style, you are probably going to find it hard to get through.  This game, although having actual game mechanics, is classified as a visual novel.  And carries a lot of the troupes that come with this Identifier.
2nd thing is the curve of play.  It will take you hours to get through one level as dialouge is incredibly important in the visual novel format.  Most of your play time will consist of speaking with the in game characters.  There is no way around this unless you've played the game before.
Now the positives, the Story is fun; name another game in which you are tasked by your school principal (who is a Robotic Teddy Bear) to kill your classmates to graduate; and then hold a trial for the deceased where you will execute the perpetrator if he/she is caught, and if not all of you will be executed in their stead.  This game is the definition of weird, but it's so wierd that it becomes entertaining.  Every character has their own quirks and perosnalities that bring them to life.  Every character you hang out with during free time gives you different skills and more power.
This game is reminicent of Persona in the way it plays (aside from the RPG elements), splitting its game sequences up into 2 (in this game 2.5 parts) in system called Daily Life, in which you are free to do what you want (but speaking with classmates is a must if you even want to beat the game), and Deadly Life, in which you investigate the death of your classmate and then present the evidence gathered during the class trial (thats the .5 part).  The game has several difficulty levels and each level of difficulty adds more and varying obstacles (somethimes an unfair amount of them) to challenge both your reflexes and your ability to make decisions under pressure.
If your looking for a fun murder/mystery, with some ridiculous characters, a kill happy mascot, and a levle of difficulty that you yourself can control, then this is a must add game to your Library.  Have fun, and feel the Des"Bear."  Ouch that pun hurt.

BoomTown! Deluxe is a cynical time-waster that tries to be too many things and basically fails at all of them.
First there's the mining sub-game.  A lotto where you place explosives on a grid and hope to explode gold out of the ground.  The bigger the charge the more ore is thrown out, hopefully with gold in it.  Collecting the ore involves driving a mining truck that would have been better suited to a Tokyo Drift game.  It's pointless and tedious and shouldn't have been included.
Worse the truck is a major money sink and the root of most of the mobile style grinding that plagues the game.  Upgade the truck so it can carry more ore so one can afford to buy better upgrades so it can carry more ore.  Repeat ad-nauseam for control and fuel efficienc too.  Similarly for the explosives.  Buy permits so you can buy bigger and more expensive explosives so you can mine more ore so you can afford better permits.
The town building is where BoomTown! should have excelled but doesn't.  Instead of SimCity it's just shallow slider management with no real fail condition.  Are people in need of a water?  Then build a water tower.  There's no management of water resources or scarcity, no piping.  A water tower covers a certain sized grid block.  Once the city grows outside of the coverage area then build another which doesn't overlap the first.  Repeat for every other type of building.
All-in-all I'm not impressed.  There's little reason to play for more than an hour and even that felt like a waste.  Spend your time and money elsewhere.

The full title of this game is "The developer has no brain, and yet it moves".
This is a godawful shovelware 2D platformer.  Some recognition should be made for them not going down the "Retro pixel" route that most talentless developers at the bottom of the development ladder take.  Instead they decided to attempt actual art, despite being talentless.   A bold move which results in predictable disaster.
Shoddy scanned in textures and the most abysmal hand drawn art that makes Napoleon Dynamite look like Leonardo DaVinci assault your eyes in this monsterpiece.   I actually had to rinse my eyes out at a chemical spill sink.
Gameplay is woeful.  It's a bland platformer with a level rotation mechanic (this is meant to differentiate it from other platformers, but many of those have already tried this). This has to be one of the most underrated games on Steam and I can't believe the negative reviews that it's getting. This is an imaginative game that breathes a lot of life into the platformer genre.
The mechanics are pretty simple: your character can walk left and right and jump, but you can also rotate the game world 90 degrees in each direction which affects the gravity of the game. Each level plays out like a semi-linear puzzle where you have to time your jumps and map rotations perfectly in order to avoid hitting the ground too hard, flying into black holes of oblivion, catching fire, and various other obstacles that beset your journey on your way to the exits. There are plenty of surprises along the way, too, and the game seems to reward your progression in its own subtle way.
Its graphical design is reminiscent of Paper Mario but has a style all its own. The soundtrack and sound effects are strange but satisfying; they have a sort of wild yet subdued mystery to them, filled with jungle inspired drumbeats and oddly simple melodies.
To me, the game's difficulty was just right. There were a quite a few points throughout the levels where I'd get stuck, but it would not take hours to progress. I beat the game in about 5 hours, but those were quality hours. There is additional replay value considering some difficult achievements and bonus levels. As far as I remember, the story is non-existant, so don't play it if that's a dealbreaker.
All in all, this is a unique platformer and worth your time if you enjoy indie games.

Well, this game is a mixed bag. There are things I love but also many things which are just plain wrong. Let me recap:
Good:
- The puzzles themselves are pretty good. It's fun to discover and learn each new mechanic and they all work nice together. It really is a brilliant and tight design at its best.
- The environmental puzzles are the best - the play with perspective never gets old.
- The graphics are pretty nice, with their own unique art style.
Bad:
- No narrative whatsover. This is the game's biggest flaw, but a major one. You get the
and
, but those have no connection to the game, other than celebrating the greatness of human intelect. With no story to tell, the whole experience feels very shallow in the end. Even a crappy story would have been better than this. If you compare it to Talos Principle, it's obvious how completely missed opportunity it is right there.
- The Island opens up pretty quickly and you initially spend lot of time travelling around without actually achievening anything, as you have no idea how to solve most of the mechanics. In comparison, navigating the corridors of Antichamber provided much better scope for learning each mechanic. Fortunately, once you find
it's smooth sailing.
- The normal puzzles themselves become tedious pretty quickly. Once you learn the mechanics, solving the more difficult puzzles just takes more time but gives little joy in return. There is an occasional new twist thrown in from time to time, but eventually you start to wonder "why exactly am I spending my time with this?".
- The most anticlimactic ending I have experienced in a long time. Like for real? In Talos Principle, even the "bad" ending had a strong meaning as it was part of the story arc, but in this case, it just emphasized how meaningless it all was. After watching it in disbelief for couple minutes all I felt was the strongest sense of complete waste of time. Even though I did all the lasers already, I couldn't be bothered to hunt the remaining puzzles anymore and will just uninstall the game with bitter aftertaste.
So, is it worth the purchase? If you have enough time and enjoy puzzles, I guess it is (on sale), but if you are looking for a Myst-like or Talos-like experience, you won't find it here. I give it a thumbs up anyway, but it pains me greatly that with little changes it could easily have been a true masterpiece.

Sure, I know some stuff about the Scandinavian Folklore. Just ask me. I've watched Moomins when I was young, you can't scare me that easy. I know what to expect and I expect a lot of snow, some weird creatures hidden in the darkness and the flickering lights in the distance. So, a year walk? Sign me in.
First of all, you go into a forest, a creepy one, expecting to find an answer you were seeking for so long. A Year Walk is nothing more or less but a complex, eerie adventure which uses no cheap horror elements to scare you. You will feel insecure anyway because of the overall atmosphere and music emerging from all the characters and the places you will encounter. And then, when you start solving the puzzles you will uncover the truth, meeting more and more strange beings taken directly from the folklore. Thanks to the encyclopedia provided you can learn more about them.
So, you expect a big reveal, a true horror at the end, going there tirelessly, only to be left with more answers and a chill down your spine.
You will travel a lot, but the map is a great asset, marking all the important spots, allowing to find more information. Traveling from a place to place you solve simple puzzles and receive just some basic hints (and you can get more of them on demand if you are stuck). At some point, you will also get an opportunity to unblock some additional features, a journal, and a hidden ending. So, yes, there's a replay value, but as you know the solution to most of the riddles you can complete the plot faster every time (and there's an achievement for that). Your dedication is always rewarded.
The visuals are the strongest part of the Year Walk, creating a great atmosphere, which allows you to experience the game fully. It's a short, yet nice game for a long winter evening. After all, when else would it be relevant...
My final rating? - 8/10
+ The overall atmosphere of the game.
+ The well captured beauty of a Scandinavian folklore.
+ All the lore provided by the developers.
+ A mix of both horror and an adventure game.
- Some puzzles might be too complex (but there are hints provided by the game!), requiring taking some additional personal notes.
- The controls might be annoying at first.

First played this game on mobile back when it initially came out. While the graphics and gameplay are identical on the PC version, some of the puzzles have been tweaked and lengthened to cater to the new platform. The PC version also edges out a bit in that the experience is not divided across multiple apps, and it comes with some helpful additional features such as a map and a hint system which make the game much less frustrating than it used to be.
As for the game itself, it is still weaker from a gameplay and narrative standpoint than the developer's mobile-exclusive follow-up, Device 6, but it has some really lovely graphics, great ambient sound design, and a unique and quirky endgame that does some fun things with genre. While the game is not the survival horror it sometimes gets marketed as being (it's really a mostly harmless Myst-esque point-and-click), it does have a fantastic atmosphere of dread and isolation and the occassional clever, well-earned jumpscare.
It's sharp and challenging, but also has a fun, intuitive design that makes it accesible for "casual" gamers.

So I last made a review on this game in the middle of August, 2016. I felt it was necessary to update this review especially after a new update coming out, and the Developer telling me they didn't believe my review to be "fair". So, I'm revamping my entire review from the ground up. I'm going to start with the bad first, since thats what people like to read first, and then later will be te good.
I bought this game in late 2015 for the price of $19.99. The first thing is why does it cost $20? It has so little content. The game really gets boring after a while. And you wonder why is that, well its because of the lack of content. Honestly this game should be $9.99 or even $5.99 with the amount of content it provides.
Secondly, Thanks to Martino he told me that they have had over more than 20 updates, as I have been only playing this game since when I bought it in late 2015. So I decided to do a check on this given information. However with a quick check of the games update history on steam it shows a total of 18 official updates.
I would like to take this time saying that I am not attacking them. I'm just a little dissatisfied with their, let's say, game.
So, lets talk about the content. Like what content? Have any real new buildings been added recently? Not really. The last major big update was on March 23rd, 2016. The version 1.1.0 patch, brought a lot more to the table, like new structures, leading to more gameplay, resulting in more game time. This update gave players even more things to do, more things to build. However, this update only helped for a little bit. After a week of playing I got bored. And many other people did to. This game doesn't hold you too well. I end up playing this game for a shorter duration everytime you start it up. Why? Because the same old content gets boring after a while. They have to build it two ways in order to keep people interested. Focus on replayability. This is a big one.
This can be solved by adding more goals for the player to complete after the main game is completed. They have sorta added a little replayability to the game, however its a very small amount. It's not in any amount to hold people in this game, and keep their attention. Another thing the Dev could do is add more diversity of structures to the game. Its the same old glass buildings. There is zero diversity, other than the size of the buildings. Why not have buildings with different outsides, or designs. Building, get really boring, especially with the set of buildings that we have at our disposal. Commandos is one of the greatest classics of squad-based tactical combat games, where you command a group of elite soldiers through twenty maps of sabotage in semi-realistic World War II scenarios. The map and control design were so well made that this game still shines as bright as it did in 1998.
Commandos: Behind Enemy Lines combines isometric tactical combat with real-time strategy and stealth. This mixture works so perfectly that it is still remembered by many to this date not just as a beloved childhood game, but as something revolutionary.
And Commandos achieved this without any real plot. All twenty maps are more or less based on real WWII events, but they don’t have much story other than a historical introduction piece and a short mission briefing. No underlying plot, no character drama, just meticulously designed levels with several objectives.
Achieving these goals usually requires careful planning, lots of sneaking around, and diversion tactics. Enemy guards are placed in strategic ways, and getting discovered or leaving a body in the open results in an alarm, which usually leads to mission failure.
To finish the task, the player gets control over six commandos, all with distinct, unique abilities. Sadly, all but two of them are useless for almost anything apart from one certain task (driving the getaway car, rowing the boat, and so on), since only they can move dead bodies out of the way – something that is crucial on all levels. All the others usually just camp in one safe corner of the map, unused for most of the mission.
The game was well-received and spawned an entire franchise, which in retrospect made Behind Enemy Lines the one with the shortest and easiest levels, but also with the biggest variety. It’s not as difficult as Beyond the Call of Duty, as complex as Men of Courage, or as action-oriented as Destination: Berlin, but still retains most of its old charm.

Yes, it hasn’t aged as well as it could have, but I think for those nostalgic people like me it is still quite playable and definitely a good challenge. To be honest, I don’t think I ever made it past the first few missions as a kid, but I’m happy I managed to beat the whole game now (even if it took 28 hours to do so). And I have also confirmed something that hasn’t changed since I first played Commandos and that is: “I really suck at this”.
Definitely a game for those that like challenges, but I’d recommend it mostly if it’s not your first time playing Commandos. Save often, save in different slots and use all your commandos wisely (although the Green Beret does most of the job, 99% of the time) And yeah, I had a few technical issues, but not anything a reload wouldn't fix. Have fun!

Overall, I'd say it's a good game but it's a reluctant thumbs up.  If you like GTA type games, you'll probably like Watch_Dogs.  It's like GTA meets Person of Interest.
It does have some annoyances though.   The load times when you initially fire up the game is pretty long coming in at 3-5 minutes.   Add to that, the maps and assets are streamed into the game as you move through the city.   During normal free roam, it's no big deal.  However, when you're on a mission, whether it's a main quest or side quest, this pops up a lot.   In the middle of a car chase, the game will freeze up several times, during which the streaming load symbol pops up.   This freeze/load takes about 30 seconds, which isn't a long time, but it shouldn't happen in an action sequence -- especially one that expects you to cross one of those imaginary borders mutliple times.   It throws off your aim, and your reactions during car chases.   Enough that your quarry gets away, or you spin out of control and slam into a tree or worse, you mow down a bus shelter full of people (which affects your reputation score).
Then there's the matter of the camera.  For some sadistic reason, the designers thought it would be stylistically cool to yank camera control away from you during those same action sequences.  Maybe they figured it would give it a cinematic feel, but the randomness of the camera at times just makes the game awkward at inconvenient times.
I'm not going to harp on the textures and frame rate cap because they're really not that big a deal -- certainly not as big a deal as some have made it out to be.  The game's graphics are fine.   It may not be as detailed or gritty as the E3 pre-release videos, but certainly on par with competing AAA titles and not bad by PC standards either.
The in-game economy is kind of messed up though.   Money is easy to get by hacking people's cell phones and stealing from their bank accounts.   Trouble is, there aren't enough things in the game to actually buy with it.

This game is a lot more relaxing than I thought it'd be. When I first heard about VA-11 Hall-A, I thought it'd be a less hectic version of Cook, Serve, Delicious!, where the focus is serving customers and getting drinks out quickly. But it isn't. It's a visual novel where, instead of making dialogue choices or choosing actions, you mix drinks to progress the story; the drink you make, and how you make it, is what causes the story to branch in different directions. Mess up a patron's drinks too often, and they'll leave earlier than normal. Mix a drink with a ton of alcohol, and you'll get different dialogue than if you'd used none. If someone ends up asking for two drinks, which one do you decide to make them? But unlike other adventure and dialogue-based games, there's no time limit; take as long as you want, and even make a drink for yourself if you want, to enjoy while you play. The game even recommends that you do.

This game has so many design shortcomings I actually wonder if the developers had any idea what they where doing or even wanted people to enjoy their game.
First of all, the jumping. It's like if you took castlevania jumping, where you can't control your descent, and tried to fix it but stopped halfway through, Point is it feels weird.
A bigger issue is the level design and enemy placement. This game opts to have single screens with a scroll kind of like zelda but with gravity. This can be done well, but here the enemies and obstacles are placed in a way that it's extremely likely for the player to get hit by something they can't see coming, and if they do see it as the screen scrolls they can't react because of the poor to nonexistant mid-air controls. And there are some places where if you jump off the side of the screen, the next screen has no floor and you'll fall. It requires so much caution that it ruins the point of playing a video game.
Another small issue is that you can't grab onto ladders while jumping. It's small, but it goes against my instinct and really should have been fixed seeing how many ladders there are.
The platforming is a hassle, partially due to the jumping but also because the platforms are often placed badly. The jumping and the way the platforms are placed remind me of Castlevania 2: Simon's Quest. And the main character has a whip. It's almost like the developers looked at that game as inspiration.
I wanted to like this game but it's so flawed I can't enjoy myself while playing it. You're better off just renting an Indiana Jones flick.

There is almost no irrelevant information provided by the game. Not just a notepad is needed, a notebook even. Keep track of clues, deity and lore names, places, room names, where those unreadable tablets that you ignored are, anything and everything. That information will come into play at some point, in some way. Cross off clues and puzzles you've solved, keep it organized. The last thing you want to do is to have scour the game for the hint, tablet, mural, deity statue etc, to progress that you only read/researched not realizing it's importance.
Well, when the sequel is finished and released, atleast I'll come prepared for it.

You're not controlling a character that moves around the screen here. there are 20 or so areas in the game world and each one is one screen.  You go from screen to screen taking quests clicking on objects to collect them, clicking on NPC's to buy, sell or craft items, and taking the items into battles. There is no tactical combat and no possibility of defeat unless it's in the script, everything is resolved with a click. (You can fail in some harvesting and any animal hunting situation, which just means you have to replace your tool or weapon. Always carry two of each item just in case.) There are no puzzles, you just need to find people or items and click on them and you're usually told which area they're in.  There is a hint system (well, more like even clearer instructions on what to do next) but I don't think anyone would actually need it. The story is a bog standard fantasy yarn with all the tropes and cliches and is completely forgetable. Despite all that it's a pretty enjoyable way to spend a few hours.  In the six hours I played I got all the achievements and finished the story. Having done that, there is no reason to replay the game. There is only one ending and nothing new will happen in a second playthrough.

There is no story in The Witness, no flashy soundtrack, just pure gameplay. A masterpiece.

I struggle to articulate what it is about this game that left such an impact on me, but I couldn't let Year Walk go without giving it my recommendation.
I've always enjoyed subtle horror elements in video games, but never been a fan of pure horror games for mostly one reason. The jumpscare as of recent in horror has become what autotune is in the modern music industry. A tool for an artist to improve their art, not a means to cover up a lack of talent by littering one's creation with it, and Year Walk does a great job of using this tool alongside it's many others to craft a uniquely unsettling experience.
Horror as a genre in gaming is something that can be hard to keep consistently impartial. When a player only ever sees other characters as something to be scared of, the fear becomes one-dimensional very quickly as almost everything that moves is an obvious threat to the player. I've dropped horror games before because i'm sick of being pulled along while the game rapid fire tries to scare me with loud noises and flashing imagery. However the eerie creepiness of Year Walk just comes naturally as it's often unclear when and if the player should be scared. Between the light safety and the dark horror lies a gray area that Year Walk hides itself amoung: fear of the unknown.
The in game encyclopedia, should the player chose to read it, gives information about the act of Year Walking as well as the five supernatural creatures asociated with it who are all said to pose a threat psyically, mentally, and spiritually. This, alongside all beasts being associated with death or murder in some way immediately sets the expectation for them to be the enemies, or the "scary" part, of this horror game. However there is no terror in the bang, only in the anticipation of it, and the entire buildup for said bang is done inside the player's head. This also creates a sharp contrast with the rest of the game, as the player is put on edge, yet the snowy landscape and ambiance is eerily peaceful.
Year Walk is a puzzle game that is a compelling narrative first, and also just so happens to be scary because of the expectation that the game influenced me to create for myself by making me come face to face with the unknown and entrusting it to continue. This game is horror done so so right, and it's a shame it almost went under my radar, don't let the same happen to you. It's an experience I wish more could experience so that we could stop giving attention to the♥♥♥♥♥♥that Youtubers play for reactions.
10/10 Redefined my standards for horror games.
