30 hours of play time, and I feel I can give some feedback on this game that may help developers, as well as other people considering buying this game.
Let me start with, should you buy this game? The short answer is, yes, yes you should buy this game... if you enjoy micro-managing survival games, and are into the space themed stuff, this is fairly good game that can give you lots of play time and enjoyment. The game really forces you to pay close attention to a lot of different aspects of your space station to keep your people alive, fed, and happy. There are quite a few factors that really play into how efficient your base is managed, and the civilians respond to your actions.
I've completed the first 3 planets and enjoyed the game a lot, but after really building up a base in the most recent planet, my OCD-side/attention to detail is beginning to get a little frustrated with some aspects of the game, such as poor AI decisions... Heres a short list that, in my opinion, would like to see adjusted in future updates to make the game more playable and enjoyable..
1. The AI need to choose where they enter and exit the base better. It's amazing how many choose the longest paths and die of asphyxiation when they could have just walked through the base to another door.. I've also had engineers built connections and trap themselves inside, and later find out they die.
2. In-game adjustments of settings would be cool. For example, choosing how fast the screen scrolls to look around. Currently, you have to save your game and back out to the main menu.
3. An added menu to track and adjust more aspects of your base. For example, currently if you want to change which bots are being manufactured, you have to click on every individual unit where engineers make bots. This sounds easy, but when you have a large base with 10 very spread out places bots are being made, it gets annoying. Same thing applies to the synthetic meat-making units (can't rememeber their name).
4. The radio plays no part in the game?? It says you can intercept calls of distress and are prompted to decide if a ship can land at your base, yet I've never had a single one over 30 hours on 3 different planets.
5. Having an ending to the game would be really nice, with the option to continue building if you enjoy the freeplay style. I feel I have a massive base and never get the reward of saving everyone's♥♥♥♥♥and building this awesome base.
6. Option to stop continuous prompts of things happening in the base if I choose to ignore them. Getting prompts such as low oxygen in an area of the base is comparible to my iphone trying reminder me everyday to update.
7. An option to stop gameplay speed interuptions when intruders attack, or when an environmental storm is happening. At some point these things don't affect the bases I make and its annoying to keep setting my speed back to 4x (which is the speed I play at 95% of the time).
Thats pretty much the bigger things I can think of at the moment. I really am looking forward to continued developments for this game, and I hope my comments may help other people or the developers!
Will update as I continue to play more.

TLDR:  Buy it.  You won't regret it, but you won't play it forever, either.
This is a good game.  It's not a masterpiece.  It won't remain on your harddrive for years to come, but you'll play it and get many hours of enjoyment, and then move on to another shiny toy and eventually forget about it.  It's one of those.
The graphics, sound and game play are all above average.  It could have used a bit deeper economic model.  Another level of graphics to zoom-in or some less restrictive camara views.  Maybe some additional sounds effects and background music to make it less repetitive... but it is really a pretty good game as it stands.  The biggest problem with this game is a lack of challange in the mid to end game section.
I didn't find it all that difficult.  There are four basic planets to build bases on, and personally I didn't have to try more than twice on any of them to build a successful base.  Some people may find it more difficult, but if you're experienced in this genre and have a good concept of how base building games work, you'll be fine.
If you've chosen a somewhat decent starting area and have chosen the correct initial buildings, then barring some very bad luck you should have a successful base up and running soon.  Therein lies the problem with this game.  Once the initial base is established and you're "out of the woods" so to speak, then there really isn't much point to developing the base further.  Making redundent buildings to further enhance your production becomes pointless except to just expand your population.  There is very little real danger to the colony once you've got the infrastructure in place to support a decent security force.
It's not a fatal flaw to the game while you're in the honeymoon phase with it, but once you've discovered all the ins and outs and played it through a couple times, it really shoots down the long term replayability.  The buildings could all be more diverse, the finished products could be much more elaborate, there could be more economy of scale advantages and disadvantages that really put emphasis on building a efficient, not just survivable colony, but none of these factors come into play.
If we were using a rating system, I'd give this game a 3 out of 5 stars.  Good enough to buy and play,  And good enough to delete later on and feel good about your purchase.

I give this game 8 out of 10. Love the game so far.
In the early stage of the game, the aim of harnessing energy, growing food and optimizing the use of limited resources creates a lot of fun. The most fun I had is surviving in the last planet (Class S), where resources are scarce and energy generation is unstable. It is a fabulous game of space colony building.
However, once I managed to balance energy, food, mining and trading, the game started to become boring. The only way through technological advancement in the game seems to be trading with space traders. But the acquisition of new technology doesnt add much to improve survivability if the player has already managed to accumulate so such wealth and resources to purchase them.
Trading is a bit of pain as the colonists have to carry lots of stuff around and desert work for that. The commission paid toward the trader is quite heavy, especially in desperate time. Please add option to attack the traders' spaceship so I can rob them of the resources without paying. :D
Once past mid game, the game is pretty repetitive and mostly waiting for new events to happen. I think better technological advancement for the colonist would be the ability to grow on the planet soil itself or to fill the whole planet with sufficient O2 and water. Buying patents to build bigger structures seem quite lame.
The colonist AI seems a bit stupid sometimes. Once there was a colonist in the middle of carrying out a task but was suffering from lack of water or O2, he still tried to finish the task and died in the process. There was no way of micromanaging the people or robots in the game.
I hope there will be new patch or DLC to add more fun to the late games. Maybe like colony politics, alien invasion, expedition around the colony, etc. For the late game, maybe there can be a chance to create a spaceship to fly to another planet with the resources and crews of your choosing and start a new colony all over again?
The game has very nice concepts and mechanics. I hope there are more contents coming up.

I was very apprehensive buying this game at first. With games like Gnomoria that I felt pretty burned about base/city building. However, I found this game to be highly entertaining! I highly recommend this game to people that just want to waste a few hours. It seems like there needs to be a few updates to content or at least open up the workshop for players to create their own custom items and modules.
Now for the bad part.
So the game doesn't give the player much micro-managing control over certain things in the game, such as priority in building certain modules. Instead, the AI simply moves resource to the nearest empty or needing module blueprint and then they move on. Additionally, when times get tough and a certain resource such as energy get scarce, you only get two options, full on, or emergency only. I think a great addition would be a simple on/off switch on every module and every component within the modules. This, I feel, would be a great help, especially if a player is having a problem progressing their game because they are overextended because they have too many gyms and not enough power plants because the AI keeps building the gyms first (see problem above).
The last thing I can come up with is that excluding the challenge levels, there doesn't really seem to be an end to the game. This has good and bad sides. The good is that I can just infinitely expand and as long as armed terrorists don't come in and gun down all of my biologists, we're good. The bad part is that I felt myself drifting. If, per se, the game gave me a goal like "build a spaceship to move on to the next planet" or "build a new colony ship and fill it to capacity with the stuff that you think you would like to have on the next planet, including colonists you are going to voluntarily give up" would be a really simple, yet satisfying way of ending the game.
I know this review may fall on deaf ears, but I have to say, this game is fantastic, just needs a few adjustments.

- It's not a perfect adventure, but it's a unique one. Think Bladerunner meets The Cell (the Jennifer Lopez movie). The attempt to blend horror into a setting (cyberpunk) that is fairly unorthodox for the genre is pretty great, and lands with more hits than misses. Some of the hide-and-seek sequences typical of this style of game feel a bit shoe-horned in, and it draws a fair amount of comparison with SOMA (attempting to offer a deeper look at the subject matter but incorporating unnecessary enemy confrontations), though it doesn't pull it off nearly as well. It is a high recommendation for cyberpunk AND horror fans, though perhaps not either/or.
PS - For those who like trippy horror but aren't fans of hide-and-seek mechanics:

Observer is a game that, upon hearing about the setting and genre, I decided I had to play immediately. I am a huge fan of horror games (though not a BIG fan of the new walking horror genre) and I love cyberpunk settings, so I figured that it would be an interesting trip, and, at the very least, it was that.
You play as a augmented detective with a trouble past (not entirely original here) that is looking for his son after having not been in contact with him for some time. You find yourself in his place of residence when a lockdown occurs and the entire apartment complex is shut down. What ensues is a semi-investigative game where you must question and observe (no pun intended) the people and things around you in order to unravel a bit of the mystery of what happened to your son as well as what caused the lockdown.
Possibly the most famous asset for the game is Rutger Hauer as the main character. Of Bladerunner fame, he's a pretty cool guy to be playing as, though his voice work tends to range from stilted to pretty believable, leaving a wildly unpredictable range of quality for pretty much the entire game. At points, it definitely feels like stunt-casting, and the game suffers a bit for it. At others, it feels like Hauer actually enjoys delivering his lines and is getting into the character. Might just be because he has a pretty distinct and entertaining voice (when he's not delivering flat lines). It's a cool addition, but at times feels not entirely spot-on.
As far as gameplay goes, it's your typical walking-sim fare, with a heavy emphasis on using augmented vision to scan your environment. However, much like any game that uses augmented vision of any sort (Arkham Asylum, Far Cry Primal), you find yourself spending a lot of time inside of the augmented vision in order to find everything you need to interact with in the environment. This leaves you staring at incredibly saturated and ugly shades of what otherwise is a pretty game (do yourself a favor and find the community guide to turn off the abhorrent chromatic aberration that the game enables by default; everything will look MUCH nicer). Many things are somewhat useless to interact with, with tons of cabinets and doors to open, but a few collectibles are scattered throughout the building and using the augmented vision is the easiest way to find them.
The other half of gameplay is spent doing what the titular Observer is made to do: exploring the fragmented minds of people. Much, much like Jennifer Lopez in The Cell, Hauer's character is known for their ability to jack in to people's minds and discover truth hidden behind layers of information. It's a pretty cool concept, and is implemented fairly well here. Soon into the game, the "observing" being done into people's minds quickly takes a turn for the expected and everything you experience there is pretty much anybody's guess, as you're constantly bombarded with surreal and psychologically twisting environments you must navigate in order to reveal more about the person you're trying to connect with.
While the horror here definitely works, it often comes off a bit forced, and somewhat inconsistent. Once you realize that the horror in the game isn't so much in the cyberpunk environment itself, but rather in a constant barrage of bizarre and surreal scenes, it starts to lose its effectiveness. At times, I sat, hands in my lap, as I watched a twisted slideshow of mutilated anatomy, followed by wires and electronics askew, followed by a forest dense with trees. Having so much of the horror be "on rails" left me feeling not-so-scared during these moments. The game tries multiple times to catch you off guard, and sometimes it works, but many times it's predictable, and being that the setting was distinctly cyberpunk, it was my impression that they would try to provide the thrills THERE. When you rely on one's imagination, both in and out of the game, to provide your scares, you're not really staying tied to the boundaries of your setting anymore. While this is definitely a cyberpunk game with horror elements, I don't think I'd ever call it straight up "cyberpunk horror". Both elements feel a bit too separated.
: I was supremely interested in this game based on my curiosity at how they would infuse horror INTO the cyberpunk. Instead, it feels like cyberpunk with a side of horror.
The visual environment they've created here with Observer is pretty amazing. The last few scenes in the game especially are almost the terrifying cyberpunk imagery I had hoped for, giving a glimpse of what COULD have been done if they had tried to infuse the horror more directly into the imagery of the setting itself. Overall, they've done more right than wrong, and it's a good time for fans of both genres. Much like SOMA before it, it attempts to bridge horror with an unusual setting and offer a deeper look into its own subject matter, but the pace falters a little with forced enemy encounters and not knowing when to truly end (has more than a few moments where it could have ended nicely but didn't). That said, the experimental nature of everything that they've provided makes it a recommendation for those who want more in the walking sim horror genre but also want something a little fresh as well.

Oh man Danganronpa what a wild ride this game was. Originally when I first saw this game I thought nothing of it but after hearing great things about the game I just had to buy this game and see what all the fuss was about. Now after playing through the entire game I can safely say this game was worth both the money I paid for it and the amount of time it took to complete it.
First off the story manages to hook you in right you away and never lets go even at the end because of the fact that there is a sequel to this game which I am definitely going to buy. I could say some of the things that make the story amazing but that would require me to spoil most of the game.
Secondly Danganronpa has an amazing and diverse cast of characters. These characters all come from different walks of life and you learn more about them as you fill out their report cards. You fill out these report cards by hanging out with them, giving them presents, and listening to what they have to say. As a result every single character is very well developed and you are bound to have a favorite character.
Thirdly Danganronpa manages to mix fun and engaging gameplay with gripping storytelling that will keep you on the edge of your seat. One part of the gameplay involves investigating a crime scene so you can uncover the truth of what really happened. The other part of the gameplay involves trials where you must use your wits and quick thinking to uncover lies and contradictions in the statements of the characters. This is done through a series of minigames. The first minigame involves taking a truth bullet and shooting the lie or contradiction in the series of statements. The second minigame involves you spelling out a crucial piece of evidence by shooting the missing letters. The third minigame involves you taking part in a battle to try and prove a person wrong if they are being stubborn. The final minigame involves you filling in the missing panels in the style of a comic book.
Lastly Danganronpa also has an amazing soundtrack which manages to play at just the right moments. After listening to the soundtrack it made me like the game even more than I originally did.
In conclusion, Danganronpa is a game that manages to take fun and engaging gameplay and mixes it together with gripping storytelling, memorable characters, a very well composed soundtrack, and beautiful visuals which results in a amazingly crafted video game which has now become one of my favorite video games of all time. Overall I rate this game a 10/10. Definitely looking forward to playing the sequel.

To be honest, this is a "mixed feelings" review. I've enjoyed La-Mulana to an extent, but not nearly enough to recommend it to anyone. You can get a good idea of how this game's like from the other reviews and I doubt I'll be able to change your mind about anything, but I do have some points that I feel haven't been emphasized enough.
The game itself is easy enough to understand: it's a Metroidvania title with heavy emphasis on exploration and puzzle solving; save for the bosses, the enemies are only there so you have something to whack as you explore the place. However, while most games hand you a cake and tell you to have fun with it, La-Mulana gives you the cake recipe in Hebraic, divided into 4 sections whose order you're not quite sure, and actively tries to stop you from getting the ingredients. La-Mulana is maddeningly hard, though very little of that difficulty comes from the actual gameplay - it's easy enough once you get used to the purposefully clunky controls. The true beast are the puzzles.
The first few areas are manageable and straightforward enough, and it's a blast to figure out a hard riddle by yourself, but as the game goes on, the game gets astoundingly open-ended, the map is of little to no use, the puzzle clues become more cryptic and spread farther apart, sometimes not even in the same area as the puzzle they're referring to, vital items are hidden behind unmarked walls, certain items can be lost forever... The great feeling of working out a couple of mysteries by yourself is slowly but surely supplanted by the feeling of being swamped by barely coherent riddles and absurd moon logic, not to mention the fact that some of the solutions require off-the-wall stuff that you have absolutely no reason to even think they'd be feasible; one of the puzzles requires you to press Down on an unmarked spot, the riddle of which mentions "you should have the courage to get down on bent knee to look for a single item", and another requires you to equip a woman's statue and do nothing on a room with a mural of a man for about 30 seconds, upon which the statue will magically get pregnant. The reasoning? "Woman within the man should be with child".
Look, I love me some puzzles and puzzle games, Layton is one of my favorite series for that reason, but La Mulana quickly devolves into nonsense that I'm pretty sure NO ONE in their right mind could possibly figure out on their own. There's "tricky", and then there's "old Sierra game logic".

Pro-tip: Take your pen and notepad with you through this journey. You're gonna need it.

Hoo boy; what to say about La-Mulana... (TLDR see bottom)
There is no question in my mind that this game is very well polished and complete in its entirety. It has an awesome soundtrack, excellent platforming elements, a wide-array of weapons, and the few characters in the game are very loveable.
La-Mulana puzzles are deliberately unfair, obscure, and require either a RIDICULOUS amount of hours (I am talking like... 100+), or the use of a FAQ to finish without going insane. It is a Japanese Platformer, meaning the game requires utter devotion from you, or some outside knowledge to enjoy completely.
Let me outline this for you - unless you want the make La-Mulana the thesis statement of your life you WILL NOT beat it without a FAQ or without help - here's why:
-The game starts off completely solvable (I managed to clear many of the first areas without help)
-Puzzles remain contained AT FIRST, limiting solutions and "cause and effect" action to within zones
-The game VERY long for a platformer.
Things obscure as READING something in one part of the ruins may unlock an entire way to go in another part. It's true, the game drops all sorts of hints and things, and it is definitely possibly to trace some sort of information to almost every puzzle... but let's face it - are you really going to remember a sentence of text you read at hour 5 for hour 55? Of course the logical solution would be then to write it down - I did that... my word document is roughly twenty pages (single spaced) long. Even Ctrl-F can't save me from my own notes!
But at the end of the day I can't really dislike La-Mulana for being frustrating... that's kind of why I bought it in the first place. One thing that drove me crazy is that although you have awesome platforming abilities in the game, it is ultimately a puzzle game, meaning those abilities are often left on the pause screen while you pull out your hair thinking of how to progress further. On the bright side, all of the bosses and enemy placement seems to be excellent.
So if you are in the mood to spend endless hours (I am serious... 100+) wandering some virtual hallways jiving to some catchy music, you may just be THAT person who beats La-Mulana without a FAQ. Or... being rational, you can swallow your pride, progress as far as possible alone, and then use a FAQ whenever hope is lost.
I enjoyed this game; but I wouldn't only recommend it the majority with the use of a FAQ.
TLDR: Game's really long, esoteric puzzles, good music, good enemies, tediously frusterating.

At first, The Witness appears to be a quite straight forward puzzle game with a simple idea. This seems to be intentional, almost as if the game wants you to believe that there is not much more after the first impressions. However, the more you give your time to it, the more it will reveal.
It is best to make the discoveries yourself, but for recommendation purposes I will reveal that I have never played anything as complex and layered as The Witness. Every layer reveals another layer, every structure seems to hold another structure beneath it, and every mystery seems to contain another mystery in its revelation.
For people who want a straight forward story with the bottom line served to them as a whole might be disappointed. The Witness does not work in that way. It seems that there is no philosophy in the game, the game is the philosophy.
I've yet to reach the end of the rabbit hole, and I doubt I am capable of doing it either. That is the scale of The Witness, if I am even close to comprehending it.
Akin to the TALOS Principal, with the island setting of Myst, the underground facility of Portal, and an obsession for path drawing puzzles, The Witness is a must-have for puzzle game aficionados.

I'm really loving this game but I've hit a couple problems that seem like they should be solvable with a patch.
I'll put the TL;DR at the top; the colonists need to not kill themselves.
One, recycling something to build something else is nearly impossible sometimes because the materials are dropped where the thing I'm recycling is and I can't build something else there until those materials are gone. My workers don't always clear out that space in a timely fashion even if I have storage space, and this is a showstopper if I'm clearing out something like an air generator for a bigger one.
Two, building multiple paths around the base is tricky because often my engineer/bot will get stranded in the middle of the base. There should be some sort of pathfinding for the constructor to get out or to only build connectors from the direction it approached from so it will never get stuck in the first place.
Three, I should be able to micromanage a little better on the production. Maybe some sort of queue was needed. Often I'll run out of spares or something even though the factory was prioritized so that the bioplastics could be used on something not crucial, and then my power grid might fail because a solar panel went down. I understand I have to plan better in the first place, but this aspect seems punishing rather than challenging, especially for the first few bases I made where everyone died and it seemed like I could have avoided that if I could put items in a queue.
In the same category is not being able to prioritize time. For example, I can tell workers where to put resources, but it seems harder to tell them which machines to work on first to refine resources. In other words, if I could prioritize spares over semiconductors by putting them in separate factories, the workers seem to put bioplastics and metals in the spares first, but still will work on either machine if there are enough resources to fill all those machines. Also, if I need bioplastics asap and have two bioplastics refinery machines, then sometimes a worker will go and work on one machine, walk away, and another worker will walk up and work on the other machine. In the long run this doesn't matter, but if I'm in a crisis that needs bioplastics to be resolved, this is incredibly frustrating to watch.
The last one is impractical, but I wish colonists would act more like real people. Like, do you really need to be watching TV when your oxygen generator isn't working because you haven't built that second water farmer I asked for yet? Is it really impossible for the biologist to pick up the worker's slack a little when we need some bioplastics for medical supplies because all the workers have broken bones? Maybe the solution would be to have all colonists able to do certain jobs outside of their specilization if it's simple enough, but at reduced efficiency, or to have a non-specialized worker.

You use a team of commandos, numbers vary by mission, to perform assigned objectives then exit the area. It's relatively like a puzzle game where you'll have to time certain tasks right and use an appropriate commando in an appropriate situation. For the most part you'll be using one commando more than the rest however everyone does play a vital role and in order to finish a mission as "cleanly" as possible everyone will be required to fulfill their roles in each mission.
A real cool feature this game has is the ability to have multiple (I think a maximum of 8 total) windows in the game and a function that lets the camera for the selected window to follow an enemy or commando.
The game requires quite a bit of thinking and even though you've got the enemy's movements down and you know your way around you'll still need a lot of patience to get through a mission without causing too much or no fuss. Each mission also gets much, much lengthier as you progress (after I think mission 15/20 it takes me around 3 or more hours to complete).
It will be very helpful to learn the shortcut keys for each commando (as opposed to always clicking on their items) for better convenience and quicker actions in given situations. Unfortunately the keys are un-rebindable so memorizing the keys may be a bit more of a hassle.
The AI, whether the Nazis or your commandos, can be pretty dumb. The commandos will have a habit of spazzing out or maybe taking some weird extra 2-foot diagonal path or whatever when maybe all you wanted them to do is walk along the wall whilst hugging it and turn on the next corner while still hugging said wall. The Nazis, especially the ones in groups, may glitch up a bit when making a turn on their paths meaning their field of visions have a good chance of going all over the place.
With an isometric game like this I figured you should at least be able to see or go "behind" large structures especially since the enemy can do it, but you can't. If you click on a building thinking you'll go "behind" it then the assigned commando will most likely try to find the fastest route "in front" of it. It's also a pain every now and again to try and put one commando where another is specifically located because there's no option to click through your guys so you may accidentally click on your guy instead of moving one there.
Really it's a cool game and despite all its design flaws it feels good to get through a really tough and lengthy mission.

And Yet It Moves centers itself around a natural twist for the puzzle-platformer genre: if the jump is too long, then make the platform come to you. This ability to freely rotate the level does open up new strategies and keeps things fresh - though the 'freely' of that equation did not survive the transition to PC. In the Steam version of this game, rotation is locked to 90 or 180 degrees at a time, a fact the levels don't seem to have been optimized for. The main 'journey' of the game isn't terribly long - there's no story, implied or otherwise - but it does have the good grace to end before the interesting ideas run out.
A variety of challenge modes and a few bonus levels help to extend And Yet It Move's playtime, but this is where its lack of polish really shines (or fails to as the case may be). The little paper avatar is incredibly fragile. A short fall by any other platformer's reckoning will tear him to pieces. The generosity of the main journey's checkpoints ensured this didn't become too much of a nuisance, but the increased difficulty of the bonus levels and the extra restrictions of the challenge modes negated said checkpoint's efforts. This makes for a painful experience, so much so that I found myself judging what I'd enjoyed earlier in a dimmer light. The ambient noises and the constant chime of having reached the next checkpoint are absent from the bonus levels as are the strange collaged images that make up the standard levels, leaving a dull and empty world behind. It's ironic that a game made from torn pages would end feeling rough and a bit flat, but without this sour finishing note, I imagine I would have left pleased - not ecstatic, but pleased at least.

I wish there was a Neutral recommendation option for games on steam, because I'm not really sure how I feel about this game, but I wanted to write the review right after finishing the game so it would be fresh in my mind.
By the time of writing this review I have finished the main story of the game with a 70% completion score and a playtime of 12 hours on steam, but about 9 - 10 of those hours were spent actually playing the game, as one time when playing the game I got interested about the devs for the game and read about them and got side-tracked and started doing other things.
Coming into Tomb Raider I wasn't a fan of games which I deemed 'Cinematic Story Driven games'.
A lot of people love the games that focus on telling a really compelling story with brilliantly written characters that act and feel real, but have a large amount of cutscenes with a lot of qtes (quick time events) and generic third person shooter, cover-mechanic gameplay. I personally hated them. Not because of the game itself, but because of the fanbase that claim that games like Uncharted and The Last of Us were the best games ever made, when really the actual GAME part of the product was mediocre or good at best. Tomb Raider was one of these games, anyone can tell by looking at it, but the game did interest me a lot more than The Last of Us' zombie apocalypse setting, or Uncharted's Indiana Jones like feel. Tomb Raider interested me because the old games were really good, and scratched that puzzle solving itch of mine. I was sceptical about the game but played it as soon as I upgraded my PC.
Within the first 2 hours I found myself enjoying the game a fair amount.
I was rooting for Lara to survive the many unreal situations she got caught in and generally was having a good time.
I wasn't bothered too much by the qtes and got into the story. I really loved the beautiful scenery and the (mostly) fun puzzle solving and was very surprised to see the hidden tombs in the game which ramped up my enjoyment of the game more.
The gameplay wasn't half bad either, the shooting felt good but I did enjoy the traversal and puzzle solving far more.
This is where my gripes come in. This proved to be a bad thing for me because the original Tomb Raider games focused on more puzzles than combat, and the new Tomb Raider obviously focused on the opposite. This would have been alright if all the puzzles were all really good, but I'd say only 20% of the puzzles in this game actually got me scratching my head or gave me that 'A-ha!' moment. The rest were pretty dull and a lot of the solutions to the puzzles were used multiple times. I'm pretty sure I had to use a heavy object to break open a door about 3 times in this game.
The characters didn't strike a chord with me that much. Lara certainly is the best character of the game by far. I felt immersed in the game for most of my time playing and was always rooting for Lara to keep going. It is a bit odd that a character like Lara can evolve into a gunslinging, crack shot within the space of 3 days though, but it didn't bother me that much. SPOILER ALERT, DO NOT READ IF YOU HAVE NOT FINISHED THE GAME
And now for the biggest issue I have with the game, the story.
Usually they say that if a game has average gameplay, it will have a really good story, and most reviews I had seen of the game said that the story was the best part about it. For the first 2-3 hours of the game I agreed that the story was very good and well written. However, I quickly found out that this was not true for me.
This next part of the review is spoiler heavy, so be wary.
Overall I'd say the game is maybe worth a play when on sale. The story is not that good but maybe you might enjoy it. The gameplay is OK, probably the best thing about the game.

You are an Observer, a person who can hack into the minds of others, attempting to track down your son whom you thought dead. Now locked down in an apartment complex, you must find the answers you seek or lose your mind in the process.
PROS
+ Amazing atomsphere and graphics
+ Great sound design
+ Top-tier voice acting
+ The story is top notch cyberpunk/horror
+ The vision modes are cool
CONS
- Sometimes unclear which vision mode to use
- Rarely didn't realize what to do
- Encountered one bug that caused me to reload
I didn't know what to expect from this game when I first fired it up, but after playing their previous game, Layers of Fear, which I loved I expected good things from this game. I was not dissappointed! Right from the start I felt like a detective in Blade Runner ready to solve a crime.
There is a beautiful fully fleshed out cyberpunk world at work here, all shrunk down into the confines of an apartment building on lockdown and the characters you meet help bring that world to life. They are all voiced wonderfully; yourself by the amazing Ruter Hauer. Your abilities and actions add meat to the bones giving you an idea of the technology at work all around you at all times.
The story itself is a great cyberpunk/horror story that has you trying to track down your son, which pulls you through the apartment complex and interactions with the residents. In order to do this, you'll have to use you different vision modes-EM vision (elecronic), Bio vision (tissue), and night vision-to scan crime scenes and the area, and your ability as an Observer to hack into people which always leads you down an interesting road as you walk through their minds and their lives.
Ultimately, it is a great game that never felt boring, overwhelming or overly difficult. I was always drawn into the game and wanted to finish it. There are collectible photos and a mini game strewn about the game for you to collect/complete, and multiple endings ensuring replayability.
Highly recommend!

You scan some things, make a couple of dialogue choices, and there are some stealth parts where you have to sneak towards the exit without getting seen. Oh yeah, an optional reoccuring mini puzzle game can be found throughout. For the most part however, >observer_ is more akin to a (very interactive albeit terribly slow) walking simulator.
Where this game shines is its art style and design, its settings and its visual effects. The world you get to explore here is gorgeous in its unique, dark and gritty cyberpunk style. However, I feel obliged to mention that I experienced some major fps drops when the effects go all in. I feel like it definitely could've been optimized better, as I hardly ever experience fps drops in other games, having built this pc for VR with a gtx 1080, i7-6700 @4.2 GHz, 32 GB RAM.
The audio is spot on as well and adds to the overall experience, with Rutger Hauer doing an okay job. His voice is pleasant but I found some lines to be a little awkwardly delivered, bordering lackluster at times. This never really took me out of the game because the whole of the experience was just very immersive.

I'm a huge fan of cyberpunk so as soon as I saw the opening trailer I was hooked. I'm typically not one for "walking sims" and while this game almost seems like it at times, it's really not, or at least it manages to be much more than that through taking specific care in immersing the player where you feel engaged in the world as a detective and not as a disconnected "controller"
I was particularly impressed with that last part, how they managed to hide away or integrate so much of the "game" aspects where you don't end up having a lot of jarring "PRESS X TO DO THIS" or items popping up on the UI in a "game" way. They're integrated in a way (such as your 'mission' and psych bar) that it fits into the game universe. Opening doors is even done in a way beyond just pushing a button and watching it swing, as is using computers, etc. It really goes a long way. It can be frustrating sometimes because it doesn't have the typical handholding of modern video games and you end up not even realizing you're in a puzzle. But I'd rather have it this way than the alternative.
The gameworld is the real selling point to me. It manages to feel like an absolutely gritty cyberpunk universe from some fiction in the 90s, still holding onto relics of the modern day but "futurizing" them in a way that feels very natural; we still have railroads and structures built from over 100 years ago still standing today, they didn't just up and disappear, they get integrated into the future. The people you communicate with, the environment you visit which is actually on recollection 'small', but feels very very large by being filled with detail. The voice acting is a little shaky sometimes, but I feel that some of it just absolutely fits the world perfect. Some of the biggest chills I got in the game were actually from talking to various people in the building; the things they would say and how they say it.
If you're into cyberpunk at all it's worth it just for that alone. I don't want to give too much away and I think that discovering aspects of this world through exploration and talking to the people you come across is one of the best parts. It's a somewhat short game (~8 hours?) but there are hidden collectibles and tons of things to read and take a look at. There are jump scares, some I feel are pretty cheap (they serve absolutely no purpose) but it's not bad. Overall I highly recommend

Zombie party is the first twin stick shooter that I've played in my life and I found the experience quite enjoyable. Although I can't compare it to other games of this genre, I can clearly say that its a pretty well done game. It comes with lots of features, several game modes, it is vastly customizable and has huge replay value. All in all, it presents itself as an almost complete and solid product.
As a newbie in this genre, I found the learning curve quite easy. No matter the game mode chosen, you will have to do essentially the same thing: kill everything that dares to move. To accommodate myself with the game, I chose to play
first - maybe it's the easiest of all since the mobs are usually in groups, therefore the player has enough time to plan their attacks.
was pretty crazy for me, since in the beginning I kept dying over and over, eaten by those damn zombie crowds that spawned in waves. I've never been good at kiting things but this game pushed me into learning how to do it in order to survive... till the boss fight came, which was a real challenge for me. I am aware that I am inexperienced with these kind of games, but I found myself wanting to have an Easy mode apart from the existing Normal and Hardcore. However, after a couple of hours of practice, I finally managed to kill my first boss and it felt really good.
I also tried the online multi-player mode, which is in open beta. Sadly this doesn't work properly yet for the same IP, I wasn't able to connect to my partner and there currently exists no steam integration for finding a multi-player game. Local multi-player works but having 2 sets of explosions that cover your screen was damn confusing for me so I abandoned my partner shortly after a few minutes. The zooming feature contributed to me loosing focus of my character too: the zoom automatically adjusts on the current area according to the distance between the players, the smaller it is, the bigger the zoom. I had the same problems, but on an increased scale, in
, during wich the screen is covered by the explosions of 4 players instead of 2.
I wasn't able to touch the
, not even with a 10-foot pole: kill 10.000 zombies in 5 minutes. The few attempts I had at this mode ended up with me dying after around 1 minute, with with less than 1000 zombies killed.
Of course, since the main objective of the game is to kill stuff, the player has access to a vast range of weapons and customizations. The common weapons found in any shootery game are present in here too and can be enhanced by runes or with skill points and upgraded to better weapons. The upgrades are bought with the gold coins you pick up while playing, which sadly are not that easily obtained. For example, in order to afford a basic upgrade one needs to play several levels, collecting all the gold on the way. Also, having to actually step on the coins in order to collect them makes the gathering process much more difficult. If you wanna be rich, you gotta work for it and the game abides to the rules of grinding.
Apart from coins, ammo and enhancements, the mobs randomly drop super guns that have a plethora of graphic effects. You can shoot huge electric balls or rainbow laser beams that decimate everything on your screen in a second. My only complaint about these is that sometimes the colors are too crazy and one can easily loose sight of their character, buried deeply under the colorful explosions. I love hidden object games but I don't think a twin stick shooter should turn into a "find your hidden character 3 times in 5 seconds" kind of game.
So far, I encountered only one bug: the cursor is sometimes not properly trapped inside the game window, this resulting in tabbing me out mid fight when my mouse touched the edge of the screen. That is, if you play with mouse and keyboard, like I did - I found it more comfortable than using a controller, although the movement in both modes is well implemented.
In conclusion, the game is complex and full of potential, definitely worth trying. But not that easy to beat.

An 2D exploration-driven Metroidvania. The platforming and combat can be tricky. The rest of the game is much, much harder. Very well crafted, from the graphics to the action to the writing to the puzzles to the killer soundtrack,
The exploration is very open-ended and organic feeling, which makes the world feel very real. It also means it's easy to venture into places you probably shouldn't be without realizing it. (a word of advice: DO NOT leave the first area before you get the Grail). Diving too deep will likely get you killed. But then again, going where you're supposed to go next can get you killed anyway. La Mulana is not a safe place.
The puzzles and the story of the ruins are heavily interwoven. Bits of lore and puzzle hints are scattered everywhere, and the heart of the game is piecing it all together. Every puzzle has its solution implied somewhere, but percieving and understanding it may not happen on the first, or even the tenth, examination. The game starts hard and gets much harder, with the riddles, the hints, and the answers getting more esoteric as you progress, and spread over a much wider area of the ruins.
That puzzle and progression design means that it's easy to have little idea what to do next. Am I supposed to be here? Does that tablet apply to this puzzle? Do I even have all of the items I need to complete it? Was I supposed to solve that other puzzle first? Multiply that uncertainty by 3, 4, 5 partially-explored areas on opposite ends of the ruins, and the confusion can quickly get overwhelming.
If this sort of thing sounds terrible, La Mulana may not be for you, but the mechanics work wonderfully to enforce the mentality of exploring ancient, trap-filled, unforgiving ruins that nonetheless hide deep, deep secrets. That atmosphere is reinforced by stellar art direction and an excellent score (One of my top 5 VG soundtracks) You must be cautious, patient, thorough, willing to brave danger, and deeply dedicated to sifting through pieces of lost knowledge if you want to uncover just what lies in the depths of La Mulana.

Sphinx and the Cursed Mummy is a 3D platformer released by Eurocom. The same developer that made Crash Bash. It originally released back in 2003 on the PS2. It's set in a fantasy world inspired by ancient Egypt.
It's a very competent game. The levels look really nice, the characters have nice designs, the platforming is competent. But it doesn't really stand out in any real respect. The story is bog standard and generic and you really stop paying attention to it. At one point you unlock a second player character who is a mummy but all this really does is shift the game towards a more stealth focus. There is also no voice acting and this really drags the entire game down and makes it feel like it lacks personality compared to something like Jak and Daxter.
Sphinx is interesting less because of it's value as a game but moreso how it was completely forgotten after it released and only gets discussed nowadays because of a massive oversight on the developers part with the original release. In the NTSC release, if you used a specific save game station. It locks a specific door you need to get through and makes you unable to complete the game. This massive technical problem affects almost everyone who played the original release and as a result very few people actually completed the game.
This is why I'm somewhat shocked that this game was ported to PC 14 years later since I was surprised someone else remembered it. This version does fix that bug and is fairly competent aside from that. But that's the word, competent. It doesn't do very much you haven't seen done better elsewhere. It's one of the most average games I've ever played and unless you grew up with it I doubt you'd be interested in it otherwise.

As noted by the amount of time I've spent on this game, I think it's pretty obvious thatI enjoyed it. As everyone agrees with, including negative reviews, the art style of this game is astounding as well as the inclusion of Nordic folklore.

Not only is this game based off of folklore, but it even includes an in-game encyclopedia. Another thing I admire about the ue of these subjects, is the creatures and practices in this game are not really well known. The Year Walk itself has been lost through the decades and the developers resurrected the experience using this game. Not only does the encyclopedia bring real world aspects into the game, but the hidden journal at the end as well. In many ways your conventional colony/village management sim, it's got enough little twists to keep it interesting. Now, bear with me, it might sound like I hate the game from what I'm about to write, but I assure you it's quite the contrary.
There's quite a few non-fatal design imperfections, unfortunately. I get that AI programming is challenging, but the villager AI in Planetbase can be rather terrible. Four medics milling around a med bay while patients die of radiation poisoning. Okay. A hundred hungry/thirsty people walking from one end of a huge base all the way to the other and dying of hunger/thirst on the way. Great. I mean, there were water fountains and food where you were, but nobody's perfect. In that sense it's really more of an ant colony simulation than anything resembling human beings, given their suicidally incompetent lemming-like behaviour at times.
There are also some curious thematic inconsistencies that don't really make much sense, but usually get winked at because being more thematic would "make the game too easy." For example, you have to scramble to build the initial set of buildings or everyone dies immediately. Why don't people in the future send robots to build an initial seed colony structure before landing? Power generation is another thing. Your sources of power ar solar and wind. That's it. And yes, the wind strength RNG
♥♥♥♥ you at the worst possible time. It ends up boiling down to having to build enormous farms of capacitors to cushion your base against the RNG of cloud cover and wind, though either type of power generation is more reliable on some planets than on others. Did you want a more reliable power source, like a bio fuel reactor, or even fusion? Ha, silly; cue "too easy" argument.
And, of course, there's the hunger/food system constellation of ♥♥♥♥ery. Some play sessions it feels like this entire game is just a set of death spirals that you'll more or less randomly get sucked into and watch helplessly as your base falls apart (save often), and I don't think it's anywhere more true than in the food system. It's a bit complicated to try and explain why exactly, but suffice it to say the suicidal lemming AI can and will destroy your base if you ever happen to fall behind on providing enough food and enough places to eat it. Contrary to what you might expect if someone's described this game as "durr it's The Martian + Sim City!" to you, your colonists have the survival instincts of a moldy cheese sandwich. They've done a lot of work on this aspect of the AI, so it's not nearly as bad as it used to be, or maybe as bad as I'm making it sound. Again, you can play around it and, with a little luck, bounce back from some death spirals if you do happen to get sucked in.
Like I said, while questionable, I wouldn't call any of these imperfections fatal. Once you learn the way to play around them, the game's actually quite enjoyable in the same Zen gardening way these kinds of games are. I'd give this one a recommendation if you enjoy the whole survival-y management sim thing.

Was really looking forward to a Mars building game but sadly this game was a disappointment.  Its a standard God mode survival game where you just direct buildings and production of AI "colonists".  You can issue orders to build and then direct workers by turning structures or machines on and off.  You also can control the probability of which type of colonist will show up in your colony.  Its fun for a few hours but quickly becomes a tedious mess for several reasons.
1.  There isn't a lot to do.  Because of the games mechanics you basically have a dozen structures and you build most of them right away.  Every structure looks pretty much the same and you may be able to build some different sizes but thats about it.  Beyond that there isn't any intrigue really and the late game structures are extremely odd in that they don't really fit the game at all.  More on that later.
2.  The AI is ABYSMAL...  Matt Damon these guys aren't.  One would assume that Mars colonists would have some level of education but they really are stupid.  You can't issue direct orders to your colonists so instead you have to turn things on and off, set production limits, etc but somehow it never seems like these morons are doing what they should.  I had one game where early on a meteor blasted the connecting tube to my bunkhouse trapping 7 of my 9 colonists.  Adding insult to injury my 2 droids needed repair at this time.  No worries I had 2 workers in the base and they will rush to save the crew right?  Wrong...  They went and had a bite to eat.  Ignored their dying friends and refused to repair the droids.  Naturally all 7 colonists died so I thought oh well I'll keep things going as best I can until more show up.  Wrong again.  Both workers proceded to get sick because they couldn't sleep and refused to do any work.  The base fell apart while they just wandered around eating all the food and not doing a single thing I asked of them.  The mechanics are poor that you really have to turn off almost any possible distraction for your colonists when you really want to push production on something.  Need spares?  Better make sure you have absolutely nothing else for them to do.  The raise/lower priority command is worthless.   Never seen it make a lick of difference.  Also some structures are worthless.  In the 3 games I played the biggest challeneges always seemed to come when I built a bar.  The second I opened that structure my whole base fell apart each time and I would inevitably just turn the darn thing off and realized I never even needed it.  In a game with so few structures seems silly to me to have structures that are worthless.
3.  Poor end game.  Once you realize that slow and steady wins the race and get a sustained population the game gets super easy.  Just slowly expand and everything is fine.  However you will inevitably be tempted to build those endgame structures.  The security room, telescope, and base defense lasers.  Aside from the radio tower and lasers there seems to be absolutely no need for these structures.  The lasers kill meteors sometimes and the radio helps you order specific items from traders.  But thats the end of the immersion.  Once you build a security room with starport random invaders will just start showing up and attack your base.  There is no story for this and no in game explanation.  It just happens.  As a result you need to waste resources on armed guards.  But your guards suck.  I had 5 of them in one game and a they didn't even respond to the last invasion I saw costing my 8 colonists while my guards slept and my red alert alarms were blasting.
It basically feels like the devs knew the game was terribly shallow and just crammed this "bandit" system in to give one more challenge.  To me it just doesn't fit.  There is no reason for them and they just kill whatever fun you might be having since the AI is so terribly broken.
If you can get this game on sale for under $7 bucks I'd give it a weekend but it will bore you very quickly.  Any price over $7 and its a Do Not Buy.

Hero of the Kingdom doesn't look like much at first glace, and honestly, what you see is what you get as far as visuals go. There's no fancy lighting or edgy music to try and put it in the "Art" category that an ever-increasing number of indie games are targetting these days. But what Hero of the Kingdom does deliver on very successfully, is sheer enjoyment and satisfaction.
If I had to give it a label, I would say that Hero of the Kingdom is a Hidden-Object Adventure, but it's certainly not like other games in that genre that I have played. Those games tend to be more about steering an antagonist around beautifully rendered environments in which the things Im seeking stand out like dogs balls, while trying to solve a crime, or avoid becoming the victim of one. In contrast, Hero of the Kingdom's hidden objects are often feindishly well hidden simply because they utilise the same low-key rendering as the rest of the environment, and are not presented to you as a random chest that has a butterfly, a skull, a broken 17th century hand-blown bespoke led-lit gilded 1:23 scale ♥♥♥♥ing church window, and a pack of Tic Tacs to sort through, but rather, parts of a thoughtfully crafted map that your♥♥♥♥♥♥eyes are going to find challenging to identify. Seems like a really simple problem to avoid considering how long Hidden-Object games have been around, but you might be surprised how much garbage is still churned out and consumed because Kmart only stocks five PC games that aren't Heroes of Might and Magic III.
What I'm getting at (I think) is that it's pretty rare to find a game that balances all the things we tend to gripe about, and still manages to be fun, great value for money, and the right length. That last one especially, is an attribute that can never be understated in this genre either. So hats off to you, Lonely Troops, for some of the best innocent fun I have had in quite a while. It's not often I talk to mates at the pub about a little game like this and have them say, "♥♥♥♥ YES I LOVE THAT GAME" in response.

A good indie game that challenges you, makes you think of how to beat this with their clever mechanic. Recommend on getting discount and only if you love indie games because this can get bored fast if you don’t like puzzle/strategy game.

And Yet It Moves is an indie puzzle-platformer, released back when indie puzzle-platformers weren't a commodity yet.
The mechanisms are simple: navigate levels by running, (weakly) jumping and, more importantly, by rotating the level around you. Rotations are made by steps of 90° or 180°. You have to be careful though, because you can only fall from so high before getting crushed to death in the process. And you keep your momentum even after rotating, so don't expect to cheat death by a last-minute rotation.
You will suffer tens or hundreds of deaths, but AYIM remains causal and mostly frustration-free, thanks to infinite lifes and the most generous distribution of checkpoints to ever grace a video game. Which also makes the gotcha-unfair kind of deaths much more tolerable than in other games.
The graphics are made of paper collages and give AYIM a look that remains unique and distinct, even all these years after its release. I sometimes wished for more variety though, as there only are 4 or so "themes".
"Music" is made of blip-bloop noisy soundscapes, which works very well  but, again, more variety would have been welcome.
Beating the game should take about two hours, and I think that's about tight: the end came just before it would have started getting too repetitive. If you're so inclinded, various modes (speed runs, ...) are available to add replayability, but I think most people will be content to just play through this relatively basic game once.
Overall, AYIM has enough personality to warrant a recommendation. It's certainly much better than what I expected from the "mixed" Steam user reviews. Because it was offered in several bundles, it lies unplayed in many people's backlog. If that's your case, I encourage you to give it a try. I think it's good enough to recommend a purchase, but there's no question that it's a bit short to justify the non-sale price tag.

Step 1) Design a platform level -

Step 4) Let the player move...the level? -
Yeah, so...in this game you move your character through obstacles, not unlike any platformer. What sets this game aside is what the developers changed. What did they change? Well, normally a floor stays below you and a ceiling stays above you, and yet IT moves in this game. What's it? THE WORLD is IT - ROTATE THE WORLD and go with it. That floor is tired of being stepped on, so STOP RUNNING ON IT. That ceiling in the cave is tired of only being looked at, so INTRODUCE IT TO YOUR FEET. The world in this game should be set with basic rules and yet it moves to break those rules. Run around and explore in this strange paper doodled upon, ripped apart, torn out, mashed up game. Just beware because you're not the only thing moving...

Not a bad game, a very good return to the series. It doesn't play much like the original series (though I haven't played a Tomb Raider since Tomb Raider 3, so take that for what it's worth) but I do feel like that's for the better. I'll admit, I am somewhat disappointed that the origin story has changed from the original plane crash in South America to a ship crash near Japan, but the story works. The gameplay is fun and smart, with great climbing mechanics and an awesome weapon modding system, although the guns do lack impact and make you feel like you're shooting BBs when four shotgun blasts at close range doesn't kill a bad guy. The progression of gameplay really makes you feel like Lara is evolving as the game goes on, and there is a really fun bit of fan service in the final showdown with the villian.
The main problem I had with the game is that it doesn't give you much of a chance to get to know any of the characters. It feels a lot like early Playstation games: when someone dies, your response is "Who was that again?" We get some very minor flashbacks and video sequences to help develop the characters in very minor ways, but it doesn't really tell you much. By the time it was over, I really didn't feel like I knew any of them. Even the villian is kind of phoned in.
If you were looking for a more serious version of Uncharted, or a more linear version of Assassin's Creed, this is a very fun game to play. If you're looking for compelling characters or a gripping story, this won't offer much.

La-Mulana is an exploration based sidescroller platforming Metroidvania that was the inspiration for one of my favorite games, Spelunky, so I knew I had to give it a play.
After a fairly slow start I found the game to be pretty engaging. The controls are very strange, with movement being very jerky and not my usual thing, but I got used to it and was enjoying it despite. I was happily wandering the ruins, solving puzzles, and slaying monsters.
I fought a boss while riding through caves on a cart, Ellmac, which was pretty difficult and frustrating but I figure that was my fault for doing it (probably) so early with such poor gear, so it gets a pass. I die after him though in the new area so I figure I'll come back later.
So far the game was shaping up to be better than I expected! I was wondering where I should go next, so I figured I'd head to the Temple of Moonlight. I'd found it before but always died early inside it, so I was putting it off.
In I go and I get to dungeoneering. Can't attack while inside? Got it. New items, puzzles, and all that jazz... great! But where's the save point? I was very close to death when I finally found it. Phew!
Now how do I get out of this place? I spend maybe an hour or so wandering the areas I'd already been, finding a secret weapon, but can't for the life of me figure out how to escape. I love playing games blind, so I leave the game for a bit to ruminate on the area and see if I can think of something I missed.
When I come back, I explore everything one last time, smacking all the walls and trying my best to find
I missed. Eventually I break, and I have to look up what the deal is. It shouldn't be so hard to leave the area - after all, I have the map, so I know where all the rooms are...
I'm permanently stuck in the Temple of Moonlight because I didn't pick up the Holy Grail earlier. Apparently there are several locations in the game where this can happen. In a game about
, you can get permanently stuck for apparently
. The game doesn't indicate that one area should be explored before another, or that you have to have this item before you should continue on. The item is hidden too, a puzzle that I had seen but was unable to solve and put off until later.
How is this acceptable design? I was enjoying the game despite the other flaws, but that crosses a line. Maybe it's a fundamental difference in the way Japanese and Westerners design and enjoy their games, but I don't have the time or want to be forced to restart a long-winded game due to game breaking scenarios that are beyond my control.
If you are new to La-Mulana, get the Holy Grail before you explore anywhere, or your game might just end early... and you'll be left very wanting.

Edit: To those who disagree, please comment. I honestly want to hear how I'm wrong about this.
La-Mulana is a fantastic platforming adventure game that does not hold your hand. "The adventure begins" and that's all you get. The video on the Steam store page helps quite a bit, giving you the basic essentials to starting. From there, you spelunk a massive ruin with many cultures mixed into a great, nuanced, satisfying story.
I really want to just say that I love this game, everyone should play it and learn how to be a real gamer. However, there were some frustrating points that ultimately made me drop it. That's not to say that everyone will find the same things frustrating, but I wanted to give fair warning at least.
La-Mulana has a very well designed difficulty curve for quite a while, but right around the mid-game, things get very overwhelming. A number of puzzles at that point have given you so many clues and you have so many places you can go that it becomes impossible to filter between what you can and can't solve without meticulous note-taking. I found the sheer number of things that you have to keep handy just in case a tablet somewhere hints at a room somewhere else to go beyond intimidating to the point of not being fun.
A lot of things are hidden behind one completely unremarkable wall among hundreds or trial and error. At the same time I've had the most legitimate challenge that I've had in any game. I wish I could give this a neutral to say "be prepared for masochistic gaming or a walkthrough", but this is probably the closest I can get considering the majority of people. Also, my playtime is not what it appears, I've been playing collaboratively in offline mode with a friend.

Lamulana is a game where half-Japanese Indiana Jones goes into a temple for worshipping a lovecraftian elder god. He stays in there for months upon end and teleporting is the LEAST weirdest thing he has to do every few minutes.
Lamulana is a game where you MUST, and I mean MUUUUUUUST, write down EVERY glyph you find and EVERY conversation you have with a dead skeleton lying on the ground on a sheet of paper and tape it all onto the walls. Yes, your real, physical walls. Arrange them into a map based on WHERE in the La-Mulana ruins you found each note. Ready some strings and pins because you're going to need to make arbitrary connections with two notes in entirely different locations with possible relations.
Oh, the La-Mulana ruins? It's non-euclidean. That means it's full of distorted/repeating space connected by portals all over the place that doesn't make any sense at all. It drives a lesser man insane. BUT NOT YOU. NO. You note that all down, too! Oh, and you want to be able to fold each area so it'll become a 5x4 square, btw. Don't think about it too hard. Just keep that in the back of you're head because you're going to need it at the end game. Just saying, every area in the game might be shaped like a 4D donut with varying directions of gravity.

Honesly, Zombie Party just a really good bullet hell game. Sure the online play is a bit buggy at the moment, but it's fun and has plently of content for a nice price. It has a large and colorful cast of characters, customizable (and unique) weapons, a variety of pets, and even a magic system. In addition, the game features a leveling/stat mechanic that allows you to talior your character to your preferred playstyle on the fly.
"But wait," you say, "This genre thrives on simple but hectic fun and all this sounds complex. Surely this bogs down the gameplay."
And it's true that there is an absurd amount of stuff packed into this seemingly simple game, but it's all to the point. Weapon upgrades do what they say on the can. Stats are also straightforward. The bombs, magic, and items you pick up are also self-explanatory. The overall effect of all this is a sense there is more meat to the game. Theres more diversity in how you play and more you can customize to how you play. Which is a nice break from the normal progression of gun -> bigger gun -> biggest gun
Zombie party also features several game modes. From the rougelike dungeon mode, to the traditional bullet hell pvp of deathmatch, to the classic arcade mode.
On the downside, it has occasional dips in performance, and online play is a bit iffy. They don't distract from the overall enjoyment though.
If you want something that you can pick up and play anytime while still having a large amount of content to earn and unlock this is the game for you.

I played a lot of Magic the Gathering back when I was in secondary school. I got in during the Mirrodin block, a series of cards notorious for being much to too strong. It introduced two new things that upset a lot of people: 1. the new card layout. 2. Affinity for artifacts. The result was a metagame built around completely overpowered combos and cards and as a result Wizard backpedaled for the next block: Kamigawa. It was infinitely weaker and very different. Fast forward a few years and Wizard is preparing the biggest update in the game ever: Magic 2010. This changed some rules and introduced all sorts of loopholes to make more insanely powerful cards that make everything in Mirrodin seem weak.
The Duels of the Planeswalkers series in an attempt to bring the card game to the masses in a simplfied form. Basically you're given a set of Decks, each with a special theme or tactic and you have to fight your way through a series of computer opponents or against other humans with the same set of decks. This is the inherent problem with this game: everything is stripped down for the game. The inherent awesomeness of magic is building your own unique deck with over 30.000 possible cards. This game offers no such options. Obviously for dirty monetising reasons. Furthermore, the game is a complete wreck when it comes to flow. The animations are so overly long and uninteresting you'll lose attention and motivation to play before you have gotten to the core of the game.
All in all, as a player of the actual card game I cannot reccomend this. It is thin watery gruel that resembles the game in rules and look, but misses everything that inheritly makes it fun.
Paying extra for limited deck slots? Haha nope. I quit/10 would♥♥♥♥♥♥on it.

15 years ago, I started to play Magic the Gathering (paper cards). I'm still playing this awesome game now, I spend 2-3 hours each day for things dealing with MtG.
Regarding this game, it's clearly not the paper game.
- The pool of cards is not that wide, you have to play with a restricted amount of available cards, which is annoying.
- I'm pretty sure that some IA opponents have pre-determined patterns : there are playing the same cards in the same order, game after game. It's not that fun to know what's coming next, especially when you play a game that involves a random aspect ...
- The interface isn't great and doesn't allow you to use all of the mechanics of the game. In particular, it's not quite painful to use the stack.
But, in the end, this is still Magic, a great game, and you will have fun to spend around 20 hours to unlock all of the achievements. Then, you can still build decks and play with them against other players all over the world.

If you want to learn Magic The Gathering on the cheap you might enjoy this game.  On the other hand you would probably want the added deckbuilding features of 2015 (Actually you don't.  After playing DotP 2015 I can safely say that version makes this one look like the Holy Grail of gaming) or the much more fun chaos of planechase in the 2013 edition.  If you are an old hat at the game, you probably won't enjoy this much unless you cannot find anyone to play with or are currently unable to play any other way.  Basically, I cannot recommend it when the year before, much less the ancient microprose version, are so much better!
If you need your hand held while you dip a toe into MtG, consider this.  Otherwise aquire real cards, look into MTGO, download cockatrice, or dig up a copy of the far superior (although using an older ruleset) Microprose Duels of the Planeswalkers.

I was twelve when I got this game. It was my birthday and i was allowed to get 2 or 3 games for my PS2. I remember seeing the box art for this game and being fascinated. i had always had an interest in ancient Egypt, my favorite movie of the time was The Mummy, and i couldn't wait to get home and play it. I'm glad I did, too, Because it wound up becoming one of my top ten favorite games of all time. Fast forward to about two weeks ago. I find out that Sphinx and the Cursed Mummy is coming to PC. I haven't been so excited. I thinks it fair to say I love this game. However, I do have a few minor issues with this port.
First, the text is far too small. When i'm at my computer desk playing it's not that much of a problem. However, in the living room, on my big TV, it's impossible to read. I've also noticed a lot of artifacting and broken bits of letters in the text box. I hear that a fix is coming for that and I hope it's soon.
Second, there seems to be a few minor graphical bugs. I'm running a GTX 1070, so i doubt it's my computers fault. A few cases of random things losing their eyes, one or both, and other cases of Sphinx's model nowhere near lined up with objects he's interacting with. Hopefully these issues can be fixed and if so, it will be done soon as well.
Overall, nothing I've noticed has been game breaking or messed up my experience with this port. They're all just little things I notice while playing that make me chuckle and wonder what happened. Sphinx continues to be a pleasure to play and seeing it in HD makes me that much happier. I look forward to seeing what the future holds for this IP and the others THQN have.

The developer has been really good with communication and pushing frequent fixes and updates but there are still some major issues waiting to be resolved, however it is very playable right now and I'm having a blast in spite of the issues. I still hesitate to recommend the port right now, but seeing how far it's come and with it continuing to get updates, I'm optimistic with where it will end up.
There are no options to resize any of the UI elements. The game launched with the text being unreadable due to its tiny size, which was finally addresed in a patch the developer had been working on for some time, but I find that for playing across the room on Big Picture, the UI elements are still a tad too small for comfort.
There is no hot-plug support for the Steam Controller as of right now, meaning the game can not detect when the controller has been turned on and thus requires you to have the controller on before you launch the game, and if it turns off while you're idle you'll have to relaunch the game in order to use the controller again. In fact, while I don't get this issue on my desktop, trying to play the game with the steam controller on my laptop results in an instant crash to desktop upon launch. Keyboard controls are not a viable option and do not support remapping controls at this time. Hot-plug support on other xinput devices works fine, I've been told.
Glaring criticism aside, the controls are actually quite tight, it's nice that they allow a lot of freedom in the FOV. You can keep it at the original 64FOV, lower it further for some reason, or crank it all the way up to 170FOV, not that you'd want to. It's really nice being able to play this game in HD without using an emulator, and I'm glad it's gotten so much better since launch already.

I followed this game for the longest time, and bought it on release, since I loved Braid so much. I was really looking forward to it, and for the first few hours, I genuinely enjoyed myself. Then, I got stuck. And more stuck. And more and more stuck. The more I played, the less I enjoyed, until I cultivated a visceral hatred for this game. I returned a year later and beat it with the help of some guides, and here's my final take:
Pros:
- It's beautiful. It really is a pretty game to look at and has a unique aesthetic anyone can enjoy.
- It's super well designed and ingenuitive. What starts as simple line puzzles spiral out to much more. Regardless of my feelings on the game, I can't take that away from them. The team did a GREAT job and this game is incredible well done and polished.
Cons:
- It's hard. It's ♥♥♥♥ing hard. I don't consider myself an idiot by any means, but by the time I was four hours into this game, I was completely stuck, and I wanted my refund. I didn't get it, so in my library it stuck. Upon my return to it, obviously I learned the further in you go, the more complicated the rules get, and they just mix them and obfuscate them in more and more confusing ways. If you did this game without a guide, ♥♥♥♥ing kudos to you, you're way better at this than me. I can say with zero doubt that beating this game without any help would have been literally impossible for me.
- The culture and circlejerk surrounding this game are horrid. God forbid you ask for any help on any forums... all you'll get is people who think they are way smarter than they are giving you 'hints' (used VERY loosely) so as not to spoil the game for you, or telling you to 'just sleep on it'.
- The ending. If you can call it that. The camera essentially takes you on a magical trip far, far, very far up Jonathan Blows own♥♥♥♥♥ The secret ending is even worse.
Final thought:
Look, it's a well done game. If you're a clever person, and you enjoy very difficult puzzle games that will twist you brain this way and that, you will likely enjoy it. If you're on the fence, steer clear. You'll walk away infuriated, and salty like myself. I wish I could nuke this game from my Steam Library. Just knowing it's sitting in there mocking me fills me with a rage I've never known.
