If you enjoy lane-based rhythm games, get this as soon as you can. This game deserves a much higher player base.
Where to start? Well, obviously the aesthetics. This game is a visual splendor, due primarily to its backdrops (ever seen the sunset undone over a cityscape?), with its variety of projectiles lighting up around you, especially when you're in overdrive. Overdrive also intensifies the music up, down, & sideways, in a soundtrack that's already "groovy" overall. These tracks, available at 24 Carat Games' Bandcamp, stand strong on their own, most being the type of music that carries you along with it, syncing well with the gameplay, your hands, and involuntarily your body. Even at the first stage, this game secures its presentation, and playing on a laptop with headphones has only allowed me to appreciate it more. (For the less powerful machines out there, there's a few preset performance options, though you can select or deselect features as you will.)
Now, the gameplay? Truth told, this IS my personal purpose of a guitar controller, and after discovering this capability in the options menu and laughably trying it out, I'd be reticent to play it any other way. (Note that switching to any lane is instantaneous on a guitar (and I assume the same of the keyboard), but is done one at a time on a gamepad.) I am not good at Guitar Hero (save for its "just strum the bar" easiest mode, which is boring), but Retro/Grade has a wide range of difficulty levels, from two lanes with modest notes to all five jam-packed. I doubt I'd ever bring myself to handle that level, but between the campaign and the challenges (with a tutorial and full practise mode alongside), I have surprised myself with my risen capability. The base gameplay involves "undoing" the character, Rick's, actions in what appears to be a horizontal "shmup", by intercepting your shots (by strumming the bar after lining yourself up) and reverse-dodging enemy fire. The feedback for messing up (distorting the timeline, where Rick had performed perfectly; the scant story to this game is a humorous read, both in scenario and composition) is clear, and you have the limited capability of forwarding yourself back in time to re-attempt undoing your non-mistake. The overdrive mentioned is this game's version of "star power", and ramps up the presentation and boosts your score decrements (remember, undoing things, here); the game defaults this function to the guitar's Select button and tilt function, but I'd recommend a controller with a dedicated button (such as just under your wrist). The focal projectiles, yours and your enemies, vary -- from bursts, beams, and barrages on your side to bursts, spreadshots, and frickin' black holes on theirs -- and the many challenges task you to added conditions, such as no errors, single or shifting color schemes, alternate speeds, and even the original pattern of an already tricky boss.
**Because of the scheme of "reversed shmup", there are projectiles coming from both (or neither, for black holes) directions -- yours from the right, enemies' from the left -- which adds to the activity on-screen and especially as the difficulty risies requires an acute awareness from the player. The beauty of this is, as the game gradually demonstrates, dodging is as much set to the music as the target notes are, and even moving from lane to lane carries a rhythm, eventually allowing you to confidently skim just barely around obstacles as you become accustomed to the music. Still, keep wary, as the bright nature of the visuals could lead to overlooking a projectile 'til it's on top of you.
For the rest, there are unlockable galleries (photo sets and the music for use in a turntable*), ships (one of the earliest is a T-rex from Go Home Dinosaurs!), and "cheats" (such as an aptly-inflated head...), all via the challenge mode. There are also visibility options, both in turning off the aforementioned effects and in making the notes denoted. And, for you score-seekers, there's a leaderboard for anything but individual challenges (the challenge mode, IIRC, just uses a points system rather than specific score).
tl;dr - This game is great on its own, and when paired with the guitar controller becomes something even its designated games could envy outside of party purposes.
*As of my last attempt, I couldn't get the turntables to start, as they weren't reacting to my green button, nor the mouse, though the latter may've been functionally superceded by the former.

Button Frenzy is an extremely addictive score-attack arcade game. Although there are only 2 (endless) modes to play at the moment, the audio-visual presentation keeps the momentum strong, training you to become a master of your favorite gamepad in a very fun way. Simple enough to pick up and play, yet difficult enough to keep you challenged for hours, Button Frenzy will make you come back for more.
There are currently 2 different game modes supported in Button Frenzy, described below, along with leaderboards.
Since Button Frenzy is a score-attack game, the main objective and crux of the gameplay lies in improving your scores and aiming to take a spot in the global leaderboards. Training yourself to get better at performing combos faster, more accurately, and with more button prompts motivates replayability. Like in many other arcade games, after a certain point while playing, it all comes down to endurance as the difficulty spikes cease to appear.
There are currently 4 different difficulty levels supported in Button Frenzy, described below.
Other than increasing the amount of included button prompts, other factors help provide a more challenging gameplay at higher levels. These include: faster LIFE/time drain, longer button prompt strings, more diverse button prompt strings, etc. Also, local high scores are saved for every game mode/difficulty level. Online/local leaderboards are also supported to compare yourself to friends or other players around the world.
Button Frenzy does a fantastic job keeping one immersed in the gameplay, exceling at encouraging the player to keep pushing for one more round. The sleek button prompts, live button-presses and dramatic shatter animations feel so satisfying to observe, and although the music can get a little overbearing at times, the polished look makes the overall simplicity fairly attractive.
Gamepads are required to play this game. M&Ks are not supported whatsoever (not even for navigating the menu). An important factor to keep in mind, before buying this game, is that there is only full support for XBox 360/One controllers; however, there is partial support for PS4 controllers. See limitations
.
Also, using external mapping tools may cause the player to experience double input (Better DS3, DS4Windows, SCPDriver, etc.). This makes it fairly difficult to use traditional PS3 controllers (3rd party controllers not tested). Users have also reported difficulties/lack of support for the Steam controller.
There are a few suggestions that may improve gameplay; these are listed below.
The developer seems very active in increasing the variety and quality of gamepad support. If you do not have an XBox 360/One controller or a PS4 controller (and don't mind the few limitations listed above), I would wait until the developer implements a couple more patches. Other than the concerns for widespread support, Button Frenzy is a fantastic score-attack game that will continuously pull you back for more. I definitely recommend this game to all fans of minimalistic score-attack/arcade games, or people looking for a casual pick up and play title; even if the individual play times may be relatively short.

'Button Frenzy" is an old-school arcade style title under the guise of a button clicker. Much like the concept behind the 'Dance Dance Revolution' entries, this game has you pressing buttons, though not in any sort of rhythm. Instead, you are given two different modes of gameplay: Frenzy and Recall, both testing your observational, motor, and recollection skills, all to obtain the highest score possible and keep the combo chain alive.
And, well, that's about it. There's really nothing fancy behind this title. Just plug in one of the supported controllers (Xbox 360 and PS4 are the more obvious choices) and press what the game tells you to. You're also given varying difficulties to try ranging from easy to extreme. The higher up you go, the more buttons, bumpers and triggers you need to press, not to mention longer input commands.
While 'Button Frenzy' may cost five dollars [US currency], you do get your money's worth out of it for a single-player title. There are a few bugs here and there I found, such as pressing the pause/back button on my controller also counting towards the start button, or the butons you need to press not showing up in Recall mode (as highlighted in the video above).
Either way, this pick-and-play-game indie title is pretty addicting if you're into these games, though (at the time of writing this) there are no trading cards, a selling point I know some will be turned away from right now. But, there's plenty of room for this one to grow as a whole as well. Hopefully the developer keeps up with this title and implements new fun and challenging modes, even something as simple as a rhythm-based mode down the line, or even implement community modding or multi-player battles.

I have beem playing this game for quite some time now, it is addicting.
PRO:  The idea of resource management, keeping your sims alive, trying to expand, trying to keep supply at an optimal rate etc. This game has it.
However I do want to have more options, sub-management of rooms like more items for sims to interact with, or visual interaction, AI control as to where you want a particular sim stationed on. More in depth analysis on the planet, more resource parts, components variation etc.
CON:
Room expansion and upgrades: While this game allow you to make 2 to 4 levels of upgrade (stronger solar panels, windmills, storage, etc) you are limited in the option to upgrade the lower tier to a better one, first you must recycle (destroy) the existing building or structure you want to "upgrade" meanwhile the resource will remain on the ground and unable to place new structures until the resources are removed. This make upgrade very tedious and the potential to lose incoming resource in the meanwhile.
AI pathfinding: While the sims move on about on their own they often take longer route to a destination, or wait in line for example an airlock being busy with more robot or sims using them.
Uninteresting later levels: While you have expended your base, planted an airport station. The amount of disaster by visitors are at minimal at best, camera spot them right away and all the intruders seems to do is just shoot at random colony's personnel until they are shot to death by the security.
The whole visitor and radio interception to help in coming ship, to heal their soldiers, or stranded humans need a place to land and recuperate is nice and all, but it is only fun the first few times.
I would like to have prison, colony having a bad mood with other, or seems to be wreckless at their jobs, or put other lives in danger would be a nice addition. The lack of water, food, sleep, electricity, Oxygen, fellow colony member dying  etc react differently, and therefore change the behaviour of sims within an idea. or something.
This game does have lot and lots of potential, to expand with addictional resources and more mayhem that is done by your own colony personnel to control as well as more natural disasters other than sandstorm, solarflare, meteor, and blizzars and thunderstorms
Don't get me wrong, the game is good as it is but feels lackluster. As a gaming with basic mechanic and expansion building it is worth a try. I do hope the developer are working on a overhaul DLC or expansion because at it core, the idea is good, the initial impression is impressive, but after about 8 hours of game play it seems to be the same thing over and over with the other planets, except they have their own version of enviromental disasters which isn't that big of a difference to the other planets other than visuals, windy or very sunny, or hardly no wind but lot of sunlight and vice versa.
Final Verdict:
Do I recommend this game? Yes.
Do I think it is worth full price? No.
Do I expect an expansion that fix the issues mentioned above? Hopefully.
Does it desevers a DLC pack or big content updates in the future? Definitely a big Yes.

I have been playing this game since it first went into early access and now that it has been released I can say that it's not that good. I was hoping that the issues I was having would get fixed up but now that it's been released I am giving up on that ever happening.
The game isn't terrible by any stretch of the imagination, I wouldn't have played 45hrs of it if it was. Rather it has some fundamental design features which mean its just not that fun. This game is a great example of a sound game (a few bugs here and there but nothing game breaking) that falls flat because design choices which encourage unfun play.
My problems with the game fall broadly into 2 camps: The physics and the content(planes, weapons, enemies, etc.)
1. Physics:
The problem here is that this game advertises itself as "a fwooshy rogue-lite action flight simulator". However the planes handle like thrust-vectoring, V8 powered biplanes in low gravity. Low top-speed, Low max altitude, low manuverablility at speed but insane low speed manoeuvring, insane power to weight ratio and insanely low stall speed.
All but the heaviest planes can accelerate vertically, go from min speed to max speed in seconds, pull out of a stall with no problem, and pull a turn on a dime. It is my suspicion that there is almost no effect from air speed on pitch, yaw and roll rates (if anything it slows them down), this means that a plane can pull incredibly tight turns at very low speeds, but at top speeds (which aren’t very high), you end up controlling a freight train.
All this results in a flight sim that doesn't feel "fwooshy" at all. I want to avoid bringing real planes into this as this isn't mean to be realistic and I am fine with that. However I feel that it should be mentioned that real planes manoeuvre (mostly) with flaps which have an effect proportional to air speed, higher speeds should me the planes roll faster however in game they roll like an A380 (even the fighters). I feel like, for this game to deliver on "fwooshy", you want planes that are fast, manoeuvrable but only at higher speeds and which can't decelerate to stall speed in no time at all. Under these circumstances, flying would be a joy, but that is not what you get in this game. In the end all dogfighting results in you spinning on the spot at minimum speed to line up a shot one the enemy (thing banshee duels in halo 1), which really isn’t fun.
In all fairness there are a few planes which are faster and more manoverable and so almost approach "fwooshy" when flown in a certain way but that just brings me to the other set of issues.
TLDR: The flight physics are bad and the planes feel weird and slow, not "fwooshy". Also the dogfighting sucks, in an air combat game.
2. The content:
This game has 9 planes of various roles, a bunch of weapons ranging from semi-active guided terminal homing long ranged air-to-air missiles, to cluster bombs, to rockets, to Gatling guns which play in a variety of different and interesting ways and which are good in a variety of situations against various targets. You use this to take on a range of targets such as enemy fighters, carriers, buildings, bombers, and ships. All on randomly generated islands which consist of 3 different biomes, each with its own topography.
Sounds good right? Lots of variety to keep things interesting. Well, not really.
In this game, you aim is to take out the objective on a bunch of islands which consist of buildings, groups of planes flying on pre-set paths and the odd boat. They tell you what the objective is before you start the island however once you have launched you can't change your plane.
Now, to get through the game you need to upgrade your weapons and plane, this takes money. This requires you to destroy buildings, especially on the early levels when there aren’t too many threats. However, buildings have high health so you need a high damage weapon to take them out in a decent timeframe, but the more powerful weapons are heavier and so can't be carried by the lighter, faster, "fwooshy"er planes. You could chip away with smaller weapons if you are patient but the carrier and aerodrome will be launching planes as you attack them so you really want to finish them quickly. So this encourages you to use heavier planes (bombers and heavy multi-role) which are slower and less fun to fly. However you cant change planes mid mission so you also need to dogfight in said plane, this means you need aa weapons and some manuverablility. This encourages you to use lighter planes (fighters, interceptors and multi-role) which have the avionics to equip good aa missiles.
All this leaves you in the position of having to use a heavy, multi-role plane to carry bombs and missiles. There is only really one plane that fits the bill. So even though there are 9 planes in the game I found myself only ever using 3 of them tops, and mostly using one.
Like wise, the only weapons that is good at taking out buildings and light ground targets is a single type of bomb, and to take out carriers there are only a few weapons with the damage. This means that out of all the weapons you will probably only really use a handful. Online multiplayer could help with this by letting each player specialise, but this game doesn't have that.
TLDR: The design choice around the content in the game mean that most of the options at your disposal are sub-optimal. You are forced to create an all round loadout to take out buildings and fighters and only a few things fit the bill. So, there is actually a lot less variety in this game than you think.
This all results in a game that is just not worth your time/money. This game could be great, and I had sky high hopes for it, online multiplayer, maybe a 5v5 pvp where you are trying to take out your opponents carrier, a better flight model with faster planes and larger maps, weapons to fill the gaps in the current arsenal to create more interesting choices, the ability to switch planes mid mission to allow for specialisation, better enemy ai, more interesting mechanics around bombing.  Alas, it is not to be.

Sky Rogue just released from Early Access, of which I was a part of for a year or so. This is one of the few flight sim games I have on steam (if not the only) and is one of the few Early Access titles I've been a vague part of. For the 25% discount (15 USD) I'd say it's one of the best flight games for its price. It is no where near a perfect game, but there have been many improvements within its development cycle and I'd be willing to call it "complete" if it has a few more tweaks applied to it following this release.
Sky Rogue is a roguelike flying game where you take on increasingly numerous and difficult enemies. Its missions are randomly generated in 12 days on the singleplayer campaign or as many as you can beat in the Endless mode. Also supports workshop for custom aeros and custom missions. It's built in Unity which is a big detractor to many (myself included) however this is better than most of the unity "games" you'd see on the Steam Store of 2017.
PROS:
-Plenty of aeros and weapons to research, with the best ones being available after you beat the campaign
-Varied enemy types in the air, land and sea with most aeros having a veteran or ace variant with better AI and weapons
-Fast transition between menus and load times are almost nil
-Does its best to offer as much replayability as possible; every loadout is viable
-Artstyle is simple, however it is also detailed and most objects have a distinct look that can be easily recognized from a distance
-Light on resources; almost any computer can run this game
-Decent OST but may get repetitive
MEH/CONS:
-No online Co-Op. Big fat CON right there.
-Menus are simplistic and the controls menu is still defualt unity assets. Video quality is either "yes" or "no" and sound levels still change even if you have the volume sliders where you want them
-There is no tutorial, so new users will either have to look at stock unity menus or experiment in free flight to figure out how to play. Most features and game mechanics are something new players would have to stumble upon rather than learn in a concise manner
-While the models and landscape have improved since the game's debut, the artstyle itself has stayed mostly the same and may wear on you over long periods of time
-On controllers you may have to wrestle with the camera a bit if you go beyond a certain point when rotating it. The camera autoresets quickly, but can be a pain when you are trying to focus on a target without using the lock-on.
If I were to apply an arbitrary number to Sky Rogue I'd give it a light 8, but that is because of the time I've spent playing this game and how it perfectly emcompassed what I've been missing from my steam library: A flight game where you dogfight and blow things up to your leisure. It has no microtransactions, no DLC, no drama. I'd suggest buying it if you want a plane game.

Every once in a while, I find myself in a mood that makes me want to experience something different; when such a thing happens, I take a peek at a game that doesn't look like a typical game; that neither plays, nor feels, like one; a game such as Year Walk.
A chill and dark venture into Swedish folklore, Year Walk consists of a series of pleasant and simple puzzles, all set under the frame of a forest; but as the title suggests, the core of the game is rather in the walking and immersing yourself in a very unique acoustic and visual landscape, and in the story that unfolds as you progress. Do not let yourself be fooled by the "horror" tag some people have put the game under; this is anything but a horror game despite - or rather because of - its exploring of a dark folklore.
Year Walk isn't just another video game, in that you won't have fun going through it. You will experience something.
Have you ever encountered an Owl in the middle of a forest, at night? Stood silent in the dark, your breathing suddenly becoming less of an automatism, while these two bright eyes were staring at you? It is a very precious feeling; one that games such as Year Walk try to convey... and sometimes succeed in doing so.

The developer was careful not to overemphasize guitar support, to avoid giving an impression that a guitar is required (which it's not), but it's a natural fit, and anyone who did some shredding with Slash in GH3 will feel right at home.  A regular controller works very well up to about medium difficulty, but I had some trouble with the higher difficulties in having to sequentially switch multiple lines very quickly, where the guitar's instantaneous any-line switching made things a lot easier and enjoyable.  Keyboard control is another option, and might actually be a better option than a regular controller, now that I think about it..

In comparison of the previous Duels of the Planeswalkers series, mainly aimed at introducing players to Magic the Gathering.  Duels 2014 was lacking seriously creativity in deck selections, as they were mainly the same decks that were in previous versions of Duels of the Planeswalkers virtually card for card.  For example Liliana's ghoul keeper deck was pretty much the same as the zombie deck in 2012, the face of M14 Chandra and her Phoenix deck is virtually the same as the 2013 version. The challenges were extremely boring and to easy to solve, as opposed to the other versions which actually required some thought and tinkering with to figure out.  The highly touted sealed deck feature was disappointing, and continuing for another sealed pool required micro transactions.
The good side is more customization, particularly lands, which comes in handy for curving mana better and more handily.  For example, Duels 2013 had a goblin deck which featured cheap and inexpensive goblins, unfortunately far to often a mana flood was in order for the deck,  Nothing quite like having 5 lands on turn 5 played and 3 creatures and an action card.
Other good things, an improved artificial intelligence.  Lack of fun and entertaining modes such as Planechase, Archenemy leads to stale gameplay is another bad addition, especially for lack luster sealed play.  At times, all progress on your deck unlocks  often get reset, leading to having to reunlock every card once again, which can be frustrating.

NOTE - This review isn't so much about the game but the decks featured. I don't have enough space for each expansion deck.
The base game comes with 10 decks. These decks range in colour and strategy, but some are clearly better than others:
WHITE
Guardian's of Light - This deck heavily features aura's and others spells that work well with aura's. It doesn't have very much removal, so it relies on the strength of its own creatures... or really, creature. It usually attacks with just one creature that  can usually be chump-blocked. Thankfully, the deck has a good number of creature's or aura's with lifelink so you can stay in the game whether they chump-block or not. However, if your one super-powered creature is killed through removal, it's hard to come back. Losing a creature and 2+ aura's from just one spell means more mana-efficiency for them.
Overall, a very strong deck if your opponent can't remove your creatures.
Avacyn's Glory - This deck's strength comes from numbers - and removal. This is a white weenie deck basically made from the Innistrad block. The deck works like a well-oiled machine, but can breakdown if a wrench is thrown in. This deck, if played perfectly, can win in a few turns. It can also play the long game with spells like Baneslayer Angel, and obviously, Avacyn herself. One of the reasons why this is one of the strongest decks is because it has many removal spells. This means this deck can stop creature decks in their tracks.
Unfortunately, many of the best cards in this deck can only be unlocked if you buy the extra unlock key.
Without the unlock key, the deck is one of the strongest in the game.
BLUE
Mind Maze - Despite the name and Jace's usual mill deck strategy, this is a highly aggressive Illusion tribal deck. The deck is mostly creature-based and can win very quickly. The big problem is most of the creatures have the "if targetted, sacrifice" clause. This can be a problem if your opponent has creatures and spells that can target your creatures. This deck has a few counterspells and a few freeze spells, but mostly relies on its strong agressively-costed glass cannons.
BLACK
Deadwalkers - This deck is a rather basic zombie deck that is very dangerous. Many of its creatures are expendable and can also come back from the grave. This deck also has 19 pieces of removal, and can keep killing your opponents creatures while it slowly withers away at their health. Some of the removal, like Tendrils of Corruption and Corrupt, also give this deck some  lifegain.
All in all, this deck is probably the strongest of the base game decks.
RED
Firewave - This is Chandra's usual burn deck. It features a few Phoenix's with a decent bit of damage spells. While this deck can be good at removing small threats, it really suffers when dealing with anything bigger than a 4/4. It doesn't feel like it has any set strategy, and kind of stumbles between burning your opponent and punching them.
It does get bonus points for its strength in multiplayer games.
GREEN
Hunter's Strength - This deck can be summed up with just "creatures". While it lacks a real direction, this deck can have its moments. It has a few pieces of situational removal and can overpower the game very early on. As the game draws on, the deck slows down a bit and the agressively-costed Kalonian Tusker's and Garruk's Companion's feel like dead-draws. The decks main drawback is that it has very little mana ramp, despite being a mono-green deck.
The deck gets a lot better once you've unlocked a few more cards, but evolve beyond "Play Creature; Attack with Creature".
Overall, a decent deck, but can be foiled by a bit of removal.
Chant of the Mul-Daya -This deck is a fascinating ramp deck that has a few big stompy creatures to finish off. This deck really falters early game and can lose without playing anything good if you don't ramp your land fast enough. However, once you've got 6+ lands, the deck gets really dangerous. It has a few All is Dust's, which can really turn the game around. This deck suffers to most from removal. Even if you've ramped up to 12 lands by turn 7, you'll probably only have 2 big creatures that don't really have any means of protecting itself from solid removal like Doom Blade or Oblivion Ring. This deck is probably the best deck at top-decking a means of winning, though.
In the end, this deck is the strongest if your opponent doesn't play any removal.
MULTI-COLOURED
Sliver Hive - Probably one of the most anticipated decks of the game, this White/Red/Green deck is a relatively new imagining of the Slivers from M14. This deck features a bunch of Sliver's as well as some mana ramp and small bits of removal. On paper, it seems like a strong deck. This deck can win quickly if you get all of the pieces assembled quickly and efficiently. However, this deck suffers once one of the Slivers are destroyed. Since they all build off each other, removing one can mean the difference. Even if they have no removal, you might still be unable to deal with them if they have one bigger creature than yours.
This deck gets a little off-focus when you add more of the unlocked cards. While this can diversify the deck, you start to lose your win condition as you start veering off the Sliver strategy.
Masks of the Dimir - This deck is basically a Black/Blue control deck. Its main focus is on discarding your opponents cards from their hand and chipping away at their health. Unfortunately, this deck really doesn't know what it wants to be: It doesn't have enough removal to really stop big threats and it doesn't have any counter spells to really control how your opponent plays. The only victories I've earned for myself was through attacking with my 4/4 flyer. Once it's killed, I rarely win afterwards.
A really disappointing deck; one of the weakest in the game.
Enter the Dracomancer - This Black/Red/Green deck's main focus is playing dragons. This deck has a decent bit of ramp spells that go into the few dragons (7) the deck starts with. It has a few weenies that can protect you and deal small bits of damage, but after a while, they're only good for chump blocking. They can later be used for the few cards that can Devour them.
Similar to Slivers and Mono-Green ramp, this deck gets bowled over once you've destroyed the few big creatures this deck plays. Devouring the weenies sounds like the right thing to do, but it actually helps your opponent pin-point which creature to destroy. Removal is minimal in this deck.
This deck does get better once you've unlocked more cards, but initially, this deck is weaker than the Dimir deck.
So there you have it: the initial ten decks this game offers. I hope this helps you decide whether this is the right version of Duels of the Planeswalkers or not.
I've even taken the liberty to rank the decks personally, based on how well each deck has played against each other:
1. Black - Deadwalkers
2. White - Glory of Avacyn
3. Blue - Mind Maze
4. Green - Chant of the Mul Daya
5. White - Guardians of Light
6. Green - Hunter's Strength
7. White/Red/Green - Sliver Hive
8. Red - Firewave
9. Black/Red/Green - Enter the Dracomancer
10. Black/Blue - Masks of the Dimir

Being my first real video game, Bioshock Infinite has a special place in my heart. The gameplay aspect is well done, but the main thing that people usually praise this game for is its story, and with good reason. Infinite does a great job of expanding on the world and themes explored in the first two games while also managing to be a relatively standalone experience that doesn't need the context of its prequels to be fun and enjoyable, even if the gameplay - while once again, is well done - can get a little stale at times. 9.5/10 recommend.

Addictive as hell! I like that there are waves of different types of button inputs so that you constantly have to be on your game. Really great polish on this one too, it's lesson in how to make a simple concept look and feel amazing.
Rich Story

My biggest issue with Infinite, is that they went with a form of time-travel/alternate-universes that makes any plot entirely pointless/meaningless. As soon as those elements really entered into the story, the entire plot/story of the game lost any hold for me as a result, because literally anything could be rewritten at any time.
The game also felt very very linear. This is normally fine from a story perspective, except a linear story makes no sense for the open-ended ("infinite") time-travel/alternate-universes based story that the plot is based around. But where the linear nature really comes through is in the level design. I don't remember the level design of either previous Bioshock feeling this linear (though they might have been), but at least some of that is probably due to the difference in setting.
Mentioning setting, Columbia is amazing, so amazing that I just want to go and explore it. Unfortunately this highlights how linear the levels are, because Columbia makes you want to just wander around it, it is frustrating to be limited to the linear path.
In all, Bioshock Infinite feels like a missed opportunity. It really feels like the story and setting would lend themselves far better to an open world type game, while combined as they are to very linear levels and a linear plot, they feel constrained and held back from their potential. That said, considering the game came out nearly five years ago, and its low price accordingly, it is well worth the price, and practically a must buy when it's on sale.

I mourned the loss of so many colonists only long enough restart the game. After getting the hang of things, though, I found my storage domes full of food and other supplies. Now, I've got a pretty big colony going that's self sufficient and overflowing with food to the point I turned a large section of the planet into a damn parking lot to let people land and use my facilities in exchange for prestige or cash. To be honest, I think the colony feels more like a truckstop now than somewhere that's trying to survive. I even have a sign out front next to the landing pads welcoming people to "Circle J's."
Overall, I think the game is on the right track and the price point is fair. It's definitely fun to play. I do agree with other reviews, however, that the game lacks content. I think there needs to be more things to build and aim for. Once you find the sweet spot between building to survive and whoring your resources out to the needy, you pretty much lose the need to do anything, except for replacing colonists who either found themselves on the wrong side of a meteor or died gloriously in a gun fight. Other than that, it's like watching an ant colony.
But I'm not sorry I bought it. It's definitely worth a play.

Year Walk is a beautiful, unique experience, and despite its length, it is well worth the price. While this is considered a horror game, its primary draw is its clever puzzles and deceptively quaint and calming atmosphere that seem to take some inspiration from Tim Burton films. The sound design is excellent; both the music and sound effects are extremely crisp and know exactly when to go all out and when to draw back. There are even some music-based puzzles that will rely on your sense of pitch to be able to solve. However, most of the game is very quiet, with little to no music in many sections (though what music is there is quite well done), and only the eerily realistic sound of footsteps crruching in the thick snow will accompany you.
One of the key selling points of the game is its focus on Swedish folklore, which is told through a companion app (included in the Steam version) and, while it is not necessary to read, I highly recommend going through it so you will know about the different creatures you will encounter on your journey. I found myself fascinated with the folklore itself, and some of the legends are truly frightening. However, the horror elements are mostly intermittent and not exceptionally scary (most of the "scary" parts I would classify more as unnerving than outright terrifying), I think this game is perfect for anyone who is new to horror games and will do a good job easing you into the genre.
However, despite my glowing recommendation, I would not recommend playing it on PC if you can get it for another device. This game was originally developed to be played on mobile devices, and while the cursor is perfectly functional, it feels a bit clunky and does not have the same seamless feel of dragging across the screen as using your finger. I would say the ideal version of the game would be the Wii U version, as it has the touch controls of the mobile version, the convenince of having the companion act on the GamePad, and is presented on a large TV to let you truly soak in the visuals. However, if you don't want to play on mobile and/or don't have a Wii U, you experience will not be significantly hampered if you choose to play it on PC. Highly recommend,

I'm not sure I get the hype here.
First, I'll say this game is a port, and it feels like it. There are some graphical issues, and the slowing down thing when you accidently hover over an investigatable point is annoying.
The Characters: All pretty stereotypical anime characters, The macho gang leader, the fat fan fic writer, the loli goth, etc. I don't really have a problem with it, but some people might.
The Mysteries: I wasn't a fan of how this was done. Part of the game is gathering clues, but when it comes time to present the evidence, the clues you gathered often seeem to take a backseat to the "plot twists" the npcs provide. Makes you feel like you wasted alot of time, and you kind of did.
The Mechanics: Past gathering clues, The rest of the mechanics are basically a series of minigames, none of which I found that interesting, and were sometimes downright frustrating. The worst part is you have to suffer through these crappy games, after you have already figured it out, and made a pretty good case for it,
The Dialogue: Good Lord! I would not call the writing good. Some of it might be translation, but some of it is just bad. However worse than all that, is that there is soooooo much of it. I'm fine with dialogue heavy games, but I was bored to death scrolling through the mountain of often repetitious, poorly written text. Tack that on to the "Trials" taking forever, when you have already clearly established the culprit.
Plot: To summarize, you go to a school that is supposedly for high school students who are the best in their particular activity, only to discover that you are locked into a murder game with said students. This is of course all overseen by an evil (maybe robotic) teddy bear. I didn't get far enough to really get into the overall mystery of who the bear is working with or who the actual mastermind of the murder game is, but just the character actions were baffling. That might be because I started skipping large swathes of dialogue.
The Price: 30$ for a port from a 2010 handheld game? Glad I got it on sale.
Edit: Someone pointed out that it's for a 2013 remaster. I stand corrected.
Basically, I wouldn't bother with this game. If you are really interested in the story, go watch the anime. I heard there is almost no difference plot wise.
TLDR: Handheld port, with annoying mechanics, poor writing, and clue gathering that doesn't amount to much, all hidden within mountains of text. Do not recommend.

Just finished playing The Witness and oh boy am I glad I'm done. What felt like 200 hours and like a bad crack addiction is finally over. The game is set on a beautiful island and bear some similarities with the Myst series. In The Witness you play an individual that wakes up in a dark tube that is set underground. You soon find yourself trying to get out and what meets you are puzzles, puzzles and more puzzles!
I didn't really know what to expect from the game when I first booted it up. I have always loved games like Myst, Syberia and Riven and at first I thought The Witness would be something similar. While Myst is more of a clue solving game The Witness is straight up a puzzle game. At first that really put me off. I was really looking forward to explore this beautiful island, find clues and solve them da Vinci Style, but the game soon had me hooked and I was solving puzzles left and right.
The Witness is is really a beautiful game, the scenery changes throughout the island and so does the puzzles. Some of the puzzles are really easy and some of them makes you pull your hair in agony. There's also a story element to the game, and as you go along you will find yourself closer to an understanding as you gather bits and pieces of it.
Overall I would say that the game is really captivating. In the beginning you feel like a fish out of water, but as soon as you get the hang of the different puzzles and styles you can easily find yourself playing for hours.
I didn't 100% the game, but I did finish the story element and that alone took me about 18 hours.
Positive points
Variation of puzzles
Scenery and game engine
Length of the game
Negative points
I would have loved to have a side element to the puzzles, like the Myst series

I recently sold all my crappy csgo skins for this game.  This game is if not the best game on the steam store.  It tells one of the best stories in gaming that not everyone can pick up on in the first playthrough.  It tells the story of a pug running away from his past.  He has the face the trials of life, both physically and metiphorically.  On his long journey, he faces everything from his own imagination's problems, like desire (thus shown by currency) or his own physical fears, like heat and water.  He has to travel through a near future's war-based economy and landscape.  This can be shown the traps set up and the currency without a value.  Weather itself even poses a problem for him.  When defeated, the end can be shown in two different prespectives. The first is an infinite time loop.  He could very well be trapped in his own personal inferno that he can't cope with.  He has to keep traveling until he can conquer his inner fears or reach happiness.  Either that or whenever one pug is defeated, another follows his leaders path, giving the game a good sense of leadership and belonging.  The gameplay alone is a reason to buy the game.  It is simple yet innovative.  Unlike other games today, like Battlefront and Fallout, it brings something new.  Save your 60 dollars and buy this work of art.  GOTY.

Hero Of The Kingdom is an adventure point and click R.P.G. developed and published by Lonely Troops. You are the young son of a humble farmer and you're thoroughly enjoying your peaceful life of agricultural management until one day when malicious bandits suddenly raid your homestead and burn it to the ground. Worse yet your beloved father has also gone missing just as a darkness begins to fall over the entire kingdom. What's a boy to do...overcome his fear and set off for adventure on a dangerous journey to places unknown as you try to find your father of course!!!
Hero Of The Kingdom does an excellent job of mixing multiple genres into one solid package...lite roleplaying, adventure, hidden object and point and click. This was my very first foray into a hidden objects game and I must admit that I rather enjoyed it. The visuals and animation are nicely done and fit the game perfectly. The title has a terrific soundtrack and the sound effects are fantastic as well. One downside, however, is the length of the title as I finished this game in under five hours but it was well worth the time spent. There are also some achievements to hunt for if that is your bailiwick.
I was also pleasantly suprised to find out that there is a sequel available, Hero Of The Kingdom II, which I plan to play as soon as I pick up a copy. Anyone looking for a casual game that covers more than one base, genre-wise that is, would be remiss to give this little title a chance. I don't think you will regret it...recommended.

The word game is being generous.
Broken match making across the board PVE, PVP, CO-OP.
Half the matches start with no players.  Then other players trickle in.
No good if you are the first one in the match then all of a sudden it is 6 on 1.

Match making is also sorted by 3 levels of ships.
For example you might be in a level 7 ship fighting against level 7 and 8 and 9 fighers.

Extremely pay to win.
Premium ships start at full synergy, max level.
Premium ships never die, you never have to pay to repair them.
Nothing is cheap either.
For example, it costs $10 in premium currency just to change your name.
Premium ships are way overpriced.
Broken trade system.
Game was never meant to have trade at all.
Congratulations, it still does not.

Watch_Dogs has received very bad press, and to be perfectly honest, I see why; however, I personally enjoyed the game and found it to be well crafted. I admit, there are many problems with this game, and there were many times when I was ready to give up on it all together, but I am glad I did not, for I ended up enjoying it greatly.

Many say the story was unsatisfying and short, but it was refreshingly new. How many times has there been a video game made wherein the main character's emotional attachments were his sister and nephew rather than his significant other? I found the lack of a romantic story to be very relieving. I will gladly conceed that his technology based, scratchy voiced vigilantism was not new or original, but given the situation and "context" of the game, everything but the scratchy voice was fitting and well placed. If you did not find the story satisfying, I do not believe you were playing it correctly. Additionally, if you did not play any of the "Digital Trips," you missed out big time.

The gameplay itself was intricat and rewarding at times, but it was also over complicated and frustrating at others. Like most games that have open-world driving, the driving was, well, really bad. The on-foot movement was more than acceptable, allowing players to climb, run, and mantel with ease. Combat was actually pretty well done. With the exception of the occasional "What the F**k? I didn't want to get in that cover!" it was acceptable as well. The stealth was, like most Ubisoft games, absolutely the same; there is a bar that appears when you are sighted, and if it fills up, they are alerted to your presence, which isn't a bad system by any means, just the same. They did, however, seem to put a lot of work into stealh, and because stealth was such a large part of the game, that was very important. The multiplayer was original and weird, but I cannot say I enjoyed it. I am a very unsocial person, which is why I tend to play singleplayer games more than multiplayer, but I decided to give this one a try. I got hacked twice and hacked someone once; I foiled both hackers and prevailed when hacking, but I did not enjoy it. Well, I did enjoy the second time I got hacked, as I randomly saw an NPC run through a crowd and almost run into me, so I pressed melee, beat the crap out of him, and won the hacking scenario even before it alerted me that someone had hacked my game. I feel sorry for whoever it was, but if you want to hack me, you'd better be ready for me to fight back.

The performance is highly debatable. If you were running an Nvidia and Intel based PC, you would have no problem running it at high settings, but if you had an AMD based PC, well, you were out of luck. It was very amusing and interesting for me to see how horribly AMDs could run the game and how Nvidia partnered with Ubisoft to "optimize" the game for Nvidias. I am not saying Nvidia screwed AMD over, but let's just say I will never buy an AMD, especially because of all the game developers that Nvidia is "partnered" with. Additionally, there's Uplay and all of its lack of anything good. It has gotten better, but for a while, people could not even log into Uplay to play their games. The downloads were slow, and it was just plain horrible.
Overall, like I said, I was fond of this game, but it has obvious problems that I know a lot of you will find to be deal breakers, especially you, AMD peasants. If you don't mind them, however, feel free to buy the game and decide for yourself whether you like it or not.

Ubisoft makes some INCREDIBLY hard games to understand sometimes, and almost IMPOSSIBLE games to review. Still, I think I'll try my hand at this:
Amidst all the criticism, I find myself on the fence between what works well and what doesn't in Watch Dogs. Lots of people claim the driving sucks, the hacking is too easy, Aiden is a ridiculous cardboard mash-up, and those abundant lots of people are basically correct; Watch Dogs struggles with its own identity as an open-world stealth-action game. Honestly, the trailers were pandered toward the GTA crowd, and the game sells itself as a "do-whatever-you-want-because-no-morals-on-the-streets" type. That's quite literally EXACTLY what the CEO of Ubisoft wanted, and maybe what a few paying customers wanted as well. Strangely enough, when looking deeply into the eyes of this game, a trace of desperation can be seen glaring through the right angles. This is what I mean: GTA ruined this game. Let me explain that which I mean:
GTA's got that running stuff? You can run around and shoot people and hookers and whatever? I don't own them, but I've seen enough of those games to understand why people like them so much. You can do whatever and shoot and run and die and it's all fun and it makes money. Something in these faint glares of desperation tell me that Watch Dogs didn't want to be the game it became. Look at that sad excuse for "online open-world with up to 8 players". You can't do ANYTHING but shoot people with 7 other people who can also be shot. Does that look like a well-thought-out feature? Does it look more like someone from upstairs slapped that on the finished (or should I say unfinished) product? Now look at all that phat loot someone can rack up with a few presses of the X button (don't lie to yourself and say you used the atrocious keyboard controls). Money signs! Yeah! What do I do with it after I bought all the sweet guns? Wait a minute, what do I do with the sweet guns? Where's the value in all this crap! I thought I was supposed to be hacking stuff!
The point is Watch Dogs was a would-be underdog turned manufactured sludge that ultimately proved rough for the people who didn't notice those desperate glares and smooth for the people who did. Look at my freaking play time. I've proabably played more of this game than anyone else on the review board (entirely because I spent 90 hours completing the game and another after Uplay deleted my save). Personally, I look on the bright side of what the game could have been and actually mananged to be. For example, I find Aiden a hollow enough character that I can freely step into his shoes and be the raspy-Batman guy I've always dreamed of being, and I often take some long walks and drives around the grey cityscape and think about the modern life and how drastically the reliance of technology has changed our society. It's a kind of dream game for me, and for everyone else who was perfectly aware of how painfully hollow and pointless the gooey center is. For those who couldn't really figure out how those remnants of an excellent game were supposed to be played, frustration was much to be had.
All in all, this game shines brightest when it's telling you what to do, taking you through epic and explosive missions, and refusing to let go of your hand. You may WANT to let go of it, but doing so will force you to realize that nothing valuable actually lies beyond it. Those worthless parts are where GTA laid waste to the open-world genre in its entirety, and forced Watch Dogs to pick up the pieces in an attempt to catch up. What proves to be actually fun and engaging will make you wonder why this game is an open-world game in the first place.
Buy it on a REALLY good sale, and maybe it'll pull you in for a good while (probably not nearly as long as me). If not, well, at least you didn't spend $70 on it like I did. Throw yourself a party in that case.

before i begin id like to state that i thoroughly enjoy rts and base builders, and clocking in over 600 hours between starcraft 2, command and conquer, and age of empires series so i can easily say rts is my most played category of game.
pros
-unique game in a changing environtment
rng environtment every time you play

cons
-terrible ai, just god awfull
simply put the dumbest, faultiest AI i have seen in any game. I've played games where the ai killed them selves as they started construction on non critical strucures before connecting water scources to produce 02. this means that they can only work one task at a time, wich is gives you almost a 50% chance to fail right off the bat as you are pressed for time, cant set up more than 3things at once and need at least 6 structures before night fall to live. its worth noting that if you dont make a storgae before at minimum ingame noon and have the means to charge it, you will fail.
-unable to macro
the game at its core is a survival, rts with economic elements, so it would stand to reason to give the player macro elements to better manage a large scale base. these however are not present untill aproximantly your 15th to 20th building providing you build to survive [counting outside structures] and these macros are simply 1-work normal 2-stay inside 3-no work and stay inside [3rd used only when a shooter infiltrates]. on top of this you have no control over which structure is built first. you may put it on a higher priority but the ai chooses to ignore this.
-unable to micro
there are several types of units in game ranging from medics, to biologists, workers and engineers (additional units/bots are used later), all of wiich are used for unique tasks. you start with several workers, and after the 1st night or so you will need to become self sustaining so you will need a working mine and production center. for the mine you may have up to 3 workers to mine ore, then workers send the ore to processing where additional workers will process it. in most rts or even base builders alone, you would be able to set workers to tasks or production areas (ie mine metals, or work feilds) but this base has no way to instruct workers to any task. you may put a room on a high priority but the workers will ignore it just the same. This game is probably one of the simpler simulation games out there, but it's consistent in it's world engine and rules. There are few surprises once you learn the mechanics of the game, and the game allows you to fail due to dumb decisions or just dumb luck.
From a challenge perspective, once you achieve a foundation you're most likely going to succeed unless dumb luck happens - ie days worth of no wind and storms, so your power accumulators all dry out. However, I see that as a bit of realism, we cannot always just use math and rules to predict success. I like the randomness and just having to abandon a base where you just messed up.
I would like to see the game evolve even further. More complex dependencies, a bigger world, capability to teraform parts of the planet (in particular the hard levels you may find yourself surrounded by mountains making you unable to build out).  It would also be interesting to see procreation so a base could grow without having to receive immigrants. Having skill levels for the personnel would be interesting too. Anyway - you get the drift.  It's a nice game to just kills some hours with now and then.

First, the bad parts: ♥♥♥♥♥♥ grammar of the english translation and some technical issues here and there. It can get pretty annoying if you are a grammar nazi, but in my case i got immersed in the story enough to stop noticing the errors. The most annoying feature are quick time events... i mean really? In a visual novel? And they are an instant game over without explaining what happened?
Thankfully, the story is very well constructed, and the game was cheaper than a potato(it cost 0,09 euro at the time that i bought it), so it's very hard to complain.
The postapocalyptic(or present-apocalyptic, since the apocalypse starts during the game) setting is crafted pretty well, though not without plot holes.

The Witness is a beautiful and intricate game that guides you into it's puzzles efforlessly.
Pros:
* Beautiful Visuals (Crisp simple textures and geometry with just the right amount of detail.)
* Easy to understand puzzle mechanic that has tons of depth.
* Themed puzzle areas are well defined and fit together nicely on the island.
* Lots of "Aha!" moments!
Cons:
* Sometimes puzzle difficulty can ramp up quickly.
* Some puzzles rely on color, which can be extra difficult for color vision deficient folks like myself.
I would say this is a must-have game if you enjoy more slow paced puzzle games, especially ones set in a world you can explore and try to understand and piece together like Myst.

In its own, quiet way, The Witness seems to read you and determine your reactions before you can even think about it.
The setting, dreamy and eerie at the same time, will have question the nature of what surrounds you, craving for answers that will hardly come.
Aside the fact that I loved the simple genious of the puzzles, I loved the whole concept.
Every piece of information counts. Without information we are just characters in a pretend world, only knowledge makes things real.

I'm not sure I get the hype here.
First, I'll say this game is a port, and it feels like it. There are some graphical issues, and the slowing down thing when you accidently hover over an investigatable point is annoying.
The Characters: All pretty stereotypical anime characters, The macho gang leader, the fat fan fic writer, the loli goth, etc. I don't really have a problem with it, but some people might.
The Mysteries: I wasn't a fan of how this was done. Part of the game is gathering clues, but when it comes time to present the evidence, the clues you gathered often seeem to take a backseat to the "plot twists" the npcs provide. Makes you feel like you wasted alot of time, and you kind of did.
The Mechanics: Past gathering clues, The rest of the mechanics are basically a series of minigames, none of which I found that interesting, and were sometimes downright frustrating. The worst part is you have to suffer through these crappy games, after you have already figured it out, and made a pretty good case for it,
The Dialogue: Good Lord! I would not call the writing good. Some of it might be translation, but some of it is just bad. However worse than all that, is that there is soooooo much of it. I'm fine with dialogue heavy games, but I was bored to death scrolling through the mountain of often repetitious, poorly written text. Tack that on to the "Trials" taking forever, when you have already clearly established the culprit.
Plot: To summarize, you go to a school that is supposedly for high school students who are the best in their particular activity, only to discover that you are locked into a murder game with said students. This is of course all overseen by an evil (maybe robotic) teddy bear. I didn't get far enough to really get into the overall mystery of who the bear is working with or who the actual mastermind of the murder game is, but just the character actions were baffling. That might be because I started skipping large swathes of dialogue.
The Price: 30$ for a port from a 2010 handheld game? Glad I got it on sale.
Edit: Someone pointed out that it's for a 2013 remaster. I stand corrected.
Basically, I wouldn't bother with this game. If you are really interested in the story, go watch the anime. I heard there is almost no difference plot wise.
TLDR: Handheld port, with annoying mechanics, poor writing, and clue gathering that doesn't amount to much, all hidden within mountains of text. Do not recommend.

While I enjoy the story of this game (particularly some massive twists towards the end), I found the gameplay itself very slow and tedious at times - so much so that I preferred to read a summary of the story of the current sequels rather than play through them. I like puzzles, and I like logic, but this game used them in a way that slowed down the story and made it less compelling. I've ticked that I recommend this game, but that is only true with the condition that you are okay with playing a slow-paced game, and playing over a number of sittings over multiple days or weeks (there are 6 chapters, so about a day per chapter would make sense). The pace is really more like reading a book than playing a game (it is a visual novel, after all).

Incredibly written, incredibly stylish, and incredibly enjoyable. If the idea of Ace Attorney meets Persona (with just a tiny sprinkling of SAW, as it's set in a death game, on top) seems good, this is the game for you. The sequel's just as good too.

Danganronpa is a murder mystery visual novel and it is incredible. I went in not knowing much about the game, not expecting much either but I was blown away by the captivating story, memorable characters and stunning art. After an hour of playtime I couldnt put it down, even after finishing the main story Im still having so much fun working for achievements and entertaining myself on the extra game mode.
To summarise the plot, you are locked in an academy with 15 other students and the only way to leave this school, is to kill another and get away with it. Once a murder has taken place, a trial will be held in which you must reveal the killer based on the evidence you have found.
Characters develop throughout the game as more gruesome murders take place, paranoia become a common theme while true intentions and secrets are revealed. The students are so well written, all having vivid backstories and deep personalities it is easy to become attached to them, causing you to fear for your favourite characters life.
If you love solving mysteries, plot twists, eccentric humour and compelling characters then you will love this game. I didnt think Id enjoy continuously clicking through the novel and although it was tedious to begin with for me personally, it quickly faded when i felt myself fall immersed and in love with this engaging, fascinating, wonderful story.
If you like the Ace Attorney franchise, you will love this game.

It's a combo of the Phoenix Wright & Persona games! You solve murder mysteries (This game is graphic & doesn't pull any punches with its content so be prepared for a lot of bloody deaths) using the Phoenix Wright gameplay style with the artwork of Persona.
There is a lot of dialogue in this game so be prepared to read and follow along with the story. The story (Much like the games it's based on) can be convoluted at times, but it'll click by the end. This game does not pull any punches with its content so be prepared for a bloody game with gruesome deaths.
The voice acting & music are awesome (really gets you pumped up in solving crimes).
I would highly recommend this game if you are into Phoneix Wright & Persona!

Danganronpa almost always puts Style over Substance and it may take some time for the player to care about any of the 15 characters in this visual-novel-murder-mystery-mash-up. But the murder cases are fun and most of the time filled with unexpected twists.
The gameplay is basically Ace Attorney with a timer and an overall more fast-paced way of presenting evidence. Also the soundtrack is pretty great.
If you are not into Anime, don't bother with this game unless you really need some more murder mystery in your life. And if you are into Anime, don't watch Danganronpa. It's bad. Get the game instead, it's pretty good actually.

Battle Royale meets Ace Attorney's fever dream. It's balls to the wall.
Just look at that title, rolls right off the tongue. "Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc." On that note, what the ♥♥♥♥ is a Danganronpa? According to four seconds in google, it means "Winning an argument with a bullet" which is surprisingly accurate and not at the same time.
The plot goes as such. You are an average Joe Schmo high schooler by the name of Makoto, who is so painfully average that he might as well be a harem anime protagonist. But out of sheer luck, you get drafted to Japan's premier high school by getting your name pulled out of a bag. On the first day of class, you waltz in and promptly black out, only to wake up and find yourself along with fourteen other unlucky sods that are trapped in a barred-up school with no way out. Your captor is none other than an animatronic, temperamental bear by the name of Monokuma. There is a way out, but with a catch - you must kill somebody and get away with it. If a body is found, an investigation is held, followed by a class trial. If the killer gets away with it, the rest of the class dies. If the killer is caught, they die.
As a result, the game starts off with a proverbial bang, and the tension only surmounts from there. As you navigate through each twist and turn of the story, getting clues as to how everything got to that point, you learn more about your fellow classmates, their quirks and flaws. Tension is the name of the game, and boy, it delivers it in spades. That's as much of the plot one can divulge without getting into spoiler territory, but my recommendation is to not look at a guide or anything else related to the game's story, as you'll probably end up spoiling yourself. Going in blind is giving yourself a real treat.
Gameplay-wise, it's like a cross between a visual novel with occasional minigames and first-person "dungeon crawling" in it. In this regard, it's very similar to something like Ace Attorney, in which you gather up clues and facts before the case begins in hopes of finding out the truth. But at the same time, the game is far less restrained in its presentation and comes off as incredibly brutal. The trial system is also interesting, as rather than presenting pieces of evidence at a certain line through a simple select, you aim a cursor at moving dialogue to counter a false statement or press an argument. There are other minor things that come with it, such as a tempo-based game to shut someone down or a hangman's gambit, in which you need to guess the right letters to form the right word. Not to mention, there are upgrades you can obtain and you can also hang out with your classmates in order to get more backstory as to who they are and what they do. To top it all off, there's an extra gamemode after the story which adds a fair amount of replayability and also allows you to revisit things you may have missed.
Graphically, the game is unique in the sense that it consists of a dreary, punkish anime aesthetic. In an age of boring, mainstream moe garbage, Danganronpa is a breath of fresh air. Even the cutesy characters are uniquely styled. In a way, it reminds me of the earlier Persona games in its presentation. While the standard large eyes and simple-faced designs are present, each character looks and feel wildly different from one another. No two character could ever be mistaken for one another or swapped without losing a core feature of who they are. The 3D segments are servicable and the paper cutout design choices evokes an odd sense of nostalgia for the Paper Mario days.
And last but not least, the soundtrack is badass. Tense moments are often riffed by the sounds of synthesizers going ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and robotic voices bringing you to the beat of the mood. Even the more ambient tracks are forboding, often blending in hints of classical instruments with modern machinery to create a disgusting amalgam that'll stick in your ear for a long time to come. I find myself of the opinion that a visual novel without a decent soundtrack is a terrible one - even with one that has a lot of gameplay elements such as this. Music is an important part of these sort of games, and if it's ill-fitting or shoddy, it can make it a forgettable experience. Danganronpa went above and beyond to make a stellar soundtrack that's catchy and rarely grating. That said, there are a couple of tracks that can get on your nerves. You'll know which ones if you play this game.
Danganronpa was a pleasure from beginning to end and I can't wait to play the next installment. While there are a couple of questionable moments of writing, it's not enough to knock down the score. The questionable English dub, however, does deserve to knock off half a point from the game's overall score for Byakuren's voice alone. All the range of a dying cat and a snoring dormouse.
At least you can choose the Japanese dub!
9.5/10! Worth every penny!

Since Danganronpa is a visual novel, the game's main focus is reading. As such, if you aren't into visual novels, I'd suggest you to look for something else.
The game's main gameplay revolves around you investigating places, talking to people and spotting contradictions during the class trials. In this aspect, it's VERY similar to the Phoenix Wright games, only changing the famous "OBJECTION!" to "NO, THAT'S WRONG!". If you love those games, you'll probably enjoy this as well. However, it goes a step further and throws mini-games during the trials to make things more fast-paced.
During the trial sections, you'll have to actually aim at the statements of people while they auto-play on the screen and shoot them with your evidence. Think of it as a mini-shooting game. You'll also have to play a mini-rhythm game when certain characters do not want to accept something. By the end of the trial, you have to select images to reconstruct the events that happened during the chapter.
All of these are fairly simple and fun. However, there is one more mechanic that I personally dislike due to how intrusive it feels, and that is the Hangman's Gambit. As you expect from the name, it's basically hangman where you shoot the letters that are missing from a specific word. My problem with this is that, while all the other mechanics feel fluid during the course of the gameplay, this one seems to just put a stop to the action for no reason. Most of the times, it's a pretty obvious word that you know 5 minutes before even going into the mini-game (and when it isn't, it's merely a synonym). It feels as if you are wasting time. With that said, it's very short so it's not as if  it's a major problem.
The game has another mechanic that has nothing to do with the Class Trials/investigation themselves, but exists to further develop the cast. During your "Free Time", you can spend time with any of your classmates. This leads to them receiving more background and leading the main character to understand them more. Since the main story can't really give every student the spotlight, this a nice little way to make you care more about your friends.  However, the "Free Time" feature is certainly not a big part of the gameplay. They are generally short dialogues and don't affect the story in any way and are completely unneeded if you choose to ignore them. Still, even if unneeded, they are still very entertaining to read.
I really loved the story and (most of) the characters. Yes, they are very anime-esque so if you are not into that you should avoid this game at all costs. Most characters are exaggerated archetypes that will grow on you throughout the story. Their interactions are very interesting considering how different everyone is, with each character choosing their own way to deal with the situation.
The story boils down to this (no spoilerinos): "Ultimate high school students are trapped inside a school with a perverted bear-thingy and the one who kills someone and is not discovered will be the one to leave. All the others will be executed."
Bias: The art is awesome. I just fell in love with it the first time I saw it. It just has a very distinctive feel to it. The English voice acting is mostly amazing. There are only a few lines here and there that I found weird, but those are very few. The music is also great.
I was completely blown away by how good this game is. I honestly did not expect it to turn out to be this good. I actually feel kind of bad by waiting for a sale since this game deserves its full price. It certainly is one of the best visual novels I've ever played.
TL;DR: Buy it or face despair~!

When you're dying from Ace Combat 7 News Drought™ and you see a game like Sky Rogue during the Steam summer sale (perhaps assisted somewhat by Ace Combat Fan's livestream), there's only one thing left to do. This marks my second (and perhaps last) purchase during the 2017 summer sale, and I must say it was a good decision, indeed, especially for an Early Access title.
Sky Rogue hardly stands up to recent Ace Combat titles (or similar) in terms of detail, but this game isn't trying to - it has a charming, simple, yet consistent art-style that is easy on the eyes, and it contains plenty of varied, unique designs for aircraft to go along with that style. The heads-up display is easily readable, and the UI is also simple and easy to use. Unlike some titles, I won't be able to ramble on here about graphics artifacts or the rendering of bees flying between the blades of grass, but this game nonetheless more than 'does the job' visually.
Sky Rogue comes with an array of unique retro-style sounds for its weapons, aircraft, and UI, and all more than do the job - weapons, in particular, sound distinct from one another and memorable, especially the long-range air-to-air missiles. The soundtrack is quite fine, though it can become slightly repetitive as each particular 'zone' in the single-player mode uses one track at the time of this review. While you might opt to turn down the in-game music and start playing
instead, the game's own music is quite alright by my book.
While I have yet to test it on a laptop, it performs perfectly on my desktop, as one would hope. I have also yet to encounter any bugs that impede progress in any way, leaving me quite impressed with this Early Access title. In fact, the only bug I have encountered was when a ship decided to sail through the land - hardly game-breaking, but...
to say the least. Based on other reviews, however, I have no reason to doubt the performance on less-than-stellar machines.
As a fan of the classic Ace Combat formula, I found all that (and a little more) here in Sky Rogue. The basic premise is simple: Choose an aircraft (or, as the game calls them, an aero), pick out up to four weapons and a piece of specialized equipment to load on-board, then launch off the deck of your floating carrier-blimp to complete your objectives. Weapons come in a variety of shapes, sizes, and for different purposes; various types of guns, air-to-air infrared, radar-guided, and dumb-fire missiles and rockets, plus bombs, and some unique pieces of kit to replace the ordinary flares ensures the game not only has plenty of replayability, but also supports various flying styles to complete your mission. My only real complaint in regard to the gameplay overall would have to be the lack of proper dogfight AI as of the time of this review. Enemy aeros will happily chase after you and fire off a missile or two, but will then veer off in another direction before coming around again - I haven't been in any tight turning fights yet, something I hope to see in later versions of Sky Rogue.
Most of the time you'll spend in Sky Rogue will be in singleplayer, either in the dynamic campaign, endless mode, or custom scenarios. The campaign starts off simple and ramps up in difficulty the more missions you complete, and as the name suggests, your progress will be reset if you crash. Fear not, however, as any unlocked weapons and aeros will stay; only upgrades and campaign progress are lost - though this is for the best, as the upgrades do significantly empower your aero and its weapons, and would make the early stages a bit too easy. I have to say, though, that there is plenty of replayability in the singleplayer alone, and it is, no doubt, enough of a draw to bring in most fans of arcade air combat.
As of the time of this review, multiplayer comes in the form of a local split-screen cooperative campaign mode, with two 'aeronauts' for the price of one Sky Rogue. It's just as fun as single-player (if not more so thanks to the addition of a comrade to help you down your foes), though I do hope to see proper online multiplayer in the future, as well as perhaps an adversarial dogfighting mode in addition to cooperative play.
Sky Rogue does come with Steam Workshop integration, and much to my adoration the first mod to appear on the Workshop was the ADFX-01 Morgan:
A host of other mods, including new aeros and missions, have already been released, though one might want to keep in mind the less consistent visual style with community-created aeros. Still, having reached this point, I can say Sky Rogue has checked all the boxes I hoped it would.
For any would-be Aces in search of a respite from that insatiable excitement for Ace Combat 7, Sky Rogue may prove to be just the game for you. Indeed, I can see myself still playing it long after Project Aces' newest title finally releases, as it is just that fun and dynamic - and, of course, just different enough - compared to replaying older Ace Combat titles again and again to earn a spot on my favorites list. Forkbeard, you've done something not many others could, and I commend you for it, and hope to see it grow further as time goes by.

Guitar Hero x shoot em up
The game is basically a guitar rhythm game mixed with a shmup. You have notes coming at you from the right side of the screen which you have to hit at the correct time. At the same time, there are projectiles coming at you from the left side of the screen which you have to avoid. When done properly, your "avoidance" maneuvers and your "strums" follow the beat of the music.
There are three control schemes, all of which are viable. If you have a guitar from a console rhythm game (360, PS3, Wii), that can be used to play the game. Alternatively, you can use your keyboard either to mimic a guitar, or in shooter-style, where you move the ship up and down with WASD or the arrow keys. Shooter-style is a bit more precise, but more tiring on the finger you use to control ship movement. Guitar-style is a bit more fun and spreads out the workload over all of your fingers, but certain maneuvers are a little tougher to pull off accurately.
There are multiple difficulty levels, ranging all the way up to five fingers. You cannot use your own music -- you play one of the ten premade tracks. Fun party game in any case, and can accommodate various skill levels.
