I finished Retro/Grade in 1 hour. No, that's no typo, you read it correctly: ONE hour. It consists of 10 levels, ranging from easy to medium mostly (also depending on the difficulty you pick, obviously). Don't expect a shoot 'em up here, as the screenshots might suggest, but a rhythm/music game where you have to press or hold buttons at the right time.
It's definitely colorful and the music is pretty good, but the game is just too short and way too expensive. Yes, there are challenges to be completed which might increase the replay value a bit and yes, there are other difficulties to choose from. But to be honest, I doubt anyone will actually play or try these after completing the game, except for the gamers who want to 100% every game out there.
Retro/Grade is a solid game, and believe it or not, but despite it's shortcomings I did enjoy it. But considering the current asking price I'd suggest you wait for a sale.

Definitely worth checking out as a strange little indie rhythm game, especially for a low pricepoint.

This game was very overhyped and that was its downfall.  This game is good, but not in the way Ubisoft made it seem.  It is missing many features that many people, myself included, would have liked.
You take on the role of Aiden, a freelance hacker who is trying to get revenge on the people that ordered the hit on him, which in effect killed his young niece.  You fight using your wit of computers and a very nice extendable cane.
The Story: 7/10
The story of Watch Dogs is decent, but lacking many things.  Aiden isn't relatable as a character which makes him very hard to relate to while you play through his adventure.  The story has a couple of plot twists but nothing that a person who is paying attention could have caught onto at least half an act before the event.  The story split into parts is nice and allows the player do go off and do their own in between story acts.
Side Activites: 4/10
This is where this game falls flat.  There are plenty of side missions like taking out gang hideouts, stealing cars and taking them to a drop off point, poker, virtual reality, taking down thug caravans, and hacking passerbys as you walk down the sidewalk.  However,  these activities are very lack luster and quite repetitive.  The fixer missions(stealing cars) are very annoying at sometimes and seem almost impossible to complete.  The same goes for the caravan missions.  The virtual reality and poker are boring and nothing fun is implemented in them. Hacking pedestrians is a way to gain money and unlockables at first, but as the story progresses it just becomes useless because  you can buy materials for crafting or the craftables themselves and not to mention you have a million dollars to do it with.
Multiplayer: 6/10
The multiplayer was a great idea in concept, but fell short in execution.  You can get into other peoples' games and try to implement a back door virus (which basically means walk near them and hold the execute button than go hide) is fun for the first couple of times but is very annoying because the game gives the player your hacking a circle on their map which shows where you and it gets smaller the closer you get to winning.  Unless if your very good at hiding, the player with usally find you because they can hover their reticle over you for half a second and it tells them that your are indeed the jerk that invaded their world while they were heading over to play high stakes poker.  The race games are horrible because driving in general is like your on ice sliding back and forth.  The free play is fun if your playing with a friend, but Ubisoft didn't implement any activites for you to do while in freeplay.  You can't redo any of the side missions and basically all you do is run around shooting civis so you can get a car chase going.
Combat/ Crime Mechanics: 7/10
The combat in this game is one of the redeeming factors in my book.  Your hacking is actually viable because you can distract a guard with their cellphone by making it go off which also distracts people near them.  The stealth is good and if you play your cards right you can take out a whole enemy group by distracting them, taking them down with either a melee cutseen or shot to the head with a silenced pistol (which is unlocked from the beginnning of the game :)).  The car chases were okay.  The whole idea of taking down the cops with barriers and then hiding with a blackout is fun, accept the godamn cars ARE ON ICE.  Another pet peeve of mine is your crime scale. You can run drive around breaking property or smashing into other cars being a♥♥♥♥♥♥  But the second you hit a pedestrian(which is going to happen since your DRIVING ON ICE) or shoot your gun, the whole goddamn police force is on your♥♥♥♥♥ready to kill you.
Music: 5/10
The sound track is horrible in my opinion. It matches the feel of the game but the music is by people you've never heard of and usually you just turn of the radio and go on youtube on your browser.
Closing Opinion:
This game had potential. The setting and whole aspect of the game is cool.  But in the end, execution fell flat and this game is just another play and pass type of games.  Maybe Watch Dogs 2 will redeem this series?
Story: 7/10
Side Activities: 4/10
Multiplayer 6/10
Combat: 7/10
Music: 5/10
Final Vedict: 6/10

Ive played this game on and off since I first saw it, the gameplay is very fun is you like fps shooters and are too lazy to play actual flight simulators, but the game is built around addiction and grinding.  If you never put any money into the game you will progress very slow, and if you do put money into the game you progress slightly faster and will be baited at every corner to put more money into the game.  The developer is quite possibly one of the worst as far as updates, any new content will be overpowered and very grindy or very pricey on the loot crates.
The US population has always been scarce with many changing their setting to "any region" this means they get into combat quicker but pings will range from ~120 for europe which is playable to ~180 for Russia which is not competitively playable, the lag effects the handling of your ship, quick ships such as interceptors wobble around like they're drunk and if you're attempting to use anything for cover you'll smash into walls because you can't control your ship.  I havent been sucked into south asia for a while cause I never do any region but the ping for me there is ~280
Some of the  "end game pvp content" of dreadnaught battles is overtly more focused towards the russian/eu timezones, PVP for these in US timezone is typically non-competitive which a few corporations tending to control the game.
The game is not just pay to progress it is also pay to win, there are some "premium ships" that have slot layouts and bonuses superior to other ships of their class in the same rank/tier.  Example Sigurdr > Cerberus
last night I queued into pvp for us with a T11 interceptor I was in a 10min 1v1 with a fellow with a T13 Long range Frigate and Tackler,  After I killed him 6 times to 0 I sent him a tell and apollogised for being stuck in a 1v1 match, and we ultimately stopped shooting each other and let the match count down in the last minute.
Typically the only time we get US pvp is when you get a group of 6+ people to set region to us and queue into pvp at the same time with the same tier ships, otherwise you're likely going to be sitting there for a while.
I do not suggest this game to anyone, I've put time and money into it, the developer has taken it nowhere postive, and each patch seems to effectively make the grind to the end even longer.
Also a large part of the us population being so past ~T9 is the grind, It also feels like since the US pop is so low they've adjusted the prices/grinding in an attempt to raise profits but its probably having the opposite effect.
Even if the grinding wasn't so terrible the consistent "new content" balance issues are a deal breaker,  Any new content will be overpowered to fuel demand for loot crates and it will be nerfed once the sales quota has been met.  Also some of the GUI is designed to misdirect you like "currency exchange"  At the top it says exchange of galactics standards(cash bought) for credits, in the chart below it lists Credits first then GS and at first glance it looks like you're able to buy gold for credits.

There is not enough community, you have to wait several minutes to find a match.
Key parts for building ships are not available as battle loot or mission rewards. Basically, you have to buy game gold if you want to build good ships.

I just finished it and I'm too flabbergasted (positively) to write a proper review. And besides, I don't want to risk spoiling it. It's an enchanting, worthwhile, paranormal experience that goes in unexpected directions. A bit spooky, but never scary. I wouldn't call it an "adventure game" proper (point & click) since it's so short; it's more like those artsy walking simulators but I don't mean that in a bad way. Again, it's great though not everyone will appreciate it. Learning about the ghastlier aspects of Swedish folklore was fun, too. Make sure you get the second ending as well, even if you have to use a guide (I did).

This game manages to take mythology, folklore and tales from Sweden's past and weave them into a pilgrimage of sorts with an interesting narrative with nothing more than simple puzzle mechanics. It's a lot more fun than many other games of similar ilk and it's clearly down to a lot of care and attention during development as well as a knowledge and emphasis of the lore. I found it short, quite different and refreshing and interesting to play through.
The things that carry Year Walk are most definitely the simple ambient design and the weaving of the story and lore into the world while staying true to the subject matter. It's carefully and smartly done and often feels as though you're part of a fairy tale or dark bedtime story as much as a video game.
Being a port of a mobile game, it suffers from a lack of depth from the gameplay, and while the hands off approach definitely works well with the narrative and story, it's still an issue when compared against other longer, deeper titles at the same price. Having said that though, I feel like had the game been any longer it may've run the risk of adding less enjoyable puzzles for the sake of length rather than story and ultimately, while short and simple, everything is fun to experience and discover.
Priced at $5.99/£4.79/4.99€ on the Steam Store at the time of review, Year Walk isn't expensive and probably isn't overpriced, but there may be better alternatives around the same price range on Steam and mobile. Due to the interesting world, atmosphere and content though, and the simple enjoyable play-through, there's no reason to avoid Year Walk and it's worth a play for anyone looking to waste an hour or so.

Plenty of things to optimise and figure out, all mildly challenging; it's a more casual base building management game. It's a bit lacking in control over the AI (see next paragraph) and has no story. It's entertaining long enough to be worth the money.
There is no base planning mode and you cannot pause construction, while getting your base design right without planning is hard; it will work, but it will contain errors that are costly to undo. While you can prioritise a building, it doesn't always work, e.g. bioplastic is not taken to a prioritised lab while a non-prioritised construction is being built (turn on yellow alarm to work around it, or don't plan ahead).
There are a lot of artificial constraints, some make the game more challenging, some just don't make any sense, e.g. in order to build a wind mill you need to first have built a solar panel. What makes the game more challenging is that your whole base needs to be connected. Connections cannot bend and have a min and max length.
The UI is good, though the top left build menu could have been replaced by circle navigation menus or a hotkeyed popup in the center of the screen to reduce mouse travel.
The AI is good enough, it works well, you just have to accept that colonists are selfish shortsighted beings. If there is one meal left, a colonist may starve because another colonist with 20% hunger felt like having a meal. A colonist may die because his O2 levels dropped too low for him to feel like doing any work while he would have lived if he simply had finished the O2 generator he was building. In some regards your colonists are just plain stupid for the sake of adding a little challenge, e.g. when there is a sandstorm, your colonists will continue working outside even though they are losing health; they need you to sound an alarm (which requires a control center) to realise they probably shouldn't work in a sandstorm.
As you play the game, you'll find out some buildings should never be used or some things are best bought through trade instead of built yourself. This is alright, having every element in the game have its use in one or more situations is better.
Replayability is low. Once you've got it figured out, it will become grindy. But it takes long enough to figure it out to make it worth 10 euros if you're a cheapskate. It's worth the 20 euros (about 1 euro / hour of fun).

* What do you do?
You build a base to house colonists, you rush to get the first roots grounded then work on balancing your whole self significant thing between usage and storage.
* Initial thoughts?
I have been playing these types of game for years because they are fun, challenging and allow you to be creative. From Warcraft to Sim City, through Command and Conquer to Banished (each being totally different). This game had me playing for 2 days, finding new features and unlocking new ways to advance your colony.
* What about after that?
Once you unlock each (limited) "tech tree" item, passed the first planet. Your not really left with much to aim for. You will move onto a couple more planets, but your left with the same tech to unlock, the same patten of "build-reduce-increase-build more". Your only aim now is to just expand that particular colony until you question your time. You repeat the same housing, food, O2, water and energy arrangement over and over again. Creativity then become monotonous.
* Well, what you you suggest?
Again I like these types of games, but something is missing these days with this and Banished for instance. Its lacking anything fresh, its watered down.  I get the feeling its half finished, one day the dev team gave the game a whirl and thought "thats alrite" "I'ld buy it" rather than "how about ground water levels" or "research into better robots etc". Maybe something more to manufacture.
* Verdict!
It is a well balanced game, everything is weighed out nicely. The initial challenge is good and rewarding. But I just wished it had a little more to do, I would have liked a more adventurous dev team. I would love a game with the depth of games from times of past, but feel like they stopped half way out of boredom. Its worth the £15 and you will have fun, but like Banished (for me) you get to a point, click quit and wont be bothered with it for some time.

The Witness is arguably the best game I've ever played.
Yes it's just line puzzles, but they're some of the best damn line puzzles in an absolutely beautiful environment. That's not why I adore this game though, I love it because it doesn't teach you anything.
There's no tutorial, no popup, no explanation, nothing. Every single new puzzle element is learned through discovery, but your first encounter with each element is a beautiful introduction to each element.
Say for example the first set of panels that introduce white and black squares. The first one can be solved entirely ignoring the new element by going straight to the goal. The second one doesn't accept that solution, so you have to figure out why. Once you've figured that out, it's twisted again to make sure you absolutely understand what you're doing. From there it's evolved and extra elements are added until you're entirely sure of the concept it's showing you, and then it starts giving you more and more difficult puzzles.

This game is longer than it easily could have gotten away with for how much quality and depth is put into it.
Unlike most detective games, I've actually had to use my head the whole time, remember things people said, and pay attention from the start, not just click things till the game told me I did good (cough LA Noire cough)
The way it does this is through the trial system, and trusting you to piece together clues and recent events you've hopefully remembered.
It has to help you a little bit since it's a video game and not real life and it has no way of knowing what you know otherwise, but it tries to not settle for simple (process of elimination) multiple choice situations, which is really important. It usually has you go through several links so that you can't just guess or assume, you have to have figured out the answer for yourself ahead of time, if you mess up enough you'll take enough damage to lose because you lost credibility.
It's maybe ~20 hours of gameplay per run, it doesn't have much replay value once you know how the cases work, but it does have a bonus mode at the end which is neat. And I'm even then replaying it now even like rewatching a movie.
Also worth noting, the plot is great, it's not just a convenient setting for murders, everything was well thought out, I didn't find any plot holes. It has a great mystery to it.

The PC version of Final Draft is possibly the most comprehensive bit of kit for embarking on this screenwriting malarky, but MovieWriterPro is worth having as a backup, or even as a cheaper alternative. Oddly enough, it loads up with a hideously written demo. The first thing to do is erase it, as it appears to be written by someone who has just emptied a tin of alphabetti spaghetti all over your monitor. But once you remove the graffiti, MovieWriterPro does have all the nice little features which are very helpful to those of us who are terrible at organising their work. Simple things such as character profiles, backgrounds, objectives etc. are all neatly catagorised so the author can drop in and out and tweak / save progress with relative ease. All the basics for screenplay writing are drawn from the rather simple, yet effective template. You can insert 'INT.', 'EXT', 'DAY', 'NIGHT', 'LOCATION' etc. into each portion of text with simple clicks of the mouse. Stuff like that might sound marginal, but it does help speed things up. You can use this software without the need for any extensive tutorial, so it's basically straightforward. I can't say I'd use only this to write a screnplay, as that would involve being stuck at the monitor too long, and that apllies to the desktop version of Final Draft too. I personally find using the iPad version of Final Draft the most practical, although it's features are limited. But I would recommend MovieWriterPro as a helpful assistant, as you can keep plenty of helpful information nicely and neatly filed, for any project.

Despite being Early Access, the game is fully playable and even has a proper (and difficult!) final level. The selection of aircraft is quite varied and overall fairly balanced, and the same can be said for the weapon selection. The workshop is crammed full of custom levels and aeros, which I believe will continue to make this game worth coming back to for years to come. If you want a fun, challenging flying game, this is worth looking into.
The single player 'campaign' spans a 13 day/level offensive on a bunch of randomly generated islands out at sea. Each day sees the player given a random key target or several to eliminate. Once the mission is complete, the player then has to return to base alive - or can hang around and bomb more ground targets or shoot down waves of aircraft. The longer the mission goes on for, and the more damage the player causes, the harder it gets.
You earn cash/credits for every kill, with the reward set proportionally to how valuable the target was. This cash can be used to either purchase upgrades for unlocked weapons and aeros, or be able to make mid-mission landings to repair and rearm. If you get seriously battered in combat, you might want to run home and pay the repair bill, because if you get shot down, you start over from the beginning with no upgrades and no cash.
Dying isn't a wholly bad thing, however. In fact, death is the only way to unlock and obtain new weapons and aeros. So though death may set you back to the beginning, you may now find yourself having access to better equipment, too.
Overall, the game is very addicting. Thanks to being easy to start playing, and quick to becoming brutally hard, I certainly can't seem to stop playing.

Some features I would like to see:
- I'd like to have it when I select one of my equipped weapons in the loadout menu, the menu would jump to my current weapon and show its stats rather than the last one highlighted. It makes it a little difficult to compare weapons as it currently is.
- Since this is an arcade style game, I'd like to have a timer on missions. Completing the objective and turning in earlier would yield additional rewards. This would make the mission objective a priority, rather than clearing everything in each stage to get the most money for upgrades. Total anihilation is fun, but I tend to pick one plane with one loadout every time, instead of upgrading planes for different purposes - making combat a little repetitive. The timer would give players motivation to focus on creating the best plane for the mission and a greater sense of accomplishment when their creation took out the target in a single strike.

Now that I completed almost all achievements with only two challenges left to try it's time to write a review on this enjoyable and extremely addicting game. If you love city building strategy games and survival ones like Banished, you should definitely check out this game, as this is essentially a space variation. You will -- presumably -- have to restart each planet and each challenge multiple times to perfect your strategy, but that's exactly where the fun starts, at least for me. In fact, after a hard start it can feel really cozy and quite satisfying to see your base safely secured by lightning rods amidst a thunderstorm. Especially as the graphics are beautiful. The mechanisms are logical even though they're sometimes not what you would expect -- e.g. if you can build a spaceship why are you not able to dig a tunnel through a mountain or build a floating component on a sea? -- and as probably everyone else I would wish for more planets, more resources, more buildings. is one of those abstract games that more closely resembles a piece of art than a video game.  The gameplay is extremely minimal, while the true soul of the game lies in its ambiance, art direction, and core concept.  This is the type of game which won’t appeal to everyone.  For those who appreciate the occasional artsy game with minimal gameplay, then you will probably find
interesting, relaxing, and enjoyable.  If you are looking to play a traditional video game, you shouldn’t be looking here.
The gameplay is roughly 3 parts “walking-simulator” and 1 part puzzle game.  Navigating the area is your primary “challenge,” with the addition of a few puzzles you will have to solve.  The answers to these puzzles can be a bit obscure, but there is a competent hint system if you want to avoid being stuck for too long and just want to enjoy the
of the game.
The core concept of the game is also quite interesting.
is based on the Swedish folklore of
, which I had never heard of before playing this, and which I found to be interesting.  After learning a bit about it, I was able to see that the developers did an outstanding job bringing the idea to life in video game form, even despite its inherently simplistic design.
The art direction, soundscape, and overall ambiance of the game make for a mysterious atmosphere which is very well aligned with the core concept.  Admittedly, the graphics are quite simple; but the simple graphics fit the simple game.
Short, interesting, and atmospheric:
makes for a fun little experience that is well-produced and should be easily enjoyed by anyone who truly appreciates the genre.

I like to think of this game as a puzzle inside a puzzle inside a puzzle game. The game begins with the simplest iteration of its 'puzzle', with a line and a dot that you draw to open a lock; and before you know it, you're seeing those lines and dots everywhere - even outside of the game itself. In that sense this game is maddening, and some of the puzzles are infuriating and perhaps even impossible without cheating if you have colour blindness or a bad monitor or hearing impairment. The island itself though looks absolutely stunning, but what sets this game apart from a lot of other puzzle games is what's going on behind the scenes. I mean, to some extent the game does that for you anyway, but like with the ending, sometimes you just have to step away from the whole thing, clear your head and start again. I can totally understand why this would put some people off, it's certainly not for everyone. Recommended for those that enjoy aimlessly walking around beautiful scenery, and for those that enjoy overthinking maddeningly frustrating puzzle games.

This game is longer than it easily could have gotten away with for how much quality and depth is put into it.
Unlike most detective games, I've actually had to use my head the whole time, remember things people said, and pay attention from the start, not just click things till the game told me I did good (cough LA Noire cough)
The way it does this is through the trial system, and trusting you to piece together clues and recent events you've hopefully remembered.
It has to help you a little bit since it's a video game and not real life and it has no way of knowing what you know otherwise, but it tries to not settle for simple (process of elimination) multiple choice situations, which is really important. It usually has you go through several links so that you can't just guess or assume, you have to have figured out the answer for yourself ahead of time, if you mess up enough you'll take enough damage to lose because you lost credibility.
It's maybe ~20 hours of gameplay per run, it doesn't have much replay value once you know how the cases work, but it does have a bonus mode at the end which is neat. And I'm even then replaying it now even like rewatching a movie.
Also worth noting, the plot is great, it's not just a convenient setting for murders, everything was well thought out, I didn't find any plot holes. It has a great mystery to it.

A Low poly, fast running shoot 'em up flight sim with excellent gravity and some really fun newtonian physics. The game looks and sound great, I particularly love how the sky is visualized in this game. The designs are great, i'm a sucker for low poly, retro and minimalism and this game really satisfies all of those wants for me. The controls took a while to get used to. I've got a keyboard and number pad, so i'm not able to get any sensitivity in my roll, which to me is the biggest downside of not having a controller. Once i got deep into rebinding the controls i was able to dial a setup that i like quite a bit right now.
Once i became adjusted to the controls and felt a little more confident, i realized just how much FUN this game is! I feel like I have been waiting for this game for a long time.  The way certain the rockets deploy and smash your target is so satisfying, and there are so many different missiles that all seem to have a real functional and balanced value. I've not unlocked all the guns yet, but the ones i do have feel fantastic and once again INCREDIBLY SATISFYING to kill targets with. I have never felt more like an airborne badass than while playing this game.
The physics really take this game to another level for me. My craft always feels really heavy, and i'm having such a great time pulling all the way back on the throttle, and using the gravity to pull myself around a corner. It's hard to explain, but i feel like a viper pilot in the BSG reboot, and i've not really played a game that's been able to capture just how much i have wanted to do that. It feel like 45% BSG, 35% realistic sim, 20% Star Wars. I don't know, i'm really going out far for this interview because i'm so passionate about this game.
I love the fact that i lose all my money and upgrades upon death, it really makes this game feel like a great arcade game that i can play over and over again. If there is one thing i could ask the developers, it would be to implement a handbrake command. I would love the ability to just kill my engines, free fall and flip through for a second and gun the engines so i can be right over where i would want to be on the target. This would push the game to stratospheric levels of entertainment for me, and i imagine it would put a considerable impact on the total amount of sun on my body over the course of my human life.
I really do feel like i have been waiting for this game for years, and i'm so happy i spent the money to buy it, and i'm THRILLED to see what's to come. Thank you developers for making something that I really enjoy!

I purchased this game while having the winter/Christmas season in mind. I paid $5.49 CAD so my expectations were not that high at all, but I ended up having a ton of fun.
The game consists of 2-4 players having a snowball fight (Human or AI). You start with 5 hearts each and the aim is to “kill” the other player. During a match you can use a light or heavy shot. A heavy shot being performed while holding the throw button to charge it up. The winner being the first to kill X amount of people or being the leader after the time limit is up.
This game contains 4 maps: Park, Graveyard, Castle & Mine. While they do not affect the gameplay or strategies you will find different objects to take cover behind in each. The store page boasts 30 characters to play, but 25 of those characters need to be unlocked. This isn’t a bad thing though. The character does not affect the gameplay either and from what I could tell, are completely aesthetic.
If you want to unlock everything it the game, you will need to play a minimum of 73 matches. The matches being broken down into 17 for Park, Graveyard and Castle, with the Mine level needing 22 matches to obtain the unlockables. The unlockables in the game come in the form of characters and powerups. Power ups range from grenades for higher damage to a snowman sentry which will fight the enemies for you. The matches themselves can be set from 2:00 – 20:00 and from 5 – 100 kills.
Besides the single player deathmatch modes, you can also have teamplay deathmach modes as well. I’ve only had a chance to play with one friend locally, so I can’t say if it can support a full 4 player local game or not. The settings for the team-deathmatch can be set to 2vs2 or 3vs1.
Overall, I enjoyed the characters/costumes and the gameplay was fun. For the price, I would recommend this game.

VA-11 Hall-A is an incredible experience. This game is one of my all time favorite visual novels and checks off so many pros in my needs and wants in a game such as this!
+The characters are memorable and beautiful designed. The protagonist is a very relatable and likable character as is with all the patrons you serve, your collegues and even your own cat!
+The overall pixel art atmosphere of the entire game is addictive and never becomes an eyesore (unless you aim to design your bedroom to be a visualized LSD trip!).
+The sountrack is composed by Garoad Music, a really fun and friendly company whom I've even contact before regarding work for my own project. The soundtrack is beautifully done in VA-11 HALL-A and is even a central rise to Garoad's usual popularity! Well deserved, I'd say.
+The story and narrative is incredibly well done and presents such an amazing quality and consistancy similar to that of other excellent story-driven games!
+The Cyberpunk world is immersive and incredibly interesting! I'd love to get to know more of it, though the game goes over a lot of aspects of their dangerous daily lives in VA-11 Hall-A.
- The bartending gameplay quickly becomes dull and no real difficulty gets posed besides when you happen to not purchase something Jill (The Protagonist) is interested in, which even then, only makes you not have a tooltip shown of what you're making while you're making it, which doesn't matter much anyway because the patrons tend to just say what they want right before you make it!
- There's not a whole lot of choice present in the game and not too much that can be accomplished regarding alternate routes, resulting in little replayability.
Overall beautiful and amazing game and I recommend a good playthrough!
(Guilty confession: A group of friends actually held an online text-based roleplay completely based on VA-11 Hall-A and it's expansive world potential. Thank you Sukeban Games and Garoad!)

Going to post a review for Space Colony and Planetbase in the same review, as the games are very similar, yet at the same time very different.
I bought Space Colony first, expecting the game to play like Planetbase.  While both games involve planet exploration, and creating a base, and surviving and thriving, eventually making a profit, that's where the similarity ends.  Both games play alot alike in those aspects.  And both are quite fun with the "base" demands of the game.  As they both play like Space City sims.  If you like games like Banished, or maybe even Cities:Skylines (A bit of a stretch) you would probably enjoy both games.
Now for the huge differences.  Planetbase plays alot like a simulator.  The base game is a bit more difficult, as you need more juggling to keep your base alive, as more colonists arrive, you need to balance alot of aspects such as food production, Oxygen production, Electricity production, water ect.  Even though the new colonists are a welcome sign to your base, they are also a detriment.  Your colonists themselves handle as you would expect them to.  They work to the best of their abilities, but need the basics including some relaxation to keep from losing morale.  The lower their morale, or the more injuries they have, the slower they will work.  But they are astronauts, and know what their job is.  They also aren't afraid to share beds, or other equipment. You also have to grow food for your astronauts, or create bio meat for your team to survive
Space Colony on the other hand is more like Planetbase if it was on the Jerry Springer show.  The astronauts all have their own set of skills, and likes and dislikes.  The base game seems easier, but you have to deal with clashing personalities, and each astronaut has a very flamboyant personality.  And part of the job in the game is to get your astronauts to go talk to each other on couches, to help them gain friendships.  Some you get to fall in love with each other, and they all need separate assigned beds or they won't sleep.  You also have to deal with what seems like constant spawning of aliens, which will destroy your equipment in your rooms.  As far as food production, in this game, you build a mower, and you need to find plants growing on the planet and the mower turns the plants into green space juice.
Personally I find Planetbase to be the much more enjoyable game of the 2.
Space Colony 5/10
Planetbase 9/10

DISCLAIMER: I would ABSOLUTELY recommend the physical board game! My reasons for not recommending this game are entirely around the digital game.
Also: SPOILERS. Odd to hear for a board game... game... but believe it or not this review will spoil the solo games for you.
So. I can't recommend this game for 2 primary reasons:
1: The online is absolutely dead. Any time I have tried to connect there have been less than 30 souls online with less than 5 games (typically full and in progress). Suffice to say, unless you are gathering a group of friends there is not much multiplayer opportunity here.
2: The single player is poorly coded. I very quickly learned that no matter what, the "murderer" at the end of each solo mission was predetermined. This is to say that if the doctor was the murderer on a given solo mission he would be the murderer every time on that mission (even if the companion cards were different). It got to the point that I could just get to the end of a level if I lost it the first time without bothering to get any of the clairvoyance tokens and just select whoever I saw the murderer was in the final voting. Pair that with the fact that you will quickly learn exactly what picture to play for what outcome because the computer's "scoring" of each card seems pretty static as well. You really miss out on the human element of variance and your gameplay becomes very rote. Luckily there are very few levels in solo.
All in all a disappointing rendition of a great board game.

This game is so simple but awesome enough to play twice! It doesn't take a nice PC/Mac to play this because it's simply clicking (but it feels like you're doing more). Here are the things I love about this game:
It's sort of like an I Spy game in which you're trying to find resources in various landscapes - so that feels like a mini game in and of itself. And as you progress, you have to go back and look at old maps/landscapes to see what suddenly appears now that you have the skill to gather/hunt it, etc.
There are a few crafting/assembly lines you can use to make money. Many you must use to progress in the game because you need a various item. For example, you end up needing bread quite often to heal/sleep and to help others. You can buy the grain, take it to the mill and pay for it to be ground into flour, then you take it to the bread maker, and then you sell it for a small profit. It takes patience but I love that it does because the reward is all the greater.
It has acheivements which are super fun for completionists. I am still trying to get all of them - so close! I can't find a couple of things on any of the maps! But that is fun to me because it means more time playing the game of I Spy.
The story progresses perfectly without hitches. There are no glitches and everything you need is basically given to you if you focus on progressing through each map before you complete everything in it. The more maps you have the more opportunities you have to gather/hunt/find the stuff you need for free. It also unlocks more things in the maps you need to go back to anyway. I can tell this game has been thouroughly tested for bugs.
It's fun to make money in this game! Due to the assemply-line type of things like bread or potions, you end up doing some simple math to figure out who gives you the best deal on the supplies to gather, and who will buy what you've gathered for the highest price. Also, it's fun to figure out which camp is cheaper to camp in based on what resources you need to camp there.
I can easily play this game in windowed mode at work. When I have nothing to do but want to look busy, I just pull it up and play. The simplicity of it makes it easy to be disracted from and come back to just to pick up where you left off.
My only complaint is that the story is your typical saving someone you love just to find out that you have to defeat a bad guy to save everyone. That being said though, the story was fun enough.
This game has obviously been translated from another language and is hilarious to read sometimes. Everything makes perfect sense but it's said in a way that sounds like a literal translation from one language to another with no account for the differences in grammar/common use of words between the languages.
I think anyone who likes the types of things I mentioned above would love this game. My mom doesn't like most games, especially not adventure/RPG games, but I honestly think she would find this fun due to the "puzzles" (where to go to get what to solve various tasks) and the I Spy part of it. Be warned though - if you play windowed you need good glasses or good eyesight because things are tiny and very subtle. To me that makes it more fun though.
PS the only reason I have logged over 100 hours on the game is because I've left it open in the background at work. Being anal about all the acheivements has given me about 10 hours of gameplay, versus the 4 others claim to have gotten out of it.

I originally wrote this game off as nothing but teenage pandering visual novel drivel, considering the type of people who sung this game's praises were the type of people I'd want to avoid, but it finally went on sale and I figured I'd give it a chance, because there's nothing worse than staying ignorant. And I'm very happy I did, as a huge fan of the Phoenix Wright series I feel like I wasted too much time not playing this game. I've played a decent amount of visual novels, so I'm used to the short-ish playtime. Not so much this game, it's absolutely packed with content and collectables.
The characters are all written to be large stereotypes straight out of japanese culture, which I expected, but it makes for some interesting dialogue during downtime. The game really harkons me back to Neon Genesis Evangelion where there's a great balance between the constant threat of doom looming and the casual cheerful interactions between the characters which makes for a great best of both world scenario, a wide range of emotions explored. The fact that the friends you make die constantly is a big reminder of this.
My favourite part about this game is simply how satisfying it is to play. The very first trial, despite being incredibly hand holdy, had multiple twists that made me feel smarter than any case in Phoenix Wright 2: Justice for All did. Making "relationships" with multiple characters and learning more about them is satisfying, even if it is behind your average gift giving system. Even the animations during the trials scene make all your choices satisfying.
I was spoiled for this game a long time ago, I knew the first trial inside and out and I know the ending too. That hasn't stopped me from enjoying every minute of this game, and I'm looking forward to playing the second one, which I know little to nothing about.
Detective games like this exist in a very tight genre, there aren't many titles that give the authentic mystery solving experience quite like this outside of Ace Attorney and the Zero Escape series (Both of which you should play, by the way) But not only does Danganronpa deliver, it does so while also having a perfect marriage with the visual novel genre makes for a really satisfying playthrough.

Random, unsorted thoughts on the game:
Danganronpa is like Ace Attorney on drugs, LSD to be specific. It takes the general, for lack of a better term, havoc of the courtroom sessions from that and ramps it up to incredible portions while adding some new things in. The game itself is much more brutal than any AA game with its crime scenes, with you actually observing bodies instead of just recieving an autopsy report and the scenes themselves being pretty gruesome at times. The game is styled off of carnival shooting games, hence the subtitle, "Trigger Happy Havoc". Personally, the way the gme was presented initially gave me a headache, but I grew to enjoy it; especially within the cutscenes.
The game has three sections: Daily Life, Deadly Life, and Class Trial. In Daily Life, you have around four "sessions" between cases to spend with others and learn more about then while gathering skills to use in trial such as increased time per testimony or more on your "Focus" gauge. In Deadly Life, you go about the school investigating the current murder; if you get lost, pull up the map, there will be an exclamation point wherever something important is. And finally, the Class Trial is the main reason you're gonna want to get this game, as it's where the majority of action takes place.
The Class Trial plays out like a regular Ace Attorney trial session if the judge had gone insane. You are timed on presenting evidence, you can only object to certain statements, you can't press statements, and you seem to have been hit over the heads as words are spinning everywhere. However, you are given the ability to use previous statements in testimonies against later statements and your health is replenished whenever you correctly answer a multiple choice question.
Though, this is best classified as a Visual Novel, so a basic explanation of the plot is mandatory. Basically, you and fourteen other students of various likability get trapped inside of a school with no way out but a strange bear name Manakuma's "Graduation Clause": If you can kill someone and not be found out during the Class Trial, you're free to leave and everyone else dies a painful death. So now, it's up to you, the ultimately average boy named "Matoko Naegi" to uncover the truth behind the murders that take place and find a way out of the school because everyone else is an idiot who couldn't find their way out of a shoebox.
Except Kyoko and Byakuya, but they're not main characters so it's up to you.
The soundtrack is phenomenal, "Danganronpa", "Box 15", "Box 16", and "Discussion - Heat Up" being my personal favorites.
I'd recommend getting the game, though when it's on sale may be the best time for it.

I wasn't sure quite what to expect with this game, so I came into it with an open mind ready to play a casual game. Right away, I felt lost. There's nothing to indicate from the on-game screen or GUI exactly what the objective of the game is or how to play it.
A basic Google search for, "How to play Super Bomb Rush" led me to a post in the Steam discussion forum asking exactly the same questions that I had. "What do I do?" "How do I play" What's the objective?" I saw a response from the developer to, "adhere to the help menu," and of course, that was not at all helpful. Still at a loss, I went back to the game and looked at all the menus that were available to me. I came across the instructions stating to, "attack the directional arrows," but that just confused me even further. How can I attack the arrows on the left side of the screen when the bomb vibrates but doesn't move? Is it a racing game? A combat game? Tower defense? What the heck is this crazy little game?
I then came across a post from another player explaining that we were to, "copy the arrows." From there, I figured out exactly what this game is. It's like Simon, a game where you need very quick reactions to mimic button presses that are being randomly prompted by the game. Mimic the directional arrows with your joystick quickly enough, and the bomb is "diffused." This process then becomes more difficult with more complex combinations of arrows. Having gotten at least that much out of the way, I went back to the game prepared to diffuse some bombs.
It was at this point that my confusion turned into frustration and flat-out being underwhelmed by the entire experience. There were countless times that I knew I was completing the arrow combination correctly and quickly enough using the joystick on my XBox360 controller, and yet, the stupid little bomb blew up anyway. There just didn't seem to be any rhyme or reason to the game itself and no consistency to the controls.
Graphically, it was mediocre. The colors were bright and even distracting, but didn't appear to require much thought. However, when you're staring at the left side of the screen at the arrows, I guess it really doesn't much matter what's happening on the rest of the screen.
Audibly, there's also much to be desired. The sound effects give the impression of a classic standup arcade game from the 80s, and if you were gaming at that time like I was, then this bit of nostalgia might be appealing, but overall, there's just not much to it.
The user interface, sound design, and graphics all left a lot to be desired, and the lack of direction is noticeable to more players than just myself. If that weren't enough of a deterrent, the gameplay itself was inconsistent and underwhelming. I simply cannot recommend the game, but I do applaud the concept. It's got potential, but there's work to be done here.

I always have a hard time recommending Early Access games. On one hand we can have an incomplete product with the promise of future developments, on the other hand we can get in on the ground floor and help get these games through their Early Access phase. Super Bomb Rush is a game based around Dance Dance Revolution style inputs and Score Attack Gameplay while defusing bombs that currently has some weird design decisions.
Review -
The enjoyment of the game comes from the quick thinking mixed with high pressure situations. The game mixes it up by showing ‘special’ inputs, for e.g. a red arrow means you do the reverse of the direction show, a silver arrow means you have to click it last and do the opposite direction, confusing stuff. The game is paced pretty well though it can be pretty discouraging as there is no difficulty system so you’ll always hit a wall, possible game mode in the future maybe?
It also features a versus and co-op game mode, sadly these are stuck behind an in game progression wall, either score highly or play a lot of games. It feels a little silly to lock out the most interesting part of the game to players. The ‘Rush Coins’ you gain from playing the game can be used to unlock them, but you’re looking at an hour on gameplay just to unlock versus mode if you’re unable to get a high enough score in arcade.
The overall presentation is good, the game is easy to read when it comes to inputs and your current situation, the sounds really add to the game with special mention to the banging soundtrack. There probably could be some changes here and there which I discuss in the video review, but it gets the job done.
Overall I think Super Bomb Rush is actually a pretty interesting game, it’s just that the most interesting features are stuck behind weird progression walls, but that’s how Early Access works, it’s out there in an early state so changes can be made. The base game by itself it quite difficult, and fans of high tension, Score Attack, DDR style inputs will love the game, for those not as interested in pushing leader boards or grinding to push it to the limit, the game doesn’t really offer much for you.

I loved Gabriel Knight - Sins of the Fathers - the updated version and couldn't wait to play Gabriel Knight 2 - The Beast Within. Even though I knew that the quality of the game would be far inferior and was prepared for that, the only thing that kept me going throughout this game was the love of the story. I felt that the price, even at only £4.99, was still too high for the quality and age of the game. I did like the characters that played Gabriel and Gracie and I did kind of like the video cutscenes and cinematic feel. The game did not display well on my laptop and it was difficult to keep watching but what did it for me was the tedium I felt when the game was still only halfway through. What felt like aimless wandering around not really sure what I needed to do next and a small (poor quality) or tiny (better quality but difficult to see) game screen. The story kept me going. I did have to use a walkthrough more often than I would have liked due to being bored with certain parts that I really just wanted to get through as fast as possible. Sadly, I was unable to complete the game because in the final chapter the game just kept freezing just before Act 1 and nothing I did stopped that from happening. In order to finish the story I had to watch the last chapter on a youtube walkthrough! After watching it I really didn't feel that I had missed anything from not playing it myself, in fact, some parts I know that I would have struggled to complete without becoming completely frustrated. But would I recommend the game? Because I loved the first then yes, it is lovely to continue a story with characters that I like. You really need to do the first in order to understand the second. The quality may have been poor on my laptop but I am guessing that it was a fantastic game to play when it was first released. If this game was enhanced in the same way that Sins of the Father was then I wouldn't hesitate in recommending it as I loved the voice overs, the humour and the ease of play.
Much as I hate to do this, there were too many 'cons' and not enough 'pros' for me to recommend this game. Just my personal opinion.

Imagine you are watching an old movie. Technically, it's out of time...the actors look different, the colors are washed out, the sound is plastic, the movement is clumsy. But still, you like it because of what it is at its core... now, imagine  you played this one game when it camed out, when technically it was something else, and when, besides the thecnical distractions of the time,  you stood there, watching, an amazing story, with interesting and engaging characters, and you watched until the very end when you didn't have any more words, you just stood there in silence, thinking of what you have just watched. You were amazed at what video games may become, one day, some day, but today, today you are just sixteen years old and you feel lucky , because you travelled the world, across the ocean onto far away lands, places you never been (and probably you'll never be, but you never know) you travelled to europe, you don't speak german, (And you barely speak english, wich you are just learning ) and travelling (for real) is so impossible, so expensive for someone of your class, so out of reach for you,  and still, you have travelled the world, you felt in love with the romantic, the wild, the unknown. And you are just sixteen and you are so far away from all of it, but life is just beginning.... and you've already experienced something special.
That's how it felt when i first played Gabriel Knight 2: The Beast within and it still does, but in a different a way, today.
Years have passed, and of course, technically, the game is very old, it would be impossible not to note that this game is from another era, before high definition, 1080p, streaming, online movies, even before dvds, this game was on 6 cds at the time, a time when vhs analog tapes were the way to watch a movie at home, and also a time of full screens (wide screen didn't exist), and dolby digital was just something for the theaters. Sound was in mono... Its' impossible not to note that because it will be a distraction first, the same way it was a distraction at the time how good it was technicallly (during the 90s) but once you look behind all the thecnicallities (even if you played it many years before like i did you will get distracted by thecnical stuff) you will still find (hopefully) the amazing story, that is the beast within.
When the main character of this story, who is a sort of detective of "special" cases, is hired by a group of people of a small german town to investigate the dissapereance of one child, that they believe was killed by a werewolf... (yeah, of course it sounds cliche i know) you will start an expansive investigation across time and history, mixing real places with real storic characters, with some fiction. An investigation that would make you learm a little of european history, about king Ludwig II , some of his castles (that still exist to this day) the story behind them and his friendship with composer Richard Wagner, a supposedly lost wagner opera (oh yes, theres and opera somewhere, there) and all this mixed with some part fiction and lots and lots of historical research.
Jane Jensen, the writer and designer of this game is at her best here, creating a story that even played today, still resonates with all the right notes, mixing history and fiction , with the romantic, the poetic and the grotesque (and a little ghotic, allthough historically is more romance than anything else)
The final confrontation of the last act, when all present and past stories and characters come to an excruciating and devastating end, reaching from the late 1800s to the (at that time present) 1990s was something so well done, so emotional, that even today makes you stop and take notice.
Whats even more incredible, is that, many of this places exist in real life, (specially the castles) and is amazing to look and see them after playing the game for real (in youtube, or in person if you can) and how jane jensen creates a story of her own based on real characters. What's best is that it makes you wanna learn more about it, and that i can appreciate it a lot.
Finally, the music is something special in this game, made by Robert Holmes, is one of the main things that gives character to this game, the music is not only great, but it is so unique and original. Really timeless i would say. Compression wise, the music and sound in game is not very high quality. But if you are lucky enough, you may found one special CD edition that camed out many years ago wich featured all GK2 music in cd quality. The soundtrack is haunting and dark, it's like travelling to the past, walking beside kings and reaching to classic composers, all at once, is like that.
The acting and the actors in this game are at times good, and other times.. not so much, it is a mixed bag of quality, thats what it is, but still in general is good, some characters like the main villain are really great (very well acted) wich makes a difference, and the main character(s) have their moments too, for sure.
The game itself is pretty good and straightforward for the most part, excep certain parts during the final chapter wich to be honest are not very intuitive (specially by today standards of gaming) so it might be difficult there, but nothing that can't be solved with a walkthrough.
With all its negatives and many many many positives, this is the best game in the Gabriel Knight Saga, and quite possible one of the best games by Jane Jensen.

GK2 is the 'Star Wars:Empire Strikes Back' of the series, a really strong follow up to a fantastic first game, that may actually be even better than the original.
I'm on my 4th or 5th playthrough of this game since it came out many years ago, and it has singularly spawned my interest in topics such as Bavarian/German history, Werewolves and Wagner.  It's a 'pilgrimage' type game, which has me coming back  and that in itself tells you a lot of about the quality of this game if i'm willing to do it over and over again.
It's all down to the live action video, how it blends with the 'point-and-click' adventure gameplay and - most importantly - a really strong cast of actors. The star of the show/game is the 'sassy' Grace Nakamura (her relationship with Gretta pre silver heart scene, is laugh-out-loud funny!) with the actress playing Grace absolutely nailing her role in all her scenes.
Which brings us to Gabriel which, sadly,  was such a wet noodle compared to the the 'boss' he was in GK1.  Admittedly, trying to fill Tim Currys shoes is a hard task, and while the actor who plays Gabriel is endearing in his own way, but some of his scenes were awkwardly acted and worst of all was the general vibe that Gabriel's character was taken too by a politically correct stick and all had all the 'sexy ' beat out of him. He's not a complete disaster, just different and i would love to know if this was a conscious decision from the game's creator Jane Jensen and maybe even Robert Williams.
Lastly it's important to note that the game is stuck in its old resolution (probably around 600:480) which does take away from the quality of this game as a final product, but is still playable.
I'd love to see more games like this that have a strong story on real issues / places dealing with real content or 'heart' as it makes the gaming experience more meaningful.

I must admit I have been a bit torn whether to recommend this episode of "Gabriel Knight" or not, because it has a lot of cons and it really is quite trashy, but then again the plot drove me to the "Yes" side.
I had never played anything done with the FMV technique before so it made me laugh from the very first moment; in my opinion it somehow deprives the game from its typical atmosphere of tension because I think it is difficult not to smile even in front of the most tearing scenes - and there are a few - but in the end it was interesting. The nicest aspect is the high fidelity to the places which are sets to the scenes: even though the resolution is really low, I can tell you (for example) that I have been in Munich and Marienplatz DOES actually look quite like that!
The adventure is pretty impossible to play without a guide, unless you are one of the developers - or extremely smart/lucky: from the very beginning, the majority of the actions are very unlikely to be figured out by oneself but they are all obviously needed not only to reach the highest score but also to continue the game; so keep your phone/tablet at hand because you will really need to consult manuals and/or videos.
Now maybe the worst part of it all: when you launch the game, a DOS BOX emulator will start and you'll be shut out of Steam for the whole time; you will play only through that and this means:
- no access to the community nor chance to make screenshots;
- ridiculously poor video quality;

I picked up Mysterium in the hopes that it would be entertaining enough to play with my brother. I didn't realize when I purchased the game that Mysterium was based on a board game. I still haven't had a chance to play a physical copy yet. But if the physical copy is better than the Steam version, I'd like to try it one day.
In the Steam version of Mysterium, there are two different roles a player can take: a ghost or a psychic. There is only one ghost at a time. There can be any number of psychics up to seven in online multiplayer. Each psychic is given three cards that they have to guess - a person, a location, and a weapon. The cards they're guessing are unique to them. However, anyone can guess any card that's still available on the table. The ghost helps the players guess their specific cards. They do this by handing over vision cards that match up with the target cards in some way. Using the images on the vision cards, the psychics can work together in order to determine who has what cards. At the end of six rounds, the players then determine what murder the ghost was killed in.
Pros:
- Comes with a story mode that doubles as a tutorial.
- The story in said story mode is actually pretty interesting.
- Graphics are smooth and polished.
- Cards can be expanded and magnified so viewing is easier.
- Has local and online multiplayer.
- Online multiplayer has a chat so psychics can easily speak to each other.
- Audio enhances the game nicely, but is easy to turn off.
- Many promos and expansions can be unlocked - only one requires DLC.
Cons:
- Visuals seem clucky because there's so much on screen.
- Sometimes it's hard to understand why the AI guessed certain cards.
- The parts of story mode where you play as the ghost can be frustrating.
- The story mode killers are always the same, so story mode can't be played twice.
- Navigating the multiplayer window is a little confusing at first because the screen is so busy.
- It's not clear how the promo/expansions unlock, aside from the ones offered to you when you complete story mode.
In truth, I really would like to play this game with my brother still. In fact, I plan to. But if it wasn't for that, I likely wouldn't pick up the Steam version of Mysterium again. It has a lot of potential, which is why I'd love to play the physical version of the game, but something's lost in translation. Unless you're aiming to play this with friends in person without AI, I wouldn't really recommend buying this. Even then, you might be better off buying a physical copy.

It's a great game, first and foremost.
You manage a space colony, starting with about seven settlers and two robots. You have to build the basics to stay alive: an O2 generator, power sources, food etc. And it builds from there - medical bay, dorm, processing plants, bar...
It's beautifully simple in its design and it's incredibly addictive. It's also brutal - a bit of bad luck and bad timing and you can cause a chain reaction that kills everyone. For example: run out of spares? No problem - there'll be a trade ship along soon. Except just then, your wind turbine breaks, meaning your power storage starts draining, meaning you won't have enough power to last you through the night. The power out, the O2 generator stops working. And everyone slowly starts to asphyxiate. Just hope that the morning's light won't be blocked by a dust storm and will power up the solar panels enough for everyone to not die.
It's stuff like that. I've also seen some flat out weird stuff - I'm not sure if it's a glitch or a delightfully morbid game design thing, but one day one of my medics just decided he'd had enough and wandered out into the wilderness and just kept going, off the screen and presumably to his death like "nope. I am so done."
It's not perfect, however - you can't directly control the settlers or give them orders. The AI is pretty good but not perfect, so I've seen Workers who are so hungry that they're nearly dead keep on loading supplies into a ship (even though there's food nearby) to the point that they die of starvation rather than just eating and loading the supplies later. Wat. Also I've played it for 34 hours and while I've only done the first planet it does feel like I've explored all the rooms the game has to offer. It's replayable, though, to some extent.
Planetbase 2 should definitely be made and I hope they keep simplicity of the first game's design but with more control over the settlers and add more room types.
Definitely recommended, though. 9/10

This is my review of Year Walk.
Well, what a game that was. Or maybe it shouldn't be called a game. Instead, an experience in solitude. I had owned this game for over a year before finally playing it, and I can't lie, I’m kind of annoyed I waited that long. Me and My Associate decided to go through all of the games that I have not played in my Steam Library and this was one of them.
I had no idea what to expect when we started up the game. I was pleasantly surprised by how much we enjoyed it. This game is an Exploration Puzzle game with odd navigation controls. You soon get used to it and the game becomes a blast. You navigate across 2D planes in first person and hop between layers of the world. First of all, the sound design is peng. The crispyty crunch of the noise of snow under your feet is a very nice and subtle choice and puts you right in the Snowy Swedish Wilderness. The art style was reminiscent of "Fosters Home for Imaginary Kids" and really suited the shifting tone of Wonder and Dread (Not the Judge). The story is difficult to explain and should be experienced first-hand with all the pieces of the puzzle aligning to make a beautiful mosaic of Swedish folklore. I would valiantly recommend giving this Modern Masterpiece a couple of hours of your time.
Remember Dear Readers, You heard it here first. Off the record, On the QT, and very Hush-Hush.

A classic point and click adventure game with a hint of horror, Year Walk is one of those games that sticks with you long after you've finished it. Though to get the full value out of the game requires more reading than expected, it is well worth it to sit down and read until you get to the end. It's a good reminder that a game need not be lengthy in order for it to be great and it was a great game to play late at night just before Halloween.

Random, unsorted thoughts on the game:
Danganronpa is like Ace Attorney on drugs, LSD to be specific. It takes the general, for lack of a better term, havoc of the courtroom sessions from that and ramps it up to incredible portions while adding some new things in. The game itself is much more brutal than any AA game with its crime scenes, with you actually observing bodies instead of just recieving an autopsy report and the scenes themselves being pretty gruesome at times. The game is styled off of carnival shooting games, hence the subtitle, "Trigger Happy Havoc". Personally, the way the gme was presented initially gave me a headache, but I grew to enjoy it; especially within the cutscenes.
The game has three sections: Daily Life, Deadly Life, and Class Trial. In Daily Life, you have around four "sessions" between cases to spend with others and learn more about then while gathering skills to use in trial such as increased time per testimony or more on your "Focus" gauge. In Deadly Life, you go about the school investigating the current murder; if you get lost, pull up the map, there will be an exclamation point wherever something important is. And finally, the Class Trial is the main reason you're gonna want to get this game, as it's where the majority of action takes place.
The Class Trial plays out like a regular Ace Attorney trial session if the judge had gone insane. You are timed on presenting evidence, you can only object to certain statements, you can't press statements, and you seem to have been hit over the heads as words are spinning everywhere. However, you are given the ability to use previous statements in testimonies against later statements and your health is replenished whenever you correctly answer a multiple choice question.
Though, this is best classified as a Visual Novel, so a basic explanation of the plot is mandatory. Basically, you and fourteen other students of various likability get trapped inside of a school with no way out but a strange bear name Manakuma's "Graduation Clause": If you can kill someone and not be found out during the Class Trial, you're free to leave and everyone else dies a painful death. So now, it's up to you, the ultimately average boy named "Matoko Naegi" to uncover the truth behind the murders that take place and find a way out of the school because everyone else is an idiot who couldn't find their way out of a shoebox.
Except Kyoko and Byakuya, but they're not main characters so it's up to you.
The soundtrack is phenomenal, "Danganronpa", "Box 15", "Box 16", and "Discussion - Heat Up" being my personal favorites.
I'd recommend getting the game, though when it's on sale may be the best time for it.

Boy this is a hard review to write. I love this game but at the same time have so much wrong with it, even more-so than positives. (skip to the bottom for the Tl;Dr)
Starting with a brief look at the positives, the art design is fantastic, like, really, considering there really isn't all that much variation in location, there is enough color and character that the game is just a joy to look at.
The story is great, but the writing is awful (explained later on). They create the right blend of humor and progression keeping a pretty fluid pace to the game. Hell despite how much I hate the writing the way they make you care about the characters, even I can't fault that
.
MOST of the voice acting is pretty decent, which is quite refreshing to see for a dub (played in English not Japanese). That being said naturally there are a few voices which make you want to tear your hair out (though in comparison is flawless compared to the anime which is awful voice acting).
The soundtrack is one of the best anime soundtracks I've heard and for the most part fits in well with each part of the story, even if it means putting in new music for just a few sentences.
The game-play, again for the most part (I'll come back to this) is pretty solid, progressing through the story opens up chances to get to know the classmates more and allows you to have a stronger connection to the characters as it progresses. The class trials are a lot of fun too, usually keeping it quite high tempo forcing you to stay focused and offering plenty of variety adding new elements with each trial making it so the game-play doesn't feel stale.
Now for the bad.
The writing, holy hell is the writing awful. Which really isn't a good thing for a game that is very story/text heavy. For the most part the story is incredibly predictable (though I wont deny there are one or two curve balls that threw me off) making a lot of the 'who-dunnits' boring and obvious. For example

At the same time its not just predictable it can also be absurdly stupid. One thing I was never able to let go with the first case
The poor writing leads the game to be far too easy for someone who's played plenty of murder/trial/investigation games and there was only one instance I can think of where I failed a trial but that was due to learning the mechanics as opposed to not knowing what to do/say. Though if nothing else the cliffhanger of an ending does pretty much force you to continue to play the second game to find out what happened.
The characters are also incredibly generic. While they flourish in design due to their 'Ultimate' ability they are all given a stereotypical look for said ability. Hell I haven't played much of the second one yet but I've seen enough of the characters to know that a lot of them have far too many similarities to characters from the first (but that doesn't really belong in this review). Another issue is A lot of things that happen through-out the game make most of these characters hard to believe sometimes. Like how your character goes from a total dim-wit to a super-sleuth after just a few trials is ridiculous. Or how a certain character
is easily one of the most stupid and aggravating characters yet somehow can survive this whole killing game.
Going back to game-play, there are somethings which just don't feel like they fit. Like the gifting presents to class-mates to 'make them happy' is completely useless, only there for you to progress in their report card, which in reality might as well just be updated after each free-period 'hang-out' anyway.
Even though it isn't bad per-say, the investigation portions of each chapter is dull. There are so many other better ways of making the investigation feel more engaging and actually feel like an investigation. To be fair its a similar investigation tool to the Phoenix Wright games only taking out the difficulty. By opening the map you can see the rooms with points of interest and quite often they won't even let you leave the room if you haven't done everything therefor making it impossible to miss something causing you to... y'know, investigate.
As for the class trial, for the most part like I said its solid, however there were 2 parts of it which bugged me. The hang-mans gambit was stupid. It was painfully easy and provided no usefulness what-so-ever. The real kicker though was the 'Bullet Time Battle'. While the music to this mini-game was really good and the tempo increases the further in you got was fun, the main-issue was the talking. Oh my god its just nothing but that character saying the same 3-4 lines every second which no matter which language you used, is annoying beyond belief. The tempo itself didn't change enough for the mini-game to be fun in general however meaning the later the trial, the longer your sitting there hitting the same 2 buttons for too long as their voice grates into your ear.
This ones more of a nit-pick but I personally wasn't a fan of the pink blood thing. I get that its in the art-style and it really does fit it well but honestly it just really didn't do it for me. Even more so when you come across a room smothered in blood, and its red. Like really come on please have some consistency if nothing else.
Tl;Dr, So yeah, the game, for me at least has SO many faults, from bad writing to useless/boring game-play mechanics, hell, in reality to me there are far more faults than positives to this game for me but there is something about it, some charm that it has that makes me love it anyway.  I  seriously think that anyone who's into murder mystery games or anime in general should play it, otherwise you might have a hard time getting around the writing alone.

Short Summary: Your name is Oleg. You boarded a train to Moscow, but around sixty kilometers 'til Moscow, the train suddenly stops and people start dying everywhere around you. You suspect the pink mist that suddenly appeared over the sky.
A Visual Novel with very interesting art. People are very realistically drawn, and might I add that some of them look absolutely fabulous (Nicolay and Irene, I'm talking about you!)
There actually is one sex scene, so be careful not to repeat my mistake and watch it while your mom is entering the room..
The game has actually 21 chapter, so if you finished in, perhaps, 2 hours, then you've made the wrong choice and wouldn't last two minutes in a real apocalypse.

Do not get me wrong, there really are some game-altering choices in it.
The game is very depressing throughout the whole playthrough, and I hate to admit that I almost cried at some points.
I still regret making some choices, but I refused to go back a few chapters and re-do them. I'll probably never play this game again, as it'd destroy the feelings I have about it.
Those were the most well-spent 6-7 hours I've had for the last few years.
Thank you, game devs, for this wonderful piece of art.
Thank you, for making my life a more tolerable experience.
