Sky Rogue is just as fun as, if not more fun than, I anticipated it to be when I first saw it! As a fan of arcade style games, especially ones that hearken back to the 80s and 90s, this one does just that, and flawlessly!!!
Arming my unlocked fighters with unlocked weapons and special abilities, trying things out and seeing what my favorites are, keeps me entertained and on my toes. I especially love mixing and matching various fighters and weapons too, like putting bomber weapons on an interceptor, and interceptor weapons on a bomber...! (although you have to mitigate the weapon amount to make a few of these possible...) The possibilities can get quite frantic, just about as frantic as the missions are themselves!
Speaking of missions, the missions in Sky Rogue always give me something to look forward to as well. No matter how many times I play the same three missions over and over again, trying to better my score while staying alive (because if you die, you have to start from the beginning) never gets boring, thanks to the procedurally generated landscapes and enemy placements. I can never expect to find the same set of factories, satelites, command towers and surface defense guns to be in the exact same place all the time, and that keeps things fresh. Not to mention, the missions are always straightforward as well. No special requirements or objectives, and no limitations of fighters or weapons. Pick a fighter, arm it, and go take out the mission targets. That's it! Nothing fancy! Just get out there and take 'em down!
One thing I did not expect is that after I destroy the last mission target and complete the mission, the mission doesn't necessarily have to be "over". If I want to, I can still take down the swarms of drones and fighters that have been pestering me throughout my struggle to take down the mission targets, or clear the rest of the island of its ground and sea targets.
Another thing I didn't expect from Sky Rogue is the absence of a story, or at least some form of story-centered series of objectives within each consecutive mission. However, because of how much fun I was having taking down targets within each mission, I didn't really see a need for one. And honestly, that's the best part. Because the way I see it, just as I do with any other story-lacking game (i.e. Terraria), it provides room for the player to make up their own story from their imagination. And I truly believe, beyond the shadow of a doubt, that the same can be said for Sky Rogue as well.
What really caught me by surprise about Sky Rogue was that it also has a Workshop page. Little did I imagine that people in the community of this game would be making their own custom fighters to share with others! And even though I have not yet downloaded any fighter models from the Workshop, I still think it's worh it to check it out, by all means.
Of course, I can't finish this review without talking about the graphics in Sky Rogue, and boy do they fit the gameplay style very well...! The graphics are very reminiscent to what a handful of arcades had back in the early 90s, games like Air Combat, After Burner, F-14 G-Loc, or Solvalou. While polygonal shapes and seemingly solid-colored textures can be unappealing by today's high definition/high resolution standards, Sky Rogue adorns this kind of aesthetic beautifully, and in a way that make the objects easy to discern from one another, and the game generally easy to look at.
Overall, this game, at only 4.2 hours on record as of this review, has me hooked. I think it's safe to say that Sky Rogue is the kind of Top Gun/Ace Combat flight sim arcade game that I've been hoping for. Because I never truly got a chance to play games of this style at my local arcades when I was younger, it always makes me ask myself: "Is this what it was like to play a game like this back in the day???"
So before I take off from the carrier to destroy some more drones and command towers, I'll part by saying, that this game is worth its price of $9.99, without a doubt!
*Fighter screams off into the distance.*
EDIT: I just found out about camera view changes, which include third person, first person, and cinematic mode. And while the camera in first person seems to slightly glitch through some of the fighters' models, it's nothing to be overly concerned about, and doesn't look like something that can't be changed as the game updates with time.
EDIT: Sky Rogue also detects and supports a wide variety of controllers, and especially flight sticks. However, here's a fair warning...
Once you go flight stick... you'll never go back...!!! (although I guess this is true for many other flight sim games)
After successfully being able to connect both my Logitech Extreme 3D Pro Flight Stick AND my new Thrustmaster T-Flight HOTAS 4 Flight Stick and Throttle, I have to admit it changes the game play and controls for the better, and I haven't brought myself to play it with a mouse and keyboard ever since...! So if you have a controller or flight stick of any sort, I suggest using them with Sky Rogue; you won't regret it...!

Sky Rogue is one of those few games that is a mis-mash of a couple different genres that actually works. What do I mean? Well, it's an arcade-flight sim similar to games like Ace Combat and Crimson Skies, with many many planes and a lot of action. It has a fairly unique randomly generated system where the various islands and missions are completely randomized. While this normally is a good thing, randomly-generated missions does have its drawbacks, meaning that you could either have a mission where you have to shoot down multiple Kondor bombers, followed by a mission where you have to destroy a flying corvette (not the car, but the ship), followed by a mission where you have to shoot down a Gryphon AWACS plane, etc etc. OOOOOOR, you can have multiple missions in a row dedicated to destroying command buildings or X-Labs. Which, that can just get boring after a while. However, that doesn't detract from the overall experience of playing Sky Rogue. It is a game DESIGNED to be quick to pick up, but difficult to master. And if you've ever played either Ace Combat or Crimson Skies, you should be right at home with this game. The art style is fairly unique, with bright, colorful aircraft signifying the enemy, and a slew of different paint schemes for your entire fleet of planes. Oh, and you get MANY planes. From fighters, interceptors and even HEAVY BOMBERS. I would love to see this game evolve over time, maybe with more useable aircraft added, and an actual plot. Speaking of, what IS the plot of Sky Rogue, anyway? It... Doesn't exist. It may be because this game is still in early access (and it's one of the more complete early access games out there to boot!), but as of right now, March 19, 2017 (for those reading this review on dates that are NOT March 19, 2017), this game has no discernable plot. Which, really is a shame, because this is the kind of game that NEEDS a plot besides mindlessly blowing sh*t up. The soundtrack is very good, and fits the overall tone of the game, with the same style.
Overall, I'd strongly advise spending the $17.80 to get both the game and OST.

Sky Rogue is in beta now and already feels like a finished product.  Definitely worth the $10 to take a fun trip down memory lane.

This is a desolate, surreal walking simulator adventure game with jump scares and ARG elements. Its tone is both wondrous and depressing, dictated very firmly by the Scandinavian folklore on which the game heavily leans. The game uses all the tools at its disposal rather impressively, creating auditory puzzles as well as visual ones and hiding relevant information in plain sight. Unfortunately, this may make some puzzles come off as obtuse and force people to look up solutions outside of the game proper.
I'm giving this game a "thumbs up" despite the fact that I don't want to play it again. True to the folklore that inspired the game, there is no happy ending to be found in it. From the perspective of someone who appreciates game-world lore consistency, I love this, but it still does not compel me to replay the game (for achievements or otherwise).
Personally, I find the experience to be worth the full admission price, despite the tone. You may disagree, but I still recommend picking this game up while it's on sale.

WoT-style arena shooter at its core, with some instanced open world MMOish trappings and team based PvE options, all of that in 3d and with nicely designed ships.
On top of that, the game has fairly low system requirements for what it offers, and boasts frequent updates.
Does all of that sound too good to be true? It better - while once a true F2P title with at most "pay for faster progress" options and reasonable free ways to earn premium currency, around the time destroyers were introduced, devs have been cranking up the aggressive monetization by reducing the availability of free premium currency sources and cranking up the grind for anything but the basic ships up to 11. This wouldn't be too much of an issue if the basic ships were to remain competitive, but at the time I left the game a bit under a year ago destroyers were on their way out (still overpowering the basic ships in general, they were at least given some considerable weaknesses), but the premium ships, even the downright OP ones, were summarily boosted across the board while the new "evolution" content (locked behind severe, time-limited grind) turned out to be little short of an "I win" button. This all led to, and is compounded by, the supposed exodus of players (the company behind the game refuses to release any hard data obviously, but many folks have noted long time players disappearing with fewer and fewer new bloods showing up to replace them).
All in all, great game at its core warped into toxic tripe by greed on the side of either the developer or, more likely, a meddling publisher. Give it a go if you'd like, but avoid getting attached.

Arma 2: Private Military Company (PMC) is a first person shooter simulation game developed and published by Bohemia Interactive and released in December 2010. PMC follows the events in British Armed Forces (BAF) following the success of Operation Crimson Lance and the gradual withdrawal of British and American forces from Takistan. In this DLC, Ion Incorporated have won a contract to protect United Nations nuclear weapon inspectors as they investigate the abandoned Takistani Nuclear Programme.
In PMC's Operation Black Gauntlet, you play as Brian Frost. In BAF, Frost came across as an appealing individual that was cheerful, driven, and was very caring towards the safety of his squad mates. In PMC, Frost gradually develops post-traumatic stress disorder and evolves into a mentally unstable individual because of circumstances in the campaign. Bohemia manages to deliver a story that showcases the change in mindset of Frost from BAF and PMC. The storytelling allowed me to clearly comprehend the issues he was in, the struggle of the overall operation, and how it all affected him. Furthermore, the game includes choices that have consequences and alter the story of the game, which also provides some replayability.
PMC features eleven missions. These missions include mediocre cutscenes, a first in the Arma 2 series, which help tell the story and lengthen the game. Furthermore, I completed the campaign in seven hours. Overall, PMC's campaign is fairly standard and for the first half, I was bored. For instance, I waited twenty minutes for the inspectors to complete the objective in mission three. Following mission five, the game did pick up in action and in intensity because it felt like something was finally happen, not just in a waiting pattern.
I noticed a variety of issues that affect the campaign. For instance, in mission two I was tasked to defend an airport with others. As a side task, I had to kill a sniper in a tower. Following completion, I checked the map, the squad ditched the airport and ran north towards the Nato base, allowing insurgents to occupy the airport. So, bugs like this were very frequent throughout the campaign and I noticed them more in the early portions of the campaign rather than the latter stages.
Private Military Company is an above-average DLC. The highlight of it is in the characterisation of Frost and how he changed from BAF to PMC. The campaign has eleven missions and the first five missions were fairly boring, but needed to provide background towards the operation, while the second half was much better as it picked up in intensity. There are issues that affect the game, affecting my experience of it. I recommend this on sale. It's fun and it provides a story, even if not a good one. If you have to choose between Arma 2 DLC, I would recommend British Armed Forces, then this, then the Czech Republic DLC.

Some improvements needed, but overall this is a really great game.
Gameplay: 10/10
If you enjoy either Dixit or Clue/Cluedo, there is little reason for you to hesitate purchasing this game.  At a 1/5th the price of the physical copy, with Pass & Play capabilities, I found this purchase to be a no-brainer.
If you're interested in seeing how this game is played, watch "TableTop: Wil Wheaton plays MYSTERIUM," on Youtube, to find out more!
UI Aesthetic: 10/10
The UI successfully captures the mood and keeps players engaged in the game's narrative.  There appears to be just as much artistic design included in the UI as there was in the original game pieces.
Additionally, the soundtrack is on point!
UI Design: 7/10
Functionally, the UI could be optimized in a way that is more user-friendly.
The magnifying glass capability seems useful on a tablet or mobile device, but it feels unnecessary on a computer.  With larger monitors, it would be more effective to have a "closer look" option, that scales each card up to the constraints of the monitor.
When the ghost reveals who was correct in interpreting their visions, players lack two basic functions:
1. Players cannot pause play and take an extra second to evaluate who was correct
2. Players cannot review the incorrect guesses made by fellow Mediums.
The latter can be seen prior to submitting predictions, but it would be nice to toggle that information during the reveal.
As a fellow designer, I also believe there is a better way to represent player guesses (in full table overlay), than to place small colored tokens atop images to which they often share similar values or hues.  It took me a number of play throughs to not only notice, but recognize their significance on the board.  Black is a frequently used color character, and his token looks like a paperweight that adds to the aesthetic, rather than serving a functional purpose.
Paperclip-style markers might prove more effective or, at the very least, more legible.
Online Multiplayer: 7/10
The multiplayer lobby definitely needs improvements (though this shouldn't discourage anyone from purchasing the game).
If you are looking to solo queue online, you should have little qualms about multiplayer effecting your decision to pick up this game.  So long as there is an online presence, there is an opportunity for you to play.
For people looking to join games with a buddy or two, however...  the multiplayer lobby lacks incredibly important features for creating games--a "start game" and "kick" button.
When a lobby reaches its maximum number of players, the game begins immediately; oftentimes without players being able to see who was last to join.  So, in theory, you may join a game and, just before your friend hops in the lobby with you, a stranger takes the last seat.  The game begins right away, and you won't discover that your friend was left high and dry until they tell you via 3rd party communication programs, or you deduct their absence when they fail to respond to in-game chat.
This leads me to another necessity in multiplayer...
When playing online, the only way to identify who is which character is to associate the color of their name in chat with the background color of their character's icon.  One would think it more userfriendly to provide the username of each player when a character token is clicked on, or hovered over.
Though i've yet to encounter anyone who wishes to troll games online, I find it naive for programmers to assume that a host might not want particular players joining their games, if they have a reputation of crashing the party.

For its charm, this is one of my personal favorites in the survival/city builder genre. It's certainly no Cities: Skylines, but its small-scale nature means that player decisions receive almost immediate feedback and that is perhaps what I love most about Planetbase. The slightest alteration to your production chain can mean all the difference for your colony, for better or for worse.
My only real complaint is that there isn't an option to truly customize each colonist's AI behavior, as each colonist is permanently classed as either a Worker, Medic, Biologist or Engineer. I understand that it unit classes are a vital part of the game design, meant to add a layer of tactical depth, but the ability to 're-spec' at least would be helpful, because colonists cannot be produced on demand -- you have to build a landing pad and wait for them to arrive on random chance.
Also, I was at first very apprehensive to the map layouts, which basically force you to keep the shape of your base quite narrow, but I ultimately came to appreciate the level of challenge it presents, as you really have to plan ahead for where that next building will be. I still think it would be very neat if there were an option to build up in addition to building out however. That said, don't expect to be able to build full-sized sci-fi metropolises. It's important to understand that this is a small-scale tactical builder with a micro-management focus. If that's your thing, I recommend.

I have played on Aeria Server for 4 years, I feel that within that time I can write a proper review even though I have not played on the Steam server.
Despite all the negative stuff about the game, I feel its still good. So First lets start with the negative, and then we will move on to the positive.
This games graphics are extremely dated, and they were at the time of release too.
This game is a cash cow. Which requires many micro transactions. And the majority of the items you will purchase are RNG based, the RNG IS set AGAINST the player. (examples are low hatch rate percentage when you want to hatch a new Digimon, also rare items that are required to make you stronger, and items for rerolling gear.)
You'll find GameKings tech support is really bad.
Now lets talk about the positives of the game.
If you enjoy grinding, and simple MMO mechanics you will love this game.
If you have money you can spend the gameplay is a lot more enjoyable and is catered to premium users, however most essential premium items are available in game through events or specific quests. Also cash shop items can be bought from other players for in game currency.

The game is set on the theme of Digimon Data Squad, which wasn't a bad series. compared to the majority of seasons that came after season 3. You will also find locations, and heroes from Season 1. That is the majority of the demographic that play, Its the hardcore Digimon fans.
Raids in this game are really fun, if you like to grind. World bosses appear hourly. There are also the end game raid locations that are instances which will allow you to grind them to your hearts content.
Daily items are given out for attendance, and login rewards. They also give rewards for server downtime.
Now lets talk about GameKing as a company and their plans for DMO.
For the past few years GameKing has really lacked on this game. But I strongly believe they are turning this game around, as well as their company. The reason I say this is because GMs are more active, and events are happening monthly. Updates that they promised a good while ago are now rolling out every month.
GameKing has also released a year plan for 2017 which includes. A new UI, PVP, New Raids, New locations. And I imagine more Digimon will be released as well considering what the Korean version already has.
So, I strongly suggest this game if.. You love Digimon, if you have money to spend. And if you have the time to spend. This game shouldn't be called Digimon Masters Online. It should be called Digimon Grind Masters Online. I hope this review was helpful.

It tends to be, it can't get Japanese enough for me. Just how I'm wired.

Danganropa, in many ways, is a Japanese culture mesocosm. Both of the story, the whole genre of 'entrapment game' is not uniquely Japanese but they do seem to embrace it widely, as well as the characters themselves. From the pop idol, to the baseball prodigy, to biker yankee, to hard-body martial artist, to the insufferable otaku... it's a solid selection of archetypes with a good justification for the diversity.

Visual novels, as games, will always struggle with interactivity. Get too interactive and you're no longer a novel. Not enough interactivity, and you might as well be an anime. "9 Hours, 9 Persons, 9 Doors", as an example, can be played to completion several ways and discovering the 'path' to the alternative endings is really interesting.

Danganropa's greatest failing is in the interactivity department. There is the entire 'courtroom' setting with different 'bullet' mini-games. Yes, you are able to build relationships to access more story and acquire perks, to modify those mini-games. The interactive portions are, essentially, presenting an interface where it's difficult to select the correct answer. And all the perks do, is make it easier to select the correct answer. Ultimately, it's pointless. There is one solution and only one solution for each phase.

Even if intuitively what you are doing makes sense. As a hypothetical example, we have two statements 'breakfast was ready at 8 A.M.' with 'No one had a chance to eat before noon'. Logically we should be able to present either phrases to contradict each other, but the game will only accept using 'breakfast...' as a counter to 'No one...'.

This can be incredibly frustrating as you cant figure out how they're not contradictory, and begin to desperately search for other contradictions, finally realizing you were right initially and no one bothered to allow for that flexibility. That if A contradicts B, then B also contradicts A.

Ironically enough, only after the game is finished will you find increased interactivity. Surprisingly well done interactivity, and actually something I'd like to see as a stand-alone.

All said, I do recommend it because the story is good. It's interesting and well put together. I'd probably have enjoyed it more as an anime, but the above mentioned post-game elements are a lot of fun, although it's clear that it won't have more than 5 or 6 play thrus before no challenge will remain.
Going forward as much as I found the story interesting, unless the gameplay is improved, I don't think I'll be checking out the other games in the series. However, I'm really looking forward to to new anime.

Oh those little mushrooms. I purchased this game for almost nothing and received several hours of 2D, discovery and clicking fun while under a  relaxed and entertaining atmosphere. Overall, I would have to say that I do recommend this game.  The gameplay mechanics and graphics are incredibly simplistic, but design choices and details help give the player motivation to keep playing.  A simple one was how as you progress through the game you'll not just expand your inventory, but also develop skills, which give you more options on tasks that you can complete.  This ranges from fishing to hunting, though the chief mechanic doesn't change at all; everything is accomplished with a simple click, if you have the necessary tools and stamina for it.  Part of me thinks that some simple mini-games might liven up those tasks, but part of me also thinks that could become tedious with how often you do it.  Regardless, as you complete quests you will advance in these skills, allowing you to achieve more, and find more hidden objects lurking on the screen.  I found this motivating, as I would scour the screen looking for items that I could sell, as gold is absolutely vital to get anywhere in the game.  In general the game gives you enough freedom to achieve certain things in the order you deem fit, as well as how far to advance in certain aspects, that you don't feel stuck or too tied down, even if there is a degree of linearity in quest advancement.  It does help that the game is short as you never feel like you're straying too far away from your main quest, as inevitably you will finish any side quests and only have one method available to you to move forward.
I wouldn't say this game couldn't stand some improvements though, as there were some design choices that I wasn't a fan of.  For starters, considering how simplistic everything is in the game, I would have hoped that when you click on a task to complete that it would process almost instantly so you wouldn't have to wait to get your results.  This was especially annoying as you discovered mushrooms, eggs, and chests, as you'd see several of them in a new area, but have to wait on each one before you could click on the next one.  This same issue plagued the market system, as you could only purchase in the increments shown, which was usually only one and you have to pause inbetween each individual click.  Streamlining these aspects would make the flow feel better.
Another aspect that disappointed me was that despite starting off the game using an axe and saw in order to chop down trees and produce lumber that mechanic was very sparsely used throughout the entirety of the game.  Other tools, like the sickle, were used heavily to gather flowers, so it felt a bit misleading to start off that way and almost never do that again.  That seemed especially pertinent when you'd need to get lumber a few times in order to build things like a water mill and a house, so I would have liked to see a bit more balance and distribution of those less utilized abilities/tools.
This might be something only I missed, but one aspect of the game that threw me off was replenishing stamina.  Since the game throws you out of your home after you've only regained stamina once, as I progressed and kept healing, I was under the impression that the cap on my hearts was something like 20.  That's the highest amount you can heal yourself for and what you start off with in the game, so I never questioned it.  As I got to the point where tasks took 8+ hearts, you can imagine how often I was going back and forth in the game.  However, I eventually experimented and found I could go higher than 100 actually.  If I had known that sooner, I would have spammed those camp sites in order to stock up on several hearts before getting back into completing tasks.
A word of advice if you're going for all of the achievements - I found the last treasure when I robbed the three crypts in the cemetary.  Since that lowered my fame after I robbed the first one I didn't end up going through the other two.  After all, I was afraid I'd end the game with too low fame to get my achievement or otherwise harm my ending somehow, but as long as you complete everything you'll be just fine in both the storyline and in achievement hunting.  So you may as well just do it when you can, or otherwise you could miss out on that last treasure by accident.
I already said that I do recommend this game, but it's the sort of experience I'll likely only play through once.  Maybe years from now I might want another go through, but there's little to offer for a 2nd playthrough in either the gameplay or the story.  Also, I have played games just like this for free before, that varied only slightly in overall game mechanics or even in the overlying plot behind the gameplay, which doesn't motivate me to want to pay for a game like this (or in my case trade it for another game).  I doubt I'll bother getting the sequel, as I don't think it'd offer anything more than this game did.  A one time playthrough that's harmless enough, but doesn't give very much meat or fulfillment either.

text:
Possibly the best puzzle game ever made. It takes dedication, but it's worth it if you like the puzzles.
This game feels like being born again and living a brand new life in an unfamiliar world. Without any guidance, you have to figure out how the world works on your own. You will wonder, get frustrated, and have epiphanies. You will think you have all the answers, until a something new arises and you will have to question your assumptions. You will desprately try to figure out why you're here and what it all means.
Everyone says this game has no plot, which is kind of true, but this game has given me more of a sense of adventure and intrigue than most other games with a heavy storyline. There were moments that made me stand up and walk around the room in awe... no game with a strong plot has made me do that. It might not have much of a plot, but that's because it puts you in driver's seat. Your character isn't experiencing the adventure, YOU are experiencing the adventure. That might sound kind of cheesy, but The Witness really pulls it off.
I wasn't sure if I would like the puzzles based off the trailer, but the line puzzles are one of my favorite puzzle "systems" ever. The game takes this simple idea and gets a lot of gameplay out of it. The puzzles have just the right difficulty: hard enough that you'll have to put a lot of thought into each puzzle, but easy enough that you almost never feel like reaching for a walkthrough. Because of the open-world style of the game, if you get stuck on a puzzle, you can go somewhere else and work on something different, then come back later. The line puzzles never felt repetitive to me, but some disagree with me on that.
The core of the game relies on these line puzzles, so if you don't like those puzzles, then you won't like the game. I think the puzzles are strong enough that they would still be really good if there was no island, and the game was just these puzzles. But don't think the game is just about the puzzles. It's really easy to say that this is a game with a bunch of puzzles on an island, if you don't pay attention. There really is a lot going on here, it's just subtle.
This is one of a few games I would call perfect. It's beautiful in appearance, mechanics, meaning... it's impressive. It's the only game out there that belongs in a museum. If you like puzzle games, give it a try. It takes dedication, but it is absolutely worth it.

I finally just beat the final day (10) solo. It was really, really ♥♥♥♥ing hard but god damn was it satisfying. So now that I've finally beaten Sky Rogue, you better buckle the ♥♥♥♥ up buttercup 'cause here comes the review train.
Sky Rogue is ♥♥♥♥ing rad. It's a great mix of what feels like Ace Combat and roguelite elements, with a sort of Starfox 64 graphical vibe. Islands and missions are random, giving you nice variety every time you play. I would highly reccommend a controller or flight stick, because playing with mouse and keyboard is like trying to find the cheesecake crumbs inside a fat ♥♥♥♥'s folds. You just can't do it, the cheesecake is gone, just like your will to live will be if you play with mouse and keyboard. There are 10 days to get through, and after day 3 you better put on your big boy pants before the catholic priest that is this game rapes you with difficulty. Seriously, day 4 will ♥♥♥♥ your brains out till you're a steaming pile of sweat and♥♥♥♥♥on the floor. This game is very Dark Souls-esque difficulty wise, meaning you need to train yourself on every mechanic of this game and perfect everything or else you'll get ♥♥♥♥ed like mommy on valentines day. There are upgrades that only stick with you throughout your one life, then there are points you get every death to spend on unlocking whole new ships/weapons/abilities that stick around forever, like a fleeting meth addiction. I give Sky Rogue a wank and a skeet outta ten.
In all seriousness though, Sky Rogue is a fantastic game, and if you're a fan of rouglites, flying games, or are just looking for something new, I seriously reccommend you give it a shot.

I'm a 3dsmax user, and I think nvil is really something that you need. You can even use the script to quickly pick something up in 3dsmax that you created in nvil without export obj and import. Really handy!

I just recently bought nVil because it was time to look for something to replace my favorite (although aging sub-D modeler, Silo 2). If you loved Silo 2, you will quickly find yourself at home in nVil. It's an amazing subdivision modeler with a slew of features and options that make modeling complex or organic shapes a breeze.

nVil holds the truth, that a dedicate tool for a task will do that task better than any multi-tool ever could.

I am not one for writing reviews but feel the need to do so for Nvil.
I am a professional ArchVIZ artist/designer moving into the world of game engines.
I am only a few hours in with Nvil and it has become my goto subd modeller. It just does what it says on the tin and very quickly and intuitively. I have had to figure everything out myself as there is little guidance or tutorials - that has not slowed me down at all.
Modelling is enjoyable fast and fun, FBX files play nice with Substance and Unreal Engine and demo versions of Modo and Houdini. I will be adding Houdini Indie to the toolset shortly on the basis that my main modelling will be an Nvil-Houdini combo.
I tend to favour separate specialist tools over huge beasts that do everything but that's not to say that there is anything wrong with using the Blenders, Mayas and Maxs of this world. (Am I allowed to put s after x?)

In a world where Blender exists, Nvil is a peculiar beast.
On the one hand Nvil fills a void left by Nevercenter Silo, which has existed as zombieware for the better part of the past decade. I feel that there's still SOME need for a small footprint, customizable SDS modeler in this crowded market. Nvil is exactly that.
On the other hand, one has to wonder if Blender's very existence makes Nvil more of an artifact of a bygone era of 3D. Nvil is the sort of app that would have been the top dog for indie art some 10-15 years ago. It's not 2002 anymore though. Why spend $119 for a SDS modeler when you can get a far more complete and robust suite in the form of Blender for $0 instead? That's the real question.
If you're looking for a Silo replacement and are willing to pay Silo prices then Nvil is your guy. If, however, you want to go beyond poly modeling then opt for the Blender instead. Blender is every bit the pro-level app as something like Maya or 3dsmax. Nvil is more of a niche product, designed to fill an ever shrinking hole in the market.
And that's the problem. Nvil isn't a complete app unto itself. You can't animate, render, sculpt, or do any of the other big picture things that you might expect of a modern 3D app. Don't spend $119 on Nvil expecting it to replace the $300 MODO Indie. You'll be disappointed. Nvil exists for one reason and one reason only, as a replacement for Silo.
That said, here are a few basic pros and cons.
PRO:
- Customizable
- More stable than Silo v2.x ever was
- Easy to learn
- Small footprint
- Pure poly modeling
CON:
- Overpriced at $119.
- Customizable GUI suffers from slightly laggy button/element redraw
- The odd clipped button text in the latest April 14, 2017 build
- Default radial menu is a little twitchy and too quick to move from one level to the next
- Dated overall design. Very 2001.
RECOMMENDATION:
It won't replace, Blender or any other general purpose suite app. Then again, it's not supposed to. If all you need is a pure poly/SDS modeling solution then you could do worse tha Nvil. Nvil is what Silo v2 probably should have been. If, however, you already have a more robust app available to you then Nvil doesn't bring anything new to the table.
Nvil is good for what it is. Just wait for a sale.
NOTE: I tested this on Win10 (ver. 1703) with a Core i7-6700K @ 4GHz, 32GB RAM, and a GeForce GTX 970 4GB.

I wrote a review for the game here:
I have an affinity for board games. Games like Lords of Waterdeep, Pandemic, 7 Wonders, and so on. When one of the games I enjoy get a videogame adaptation, I’m usually right on top of it. Some of the best adaptations include the iOS version of Lords of Waterdeep and Puerto Rico. Others, like Ra, aren’t as well translated. One game in particular, 7 Wonders, seems to be in an eternal beta.
However, one of the less likely board games to get a videogame adaptation is Mysterium. The game can best be described as a cross between Clue and abstract picture game Dixit. The theme of Mysterium is that one player is a murdered ghost, and the other players are psychics at a seance. The ghost sends the psychics clues related to their own murder, but the clues come in the form of wildly abstract pictures that Salvador Dali would be proud of. Using those vague clues, the psychics have six game turns to determine who killed the ghost, with what and where.
The game manages to represent the board game well, which lush, moody 1920’s art deco graphics.
The single player campaign is basically an extended tutorial, framed in a story where the player spends time as both a psychic and a medium channeling a ghost. The game features multiplayer modes, including a Blitz mode that promises a faster game.
The game plays best with other humans, because playing with a computer requires the player to do a sort of reverse Turing Test in figuring out either what the computer ghost is trying to say or, even more difficult, figuring out how to find out what connections the AI will make. For example, putting 4 yellow cards may not influence the computer to select the yellowest option in front of them.
Playing with other humans is a pleasure, as always. A co-op game, you’re not going to find hostile players. The interface is good enough to allow players to communicate with each other, advising which evidence they should vote for or against. Mysterium is one of those games that never fails to present a compelling session.
It’s unfortunate, then, that the population of Mysterium players is very low; matchmaking is poor, and it’s very hard to coordinate with strangers to start a game. Gamers are lucky to start four player games (1 ghost, 3 psychics), and the game really sings with far more psychics than that. Tn fact, I was never able to get a game of Blitz going.
For fans of Mysterium, this game is a must-buy, but it’s advisable for players to coordinate scheduled games to avoid the dearth of online players out there. The game is currently only available on PC, iOS and Android — hopefully, word of mouth will get more players to enjoy this faithful adaptation.
Great concept. It's a nice multiplayer game that demands some reflexion. The real downside is the lack of players and the few bugs here and there.

If you don't already know, Mysterium is a murder mystery table-top game for 2-7 players. It's asymmetric, with one player taking on the role of a murdered spirit, while the rest - playing as psychics - have to figure out how they died, and who did it.
They figure this out by looking over vision cards, each illustrated card guiding them towards a specific suspect with its abstract art. Players can also share their visions with other psychics and approve or reject their choices with Clairvoyance Tokens. In Mysterium, up to 7 players can join together for fun, engaging games.
In the new, digital version of the game, you have the option between a story mode and a "play" mode. The story mode puts you through the tutorial first and lets you get the hang of the game. The play mode lets you play online games, host an online game or play against, or rather with, the AI.
All and all, I can say this game is a masterpiece in the digital tabletop section of Steam. And for a little under 10 bucks, you can't go wrong with it if you like these types of games.
PROS
+ Amazing artwork
+ Good atmosphere
+ Fun to play
CONS
- Crashes on quit
- Don't know how the AI "thinks"
- No real single player game
- Story mode gets pretty hard pretty fast

Year Walk is based on Swedish lore about vision quests. You embark on a long walk in the woods, looking for signs and meanings, and you come across some very strange stuff. There's a very dreamlike quality to the game where the odd glyph or ghost you run into feels almost expected, but it also serves to take you out of the real world and immerse you with very simple, beautiful graphics. This makes the horrifying bits all the more effective, because they come in rough contrast to the feel of the rest of the game. I won't lie, there have been a few jump scares, but the feel earned instead of cheap. It's like a nightmare intruding on the edges of a pastoral dream.
Gameplay is simple, moving left or right through pretty landscapes, moving forward or backward to different areas, and clicking on things to interact. You have a useful map and an encyclopedia that helps flesh out the legends and signs you encounter. The game also has a very clever way of getting you to use the encyclopedia later on, which I found very effective. The puzzles are pretty simple as well, so don't go in expecting a lot of gameplay. It's mostly exploring the woods and delving into the myths you encounter, which for the price, I think is well worth it. An entertaining, chilling experience.

I got into this game expecting a fairly open Persona-style game to blend with Ace Attourney-style mystery. As far as that's concerned, I absolutely got the latter (and just a little of the former). The murder mysteries start out strange, get increasingly more strange, and are strangely satisfying to solve.
The game has large sections of Visual Novel to it, and this may be a let-down if you're expecting agency. Not only do in the sense that you will read *a lot* of dialogue and narration, but also how the game can restrict movements to make sure you do things in the order the game desires (e.g. me: "oh, a body - hey, is that the weapon?", the game: "Stop! The plot mandates you see the body now"), including the detective and trail sequences. Play the game knowing this made me feel more safe, release any sense of regret, but also capable to move forward and focus on the details.
Monokuma really deserves mentioning. As a villain, he could be described as if the Joker and Deadpool had raised a bear. He's unpredictable, has a deeply dark sense of humour, and breaks the forth wall when he feels like it. As I see it, it's clearly "the star of the show".

This game is a funny visual novel with this nice "Ace Attorney" feeling. You play as Makoto, a
kind but average high school student entering Hope Peak's Academy, a kind of "genuises only" high school. Unfortunately, the school is quickly overtaken by Monokuma, a sadictic, perverted, talkative
bear who intends for the students of the Academy to kill each other if they want to survive and to regain their freedom.
This is the basic plot. It doesn't make a lot of sense? That's normal at the beginning, and let me reassure you: the more you'll learn from what actually happened, the more confused you'll be about this plot, until the very end. Nevertheless, I highly recommend this game
, for several reasons.
(but seriously, why would you even read the positive reviews in that case?).

The game will last for at least 25 hours even if you're rushing through it, and it has some nice plot-twists with a few

Despite all these good points, I
recommend this game if you don't like visual novels or if you played an Ace Attorney game and didn't like it. If that's not the case, you should be more than fine with this (awesome) game.

As for this day, this is my favorite visual novel and I don't praise games like that lightly. It's been recommended to me by so many people, that I was actually afraid to play it, because of possible disappointment, but despite all the hype, Danganronpa managed to surprise me only in positive way.
The whole story is great, including concept itself and payoff. Music is amazing and partial voice acting very well done (I was playing with original voice acting, not English one). Great plot, solid writing, no issues with translation or anything like that. Characters are all well designed, not only in terms of look, but also their personality, past and goals. There is gallery, extra modes, chapter selection - all additional little things, that should be basically part of every visual novel these days.  Solving mysteries (which is the most important part of the game) is pretty fun, since all the cases are unique and interesting. Art... Art is just great. Animations are beyond awesome. So many CGs - almost every important scene has it's own graphic, which doesn't happen that often with these sort of games. It's long, absolutely worth the full price, considering it's value and deserve every recommendation.
I have some issues with this game. First of all, it's a game with almost no replayability. I cannot imagine feeling even similar sense of excitement while playing it again, when you know exactly what is going on. This isn't necessary a flaw, there are many great linear games and Danganronpa is one of those, but a lot of people (including me) associate visual novels with important choices that affects the plot and/or the end result. If you are looking for something like this, you may be disappointed.
Everything I wrote above also means that if you read any spoilers or even accidentally encountered something that could be consider one, the game may lose a lot of it's uniqueness and charm. It's basically an experience - a great one, for sure, but the less you know and expect, the better it is.
The thing that annoyed me in terms of writing was a great deal of recap within the narration. Not only during trials/investigations, where it can be explained, but at almost every step - protagonist just revise over and over again things that basically just happen. This also has a slight impact on lack of replayability - everything gets so obviously stated that playing game again, with this knowledge, just to see what sort of clues you've missed is pretty pointless. Those clues will be specifically mentioned to you at the end.
I think the biggest flaw for me is that  sometimes game gets too obvious and, via protagonist, explains everything to you, like you just couldn't draw your own (usually pretty obvious) conclusions by yourself and after someone stating "Oh, so it's 1+1, huh?", protagonist gets on: "1+1... Hm... 1+1... This must mean... 2! Right?!". There were moments when it was getting really tiresome.
Still, with so much amazing content, these flaws are almost non existent. I sincerely recommend this game for every fan of mysteries/visual novels/good stories/anime out there.

This game is beautiful, no question about that. But that's pretty much the only thing it has going for it. I only played about an hour of this before I had to quit because I was so bored. I can appreciate exploration-type games like Dear Esther, but they rely on compelling the player to want to continue to explore the landscape to progress the story. There is no story here...  Also, the scattered puzzles are drab, repetitive to the point of being tedious, and unsatisfying to complete. I am seriously mad at myself for spending $20 on this.

The Witness kept me consistently entertained for the time I played it. The puzzles were unique, challenging, and placed in a visually appealing world where your perspective and understanding are your only limitations.
There are puzzles in this game that are impossible to understand in the beginning. You cannot solve them yet, as you have not learned how each individual mechanic works. However, each and every symbol and trick will be taught to you in relative simplicity before being expanded upon.
There are even puzzles that are so well hidden that you will be unaware of their existence until a specific moment of epiphany somewhere (likely later on) in the game.
Some puzzles (especially in the swamp) contain random twists that are unnoticeable and more than just difficult to understand, let alone NOTICE. These are the only problem I have with the puzzles in the game.
The philosophical value of the audio logs is interesting, but only if you intend on listening, and you are interested in the topics of self-reflection they present. Additionally, the audio logs are incredibly well-hidden, sometimes to the point where you will not find them without external help. I found this to be a useless and arbitrary task, and it is the only thing I bothered using a walkthrough for, as there is no real "challenge" besides aimless wandering.
Also- I'm calling out the developers on false advertising here, as there is no single part in the game that involves you in any way "regaining your memories". As someone who has been a huge fan of the Myst series for years, I truly enjoy the subtle, nuanced way in which you discover the plot in the world around you. THE WITNESS DOES NOT HAVE A PLOT. Do not buy this game if you're looking for anything more than a beautiful, quiet, challenging and rewarding puzzle-based experience. I was expecting an interesting ending to the game (which I grew high hopes for due to the store description), and was kinda let down big time. The ending gives you no reward besides the knowledge that you beat the game.
All in all, this was fantastic, and I enjoyed the whole game. It was probably my favourite game of 2016. The puzzles were great, the ending not so much. I'd give it about a 9/10, but a 7/10 for anyone who hates puzzles and is looking for plot.

Would recommend but only if its on sale for $20. Some of the puzzles are pretty infuriating, but I like that it is open world and I can leave at any time and go to another area if I get tired of where I'm currently at.

I have to begin with this point: If you've NEVER played Magic: The Gathering (MTG) before, then you might actually have a chance to enjoy this game.  Anyone who is a veteren or even moderate MTG player will immediately HATE this game.
The graphics look great.  The interface is a little touchy sometimes, but works pretty well as long as you remember to hit the pause button while you read card specifics.  The music is pretty well done, especially for a side-game that really never was intended to have a huge player base.
The biggest beef I have with this game is the fact that it violates the rules of MTG.  There were two giant rule violations in the first 2 battles you go into.  There's one deck that included over 10 of the same creature card (You can only have a maximum of 4 of a unique card other than basic lands in your deck).  The rule for damage allocation for combat phases was completely off.  Attackers get to choose where damage is dealt, not automatically chosen by the computer.
Since this is a Wizards of the Coast game, you would think they would be able to follow their OWN rules!
Long story short - if you know anything about MTG, don't bother wasting your time and money on this game.

Wow, would you look at all the negative reviews. Does that scare you? It scared me.
I probably wouldn't have bought the game either, but I got it in a bundle with some other farm simulators. Despite my reluctance I decided to give it a test drive one day and see what all the hate was about.
Ten hours later I came to a conclusion and can now tell you what I think about this unusual game.
First of all, you have to be familiar with farming sims and understand how they are played. If you don't know how to operate the machinery then you are not going to have fun. That brings me to my second point: half of the reviews on here are from people who have absolutely no idea what to do and, instead of looking for help, they decided to nix the game altogether. The other half is from jokesters who jumped on the hate bandwagon because that is the popular thing to do nowdays.
If anyone with the least bit of interest in the subject would have taken the time to learn the game then I think they would have appreciated what the developers have almost succeeded in creating here. I say "almost" because I can admit that it is not a perfect game. Yes, it does have lots of bugs; and yes, it is slightly underdeveloped. But no way is it the unplayable disaster that the reviewers here would have you believe. I have played games far far worse than this one.
It helps to have some prior experience with farming, but the game itself is quite easy to learn. I have a rudimentary knowlege of the subject and still didn't know what to do. I found the tutorial videos from the main menu but they would not play. However, with a little bit of digging you can find the videos in the game's main folder and watch them from there. You can even read the subtitle files that accompanied the videos with insightful tips. Reading and watching those made the game so much more easier to understand and I have been having fun playing it ever since.
My gameplay experience so far has ranged from average to great. It is a small game without a lot of replayability; so I can't see myself spending any more than 25 - 30 hours on it. But I am enjoying the game for what it is. It's a farm sim set in an historical period; and it's not trying to be anything more than that. The sooner you can accept that the less disappointed you will be.
Maybe I am a bit biased for having such a strong interest in antiquated farming. I've tried recreating the same time period on the more popular farming games without success. Their antique tractors were nice, but in the end all it is is modern farming using old machines. But this game is so much more detailed. You actually have to connect implements by hand and get off your tractor each time you want to lower the seeder for planting. And the plowing itself is the most real I've ever seen in a farm sim. Instead of having ready-made fields for you to plow, you have to decide where you want to grow and start digging up the green. I spent hours on my first day outlining a field in my backyard and plowing a sizable portion of the yard. After cultivating, fertilizing and planting I'm now waiting for my first crops to show.
This game also features the most animal interaction I've ever seen. You have to keep them stocked up on hay and grass. The bales can be stored in the barn loft and, just like any farmer, they must be thrown down to the bottom floor and placed in designated locations. Milk and eggs can also be collected and sold at the local market. Unfortunately the animals do not move much, but you can walk them to places you want them to be. You can also breed them for their offspring and sell your old animals. And make sure you don't scare the chickens too far away or they may die of starvation.
The machine models, I think, are some of the best-looking in a game like this. They all look beautiful and shiny and historically accurate. There are a few different tractors you can purchase, including a John Deere model; not sure how they were able to acquire that license. The implements are varied and also look good. Antique plows, cultivators, seeders, balers, wagons and more have been perfectly modeled. Even the harvester is one of the old ones that is pulled behind the tractor; something I haven't been able to find in any other game.
I plan to spend more time on this game because I am actually enjoying it. However I do wish they would patch it with fixes and added incentives. There is a gas station in the game, but you never run out of gas. Was this a planned but cancelled feature? Also you can sell logs, but no way to chop down trees? That's disappointing when you realize that the game could have been so much better with a little bit more work. But, still, it is not a terrible game.
So far I have experienced no game-breaking bugs. There was an incident in which all of my animals disappeared, but I reloaded an older save and they returned. Some times the game does lock up when launching, but closing and relaunching usually helps. There are some minor physics issues, but the solution to that is don't do stupid stuff. This is not an FPS. Treat it with a little bit of delicacy. Why would you be doing silly stunts when you should be farming? The only real annoying thing that occured was when one of my pigs and dog became stuck and I couldn't move them. I drove the tractor through them and they returned to normal. Sometimes it's the simplest solutions that save the day.
Even though I wish more work could have been done, I am still happy to have discovered this fascinating game. I would like others to enjoy it too, but I guess you can't please everyone.

Well, you look around and find yourself in a farmyard that might have come from an old picturebook of the early fifties. You turn around and see your dog, running towards you. You see your chicken, your pigs... well and Bessy, the old cow. And then you see your old tractor and...

So this was a quirky little game I've had my eyes on for a while. Having picked it up on offer, I decided to give it a run-through, and it was a generally pleasant experience. Nothing that stands out in particular in terms of what would set it apart from other games, but nothing that felt like it hampered my experiences either. If you have a few hours to spare and a bit of change, this is worth at least one playthrough to pass the time away. It doesn't have much of worth to bring you back for a second playthrough, but given a reasonable price point and it's worth the one time.
The game is essentially a resource management simulation where you have to manage what you have, your energy, money and your skills to eventually become the "Hero of the Kingdom", and honestly, it's not too challenging provided that methodical progression is applied to everything, from levelling your capabilities to ensuring you have enough food or money for the next event you have to overcome. It does have some strategical layer of depth to it (case in point, you can simply buy certain things you need, but if you work on your skills you can get items for much cheaper than you would buying them) and I appreciated the layers that had been taken to reward those who did go a little extra in managing their resources more efficiently
A lot of the gameplay elements are easily visible event points, though one of the other draws of the game is an element of hidden object games, where you find items such as mushrooms or crates for extra items and money. Beyond these elements, it tends to play forward in a more point-and-click adventure game than your typical RPG (a great number of RPG elements are not present here, so if you are looking for an RPG experience, I would advise seeking this elsewhere) and the story it does tell through the story is a simple one, with a neat bow finish after the ending progresses. If any complaint could be thought of, it would be that there's no real sense of time passing by as any of these events transpire - and given that you can rest in camps without any effect to the story does not help in this regard.
In terms of the art assets, the landscapes, the various icons and the people you get to see are pleasant to look at, with nothing looking out of the ordinary for a fantasy adventure. The game has a good sound quality to it, from the effects to the music, though it can sometimes be distracting when the track suddenly changes while you've been on a screen for a while without any change. All-in-all, though, the complaints that I have are minor and nit-picky, and did not detract from the fact that I did get enjoyment from the game overall, and while I clocked only about 4-5 hours and obtained all achievements (with others completing it in less time), it was a worthwhile 4-5 hours that I had spent without any regrets.
In summary: While a short point-and-click adventure experience, it's hidden object and resource management elements helped keep the gameplay varied and entertaining, while the story and progression was balanced enough that it did not feel like it carried on for too long or too short a time, and it didn't leave any loose ends. It's lack of difficulty or replay value is an appeal for anyone seeking something to plug into for a few hours of their time, and the price value makes this at least worth a purchase on a sale, if not at full price.

A simplistic, arcade, rogue-like dogfighting game that is an absolute blast. I played the hell out of the Ace Combat series on the PS2 and this is easily the most fun and closest game to Ace Combat. If you like arcade flight games then I highly recommend you slap this on your wishlist. Now just to quickly summarize:

As for this day, this is my favorite visual novel and I don't praise games like that lightly. It's been recommended to me by so many people, that I was actually afraid to play it, because of possible disappointment, but despite all the hype, Danganronpa managed to surprise me only in positive way.
The whole story is great, including concept itself and payoff. Music is amazing and partial voice acting very well done (I was playing with original voice acting, not English one). Great plot, solid writing, no issues with translation or anything like that. Characters are all well designed, not only in terms of look, but also their personality, past and goals. There is gallery, extra modes, chapter selection - all additional little things, that should be basically part of every visual novel these days.  Solving mysteries (which is the most important part of the game) is pretty fun, since all the cases are unique and interesting. Art... Art is just great. Animations are beyond awesome. So many CGs - almost every important scene has it's own graphic, which doesn't happen that often with these sort of games. It's long, absolutely worth the full price, considering it's value and deserve every recommendation.
I have some issues with this game. First of all, it's a game with almost no replayability. I cannot imagine feeling even similar sense of excitement while playing it again, when you know exactly what is going on. This isn't necessary a flaw, there are many great linear games and Danganronpa is one of those, but a lot of people (including me) associate visual novels with important choices that affects the plot and/or the end result. If you are looking for something like this, you may be disappointed.
Everything I wrote above also means that if you read any spoilers or even accidentally encountered something that could be consider one, the game may lose a lot of it's uniqueness and charm. It's basically an experience - a great one, for sure, but the less you know and expect, the better it is.
The thing that annoyed me in terms of writing was a great deal of recap within the narration. Not only during trials/investigations, where it can be explained, but at almost every step - protagonist just revise over and over again things that basically just happen. This also has a slight impact on lack of replayability - everything gets so obviously stated that playing game again, with this knowledge, just to see what sort of clues you've missed is pretty pointless. Those clues will be specifically mentioned to you at the end.
I think the biggest flaw for me is that  sometimes game gets too obvious and, via protagonist, explains everything to you, like you just couldn't draw your own (usually pretty obvious) conclusions by yourself and after someone stating "Oh, so it's 1+1, huh?", protagonist gets on: "1+1... Hm... 1+1... This must mean... 2! Right?!". There were moments when it was getting really tiresome.
Still, with so much amazing content, these flaws are almost non existent. I sincerely recommend this game for every fan of mysteries/visual novels/good stories/anime out there.

As someone who loves anything to do with space, I find this game is right up my street. It is a very fun game, that I believe and hope will be continued to be developed. It seems like there is a large amount of pathways that can be taken to further expand the game, which I hope will happen.
Overall a very cool game, which I think is one of the best of it's kind. It's not overly complex, there is a little bit of thinking, such as what to build first, and the sub-sequential build order, as well as the positioning of structures, and what colonist ratio is needed, which makes a nice challenge.
One thing I will pick up on though, is the level difficulty of the planets. There are four planets with different environments;
- Class D (Desert Planet) > ACCESSIBLE < Meteor's + Sandstorm's + ~50% Flat Surface
- Class F (Frozen Planet) > CHALLENGING < Blizzard's + ~45% Flat Surface
- Class M (Gas Giant Moon) > OVERWHELMING < Meteor's + Solar Flare's + No Atmosphere + ~55% Flat Surface
- Class S (Storm Planet) > SUICIDE < Thunderstorm's + ~30% Flat Surface + ~10% Water Covered Surface
Now I believe the level of difficulty to be in the wrong order, not something that ruins the game, but still annoying.
The Desert Planet > is easy. The unique Sandstorm's really aren't that big of a deal, they do mild wear to certain power structures, and mild damage to colonists overtime, but they also provide a large amount of Wind power. Meteor's are rare but can still be a pain early in the game. Space is a mild concern.
The Frozen Planet > is very similar to the Desert Planet, but easier. Sandstorm's are replaced by Blizzard's, which also deal mild damage to colonists and certain structures overtime as well as increasing the Wind strength. You may have slightly less space, but the fact there are no Meteor's at all, makes this planet easier.
The Gas Giant Moon > is by far the hardest. There is no atmosphere so you don't have the option of Wind power to sustain you through the night, so you must solely rely on Solar power. You are constantly bombarded with Meteor's, and additionally there is now Solar Flare's which are a real annoyance. If it's early in the game and your colonist is outside when it hits, you can pretty much say GAME OVER!
The Storm Planet > isn't the hardest. You may have slightly less room to operate in due to lakes and large mountains, but there is still adequate space. Instead of Sandstorm's or Blizzard's, Thunderstorm's take place. This is by far nicer, as they are much more regular then the other two. You may wonder why I say "nicer", and I do because they provide energy more frequently, and with the simple addition of one building (which you can easily build from the start without drawing to much from your resources) protect your buildings and hence your colonists, and pretty much take the only danger of this planet out of the game, leaving it as not a 'Con' but a 'Pro'.
So in my opinion, the planet difficulty should be more like this;
- Class F (Frozen Planet) > ACCESSIBLE < Blizzard's + ~45% Flat Surface
- Class D (Desert Planet) > CHALLENGING < Meteor's + Sandstorm's + ~50% Flat Surface
- Class S (Storm Planet) > CHALLENGING < Thunderstorm's + ~30% Flat Surface + ~10% Water Covered Surface
- Class M (Gas Giant Moon) >  OVERWHELMING/SUICIDE < Meteor's + Solar Flare's + No Atmosphere + ~55% Flat Surface
If I could change one more thing, it would be that something happens after you have built your base. Although a challenge, in reality one would not simply stop at building a base on a planet, you would then proceed to terraform, but as I mentioned earlier "there is a large of amount of pathways that can be taken to further expand the game"!
Overall?
In my opinion it's worth a try.

I beat the PS4 version of the game first, then bought it from Humble and beat that, and then bought it here because it was on sale and why not.  First playthrough was easily over 100 hours.
I think this is probably the best video game that's ever been made.  It's certainly my favorite, but beyond personal preference, what it accomplishes is mind blowing.  I've never had any piece of art make me feel as much a part of the human race as this does.  There's a million things about this I could talk about, but two things I'll mention here are:
1. The realization that, whether cultural or biological, our brains are very predictable.  When there's three different ways to solve a puzzle, the game seems to have already known which one you'd pick first, second, and third.
2. At first the game seems like it's about solving puzzles, but as it goes on, you realize that the game is actually about getting stumped, stepping back, and after some amount of observation of the world around you, having that immediate realization of the solution.  It teaches you how to learn, and in a way that's applicable outside of the game too.
The game is also constructed like a classical symphony, with motifs used to build themes, and themes in various structures, but even though they start as abstract imagery/concepts, as the themes build, the abstractions fade and you are given some suggestions as to what these things all mean, much like in a film.  There's other, even more meaningful things I experienced with the game, but they're too abstract to talk about in a review.  And I could talk about this for hours.
If you're looking to burn through a puzzle game, there's amazing puzzles in this, but like I said, it's not set up as a pile of puzzles to solve one after another.  If you're looking for a game with an explicit story that bangs you over the head like almost every other video game I've played, you'll be furious after playing this.  But if you're open minded and want to explore the inside of your own brain to any extent, this might be the best game you ever play.

The one caveat is that while all of this fast paced stuff is going on, you may as well be playing with the controller upside down, backward, and behind your head. It's almost expected that to fall through a floor in a game, you press down and jump. When you want to jump higher, you hold the button down. What we get here is you hold the button to fall through floors, and "down and jump" doesn't exist. Going up stairs requires an "up-angle" command, and pressing jump to leap off the stairs results in simply falling through them, likely into a horde of enemies as the power up you were after vanishes before you. Hope you weren't needing ammo! It results in MANY frustrating moments, and could have easily been avoided.

Year Walk is a very interesting Adventure horror game. But will you want to play it ?
Year Walk story is really hard to explain. You play as a man trying to do a year walk on New year's eve. It's based on Swedish mythology. It's one of those games where you piece the story together when you play it.
Gameplay is really simple. You use the keyboard to move around and the mouse to click on stuff and the goals vary on the cycle you're on. It can range from trying to find ghost to trying to find a way to a church.
The art style is amazing to say the least. The hand drawn environments and characters are really amazing to look at. The style is really well drawn.
Audio is amazing. The soundtrack and sound effects are both really well made. It makes you feel tense and relaxed. It really makes you immersed in the world.
The game isn't difficult. Some of the puzzles are difficult but nothing too head scratching. The game gives you clues  and even then you have hints which are helpful.
The map layout is the only bad thing about this game. It get's confusing really fast and it doesn't help when all environments look the same. I wish they could have given more indication where you need to go.
Game is really short. It took me 1 hour to finish it. There is an alternative ending which can be unlocked, but overall don't expect much replay value.
The game didn't have bugs what so ever. Any rig could handle this game. Don't expect to run into bugs while playing this game.
Year walk is a really tough game to review and to explain why you need to play it is even tougher, but you must play it no matter what. Year Walk was an amazing experience and the whole lore behind it is really interesting. Adventure game fans must own this little title as soon as possible. It's worth it at full price without a doubt. I give Year Walk a 8.5/10

Oddly enough, it was a negative review that actually convinced me to buy this (on sale). I was looking for something casual that wouldn't frustrate me with arbitrarily difficult mechanics. Six hours later, I'm exactly 15 mushrooms away from completing every "achievement" in the game (37 of 38). All the little side quests and object hunts kept me happily engaged and distracted, going back and forth through various areas to discover newly revealed items, and kept my completionist impulse throughly fed. For $0.59, the value can't be beat (even if, as I suspect, the game offers no replayability of substance).
Fulfilling the requirements to complete the major "quests" required at least a little thought and planning to ensure that I did everything in the right order and didn't run short of resources in the process. I agree with critics who say this game is not difficult. If you're looking for hardcore gameplay, this is not the game for you. Short of being so stoned that you fail to figure out the basic resource gathering / cash generation loop, there's no real "challenge" to speak of, no combat mechanics, and the game, while not putting you "on rails" completely, doesn't let you get ahead of yourself... you have to complete each step before new areas open up for exploration.
I'm pretty sure it is impossible to "lose" the game, or to "die". The "hint" mechanism is helpful, but barely necessary... the game makes what needs to be done next pretty obvious, if you're paying attention. You're free to roam around within explored areas, and to pursue quests given in whatever order seems sensible (not all quests are immediately achieveable, you have to build up to them by gathering resources and generating "fame" through completing a large variety of simple side quests), but as indicated, unexplored areas can only be opened up by completing quests, and the mechanics ensure you complete the quests in the appropriate order.
All in all, a nice, satisfying, rewarding "casual" gameplay experience. 7/10, and that's not a complaint. No regrets about the six hours / sixty cents invested. Sometimes, you just want to "play", not "compete". I'll buy the sequel whenever it comes on sale, too.
