Strap in folks, this is going to be a loong review.
Let's Start at the beginning, way back 3 years ago. 3 years ago, I began playing this game. And I sucked at it. At this current point in time, I think there was actually a skill curve. (or I just sucked badly). It was during this beta period that Aliens were first introduced. The developers began what was known as the "alien invasion." Aliens were now everywhere in Open Space, one of the game modes. I ended up taking a break from the game.
Later, I redownloaded the game. Either I had gotten better, or something, because I was able to effectively complete missions.
. This was back in 2015/ early 2016. Things have changed. I suppose I should cover the modes and stuff in the game.
At the prime time, there were 6 game modes: PvP, PvE, RAID, DREADNOUGHT, TOURNAMENTS, and OPEN SPACE. PvP consists of 5 different modes played across 15 or so maps, PvE has about 12 different missions, Raid is 2 different missions, Dreadnought and Tournaments are effectively PvP, and Open Space is flying around various different maps (some including the maps other missions are in). There were also quests for each mode.
The controls were excellent, it was very easy to learn the controls and utilize them. At this time, there if you went deeper, you could utilize something called "turn-keys." Interceptors sucked to fight against. Overall, at this time, it was pretty fun.
My timeline on this is kinda fuzzy, and I can't give enough s**ts to actually root through and sort it out, so I'll do my best. The first thing introduced were special manufacturing ships at mid-tier levels. There were max tier special craft, which is fine. These special mid-tier ships had exclusive modules that only that ship could use. Previously, so long as a ship was a certain class, whatever module could be used for them. This statement was no longer true. To add more to the sting, these special ships were slightly more powerful than the rest. In addition, the ships required special parts to build, which naturally could only be bought using the premium currency or grinding for hours per day for a chance to get it. Then they removed the ability to get the parts for the ship.
Shortly after, they introduced Destroyers. This is when s**t started hitting the fan. Destroyers are bigger, stronger, and more durable than ANY other ship by 2 to 4 times. Games started being "who had more dessies." Again, you could spend money to buy a chance at getting them, or sit and grind for hours per day. I managed to get my destroyer. However, the destroyers use the same crafting components as the max tier special crafts.
This was only one tier of destroyers. They added two more tiers. The second tier included some annoying modules, like a gravitational lens, which when placed over an objective in PvP, resulted in the enemy team being unable to capture the objective due to damage taken. I don't have much experience with the top tier dessies, but based on my limited interaction and comments on the forums, they broke the balance as well. Then, at the end of each top tier event, they removed the ability to even MAKE the dessies (which by the way, required special parts that you had to grind for.)
But these reasons are not not what ultimately caused me to not recommend this game. Rather it was the next few things.
Firstly, they removed premium currency rewards from achievements and from answering polls. (you got 10 currency per each, which wasn't really a lot,)
And our second reason is what quite a few of the negative reviews say:
Oh boy did these break the game. The ships are literally Over-powered. To give you some prospective, in one of the Tournaments my team was up against another team with two of the first alien ships. We went 0 - 38, out of 40 ship lives. Top rankers? The alien ships. They could fly at the max speed, teleport, pop a secondary shield, and immediately blow through your ship in 4 secs. It was at this time that I quit playing PvP (i'm not competive anyway). Then they introduced the second alien ship. Even more OP. one of it's weapons is auto-homing missiles that you can no longer evade, it can also teleport, can insta-heal after teleporting, secondary shield, and squirt ink that kills dessies in 5 seconds flat (had this happen to me).
To hit the nail home, the ships require a massive amount of grinding (or some money) to fully max out to get these modules. On top of the grind (or payment) to get the ships in the first place. As of current you can buy the first to alien ships for effectively straight cash. They have just released another alien ship over the summer. As I'm not playing PvP, I cannot say how OP it is in PVP. In other game modes, it appears that the ship has followed it's predecessors and become OP. (Not to mention they released it unfinished.)
Then the absolute last reason why I highly suggest you play some other game:
Blueprints that are pretty much only available from random chance boxes that you only get by random chance. No buying your way through this one. That shiny dessie you just built? You'll need to get these blueprints to make any modules that don't come with the ship.
Oh, and once you get the blueprints, you need the premium premium currency "Monocrystals". Why are these premium premium? Because they are ridiculously rare for the amount you need (457 for a max tier dessie). The level of rarity is you can get maybe 15 a day if you have premium and grind for several hours. Or you can potentially pay a ton of money for a chance at getting them.
This monocrystal revamp is the nail in the coffin for me. After I found this out several weeks ago, I vowed that I would call this game finished at 1000 hours no matter if I didn't reach my goal. I managed to reach my goal of obtaining all the regular ships at 996 hours. I am literally wasting game time to write this review because of how badly I do NOT want to play it.

I 100% get why people are in love with this franchise, I really do, and this review is not meant for that crowd. I'm just gonna write the review I wish I'd seen on Steam earlier, before I purchased this game.
These are the things I wish I'd known beforehand:
- This is a game strictly for anime fans, especially if you're into high school themed anime.
- It's NOT meant for the vast majority of adventure game lovers out there, like the Monkey Island Series, King's Quest or the latest Telltale games. It's an entirely different beast, the dialogue and plot are VERY Japanese (which is not a bad thing necessarily) and all the characters, especially their looks, are extremely anime inspired.
- Every single character is basically a by the numbers, personification of an extreme type of personality, with a few exceptions (You got the angry, loose cannon type character, the extremely cute and popular high school girl, the posh kid that everybody hates, the fat nerd who writes fanfic and so on...). There are some twists and turns here and there but I'd say that, for the most part, the characters are pretty cut and dry and in no way represent realistically anyone that I've ever met in real life, they're all pretty exagerated.
- There's little to no actual gameplay, which wasn't all that surprising considering it's a visual novel type game. However, I wasn't expecting the first three hours of the game to be basically one, big cutscene. You gotta be ready to read A LOT, and the game expects you to pay attention to every single bit of dialogue uttered by these characters. It even goes as far as to literally point it out at the beggining of the game.
- Now this is probably the most personal out of all my gripes with this game, but if you're not the type of guy or gal who has an easy time feeling sexually attracted to anime characters, this is DEFINITELY not the game for you. Not that there's a lot of sex in the game or anything, but right off the bat, the game throws this cute female character your way and expects you to feel some sort of physical attraction towards her and it just didn't happen for me. More of a personal gripe, but I feel it's worth mentioning anyway.
- If you're like me, and you don't have a lot of patience for literally thousands upon thousands of lines of dialogue, and LOTS of reading, I'd say you'd have a pretty miserable time with this game. The dialogue is decent, but like I said before,it's very Japanese, and very anime inspired, so be prepared for a lot of outbursts and stereotypes.
Like I said before, this is just a heads up for people who aren't particularly into anime and were perhaps recommended this game, like I was, after showing an interest in the Telltale games or in other western adventure games out there. So if by any chance you agreed with any of the points I made in this review, then I'd say skip this game and spend your money somewhere else. Not a bad game by any means, it's just not for me.

The mix of whimsical hand drawn style and gore is easy on the eyes and helps distract from the hand cramps of constant restarts.
Room 13 is a fast paced arcade experience filled with giblets, gun mods, and face collecting. With little direction given to players outside the tutorial, they are tasked with tearing apart waves of the undead in an arena style setting with guns that are limited by ammo, and melee weapons limited by durability. This means that avoiding and dealing damage is tricky and puts players constantly on the move up and down stairs. After each wave some piles of boxes and supplies pop up that can offer players gun mods, pickups like medkits, or a surprise zombie that could ruin a good run.
The mods can alter gun stats as well as how they behave, like the chaser gun part that makes bullets track down enemies, or the motorized arrow launcher which allows you to pick up the arrows after use. Surviving waves and obtaining mods unlocks mods that later have a chance to appear in boxes between waves.  After surviving a few rounds players will be able to carry secondary weapon that is also customizable. There are lots of mods to unlock, and while some are flat upgrades (like stocks that increase rate of fire), the finer parts of customizing are fun and keep runs fresh due to the random nature.
Another reward that keeps the game moving are the faces. The mask unlocks come in the form of 2 types of unlocks: a more forgiving tally of cumulative rounds survived, and the other masks are unlocked by surviving a certain number of rounds in a single life. These masks all come with a certain health amount attached as well as an ability such as eating enemies, releasing toxic gas, or charging across the screen. They are fun to collect and allow players to try out new strategies and push themselves to earn the next reward. The one small complaint here is that the masks seem a bit imbalanced: the earlier masks mostly have lower health and less potent abilities than later masks that have more health and powerful abilities.
In its current state there is only the arcade mode to get new masks and unlock mods, and it is a fun experience worth picking up. With only 2 recorded hours I have unlocked a fair bit, but the later mods and masks are still very far my reach and I am having fun hitting quick restart. The levels, each housing a different trap that hurts the player and enemies, are fun if not a little bit too much alike. The early access page states that there will be more levels, a story mode, and bosses, among other bits of content which should make this a stellar title. The developer also interacts quite a bit with community and is transparent and constantly bouncing ideas with everyone, which is always nice to see in an early access title

“room 13” is possibly the best combination of violence, extreme gore, amazing graphics, simple controls, fun and humor I’ve seen in quite some time. And there’s a distressingly large selection of games in exactly that genre, so that is high praise indeed.
In “room 13” you are given a minimal amount of instruction, with the exception of making it clear that playing with a mouse and/or keyboard is tantamount to near instant death. The player starts in a room with a weapon, and very quickly you are assailed by many varieties of what can best be grouped into “the undead”. And not 1980s undead, but 21st century “darn near fast as you” undead! (And just SO cute!) You have a limited amount of life and ammo, but there’s generally enough of both health and ammo to be found and collected. And you can find melee weapons such as pipe wrenches, hammers or crowbars (or you may pull one out of the head of some of your victims.) Melee make quite excellent weapons, in no way secondary to projectile weapons, but they wear out quickly. Killing in “room 13” is just about as fast and bloody as any I’ve seen. And just as quickly you will need to collect the gobs of flesh and brains before they dissipate.
In addition you occasionally notice a sort of breathing lung machine to be collected, and when you have enough of them you have won the round. At that point the player gets a brief respite from attack…..and choices to make.
Certainly, as a beginner the choices are simple. The immediate goal is to gain the ability to advance. As such, all you’ll want to do at first is survive. As you do, and cumulatively kill more undead (“kill more undead”. Hmmm…), you gain “faces” and weapon parts. Faces and weapon parts are awarded for rounds won (but not likely as a beginner) and the number of dead. Each face has a set amount of life and perhaps a specific unique skill. Having more life and further skills is the key to the choices I mentioned earlier.
Once you clear a level, a door will open to the next room. The choice you have is “do I go through that door, or continue fighting in this room?” The reason to stay is you will be given the option, for a few seconds, to open boxes in a rapid search for weapon parts to build the most powerful weapon possible, from parts awarded as mentioned above. Then and only then will it be feasible to move on to the next room…IF you manage to stay alive for the entire next round, so you can take that more powerful weapon with you. This is not an easy game, but not stupid, crazy hard either. And SO MUCH fun!
There is far more to this game than in this brief description, but if this doesn’t get you interested, I suspect nothing will, since perhaps you think this just isn’t your type of game. But, in full disclosure, I would have said the same before I began playing. (I was swayed by the stellar graphics and the low sale price.) For five minutes or five hours, an excellent game (even at full price.)

I wish there was a neutral selection.  Because that's really how I feel about this game.
I don't hate it, but it really isn't very interesting either.
I don't mind the almost entire lack of graphics - graphics in the game pretty much consists of still painted scenarios.
But there is really very little going on in the game.  Oh sure there are step-n-fetchit "quests", but the game is so entirely linear that its like reading a choose-your-own-adventure that somebody else has already gone through, and you have to follow in their footsteps.  There is really very little choice in the game.
Also this is THE GRINDIEST game I have ever had the misfortune to come across.
One of the major flaws in this game (so far) is that you are constantly being given "quests" that you have to spend your own money on - of which you have very little.
And more often than not, these quests don't even make sense.  For example, once you join the army, you are given quest after quest that requires you to go out and hire workers, hunters, and soldiers, and buy materials, weapons, and supplies, to perform tasks for the army - and you are expected to pay for ALL of this out of pocket.
In what army are the privates and new enlistees expected to pay their fellow soldiers to do the jobs those soldiers joined the army to do, such as fight battles with goblins and bandits?  And in what army do enlisted personell go to the armorer and then have to PAY for their weapons, supplies, and armor?
While there are mushrooms to pick and sell, and fish to catch, etc, these items quickly disappear and then you have to wait a long time for them to respawn.  So you can't really forage your way to wealth.
The only way I've found to make enough money to do the quests is to literally grind - grain into flour, then take the flour back to the baker and trade it for bread, then take the bread into town and sell it at the inn.  And you have to do that a looooooong time, over and over and over again, as you are only making a little over 1 gold per loaf.
Some of these early quests take THOUSANDS of gold worth of materials and hired help.  And you can't "sell all" - you have to click to sell each individual loaf of bread.  I literally have spent hours reading a book with one hand and methodically clicking over and over again to make enough money to do the stupid quest that I shouldn't have to pay for anyway because its the armies job in the first place.  What IS the general doing with all that money he gets from the royal exchequer?  He's sure not spending it on personell or supplies.
Overall I'd not recommend this game.  People complained about Titan's Quest being too linear - they should take a look at THIS one.  This has got to be The Definition of a linear game.
Grind grind grind.  And then virtually no choices anyway.  I don't see the point.
Also - the main character (who you are following around throughout the game) is pretty much of a jerk.  He self-proclaims his own heroism every time you turn around.
Actually, the more I think about it, I would not recommend playing this game even if you got it for free.  Guess I'm not so neutral after all.

I'm a cynical sort when it comes to games. There are so many of them on Steam, and with debacles like NMS, it's easy to become a bit jaded. I typically avoid most hidden object games to boot, so when I fired up Hero of the Kingdom I expected something pretty boring and tedious. I'm happy to say that I was wrong - and what I found recaptured some old memories for me.
Remember when you were a kid, discovering games for the first time, and letting your imagination whisk you away? I'm nearly thirty now, and that feeling is too rare these days. Hero of the Kingdom didn't blow me away, but it did help me remember that sometimes games can be like a cosy blanket that you settle into at the end of the day. A hot mug of tea and a crackling fire in winter - that's what this game is. The simple, rustic fantasy setting and verdant aesthetic, the gentle score and straightforward-yet-rewarding gameplay all combine very well to create a surprisingly immersive experience. The whole is much greater than the sum, I feel.
You start out with a pretty typical fantasy trope via your farm being burned to ashes by bandits, and your father going missing. From there, you embark on an adventure to capture all the krayfish and mercilessly steal eggs from nests. I mean, erm, 'helping fellow villagers'. These tasks range in importance...some are incredibly menial, some revolve around the livelihood of an NPC, and others up the stakes towards the prevention of an apocalypse. It's all quite homely, although the game doesn't shy away from generic soldiers getting killed. Essentially, the gameplay revolves around resource management in a point & click environment - collect materials, trade them, sell them for cash, and so forth. You're fairly well railroaded at first, although at around the halfway point you can elect to ditch the sidequests in favour of just buying everything, if you're happy to buy/sell accordingly and get an endless profit going.
I was sceptical, but Hero of the Kingdom won me over from the outset. I beat the game in six hours, and I was thoroughly impressed. Well worth the cash when it's on sale, if only for being able to indulge your inner child for a few hours. I didn't even find all the collectables, but I don't mind that - it just gives me an excuse to come back and play it all again in a few months time...

I beat the PS4 version of the game first, then bought it from Humble and beat that, and then bought it here because it was on sale and why not.  First playthrough was easily over 100 hours.
I think this is probably the best video game that's ever been made.  It's certainly my favorite, but beyond personal preference, what it accomplishes is mind blowing.  I've never had any piece of art make me feel as much a part of the human race as this does.  There's a million things about this I could talk about, but two things I'll mention here are:
1. The realization that, whether cultural or biological, our brains are very predictable.  When there's three different ways to solve a puzzle, the game seems to have already known which one you'd pick first, second, and third.
2. At first the game seems like it's about solving puzzles, but as it goes on, you realize that the game is actually about getting stumped, stepping back, and after some amount of observation of the world around you, having that immediate realization of the solution.  It teaches you how to learn, and in a way that's applicable outside of the game too.
The game is also constructed like a classical symphony, with motifs used to build themes, and themes in various structures, but even though they start as abstract imagery/concepts, as the themes build, the abstractions fade and you are given some suggestions as to what these things all mean, much like in a film.  There's other, even more meaningful things I experienced with the game, but they're too abstract to talk about in a review.  And I could talk about this for hours.
If you're looking to burn through a puzzle game, there's amazing puzzles in this, but like I said, it's not set up as a pile of puzzles to solve one after another.  If you're looking for a game with an explicit story that bangs you over the head like almost every other video game I've played, you'll be furious after playing this.  But if you're open minded and want to explore the inside of your own brain to any extent, this might be the best game you ever play.

Planetbase is a quintisential survival/RTS/city planning hybrid that takes place on different planetary bodies with differing levels of difficulty. After having FINALLY completed all of the milestones for the first planet class, I figured it was a good time to write up a reveiw on the current state of the game, but before I do that it begs mentioning that the development team is continuously updating the game and fixing bugs; something that is awesome coming from such a small development group.
Now, for the quintisential pros and cons:
Pros:
Visually pretty- the Unreal Engine, while not my favourite, provides a visual beauty to the game that balances out ambience and detail with performance.
Challenging- Random events, random starting locations, and varying challenges thrown at you make the game especially challenging even in the first scenario. The balance of choosing what's best for the moment, versus what's best for the future is one of the knife-edges that makes this game a blast and very satisfying when you "win".
Intuitive- Camera controls and choices for items and expansion are fairly intuitive.
Replayability- Just to try to do better, I have played the first planet multiple times, despite having gotten successfully growing bases in previous playthroughs. The randomization and challenges make the game more fun the second, third, or tenth time around!
Depth- The game is fairly in-depth with the facility types and levels that are possible.
Fun- I have played this game longer than many of my AAA RTS/Survival/etc... titles. Awesome bang for the buck!
The Meh:
Soundtrack- While the sound effects are great, if you're wanting a game that has decent audio for the soundtrack, this isn't it. While it's very appropriate for the genre and sci-fi aspects, it's very limited and somewhat repetetive.
Unable to upgrade existing facilities- As of this review, the ability to upgrade existing facilities has not been implemented. Whether this is a design decision, or something to be implemented later, it's exceedingly annoying to not be able to upgrade existing facilities.
Cons:
AI is stupid- Whether it's a pathing issue, or the fact that the game's only "control" you have is by raising the priority on a specific building, the AI for your colonists is oftentimes stupid. I have had many games where I've had an overabundance of food, but the AI is so stupid that it would simply just starve to death as opposed to moving to a different canteen facility for food. Additionally, there's no way to prioritize the removal of resources reclaimed form having recycled a facility, so you have to wait for the AI to eventually decide to clear out the resources before you can build again.
Control- Going off of what I've said above, the complete lack of control of anything other than a simple "priority" button means that when things get really dicey it's impossible to actually direct the people to do something simple like re-locate to another area of the station. If they would add a simple "tasking" section where you could assign specific people to a job manually if you wished, this would make the game a lot less frustrating, and add a fun micro-aspect to it if you wanted to use it.
Overall a 7.5/10

let me put this into perspective.
I'm currently playing through this game (and sinking good revising time) when i have exams in a few weeks.
i read a few reviews before purchase, and i think some people forget how small this game is.. it's not a serious title, and it's only £15..
recommend, obviously. what i wouldnt recommend is wasting revising time. unless its on this game....

GAMEPLAY
I am using the Thrustmaster T.Flight HOTAS X Stick and it works out perfectly well. Although there are no presettings for using a Joystick, the setup is pretty quick and easy. You can personalize all buttons very well and thus, I strongly recommend using a joystick or better a HOTAS for the game, which I believe is crucial for the fun factor of the game.
Gameplay feels GREAT. You can literally feel all the properties of the different plane types you are flying and the effects of how you fly. The principle is very easy to learn and becomes more and more challenging, as you fly different random mission from your base (A flying Aircraft carrier). You will have to either destroy enemy bases on the ground in awesome bombing runs or battle bogeys and aces in challenging dogfights with your steadily growing arsenal of all different sorts of weapons. Once you successfully complete a mission and return to your base, a new mission will wait for you. With every mission you complete, your enemies will get stronger and harder to ward off, but if you die once, you will be back at the beginning and have to start all over again. All upgrades you afforded will also be lost.
For each kill, you will earn Tech points (which are not going to be reset) and proceed in your Tech Level, wich will unlock new planes and weapons. The planes not only differ as to how they look like, but there is also a great deal changed about their handling, speed and their payload (How much weaponry they can carry)
The gameplay itself is pretty easy to master but still quite challenging. Your weapon pool's arsenal consists of guide Air to Air missiles and Air to Ground missiles which will have to be locked on to an enemy before firing them off, bombs, unguided missiles and machine guns/Flaks. You always have to carefully chose, which weapons to take with you in which plane, as they have limited payloads and only four slots.
You also have the ability to equip a fifth slot either with flares (You can dump flares to ward off enemy missiles), drone wingmans which can be launched to help you or a speed booster.
There are different skins you can fit to your planes for every personal style. All of them look good.
GRAPHICS
There isn't much to say about Graphics. Sky Rogue's Graphics are not at all impressive, but they have a very nice low-polygon style. Though there are many low-polygon games, Sky Rogue maintains a very personal style, making the game charming and unique. Thus, the performance is great, even on low-end PCs like mine (Intel Core 0.03 at 1Hz), even at highest graphic settings.
MODDING
Modding is one of the most important features of this game. Even if you might get tired of the main game after a few hours of playing it, there will be always an extremely wide range of mods which feature awesome fictional and real-world airplanes to get a new shot of enthusiasm into your veins and also custom missions. Mods are also verz easz to create and if you are looking for a particulat plane and can't find it, there are plenty of guides to help you create your personal mod.
*HOWEVER* Don't tap into the trap of downloading OP planes like I did before, as this will destroy the fun factor completely. It should always be challenging!
REVIEW
This game is AWESOME and well worth the 10 quit. You will get that top gun feeling, shooting down endlessly many bogeys and bombing infinitely many buildings, Dodging enemy missiles with daring barrel roll maneuvers and dumping flares at them. This game is what you are going to be in the skies. an ACE!

If you're not careful, they can drop on your head very quickly as well.  It's a little hard to tell where the platforms allow for that.  Visibility is also a recurring concern - platforms are hard to make out, and the screen shaking from various events is overdone.
Being able to pick up a diverse number of melee weapons is pretty fun, though using them is so much more riskier than simply firing your gun - you get a lot of ammo and it's very easy to miss or take damage after you swing.  It's troubling because it's a lot of fun to melee, while firing your gun feels pretty mindless.  Nerfing ammo drops should help with this balance.
Finally, the subtly different enemy types are also a nice feature.  The dev continues to polish, and things are looking good for a recommendation.

This game has a lot going for it so early on. I haven't mastered the game but there is a lot to keep it fun and the developer has a lot of realistic plans for the future.
Current game flow: Pick a mask, fight off a wave of monsters and collect their guts to make a red potion thingy. Get three and you finished the round! You can collect from packages that will appear or move to another room, or try a bit of both. You don't have a lot of time. If it sounds boring, I found it definitely a fun experience.
The art is just too good for words. You don't need to pay to see that. Or just judge for yourself.
The controls are great, I have trouble when trying to jump on the stairs in some rooms, while in other rooms it's easy. It might be my controller though since it sometimes sticks to move left now and then. There is no story mode yet but it's planned, and the game is most definitely a complete experience. Though I'm sure it will be much further improved even before full release out of Early Access.
The masks. There are quiet a few each with their own abilities. Most increase your health but all do health upgrading and/or an ability. The developer has stated that the final count will be around 33. Off the top of my head, there are around 9 now. One example is a gas mask that after enough shots or kills [forgot which if not both], will spew a gas when activated. I find it useful to say the least.
The music goes with the gameplay. I find music necessary but not a big thing for me so you might want to read other reviews regarding it. For me it's enough to keep the gameplay flowing.. but again I'm not big on music unless it's a game where music is part of gameplay or just super super great. Though it's absolutely not bad at all IMO.
I almost forgot, the enemies aren't super varied but the individual enemies aren't your only concern. You have to deal with more and more of them, some different as you go each round. But also, there are unique traps for each room. I won't spoil them, but each is different and I think at least one room has two. I can't really remember in detail. I just know they aren't only against you.. if you are smart you can use them to kill enemies.
Most importantly aside from me really enjoying the game at an early stage of development.. I have to vouch that the developer is on the best end of Early Access and after seeing them keep up with their work I found enough interest to give it an in-depth try.
I am definitely looking forward to more of the masks and game design. I'll try to update this review again at least when out of E Access. MIGHT update now and then as it develops.

room13 is an action platformer featuring everyone's favourite enemy, the zombie, that's currently available through Steam Early Access. In room13 you fight your way through thirteen rooms filled with zombies as well as deadly traps. Progressing through these rooms or staying in the one you're currently in increases the difficulty of what you face.
+Cool black, white and red based art style. The blood red provides a satisfying contrast with the black and white colours of everything else
+Great customisation, not only can you customise your character with different helmets/heads (which also provide special bonuses) you also get weapon parts at the end of each round which can be used to customise your gun
+A lot of gun parts to choose from, more heads and gun parts are unlocked as you play through the game
+The death traps are very creative
+The game keeps a count of all of your kills, it's a simple feature but I really like it
+A few different types of zombies, each one behaves in a slightly different way
+Simple gameplay that's very addictive and challenging
+Good soundeffects and soundtrack
+/-The controls aren't the best but they are improving (I played with a 360 controller)
+/-Only thirteen rooms, if you aren't too good at the game it will keep you entertained for a while but if you manage to burn through them you're not gonna have much to do
+/-When a round ends you don't have enough time to get all the items as well as leave the room which I found annoying
-The mouse cursor doesn't disappear under any circumstances which is rather irritating
-Can get a little frustrating when an ammo, health or battery drops on the other side of the room when there are a lot of zombies there
Verdict:
Worth purchasing (7.5/10)

To be fair, you have to have a very high IQ to understand The Witness. The story is extremely subtle, and without a solid grasp of theoretical physics most of the storyline will go over a typical gamer's head. There’s also Jonathan Blow's nihilistic outlook, which is deftly woven into his characterisation- his personal philosophy draws heavily from Narodnaya Volya literature, for instance. The fans understand this stuff; they have the intellectual capacity to truly appreciate the depths of these puzzles, to realise that they’re not just difficult- they say something deep about LIFE. As a consequence people who dislike The Witness truly ARE idiots- of course they wouldn’t appreciate, for instance, the insight in the silent protaganist's existential catchphrase “...” which itself is a cryptic reference to Turgenev’s Russian epic Fathers and Sons. I’m smirking right now just imagining one of those addlepated simpletons scratching their heads in confusion as Jonathan Blow'ss genius wit unfolds itself on their television screens. What fools.. how I pity them. 😂
And yes, by the way, i DO have a Braid tattoo. And no, you cannot see it. It’s for the ladies’ eyes only- and even then they have to demonstrate that they’re within 5 IQ points of my own (preferably lower) beforehand. Nothin personnel kid 😎

Alright let me say this first: If you want a game that's got lots of ..."Game" in it? You might possibly want to give this one a miss.
This game is more in the vein of say Phoenix Wright but with less investigatey stuff and far less choice in matters. This however isn't really a bad thing? It's a strangely calming experience. The only actual game parts of it are picking what music to set up at the start of each day and after each break (has no in game effect other than playing different tracks and there's two achievements centred around the jukebox), mixing drinks (of which you can choose to give them what they ask for... what they REALLY asked for, what they actually would normally WANT, or...something else if you're feeling mean, spiteful, or curious...or just make a mistake), and buying certain things to make sure Jill, your character, stays focused (so you don't have to manually remember what the client wanted and said) and making sure you earn enough to pay the three bills that turn up in ever increasing cost throughout the game.
That's basically it.
You can't choose what to say to people; you're seeing a month in the life of Jill Stingray, a bartender, at a very out of the way bar in a highly dystopian cyberpunk city ruled by corruption, rife with greed, and plagued by rampant capitalism (...or was it plagued with greed, rife with corruption, and ruled by rampant capitalism?... Hm. No matter). You experience her life, trials and tribulations, and just try and get by day by day.
Surprisingly it turned out to be a very deep and engrossing game for me. There's so much lore and background detail and interesting story to read and experience in the game. Glitch City has got so much life  that it's almost impossible not to want to know MORE about the city and indeed the rest of the world.
There's some very heartfelt dialogue, some great writing, some genuinely hilarious moments, a whole cast of interesting characters (even three secret ones you can meet with the right circumstances... though that requires either having played Read Only Memories, or looking up a guide tbh. It really is a secret), and some amazing music to go with the whole experience. Mixing drinks is kind of fun as it turns out, if simplistic.
If you want a game heavy on narrative and worldbuilding, one which you will likely find yourself invested with the characters, I will absolutely recommend this game to you. Fair warning however, there is a character who you may really enjoy or find completely offputting. I'm speaking of course about Dorothy, the sex worker Lilim (sentient android) whose body remains in the appearance of a 10-13 year old :/ who talks rather frankly and cheerfully about how she keeps her body that way because it grants her a very competitive edge in business.
Personally I see Dorothy as a damning indictment of the fictional world she lives in and Glitch City in general, that this situation is apparently normal and accepted, even by the character herself, who seems to apply herself with quite a lot of gusto to her job with very few complaints, and who often flirts mercilessly with various members of the cast. She doesn't glorify her situation, nor does she judge her clients. Others however may find, quite understandably, her presence and the themes she covers to be very distasteful, if not outright abhorrent, and I cannot blame you at all. So it's only fair to warn you of that.
There is a far deeper side to Dorothy however, and the Lilim in general as a whole, as well as various other setting details I won't spoil if you decide to pick up the game. Despite the inclusion of Dorothy I still had good fun with the game, and Dorothy as a character is fascinating, if deeply uncomfortable. Depending on choice of drinks you give to people, you can have some interesting conversations with many of them. It plays out almost like a visual novel in that aspect, except it's far less about dating people and getting to the porn (there is no porn after all, or dates exactly), and more about just getting by, day to day, dodging whatever spanners life throws at you.

Like any game on Steam, Laserlife has its ups and downs. Luckily the ups far outnumber the downs.
Laserlife has a story at its heart, as in the description, it is the story of a dead astronaut from childhood to death. And its a good one.
Telling a story without any words* is always a challenge, relying upon visuals**, sound and imagination. And let me tell you, Laserlife has all of the above. It delivers a beautifully crafted piece of storytelling with brilliant creativity that really does make you stop and think. Take it from me, I'm no sentimentalist.
There are three "Acts"; Childhood, Adulthood and Death.
Each Act has 4 levels, each leading to a different milestone in memory.
Each level in the game is made up of 4 phases and is set up as a kind of twin-stick runner, utilising 2 lasers.
The environment of the 'Collection' phase is the same over the Act, therefore there are only 3 'Collection' environments in the game.
They are a kind of pseudo-psychadelic representation of that certain stage in life. They are meant to stimulate thought, emotion and - most importantly - your imagination.
The environment of the 'Harmonising' phase is where the story really comes into play. Using the same kind of style as the previous phase, only much clearer, they tell a certain aspect of the story - a significant part in the astronauts' life.
The 'Warp' phase has a tunnel environment, nothing other than that. Various obstacles block your path, easily navigable...mostly.
The 'Power' phase revolves around the captured astronaut as the memory is vigorously extracted.
The music is a fine example of techno done right and complements the gameplay fantastically.
Overall this is a triumph of modern day storytelling, employing original and highly creative means.
However, I did mention downsides.
The primary downside is that this game is far too short! I completed it within 2 hours and that includes a few repeats. The only way to make it longer is to aim for perfect scores.
I implore the devs to add some more content, another story, anything!
This leads me onto the second point which is that the price tag is, for the gameplay time, pretty excessive. When you play, you can see where the money has gone and I, for one, can understand that but charging £11.00 (~$16.00) for just a few hours isn't something many can commend.
As such, I can't recommend full price for this game, brilliant as it is - buy it on sale.
*The only words in the entire game come from random excerpts of real dialogue between NASA astronauts and ground control (added for effect) and the poignant explanation at the end of a level.
**The visuals are truly great, however if you are playing properly you will only see them in your peripheral vision. I honestly recommend you to start up a Phase 1 or 2 and not play it, instead focus on the exquisite background.

I grew up on Parasoft's
for PC and Majesco's
for the Gameboy Advance, and Sky Rogue is next in my lineup of combat flight games.
This game is a light alternative to intense simulators for those who just want to get airborne, blow stuff up, but also want challenging opposition instead of enemies that couldn't hit a barn.
That leads me into the one thing that sets this game apart from most others in its genre:
. The latest updates have made it possible to get to levels without dodging missiles left and right. Don't expect to fly in and out without a scratch, but the looming bullet hell common with rogue-likes is absent during earlier levels.
If you have a spare controller, you and a buddy can play through missions co-op, which in my experience is rather fun.
Now that I've praised the game, I must also point out some of its flaws. The first and most irritating (to me) is repeating missions. The first time you bomb some enemy HQ it is alright. Not after the 5th time.
My suggestion would be to stack mission objectives, but hey, this is a review.
The second game aspect is the lack of online multiplayer and/or a dogfight mode for multiplayer. That's just something I feel that a fly-em-up should have if it includes multiplayer. At least some local network co-op would be nice.
When all is said and done, Sky Rogue is a great early access game that has potential to be that title that fills the gap between hardcore flight sims and flight games that just don't offer much for those looking for replayability. While I love my DCS: A-10C, after a long day it's nice to have a game that forgoes the simulation stuff, offering something that everyone can jump in and enjoy.

The Witness is a pretentious and vague first person puzzle game centered around line-drawing puzzles. Every puzzle in the game is some variant on a puzzle whereby the player drags their mouse across a grid to form a line to some destination point, following certain rules of construction along the way.
The game lacks any real story; you are on a mysterious island, and you explore it. There are various recordings of real-world quotes and even video clips scattered around the island, but all of these are very vague, nebulous, wordy, and ultimately pointless. They are of variable quality; some of them are more interesting than others, but there isn’t any sort of story to the game. The only objective – which is never explicitly stated to the player, as the game is totally lacking in instructions either – is to reveal laser beams which then ultimately open up the area where you solve some puzzles to end the game. There is no real purpose to this; it is all just about solving puzzles.
This, unfortunately, is one of the major problems with the experience; the game is lacking in both story and context, and while some pure puzzle games function in that way, this is a game with a complex 3D environment – its lack of any sort of coherent plot is really puzzling. Worse, because there is no real goal, the game often feels unrewarding – your “prize” for solving puzzles is even more puzzles to solve.
And the puzzles, unfortunately, tend to be pretty repetitive. The game is all about grid-drawing puzzles, with various obstacles thrown in the player’s way. Some of these are rules – you have to make specific shapes with the line, say, or separate out colored dots. Others are the result of literal obstructions – there is something in the way of the puzzle, and so you have to draw around it. Some of the puzzles rely on you looking through them to trace environmental features, or obscure portions of the puzzle from your view, requiring you to deduce what you’re supposed to do. Some involve lining up objects in the environment in order to draw lines across them, and there is a secret set of environmental puzzles which function like a hidden object game, where you click on environmental features and draw lines on them.
While the game manages to mix up the line puzzles much more than one might expect, unfortunately, they still become samey after a while. While many of the puzzles are easy – especially while introducing some new concept – some of them are quite difficult, and while it never takes very long to solve a puzzle in the sense of actually drawing the lines, it can take you a very long time to figure out what, exactly, you are supposed to be doing. Worse, if you are stuck, there is nothing really for you to do except keep plugging away at the puzzle or wandering off and doing some other puzzle.
The island itself is rather pretty – the graphics are simple, but attractive. Unfortunately, the game seems to believe that walking around the island a great deal is part of the experience, so there is no quick-travel system – if you get stuck on a puzzle and want to go elsewhere, you’re going to have to walk there manually, and while the island isn’t huge, it can take you a couple minutes to get out of the place you’re in, especially if it involved puzzles that moved the environment around in response to you drawing lines (such as drawing lines to move a ferry from one place to another, or to open up a specific path through a location). While this mostly isn’t too bad, it does discourage the player from walking away from a puzzle set.
The game is, on the whole, just okay. The puzzles are quite challenging, but the lack of any motivation to keep playing is wearing. I played the game for about ten hours when I first got it about six months ago, then set it down and didn’t touch it again until tonight, when I solved the last two areas and beat it in another five hours or so, totaling up to about 15 hours of gameplay. Beating the game felt like a pretty empty experience, without any real payoff, and really, the game in general just lacks any sort of sense of reward.
If you are really fond of puzzles, this game has a number of fairly clever ones, even if they’re all based around the same system. But this game can be frustrating in its lack of instructions, won’t help you out in any way if you get stuck, and there is no story or overarching plot. What little dialogue there is in the game is in the form of recordings of real-world quotes, all of which are intended to sound deep, but they don’t lend the game any sense of depth, merely of pretention.
All in all, I don’t think most people would enjoy this game, but people who are big fans of puzzles might get some mileage out of it. But even they are likely to be disappointed if they’re hoping for some sort of payoff like The Talos Principle or the Portal games, or even something like The Turing Test; none of that is present here. There are no characters, no plot, and no story. Just lots and lots of line-drawing puzzles.

Who likes shooting zombies and collecting organs?
I do! And that's what you get to do in room13.
room13 is a 2D shooter where you must collect the delicious giblets of destroyed zombies. After you collect enough parts you will spawn a battery which you need three of to move onto the next room.
As you move from room to room each round gets harder, you face different enemies and each room has a unique trap that can become activated. At the end of each round you'll have a few seconds to search some crates to upgrade your weapon.
The game is a little rouge like, in its mechanics. As you progress you'll achieve different milestones which unlocks new weapon parts and new masks. The masks to my knowledge only increase your health(although the trailer does show a shark mask that seems to eat zombies!) . While the weapons upgrades are random drops in those crates at the end of the rounds. You'll die plenty and as you do hopefully your runs will lasts longer and longer.
room13 is a fast paced addicting shooter while plenty of zombie destruction to go around.
My only gripe is the controls, when moving up and down stairs you must go all the way up or down. You're unable to just jump up onto them, which makes it hard to get out of tight spots.

This game has a lot going for it, even in an early state. It's challenging, requiring a pretty good awareness of ammunition, timing, and health amidst some pretty frantic action. Maybe I suck, but most of my games are about 2 minutes long, leading to the inevitable "one more" feeling. There are leaderboards tracking several categories, and that helps with a sense of reward as it finds its legs. There are already numerous unlocks in place, and what I'm digging most is the variety of means to play, even on a limited stage. Staying on one floor longer has its own rewards, and changes occur in the environment if you decide to push your luck (death trap activated!). Pushing on to the next floor is too tempting, usually, as I'm eager to see the next layout.
Good job devs. Don't hate me for this, but it really does have a Binding of Isaac meets platformer feel. Can't say enough for the art direction and cinematic effects during play, either )

Danganronpa is a murder mystery, pseudo-visual novel-ish game similar to the Phoenix Wright series, but with much more mature, well developed, and interactive plots and a variety of unique, interesting characters who bring different views and personalities into the fray. There are some times when the case seems obvious and in your face. At times, this is the case. At others, however, these initial impressions are flipped on their heads multiple times during the Class Trials. I would highly recommend this game to anyone looking to spend 15+ hours in a gory game of cat and mouse.
I have already watched the anime version of this game, and it is a very faithful adaptation, with no cuts or changes that Inoticed.I played the game mostly as a refresher before I start playing Danganronpa 2, so I am caught up when the Danganronpa 3 anime comes out in a few weeks.
I do, however, have one complaint about the game: during trials, there are a lot of cookie cutter animations and transitions that occur ever single time an even happens, and these are unskippable. While they are only 5-10 seconds each, when they happen repeatedly, one after the other, they themselves add about 10-15 minutes to every hour of actual gameplay. Also, at times, the main character comes accross as incredibly oblivious to obvious facts, making you as the player "discover" them after sitting through the aforementioned animations that happen before and after every minigame during the trial.
I will admit that I played this game at its easiest difficulty, so the mileage others get may differ. However, from what I understood throughtout the game and tutorials, the difficulty simply changes the timings and difficulty of the minigames, at times completely disabling debuffs the AI can use to make minigames more difficult, while the actual plot remains the same. Use that information as you would like.

Side-scrolling horde-mode
The Paper Robot
Clickteam
is side-scrolling horde-mode game developed by The Paper Robot and published by Clickteam and is currently available on Steam Early Access.
The black-and-white art style is rich of detail in the different rooms that you explore, and the walls quickly turn red when you blast your way through zombies.
Your objective is to avoid dying while exploring the different rooms of the mansion. In order to proceed, you have to collect the blood and guts that the zombies eject, to then grab a vial of blood: after getting three vials of blood, the doors of the room open up and some crates appear. The crates either contain weapon improvements, weapon receivers, a secondary weapon, health or nothing.
The keyboard controls are rather awkward, so I recommend using a controller (if you own it, of course). The shooting feels really good, and the controls are responsive enough. Like with many horde games, it does tend to get repetitive after some time, and there currently isn't much variety in enemies and weapons, but the different rooms have various environmental hazards and the zombies are satisfying to kill.
The game tends to be more frustrating than challenging: you will finish your clip too fast, and you are armless against the horde of zombies that's trying to eat you. It is also really easy to don't notice the vial of blood spawning, and if you don't take it, it will explode and damage you.
The noises of the zombies and the gunshots are really good and effective, and the music gives you enough adrenaline and hurry to fight the zombies.
The game does get really addictive, and you will want to unlock all the different masks to get perks and gameplay variety. Plus, more features will be added in future updates.
Overall, the game is well developed, but it does tend to get incredibly frustrating rather than enjoyable. Those who are looking for a good challenge will be more than satisfied, while other players won't pick it up that often.

Planetbase is a colony building strategy/simulation game from Madruga Works. In Planetbase, you first start out with a handful of colonists and bots with respective profession and duties. Your primary job is to create a self-sufficient colony to sustain your population and gradually improve and expand your colony to support increasing colonists and visitors. In such a dire condition, your survivability depends on your management skills and strategic thinking.
Despite being a colony building game, Planetbase did not fail to deliver stunning graphics with amazing clarity. The texture and shadow is exceptionally well-done. The game is designed down to the smallest detail, for example, the beautiful and starry night sky can be seen reflected on Solar Panel. The UI is great, the menu is easy to use and only allocates a small space. Besides that, there is a notification system which will alert you when there are surfacing issues such as the death of colonist, a sandstorm, etc.
As an impatient person, I enjoy the fast forward feature very much. The game will revert to its normal speed when an issue occurs which I found either annoying or helpful at times.
There are 4 planets to choose from with increasing difficulty and different conditions. Choose the location of your base wisely, the geometrical factor will affect the expansion of your colony. Besides that, Planetbase offers a respectable type of buildings ranging from solar panels to wind turbine to processing plants. Each and every building plays an important role in the development of the colony and the production chain. One thing that I absolutely love about the game is the ability to place various equipments in the buildings. For example, you may place a water dispenser in the Canteen

As mentioned, management skills is compulsory for a successful colony. During the later stage, you may construct Starports and Landing Pads to welcome colonists, traders and visitors. Hence, you would need to carefully manage the colonist immigration flow to ensure you have the people with the right skills. Terrorist would start to appear gradually as your prestige increases, those ****** would disguise as colonist or visitors, so be extremely cautious. This game encourages a strategic mindset, it makes you think twice before doing carrying out an action or building. You will most certainly ask yourself if placing a certain building at that location lengthen the time of processing a certain material.
As a HUGE fan of colony-building games, I would say that Planetbase is one of the best out there. Many people said that it’s hard but you’ll manage after a few retries. Hopefully, the developers would add choices for guns and include aliens as well! But as for now, it’s time for me to continue my 9-hour Planetbase streak.
: 8/10

I really want to recommend this game, but it has too many issues for me to do so.  Technically there is no problem with the game (no crashes or anything like that), however lack of a windowed mode in this kind of game is quite frustrating.
The main issue I have with this game is how increadibly unbalanced it feels.  It's very challenging to keep your colonists alive, but when they do inevitably die, it feels like it was the games fault and not yours.  Upon completing the tutorial, I attempted to replicate what it had taught me, only to have most of my colonists die of asphyxiation.  This is due to you having to build solar panels (which only work in the day), before wind turbines; the day-night cycle is faster in the real game than in the tutorial, so you quickly run out of power and your O2 plant shuts down.
My next big gripe is that the economy is pretty dire.  The cost of buildings compared to the cost to connect them is very low (meaning that a solar panel is as expensive as the wire to connect to it.  This also makes it quite hard to scale up the size of your base because building the cabling infrastructure is very expensive.  Also, I really dislike that way that everything needs to be connected together in a tree like structure.  I understand the thematic reasoning for it, but it make refactoring your base design undesireable.
My biggest peeve however is that the game never seems to balance.  You indefinately have colonists pouring into your colony with no management (or easy management) of limiting them based on the amount of resource you have available.  This means that you'll create a nice 'sustained' base, and over (relatively short) time, it will decay, your consumption will out compete your production, and ultimately your colony will collapse because there isn't any real way to dig yourself out of situations.
Here's an example: I build a mine before a medical ward (because I didn't have enough metal to build both, it made sense to build a mine, to get metal, to build the other), all my miners broke their bones so would not work, so I couldn't get any metal.  I had to recycle some buildings to scrape together enough metal for a medical ward, which then made production somewhere else drop below critical level.  I then had to do the same else where, and eventually I just gave up because a minor timing issue caused everything to halt.
Love this game! Definitely worth looking at if you like strategy based games, without the worry of getting attacked and your whole base destroyed...

Possibly the best VN I've ever played, certainly the best western developed VN.  The music is absolutely incredible, the art is beautiful, and the writing leaves very little to be desired.  Keep in mind you shouldn't go into this looking for a dating sim or a plot with a big start and finish, it is more like a great number of days in the life of the main character, who I must say has much more personality than most VN protags in my experience.  All of the characters are well fleshed out, and in a rare twist for visual novels, three dimensional in personality without requiring some sort of "twist" or hidden trait.  Everyone seemingly has a good and bad side, rather than the sort of black and white I'm so used to seeing in visual novels.  Just hanging around these unique characters in this very fun setting is what drives the game forward rather than an A to B traditional plot, and I think it's better for it, (though if this game were to feature romance options I wouldn't complain).  Can I recommend it to everyone?  No.  The lack of romance options and plot may be a turn off for traditional VN players, and the topics the characters cover could lead you with a bad taste in your mouth if you're looking for something completely innocent and fun.  However, if none of that bothers you, and the trailer seems at all appealing, it is easily worth the price.  You'll know if you like it or not within the refund period anyway, more likely than not.

VA-11 Hall-A: Cyberpunk Bartender Action was an idea that struck me as one that I feel really should have been used before, and perhaps has. After all, a bar is a pretty good setting to find people from all walks of life coming to the same place for different reasons, be it as a distraction from the lives they live outside the bar walls, a place to try and meet new people to stave off the loneliness they’re living with, a place to unload their problems onto others without the fear of judgement or guilt, or even just a place to enjoy a drink.
VA-11 Hall-A, is a game about these people and more. It’s like a snapshot of their lives, some we only see once, some we get to know better over time. We play the game from the point-of-view of the bartender who see’s these different people come and go, seeing only a few moments of their lives but not before changing them in some way, be it big or small. This is all set over the backdrop of a futuristic dystopian society, a world whose politics and background we learn more about throughout the game.
In terms of a story, it’s a bit tricky to nail down a particular summary. As mentioned, the game is really about the characters we meet and not some overarching plot we follow throughout. Because of this it feels like the beginning and ending held almost no significance, although the ending does tie things up with the main character well enough. I know this game is really meant as just a snapshot in time, but a bit more significance to start and end things off could have improved things.
The people themselves are great. Fun, interesting characters with compelling, sometimes quite tragic backgrounds and stories to tell. The contrast of people we meet is one of the great things about this game as well. Each character is so well devised that each of them really feels like they’re their own individual person, which when the game is pretty much only about the characters, is a very good thing. Even the main character who we see things from, Jill, is unique in her own way. She’s a person who tries to help others see their problems logically and deal with them head on, yet is unable herself to heed her own advice. The characters have their strengths and flaws, and they only help deepen our affinity for them as we seem them change over time and reveal pieces of themselves that may not have at first been clear. The futuristic setting also plays an important role with the characters. I won’t go into any specific details, but it’s nice to see both the characters and setting play an important and interrelated role together.
Since it’s a visual novel, the only real gameplay is the ability to mix and create the drinks that the customer asks for. Sometimes they’ll tell you exactly what they want, sometimes more choice is given to the player. Different drinks are created by mixing different amounts of ingredients together. While it’s simple, I quite like this feature. It helps with the pacing of the game and gives an opportunity to gain a bit of a breather with the dialogue. While there are no dialogue options, different drinks will often lead to different branches in the story, affecting who some characters meet and and don’t meet. There are also a few bills you have to pay over the course of the game, so you still have to earn money. While the costs start low, they build up, and it’s interesting how near the end you find yourself giving more expensive drinks to customers just so you can hopefully pay your rent. Also, on most days, there are items you can buy that keep Jill from getting distracted, which essentially makes it easier to remember the drinks the customer's order. While the game is very relaxing to play, these small expenses keep you on your toes enough for you to want to pay attention.
The soundtrack is also quite good. You can choose which songs play during the course of the night and in what order, but some songs can only be unlocked as you play. While the songs are good, the fact that the player picks them can sometimes be a bit awkward story-wise, especially when a someone is giving you their tragic backstory and some heavy techno-rock song is blaring in the background, but this is only a small nitpick.
Overall, this is a very enjoyable and relaxing character-driven game. A lack of beginning and ending shouldn’t hinder your enjoyment of it too much, and it’s certainly worth trying if you get the chance.

This game is exactly as cool as its premise. You are assembling a dead astronaut's memories in a very alien way through a really neat rhythm game.
Pros:
+Visually impressive and well optimized (except right after level completion, occasionally)
+Really fun and unique gameplay. I haven't played a rhythm game like this before (although I have seen comparisons made). If you could somehow put in your own music, this would replace Audiosurf 2 for me.
+Futuristic and alien music. The music is easy to "feel," which is obviously important in a rhythm game.
+Again, the premise and concept are just really cool. You'll be fascinated by the story and visuals by the time the menu screen shows up.
Neutral:
=Some of the fragments that you have to push an analog stick just partially to get are nearly impossible with the first person moving forward setup. You'll see what I mean in later levels.
=You'll hear the same songs over several times in the first and third stages of each memory in a group.
=The game is <2.5 hours. Concise, yes. But you'll probably want more!
Cons:
-You have no idea what the camera/your trajectory will do, causing you to miss some fragments.
-Your lasers move much too slowly for some of the fragments in later levels. I know it's possible, but it just feels unfair and clunky.
As you can see, my issues are mostly just minor gameplay complaints that can be overcome by getting good. If you have doubts about the game, I recommend just tossing it on your wishlist and waiting for a sale, as the game is short.

-slowly uncovering memories is nice, while there's no real story discovering the astronaut's life and what happened on his last trip was intriguing
-leaderboards for each game level and difficulty setting for those so inclined
-a few sections get a bit too crowded on the background, making memory pieces hard to see
-a slight framerate drop at the end of some levels ( no impact on gameplay, but was a bit annoying)
-short, it'll take you 1,5/2 hours to finish and, unless you want to go for an high score on certain levels, there's no replay value
I really liked Laserlife, the gameplay is fun and keeps you on your toes, the levels sport nice and trippy graphics, the soundtrack alternates between high tempo and slower tracks to mix things up a bit and the various memories were interesting enough to keep going for more.
It's a bit of a shame that it's so short, the 12 levels go by quickly (in fact the devs recommend playing through the game in one sitting) and once you're done there's not much else to do, they'd also have done a bit more with the story rather than just giving us bits and pieces of memories.
All things considered if you're a fan of the genre or just want something different Laserlife is an easy recommendation, just avoid getting it for full price since I feel it's too much for the amount of gameplay you get: thankfully it goes as low as 5$ when on sale.

With the lack of real triple-A flight simulators coming out lately, Sky Rogue attempts to take the reigns and create an arcade-like aircraft game. But does it succeed?
I'll be happy to report that the gameplay is the highlight of Sky Rogue. Choosing from a variety of planes which you unlock, as well as a loadout from a colorful and fun weapon pool, you take to the skies in a brillant fashion. Launched from your mothership, you complete randomly assigned missions. This can range from average bombings to taking on entire battleships.
Movement feels fluid, and you can feel the agility and weight of your planes with every sick turn or twist. For evasion, you have a simple, but effective dodge roll which usually throws missiles off. Barring that, you can equip flares for a big middle finger towards your missile slinging foes. Your weapons are large-scale and always ready to chew up the opposition. Explosives, lock-on missiles, machine guns, and much more are available as you steadily progress through the game. When you inevitably get shot down, you are sent back to mission 1, but not before unlocking some permanently acquired equipment with your hard earned "Tech" points.
Note that this game works with your HOTUS setup, and (apparently) feels great!
The graphics of Sky Rogue aren't exactly impressive, but have a very low-polygon charm that is done intentionally. It looks great and doesn't seem to impede with performance too much. Certainly colorful as well, with bright explosions, gaudy color schemes, and a blue sky at your hull.
Runs great, even on my potato of a PC. Supports DirectX9 and DirectX11. Solid 60 while playing on the highest graphics, and even runs at 50-60 while recording if I bump the graphics down to low.
Sky Rogue has a modding community that seems fairly talented and dedicated to making up some ridiculously cool or funny looking planes. Custom missions are also littered through the workshop, though I haven't personally tried any of them out. The developers are responsive and work at a moderate pace. They seem to have things sorted out, though they also seem behind schedule. Still, the game currently has a fairly good amount of content, well worth its 10 dollar price tag.
Now this is what I'd call a great flght-and-flight game. You'll feel like a real badass ace flying through the skies, shooting down enemy drones and bombing countless amounts of buildings, all while dodging the wall of missiles and flak that impede you fruitlessly.
Well worth the 10 dollars, be sure to get it while it's hot!

This game has a lonnnngggg way to go before being feature-complete, but here is The Story So Far™
The base game itself has a wide range of specialized fighters and weapons with either minor or major differences, a well put-together ordinance system revolving around either sheer demolishing power or electronics, with most weapons requiring at least a bit of both, with the standard GUN being one of few exceptions.
The fighters all have a place in combat, and the only ship with ballanced stats, the namesake of the game, the Rogue, is basic and expensive to upgrade, but so worth it as the stat boosts are one of the highest in the game of basic fighters.
Although it
a stinkin' rogue-like* tech points you earned can unlock new craft and ordinance. Protip: get the turbo micros and the 30mm.
And most importantly is the sheer level of community support to and from. Custom ships, missions, and now weapons. The lowpolly and arcade nature of the game attracts all kinds of gamers especially that of Ace Combat. It's basically that game, but much, much more instant-action with even less realistic physics. None the less, it is a
yet challenging and welcome addition to the seemingly forgotten world of fighter-jet games.
The physics, AI, world detail, and ship specialization, especially the superheavy ships like the Medved strategic bomber, all feel like they need a bit of work but I see a fairly consistant stream of it.
Three or some odd years in the making and it's not even in beta yet. Alpha 29.1 as of writing this. I'm pretty sure they're just getting started, even though I've had this game for a year now.
*protip: IT'S JOKE

It's still in Early Access, but easily worth the entry price with what's already in the game. It's basically an arcade-y dogfighter, but with a massive number of weapon and aircraft choices available. Any playstyle you can think of is viable once you get the right unlocks, which helps keep it from feeling stale even when the variety of land targets isn't quite there yet. That said, the enemy has access to all of the same planes as you do (and a few drones), so there's no shortage of variety in the air.
If there's anything I don't like about it, it's that there aren't enough upgrade tiers in a run. All your weapons and planes can only go to level 3, and you probably aren't using anywhere near all of them in one run, so you can get everything maxed out after just a few days. I'd like something useful to keep putting my cash into in the late game. I've also had some issues with the air-to-air rockets not locking on to enemies unless I cycle through my weapons first.
It's still in Alpha at the time of writing, but it feels more complete than a lot of released games. Easy recommendation even without considering the improvements to come.

I am in a love hate relationship wih this game because it is the prettiest thing but dear lord can I be thick as bricks sometimes. The excellent thing about this game is that whole island is moslty open to you right from the start, so if you can't solve a puzzle you can just walk away and do different ones, you never really get stuck as such because there's always more and more to discover.
Those saying it doesn't have story, well they aren't paying close enough attention. A huge part of the game is paying attention to the environment and playing with it to solve or find puzzles and in the island there lies strange things that give you more and more strange images and half clues as to what happened on this strange island. (I actually am pretty sure I've spoiled it for myself because I was looking to confirm if I knew the pattern of a puzzle or not and read a couple of lines about a future puzzle so be careful with your solution finding)
The advice I have is wander away is you're stuck because sometimes all you need is to wander back with fresh eyes, or in my case hand it to someone going "I know what I'm doing but I don't know why it's working" and then understanding the next set of puzzles because they solved one and you can now see the pattern.

FIRST IMPRESSIONS
If you thought Braid expanded your mind, get ready to have it fill an entire world. As close to art, the HARD stuff, as games get. Not for the mundane.
It really is a game that you need to go into cold if you have any interest in it at all. Last warning.
MIDDLE THOUGHTS
Witness is uniquely well designed. An exploration/click-puzzle game where the diagetic and atmostpheric elements blend seamlessly yet you are never confused or waste time on something which isn't part of the game. Loaded with intriguing atmospheric art and, for real, lectures and quotes from some of modern history's greatest minds, Witness is a game about learning.
As you begin, you are taught the game's singular mechanic. There is a ray. Trace a line from the point to the rounded-end. As you continue you find puzzles of increasing ambiguity, shapes and glyphs with meanings you can't discipher. Yet as you continue, you learn how each of them works, one at a time. It's empowering to learn these rules, open new areas. It's something like Metroid, something like Myst, and unlike anything I've ever seen before.
If puzzles are your thing, and zen is your element, this is your game.
CONCLUSIONS (PREMATURE)
The "End" of the game is quite... unusual. I can't say I was disappointed because I had no idea what to expect. The island is, and the title implies, subject to some event but that never really becomes clear. Like Braid, it's possible there is no story and the ludonarrative is the entire point.
That said, my emotional journey rapidly went from awe to pride to frustration to wonder to confusion. In other words, like learning itself. We are amazed when we first comprehend, enthralled when we are rising fast, then as we reach our limits.... and maybe that was the idea.
I did not get 100%, and am content with that. I enjoyed my stay on Johnathan Blow's Island and would reccommend to anyone clever enough, curious enough and willing to be patient and observant
TURNS OUT...
There's actually another 10-15% of the game I didn't find yet, and will be working to do so.
I don't exactly "hate" this kind of thing in games, but I don't think it's awesome either. Hiding an extra room or two in the old 32 Megabit Day was cute, now it's just obnoxious.

That being said, I still really enjoyed playing "Year Walk" and would recommend it to others.
