The Witness isn't for everyone, but it was for me.  Easily one of the best gaming experiences I've ever had.  It's true, you're in hours and hours (in my case, 22 hours plus a four-hour false start last year) of line puzzles, and its a slow, meditative experience that expects you to learn the mechanics and do lots of extremely clever problem solving.  Playing the Witness feels a lot like learning, because you do a lot of that.  There's a lot of the poke-it-to-see-what-happens-ness in it too.  By the end, the puzzles have gone in brilliant but completely obvious, now that you think about it ways.  I went into this thinking it was going to be a brutal puzzling experience, and in some ways it was, but the game really wants you to succeed.  There's a lot of opportunities to learn the lessons its trying to teach you, and if you don't get it you can wander off and tackle some other puzzles that might help make the connection.
Its slow and understated, and exactly what I was looking for.  When you get in the mood for something similar, please give it a try.

In brief, you fly around in spaceships shooting other spaceships. Hardly a novel premise, but well executed in this instance. If you have played games like Freelancer but got tired of having to fly around looking for a fight before you actually got one, this is the game for you. You queue up. You're put on a battlefield. You fight until the battle ends. You move on to the next one. No jumping from system to system, (practically) no waiting, it's just the battles.
There are three main game modes (there are others which I haven't tried as they require the local clan-equivalent):
- PVP: As it says on the tin, player versus player. No Bots.
- COOP: Players versus a team of AIs flying player-class ships. PVP against bots.
- PVE: Missions with specific objectives while fighting NPCs
For PVP/COOP you get the usual selection of modes, e.g. team deathmatch, capture waypoints, and so forth.

If you do want to do some flying around and exploring, there is also an open space mode but, well, it wasn't for me so I'll skip over that. In my experience it involves being blown up a lot by various roaming NPCs that tend to have a suprising amount of firepower.
Of course there is grinding. What do you grind?
1) Experience, research and credits to get ships and equipment.
2) Rare resources to construct certain ships or equipment
It sounds worse than it is. The first three are easily acquired from battles and the game is quite generous with daily extras, special events and even one-day-premium licences, which speed up the process quite a bit. Once you figure out which bits you really want or need you can comfortably get by.
Resources are a bit tougher but again, as long as you focus on the bits you really want to have, you can mostly get by. Just don't expect to build any of the large destroyers. Your grandchildren might, though, assuming there are some significant advances in healthcare.
Generally speaking, the game is fun to play. Or could be, anyway. It isn't pay to win. I'm still giving it a negative review despite enjoying it (where possible) because there are quite a few caveats.
1) ALT-F4 to quit has been disabled in a recent update
2) You can’t leave or quit during a match
3) COOP enemies are now exclusively using alien ships (player-accessible) that have been introduced in recent updates
4) Those alien ships lack any balance whatsoever.
5) PVP matches aren't really 'matched' at all, as far as I can tell
(1-2): No idea if this is supposed to be accidental or trying to coerce you to sit through a match. Either way, it's not okay. First off, you do not interfere with system shortcuts, especially the universal quit button. Secondly, I will leave the game when I want to, not when I am graciously allowed to. As it is I may have to peel it out of the task manager, but I'm still not going to stay in the game if I do not want to. The developers are not endearing themselves to anyone by making this annoyingly difficult.
Incidentally, if you do quit and relaunch the game, you may find your ships are still "in battle". I.e. you still have to wait until the battle ends or pick a different set of ships. Another unfun mechanic presumably designed to keep people in the match. (Still not making any friends over here) When people do leave, by the way, there's no way for new players to join and fill the vacancies, unlike in any other team game anywhere, ever.
So, a colossal, sun-blotting negative point for haranguing players into playing - or at least staying. "You'd better stay in this obviously doomed battle or else". Nope, don't think so.
(3-4): Damn shame. COOP was my favourite but it's decidedly less fun facing an armada of unbalanced ships. Bots with lightning reflexes, perfect aim and good ships were a challenge. Bots with all that and completely overpowered equipment and, ye gods,
are a nightmare.
To be fair, the balance is a work in progress, but that process is painfully slow. With recent patches, you no longer die instantly when all nearby enemies pick you as their target. You now have time to
you are about to die, which is
much better.
You'd think there'd be some balancing
release but instead, I guess, COOP was turned into a sort of beta test. "Guinea pigs, meet modified flesh-eating bacterium sample #482-B. Now, let's start the stop-watch, please".
Taking one of those things on 1:1 is generally futile, by the way. Usually these battles are won by all players bunching up and focus-firing those tough little ships to scrap one by one. In some game modes you can also win by staying out of the AI's way, which doesn't make for riveting space battles.
(5) I'm not sure about this one but it certainly
like the game just scoops up the first x players and sticks them in a match at random. There doesn't seem to be any attempt to get teams that are evenly matched. If there is it doesn't seem to be working very well.
The net result is that most PVP-matches are extremely one-sided. Not being an ace myself, this results (for me) in one of two outcomes: a) a very dull match or b) an extremely frustrating match and a major repair bill. Full disclosure: it's usually the latter and I avoid PVP for anything except the daily bonus because of that. This is also why (2) is so annoying – you’re stuck wasting your time in a match that’s most likely boring for everyone involved.

Year Walk is a game that requires and rewards obsession. This isn’t saying  so very much. It’s about two hours. You only have to work up a little obsession, a little checking and rechecking, a few scribbled notes, light diagramming. Year Walk is not difficult. It only asks mindset enough to engage with its premise. Yes, engage in minor self-deprivation, fast, avoid festivals, and set out into the night to find the future, if you can only face everything within these woods.
I am not always the greatest player of games like this, due to impatience and a tendency to try to solve even straightforwardish puzzles by overthinking, but the strength of Year Walk is its dark folklore tone, its eerily blocky art, the loneliness of the forest until you’re suddenly not alone. This is 90% atmosphere, but it’s great atmosphere. And you do have to read the encyclopedia, which contains my favorite style of game lore, all mildly oblique supernatural rumor contextualized with cultural rooting.
The story framing the Year Walk itself relies on some tropes that I won’t spoil, but don’t do much for me. However, it’s also beside the point. The presentation is creepily fantastic, the mood is perfect, and what else are you playing for?

This game has nothing in common with RPG genre (perhaps except the storyline, from zero to hero, which is often associated with RPGs). There is no character created by player and player has de facto no infuance of its further development. Story is 100% linear and you have literally zero options to choose, except skipping the whole game if you want to skip any particular task. Dialogues means just clicking and confirming predefined statements.
In fact (from game's mechanics point of view) it's just casual economical game, based on simple rules of collecting and exchanging resources. It has even graphics similar to Settlers. But you cannot lost here. Even the battles cannot be lost! To join the fight you need to provide a specific number of resources (soldiers, tools, weapons, healing potions etc.). Encountered enemies will wait for you until you have all you need to start a fight and automatically win.
HotK is about 3,5h of gameplay (don't be mistaken by my 7h hours caused by idling scripts). Replayability factor equals zero due to linear story mentioned above.

As for the gameplay, I guess I'd call it a "resource manager RPG", especially because most of the time you need to go after this or after that in order to complete the given quests that are required to advance further on the story. The graphics are ok and the soundtrack can get old after a while so it's not a bad idea to have your own playlist available. There're also the trading cards and the achievements, so it's needless to say that it brings some added value. Overall, if you enjoy the casual genre, this title is for you.

I'm very much a fan of this game. I think that the very core nature of The Witness is about how we learn through example. If you're stuck on a puzzle and feeling frustrated (like I have done on multiple occasions), go back and look through the tutorial puzzles for that section. The game
teaches you how it works in incremental steps. Always.

The Witness is simultaneously a triumph and a huge letdown, and thus, a hard title to review. Visually, the game is stunning. The game plays with perspective in a way that will consistently delight. However, you will be spending the majority of the game staring at line puzzles on panels, completely motionless. The puzzles are, however, wonderfully crafted. Teaching the game by forcing you to learn is a refreshing take.
The ambiance is mysterious and haunting, as you puzzle your way through this lonely island, whose only inhabitants other than the player are strange statues. I was stoked to unlock each new area, voracious to discover the hidden truths of the place. But much like a famous TV show also set on a mysterious island, it never follows through. I don't mind a game where the story isn't handed to you on a silver platter. In fact, many of my favorite video game plots have asked that the player do their own share of the thinking. However, The WItness barely has any story at all. There is one, to be sure, but the developers simply decided not to engage with it. It's almost as if they created the island and puzzles with the intent of filling in the story elements later, but never really did. And before you ask, yes, I'm aware of all the hidden easter eggs.
It's an important title, to be sure. But where the game awes you out the gate with A grade visuals, ambiance, and puzzles, it followed through with an overall B- execution. It's worth experencing, especially for a Puzzle/Adventure fan, but I would wait for a sale these days.

Holy Gaben, this is some really hard hitting stuff!
Year Walk is a extremely strange game, that may be obtuse at times, but still generates so much genuine suspense and fear that you will be TERRIFIED to play this game for more than few-minute sessions. Interestingly enough, this isn't a pure horror game. While there are some jumpscares, they are not very common. They won't throw you out the experience. A really, REALLY CREEPY experience.
The subject matter is extremely interesting. Swedish folklore is used here to the full extend and it's really fascinating. You are often encouraged and rewarded by checking game's implemented mini-encyclopedia, which is full of interesting reads. To all new players who's looking to get into this game!
This game is a heavy grind, it's mainly about leveling your digimons and tamer to max level (99).
There is a few dungeons, but the ones that really matters are unlocked at Tamer level 70 and are incredibly hard and require an absurd amount of gear stats and a Jogress level digimon.
There is an easy version of them, still unlocked at Tamer 70, which you can do with a group of burst mode digimon.
A lot of people say it's P2W (Pay to Win) but they don't understand what P2W really means.
P2W is a term used in games who are competitive, where there is PVP or ranking, this game doesn't have any of these things, in this game you only grind to improve your tamer and digimon to kill stronger digimon.
In the end, if you buy costumes who gives you stats (1000% XP)(which are event only, around 3 times a year at the most) it's just a pay to progress faster, you aint winning any real advantage over other players since there is no ranking or pvp.
The game is build around the cash shop, i won't deny that, but you're never forced to buy any item since other players already buy and sell the items or Cash Shop currency for in-game money.
If you want to put money into the game don't buy digimon eggs, they are randomized and the odds are, you'll get the lower tier. You can get almost all the digimon in the game (except around 10 digimons who are cash shop or event only) by farming mercernary eggs from the specific digimon you want. Don't buy evolutors too, they are simple to obtain (From Monster Card level 7) when your starter digimon is high level enough (level 90).
The best item to buy are Burst Modes or Riding Items or Digidestined Tamer package.
So in the end, play the game casually, don't aim for the end game you will mostlikely stop playing before reaching the requirements for doing the dungeons, take your time there is no rush, do the events since lots of them give cash shop stuff, explore the maps, be nostalgic if you are a digimon fan. If you're looking to make in-game money to buy cash shop item from other players, i recommand you farm "Monster Card level 2" and sell the "beast low data" these data sells incredibly well.

D'aww, this game, guys.  It's just...not to sound girly, but it's friggin' cute.  And a pretty good murder mystery, to boot.
The good points: relatively good cartoon animation, as you already see, as well as professional voice acting that at times made me forget it was a game, though that's not to say the 'cutscenes' are drawn out, as you play those parts as heavily as anything else.  It's simplicity means no glitches, and it's good for a wide range of ages (I'm 27, and played it with my 8-year-old nephew, and neither of us lost interest until the end).  All of the characters were interesting and fun to watch.
Some puzzles threw me for a loop (well, one did) to the point where I just cheated and googled the answer while my nephew was in the bathroom, so adults shouldn't get cocky.  It's fun.  I'd rank it higher than Murdered: Soul Suspect, anyway.  It was more fun than L.A.Noire, though I won't claim that it's as authentic.  You'll have a good time.
The bad points: it's only one murder mystery, which lasts around 3 hours if you're not cheating.  As far as the murderer goes, my nephew and I both called it as soon as we started talking to that person, so you might find it too obvious.  Figuring the murderer out isn't the hard part, though, you have to prove it by having the evidence and using it at the right time.  It's not exactly Ace Attorney, but it's interesting.  Oh, and if you're worried about a rating for kids, it being a murder mystery is about as bad as it gets.  The detective says 'damn' once, there's a flirty souvenir seller, and you have to walk into a room filled with cartoon taxidermy, but that's nothing compared to Simpsons, Futurama, or Family Guy.  Honestly, it's more along the lines of Gravity Falls.
Tl;dr, you should get the game.  It'll be fun.

is a charming investigative Adventure game. With an unique visual style and a whimsical cast of characters this game hooked me right from the start.
Playing the eponymous Detective Grimoire, you are charged with solving a mysterious crime, that happened at a tourist attraction, located in the depths of a swamp. During your investigation, you will examine and pick up pieces of evidence, solve basic puzzles, as well as interview the inhabitants and workers at the tourist attraction. While these gameplay mechanics are nothing new, SFB Games make the best of it: Every once in a while you are faced with the task of forming a sentence out of pieces of evidence, characters and phrases (it is a rather simple system, but has lots of possible combinations, making a random success unlikely). This way, the developers make sure that you really understand what you are doing. If you form the right sentence you are rewarded with a "challenge", meaning that you can confront one of your suspects with your conclusions, often revealing important information. These systems are a perfect fit for the game and i found them to be very engaging.
Detective Grimoire's Story is nothing exceptional, but rather well-crafted; the characters are distinct and intriguing with nice animations and well-written dialog. The visual design (most notably character design) is the most apparent selling point of this game and really gives it a special flair. Together with the athmospheric soundtrack it creates the impression of a lovingly created game.
Being a casual/children's game, Detective Grimoire will be pretty
for most adult players (, but I think a perfect fit for younger audiences). Also, the game is available on mobile devices, too; which is basically a good thing, but is reflected in the rather
the game is displayed in on the PC. This dampens the quality of the artworks a little and makes the menus appear a little overbearing.
Last but not least: This game is
. I finished it in two and a half hours, and you might do so even faster. While this does not particularly bother me, many people on Steam seem to be very attentive, when it comes to game length.

This was not a satisfying game to play. Let me explain, why.
Some people dismiss this genre of games, wittily called "walking simulators" as not engaging and generally boring. And, true enough, the common theme for this kind of games is lack of agency or interactivity. But if these components are missing what makes a good "walking simulator"?
Generally the games of this genre rely heavily on observation and exploration, allowing player to experience story and world crafted by the developer via bits and pieces of information, spread across levels, something called "environmental storytelling". Walks between these objects and reveals serve as a sort of a mental buffer for a player, a way to process new information and tie it into the mental model of the game universe he's building in his head. Additionally, such walks are best accompanied by expressive environment and music, serving to cement mood and impression the game is going for. And of course the centerpiece of this exposition is the story that is woven into gameplay, the characters, the mysteries.
Unfortunately, De-Void does none of it right.
Perhaps, the best parts of the game are voice acting and music. That's not to say that they are excepionally good or memorable, it's just that these components of the game were good enough. Other than that the game fails miserably at what it's trying to be. The levels and environment and bland and washed-out, offering little to no entertainment during the soul-draining walks from one point of interest to another, some of which can take several minutes. These points of interest themselves are mostly audio or text logs from other people you never encounter and have absolutely no emotional attachement to. The protagonist is similarly bland and uninspiring, simply a vessel, moved by players hand through empty vastness of scarcely populated levels. The only discernible purpose such long walks serve in this case is to pad the length of the game. On top of that at times your vision will be obscured by weather, making navigation all but impossible. And no map, of course. Where we're going we don't need maps.
It all could've been saved by a good story, a decent mystery to solve. But unfortunately, no, instead of such we get pretentious and obtuse pseudo-philosophycal ramblings about the nature of man and abrupt ending, which ties none of what we've seen up until this point together. The parts of story and world feel disjointed and don't fit into a whole.
Throw some gameplay bugs on top of that (I've got stuck into tight spaces a couple of times) and you've got a failed attempt at a "walking simulator".
I urge you to not buy this game.

The Witness is simultaneously a triumph and a huge letdown, and thus, a hard title to review. Visually, the game is stunning. The game plays with perspective in a way that will consistently delight. However, you will be spending the majority of the game staring at line puzzles on panels, completely motionless. The puzzles are, however, wonderfully crafted. Teaching the game by forcing you to learn is a refreshing take.
The ambiance is mysterious and haunting, as you puzzle your way through this lonely island, whose only inhabitants other than the player are strange statues. I was stoked to unlock each new area, voracious to discover the hidden truths of the place. But much like a famous TV show also set on a mysterious island, it never follows through. I don't mind a game where the story isn't handed to you on a silver platter. In fact, many of my favorite video game plots have asked that the player do their own share of the thinking. However, The WItness barely has any story at all. There is one, to be sure, but the developers simply decided not to engage with it. It's almost as if they created the island and puzzles with the intent of filling in the story elements later, but never really did. And before you ask, yes, I'm aware of all the hidden easter eggs.
It's an important title, to be sure. But where the game awes you out the gate with A grade visuals, ambiance, and puzzles, it followed through with an overall B- execution. It's worth experencing, especially for a Puzzle/Adventure fan, but I would wait for a sale these days.

Without giving away any spoilers, I will do my best to give some objective opinions about The Witness. I didn't finish the game, hell I probably made it about one third of the way if that, but I can at least try to give a decent assessment of what I saw.
I really... REALLY wish I could recommend this game to others. I really do. But due to the fact that the only real satisfaction I had in regards to this game was writing this review about it, I simply can't. Here's why:
Unless you are the president of MENSA, the puzzles in this game will drill a hole in the side of your head and mercilessly f*ck your brain until it turns into jello. Be prepared to get frustrated, swear a lot, pound your fist on the desk, swear some more, feel like a complete moron, and use Google time and time again for hints. (I did that with a few of the puzzles until I realized the only way I was going to finish this game was by cheating. At that point I gave up on the game entirely)
When you first start playing, the opening puzzles are kind of a "intro" to what you will face later on. I won't say what kind of puzzles the "intro" ones are, (again, trying for no spoilers) but it will at least give you a general idea of what is to come. I will say however that if you are expecting the puzzles in this game will be like the ones in MYST, you will be very disappointed.
Unfortunately, the puzzles after the intro area get
more difficult and confusing the more you explore the island. Some of the puzzles may look similar to ones you may have already solved, and some will make absolutely NO sense whatsoever, even after solving some of the "example" puzzles provided. I'm also 75% sure that at least two of the puzzles I came across were bugged, but the only proof I have of this theory is that I had to Google the answers to solve them, and even after cheating, the puzzles still made no sense.
Another theory I have (which will sound ludicrous and/or like "sour grapes" but I'm still considering it) is that the developer created this game simply to troll the average player. I really hope this wasn't the case, and I'm not trying to make wild accusations, but after trying this game, I can't rule it out entirely.
Now unlike me, if you decide to stick it out and keep playing, and you get stuck on a particular puzzle, the best advice I can give you is don't spend hours banging your head against it. Go explore another section of the island that you haven't been to yet, enjoy the sights, and crawl around the nooks and crannies. At the very least, it may help clear your head. You may even come across a different puzzle that is easier to solve, and this may help decrease the frustration factor. If all else fails and you absolutely don't want to cheat by Googling the answer, just shut the game off and play something else for a while. You can always come back to it later. Or just do what I did and quit playing altogether. I know, I'm a quitter, and in this case, I just don't care.
Oh, and one more thing... and I felt this was very important to add...

In summary, after logging in 15 hours over the course of a few days, my brain wanted to puke, and unfortunately I had to put it in the "f-ck it bucket" and move on to other games. Who knows? You may have better luck with it than I did. But I'm not gonna put money on it.

The Witness is one of the most fascinating and exciting games I've ever played. Unfortunately, it's also very likely going to frustrate you at some point.
It's got really good puzzles. Like, really, really good. Thing is, you have to figure out the rules to the puzzles yourself. Which sounds a bit counter-intuitive and possibly annoying, but it's neither. Experimentation is encouraged and enough feedback is given that you will be able to figure things out well enough. If you do get stuck, there's usually a wealth of other puzzles to make progress on and being introduced to new mechanics there might help you come up with new solutions to previous blockades. Which yeah, sounds like a pretty standard puzzle game thing to do. But trust me, The Witness just absolutely excels at it. Figuring out rules, not just solutions is exciting. Many rules are just so creative and require thinking outside the box. Having a theory you suspect be proven right or suddenly realizing a solution is just this wonderful, joyful experience, and the game has so many of them. It's really quite something.
And then you get to the ending. Which is about as unsatisfying as it gets, but hey, I didn't enjoy this game for it's non-story (there's a bunch of audio quotes and video footage of various sources scattered around, some more interesting than others), I enjoyed it for its puzzles. And the thing is, by the time you've reached the ending you probably will know of a few puzzles you haven't solved yet. I'm not one that always has to try and complete every last bit of a game but The Witness was so fantastic, so exciting, that I just wanted more of it!
Which sadly is where the problems start. You're navigating around this island to find the puzzles, yeah? There's no menu where you can see, oh I haven't beaten this puzzle yet. And I'm not saying that there should be! Exploration is fun, the visuals are gorgeous and there's such a wealth of puzzles on the island that there's a constant sense of progression and reward. But once you get to that ending, and you know there's more, you've probably already solved the majority of the puzzles. And the more of them you solve now, the longer you have to walk around the (pretty sizeable) island that is starting to feel increasingly lifeless. You'll be retreading the same paths over and over to find less and less puzzles. You can take a boat for shortcuts, but it becomes an exercise in patience and it's easy for the game to start lacking the magic it had before.
Some of the puzzles you find will also feature a new rule that you don't encounter a whole lot. Usually there's a bunch of puzzles in one area to help you try and figure out new rules. In this case, all these puzzles are spread around the island. The experimentation that you previously could rely on now is actively disrupted if not discouraged. A similar issue is that a few puzzles escalate the difficulty not by increasing the complexity of the puzzle but rather by introducing barriers such as flashing colors or distracting sounds. I didn't find this to be a huge issue, but plenty of other players have, and combined with the two other things I've mentioned it adds up to the frustrations that can be found in the game.
On one hand I can appreciate the game's difficulty. It's a challenging game, and I've greatly appreciated all the headscratchers it's thrown at me. I can also appreciate it trying to make you work for the epiphanies and surprises it has in store. But it's a fine line between challenging the player and making the game feel like a chore. It's a fine line between allowing the player to be surprised and excited at
discoveries and providing so little sense of direction that the player might get bored and leave and potentially miss out on truly brilliant content. And I'm afraid The Witness doesn't always manage to tread those fine lines perfectly.
I've talked about what frustrates me about The Witness more than I have about what I love about it! Please don't let this lead you to think that the game is just a big series of frustrations. They are there, and they make the game as imperfect as surely anything is. The fact that they stick out as much as they do, merely is a testament to how wonderful and great everything else about the game is. Even if you encounter these frustrations; do work through them, because the game will continue to reward you with amazing experiences.
To sum up, if you are into puzzles and having your mind blown by video games, please play The Witness! (And Antichamber, which also blows your mind with puzzles, but in a very different way) Do be aware that the game might eventually frustrate you, and do be aware that it's also absolutely worth to keep going anyway.
Also, if you are playing the game, here is some advice that I hope will help you avoid a few frustrations:
- If you come across puzzle panels that seem out of place and don't seem to do anything, take a note. Make a screenshot.
- If you're trying to find hidden puzzles, there are useful, non-spoilery hints (

will help.

this review may seem a little ridiculous, coming from someone who had played over 70 hours of the witness. in all honesty, i accidentally left this game on for 24 hours, and there are a couple other reasons figuring into this huge amount of hours spent on a game i didn't really enjoy.
if you're looking for a good puzzle game, the witness is a puzzle game. it's good, in some means, and terrible in others. if you'd like a spectacular review of this game that genuinely shows it in its true nature, please check out joseph anderson's review of it on youtube. i highly reccommend it, and it's humorous, extremely well done, and can keep you interested for 40 straight minutes.
let's start with the basics. the main problem with this game is how frustrating it can be. the main point, as one probably knows, are mazes for you to solve, scattered throughout an island. as you progress, the puzzles gain symbols that have a specfic property, from drawing shapes with the lines to separating blocks of different colors. the idiotic part of this is that, with no specfic instructions, you're left to figure out what in the hell each one means. this of course, means that everyone will end up with different interpretations of what the symbols mean, and not neccessarily what the developer wants them to think. this creates an artificial difficulty where you think the puzzle is legitmately hard and you think you know all the rules, but then it turns out that it was trying to introduce something new to you. the difficulty is artificial because it's less like it's difficult for you to solve it because the puzzle is actually hard and more like it's because of something that you didn't even know. some parts were extremely easy for me, but others found them very hard, and vice versa. this results a lot in you staring a screen, failing and failing over and over for hours on end. and i mean literal hours. this game is not something short - no, puzzles for me have taken 2, 3 hours just for one. joseph, above, pointed out that the steam page literally says that this game treats your time as precious, which as you progress, continually shows itself as a blatant lie. and you may assume that with a game with "500+" challenging puzzles, this makes for a huge time investment. except for one thing.
there aren't really 500+ puzzles.
it's pretty clear that this is just a marketing tool, and because as you progress, simple puzzles that consist of a LEGITMATE STRAIGHT LINE add to this count. it's ridiculous and annoying.
that's not even to the main part yet - the story. this is what drew me into the witness, something that made me so very inclined to buy it - this mystery of an abandoned island, frozen stone figures, a town in shambles, and a plot, or so i thought, to unfold.
this is honestly the most ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t i've ever heard, because this game has zero story at all. zero. the "ending" consists of you flying around the island as all of the puzzles that you've done, all of the work that you've put into this, slowly unravels. the puzzles turn off, and you're back were you started the very beginning of the game. the game quits. and that's it. t h a t s  i t.
there is, of course, a "secret ending" which is even more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t than the first. finding a secret entrance to a "lobby" as it's well-known, you walk around this sky palace, then through what appears to be limbo, and then you wake up. a video plays for a solid ten minutes of a dude stumbling around an office before laying outside in the rain and going back to sleep. honestly, i was a little confused too.
the part of the game that annoyed me the most, however, was how stupid half of the puzzles were. there were many sections that i enjoyed - the quarry was probably one of my favorites, as was the shady trees and the keep. besides that, they confused the hell out of me - so much that i didn't know what to do. the jungle was nice for the first few levels, but then spiraled into random puzzles that didn't make sense even after i knew the answer. the swamp did a terrible job of explaining that i could combine tetrises in different ways. for half of the desert ruins. i had no idea how to obtain nor even start to obtain the answers. i get that the glare was the answer, but for most there was no glare to begin with, and experimenting with lights and water levels did nothing to change that. the town was great. i enjoyed it immensely. the mountain was great, but still had some puzzles that still today confuse me. i have no idea how in the hell to solve the puzzle on the final floor of the mountain, and i hated the puzzles on the first floor stuck in that jumble of trash in the center.
this isn't even to mention the obelisks, which were some of the best and worst moments i had in the game. the problem with these obelisks puzzles were how contrived they were. when they were in accessible locations and required little effort to solve but actual effort to find, they were at their best. some however. were stupid for the point of being stupid. the main example of this is the one found in the theater as the psalm of 46 plays, where YOU WAIT FOR A ♥♥♥♥ING HOUR FOR THE MOON TO MOVE SO YOU CAN FINISH OFF YOUR PUZZLE. you cannot move. you cannot do anything but sit and wait for it to finish. this similar concept of waiting for a ridiculously ♥♥♥♥ed up amount of time for something to happen also happens in 4 to 5 other places throughout the game, most notably the bridges in the swamp.
finally, a little suggestion - for some reason the pc port of the game has only 2 achievements, while the ps4 port has at least 14, including one for each of the lasers. i feel like i would've enjoyed the witness more if those achievements were added to the witness, and gave me feelings of accomplishments while also allowing me to compare myself to other players' standings. with only 2 achievements that you can only get about 20 hours into the game, there wasn't really any way for me to feel good about myself after completing a section. just something to think about.
tl dr; this game is great in some aspects, but generally terrible in many. i enjoyed some of my time with the witness, but also hated most of it as well. if you're looking for something in the same vein as braid, look somewhere else. i loved braid. this is nowhere near as good as braid. period. i advise against buying unless you can get it for $5. i got it for $10 and i still think that that money would have been well spent elsewhere.

You wake up in an unknown place, a small room. Where are you? Why are you here? Doesn't matter, here is a puzzle. A very simplistic one. Draw a line from A to B. It opens a door, leading to another puzzle. This time the line has a knick in the middle. Fair enough, it's more complex than a line. This opens a second door, leading to the outside, where you can see the blue sky...
The game takes place on an island where you can wander around, look at the beautiful landscape and find lots of puzzle panels. The core mechanic is always the same: Draw a single line from a valid start to a valid end. It does collide with itself, which means that intersections are not possible. That alone doesn't sound exciting, right? But there are lots of additional mechanics the developers have in store for us. What starts simple soon becomes pretty complex, when different mechanics start interacting with eachother.
As you may already guess, it's far from an action game. You can walk and you can look around. Jumping or falling of ledges is not possible. And there are no enemies that can attack you or distract you from your puzzles. You can take all the time you want, thinking about the problem before your eyes, maybe scribbling some shapes onto a piece of paper next to you. The graphics are beautiful and very colorful, the whole island feels very calm and peaceful.
Also, there is more to the game than just solving one panel after the other. The developers put an extreme amount of thought into the game. If you are observant, you might spot some secrets about this island. Those are the moments that really made me appreciate the game. "So, that's why they made it like that. clever!"

You should play this game if you love Wizardry: Labyrinth of Lost Souls.  Operation Abyss: New Tokyo Legacy is practically a clone of Wizardry: Labyrinth of Lost Souls but way more advanced, as it offers everything you would love about W:LOLS; but with better storyline and includes a crafting system reminisent of Shin Megmi Tensei Strange Journey.
The storyline gets pretty interesting as you progress, though it starts a bit slow.  If you like a bit of anime cyberpunk you may enjoy this game.
You can play in 2 modes; Basic and Classic:
Basic allows you to customize your character's appearance
slightly, with beautiful preset character art, but equipment does not show on your character.
Classic allows you to customize your character's' appearance in depth, but with less "stunning" artwork, and equipment does show on your characters.
(You can not switch modes once you pick a game mode, so pick wisely.)
My Experince Between The Modes:
I first started a Basic mode game and reached level 7 and got bored with the preset art.  I decided to start over in Classic mode and I am so glad I did.  The art in Classic looks more dated, but it was much more fun creating myself and my friends. Seeing them in the equipment (weapons, armor, bunny ears, bat wings, hair ribbons, etc.) was really cool and also hilarous at times.  For me, Classic mode fixes what Basic Mode & W:LOLS bored me with (preset character art).  So it is up to you whether you want detailed preset art or to add a bit more personal creativity and humor to your game.
FEATURES & PROS:
• Full Controller Support (Xbox one controller works amazing)
• Grid-Based movement dungeon crawling
• In-depth Crafting System
• Character customization
• Lots of missions
• Nice 1080p Graphics & Art at 60fps
• Balanced combat (if it gets too easy you can equip an item you start with that increases enemy levels, this also affects drop quality. If the level increase is too hard just unequip it.)
• Auto-move; You can click on an area of the map where you have previously visited and move automatically.  This makes grinding a breeze and I'm terribly spoiled now for future games.
CONS:
• Interface can be awkward to learn at first but you get used to it
• Comparing new and old gear can be a challange, lots of back and forth from menus
• Occasional annoying/boring short story fillers
• Some people might not like to grind
• Classroom setting that seems out of place from this type of storyline, also a bit too predictable for an anime game.
I'll keep updating my review as I play.

I've played this game over 350 hours at this point.  I've read the complaints about it being pay to win, but that's just not the case.  People who think this game is pay to win don't know how to play the game.
They want to rush at the endgame content because they believe that they need the power of the rank 15 ship to do open space, or compete in pvp, or do well in pve.  They strive for personal score, over perfected teamplay.
This game is a teamplay based game, yet some want to play it like it's not.  If you play this game, starting at rank one, working your way up slowly, doing the dailies as you level up your ships, you'll come out in the end with far more than someone who tries to buy their way to rank 15.
Lower rank gameplay is very enjoyable to new players, or long time players returning.  I've been spending time going back over ships I don't have max level mods on to make them the best they can be for when I want to play lower ranks.  If I hadn't jumped ahead, I'd be in a MUCH better place leveling up the ships and mods each in turn.  if you skip, you also miss a ton of daily quests to get loyalty, which is a currency type required for leveling weapons and ship mods.
These dailies always require the players to use a max level ship to complete them, so going slow, not trying to buy your way to rank 15, will be far more rewarding.  You'll also enjoy playing the game far more.
Players miss learning how to play roles.  Ship roles are very similar in concept to League of Legends or other MOBA type games in that the roles can heavily effect win or loss scenarios.
Tacklers and ECM - crowd control and disablers
Gunship - much like attack damage carry in MOBA high damage output
Destroyers - the primary tanks of the game
Guards - secondary tanks of the game, also very useful in gguarding other ships against damage
Engineer - the medics of space.  These guys are highly undervalued, and extremely important to successful use of ship roles.
recon - very adept at long range beacon capture and essential for beacon capture game modes
covert ops - secondary beacon capture, very adept at doing massive damage to destroyers in a short amount of time, especially if  after using the cutting beam they die with the reactor trigggered.  (looking at over 30k damage in about 5 seconds roughly)
long range - the sniper ship of star conflict.
If you do decide, after trying out the game, that you want to spend money on it, I suggest waiting for the DLC sales that happen on steam because if you buy all the DLC at one time you spend about 230$, you get a ton of ships to play around with, you get over 240 days of license (gives you 50% more of drops, currency, synergy (experience points), you get 5 different permanent bonuses from the DLC packs, and you get over 65000 glactic standards (approx 150$ worth of in game premium currency) all from the DLC.
If you enjoy dog fighting that progresses into dogfighting in the middle of destroyer wars, this is the game for you.  No other game out there right now does it this well, and has it this well balanced.

An odd game, or rather mini-story, that I would recommend, but DO NOT pay the full price. Here is a time where I wish Steam would have an "OK" recommendation instead of Yes or No.
Length-wise, Year Walk is rather disappointing. I do not understand that some people can take hours with it. Just by wandering around helplessly, and using only 2 hints, I ended up finishing in around 30 minutes, and that's with seeing everything that you can see except for the alternate ending. Immediately afterwards, I got into the journal, and I racked up my game time from sitting there at different pages--because I saw how many entries there were, I started cooking myself dinner while going back and forth to the journal. In reality, you can probably read and fully engross yourself in the journal within about 20 minutes, and I picked up on what I was supposed to do and got the alternate ending immediately. After that, there is no replayability to the game at all.
Now, when I first started the game, I sat down and read the Encyclopedia without going anywhere, and I was greatly interested in the folklore as it was described there. Afterwards, I ran through the whole game in one sitting. To be honest, nothing special seemed to be happening the whole game other than "Hey, look, you're encountering everything you just read about!" But besides solving a puzzle or two for each being, nothing really happened. Then you get to the end of the game and you're like "What just happened?"
By going through the alternate ending, you understand what happened. And as some people seem to argue that the ending means that the story can change, I argue on the other end. The alternate ending implies that everything is completely fixed and has no leeway.
What I liked about the game, essentially, boils down to the Encyclopedia, the Journal, and the alternate ending. I was rather okay with the first ending being this weird ambiguous mess, but to be honest, I didn't really like much of your first playthrough. You're given all of the beings you just read about... but it just felt somewhat cheesy and slopped together. The atmosphere overall was alright though, but I never once got a scared feeling from the game (even with my headphones and the dark).
I didn't pay full price for the game, and I am rather glad. Altogether, it is an interesting idea, but it is not much of your time. I understand everything in the game, but it's not going to engulf me and fill my mind forever like some people are posting on the forums. Rather, it's just a one-shot story that, while I did enjoy the story, could have used more development in the actual experience of the Year Walk itself.

TLDR:  Fun enough game, but the level design and boss fights arent that special.  Overall 6/10
Before I purchased this game I saw a lot of complaints in the reviews and I want to address some of the issues that people usually complained about that I don't think were accurate.
#1.  I felst that the controls are 100% fine and responsive.  I'm guessing what is bothering people is that when you jump you lock into a direction.  No Mario style easing one way or another.  You jump straight up you will land straight down regardless of how much you hold left or right. But... you have a double jump to let you re-direct once. But after that you are just going to go that direction regardless of what you press.  That style is a a bit odd to start with, but you get used to it pretty easily. Also, there are a lot of enemies that can be above the normal attack and between normal and ducking attacks.  Feels awkward at first but you can see it coming after a bit of practice.
#2 The game just isn't that hard.  Every enemy and boss has a simple and predictable pattern.  It just takes a while to map out the level.  But once you do you can get through it pretty easy. (For me it was an average of 45min per checkpoint.  2 checkpoints per level.  6 levels.  For a 9 hour play through)
#3 Checkpoints distances are fine.  It feels really hard to get from the start of a level to the the next check point for first time.  But due to how predictable everything is, the more you play the easier it will get because everything can be mapped out and anticipated.
As a whole I think the game was fun, but not something I would recommend to many people.  The boss battles were pretty meh with way to little pattern variability.  There was a lot of cheap deaths/overly awkward places to fight in the levels. And the last couple levels felt like the devs weren't trying as they were soooooo much easier and less inspired than the rest(and no not becuase I was used to the controls).  But overall I liked the game, so if you like old school hard games that require a lot of pattern recognition/grinding then grab this one... on sale.

Tough but fair memorization oriented platformer. It's superficially similar to the arcade game Rastan, but where Rastan has a constant stream of semi-randomized enemies coming at you from all sides, plus a lifebar which doubles as a timer by continually depleting whether you take hits or not, Volgarr goes for specific and consistent enemy placement and ghouls'n'ghosts style "one hit you're dead or two hits if you have a power up". This gives the game a more methodical pace and loses the sense of urgency and need for on-the-fly improvisation that makes Rastan so challenging and frequently frustrating.
You'll die a lot, but you'll probably get a little further with each retry. This is the kind of game that's meant to be winnable by playing from beginning to end without taking a single hit. Restarting from the beginning is always a good idea, because with each successive run you'll be fine tuning your technique and deepening your understanding of the level. This will make later levels easier because you'll be able to accumulate a greater number of power ups as you run through levels more efficiently.
Well that's it. There's no story, really, no roguelite-style "do X number of runs to unlock Y," it's just tight controls and solid level design. Your job is to play from the beginning to the end while making as few mistakes as possible.
Biggest criticisms are the pixel art graphical style and the music. The graphics don't look like real pixel art, they look like regular cartoon drawings that were passed through some kind of pixel art filter. I would rather have had high resolution detailed cartoon drawings. And the music is pretty ambient and boring sounding, it just doesn't drive the action at all.  I like to turn off the music and put on the music from Rastan or Golden Axe instead.

Some simple stuff in this game: Gather this and that, trade this for that, keep a lookout for hidden objects in the scenery, rest when necessary; yet it never really grows old on you.
I don't know what else to say really, it's a surprisingly addictive game. And even though the main gameplay consists of gathering, trading and doing quests, the inclusion of some objects hidden cleverly in plain view makes for a game that keeps you engaged.
The story is pretty standard, but it's not bad by any means. And whether or not you're into the tropes of RPGs, the simple beauty of the graphics will certainly sway you.
I don't know why it's so charming, but I don't care really. This is a good game. And it's certainly worth five dollars. But if you're unsure, get it on a sale. If you like these kinds of games, you'll not regret it.
Edit::
I still recommend this game for its simple charm, but I should warn you that it's a very casual game. I managed to beat it in about three and a half hours, and earn the remaining achievements in 15 minutes. Granted, I'm the kind of guy who used to pick up Dark Souls and play it casually, so take from that what you want. Still, my point stands: This is a fairly easy game. But that doesn't make it bad. So again: Still recommended.

Excellent little game! At first I was worried because of the way it took me by the hand during the first 5 minutes or so. The story, although not very original or believable, is imersive and entertaining.
I see people complaining about 2 things and I'd like to adress them.
1 - "It's like a facebook game". People say that because of the energy system and kind of exploration + completing quests gameplay. Yes, the gameplay is really an interactive story with exploration, hidden objects, collection and trading, so be aware. On the other hand, it does not have those annoying time limits, inviting friends and premium currency. You don't even have to wait for your energy to be low to recharge it - there's no limit to how much energy you can carry so although it's not realistic, you can rest repeatedly and build up lots of energy to then do your actions. Also, this game has an END. It does not have seasonal events and added content. So I see a monstruous gap between this game and a facebook one, I love this game and hate the ones on facebook. Huge difference.
2 - "The game is too short". For the people who say that, I recommend a youtube video called "in defense of short games", from the channel Extra Credits. They explain it a lot better than I could write here. But basically if people keep on judging games only by the lenght of the gameplay, we will get longer games that provides us a poorer experience. Everybody knows at least one TV series of movie franchise that got streched to the point it became so bad it was not worth watching. We need to end this way of thinking. The lenght was perfectly fine for me. I finished the game in 2 sittings of about 3 hous each, reading every dialogue line and getting all achievements before ending the game. Isn't that enough gameplay? There are too many other games out there I'd like to experience before getting stuck with a single game that provides "endless gameplay" or something.
If I had to complain about one thing in the game, would be the pace of the action resolution sequences. Everytime an item drops, I need to collect it before moving on. Everytime I choose to perform an action, I need to wait until it is done to do something else. I'd like to be able to do several actions at once, clicking the next one before the previous one is completed, then collect their rewards. Or at least click several actions and "queue" them. It would make the game more dynamic. Also, the nighttime sequence is too long for something that will be repeated several times during the game.

Detective Grimoire was a fantastic little story, though short(it took less than 3 hours to 100% the game) though that doesn't determine the quality of the game, just how much money that time is worth to you.
The game is a fiarly strightforward point'n'click adventure with art that was clearly lovingly made. The characters have some fun interactions with Detective Grimoire. As the player I found the repsonses you can say are surprisingly funny compared to some other games, I have some trouble deciding which I like more. The investigation itself is intuitive and the background story is very scooby-doo. There are small puzzles every so often, mini-investigations and I gotta say we don't get enough games where you get to play detective(in a non-linear way).
The voices are very fitting to the characters, every bit of dialogue has got a voice over it. Grimoire is pleasant to listen to, which is good because he's the one you'll hear the most, but something must have gone wrong in the audio mixing stage of production. Sometimes the dialogue sounds completely off and two characters sound like their voice was recorded with a cereal box. I suppose this could be from casting VO talent from different locations on the planet with different recording setups, but overall the game sounds great and I wouldn't call this a "con" to buying the game; just a gripe. As I said before the visual aesthetic is wonderful and although the cast don't have many animations I still love watching each idle movement when they talk.
It's a fun game I would recommend, a good story, decent gameplay, fun to unravel the mystery and put together clues, as well as refreshing to walk around and chat up suspects at your own pace and not be forced down a single route.

is a point & click adventure game based around a whodunit story. You play a detective who's sent to a tourist attraction in a swamp to investigate a murder that took place there. You need to talk to the suspects, gather clues and then piece together the clues and the statements from the suspects to find out what happened and who's the murderer.
In most point & click adventure games you collect items and use those items on objects in the game world, sometimes after combining them with other items in your inventory first. In
, you just gather clues. Clues can be items or they can be statements made by the seven suspects. You don't use your items on objects in the game world to advance, you only collect them to puzzle together the whole story behind the murder.
To gather clues, you investigate objects in the swamp and talk to suspects by simply clicking on them. Sometimes, investigating an object leads to a puzzle you need to solve in order to advance. The puzzles are very easy though.
When you're talking to a suspect, you have a plethora of topics to bring up: there are a few basic conversational options, you can bring up an overview of all the items you collected and ask the NPC about any of them, you can ask their opinion on each of the other suspects and finally, you can unlock one conversational 'challenge' with each suspect, which is a conversation during which you deduce an essential clue.
Richard Remington was the owner of a small tourist attraction that revolves around a mysterious creature known affectionately as Boggy. When Remington is found dead and it appears none other than Boggy is the culprit, detective Grimoire is sent to the swamp to investigate.
The story plays out as a typical whodunit. Everyone is a suspect and clues are everywhere, waiting to be found and pieced together.
is a short game, about three hours playtime, so the story and its people don't get described in great detail but you do get a very decent narrative for your money. The swamp has a whole history that revolves around Boggy, the mythical creature that supposedly lives in the swamp. Each of the suspects has a distinct personality and has a personal view on the story of Boggy and on recent events.
Somehow, despite showing some flaws, this game managed to get me invested in the story and its people. Important note, though: don't skip the credits that roll after you pieced together the mystery, as a final scene is shown that wraps up the story. And still the developer found it necessary to tease the player by ending the game with a
message. I looked into it a bit. In december 2015, the developer was awarded some funding for making Detective Grimoire 2 and promised more news 'soon'. But there has been nothing but silence since then. So it's not clear if the sequel will ever be made. Again, it doesn't really matter as the story of
is perfectly wrapped up at the end, provided you keep watching while the end credits are rolling.
The graphics are crude and artsy, so whether or not you like that style of graphics is an entirely subjective matter.
The voice acting ranges from okay to good. It's never bad but unfortunately it's never great either. Most of the times, what you hear is a voice actor delivering lines skillfully, but you don't hear the character come to life because of the voice acting, which is of course what's desired. In my opinion, there was only one voice actor who managed to rise above that level.
The music is atmospheric and sounds very nice. Combined with the ambient sounds of the swamp, at times it even sounded genuinely soothing and relaxing.
has 10 Steam Trading Cards. You get 5 while running the game.
Of the 9 Steam Achievements only two are unmissable. The remaining seven are awarded for doing a little more investigating than what is strictly required to finish the game.

To get it out of the way: this game is a walking simulator, and one built on a fairly old technology.  The levels are vast but bland; impressive distant vistas are marred by the near flat, featureless landscape you walk through.  Textures are blocky.  The level design is that of someone with too much time on their hands and no real theme... items are strewn around.  To make it worse, there's no in-game map, so it's very easy to get lost.  There are doors that are not doors, and doors that only become doors when the game is ready to let you through them.
That said, De-Void has an interesting story underneath it all.  Unfortunately, I'm not sure it's enough to make up for the lackluster presentation.  If this was a movie or television show, with a lonely protagonist (like The Martian) exploring and figuring out what was going on, I'd watch the hell out of it... but in-game, just getting around takes so long.  The ease of getting lost discourages exploration.  And finally, without spoiling anything, the ending is... unsatisfying.
Is it a good story?  I think so.  Is it a good *game*?  Eh... not really.

Okay, first of all, I'm a guy in his 30s, and I am really, REALLY into adventure games that are really just about story and wandering around. Truly! And I am also really into indie games, that we had some VERY GOOD ONES so far.
But this game is utter BS.
This game is about nothing else but pointlessly wantering around in very poorly designed areas that are completely and utterly without any purpose. The story is.... a piece of pointless nothingness (see more at the spoiler part).
The interactivity is near to 0, you can use ONE ITEM in the whole game, all the rest is automatic doors and about 5 elevator buttons. That's that. Even though it wouldn't be such a bad thing, as the game could be awesome even like that - it is NOT.
**WARNING, SPOILER ALERT**
Okay, so seriously, the story is basically nonexistent. There's this girl who wakes up, we have no idea about who she is (player character), or what is her purpose here. Then we find out that "something is very wrong" and all people are gone. So we start to work together with this AI, then we get a helmet TO BE ABLE TO LIVE/SEE EMOTIONS (this is the only item we can take in the game) and then we wander around. Then it turns out that they found some alien mind, that is communicating only via emotions (that's why they made that helmet) and then we wander a bit more and then we meet with a physical, real robot that says our names. Then we pass out and we are in the desert. Yes, no point, nothing. Then we go back, the AI friend does an examination, turns out we have about 37 thousand people's neural activity, then we wander around and then we have the truth: this alien is here to destroy, or whatever, but it just used us and it says thank you. Then the credits roll.
There is no real story here, no point, no ending, no nothing.
Not to mention the pointless "emotion scenes" where all becomes black and foggy and we can see some ppl's shadows and hear voices.
Not recommended, even for free it was basically a waste of time.

The Witness is one of the most fascinating and exciting games I've ever played. Unfortunately, it's also very likely going to frustrate you at some point.
It's got really good puzzles. Like, really, really good. Thing is, you have to figure out the rules to the puzzles yourself. Which sounds a bit counter-intuitive and possibly annoying, but it's neither. Experimentation is encouraged and enough feedback is given that you will be able to figure things out well enough. If you do get stuck, there's usually a wealth of other puzzles to make progress on and being introduced to new mechanics there might help you come up with new solutions to previous blockades. Which yeah, sounds like a pretty standard puzzle game thing to do. But trust me, The Witness just absolutely excels at it. Figuring out rules, not just solutions is exciting. Many rules are just so creative and require thinking outside the box. Having a theory you suspect be proven right or suddenly realizing a solution is just this wonderful, joyful experience, and the game has so many of them. It's really quite something.
And then you get to the ending. Which is about as unsatisfying as it gets, but hey, I didn't enjoy this game for it's non-story (there's a bunch of audio quotes and video footage of various sources scattered around, some more interesting than others), I enjoyed it for its puzzles. And the thing is, by the time you've reached the ending you probably will know of a few puzzles you haven't solved yet. I'm not one that always has to try and complete every last bit of a game but The Witness was so fantastic, so exciting, that I just wanted more of it!
Which sadly is where the problems start. You're navigating around this island to find the puzzles, yeah? There's no menu where you can see, oh I haven't beaten this puzzle yet. And I'm not saying that there should be! Exploration is fun, the visuals are gorgeous and there's such a wealth of puzzles on the island that there's a constant sense of progression and reward. But once you get to that ending, and you know there's more, you've probably already solved the majority of the puzzles. And the more of them you solve now, the longer you have to walk around the (pretty sizeable) island that is starting to feel increasingly lifeless. You'll be retreading the same paths over and over to find less and less puzzles. You can take a boat for shortcuts, but it becomes an exercise in patience and it's easy for the game to start lacking the magic it had before.
Some of the puzzles you find will also feature a new rule that you don't encounter a whole lot. Usually there's a bunch of puzzles in one area to help you try and figure out new rules. In this case, all these puzzles are spread around the island. The experimentation that you previously could rely on now is actively disrupted if not discouraged. A similar issue is that a few puzzles escalate the difficulty not by increasing the complexity of the puzzle but rather by introducing barriers such as flashing colors or distracting sounds. I didn't find this to be a huge issue, but plenty of other players have, and combined with the two other things I've mentioned it adds up to the frustrations that can be found in the game.
On one hand I can appreciate the game's difficulty. It's a challenging game, and I've greatly appreciated all the headscratchers it's thrown at me. I can also appreciate it trying to make you work for the epiphanies and surprises it has in store. But it's a fine line between challenging the player and making the game feel like a chore. It's a fine line between allowing the player to be surprised and excited at
discoveries and providing so little sense of direction that the player might get bored and leave and potentially miss out on truly brilliant content. And I'm afraid The Witness doesn't always manage to tread those fine lines perfectly.
I've talked about what frustrates me about The Witness more than I have about what I love about it! Please don't let this lead you to think that the game is just a big series of frustrations. They are there, and they make the game as imperfect as surely anything is. The fact that they stick out as much as they do, merely is a testament to how wonderful and great everything else about the game is. Even if you encounter these frustrations; do work through them, because the game will continue to reward you with amazing experiences.
To sum up, if you are into puzzles and having your mind blown by video games, please play The Witness! (And Antichamber, which also blows your mind with puzzles, but in a very different way) Do be aware that the game might eventually frustrate you, and do be aware that it's also absolutely worth to keep going anyway.
Also, if you are playing the game, here is some advice that I hope will help you avoid a few frustrations:
- If you come across puzzle panels that seem out of place and don't seem to do anything, take a note. Make a screenshot.

this review may seem a little ridiculous, coming from someone who had played over 70 hours of the witness. in all honesty, i accidentally left this game on for 24 hours, and there are a couple other reasons figuring into this huge amount of hours spent on a game i didn't really enjoy.
if you're looking for a good puzzle game, the witness is a puzzle game. it's good, in some means, and terrible in others. if you'd like a spectacular review of this game that genuinely shows it in its true nature, please check out joseph anderson's review of it on youtube. i highly reccommend it, and it's humorous, extremely well done, and can keep you interested for 40 straight minutes.
let's start with the basics. the main problem with this game is how frustrating it can be. the main point, as one probably knows, are mazes for you to solve, scattered throughout an island. as you progress, the puzzles gain symbols that have a specfic property, from drawing shapes with the lines to separating blocks of different colors. the idiotic part of this is that, with no specfic instructions, you're left to figure out what in the hell each one means. this of course, means that everyone will end up with different interpretations of what the symbols mean, and not neccessarily what the developer wants them to think. this creates an artificial difficulty where you think the puzzle is legitmately hard and you think you know all the rules, but then it turns out that it was trying to introduce something new to you. the difficulty is artificial because it's less like it's difficult for you to solve it because the puzzle is actually hard and more like it's because of something that you didn't even know. some parts were extremely easy for me, but others found them very hard, and vice versa. this results a lot in you staring a screen, failing and failing over and over for hours on end. and i mean literal hours. this game is not something short - no, puzzles for me have taken 2, 3 hours just for one. joseph, above, pointed out that the steam page literally says that this game treats your time as precious, which as you progress, continually shows itself as a blatant lie. and you may assume that with a game with "500+" challenging puzzles, this makes for a huge time investment. except for one thing.
there aren't really 500+ puzzles.
it's pretty clear that this is just a marketing tool, and because as you progress, simple puzzles that consist of a LEGITMATE STRAIGHT LINE add to this count. it's ridiculous and annoying.
that's not even to the main part yet - the story. this is what drew me into the witness, something that made me so very inclined to buy it - this mystery of an abandoned island, frozen stone figures, a town in shambles, and a plot, or so i thought, to unfold.
this is honestly the most ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t i've ever heard, because this game has zero story at all. zero. the "ending" consists of you flying around the island as all of the puzzles that you've done, all of the work that you've put into this, slowly unravels. the puzzles turn off, and you're back were you started the very beginning of the game. the game quits. and that's it. t h a t s  i t.
there is, of course, a "secret ending" which is even more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t than the first. finding a secret entrance to a "lobby" as it's well-known, you walk around this sky palace, then through what appears to be limbo, and then you wake up. a video plays for a solid ten minutes of a dude stumbling around an office before laying outside in the rain and going back to sleep. honestly, i was a little confused too.
the part of the game that annoyed me the most, however, was how stupid half of the puzzles were. there were many sections that i enjoyed - the quarry was probably one of my favorites, as was the shady trees and the keep. besides that, they confused the hell out of me - so much that i didn't know what to do. the jungle was nice for the first few levels, but then spiraled into random puzzles that didn't make sense even after i knew the answer. the swamp did a terrible job of explaining that i could combine tetrises in different ways. for half of the desert ruins. i had no idea how to obtain nor even start to obtain the answers. i get that the glare was the answer, but for most there was no glare to begin with, and experimenting with lights and water levels did nothing to change that. the town was great. i enjoyed it immensely. the mountain was great, but still had some puzzles that still today confuse me. i have no idea how in the hell to solve the puzzle on the final floor of the mountain, and i hated the puzzles on the first floor stuck in that jumble of trash in the center.
this isn't even to mention the obelisks, which were some of the best and worst moments i had in the game. the problem with these obelisks puzzles were how contrived they were. when they were in accessible locations and required little effort to solve but actual effort to find, they were at their best. some however. were stupid for the point of being stupid. the main example of this is the one found in the theater as the psalm of 46 plays, where YOU WAIT FOR A ♥♥♥♥ING HOUR FOR THE MOON TO MOVE SO YOU CAN FINISH OFF YOUR PUZZLE. you cannot move. you cannot do anything but sit and wait for it to finish. this similar concept of waiting for a ridiculously ♥♥♥♥ed up amount of time for something to happen also happens in 4 to 5 other places throughout the game, most notably the bridges in the swamp.
finally, a little suggestion - for some reason the pc port of the game has only 2 achievements, while the ps4 port has at least 14, including one for each of the lasers. i feel like i would've enjoyed the witness more if those achievements were added to the witness, and gave me feelings of accomplishments while also allowing me to compare myself to other players' standings. with only 2 achievements that you can only get about 20 hours into the game, there wasn't really any way for me to feel good about myself after completing a section. just something to think about.
tl dr; this game is great in some aspects, but generally terrible in many. i enjoyed some of my time with the witness, but also hated most of it as well. if you're looking for something in the same vein as braid, look somewhere else. i loved braid. this is nowhere near as good as braid. period. i advise against buying unless you can get it for $5. i got it for $10 and i still think that that money would have been well spent elsewhere.

You wake up in an unknown place, a small room. Where are you? Why are you here? Doesn't matter, here is a puzzle. A very simplistic one. Draw a line from A to B. It opens a door, leading to another puzzle. This time the line has a knick in the middle. Fair enough, it's more complex than a line. This opens a second door, leading to the outside, where you can see the blue sky...
The game takes place on an island where you can wander around, look at the beautiful landscape and find lots of puzzle panels. The core mechanic is always the same: Draw a single line from a valid start to a valid end. It does collide with itself, which means that intersections are not possible. That alone doesn't sound exciting, right? But there are lots of additional mechanics the developers have in store for us. What starts simple soon becomes pretty complex, when different mechanics start interacting with eachother.
As you may already guess, it's far from an action game. You can walk and you can look around. Jumping or falling of ledges is not possible. And there are no enemies that can attack you or distract you from your puzzles. You can take all the time you want, thinking about the problem before your eyes, maybe scribbling some shapes onto a piece of paper next to you. The graphics are beautiful and very colorful, the whole island feels very calm and peaceful.
Also, there is more to the game than just solving one panel after the other. The developers put an extreme amount of thought into the game. If you are observant, you might spot some secrets about this island. Those are the moments that really made me appreciate the game. "So, that's why they made it like that. clever!"

It's been a long time since I've played a point-and-click game as enchanting as Year Walk.
It starts you out with very little direction, and you only start piecing together your objectives as you wander around the eerie winter setting. There's an encyclopedia in-game that you can reference as well (And adds a bit of structure to your journey), and the lore it contains is a bizarre guide to the mythology of "year walking."
Now, the trap that most point-and-click games fall into is breaking their own logic for the sake of difficult puzzles. This results in bizarre, non-intuitive puzzles that takes, at best, some serious imagination to find solutions to, and at worst, brute-forcing. Year Walk does not do this. It stays very grounded in the world it builds, and everything can be deduced through environmental exploration and logical deduction, giving the player satisfaction with each puzzle solved.
Now, it
a short game, but it's far more memorable than most games I've played. Check it out.

Operation Abyss: New Tokyo Legacy is both fun and approachable, like the best guest at a party. It doesn't bore you with convoluted ways to make your guacamole taste better, but you know it could if you asked for it. It's as complicated as you want it to be, and a nice challenge no matter what.
+ Easy to pick up and play
+ Plenty of stats for dungeon crawling pros
+ Nice anime artworks
+ Fun enemy variety
- Images aren't crisp
- Some excessive UI clicking
- Typos every now and again
