I have a sickness that results in me seeing philosophy in everything, naturally, perhaps, since its center is everywhere. But where lies the limit of its sociability? Can you freely associate a few key words into a philosophical diatribe? I imagine some situations warrant it more than others. DeVoid's writer is philosophically inclined, this begs the player to actually focus on the the words of this experience as substantial in their own right, this justifies what I am about to write about (hopefully).
Strip a game of its gameplay and you will naturally focus on remains of this divesting. What is left is atmosphere, music, visuals, and always in a game: kinesthetics. But here the focal point is, and should be, on the writing itself, and after having played through the experience and seeing what each elements offers, the most salient element is, undeniably, the writing.
My mind immediately went to System Shock (2). John Carpenter-like electronic music, however somewhat less obnoxious than the System Shock 2 soundtrack, creates a certain tone, its sole purpose is ambiance. It does not overwhelm or beg for attention, but is there as a solid substrate for the foggy atmosphere. The visuals in that sense go along with the audio, there is no terribly great beauty to glean from this game, but De-Void never seem to have the ambition of awe-striking the player visually. It is there, it is deserted, it is structural, it serves no real purpose other than leading you through a path towards the next piece of story. It is minimalistic, truly, in that it simply gesticulates. It provides basic signs of guidance. Visually it is functional, although not without touches of brilliance.
Those touches of brilliance, among other situations, come from a System Shockean story-device, where the player is jarringly put into a new world – I suppose it could also be likened to Silent Hill with this criteria – where things are wildly different, the mindset is different, the ideology is different. In System Shock we saw the Many, here it is a fittingly Deleuzian unnamed entity that speaks to us. Without saying too much, these moments are the best parts of the game, both for its visuals and for its writing, they are bizarre and philosophical, and serve as an attack on the philosophy of the other part of the game, just as in System Shock.
I find that there is somewhat of a discrepancy between story and philosophy here. Motivation is needed for all types of progression, but the player-motivation was not in line with player-experience. By that I mean that the story lead a player into a sense of self-preservation and self-discovery, whereas the philosophy of the game seemed to disregard these human endeavors, because of the fact that it was a human endeavor:
“They tried to conquer the madness with science, to study it and disperse it with their reason. Like they had something to prove. When faced with failure, they tried to conquer the madness with administration. Unity, form and standardization. When all else proved futile, they tried to conquer the madness and call it art. Such is the movement of the human mind with its own beyond. In response to the failure of thought and the delicate inconsistency of truth, even the most rational animal begins to dream the contours of magic.”
Deleuzian philosophy runs along the same lines of the above-mentioned text, for example: “We are not threatened by error, rather and much worse, we bathe in delirium”. The game, however, skirts the line of logico-empirical rationalism and the chaos of the beyond, until it inexorably falls into chaos, into the chaosmos, into the plane of immanence, or “singularity”. Having either or in this sense becomes frustrating, and its middle-ground, the player, becomes confused about the confusion itself. A game inherently needs a goal for it to work, and in a way this Nietzschean/Deleuzian attack on human endeavors, that can be easily attributed to some of this game's writing, becomes a critique of its own existence. Not to say that isn't incredibly interesting in its own right. It does however both intellectualize and distance itself from the object of desire while at the same time forces the player into that very mindset. That is the folly of the expectation on games as a whole, more so than the writer's capabilities.
But let's say its critique directs itself outwardly. What can we gauge from this experience? I think the core of what this game does is incredibly profound. Whether this philosophical undercurrent is intentional or not in its exactness, I do not know, but within its words lies the profundity of great 20th century philosophy. It shows civilization at its brink, the desert of the world, perhaps a Nietzschean desert, and the inability to understand even our own culture or civilization's foundations. “We have been staring too long at the full painting to understand the individual strokes that constitute it” or something along the lines. What this elucidates, it seems to me, is the futility inherent to civilization and its objects of desire. Self-preservation can be taken to any extreme, and it most likely will, but what is the ultimate goal of this? Society has no entelechy, and De-Void portrays it efficaciously and beautifully. It shows the abject terror of this realization, the knowledge of death and non-becoming. Probably in a way that we'll never see again, unless this realization itself and its psychological horror becomes etched into the minds of society. At this point, however, what is left to hold society together? The interplay between humanity and chaos is within this game, with Nietzschean drabness, Deleuzian sharpness, and unfortunately it becomes somewhat of a dialectical relationship of the form both Nietzsche and Deleuze would attack viciously – but is anything but this dialectics so characteristic of humanity possible for a game, or any artistic creation for that matter? I do not think so.
For the first time in a while I see the echoes of philosophy, truly, in a game. Games like The Talos Principle tries it with a modern scientific twist and all of its subsequent quandaries, but fails to see the underlying systems of philosophy that deals with for example the mind-body problem. Ian McCamant (the game's writer) made this experience worth it. Even while finishing it in under two hours, it is worth the money. Despite some clumsy execution, despite graphical glitches that were not intentional, despite clunky voice acting at times, what you get is a solid experience with some more than excellent writing and even philosophy. If you are not already in a Nietzschean/Deleuzian mindset, it might not blow your mind (by something other than the fact that these themes were explored in a game, which somewhat blows my mind, but also makes me very happy that I bother trying these smaller interesting titles) but if you are perhaps not philosophically inclined, or have other philosophical preferences, playingh De-Void will be highly evocative, provocative and intellectually interesting.
Oh well.

First off if you wanna see some gameplay then heres a link to a video I made covering the game but WARNING THERE WILL BE SPOILERS IN THE VIDEO.

Being I haven't had a chance to play through the story all the way yet I will say nothing on the story itself, just gameplay and the like.  On to the actual review!
Graphics: Let's get this out of the way right now, graphics don't make the game but they sure help it, thats no exception here with De-void. The graphics are great for this Sci-Fi game, they are clear, crisp and I just loved the way the world looks with all the different environments shown.
Sound: The music is good and doesn't make you wanna tear off your ears after hearing the loop for the 100th+ time. There is different music for different points in the game and environments so it's not the same song looping through the whole game. The Voice acting is pretty good in the game, not great but its not bad, so its more Meh then anything, all characters are voiced and it works out pretty well for what they were going for.
Gameplay: The real maker or breaker of the game. The game plays really well with very little UI, it has smooth animations and the game world is well put together where you know where you are going next with only alittle need for help at some points (Yea I might be blind sometimes lol). along with that intractable laptops and tablets throughout the world that you can interact with so that you can piece together the puzzle of what happened to the lost colony. The AMBER Helmet is a really nice thing they added (Story point I'm not explaining) and it adds another “Level” to the levels already in place.
Story: Going to edit later with my thoughts on the story once I beat it.
PROS:
Gameplay.
Story (So far and is subject to change)
Graphics (Maybe not AAA quality but still great).
Music isn't tear inducing.
Meh: Voice acting at times is Meh, Not good but not bad enough to make it a con. It leans more on the good side but there are some characters that are worse then others.
CONS:
Lack of direction at times.
No instructions on what button does what at any given time. (Granted theres only some 7 ish buttons but still).

Como um apaixonado GAMER com quase 3 décadas de experiência em jogatinas, sempre me instigo em visitar games recentes com um teor RETRO que trazem consigo pura nostalgia e aquele feeliing da década de 80 e 90. Volgarr the Viking é mais um desses títulos que trazem consigo o ar de jogos clássicos unido a mecanicas de gameplay modernizadas. Gostei demais do game pela sua junção de simplicidade e mecânicas que funcionam muito bem, fazendo do game uma experiência prazeirosa e divertida. Volgarr parece uma versão 2D de  Dark Souls,  por conta do nível de dificuldade e seu estilo de combate estratégico que requere paciência e cautela. O game obriga o jogador a pensar na hora de atacar, defender se nas horas certas, pular e rolar para os lados a fim de escapar de inimigos mais fortes. Sem sombra de dúvidas, VOLGARR é um game MUST-HAVE para apaixonados por games que buscam vivenciar um pouco das gerações classicas, e diga se de passagem, douradas dos games.

Year Walk is definitely an interesting game, maybe less so 'game' but huge emphasis on interesting. I would call this a visual story (not to be confused with a visual novel) and while most games are obviously 'visual stories', I'll try to give a reason as to why I call it that. I'll start with the gameplay as that will help me get my point across.
Your character (never given a name) is put into this beautiful snowy landscape. The only movements you can make are to walk left and right, or forwards and backwards on paths. You have a cursor so you can click on objects here and there, but there aren't a ton of things to interact with. Hence, why I say this is more of a visual story. While you do have control, I feel more like you're just watching through their eyes.
Onto the gameplay/setting. The term "Year Walk" (Årsgång) refers to a Swedish ritual that was believed to be done by people from the medieval times to the 19th century. The Year Walk was done on either Christmas Eve, or New Years. The idea is that you lock yourself in your house, void of light, no eating, drinking, or interacting with others. After which of 24 hours, the year walker is tasked with heading to their church in order to have a vision of the coming years future. There, they will have to pass the tests of supernatural creatures in order to be granted that vision.
The premise alone is very intriguing, and I knew nothing of it while diving into this game. Let me say this, I played through Year Walk in one sitting. Now, it only took me about 2.5 hours, but that time alone was very gripping and I couldn't wait to progress further along. The atmoshpere of the game is mind blowing. Play this with headphones on and in a dark room for full immersion. The game is also genuinely terrifying through it's use of the lore. Added that the soundtrack beautiful and the art is amazingly well put together, you've crafted a very serene yet eerie world that can totally draw you in and make you lose sight of things.
While I would love to tell you much more about this game, I really need to leave it up to you to discover what it holds. It's not terribly hard, puzzle wise, but there are some here and there. Also, in game, if you'd like to read up more, they provide an encyclopedia that provides some descriptions of what you'll encounter. I've also heard you need to play it more than once to really get the full picture. So, I hope you will play this as I highly recommend it. It's something that will stay with you long after it's over.
P.S. Don't worry about the box. Yet.

Detective Grimoire is a clever adaptation of a intriguing flash game. With its unique story, quirky characters and funny detective, Detective Grimoire is a solid value game.
Detective Grimoire combines hand drawn backgrounds and characters with solid animation and voice acting. First off, this game is a low budget indie title so there is nothing realistic about the graphics. The graphics or better defined as art in this game. Each character encountered has a unique look. Locations are detailed and interesting with easy to identify interaction points. Solid lip-syncing and animation make the game shine. It really shows how much love was put into this game.
Detective Grimoire's murder mystery/who done it story is quirky and interesting. The titular hero is skeptical of the supernatural suspect, but with help from the folks in the Amusement Park, all is revealed by the end. The story does fall into some classic tropes of the genre, but is funny and strange enough to see through to the end. Simple design and art really make this mystery better than most mystery games on the market!
Detective Grimoire is a point and click game. Meaning that all movement and interactions are done simply by clicking. Puzzles and a suspicion meter system have to be completed to move on in the story. Some of the puzzles are harder than others, with some being as easy as dragging objects. The puzzles and Grimoire's comments solidify the story and bring it all together.
For point and click gamers, short game lovers, and mystery fanatics, Detective Grimoire is a fun addition to any those categories in your library. While a little overpriced at $6.99, the price regularly drops down to $1.39 on sale, which is a pretty good value.

After finishing "Danganrompa: Trigger Happy Havoc" I found myself realizing that this is probably one of the better games I have played in the past few years. The game is able to be a interesting visual novel sort of deal, but still have its own uniqe gameplay ideas that I havent quite seen before in a game. If I had to describe it in a whole package (being story and gameplay) it would be tough but I would say think something like a mix of: Pheonix Wright, 9 Hours 9 Persons 9 Doors/ Virtues Last Reward and Persona 3/4. So if you find yourself enjoying any of these games even in the slightest I would say that Danganronpa is a absolute must buy.
The story of Danganronpa is one that is kind of hard to explain so bear with me here. It stars a group of 15 highschool students who were all selected to go to a prestiguious school called "Hopes Peak Academy". To get into this school there is only one requirement. Be the best at whatever you may do, weather that be the best writer or the best baseball player it dosent matter even if you just got into the school but a lucky random vote. This is where our main character Makoto comes in, he was selected at random and deemed as "The ultimate lucky student".
Makato quickly learns however that he was not as lucky as he thought. He passes out just seconds from entering in the school, he wakes up in a abandoned class  and soon realises that himself and 14 other students have been trapped in the school by a psycotic bear with only one way to escape. Kill one of your fellow classmates and dont be caught. This story creates alot of tension and mystery as you will be wondering who will be killed next as well as alot of suspence when you are trying to figure out who killed who.
There are still issues with this story however. While the game is long in its own right with so many characters that they were trying to individualy build up, it feels a bit crammed since in most cases we barley know anything or have any kind of a connection with a character before they are killed off. For example for the first 3 or so deaths they were my faverioute characters in the story at that point. Now you would probably think that I would be sad because my faverioute characters dies right? Well I found myself as more mad then anything because the characters hadent been fully fleshed out yet and It felt like somewhat of a cheap shot for them to do. It feels as if they wanted to make a cast with 8 characters in it but realized they needed some to die so they created 15 with the extra 7 characters just being for slaughter.
Another more minor problem with the story is that it takes a while to actually get good. (Depending on your reading speed) it will take around 2 hours for the first interesting thing to happen, being the first murder, but if you can stick around the murders are a hell of alot of fun to solve. Another problem is the game feels like it has kinda all over the place pacing. This is because the game is broken up into a few different sections being: Free time, Investigation and class trial. These sections all have a very different pace with the Free time (in which you interact with other characters for bonuses) feels to few and far between because these are the only scenes where the characters actually have much kind of development and they only happen maybe a dozen or so times in the game. Investigation is a regularily long process of gather information about the murders and seeing how they happened but these are kind of puzzle peices that wont be put together for a long time. Finally we have the trial bits where evreybody works together to put together the puzzle to find out who did the murder. The problem is with this is that the trial bits were the only parts that stood out as really interested and I feel that the free time and the investigation sections at times felt like they dragged on a bit with there sometimes being no clear direction of what you had to do. However the trial bits are a ton of fun, I never left my computer once durring a trial section because it was just crazy entertaining to watch go down so it makes up for it and then some due to alot of the gameplay ideas.

Talking about this game at all is rife with spoiler-y landmines.  On a surface level, the game is about solving line puzzles and seeing how far that mechanic can be stretched or reinvented.  If you enjoy puzzle games (and especially those with a sense of adventure), you'll probably like this game.
However, there is a subtext at play that explores themes and ideas.  I won't say what, because there is a joy of discovery.  Or perhaps because I might be wrong.  You might draw different conclusions.  And we would both be right, and wrong, to various degrees.  Perhaps this is one such spoiler.
This is why it's difficult to talk about this game, so...  ABSTRACT SPOILERS HERE:
Or maybe I'm trying too hard to sound pretentious.  But it is hard to describe what
is about eloquently in words because its ideas are so nebulous.  That is why this game exists.  Many have referred to the "walking simulator" genre as "art games", and some are deserving of that title, yet
really feels like it's trying to express art in a way  that is unique to games.  There is also some great tech in this game that might take a while to appreciate, but if you ever
yourself to discover what more this game has, then you are treated to sequences of moments that leave you satisfied.
If this review has piqued your interest at all, allow me to offer some advice.  Don't approach this game as another title to be 'beaten'.  Be patient with it.  Treat it like the Sunday morning crossword.  Allow yourself the time to indulge in it and, perhaps as importantly, let yourself have time away from it and come back.  You may be surprised by what you take away with you during that intermission, and learn what has changed within you upon your return.

I loved this game but there is something I need to mention to both he devs and potential buyers: If you are colorblind, do not purchase this game.
I was enjoying this game quite alot. The puzzles were varying levels of difficult but solvable none the less. It was a very rewarding experience knowing that I was able to do it all on my own. But then I ran into a major problem. I spent hours trying to solve a particular puzzle to no avail. I was able to guess some of the solutions but the underlying logic eluded me. I got really frustrated, so frustrated that I caved and looked up the solution. Once I had done that the beautiful mystique of this game was destroyed. The gratification of discovery on my own merit had been taken away from me.
What really got me wasn't the difficulty of the puzzle, but something much more agrivating: I am colorblind. I have checked and re-checked for a way around this but there is not. I am really disapointed to say that if you are colorblind you will almost certainly hit a nearly impassible wall multiple times in this game, that will leave you guessing for eons to come or force you to look up the solution; which really hurts the spirit of this game.
That being said this game is so beautiful in a whimsical dreamlike way. The story is intentionally open to interpretation, the symbolism is rich, the outside references are well researched, and in general it just feels polished. 10/10 for content 5/10 for disability support.

When you leave this game you are different, you have a kind of non-verbal internal dialogue going on, the kind often only associated with deep reflection. In a sea of mediocre games that aim to provide nothing but escapism and cheap thrills, The Witness is a serious development in the capability games have to approach the human condition.

Fantastic, wonderful, very well made game. I'd go as far as calling it a marvel or a gem or a piece of art. Sadly, same as with art, I can't recommend it to everyone.
The graphics are beautiful, the world is very colorful, pleasing to the eye. The puzzles are wonderful - well designed and with a lot of twists. Easy to play but sometimes difficult to solve. Often they require thinking outside of the box. Like, looking at the problem from another angle. Or place.
I love the game in general, but I can't recommend it to average player for one reason: at times difficulty simply jumps up without warning. Most puzzles of the game are pretty simple and follow a fixed set of rules, but sometimes the game just throws a weird idea or two at you, or a puzzle has an unsual pattern and you're stumbled for a while. I can't say I'm fond of this thing and wish someone told me before I bought this game.
Overall, the good:
The game looks great and is fun and puzzling. You'll enjoy it the most when you solve it without a guide.
The bad:
Unjustified difficulty at certain points. Puzzles designed to be hard to solve instead of hard to understand and guess the rules. No music (practically). No sound (practically). No story. No heroes, characters, anything. Difficulty jumps at random points. One utterly broken puzzle in the jungle area. The Challenge has a time limit (it'd be perfect without one).
Overall:
Do NOT buy unless you know for sure what you're up for.

There are several reasons this game is among the greatest within it's genre. First off; it's enemies are in predetermined locations and rarely deviate from a designated pattern. What this does is allow players to develop a level of cognitive memory in the same vain as classics within the Ghosts'n Goblins and Contra franchises as well as the more recent Demon's/Dark Souls. Basically, you learn as you play and improve with each mistake. eventually you will develop the reflexes required to navigate the later challenges in the game.
Second. This games weapons are a sword and a spear. unlike the aforementioned Ghosts'n Goblins and Contra this game makes you use the same two weapons throughout. this works, in my opinion, better due to the games level design being built solely around these two weapons. The Spear is especially impressive due to it's many functions (and trick shots when you get the hang of it). It was also very smart for the developers to give the spear the same base strength as the sword so that it can be used as a primary weapon instead of a 'panic' or spamming weapon.
Third; this game maintains the 'stiff' double jump as seen in Super Ghouls'n Ghost [SNES]. The level design is perfectly catered to this jump standard and despite what you may think, it actually makes things easier when you get used to it as it locks you in almost grid like jumping patterns. This ultimately helps you gauge distances better based on the games design.
Fourth; The challenge. Although many critics and users will immediately dub this a "Hardcore retro game" it should be noted that it's actually easier than your standard early '90's 16-bit Platformer. Checkpoints can be found in the middle of each stage and before entering the next stage but, you have Infinite lives (unless you play the tougher "hard" difficulty levels). The levels aren't overly long and there is only 6 levels on the main route so with a bit of practice it's not bad at all. Enemies don't even act randomly (except the ghosts but they move very slow) so that is a huge help in the muscle memory department.The only thing I would consider "Hard" for newer players would be the fact that there is no checkpoint directly before to the bosses (like in Mega Man games). I can see this being trouble for some but the bosses have very simplistic patterns that can be learned with some dodging and observing before engaging.
Overall, being a huge fan of this kind of game, I can honestly say that Crazy Viking Studio's nailed it. I would even go so far as to say it's actually better than most classics found in the arcades or on the SNES

To keep the story short - "Year Walk" is an atmospheric mystery horror adventure with an unique presentation and splendidly unsettling atmosphere. It does everything a truly unsettling psychological horror should. The strongest point is the telling of the narrative, which is brilliant, and takes (at least) 2 play-throughs to unfold.
The game has no dialogue, and offers no backstory. During your 1st play-through you'll get bits and pieces of the puzzle, but it's up to you to connect the dots, and guess and assume much, thus creating the skeleton of a story. Then during your 2nd play-through, if you choose to do a side-quest (of sorts) the true nature of things is revealed, and the story suddenly gets a crazy spin and expands majestically in scope as everything falls into place.
"Year Walk" is not so much of a game, as it is an amazing example of story-telling. Recommended, and then some!

I have some issues with this game. I love it overall, which is why I'm recommending it, but this game screams "tumblr" to me. Not that that's a bad thing, I just want you to know what you're getting into.
There's a typical extremely sexist man, a gay guy who's dealing with trying to keep up appearances to look manly. a daughter who's been abandoned by her mother because she is lesbian, etc. Every other person is either gay or bi, and there are lots of dogwhistles that might put you off if that type of thing bothers you.
If you can get past that, the game is very enjoyable for people who just want to sit down and listen to someone else talk. The bartending mini game is pretty fun and provides a nice breather. I ended up pretty attached to some of the characters by the end of my playthrough. I also enjoy the pixel art, and the music is pretty good.
In the end, I would recommend taking the game at face value. If you just sit down and relax and enjoy it, I think you'll have a much better experience than if you try to dig into the meaning too much. Just my two cents.

A little safe haven tucked away in a grunge-esque alleyway; A post-dystopian era, cyberpunk style.
Suffice to say this is a VN (visual novel) worthy of mention time, and time again. Definitely one of those things worth running through a second, or third time - much like Fight Club for instance.
VA-11 HALL-A is a wonderfully written, and executed piece of work that you'll most likely have a hard time putting down. Amongst being one of the better illustrated story driven VN's, it boasts a phenomenal soundtrack that you (i.e. the player) may set as per chapter before the days work begins [ which as implied, can change the feel to the viewers taste ]
Playing as the lovely bartender Jill, our protagonist in this game, who's catch-all is in her ( i.e. the player's) choice in drink serving - will change the direction of the dialogue/info you're given which in turn influences one's impression on current events/people at given times.
You'll be given many concepts to ponder, and maul yourself over as well like 'solipsism' (the view or theory that the self is all that can be known to exist.) Many 'what ifs' dance around the atmosphere as you become more, and more accustomed to the way of life in which the citizens of Glitch City go about their lives. And, as you move on from one day to the next - you may soon realize some individuals and things of 'happenstance' aren't who/what they appear to be.
---
On a personal note, I am absolutely smitten to the clouds with VA-11 HALL-A and its' cast of beloved characters.
Catching up on the in game 'mundane' every day news as Jill sits in her room whilst
with her cat 'Fore' even feels fun, and refreshing.
Each clientele brings such a novel experience to be savoured - and mercy, is it ever lovely when they banter between each other!
It's that kind of game to me. Many of the events, and characters actually touched base with me on a personal level. The idea of relations between individuals, emotions, and regret are ever so grounding and yet fairly charming all the same.
The atmosphere of the bar is one that I'd wish to experience firsthand myself. It's relaxing, and particular to those intimate one on one engagements that I long for. Certainly a game to end your day with for sure.
Until the time comes for when I finish my extra playthroughs to discover the whole story, I wholeheartedly feel the need to cherish the mystery and venture that is VA-11 HALL-A.
To that end, I would highly recommend to play through it!

In the past calling this game P2W could've arguably been a subjective statement, but now there is no doubt it being P2W in my opinion.
It really started with the implementation of the destroyer class ships being able to speed the manufacture process up through buying RNG containers or otherwise grinding like crazy and these ships were OP for quite some time.
Rank 14 destroyers were even in a league of their own seeing each faction's destroyer had their own unique resource and you were only able to manufacture it for a limited time. So once again the devs not so subtly encouraging people to buy the RNG containers or grind like crazy, to a extent that you couldn't even craft the first R14 destroyer that they released without buying the RNG containers and the grind is even bigger now seeing you even need to manufacture the weapons and modules (abilities) that come with it, which wasn't the case in the past.
Though now in the present the game has hit a all time low imo, the devs are currently in the process of implementing a new 4th faction (Ellydium) with their own customisable ships and so far the 2 ships they've released both are highly favoring buying the RNG containers.
The main problem with these ships though is how OP/unbalanced they are, the first ship they released got several nerfs and i would say is still the strongest ship in its class. The 2nd ship they released is a recon class ship, which arguably isn't a main damage dealer class, yet this ship can kill even a destroyer class (which has the highest survivability rating in the game) in mere seconds, not to mention having a whole array of abilities that makes it currently the strongest ship in the game.
To me it seems these new Ellydium ships are nothing more than a way for the devs to squeeze money out of people (especially the whales) so they can craft the latest Ellydium ship, have the people who spent money have their fun with their OP/unbalanced ship, ''nerf'' it somewhat after a while, release a new Ellydium ship and repeat the process.
If the devs keep going like this, it will also mean eventually only Ellydium ships will be flying around except for new players, seeing at the moment there's no reason to use anything else.
Not to have this review focus on only one part of the game, i'll also add some short pros and cons.
TL;DR: You might enjoy this game when you just start playing, but the further you progress the more the negative sides of the game reveal itself, P2W, grind, unbalanced, etc.

A really interesting game. It puts a unique twist on city builders by having what they call "subcultures". They're arranged in a hexagon, with the higher up ones being richer than the ones below. Those touching eachother on the hexagon are friendly, and those opposite are enemies. For example, the blue collars hate the yuppies and vice versa, the elites hate the blue collars, and most of the rich classes hate the poorest class.
The key is that a fully fucntioning city needs people of every class. Someone has to be the janitors and grounds keepers. Artsy Fartsy people need doctors and firemen, and Executives need waiters at their restaraunts. People will not commute to the other side of the city for a job, so you need to manage where housing gets placed for each subculture.
It's definetly worth looking at if you want a unique twist on a city builder.

Danganronpa was quite a surprise when I found it, due to its less than appealing graphics and its overwhelmingly positive reviews. At the time I just wanted something with a lot of plot, so I decided to pick it up while it was on a slight sale. Never have I been more happier to have discovered it.
Danganronpa is an Anime style Visual Novel with heavy gameplay in addition to its strong sense of plot, making use of smart action that compensates for the amount of story and dialogue within the game. Split into 6 different chapters as well as an Epilogue and Prologue, the story begins with Makoto Naegi, the Ultimate Lucky Student, entering Hope's Peak Academy for the first time only to find that nothing was at all what he had imagined. A school meant for the 'Ultimates'(High school students that each had a special trait, such as the Ultimate Programmer), and meant as a symbol of hope to the world, Makoto wakes up on a strange desk to an unsettlingly empty school. Thrown into a deadly struggle against none other than his classmates, he must survive the brutal killing game while trying to find the killers of the murders, all the while attempting to discover what has occured within the school that led to the barred windows and the mysteirous dissapearance of any sign of living life.
The gameplay consists of walking around a school, and then using a point and click system to interact with objects and people. Dialogue has been translated very nicely, with close to no errors anywhere within the thousands of lines of dialogue. Throughout the game, the player will also be able to interact with his school mates and learn more about their history and abilities, as well as progress the game further by learning more about the events that happened in the school. After a murder has been committed, the player's enter Investigation phase, in which they must try to find as much relevant evidence as possible. After that, the player's will enter the Class Trial, the main action of the plot in which the player's initiate discussions with other characters in order to find contradictions and to discover who the true murder is. They play multiple different minigames(Includig rhythm games and hangman's) in addition to the main debate game in order to progress and discover the trail in the case.
The story itself is brilliantly handled, starting the player's off with nothing given. Mercilessly pounded by murder after murder, the story uses cold hard truth and dark events in order to give the story a deathly and hopeless feeling, all the while revealing slowly the reason why any of this is happening. For me, it had me obsessed, furiously clicking through the dialogue in order to find out the identity of the killer or to discover the history of the school. All of the murders and cases presented throughout are also completely unexpected, with major misleading clues that will guide the players to false ends and false trails, surprising me every single turn of the way.
So should you get this game? If you like solving mysteries and games with a very large emphasis on story as well as an intricate gameplay system, then I would highly recommend this to you, even if you do not particularly enjoy the anime art style. For those who have played visual novels before, or have watched anime(or read manga), than this game will definitely come as a pleasant surprise.

The real tragedy of the obnoxious difficulty curve is that it presses the player into a more narrow choice of play-styles than the game would seem to otherwise allow. There are ground attack missions, but don't try making a low-altitude loadout based on rockets or cannons because enemy fighters and SAMS will vaporize you. The only way to survive ground attack missions is to drop bombs on your target from a mile away and flee back to your carrier before more fighters spawn. Those giant long-range interceptor missiles look cool, but don't ever use them because enemy fighters turn on a dime and dodge them every time. Even dogfights are reduced to nothing but an endless turning battle with stupidly maneuverable enemies while you mash the button that deploys your (finite) countermeasures to deflect their (infinite) missiles. Half the planes go unused because they can't survive the world the game generates. It's frustrating, but more importantly it's monotonous.
I'm thinking the flight sim format doesn't blend well with roguelike elements like procedural generation and permadeath. The game gives you the tools of a traditional flight sim but they're the wrong tools to deal with the challenges of a roguelike.

Another game that pretends at being old school while missing the point entirely. Hint: old-school games were not built around speedrunning. It's like Super Ghouls n' Ghosts if that game were stripped of all its charm and built around pixel-perfect timing with zero margin of error. In short, Volgarr the Viking is a game that is trying entirely too hard.
At its core, it is simplistic and unsatisfying. There's no weight in your attacks - enemies simply explode into blood mists when you strike them. It's not nearly half as cool as it sounds. The controls are tight and responsive, but a platforming section that was fun the first 3 times is not fun at all the 40th. Checkpoints are anethema. Remember: it's all about level restarts and speedrun timers. It's a game for youtubers (I cringe just to type the word), first and foremost.
The visuals are crisiply drawn and smoothly animated, but there are some parallax effects in some places that are just downright nauseating. The second level in particular made me put down the game. That level's offensive color pallette and sickening background scrolling was just too much for my eyes. That's meaningful, because I'm about as old-school as it gets. My childhood was defined by side-scrolling platformers. For such a game to make me literally nauseous is unusual.
If I can't dissuade you, at least let me insist that you avoid purchasing this game for full price. This is no carthartic challenge of trial and triumph. Rather, it's a frustrating callback to the worst of an era: needless, pointless trial and error with a pattern memorization fixation. To those who have come after, make no mistake: few old-school games were this hideously banal and irritating.

It's a call back to games like Super Ghould and Ghosts, and it's just as hard as it's inspiration. It's a great game, just know what you are getting in to, this game pulls no punches.

Where to begin really,
The game is not great. It's okay at best, and it loses enjoyment the longer you player as the pixel perfect hitboxes start to become a serious grind. Basically, you can't touch enemies, you can't walk into any part of them, and you can't walk into any part of their weapon while it is out, even if they start bringing it back. Flames left on the ground by enemies can't be touched until they're completely gone, as even the tiniest unseeable pixel causes you to take damage.
You die in one hit, unless you have gear, I/E the shields and helmet. In total you can take four hits with full gear, and they start throwing reused enemies in some places, and others are frustrating to deal with and show the lack of actual creativity to produce challenge. Enemies that can't be hit from the front, and require you to crouch are beyond annoying, as one version can't fight back as his whole deal is to simply walk into you, and the others require two to three hits depending on colour, and will be knocked out of your attack range on the first hit, while they stay well within their own reach to hit you, requiring either a roll behind them after the first hit or for you to be frame perfect in a dodge.
You cannot start another animation before the last one finishes, meaning you can't attack until the spear throw is finished, you cannot attack until the roll animation is finished, and you cannot roll until the landing animation is finished. Some things are better, as in you can throw a spear while double jumping and your double jump counts as an attack, but has a slight window where you do not hit anything.
Levels have respawning enemies after the first, in the form of slimes and ghosts, and the ghosts are the worst offenders. They clip through terrain, simply fly into you to deal damage, and will sit watching and waiting then just slowly floating into you at every worst possible time.
Enemies are telegraphed, easy to read and the only thing the game rewards is perseverence. Eventually you will learn every spawn point, how enemies fight, and then the game becomes very easy as you don't have to explore every path to power through.
Don't buy, it's not worth it even if its on sale. It's artificial difficulty at its finest, and you'll find more satisfying challenges elsewhere.

Volgarr the Viking is not an awful game, but it just isn't fun. I'm not saying it just because it's hard. It is hard, but in the wrong way.
The BloodSouls games are, in my opinion, masterpieces of level design because they are truly challenging and they have amazing level design. They require actual skill and you have to master the combat and truly git gud. I'm comparing Volgarr the Viking and the BloodSouls games because both are trying to be hard, but Dark Souls is rewarding and pretty fun. Volgarr tries to do this, but instead of being fun and rewarding while maintaining a challenge, it fakes being hard by making you die a lot by things you couldn't have seen coming and making you do the levels again and again until you've memorised them.
This isn't being hard, this is being unfair. While having some good mechanics, for example throwing a spear and being able to use that spear as a platform, it has a lot of potential, but falls flat by making you think it's hard, when in truth it is just about learning exactly how and when things happen in the level. It isn't fun. It isn't rewarding. This sounds harsh, but it's kind of a waste of time.

Hero of the Kingdom - Game Review - 10/10
Hero of the Kingdom is a casual point and click indie game for $7 on Steam. For a dollar value hour value, it lasted a little over seven hours which is right where I think a game should be priced. I don't play a lot of point and click games, so I took a chance on this one and was pleasantly surprised.
This is one of my favourite types of art-styles to look at, so I thought this game was absolutely beautiful the whole way through. The music was enjoyable to listen to all throughout. The gameplay was simple and crisp. You get energy by resting, then use that energy as a resource to complete other tasks.
One of my favourite parts of this game was as it introduced new things to you through tasks, you would be able to go back through previous areas and find things such as mushrooms or boxes hidden in the scenes. It was really quite fun to look through everything and complete the achievements, read the story, and play through this sweet little game.
To anybody who enjoys a nice casual game, or a rest from their competitive games for a while, I definitely recommend this game. As usual, if you can get this on sale, it's even more worth the price.
For me, this point and click game is a 10/10.

Year Walk is a game that first came out on iOS, but it caught my attention very early on. Above all else, you have to know what you're getting into, to properly enjoy it. This is
a game, in the traditional sense, but it certainly requires player input! Even more than many games, somehow.
It's a very unique experience, certainly worth trying! Plus, you might learn a bit more about swedish folklore.
I find it very similar to Fez, in a way. Year Walk is a riddle in and of itself. Its challenges rely on concepts more than anything the game directly teaches you, but all the clues are present for you to succeed. Also, it was clearly designed for multiple playthroughs (at least 2.5 - 3), and it was brilliantly made, with that in mind.
I'm a sucker for mythology and folklore in general, so I had been interested in this game for a while. If you're trying it just "because", you might be lost for a while, and find it frustrating.
Going back to the Fez point: Fez was much harder and more cryptic, because its clues were very spread apart. There were lots of different areas, and it also relied on many skills completely unrelated to the game.
Year Walk is not like that. While the game is mostly a riddle, you can get everything you need inside the game. I'd advise either taking notes, or screenshots and being very aware of your in-game surroundings, otherwise you'll probably be walking in circles.
The game is certainly fairly minimalist in its design, but I think it knew exactly what it needed to be. The
are digital, but made to simulate paper cut-outs, which goes hand in hand with old folklore. Its use of color is also noteworthy, and while very subtle, it very much contributes to the overall atmosphere.
The interface looks, perhaps, a bit too modern, but it's not too bad. The port is mostly okay, although there's a bit of disconnection to the pc, clearly. While there aren't big, intrusive buttons, they haven't really mapped any hot-keys that would have been
useful (using M for map, or E for encyclopedia, for example), and you have to click everything. Then, in a puzzle, they have you use "u" and "n"! It was the hardest puzzle for me, haha! It clearly said "u" and "n" on the screen, but it felt so out of place that it took me a while to try it. Oh well.
The
are a bit space-y, which feels a bit weird, but it sort of fits. They're well done, but I would have liked something more traditional.
The
, thought, is definitely one of the aspects where it shines! (Of course, this is biased.)
It's mostly quiet and atmospheric, but it gives you an eerie feeling at times, through two main aspects: slight dissonance, and using what seems to be aged instruments, that don't sound
. These two aspects have been in my mind for a while, on how to make creepy music... So there you go. Of course, I found it great! But honestly, I think it works, and gives it a very natural feeling. Good job!
There's a problem, though:
Whenever you open the map, or the encyclopedia, the music stops. That... is a problem, and a big one, in my opinion.
In a game that relies so much on atmosphere, a continuous flow of sound is critical. If you need to open the map (which should often happen, especially during your first playthrough -- a the one that relies the most on atmosphere!), the music stops, and it completely breaks immersion. I seem to mention this in a lot of games, recently, but it's really important!
Having the music cut-out when you have to do something as simple as opening a map... that's bad. Furthermore, it makes those menus seem completely out of the experience that the game was going for.
I'd like to see this changed, at least in future games, but hey... it's not
, I guess.
To start off, this is an adventure game. Instead of being a point n' click, however, you can walk in 2D, in several lanes set in 3D. You can go back and forth to change lane, at specific points. It can be a bit confusing, at first, but there's a map, and while your first playthrough feels a bit alien, it all makes sense after that. And it's still very compelling.
I'll make this clear right away. A puzzle, in my eyes, is based on mechanics that a game teaches you. Most games work like this.
A riddle, on the other hand, relies on something beyond the game. These skills are mostly learned outside of the game, and makes what could be "puzzles", mostly unrelated to one another.
This is why I say Year Walk is more of a riddle.
There are clues inside the game, of course, but it never teaches you anything. It never starts easy and gets progressively harder. Not at all. Every riddle is like a self-contained puzzle, reliant on combining the clues, and skills you have acquired outside the game.
Some of the puzzles are based on listening cues, some are based on
cryptography, etc. But I think it's balanced. I managed to go through my first playthrough without getting stuck  at any point, and without using Hints. But again, you need to be in the right mindset to enjoy it!
These riddles are based on the mythological creatures you'll find in the game. You won't, of course, know what these creatures are, or why they're there. And that's normal. To complement the game, there's an
. This is merely a collection of texts, one about each creature or event you're playing. It's not a direct guide for the game, as it doesn't really help with the
, but it gives context to what you're doing! And may also give you some clues on where the solution may lie.
I've found it very interesting, but it's still about reading
! It's the same problem that Type:Rider had, the way it never taught you through gameplay, but through wikipedia-esque articles.
Year Walk doesn't function this way! But it has some similar problems. Still, the creatures are
in the game, but it would have felt much better to have some more integration of the Encyclopedia in the game. Maybe some more clues to the puzzles... I believe the Encyclopedia was a companion app for the iOS game, so that's it doesn't quite feel a part of the game, unfortunately.
I think this is the best part of the game, by far! Every encounter has some meaning. It will not be apparent at all, the first time. However, the game always gives you slight clues on what to do next. On your second playthrough, it's quite different. I don't want to spoil it, but it's about reading an Historian's "diary" while he was investigating the tradition of Year Walk. It's
reading (and there's a lot of it), and also taking notes to solve the last puzzle in the game. Again, it's completely detached from
the game, but it's as interesting as it makes you feel like a detective!
This diary tells the actual story of the, as if it happened a few centuries ago. While you're reading this, everything you encountered in the game starts making sense.
This is the first part of the journal.
The second is far more conspiracy-like and esoteric, but due to the very believable first part, you start questioning everything that's happened in the game, up to that point! It was one of the most compelling experiences I've recently had in a game!
Every symbol is explained in the game! Not initially, but it is. And that's the way to do it! You won't leave it feeling like it was just pretentious gibberish. It's genuinely interesting, and the questions extend the game itself!
Already out of words... Seriously, this is one of the most interesting experiences on Steam, and is one that's based on
folklore, which is always a plus!

Planetbase allows you to concentrate on Engineering without micromanaging the AI. If you enjoy Survival Sims like Sid Meier’s Beyond Earth, but want something with more accessibility, you will love this game.
With few quick-loading splash screens, and a smooth tutorial that drops you directly on a planet, you are immersed in the action almost immediately. This is one of those games that can become a “Just one more minute” time consumer. It takes a few components of the grand 4X Strategy Space genre and allows you to build a colony on a Mars-like planet where you are the Engineer.
To start you select the first unlocked planet, and you are able to spin the planet to choose a good spot for planet fall. I went to the West and took a spot surrounded by mountains for mining. Meeting various benchmarks will unlock up to two more planets. It quickly becomes a challenge to keep the power up with solar cells and wind turbines, with the dark of night and frequent storms.
I love the way the AI functions independently, unlike in similar games I’ve played. There’s no need to tell them what to do. They are hard-working and will tend to the mining and farming jobs you’ve set up. When they are sleepy, they take turns using the number of beds you’ve built with no input from you. Of course, since you want them to work in shifts, never provide more than one set of bunks for every 6 workers, and provide a dorm instead of private cabins. You also manage their food, morale, and recreation by providing a variety of buildings on the base for those needs.
Controlling the work the AI performs is as simple as clicking on a building and setting it as high priority. At first it may seem like they are ignoring your priorities, but actually they don’t have the required materials for the item you planned, so they move on to the next in the queue until you divert materials.
Resource management can become problematic on another planet so uninhabitable. But, lucky for us, these NASA guys have created fully salvageable materials. You are able to click on anything and recycle it for usually most all of the cost components back in metal, plastics, and spares. This makes it possible to be thrifty and recycle your mine, for example, after stacking up some ore, so you can use the scrap metal for building a factory while the ores are being worked in the processing plant. By the time the materials are outputted in the finished factory, you will have enough metal to rebuild the mine. This also helps keep your workers focused on the job at hand.
The cost of building is further facilitated by the trading system. Once you’ve built a landing pad, trading and colony ships arrive fairly frequently. You can trade for materials needed. Some traders will overcharge, but others are more competitive. Because you can recycle, you are able to sell anything not bolted down just about, and if it’s bolted down you can tear it down and sell the materials anyways. This aspect is one of the realistic elements of the game and reminds me of the ability to sell anything on hand in the “Gray Market” in the XCOM franchise, for extra building income.
But, beware of accepting colonists before your colony is fully sufficient; then never accept more than you have meals on hand. You are able to manage this from within the landing pad. You are able to build a security control center for emergencies to order all AI inside the base during bad weather.
The management system allows you full screen information on your power grid, your techs, and your progress. The buildings have a really cool video option that lets you change into full-screen video mode of the interior of the rooms. The camera controls are easy to work with providing everything but a vertical axis camera, which is really a minor disappointment because you can’t see enough of the sky. I accommodate for this shortcoming by centering the camera above a mountain to see more of the sky dome.
The graphics consist of a single map of the planet you are on, and you are unable to move more than a set distance from your base. But, the map changes with a variety of weather conditions: such as meteor showers, wind storms, and solar flares. Meteors fall and destroy parts of the base and you must react by repairing and diverting power sources. Audio consists of a variety of sound effects, as well as background music that is nice to listen to while building.
* Trading variety to facilitate bargaining to best the AI traders
*Fully recyclable resource management that is flexible & forgiving of changes
*You can build telescopes and lasers, and bots to do all the work
*Some battle component exists with guards, guns, and interstellar bad neighbors
*Perma-death/ failure is offset by flexible save-loading
*Polished mechanics & No bugs
*No Narrative – Only the sign that has your city name, and the monoliths you may build
*No exploration of the planet
* There are no aliens, just mining, space-farming, & building turbines, generators, solar panels, etc.
*No vertical axis camera controls/ Can’t really appreciate the sky, more than a 20 degree angle above the horizon

You start with a handful of colonists, a couple of robots and some supplies such as metal and food to get you started. Since your colonists only have spacesuits with limited oxygen, you better get building quick. The tutorial is smooth and in-depth and it walks you through what you need to know about surviving without giving away too much and ruining your ability to try new things your way.
There are three planets which range in difficulty of which two are locked. You can unlock the more difficult planets by completing 'milestones' or challenges on the first planet. These range from Surviving one day to having 300 colonists. Once you've picked your planet you can name you base and the game begins.
Planetbase seems quite hard at first, I killed off my first group of colonists in 4 minutes because I rushed to build larger buildings instead of the basics but after restarting I quickly learnt from my previous mistakes and was able to keep them alive for a whole day. Once you realise the needs of your colonists and how to manage your resources without overbuilding everything comes together nicely. Managing your power, oxygen and water levels is your main goal at first, then you'll want to start expanding your base and building mines for ore, bio-domes to generate food, labs for research and pseudo-meat production and much more. You can build a launch pad so other colonists can join you which they will as you start to build bigger and better things.
Whilst building your base you can also manage the percentage of your colonists doing specific tasks (producing food, building, guards, ect) adding a nice little micromanagement element to it and allowing you to feel more in control of what is going on. You can also change production levels giving you full control over making sure your resources are never depleted fully
The graphics of the game are very beautiful with a lot of attention to detail, however the interface is very very basic looking. Everything is just a little green square with a symbol.
Planetbase is similar to Banished in the fact that starting out can be very difficult and once you make a big mistake it's often too late to fix it by the time you realise. I find this very enjoyable as I am careful with each of my resources and have to think about what is the most important room to build with what I have rather than just placing one of every room and leaving my colonists to do the rest.
There are some negatives to the game, though none of them are too bad. It would have been nice to have a pause button without having to press escape. I appreciate that the default speed is already quite slow but when I start a new game like this I want to browse all the building types at my own pace without the game progressing without me. I also found the random meteor showers a bit problematic at first. In my first two attempts at playing I lost 2 colonists in the first 10 minutes in one, and a newly built room in my second. I think it'd be better if random events like that didn't happen on your first day or so on the lower difficulty to give new players a chance. One last little grievance is dead end rooms (certain rooms can only be built off of one other room meaning it increases walking time when colonists are travelling through he base). I don't think there is any real point to this and it does end up slightly limiting your freedom in base building.

The Witness is a weird game. Part atmospheric puzzler, part art piece, it's hard to pin down exactly what makes it so addictive, but I'll do my best. This will be stream of consciousness style, as the only way to really get the Witness is to play it.
There is no "gameplay" besides deceptively simple "Line puzzles" and world exploration. But it is the way in which some of these (I must stress that not all puzzles are created equal) are inextricably linked with the world and the moments of revelation that result that lead me to ultimately recommend this game.
The art direction is top notch, and it has an almost painterly approach to using colour, not only to define a sense of place, but a sense of mood as well, equally breaking up the world into digestible chunks (each "level" exists on one fully explorable island) as well as enhancing the recognition of these spaces with some key landmarks. This is imperative to the experience of the Witness.
So why is this? Well this segue's nicely into the next point, a trickier one to make to say the least as it is both a measure by which you may make or not make your purchase, but also attempts to find meaning in a game that may ultimately have none. I will attempt to discuss what The Witness is "about" as this is the question that crops up from friends thinking of playing it, and family members exasperated with my continuing obsession with solving all the puzzles - "there's no story, all you get for solving the puzzle is twenty more! What's the point of this? Why are you on this island?" Now, without spoiling anything, most of these questions are answered, however whether this is satisfactory is dependent on your point of view.
In my opinion, which may be coloured by my study of design and space in an architecture degree, the Witness is about discovering new ways of "Seeing", it uses virtually constructed physical spatial interactions to make a metaphysical point about the human condition. The narrative of the Witness (which ala Dark Souls is largely implied) is diminished in value next to the realisation that the game was laughing at me the whole time. There ultimately is no point to what you are doing when you solve the puzzles - they do just lead to more challenging puzzles most of the time.
Conquering every puzzle type in the Witness requires the player to not only think in new ways, as in a game like Portal or the Talos Principle, but to observe the world in new ways too. There are some areas which seem to be created simply to teach the player how to solve a specific type of puzzle, but these may be on the other side of the island to the first instance of this puzzle type that the player finds. So the player can make the choice, to stay and solve the puzzle through trial and error (there is no penalty for failure in the Witness, besides inability to progress and solve more challenging puzzles) or alternatively, to walk away, find the "tutorial" and return when better equipped to solve the puzzle. The Witness gives the player agency in these choices, without giving them all the context or any tangible result. The player did or did not solve the puzzle - the game doesn't care either way - it is not about solving puzzles, but discovering the rules required to solve the puzzles and then questioning their existence when they lead to dead ends or paths that lead to more puzzles with different rules.
So the simple joy of solving the Witness' puzzles is outweighed by the discovery of how to solve them and a pervading sense of pointlessness to the whole endeavour. The best puzzles in the Witness build on one another to teach a concept to the player, and then have a directly tangible effect on the game world.
The player's goals are not really suggested by the game, but rather self assigned. My own journey through the first play session was as follows - "Solve line puzzles. Explore. Everything available.  What's with the couches? Solve more puzzles. Beam of light - where does that lead? I'll go there. Solve environmental puzzle - something lit up. Not sure why. Solve more puzzles. Another beam of light. Excellent, making progress. Found monolith with lit up symbols. Connected to environmental puzzles? Test this theory. Find another environmental puzzle. Same effect, different colour. Return to monolith - another symbol lit up. Ah, they are connected. New additional goal - light up all symbols on the monolith. Explore island some more. Got lost. Solved more line puzzles. Discovered new rule. Found boat. Took boat trip around island. Discovered another monolith with more symbols. Must be missing a lot of environmental puzzles. Hmm, most puzzles lead to more puzzles, I wonder if there's any point to these environmental puzzles? Solve more puzzles. Another beam of light. What's the point of this beam of light? Goes up to mountain. Creepy village with creepy manikins. Ok, so it's a horror game? What the hell happened here? More puzzles - unsolvable with current knowledge. Hmm, ok well I guess it's time to shut this off for the day"
The Witness never really did anything to suggest any of these goals to me besides presenting the effect of my tinkering. Its as if I decided that Cause and effect equates to a Goal and meaning in a world devoid of both. The Witness is a large time sink, but the piecemeal approach to its puzzles leads me to suggest that it could be easily played in fits and starts.
So why do I recommend this game? If it is all pointless, has no story etc. then why would I recommend it?
1. The puzzles are generally pretty excellent, so if you like puzzles it's a no brainer.
2. The game does open your mind to seeing things from different perspectives.
3. The world is beautifully constructed and a joy to explore.
4. It asks us not only why we solve puzzles, but also why we play games, why we set goals, why we persist, why we give up, why we obsess over finding meaning in our current state and why it may be ok that there isn't any at all if the journey that led there was enjoyable, cathartic or illuminating in some manner.
Yeah, like I said. The Witness is a weird game.

Sky Rogue is a flight sim with a style reminiscent of the hit SNES game "Star Fox". Unlike Fox McCloud, however, you play as an unknown pilot, and completing missions from your flying aircraft character. Battles are restricted to the atmosphere, and take place on islands, which allows enemies to defend in the land, sea, and air. Depending on your craft, you can utilize different gear to suit a mission (for example, using a bomber with cluster bombs to destroy a ground target or an interceptor with guided missiles to take out a flying target).
Sooner or later, however, you will crash (or be shot down) and then you choose what kinds of technology to develop, either new weapons or new planes. The amount you can research is based on your tech level, which, in turn, is based off kills. This sets up a nice incentive for you, the player: to stay in a mission, getting lots of kills to upgrade your tech when you eventually falter, or to leave sooner to get a further run.
Also, theres mod support. Right now it's restricted to new ships (which are basically new models, such as X-Wing fighters from Star Wars), and skins for your plane and carrier.
Controls are good. I love the controller support, and the advanced controls seem pretty natural. Theres also beginner controls if you want something different.

My Rating: 7/10 (Pros and Cons summarized below).
I often find that this game genre ('Point & Click: Mystery') tends to struggle with actual story/game quality. IME, the games can feel tedious, boring, and repetitive. While Detective Grimoire is fun by its own merits, I especially enjoyed how it overcame these common weaknesses. The art/animation/music/color palette is lively, the voice acting is excellent, and the story has a streak of bizarre that breaks up the monotony. Yes, it is a somewhat cliched concept (murder mystery with a monster suspect). However, the game is self aware of its camp, and does a good job of humorizing it. The story/idea is well executed.
The game play is well designed; it uses a blend of interactive (and interrelated) clue/person/conversational methods, and it encourages the player the 'think through' what evidence means. While some of these methods could be a bit more challenging, I like the concept and would like to see more of it. Most characters/suspects do not say over-the-top giveaways, and it requires actual legwork to reveal what happened. E.g., you need to learn information before asking any specific questions, but you can still ask questions on your own. These are logical progressions too--no ridiculous specificity requirements. Overall, it felt like they did a good job of layering in the mechanics of game-play with a somewhat realistic story execution.
The main weak point that I contend, is that the game lacks enough 'irrelevant' clues and conversations. Although not *everything* interweaves together, and there are some decoy trails, it is also a bit too easy for every 'pocketable' object be a valid clue. It hampers the game quality. It would be more challenging/realistic (and fun) to find/receive more useless information and evidence. The game was also a bit too short (likely related to the streamlining of the mystery). And, while figuring out the mystery is a fun challenge overall, some of the individual tasks were painfully easy. The game is still enjoyable and I would recommend it; I hope that they address these sort of weaknesses in the potential sequel.
Pros:
-Great art/story/style
-Above average voice acting
-Nice integration of different modes/methods of evidence
-Interesting mystery (nice mix of mystery, humor, and camp)
-Soundtrack fits well
Cons:
-Not enough 'unrelated' clues/topics
-Short (mystery is streamlined)
-Lack of challenge for individual tasks
-Somewhat impractical controls (switching between walking/looking)

Overall, well worth a purchase if you like mystery/detective games.

But after spending a few days with the game, I can definitely see why so many people love it. The characters aren't just annoying anime tropes, they're well written and engrossing, if slightly ridiculous at times (in a good way), and their respective voice actors really bring each of them to life. However, what really hooked me into the game was the story and the incredible pacing. As you play, the morbid scenario just keeps getting darker and more complex, as do the characters reactions to them and attitudes toward each other... and there is always a shocking twist just around the corner. Just when you think you KNOW what's going on, everything is turned on it's head.This game is just really hard to put down, I found myself constantly wanting to know more, kind of like binge-watching a really great show on Netflix... just... one... more... chapter...
As far as the things I didn't find so engrossing... it's really all just nit-picking. The first-person controls in the free-roam segments are just kind of... functional. It took me a while to get used to the clunkiness, and I really dislike how the camera slows down to a crawl when you're panning across a door or interactable object. Also, this might just be a matter of personal taste, but a couple of the minigames during the trial segments of the game are a bit strange, and seem almost out of place at times... but they aren't so difficult or out-there as to substantially detract from the overall experience. You're playing this game for the story, not the mini-games.
I can't think of any reason not to recommend this game to anyone who loves a suspenseful, morbid story and well-written characters. The contrast of the disturbing story and the candy-coated, psychadelic visuals really give this game it's own unique feel.
Pros:
- Engrossing, morbid story
- Well-written, subversive characters
- Interesting visual style
- Superb pacing
Cons:
- Clunky FPS segments
- Some minigames seem out of place
