Many if not most of the negative reviews for Cities XXL seem to focus on one of two arguments:
- an engine upgrade, even tho offering 50% discount to Cities XL version owners, should be a free patch according to some. Surely an interesting topic, especially if one goes by that even on lowest graphical settings a game in its endphase (and rig filling specifications) allegedly didn't uphold a proper game experience and should therefore fix an arguably essential issue for free. Myself I don't remember free nor discounted upgrade e.g. from Windows XP to Windows 7, to name an example of where there was apparently not really addition of features neither, while it was arguably laggy or such with plenty of stuff doing in XP. So such argument sure may seem valid a lot, but it does not really seem a proper review for the Cities XXL version anyhow.
- and argument about an "either - or" approach, which may be understandable if one wants to point out what may seem a better alternative but in my view doesn't justify a negative review as such. Meaning that just because someone may have more fun with one title surely doesn't mean that every other title of such genre is bad just becuase of that.
Anyhow, Cities XXL review of my own:
Overally, I found the video game Cities XXL to be an enjoyable city building simulation, which offers complexity with not really need for tedious micromanaging (besides issue of that inter-city trading may have been made more streamlined by offering a global pool, but isn't really complicated as is).
Various resources, possibility to build roads and large zones in different ways or plop individually, demands and desirabilities and population satisfactions (where eventual problems are mentioned with top bar where icons for industries, offices and workforces), plenty large maps in various setting (snow, beach, desert, greenlands), day-night cycle having various times of day with moving shadows and possible to switch inbetween (with moving cycle possible to be turned off), city overlay maps (such as for air or noise pollution, or particular satisfaction, and more), possibility to zoom-in to street level and as if walk around looking around, tutorial, possibilities with mods, all there.
In terms of performance I can't complain. With a what I would call mid-range rig (multi 3,2GHz (64), GTX 760, and 8GB RAM) and everything set on high I didn't really experience lag, even with city size having more than 10 millions of population. That is that zooming in or out quickly from top to bottom or vice versa did show a fraction of second lag, similarly sometimes on street level looking around, and at night when zooming out it took a moment for all lights to be rendered, but besides such it was fluent all the time. In around 90 hours of gameplay I experienced a few crashes, but such as far as I remember only when leaving a map, which was not much an issue to me since it successfully saved the map before the crash, so no building time lost with it.
As for gameplay more in detail:
Cities XXL offers both sort of career mode for every map as well creative building possibilities straight on, meaning that one can go with starting with low density buildings and have further possibilites unlocked as the city grows in population (recommendable to learn the ropes and mechanics), or simply use in-game option to unlock most buildings straight away, or even called cheat to have e.g. cash added, or even have mod for such.
Game is rather resource rich, ranging based on map limited resources such as water and food, to resources such as heavy industry and workforce split into 4 categories (with each category having housing of their own), which makes it on a larger scale a good idea to develop more than one map with each city specializing and trading with each other. But it is also possible to develop only one map-city while trading as possible and needed with Omnicorp (which is in-game a trading partner having unlimited resources to buy and sell, tho usually at a rate giving 2 resource tokens for 3 resource tokens taken, but also offering easy way to increase cash flow with resources traded from surplus). Specialization also brings possibilities to increase production of commercial resources a lot, meaning that map-total e.g. electricity production can be increased by 40% by placing one building only, which has prequisites to be unlocked. Many a resource usually requires other resources (e.g. heavy and manufacturing industry needs some offices, electricity, water, waste disposal, variously skilled workers, while needing to be near a freight connection such as road connection at map border, freight airport or harbour, and so on), which is why specializations are handy to use especially where the resource production requires upkeep (with every map supporting full specializations of max. two resources). Resources get distributed automatically within a city as long a road connection is there (including water and electricity).
Inner-city mass transportation exists but unfortunately has only buses and subways (not counting mods) with no revenue from it (but limiting air pollution and usually decreasing travel time). Having to make those mass transportation lines manually is easy to do but may somewhat seem as micromanaging even tho with bus lines it requires no building of bus stops as in buildings taking up space at roads, and with subways it gives a map view where sub-stops are easily visible.
Desirability factors (especially "quality of life") are important especially with higher tier buildings, such as offices and high-tech industry but also holiday hotels, which unlike business hotels require appropriate landmarks, which on some maps may be the whole coastal area in the beginning but usually require buildings (on maps with holiday resource). So while these things offer additional variety in terms of planning, I found the holiday factor in terms of gameplay rather boring quick tho since it doesn't seem that tourists have any impact whatsoever on retail nor leisure. So while it is easy to make a sort of eye-candy district for holiday hotels with retail and whatnot, in terms of gameplay it isn't really as if connected to each other as far as e.g. holiday hotels and retail is concerned, which is why I myself ended up trading for holidays from Omnicorp.
While it may sound complicated that there are various resources with somewhat different requirements, it easy to keep track of, both in terms of having neat table overviews of which resources are lacking or too much off, but also since if e.g. offices lack business hotels the icon for offices in the top bar will turn yellow or even red with it telling what the issue is if one hovers with mouse over the icon.
All in all, even tho not having a sort of endless career mode such as in terms of SimCity 4 filling a region map with cities for sake of having a view of a huge metropolis, plenty to do in career mode and even more if one enjoys creative building. Therefore from my side a recommendation for this city building simulator.

Excellent City Builder game with a good balance of resource and base management. Definately contains a challange factor too as I have had numerous occasions where a solar flare killed half my colonists because I had yet to build a command bay to issue the alert to stay indoors. A little work needs to go into the unit AI as they will sometime priortize things weirdly. For instance, if you have placed the work order for your first water fountain the AI will prioritize things like eating (even when their hunger bar is only about half empty) before building it even if that means the colonist will die of dehydration. The best way to remedy this is to only place two to three build orders at a time as the root of the issue is that colonist AI prioritizes needs (oxygen, water, sleep, etc.) over construction duties even if those construction duties result in providing an unmet need. Placing too many build orders may also tie up your builder units with transporting materials to build sites when they could be actually constructing them. Overall though the game is great, excellent potential for future improvement & modding which should bring additional replayability to the game.

I had been waiting quite some time for another truly fresh and intensive game experience. This was one.
At first, you might think this is just a bunch of dry two-dimensional logic puzzles scattered around a beautiful landscape.
But after a while, you realize that the world and the riddles are intertwined in various creative, entertaining and spectacular ways.
So while, yes, technically, the only things you do are running around and drawing lines on boards, the resulting game experience is very complex, rewarding and full of variety. If you're looking for an adrenaline rush, this game is not the right one. There is no danger. There is no "action". Just perception and thought. If, however, you enjoy racking your brain over countless riddles that progressively cross the lines between abstract thought, world exploration and creative observation, you should definitely play "The Witness".

I think I have to agree with most of the reviewers on this one, the game is short, it's easy, and it's overpriced. However, I would still reccomend it, because despite the fact it's short and easy (and overpriced), it's stilll good. The sluthing you'll have to do to figure out the case isn't hard, it only took till I was half-way through the game to figure it out, and that was only because I didn't realize I forgot to talk to one of the suspects. Even if you couldn't piece it together based of the first few clues, the game makes sure you have more than enough evidence to convict the killer by the end of the game. Each character you meet also has a challenge topic for you to beat. Most of them aren't hard, once again I only got stuck when  I actually had forgotten clues that I didn't think were important. The actual puzzles they put in the mix up the game play aren't challenging either, but they were kind of entertaining, I just wish they were harder. Then personally I wished the characters had more connections to each other, everyone felt like they were on their own little narrative island, with no relation to the other characters except for the murderer, the victim, and occasionaly, their single "friend" character.
But all that aside, the game was still fun. The visuals are smoothe, the voice acting is good, the soundtrack is great, the characters have simple, but not boring personalities, the mechanics are fun, although the walking mechanics (don't forget you can fast travel) and navigating your notes can be a pain. So overall, I liked this game. If I had to describe it in one word, I think I would say the game is "charming." I can't honestly say the game is worth seven dollars, I typically don't mind short games that cost a bit, but this game doesn't seem like its worth that much (five dollars would have been more reasonable). But I picked this up on a steam sale for a dollar, and I feel like I got my dollar's worth. So if you can ever pick this game up on sale, and don't mind something short and easy, I'd say it's definetely worth playing.

Do you want to know what it feels like to have all your friends die while having to stay emotionally strong to win a battle of wits? Then this is the game for you! Prepare yourself for "Thrills! Chills! Kills!" as you attempt to uncover the truth of your despairful situation before you're all killed. The game's unique soundtrack and whacky artsyle will immerse you in the game's setting, while the plot keeps you hooked as you try to discover the truth amidst a fog of lies and red herrings.
Is good.

While it would be easy to constantly compare this game to the Ace Attorney series, I feel as if this game deserves to be enjoyed and praised in it's own right. There is much thought put into Danganronpa's story, as it is very fascinating in it's murder mystery plot and dark humor. If point an click adventure/visual novels are your thing, along with an Ace Attorney style court drama where you present evidence and do fun little mini games is exciting to you, then I recommend this game to you. It even has an optional "dating sim" type mode called free time where you can unlock more about each character to find out their information and backstory. They may seem like stereotypical tropes at first, but later on you find there's more layers to who they are and you'll get very invested. Again, if this type of game is your thing, then I highly recommend this experience to you and guaruntee it's worth your time and money.

The last thing I'll be able to understand is the negative reviews. Because of how poorly optimized the last Cities games were, people began developing some sort of bias that any future Cities game will always be bad. That's not the case here, anymore.
Cities XXL is actually a big improvement from Cities XL 2012.
I remember getting CXL12 back in 2013, and that was sort of my replacement for the awful SimCity game. Originally, I thought it was pretty cool. I made over 20 cities in a span of 5 months, but that's not the point. The game was no longer stable by the time my city was as big as a quarter of the map, and that's not good, of course. After a year-long hiatus from the game, I've wanted to play it again, but it's not even playable anymore. Okay, this game is good. Really good, in fact.
Is it hard as balls? Yes.
Does it rely on trial and error? Sometimes, yeah.
Is it unfair? No, not really.
The controls are perfectly fine. Not being able to change the trajectory of your jump in midair is a deliberate decision and it integrates perfectly with the game's philosophy. You can't go jumping around recklessly becasue you'll get killed, but that's kinda the point. Attacking and rolling work exactly as intended and very rarely do your inputs not translate the way you expect on screen.
Level and enemy design are actually pretty clever. Almost every action and power-up is useful in more than one way and the levels make use of it, Enemies are, on the other hand, are spread in a way that create very different situations. There are some areas where weaker enemies respawn and force you to be quick and precise, while others encourage you to be cautious and methodical, having to remember the way a particular enemy moves and being on the lookout for potential traps. Both enemies and level structure seem to vastly differ from level to level, so you'll need to approach each of them with a new strategy.
So, yeah, if you like classic sidescroller action platformers in the vein of Castlevania or Ghost 'n' Goblins you'll love this game, and even if you don't I think it still deserves a chance, because it's a damn fun game.

The AI is extrememly buggy more often than not refusing to actually do tasks, leading to station wide issues from lack of spares leading to oxygen and power problems.

A straightforward visual novel that's strong on story, very light on actual gameplay. 95% of this game will be spent reading the entertaining plot while what little game there is amounts to drag-and-dropping correct ingredients to mix drinks (you are not timed so no quick reflexes needed and the game generously allows infinite attempts to create drinks with no penalty). There is a slight puzzle factor in that you're going to want to note what's being said in the dialog (such as the drinker's preferences or a particular piece of history behind a drink) so you will need to pay attention despite some things being said seem innocuous at first.
In terms of replayability, you could potentially give patrons their requested order on the first playthrough (though, if prompted, give them their preferred drink to meet ending requirements). On the second playthrough, booze them up on Karmotrine (the "alcohol" ingredient) every chance you get to receive some revealing dialogue. There isn't anything like branching paths or affecting your relationship with certain characters here though.
Still, for what the game offers, most folks should enjoy the story presented. The soundtrack is no slouch either.

VA-11 Hall-A: Cyberpunk Bartender Action is an experience worth more than what you pay for it.
I'm slightly biased, due to having been keeping up with the game since the pre-release builds.
You take the role of Jill, a bartender at a nice little bar in GC called 'VA-11 Hall-A' (But that's too much of a mouthful, so we just call it Valhalla). You work through the daily life of a bartender working in a Dystopian Cyberpunk city, chatting with clients, mixing drinks and changing lives.
The atmosphere of this game is perfect, and is sure to be an immersive experience.
The writing and character design is top-notch. All of the characters have interesting enough backstories, and are really just well rounded and totally likeable.
I've poured 60+ hours into this game, and have loved every second of it, I've made some regretful steam purchases in the past, but this is not one of them; I would go as far as to say this is my favorite purchase yet.
If you like Cyberpunk setting and story, relaxing in your seat with a cold drink and having a nice time or just a really engaging story that you'll find yourself replaying a few times every so often when you want to get comfortable; Then VA-11 Hall-A Cyberpunk Bartender Action is the game for you.
Do yourself a favor and buy it already!

This isn't Ace Combat, not even quite an Ace Combat 'lite', but it is as good an arcade stand-in as I've found.
Basically, you unlock new planes, weapons and items (flare alternatives, boosters, etc) by playing randomly generated levels each containing a random mission from a limited selection of types. As you play and kill stuff you get cash and experience and increase your 'tech level', unlocking new stuff as your tech level increases. If you are killed in a mission, you cash in your XP and money, select new items/weapons/planes to unlock and start again from level 1.
An interesting feature I enjoy is being able to choose the load-outs for every plane you have unlocked and being able to use any one of these planes during a mission, switching between them by landing on your carrier. This lets you play with tactics, choosing planes with large load capacity which can take a lot of punishment and using them as bombers, while choosing planes with good avionics and speed as fighters. Something to note, when you are killed, your loadouts are reset and some weapons are relocked, meaning you have to repurchase the weapons you want to use (if they are now locked) and resetup your loadouts.
Tl:dr - Fun little rogue-like with a decent amount of replayability for those who like quick drop-in games (20 minutes or so at a time). Unlockable content seems to slow down by level 25 and the missions, enemies and islands are failr samey. Combat feels fun and fairly fast-paced, weapons have a decent feel to them.
For £6.99? Worth every penny.

Sky Rogue! Where do I start here? I guess I'll start with a question. You! Yes, you, Reader. Don't look at me like that. The fourth wall cannot protect you here. What did you think this was, a work of fiction? No, this is a video game review. Now shut up and listen, because I'm monologuing here and I will not have my rhetorical questions interrupted with that uncouth glare of yours.
Really. Am I going to have to confiscate your eyebrows?
No?
Good.
As I was trying to say before I was so rudely interrupted: I would like to start this with a question. That is do you, the reader with the funny eyebrows and the tendency to rudely throw a writer off his train of thought, like to blow stuff up?
If the answer to that question's yes, then you will like this game.
It's really somewhat more complicated than that - you will also, for instance, need to learn to fly a variety of aircraft in a variety of horrifically dangerous situations, many of them involving missile spam, bullet spam, enemy spam, turret spam, and very nearly every other kind of spam except the true, original, Monty-Python-Sketch-Inspiring ham-like meat product. (Incidentally, that sketch is where the term "spam" comes from. See, we can learn things even on the internet! Knowledge! It ain't just for breakfast!) Simply put, this game's a blast. The levels are procedural, with mission objectives chosen semi-randomly from a list of possibilities; the more missions you complete, the more hideously dangerous the skies become. And, of course, dying sets the counter back to day 1.
The game does have its downsides - it's an early access title, so there are some hiccups in the current build. For instance, sometimes a target won't recognize that it's dead and will linger in your targeting system until you fly away and find something else to shoot at. And in the indev version, there's that finicky little thing where pressing "back" in a menu will instantly ask you if you want to return to the title screen, resulting in some wacky hijinx and occasional selection glitchery.
But if you're willing to overlook a handful of minor flaws for the chance to fly around blasting minions like the Red Baron on way too much caffiene, then this is a game for you! The devs update regularly and respond to the community on their Steam page fairly often; mods are supported, up to and including ships from Wing Commander and Cowboy Bebop, and, of course, with a certain loadout you can barrel roll between the hails of missiles like Starfox on a Tuesday afternoon!
Final summation: if you like your flight sims, give this game a shot. If you like explosions, give this game a shot. If you like arcadey shoot-em-ups where you get to perform flights of flying-ace-like derring-do - I think you see where this is going - give this game a shot.
Part Ace Combat, part Minecraft, all radical. Strafing runs on titanic floating air fortresses never gets old.

I had been waiting quite some time for another truly fresh and intensive game experience. This was one.
At first, you might think this is just a bunch of dry two-dimensional logic puzzles scattered around a beautiful landscape.
But after a while, you realize that the world and the riddles are intertwined in various creative, entertaining and spectacular ways.
So while, yes, technically, the only things you do are running around and drawing lines on boards, the resulting game experience is very complex, rewarding and full of variety. If you're looking for an adrenaline rush, this game is not the right one. There is no danger. There is no "action". Just perception and thought. If, however, you enjoy racking your brain over countless riddles that progressively cross the lines between abstract thought, world exploration and creative observation, you should definitely play "The Witness".

A lot of things wrong here.
First, you can't configure controls.  You either move with WASD or arrows keys, and use shift to sprint.  Everything else is with the mouse.  That's literally all the controls, no crouch or jump, and you can't even customize them.  What if I want to use the numpad to move, or buttons on my mouse?  And if there is some way to change controls, the game gave you no indication of how to do so.
Next is the puzzle types.  I enjoyed the difficult puzzles, and a lot of them were clever, but a lot of the puzzles were terribly executed, namely the environment ones.  There are good environmental puzzles, like the apples on the tree branches, the birds singing different pitched notes, or standing behind the colored glass, and then there are absolutely terrible ones like requiring you to stand in one specific spot behind a tree branch to get the branches/leaves/shadows to line up NEAR PERFECTLY.  That's not challenging, it's just frustrating to look for the exact, one and only spot to solve the puzzle.  It doesn't even feel like solving the puzzle, it feels like tracing a picture.  Now the amount of puzzles that were good outweighed the bad, but nearly every section had a few of these, so you couldn't avoid them.  The absolute worst was the desert ruins, where you had to angle the sun on the board to look at the markings.  You'd have to stand in very specific spots and angle the sun perfectly to get a view of the board.  There's no creative thinking to that, it's just trial and error to find the right spot.
The ending was also lackluster, and there were no fun easter eggs.  The windmill videos didn't make sense and listening to someone monologue about an topic on the phone recordings were boring.  For a 40 dollar game it's a letdown.

It used to be fine, skill-depended game where your team's coordination was also important. Then destroyers and green nation attacked.
Devs don't have clear vision how they want their game to be. At first it was clear that its team focused game where variety of ship classes and their combination matter. Then it started to be more and more simplified to the point where even you dont need to aim on certain weapons. Devs seem to be aware that game is slowly deceasing so they decided to make last cash-grabs.
Before, premium ships were optional. While some offered increased damage output, they were balanced in being more fragile. After recent changes, some premium, especially DLC, offer unique abilities that used correctly turns the tide of battle. Certain premiums after being introduced, you could get for free with quite amount of grind. They deleted that, but you can still get them by paying or waiting for "special offer" weeks when drop is reenabled.
Then destroyers came. Totally unbalanced, with extreme survivability and firepower with only weakness that is their speed. It took them months to somehow balance that but in a wrong way, adding "danger zone" when approached at 750m you dealt ridiculous damage. Now they are close to useless, still they are fine in team in number not exceeding 2. Salt generation increases when you see price of this ship. Weeks of gathering special resources to realise you need even more grind for it's modules.
Then finally, "Evolution" patch and a new ship. With quite amount of grind, but not so much compared to destroyers now, you get ship with reconfigurable stats and special module. Cool concept, but tragically realised - this ship is OP as hek. It's faster, more maneuverable, auto healing whenever it destroy enemy or enemy shooting at it, can teleport, cuts off small ship only way of survival that is speed and deal ridiculous amount of damage, killing most of ships in 2-3 hits. Now after 7 nerfs (SEVEN!) it's still best ship in it's class. Now they did the same with new ship, interceptor. It should be weakest damage dealer in it's class, but it's weapons deal absurd amount of damage and capable of homing on target. Very hard to hit, even if you try, it could go permanently radar-invisible. Of course, grind for it increased that can be bypassed by 60 euro DLC that cuts grind in half (because resources needed for upgrade are not included).
Grind is worst way possible, as I call it "RNG-grind". After battles you have chance to get container that have random part inside, but you need to use iridium to open it. Iridium can only be aquired by first day win purple loot spots or by playing corporate wars. Holding location for more than 2 days is almost impossible if you don't flood it with players and even with that you need to win pvp after to get your location reward back. When you fail to get iridium in 2 hours, container is lost. Trading is in here, but again, focuses on getting money for devs not for players. There is only GS option, each item has minimal price, seller need to pay tax, while 60% of items is useless (like blueprints of MK.5 weapons that give maybe 3% in increase, but require lot of materials). That all combined with resource limits give overall a bad economy.
Game is destroyed by imbalance. When 2 ships outclass by x3 other 200 ships in the game, there is something not right. PvP matches are decided who has more alien ships other than teamwork. Leagues that claimed for aiming for e-sports are the same. Weekly tournaments are infested with 7 green gunship/recon + healer teams, that require close to zero skill when opponent has "normal" ships. Lags and long waiting queues. Meaningless Open Space mode with 100% accuracy bots and nothing than resource gathering.
It's not fun anymore, maybe until rank 5 where naked green ships are nothing than ordinary ships. After R5, prepare to be farmed. I suggesting staying away from it.

Is this game a detective game? Yes and no. There's clue gathering, some puzzle solving in regards to how the pieces fit together to form the transpired events, but it's not in league with other more thought provoking detective games like the Ace Attorney series. That said, if you like Ace Attorney like myself, this won't kill you.
The difficulty is pretty much all in your own endurance. There's no real penalty for guessing something wrong when it comes to class trials other than needing to start the trial over. Trials are so quick though that it's hardly worth calling it a penalty. The most gamey part is in the trials with the Trigger Time events. Wish they just passed on that as it just makes the experience frustrating.
Aside from murder and some pretty dark humor, there's some good ol' sex jokes (that are surprisingly funny), completing the circle of a good time and adding some good character to the script. Still, I could do for less panty shots, but what's to be expected from a Japanese game? Japan can't help itself.
Let's go with one more question: why wouldn't you want this game if you like the above? If you're expecting Nine Hours, Nine Person, Nine Doors or Virtue's Last Reward, you need to lower your expectations. This game is not complex. There are times it will make you think, but it won't keep you on your toes. You want to play this if you're more for finding passive interaction with a quota of gaming elements to pass the grade.

Something you should know up front about this game, however, is that part of the enjoyment comes from the surprise you get when playing it.  And people are especially terrible at keeping the secrets of this game...secret.  If you have any interest in playing the game, I highly recommend steering clear of discussion forums, comment sections, YouTube thumbnails, Wikis and even other Steam reviews.  Imageboards are also a no-go, spoilers will show up in /v/ threads even when you're not looking for them.
In any case, the game is a "Whodunit" visual novel in the vein of games like Phoenix Wright and Zero Escape.  The conceit of the game is spelled out in its Steam store page, so I won't repeat it here, but if you've never played those types of games before, the experience is much like reading a good Sherlock Holmes or Hercule Poirot murder mystery, except you play as the detective from a first-person perspective.
That's not to say that it's just a read-along story - this game gives you some autonomy.   In between murders and major story beats, you can choose to hang out with any of the remaining students and try to get to know them better.  But when a student is murdered, you also have examine the scene of the crime yourself, gathering as much evidence as you can by looking around the various crime scenes, and then debate with your remaining fellow students over "whodunit" during the class trial.  The debates are where most of the actual gameplay comes in - you must suss out contradictions in your fellow students statements based on your knowledge of the case though a variety of mini-games.
These games are kind of famous for having absolutely crazy stories with lots of twists, and this game doesn't disappoint.  There were a few things that I figured out ahead of my player character, but just as many things took me completely by surprise, a few even catching me completely me off guard.  The game is not short - Steam says it took me about 27 hours start to finish, but I was so fixated on the mysteries of the plot that those 27 hours flew by.
The art-style might lead you to believe that the game is aimed at anime or JRPG fans, but I enjoyed the story despite not being either - there were one or two scenes that were kinda "fancervice", but not enough to detract from the overall game.  The soundtrack is fantastic too.
If you're still not sure if you would enjoy this game or not, what I would recommend is reading or watching¹ a Let's Play of the game.  Reading or watching up to the end of the first chapter should be enough to tell you if this is the kind of game you would enjoy or not - there is enough to tantalize, but no major plot threads are resolved, leaving you to experience the best parts of the game yourself.
¹ If you're watching, be careful to avoid spoilers in YouTube comments or thumbnails, and also ensure you're watching a play-through of the US PSVita or Steam release, so you get fully voiced class trials.

My original review was among the first on the Steam for this game.  At the time, there were numerous AI glitches that made the game unplayable, and I felt the game belonged in early access.  I promised to come back to Planetbase later on and change my review if the problems I cited were addressed.  They have been, so I decided to delete my earlier review (which had attracted a lot of attention) and write a fresh one.
Planetbase is rather novel.  You are tasked with building a successful colony on an alien world.  What makes this interesting is that you have no direct control over your colonists.  You decide what gets built and the ratio of colonists with various jobs that you'd like have in the colony as new ones arrive, but there is no way to directly influence what any unit does.  The closest you can come is increasing the priority of a structure, and I have to agree with the folks who say this seems to have a questionable effect at times.
It is challenging at first to understand just how to build up your base.  Frankly, you can expect to lose a few bases at various stages until you work out a system for creating a successful one (and the hazards will sometimes wreck your base any way if you aren't prepared or get unlucky early on).  This leads me to two complaints I have with the game.  First, the tutorial should give better advice.  While it does explain the function of many structures and show you how to reach survival, I don't think it demonstrates a good starter base design.  Or at least I didn't have any luck following it.  My second complaint is the speed of the game.  You can make the game move at x4 speed, but it still feels like things move along a bit too slowly, especially since your liable to fail the first time your base reaches certain key points you don't yet know how to deal with.  It's sort of demoralizing to lose an entire base when they take so long to grow in size.
The main way Planetbase offers replayability is through planets.  Each planet features a different terrain design and unique challenges to make base building and survival more challenging.  There are milestones to be reached in base development, and new planets are unlocked once enough milestones have been reached.  I understand a new planet will be added in the near future in an update (there are three at the time I'm writing this).  So if you find you enjoy playing Planetbase, there is a reward to seek for doing well which in turn gives you a new challenge and an incentive to try building a new base.
As I said at the beginning of this review, my initial impression of the game was very negative due to a variety of serious bugs with the AI.  All of these appear to have been addressed and I was able to clear almost all of the first planet's milestones with relative ease (and I had fun doing it!).  I still wouldn't say it's perfect though.  My two medics became engrossed in the task of walking back and forth down the corridor to an air lock for like two days straight, leaving me without medical supplies or treatment for injured workers.  After a couple of days, they just stopped doing that and went back to behaving normally, but it was still odd.  I'm not entirely happy with how the AI manages workers, either.  I had some unexplained droughts in my production of metal that lasted for ages.  The mines were full of bots, I had plenty of workers, everyone was happy and well-fed, there were plenty of machines, and yet...no metal.  I was stores were full of ore but no metal was coming out.  This only happened a couple of times, but it dragged on long enough to be both noticeable and irritating.
I'm not upset that the AI is occasionally wonky, I just feel like it is worth mentioning.  Planetbase is a fun game if you take the time to understand how to play it.  For the aspiring player, here are some tips from my own experience playing the game.  This is just what worked for me so do feel free to experiment.
1. With the exception of the first Canteen, build everything large, especially oxygen generators.
2. Don't expand too quickly.  When you've added stuff on, watch to make sure your colonists aren't overloaded and that you have enough water, food, and power to keep the base running for a day or so before doing more.  Night is especially critical because power outages are awful.
3. Biologists seem to be able to reliably tend to three things at once (plants and meat) before getting overworked.  Rice, tomatoes, and meat seem to work well for food.  Be mindful of the ratio between rice and tomatoes because one grows faster than the other.  Naturally, you will need to plant a medicinal patch when you are nearly out of medical supplies to ensure you don't run out.
4. Be ready to start building robots ASAP.  Robots eventually fail and your base will become much less efficient as you start losing them.  I would recommend making it a priority to save up for bot designs early on unless you really need something.  Building and driller bots are awesome.
5. Cabins may hold less beds than dorms, but try to have some if you can.  They appear to boost morale by a fairly large amount in addition to providing colonists with a place to rest.
6. Don't bother building a multidome.    Bars see a lot more use, but be mindful (VERY mindful) of the resource consumption.  It became an issue way faster than I expected it to.
7. Be mindful of your starting location.  Look around to make sure you have a lot of room to expand before you start making your base.  Don't do what I did and accept a sub-optimal location only to get boxed in at the end game (if only I could fit one more large O2 generator in my base...).
8. Oxygen can become an issue in two ways:  either you just plain don't have enough for all the people in your base, or you have enough but they are too far away from certain structures in your base.  A lack of O2 kills quickly, and depending on how it happens, it can be difficult to throw down a new generator in time.
Good luck and have fun!

Welcome to VA-11 Hall-A.
VA-11 Hall-A as eponym for the game is also the name of the bar you, the player character, in the form of Jill is tending. As such you have the usual tasks a bartender has to fulfill: Mixing drinks and listening to your customers stories/sorrows and complains. I would  describe VA-11 Hall-A as a Visual Novel of sorts as the most of the time you are just reading the text. There is also the possibility to influence some minor events.
This is done in the form of the - more or less - only activity/minigame in the game. The mixing. After the customer has given his orders your job is to prepare this drink. This is hardly difficult as you can look up the ingredients at every moment of the game. And the order is always standing at the bottom of the screen unless Jill is distracted. As such the difficulty is for most of the game very easy. There are some minor challenges where customers give you a bit of choice for their drink as they don't name it specifically but only with a characteristic like it should be girly or sweet. In some rare instances the drink is described rather cryptic or you have to remember something from an earlier night. So while the game is easy you have to pay a bit of attention (unless you go the boring guy route and use a guide). By remembering the drinks correctly and chosing a suitable drink if given the choice you can influence the outcome of some minor events which will then lead to additional endings. Other than that they influence your paycheck which again influence if Jill can buy what she wants and also pay her bills which will again influence if she is distracted and can remember the order. It is always just minor stuff but it adds up. Other than those events several drinks have an optional alcoholic content which can change some dialogues. So if you want to you can make an idol spout some rather grim lines or make your favourite Streamer sleep through the entire night.
While the mini-game gives you enough to do between the talk of the characters it is rather rudimentary and would not be a reason for recommendation. So what is the reason? The strength of the game does not come from its story but rather from its cast. You have Alma your female hacker searching for a suitable love, Dorothy a sex robot earnestly loving her job, your co-worker Gillian (or whatever his real name is), Dana your boss with the metal arm, a dog wearing a hawaii shirt and and and. Most of them a very loveable and everyone should find his favourites. And all of those characters come with their secrets. Although most of those secrets are only hinted at as this game is not about the secrets of your customers. In its core VA-11 Hall-A is a game which tells the story of Jill: why she is doing this job and also her sorrows . And it is a game about friendship.
And the last one is something which i really appreciate because for one it is a game which will make you happy walking away from it. There is some tension, some drama but at the end the game will make you feel good about what happened. Even the bad ending will make you smile. All in all there are only two outcomes the good and the bad ending. If you manage the good ending you can get additional endings depending on how much you bonded with specific customers.
The game is rounded up with a good soundtrack which can be chosen on your personal preferences, a suitable art-style and some achievements. The achievements require some concentration and probably an additional playthrough (unless you bore yourself with a first playthrough guide). All of them are rather easy and fair with one small exception as it is a cameo to another game and cannot be found out with just playing VA-11 Hall-A. So all in all the game is very recommendable if you are in search for something rather light-hearted, visual novel like game with a colourful and fun cast.
PS: If you have any questions regarding the game just ask them in the comments and I'll try to answer them to the best of my knowdledge.

Some people may like this game, but it sure isn't for me. After insufferably long dialogue filled with foul words and sexual comments, you get to serve a drink or two....and then listen to more insufferably long dialogue. Positively brilliant indie effort.
The dialogue feels like is was written by William GIbson while he was reading a bad 90s manga, the cutesy graphic style could belong in any 16-bit era console game and all the little shout-outs to cyberpunk (anime and otherwise) add up to the a really consistent tone. The real star of the show, however, is the soundtrack, and its given centre stage by making the player set up the jukebox before each 'day' begins.
The gameplay reminds me somewhat of Papers, Please. Its a simple but intensely addictive formula - you get the orders throughout the dialogue, you make the order as best you can. There are some funky touches like being able to add extra alcohol to get an annoying patron drunk and it stays interesting by the number of ways the patrons order their booze.
Worth it for the soundtrack alone. Get it and prepare to lose your weekend

Year Walk is a short, creepy adventure that is 2 parts adventure game and 1 part interactive fiction.
Inspired by the Swedish folk tradition of Arsgang, Year Walk sets you in the shoes of someone who dares to undertake this strange journey.
The art and simple controls, as well as the sensation that you are watching an old film complete with tears and dust on the print, put you into a realm where anything could happen. It is not without some quality jump scares and unsettling imagery. There is a bit of Lovecraftian horror dwelling within Year Walk.
The puzzles fit into the world well, although while manipulating them you can tell the game was conceived for tablets. It should not diminish any enjoyment, however. They are clever enough to make the player feel smart upon completing them.
And the less you know going into it, all the better. Year Walk is worth it for fans of interactive fiction games and creepy short stories.

i'm a very big fan of folklore, especially scandinavian. other games i've played that try to touch on folklore either don't give enough background and end up confusing, or give way too much information and feel like a history lesson. this game balances the historical information with the gameplay very well. you get to interact with every character you learn about in the game and some levels aren't possible to beat without knowing the history.
the gameplay is a bit confusing since there aren't many games that are 2D and first person, but you do get used to it pretty easily. i wouldn't call this a puzzle game, but you do have to use critical thinking if you want to move on in the story, unless you use a walkthrough like i did. for me puzzle games have to do with finding patterns in the physical properties of objects. in this game, you are given hints as to how to get past the chapter in the story in the form of riddles, and you have to decipher the riddles. i guess this would really be a riddle game instead of a puzzle game.
the story is not linear and you only get clued into the plot at the very beginning and the end. the game starts with the main character visiting his girlfriend, where we learn a bit about the characters and get some background on what "year walks" are. you don't eat or drink for a day, then you walk into the woods at midnight in search of clues for what will happen in the future. this is loosely based on a swedish tradition. the next day you begin the year walk, and the plot is not mentioned for a while. the majority of the game is solving a series of challenges presented by and involving different scandinavian folk figures. the game provides an encyclopedia where you can read about every creature in the game. this gives clues to their nature and behavior, and sometimes helps to solve puzzles. when you finally get to the end, you get a glimpse into the main character's future, which i won't say since it will ruin the game.
however, this is not the end. the game ends in a tragedy, but it gives you a chance to right your wrongs by switching perspective to a modern-day historian who is researching the year walks. he gives you a riddle that lets you view a journal he has been keeping about the events of the game. some people say the journal is a long read, but it only took a few minutes of my time. this part of the game is almost a different genre; it seems more like a detective short story than a surreal video game. the historian is haunted by the creatures you interact with from the game as they show him how to help the main character. his research into the year walk tradition explains a lot about the plot. i will say that this whole aspect of the game seems a bit out of place: like the developers just threw it in because they felt like people would be confused by the twist ending or wonder how the game ties into the real world. ultimately it created a bit more confusion than was already present, but since you get a chance to save a very likeable character it makes a good addition to the game. the alternate ending created by the journal does involve the very overused (especially in games) cliche of heroic sacrifice.
none of this would really matter if the game didn't have nice aesthetics though. it doesn't try to make up for anything with them, but the simplistic gameplay and virtual lack of dialogue would make for a very boring game if it weren't for the way this game looks. the graphics go along very well with the gameplay and other stylistic choices for the game, like the use of runes, the setting, the light horror aspect, and the depiction of the folk figures. allegedly the developer of the game researched horror movies to get the timing right on the spooky scenes, and it really shows. right when the music gets peaceful and the graphics become fluid and lure you into a false sense of security, some spooky pagan
will come flying at you out of the blue. people are very averse to the jump scare, and most fans of horror and critics will say that it's a cheap or uncreative tactic, but just like everything it has its place, and there are some times where it's appropriate to use it. unlike most of the horror genre, where the jump scare is used so much it becomes a joke amongst the audience, this game knows when to trigger a fight or flight response.
besides minor flaws i talked about, this is one of my favorite games right now. i know most folklore fans don't give a
about games, and most gamers don't give a
about folklore, but this game has something to offer to both groups.
i am ashamed to say that this game is 2spooky for me. scurry atmosphere/10, worth the $2 or so I got it for on sale. Not sure if I'd pay full price though.

Year Walk is a haunting, creepy, beautiful experience and I loved every minute of it.  The art is superb.  The music and sound design is flawless.  The puzzles are a joy to piece together.  The ambience gets progressively more chilling as the game goes on.  There are secrets that you must discover after your first playthrough, and I say MUST because you would be doing yourself a great disservice by failing to follow through and finding the  "real" ending that can only be found using clues given to you after you "beat" the game the first time.  There is actually a reason for more than one playthrough explained in the meta-narrative you'll discover if you do.
Do yourself a favor and play this game and find all of the secrets embedded within.  The secrets aren't extras, but vital for you to get the full impact of this very unique story.  Beat the game, open the journal, and then use the clues there to finish the game.  Don't cheat and look stuff up, you will cheat yourself out of one of the most unique narrative structure and reveals of any game I've ever played.
Wonderful job by the developer. Absolutely fantastic.
(p.s. -- I would also reccomend reading the in-game encylopedia as you start the game the first time.  It gives a lot of background for the Swedish folklore that this game uses that will help establish the atmosphere.)

This game simulates NES-era action platformers, which means the controls are unforgiving.  You can't change your jump arc, for example.  However, that means once you learn a section of a level, you will be able to do it the same way every time because your inputs will always produce the same result.
So once you beat the game, it is easy to zoom through it again for speedruns or challenge runs.  And in fact, beating any stage without taking a hit will allow you to get special items that unlock bonus levels.  That part of the game was too challenging/time consuming for me, since you basically have to start from the beginning if you make a mistake.
Still, the base game is worth playing.  It has really nice pixel art, some of the best.
One of the best, challenging sidescrollers I've played.  Highly recommend it.

Volgarr the Viking is a hard game, but you probably already know that. I thought about giving up on the game when I was on my umpteenth attempt at beating the second half of stage two. But I persevered and eventually beat the entire game. Afterward, I went back and played stages one and two again and was amazed at how I could fly through them. My ability to control Volgarr had improved drastically, and it felt great.
Some of the negative reviews are saying there are no checkpoints, which is weird because there are. There is a checkpoint in the middle of each stage for stages one through five, which, I admit, isn't enough checkpoints. I would have been happy to see another checkpoint close to the boss in each stage. Toiling through the lengthy second half of a stage multiple times only to get immediately annihilated by the boss time and time again was disheartening and almost caused me to throw in the towel. But I kept coming back for more, and I think that shows how well-designed, fun, and rewarding this game is.
Just to give you an idea of how much time you might have to dedicate to this game to beat it, I beat it in less than nine hours without ever looking up strategies or watching YouTube videos.
Despite what some other reviews say, you don't have to beat the game in one sitting. If you exit the game, you can restart at the beginning of any stage you've reached previously by continuously moving left at the start of the game.
In the options menu, you can change a camera setting so that the view is zoomed out all the time, which is what I preferred; this probably should have been the default. I also disabled down + jump to roll and just used the shoulder button.
The downward thrust is your friend.

This may be quite suitable for a younger audience, although the theme is murder and there is a murder weapon said to have blood on it, there's nothing in the way of graphical violence or gore. In fact, the game's hints and clues really guide you through everything so well that I could see playing this as a child. In some ways, that's my only complaint - the game keeps telling you how to do everything any time you're faced with a puzzle, such that they're not very puzzling.
Oh, also, it seems theere may have been a prequel (from dialogue with a disappearing little girl who recognizes you) and the game 'hints' at a sequel, but neither is explicitly linked to or very blatantly described. Ssurprising, given how much else is made painfully blatant.

Note: I didn't give this game a thumbs down because it was bad. I personally enjoyed this game. I only gave it a thumbs down because I don't recommend this to anyone who has no idea what they're actually playing. If you are aware of what's actually in store, buy it!
This game is about exploring an island and solving line puzzles. That's it!
The game is very creative with it's puzzles. You immediately start the game with no menu, it just loads up and you solve the first set of puzzles. Once you've done the first area, you are free to explore the island and solve the puzzles. The game introduces you to this complicated puzzle with different types of puzzle features you haven't seen before. This gives the player the idea that he can't solve this puzzle. You see two sets of puzzles with the two puzzle features in the previous puzzle which you use to solve it. Some puzzles use the environment like one in a desert temple or a monastery where you use the patterns and trees to guide yourself to solve the puzzles. However when I finished the desert temple, I stumbled across the quarry area where there were these tetris pieces which I had no ♥♥♥♥ing clue how to solve. The game doesn't tell you which areas to go to first. The tetris pieces are introduced to the player well in the marsh area.
This game fails to guide the player how to do things. Players are left to figure things out for themselves which is where things fall flat. Areas that I did enjoy were The Keep and The Mountain and the Monastery.
I love this game and I hate this game. I do not reccomend this to anyone unless you know what you're getting yourself into. There is no story, it's just an open world with line puzzles. That's it! I only bought it because it was 66% off.

This isn't just a game, it's a masterpiece.
No trailer or gameplay video can explain it, because the genius of the game isn't a story, or gameplay, it's the feeling it gives the player when playing, you can't communicate that.
Unique puzzles, unrivalled in design and polished to perfection.
I don't think I can pick out a flaw.
Sure, there will be parts some people don't like, but everything in here is intentional, there are no mistakes.
The game took 8 years to make by a very talented development team.
There is no game that is like this, and there will never be a sequel.
I wish I could wipe my memories and play through it again, as it's not the same the 2nd time through, when you know how everything works.
What I can say is that it's not for everyone.
It's for people that like solving puzzles, that don't mind getting stuck on a problem and having to come back to it hours or days later when you've had time to think, giving up for now and walking to a different part of the island.
There's no handholding, and do yourself a favour, and don't look at walkthroughs, the beauty of this is about the "ah hah!" epiphany moments, trial and error, testing and learning, scientific method to a puzzle you've never encountered before,
with no instructions or, well any text whatsoever in the game.
You'll become an expert, be tested to your cognitive limits with harder and harder puzzles and a crazy time trial.
Then you'll be done with the game, and you'll never encounter this format of puzzle again, and maybe never play a game that has this much thought put in to it either.

You'll need a lot of patience in playing this game. The graphics are fine, it's just that you don't have any options to move forward. You would really have to solve each problem before you go to the next phase. The game is good if you don't get bored that easily.

The Witness is based on a mysterious and philosophical island not filled whith puzzles, but filled with lessons and challenges for you to face and reflect on. The aesthetic is simple and pleasing, allowing for a walk through beautiful landscapes scattered throughout. Find yourself at peace in this enormous journey for you to embark.

The puzzles are arbritrary, there are several rules to each of the different puzzles you have to discover yourself, which requires a lot of trial and error, and research.
I cannot recommend this game to ANYONE because it is simply not fun. But if you want to feel aggreviated, challenged, then feel free to pick this up.

It's been over a year since I last played Chaos Domain, and I still remember it as possibly the worst platformer I've ever played. And I've played a lot since then, including terrible parody games and utterly incompetent ripoffs of concepts that were bad to begin with. No, there's something singularly terrible about Chaos Domain, a game that sits uncomfortably between no-effort cash grabs and poorly-designed passion projects. It's a game that tries to be an action platformer in such a lazy way that it almost comes of as cynical just by existing.
If you think I'm being too hard on Chaos Domain, know this: One hit kills you, levels can be up to five minutes long, and there are no checkpoints. I'm going to talk about plenty of other facets of the game, but if that's not sounding the warning bells in your head then maybe you've never played a grossly mis-tuned game before. It's a perfect storm of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t designed to waste your time as you get wasted by common enemies and forced to play entire levels over just because one part was designed to be too punishing. But don't fret if you're already put off by that little detail, because the rest of the game is almost as bad.
Chaos Domain dumps you into the cyberboots of future Anubis, fighting hundreds of cyberdudes along wholly unremarkable cybercorridors. Levels have only two components, hallways of fixed height that only scroll in one direction, and shafts that you can platform up and down freely. Platforms mostly hold enemies that fire slow, creeping bullets and die in one hit, but can also be laden with health pickups (more like 1-ups), new guns, or point-granting ankhs. I will go ahead and tell you now that I have no idea what is up with the Egyptian theme, especially since it only extends to the player character and point items.
There are ten chapters, with three levels to a chapter. They take a few minutes to run through, assuming you are quick on the draw and don't touch any of the numerous enemies, bullets, explosives, explosive barrels, electrified floors, or glitchy crushers littering the corridors. One touch of anything instantly kills you, respawning you in place a moment later and costing you one of your three lives. Lose all three and you start the whole level over. The problem here should be apparent (if it wasn't before) because as early as the second chapter you'll be fighting shooting dudes, running dudes, grenade dudes, and rocket launcher dudes all at once.
Even if the graphics weren't bland and strangely grainy, even if the weapons didn't feel like Nerf guns, and even if there were some kind of story at all, Chaos Domain would still be too incompetently designed to stick with. The lowest bar you can set for a platformer is to have a reasonable sort of challenge, and instead of clearing that bar it smacks face-first into it and ends up in a coma. There's simply no excuse for instant kills and no checkpoints and unavoidable deaths, and with the glut of platformers on Steam there's no excuse for slogging through this garbage heap of a game.

Yeah, this is basically Phoenix Wright meets Battle Royale with an perverse stuffed demon bear as a ringleader. And it's fantastic.
Imagine a dating sim/visual novel in which the any of the characters you cozy up to could be murderers or murder victims at any point, and you're not far off.
Most of the gameplay follows the standard Phoenix Wright formula - lots of investigation and talking to colorful characters in between solving and arguing over murders. When in the courtroom, you listen to a conversation over and over and try to pick apart the contradiction with one of your argument-as-metaphor "Truth Bullets," but Danganronpa adds something deceptively simple that makes the whole courtroom scene so much more tense than Phoenix did:
A timer.
That's it, that's all it needed. A ticking clock. And it becomes so much more satisfying to shoot down even simple arguments. Add a fantastic soundtrack and you've got a desperately engaging experience.
The writing and setting is good enough to suck you in, give you a big enough mystery in a surreal nightmarescape of a high school to work through obtuse and unrebindable controls and minigames that don't explain themselves wonderfully on the first go. You can work past that. You're going to have to if you want to find out what's under Hope's Peak Academy, and I sure as hell want to find out.

Gravitar is one of my favorite arcade classics, and when I searched for similar names on Steam I found this gem.  The demo is short but it told me everything I needed to know and I spent the $5.  Gravitron 2 is what I wanted in a more modern "Gravitar-like" game.  The difficulty ramps up quickly but death isn't rage-inducing because I feel confident I can "git gudder".  I'm not very far into the levels yet, and I'm sure they get
, but so far the game feels quite fair.
TIPS: If you have a gamepad I recommend you use that.  On my Xbone controller I have A=boost, X=fire, L1=shield.  It's important that you can easily boost & shield at the same time.  Also start with "Standard" map pack.  The default-selected map pack ("OfficialPack1") is harder.
It's a great game and the price is right.  Give the free demo a try!

Criminally underappreciated retro arcade gem. It's near 10 years old now and the developer is long gone, but this is still one of the best Gravitar-style shooters ever made.
Difficult but fair, with a surprising amount of diversity in the level design. You can download the demo, or there's also a good gameplay video
so you know what to expect.
Now a few important first-play tips if you buy this game (which you should):
- The default level pack on the main menu is "OfficialPack1."
Click once so that you are starting with the "Standard" pack, which are the levels from the initial release. Otherwise the game will seem very difficult to start with.
-
It will deflect all standard bullets and is a lifesaver in tight areas. By default it is bound to the middle mouse button; I suggest rebinding it to a more easily accessible key like the spacebar, or use a controller. All controls can be rebound from the options menu, which is available after starting the game. You can also adjust the mouse sensitivity there.
- You can land on any flat surface, including walls and celings, and you will not take damage from landing at high speeds, as long as you are correctly aligned.
Gravitron is near-perfect, with only one serious flaw: There are no leaderboards. There were at one point, hosted on a third-party server, but that server is down for good. Steam leaderboards would be a major benefit, though there is little hope of that happening now.
Still, that lone drawback should absolutely not stop you from picking this one up. Don't bother waiting for a sale - it hasn't dropped in price since 2013 and likely won't ever again. Plus at $5 it's already a steal.

VA-11 Hall-A looks great. The pixel-art is consistent, colorful and atmospheric. Mostly, you will see your bar from behind the counter, as you've probably noticed by looking at the screenshots. The interface takes a majority of the screen. That means, at times the little screen you have left is quite busy while you feel like there is a lot of room that could be used elsewhere. This does, however, support the technoid feel of the game. It is a world reigned by computers, cyborgs and megacorps after all. Like it or not, the artist clearly knew what he was doing. The sprites are a bit of a hit and miss. Some look downright awesome, others have small problems with their anatomy and can look kind of weird. All of them are mostly static - the mouth is the only thing moving most of the time.
I only wished there were more scenes that do not play behind the counter - when Jill, the protagonist, leaves her comfort zone and the game changes to different interfaces (sometimes with unique minigames) and backgrounds. Those scenes are few and far between, and offer a welcome change from VA-11 Hall-A's monotonous design. Jill's apartment, which you visit between each workday, is gorgeous. You can customize it in every conceivable way, while playing and surfing around with Jill's tablet. It is a wonderful change of pace and serves greatly as a breather between the long passages in the bar.
The aesthetic of the game is largely carried by it's Cyberpunk feel and it's music. The tracks are very varied, from brooding Ambient-sounds that remind me of musical projects such as 2184, over instrumental pop to pumping and upbeat electro-tracks. You can most of the time choose yourself what is played in the bar-owned jukebox. The design of the game clearly showcases that the developers are into Science-Fiction and Cyberpunk culture and -media. Everything feels authentic and just what you would want and expect from a game like this.
Apart from managing your money (and some monetary goals you have to reach to get a nice ending for Jill are actually quite hard to get, so don't mess up mixing your drinks) the majority of the time will be spent talking to the various customers of VA11 Hall-A. Their stories range from funny to downright moving, depending who you have in front of you. The atmosphere of the entire game changes depending on which character you are interacting with; a testament how greatly varied the different personas in the game are. I liked every single one of them, and won't get into any more detail, since they are the meat of the game and should be experienced by the player.
Speaking of the player; looming over all those personal stories is some kind of main arc, involving you main character and an old friend. Let's just say: it is luckily not what you would expect from most visual novels. There is no sappy romance, so unnecessary sex, no cheap emotional punch, just an authentic, almost everyday story that could very well leave you in tears in the end. If you usually avoid this genre for fear of the aforemented cliches, give VA-11 Hall-A a spin. It really tries to be different in this regard. The writing itself won't win the Nobel Prize of Literature, but it is good enough. It never felt artificial, and the dialogue flows well. Sure, the devs are not Hemingway, but easily on par with most other video-games.
Certainly a matter of taste are the various influences on current pop- and internet-culture that are spread around the game. I for one loved them, but I can see how they can be turn-off for some, so I will address them here. You will deal with streamers, you will hear some inside-jokes, serve drinks in fedoras to slimy, fat men and even surf on a weird bizarro-cyberpunk-imageboard. It is important to note that those references are indeed noticeable, but very well integrated in the world VA11-Hall-A presents. They don't take too much room and if you can stand them, just swallow them.
After all is said and done, there is little that can be added without talking too much about the plot. VA11 Hall-A is a portrait of a city, it's about it's problems and the lifes of it's inhabitants. It's about normal people dealing with their demons, with their passions and families in a dystopian world. VA11 Hall-A is not new in this regard, there have been many Science-Fiction classics doing similar things; it is, however, almost unheard of in our new media. I can not recommend this fresh and new take on Science-Fiction enough. 15 bucks might be a little steep for some, so if you can not swallow the price for something that takes roughly 10 hours to finish and serves little to no real gameplay, wait for a sale and buy it then. If you can identify with the virtues of the game, you won't regret it.
I still can't decide whether I want this game to stay under the radar, or if I want it to become more popular. Quite the dilemma.

I don't really like Visual Novels (like, at all), but I'll make an exception for this one. The entire "game" had me glued to my seat until the end. I'll be doing another... uhh, "playthrough" soon just to see the other endings.
It's a nice little story you can read through when you've got nothing to do. If you're going in expecting some deep gameplay mechanics, you're probably gonna be disappointed, but that should've been obvious already. The bartending thing adds a nice little twist to the usual "choose-your-own-adventure book" thing that VNs usually have (not that I would know, this is pretty much the only one I've actually "played").
My favorite thing about the game is how you don't actually need to give people the drinks they ordered. I won't spoil anything, but giving people certain drinks can have different effects on the story/endings or just the amount of exposition you'll get out of them in general. I'm pretty sure I've gotten some people unintentionally drunk too (there are obvious visual cues), which lead to some amusing dialogue. I would highly suggest against reading a guide because in my opinion, it'll ruin most of the experience (at the very least go through it blind for the first playthrough). It adds quite a bit of replayability, which is pretty surprising considering the kind of game this is.
As for the soundtrack, it's amazing. I guess I'm a bit biased because I'm a huge fan of cyberpunk and synthwave, but really, the soundtrack is just great. Even better that you can customize the jukebox every time you start your shift.
Overall, I would totally recommend VA-11 HALL-A. If you still feel like it won't be worth your money, pick it up when it's on sale. The devs did a good job, they deserve the support! :)

I thought this would be the kind of difficult game I'd just chip away at over time so I can pace myself without having to break my controller from trying to play too long.
I thought it wasn't so difficult I couldn't handle it, and the controls seemed tight enough, so I figured I could get past any challenge it threw at me given enough time.
Then I decided to take a break and quit the game, only to be told that I'd have to start from the beginning of the game if I quit. You have to beat this whole thing in one sitting.
Yes, I get it, it's supposed to be like an old school arcade sidescroller and you couldn't just save those and pick them up later either. That's cute and all but that's honestly the tipping point that turns my opinion from "Get this if you want a tough challenge" to "Don't bother, just emulate something better instead"
EDIT: I've played more of the game since I wrote this review and I found out that you can skip worlds after you've  beaten them, so you can at least "save" some progress in a sense. I also found out that you can set "look ahead" to be a toggle in the options, so you want to make sure to turn that on, toggle "look ahead" on, and never ever turn it off. Honestly I don't know why the screen isn't zoomed out like that by default, because it makes planning ahead so much better and more satisfying.
That all being said, I still feel like this game's true potential is held back by the devs insistence on making it be difficult for the sake of fueling nostalgia for old NES and arcade games, and I have a hard time really recommending it. This is the kind of game that makes me wish steam had neutral recommendations.

This would be a fairly enjoyable little side scroller except for one abysmal design choice, the checkpoint system. The levels in this game are rather lengthy and you tend to get a checkpoint only at the halfway point, so whenever you die for any reason, be it your own fault, dying from a simple honest to god mistake or the game having trial and error ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, you go back to the last checkpoint. Now, I wouldn't mind this too much, except for the fact that there is no checkpoint when you make it to a boss fight. If you die to the boss, you go back to the mid-level checkpoint. This wasn't an issue in the first level as the boss was rather simple and straight forward and if used common sense you get past him easily, the second boss is when I started breaking things. The second boss in this game is PURE TRIAL AND ERROR, it has attacks that you would have absolutely no way of knowing how to dodge or even anticipate them coming your first time through. The boss arena involves two platforms and a pool of water underneath and the boss is a fish with a trident, you would have no idea that the fish's trident actually shoots electricity because nothing indicates it, so if you are in the water and you have no idea this is coming, you're gonna get hit, sometimes when you know it's coming but you accidentally fell in the water, you don't actually have enough time to get out before he does that attack. Another attack is the boss shooting a laser beam that you have no idea is coming and the way to fully dodge it and avoid any damage coming after it makes no sense and you have no way of figuring it out your first time through. This is a boss to which you have to die over and over and over again until you finally figure it out, and you know what happens when you die in this game, you go back to the mid-level checkpoint, so that means you constantly have to repeat the same sections over and over again just to have another shot at the bit you're actually having trouble with.
The developers of this game said they wanted to emulate the experience of an old arcade game with this. Guys, I don't know if you're aware of this, so this might come as shocker, but arcade games were really hard, sometimes outright unfair for the sole purpose of milking quarters out of kids, there was no good reason for them to be difficult other than that, and console games from the 80's and early 90's just emulated what arcade games were doing despite you not being able to put quarters into your console, and there's a reason games slowly started getting rid of mechanics like extra lives and started introducing more frequent checkpoints as the years went on, because having to repeat the same sections of gameplay ad nauseam doesn't add to the challenge at all. If I've made it to the boss fight, I have proven that I can get to the boss fight, there's absolutely no good reason for me to have to go back and repeat the sections I've already beaten again. It gets to the point that I can get through these sections without even taking damage so by that point it's pure filler. That's what it is, filler. This doesn't make the game more challenging, it just pads the whole thing out. A simple level and a boss that is supposed to just take a few minutes, turns into an hour. I bet that if you know what you're doing and you don't die at all, this is roughly an hour long game, probably even less, so I think the devs are full of crap and they only made up an excuse to pad the game out or to pretend it's "hardcore". The game itself isn't even that hard, it's just tedious because you have to beat the same sections over and over again. I wouldn't be complaining about this if the game was ACTUALLY FAIR, it is full of little sections that have trial and error, little bits that catch you off guard or they're designed in such a way that you would have no idea how to beat them first time through; traps that are just out of the corner of your vision, things you can't react to, making mistakes because the jumping controls are downright atrocious, a lot of deaths won't even be your fault if you're good at the game, and when you die you are sent back to the last checkpoint.
I have finished games that are infinitely harder than Volgarr, like Gothic. That game is brutally difficult and it has a full-on save system. Serious Sam games are way harder, full on save system. Guys, there's no such thing as "save scumming" because you still need to be good at the game in order to get passed a certain section, you can mash that quicksave key as much you want but you're not getting through that section unless you're actually good. There's no good reason to have such a stingy and atrocious checkpoint system. Either the devs just wanted to pad the ever living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of their game or they aren't confident in their game's challenge.
It's a damn shame because I want to continue playing this game but it's so ♥♥♥♥ing tedious and infuriating having to play through the same sections over and over again that I just don't even want to bother with it. What there is, is a lot of fun, but you're gonna stop thinking that when you play those "fun" parts for the millionth time.
All I'm asking for are checkpoints at the start of a boss fight for ♥♥♥♥'s sake.
