Note: I didn't give this game a thumbs down because it was bad. I personally enjoyed this game. I only gave it a thumbs down because I don't recommend this to anyone who has no idea what they're actually playing. If you are aware of what's actually in store, buy it!
This game is about exploring an island and solving line puzzles. That's it!
The game is very creative with it's puzzles. You immediately start the game with no menu, it just loads up and you solve the first set of puzzles. Once you've done the first area, you are free to explore the island and solve the puzzles. The game introduces you to this complicated puzzle with different types of puzzle features you haven't seen before. This gives the player the idea that he can't solve this puzzle. You see two sets of puzzles with the two puzzle features in the previous puzzle which you use to solve it. Some puzzles use the environment like one in a desert temple or a monastery where you use the patterns and trees to guide yourself to solve the puzzles. However when I finished the desert temple, I stumbled across the quarry area where there were these tetris pieces which I had no ♥♥♥♥ing clue how to solve. The game doesn't tell you which areas to go to first. The tetris pieces are introduced to the player well in the marsh area.
This game fails to guide the player how to do things. Players are left to figure things out for themselves which is where things fall flat. Areas that I did enjoy were The Keep and The Mountain and the Monastery.

This isn't just a game, it's a masterpiece.
No trailer or gameplay video can explain it, because the genius of the game isn't a story, or gameplay, it's the feeling it gives the player when playing, you can't communicate that.
Unique puzzles, unrivalled in design and polished to perfection.
I don't think I can pick out a flaw.
Sure, there will be parts some people don't like, but everything in here is intentional, there are no mistakes.
The game took 8 years to make by a very talented development team.
There is no game that is like this, and there will never be a sequel.
I wish I could wipe my memories and play through it again, as it's not the same the 2nd time through, when you know how everything works.
What I can say is that it's not for everyone.
It's for people that like solving puzzles, that don't mind getting stuck on a problem and having to come back to it hours or days later when you've had time to think, giving up for now and walking to a different part of the island.
There's no handholding, and do yourself a favour, and don't look at walkthroughs, the beauty of this is about the "ah hah!" epiphany moments, trial and error, testing and learning, scientific method to a puzzle you've never encountered before,
with no instructions or, well any text whatsoever in the game.
You'll become an expert, be tested to your cognitive limits with harder and harder puzzles and a crazy time trial.
Then you'll be done with the game, and you'll never encounter this format of puzzle again, and maybe never play a game that has this much thought put in to it either.

The Witness is based on a mysterious and philosophical island not filled whith puzzles, but filled with lessons and challenges for you to face and reflect on. The aesthetic is simple and pleasing, allowing for a walk through beautiful landscapes scattered throughout. Find yourself at peace in this enormous journey for you to embark.

Do you play games to have fun or enjoy your time? If you answered 'yes', then skip this game. The Witness is NOT a fun game (unlike Portal). The puzzles are arbritrary, there are several rules to each of the different puzzles you have to discover yourself, which requires a lot of trial and error, and research.
I cannot recommend this game to ANYONE because it is simply not fun. But if you want to feel aggreviated, challenged, then feel free to pick this up.

- The voice acting is alright with a plentiful amount of cheeseiness, so if you like people hamming up their voices this game is for you.

- The puzzles are abismal. I did not even get SLIGHTLY stuck on a single puzzle and I'm not even that clever. So if random mazes and dot to dots are your thing then enjoy.
- For a 'detective game' Detective Grimoire is not smart with ANY of its gameplay mechanics. Most of the deductive reasoning comes from basic slot puzzles that can be finished with simple trial and error giving absolutely no feeling of accomplishment when completed.
- All characters in the game can be indivisually summarised with one word each. What you see is what you get for their personalities and if you like tropes then it is chocablock with them from pompous rich guy to hippie stoner dude. Don't expect to remember their names after playing.
If you're missing a couple of chromosomes or are an unborn fetus this game might be just the right challenge for you, but anyone else will see this game as a boring slog to the finish line wasting your time along the way.

Not gonna lie, enjoyed it more than I thought I would. It has a decent story with interesting characters and funny dialogue. It's not exactly the best, but it's not horrible. The gameplay is a homage to titles like Phoenix Wright and Professor Layton (albeit with a LOT less puzzles and more just questioning the characters about literally everything).
The music is amazing, and the background art is gorgeous. It was refreshing to have a point-and-click that was not only visually pleasing, but also atmospheric, upbeat, and pleasant to he ears despite the fact that you're solving a murder.
However, that's not to say that this is the perfect casual mystery. The game is silly sometimes and it's not very challenging (probably because I feel like this was partially meant to market towards kids). I mean, you're in a swamp trying to solve the murder of the owner of a tourist attraction and you don't even know if the murderer even exists. Hell it wouldn't take anyone long to 100% this game because it's so simple. There's no replay value.
But if you're looking for a short and decent casual point-and-click with witty dialogue then give this a go. It's worth the money.

When I initially started playing this game, I became very frustrated as it is really a difficult game to master in the beginning even on the easiest difficulty.  One miscalculation and all of your hard work will be for nothing.  However, if you can get past this early point before you acheive self-sufficiency (which there is actually two levels of this; the first being basic where you can survive in the meantime and the second where you ensure your base will be truly self-sufficient).  It is important to monitor everything closely because things can go crazy real quick and this can lead to catastrohic failure for your colony.  Overall, this is an absolutely amazing game which I have already spent dozens of hours playing.  It is especially neat to see your small colony of only 7 people eventually turn into a burgeoning colony of hundreds of people plus robots and visitors.
If you are on the fence about this game, then just go ahead and buy it.  I am not saying it is perfect (as my below comments make clear), but it is still great fun and you will get tens of hours out of it, easy.
*FOR THE DEVELOPERS*: If you read this review, there are a couple of things I would like to say and I realize that you are of the belief that this game is finished.
First off, I really think you should reconsider being finished.  I would like to see some additional buildings to help with ensuring variety of gameplay which is important for replay.
I would also be interested in seeing the ability to build tunnels through rock formations.  That is defnitely something which can be annoying especially if you spawn in a bad place.
I would also reccomend that you improve the AI system.  As it stands, the AI seems very basic.  It tends to lack basic logic which is part of what makes the game so ridculously hard.  It would also be good if the people could actually interact with one another.  All of this would help enhance the realism of the game.
Finally, I would love to see greater variety of available planets.  And, I do not necessarily mean that the planets should be more difficult just different to mix up the scenery.  Maybe even have different gameplay options based off the selected planet.  An ocean world, perhaps?
FInally, I would like the ability to name my saves, the current save system is VERY tedious.
I know what I am asking is a fairly good amount but I think it would make the game that much better and so I hope that you opt to strive to make the game the best it can be and not settle for just good enough.
However, with all this being said, let me take the time to say what an amazing job you all did.  This is perhaps the best game of its kind I have ever played!  A very great effort indeed!

Enjoyable little arcade shooter, but needs work to give it staying power past an hour or two.
Currently, Sky Rogue is in alpha. This gets you: a single level, a small cluster of islands in the middle of the ocean. Not a lot, admittedly. The landmass in the middle of the ocean might be randomly generated between waves; I didn't pay enough attention to tell you if they were. At the start of play, you're given an objective or objectives ("HANGAR", "2 COMMAND", "3 AWACS" etc), and you customize your plane and weapon loadout to suit your needs. You start with a single plane with three basic weapons, but upon subsequent deaths you unlock more weapons and planes in what seems to be some hidden slot machine mechanic.
You then launch from your skybound aircraft carrier, blow up designated targets, and then fly back to the carrier to end the "Day," the game's designation for waves.  The game ups you to the next day, with harder enemies and more objectives. You're given the chance to reconfigure your aircraft before the next mission. Fairly simple.
The game's strength lies in its tight control scheme. Controls are responsive; your sci-fi jet fighter, obedient. Those who have played Ace Combat will feel instant familiarity, though the traditional button to change targets in AC is, in Sky Rogue, the button to swap weapons. I suffered several rounds of accidentally cycling through my weapons before I had the good sense to change the key bindings on my 360 gamepad. Chasing down enemy fighters, dodging missiles, and swerving out of the way of enemy AWACS tumbling out of the sky is a treat, particularly for those of us longing for Namco to revive the AC franchise.
There are some downsides that make Sky Rogue tough to recommend. For one, you're locked into a single, uninteresting map. After a few rounds, I was desperate for something—ANYTHING—different than green clumps surrounded by blue water. Second, the music. Rather, the song. There is a single tune that accompanies you in the air, a chiptune throwback to the SNES era. It's highly reminisicent of a Starfox tune, and while it starts out catchy it soon becomes irksomely repetitive.
Last, and most important, is the unfortunate fact that most the mission objectives are a chore. If the game is feeling charitable, it might throw a couple AWACS planes your way. Chasing down the AWACS and their fighter escorts is fast and tense—one might forget they weren't playing Ace Combat for a minute. Sadly, the common objectives are fortified ground targets, buildings that take many, many passes with anti-ground ordinance to destroy. From Day 3 onwards, these ground objectives are surrounded by long-range SAM sites, making carpet bombing from above the ideal tactic. This is exceptionally boring, as it requires you to line up your shots with an insufferable slow targeting reticle that shrinks when your plane is not pitching or yawing, and then turn around and repeat the process multiple times. Worse, as you'll have brought an aircraft built around bombing and not air-to-air intercept for these, you'll be at the AI's mercy when it throws its higher level fighters at you.
The game is in Early Access, but there's the rub: as we've seen over and over the past couple years, there's no guarantee that an EA game will ever progress beyond its current alpha form.  After a couple hours of play, I was stuck with the feeling, "Is that all there is?" I tend to play Ace Combat on Ace difficulty, and it does not take long for me to reach the point where I can progress no further in Sky Rogue. I hit my inevitable death after passing by for my fourth bombing run of a target, get tossed back to the beginning, and it feels like something's missing. Variety, perhaps. Or maybe I'm missing the fun. There's a game in here somewhere that I very much enjoy and very much want to play more of, but it's locked behind uninteresting, ultimately futile bombing missions on an unintersting group of islands in the middle of an uinteresting sea. Ultimate, Sky Rogue strikes me as one of those games that comes inside another game as a distraction or Easter egg, not a retail product.
Perhaps the game will expand, but perhaps not. This is Early Access, after all, where nothing is certain. I would not hedge my bets on the game making good on its implicit promise of scratching that itch we feel for a good arcade flight game, and cannot, therefore, in good conscience recommend this game. If you are absolutely desperate to feel the thrill of the Ace Combat games, wait for a sale. Yes, it's only $10, but you should still wait for a sale.
I also hear that a PS2 emulator will play AC4 just fine, so there's that.

VA-11 Hall-A looks great. The pixel-art is consistent, colorful and atmospheric. Mostly, you will see your bar from behind the counter, as you've probably noticed by looking at the screenshots. The interface takes a majority of the screen. That means, at times the little screen you have left is quite busy while you feel like there is a lot of room that could be used elsewhere. This does, however, support the technoid feel of the game. It is a world reigned by computers, cyborgs and megacorps after all. Like it or not, the artist clearly knew what he was doing. The sprites are a bit of a hit and miss. Some look downright awesome, others have small problems with their anatomy and can look kind of weird. All of them are mostly static - the mouth is the only thing moving most of the time.
I only wished there were more scenes that do not play behind the counter - when Jill, the protagonist, leaves her comfort zone and the game changes to different interfaces (sometimes with unique minigames) and backgrounds. Those scenes are few and far between, and offer a welcome change from VA-11 Hall-A's monotonous design. Jill's apartment, which you visit between each workday, is gorgeous. You can customize it in every conceivable way, while playing and surfing around with Jill's tablet. It is a wonderful change of pace and serves greatly as a breather between the long passages in the bar.
The aesthetic of the game is largely carried by it's Cyberpunk feel and it's music. The tracks are very varied, from brooding Ambient-sounds that remind me of musical projects such as 2184, over instrumental pop to pumping and upbeat electro-tracks. You can most of the time choose yourself what is played in the bar-owned jukebox. The design of the game clearly showcases that the developers are into Science-Fiction and Cyberpunk culture and -media. Everything feels authentic and just what you would want and expect from a game like this.
Apart from managing your money (and some monetary goals you have to reach to get a nice ending for Jill are actually quite hard to get, so don't mess up mixing your drinks) the majority of the time will be spent talking to the various customers of VA11 Hall-A. Their stories range from funny to downright moving, depending who you have in front of you. The atmosphere of the entire game changes depending on which character you are interacting with; a testament how greatly varied the different personas in the game are. I liked every single one of them, and won't get into any more detail, since they are the meat of the game and should be experienced by the player.
Speaking of the player; looming over all those personal stories is some kind of main arc, involving you main character and an old friend. Let's just say: it is luckily not what you would expect from most visual novels. There is no sappy romance, so unnecessary sex, no cheap emotional punch, just an authentic, almost everyday story that could very well leave you in tears in the end. If you usually avoid this genre for fear of the aforemented cliches, give VA-11 Hall-A a spin. It really tries to be different in this regard. The writing itself won't win the Nobel Prize of Literature, but it is good enough. It never felt artificial, and the dialogue flows well. Sure, the devs are not Hemingway, but easily on par with most other video-games.
Certainly a matter of taste are the various influences on current pop- and internet-culture that are spread around the game. I for one loved them, but I can see how they can be turn-off for some, so I will address them here. You will deal with streamers, you will hear some inside-jokes, serve drinks in fedoras to slimy, fat men and even surf on a weird bizarro-cyberpunk-imageboard. It is important to note that those references are indeed noticeable, but very well integrated in the world VA11-Hall-A presents. They don't take too much room and if you can stand them, just swallow them.
After all is said and done, there is little that can be added without talking too much about the plot. VA11 Hall-A is a portrait of a city, it's about it's problems and the lifes of it's inhabitants. It's about normal people dealing with their demons, with their passions and families in a dystopian world. VA11 Hall-A is not new in this regard, there have been many Science-Fiction classics doing similar things; it is, however, almost unheard of in our new media. I can not recommend this fresh and new take on Science-Fiction enough. 15 bucks might be a little steep for some, so if you can not swallow the price for something that takes roughly 10 hours to finish and serves little to no real gameplay, wait for a sale and buy it then. If you can identify with the virtues of the game, you won't regret it.
I still can't decide whether I want this game to stay under the radar, or if I want it to become more popular. Quite the dilemma.

I don't really like Visual Novels (like, at all), but I'll make an exception for this one. The entire "game" had me glued to my seat until the end. I'll be doing another... uhh, "playthrough" soon just to see the other endings.
It's a nice little story you can read through when you've got nothing to do. If you're going in expecting some deep gameplay mechanics, you're probably gonna be disappointed, but that should've been obvious already. The bartending thing adds a nice little twist to the usual "choose-your-own-adventure book" thing that VNs usually have (not that I would know, this is pretty much the only one I've actually "played").
My favorite thing about the game is how you don't actually need to give people the drinks they ordered. I won't spoil anything, but giving people certain drinks can have different effects on the story/endings or just the amount of exposition you'll get out of them in general. I'm pretty sure I've gotten some people unintentionally drunk too (there are obvious visual cues), which lead to some amusing dialogue. I would highly suggest against reading a guide because in my opinion, it'll ruin most of the experience (at the very least go through it blind for the first playthrough). It adds quite a bit of replayability, which is pretty surprising considering the kind of game this is.
As for the soundtrack, it's amazing. I guess I'm a bit biased because I'm a huge fan of cyberpunk and synthwave, but really, the soundtrack is just great. Even better that you can customize the jukebox every time you start your shift.
Overall, I would totally recommend VA-11 HALL-A. If you still feel like it won't be worth your money, pick it up when it's on sale. The devs did a good job, they deserve the support! :)

VA-11 Hall-A does so many things so incredibly right that you feel those that it doesn't do so well more keenly.
Pros:
+ Interesting characters with fleshed out personalities and backstories
+ Well-written story and dialogue that rarely got boring, there's always something to learn
+ A healthy sense of mystery, like you won't ever know all there is to know
+ Simple, relaxing gameplay: the game never demands all that much of you and its simplicity reinforces its role as a backdrop for the story, in the same way drinks act as the catalyst of interaction between an actual bartender and their patrons
+ Kickin' soundtrack, has some solid variety and sets the tone very well oftentimes
+ Not too short, not too long
Cons:
- You wish you had a chance to interact more with the characters and know them better
- The game creates so many mysterious loose ends and touches relatively few of them
- The simplicity of the gameplay highlights a few odd little additions that don't work as well sometimes
- Ends perhaps too abruptly
My thoughts: 9/10
Halfway through this VN I was blown away but what I'd found. It gave me a very positive experience in which I felt the pros far outweighed the cons, and I would say that it is now one of my favorites. I was prepared to award a higher score, except that the VN ends rather unexpectedly. There was a definite feeling that it would keep going, and that left me feeling disappointed. That may just be me, but the amount of genuinely interesting storylines introduced throughout its duration can lose their appeal as mysterious and instead become clumsy-feeling if they aren't handled properly.
But even so, I love this game thoroughly and I would recommend it to anyone. Casual gamers can find what is essentially a book with some enhancing gameplay, while more serious players will find a story no worse than some of the best out there, and perhaps a chance to relax a bit. Definitely buy this game, especially if it is on sale. I don't regret it a bit. I'm very interested to see what if anything Sukeban Games does after this, for they have earned my attention.

Detectie Grimoire is a cute point and click mystery adventure game which centeres around a murder in a swamp "tourist attraction". The visuals are very charming, as well as the music and overall atmosphere. The story was very simple, but it was still enjoyable to run around and talk to all of the suspects and their distinct personalities. It's short and sweet, and worth the time if you need a change of pace and 2 hours to kill.
However, the biggest gripe I have with this game is the very mystery/detective aspect of it. Despite this game being classed as a "detective" game--the amount of sleuthing you do is almost absent. You have a couple of puzzles to solve (around 5 I believe) which even a two year old child could figure out. If you're used to Proffessor Layton-esque puzzles or even Sherlock Holmes ones, these come off as incredibly flat and just plain disappointing. Of course, I wasn't expecting anything too complex puzzle wise but it felt incredibly lazy and just "thrown in". Even when questioning the suspects further and unlocking "challenges" to further the investigation; everything was incredibly clean cut and straightforward. No mystery, zilch, nada. Once you've pretty much questioned most of the suspects (first 45 minutes through the game or so), it's incredibly clear who is the murderer. You spend the rest of your time racking up evidence and showing this evidence to the suspects (most of which don't even have an opinion of it) to progress the story. The "detective" aspect of this game isn't fun at all, and I found myself being more intrigued in the characters than solving the murder mystery.
Though my commentary is quite harsh regarding the "detective" aspect of it, I wasn't expecting any of the mystery to be truly spectacular or mind boggling. I went in with the understanding that this was going to be a casual detective game, and didn't expect much from it. However, even that low expectation wasn't reached and you'd be off better playing a free mobile detective game honestly. The game itself is very charming, but again, if you are going to create a *mystery detective* game--I would develop and refine those aspects of the game instead of releasing something which feels half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥

Detective Grimoire takes a bit from the Ace Attorney series and adds in its own gameplay mechanism, which are sadly not well explained and could be left unused, to make a pretty good detective game with a muddling ending.
Visually I really liked the fluidity of the animations, they may have been repetitive, but they felt natural to the characters. That said the game has all the earmarks of a flash game.  It definitely feels like it could have been released online instead of on Steam.
As for the gameplay itself, it is very similar to Ace Attorney’s investigation gameplay (not the court room).  Go around talking to people, pick up evidence and find ways to open up new conversations with suspects.  The issue is there is even more to it than that, and it doesn’t illustrate how to use it.  I was expecting a standard point and click, but there’s actually a note system, a suspicion system, and map that details completion of each section.  You get a screen with about a dozen icons on it and no alternative hover text to tell you what they are.  This game really needed a tutorial case because I got to nearly the end of the game before even knowing some of those things existed.
Speaking of that, the game gives the impression that they may have wanted to do more cases, but only one case is included. There is a place to go and “lab testing” but it becomes pointless by the end, you only test for 1 substance and the test itself is laughable.
Okay but aside from all that. It’s actually a really good game. It includes some lock puzzles, it requires some searching and maintain cognizance of what’s going on in the game. The ending is a little lack luster but overall a detailed and fairly well developed story. Biggest issue with the ending is that it’s kind of obvious who the bad guy is long before you get to the end.
Overal, Detective Grimoire is a pretty decent game that could have used either pairing down of unnecessary extras that were included or a detail tutorial chapter and gameplay change to make them useful.

I'm not one to give many negative reviews on games, especially ones that I have invested a significant about of time, but for this particular game it deserves not to be recommended for a few of the following reasons, and I will do my best to remain as objective as possible without going overboard.
When starting out, it is extremely helpful to start out with the tutorial, which does a nice job of explaining and walking you through the how-to. (+1)
Now it's time to get started on your own, the real deal as it were. Yes, it does take a few times to get the hang of the game because you would expect there to be some additional logic involved in your people's activities, but no, that is not the case. I've seen situations where the airlocks are queued up with robots and then colonists die because the robots won't get out of the way of the humans. Maybe they just need a little robottie door? (-1)
Eventually you'll start to go through the various milestones in the game as you expand your base, cultivate the land as it were, and allow for the space traveling people to stop by for a break. These milestones were a bit of a double edge because on one hand, this is great, but at the same time, 300 people? It seems a little conflicting because the game instructions say that increases in populations decrease morale and also large populations as well, so wouldn't a 300 base population really bring down morale, even if you have the required resources? (-1)
In terms of the variety of things to do in the base for your people, they are pretty much on auto pilot from the player. I understand that this is space survival and management based system, but I feel like there should be other things that the player could do, such as set up an auto trader for passing ships, maybe make a guest only area of the base, restricted access, etc. Just something to help add another level of activity for the player, although this could be more annoying then helpful, but at the same time, variety in the events that we can tackle in space. The people that are trying to survive on the base have to have variety as well. (-1)
Overall, I enjoyed the experience I had with this game. My main issues with this game is how broken it is and by broken, I mean looking at the community guides and seeing that they already have guides on how to tweak the save files. So in theory, anyone should be able to complete this game 100%, if you edit the save files just right. That being said, if you are the kind of gamer who also know how to edit files and wants a decent experience, I wouldn't recommend this game for you given the price. However, if you are the kind of gamer who wants a game to kind of help pass the time at work, this would be a good way to pass the time as it would keep you engaged.
That's my two cents on this game, but ultimately, the choice is yours whether to buy it or not, but I will advise you to throughly look around the community guide section of this game and just browse the guides to see what you are going to be playing. To be honest, that statement alone is more objective than my review. What you see on the game's community page will help you in making a decision.

So right off the bat, Cities XXL is not substantially different from its predecessor (Cities XL). In my time with the game so far, I've only encountered two new features. Everything else, right down to the buildings available and the game interface, are unchanged. XXL hardly deserves to be called a sequel or sold as a new game. It's a content patch, and not even a very good one.
When I first started playing Cities XL a few years ago, I was really impressed with it. I hadn't really played any modern city-builder games since SimCity 4, and so the jump to 3-D graphics, the ability to draw curved roads, and the sheer size of the maps was enough to win me over initially. But as I've played the game more, it's limitations and weaknesses have become much more apparent and hard to ignore. This is especially true in the game's interface and controls, which are very rough and full of nagging annoyances. When compared to the much smoother and organic controls of games like Tropico 5, the modern [disastrous] SimCity reboot, and even older games like Caesar IV, Cities XL really starts to look bad.
The biggest deterrent to enjoying Cities XL is its UI and controls. There's nothing that really single-handedly breaks the game, but there's a cacaphony of small, nagging problems that gradually wear down your resolve to play the game. The first thing that you'll notice is the ugly and disorganized interface. There are buttons and widgets floating all over the screen: build icons, overlay toggles, camera control widgets, zoning sub-controls, and so on. You can customize some of the UI elements by dragging them to different places on the screen, but there is no arrangement that really feels comfortable.

I can't say I've ever played a game like Hero of the Kingdom. It's something of an adventure game that gives you a birds-eye view of your surroundings and progresses through some simple mouse clicks. I have a hard time reviewing Hero of the Kingdom, because it's so forgetable. On the other hand, it is quite an enjoyable time-killer.
Let me explain. Hero of the Kingdom is about a young man whose farm is burned to the ground--forcing him to journey out into the world to survive. From there the story becomes generic in almost every sense of the word. You'll fight skeletons, beasts and goblins before eventually taking on a dark wizard. While I can see that a lot of love went into this game, the writing could definitely be more original.
The gameplay involves a lot of trading. You'll essentially be roaming around the various areas searching for items to sell or animals to hunt so you can get gold with which you can purchase supplies you need to further the story. While I played quite a bit of the game several months ago (I don't remember how long I played, but I remember accidently leaving the game running for a while, so my time played is off) and I didn't manage to get myself to finish it until a couple days ago. For me, the concept of constantly trading like in Hero of the Kingdom becomes tedious. Especially when you unlock every area of the game and it gets tough remembering where certain merchants and points of interest are.
I'm afraid I can't give any input on the sound. It wasn't long into the game until I just played my own music over it. Despite all of this, I'm still recommending it. This game is a great time sink. While it did repetitive after a while, the first hours were pretty entertaining. It was actually rather fulfilling to trade my way up to the items I needed. While it's just not a game for me, I can definitely see Hero of the Kingdom appealing to fans of the genre. It was certainly a good time sink for me if nothing else.

I remember playing ROSE back in its open beta days.  I played the heck out of this game back when I was a kid and had nothing better to do.  ROSE ties with Silkroad for my most nostalgic MMO's. The grind is heavy (used to be much worse) and the economy is pretty terrible but is certainly reminiscent of any older MMO's where economies were generally left unchecked.  With most MMO's there a clear dividing line of prosperity between players.  So why do I recommend this game?  If you can get passed the old school MMO aesthetics, you're going to be able to find a ton of enjoyment from it.  It's a simple MMO with simple goals.  You may or may not sink thousands of hours into ROSE, but the time you spend in it should give you lasting memories.  How you look at it is up to you.

text: ROSE Online is my favourite MMORPG of all time and will probably be for the rest of my life. Of course, it most likely won't be for practically anyone who will play this game in this day and age, because the strengths of this MMORPG to new players now only revolves around the history and idea that it is a classic. If you played this game in it's prime, you would feel totally immersed in the world of ROSE and probably never forget the ride. It really felt like an adventure. An adventure that made me believe that this game would might aswell be a RPG that loved me in it's world. There are plenty reasons why this game would irritate, annoy or even anger an audience of modern gamers through it's art style, UI, stability and overall simple gameplay, but considering that this game was a free-to-play (not pay to win) MMORPG that was introduced at the time when the World of Warcraft began, it really was a nolstagic game that contained plenty of down-to-earth players that at the end of the day, you would never see again. I have picked up and dropped this game HEAPS of times and everytime I remember what made my weekends an adventure. I'm not saying it will make any of you feel that way, or if you will even get by 10 minutes of this game without poking fun at it for being last generation, but sadly, it is what it is and if you cannot accept that this game was one of the best in it's time than you haven't REALLY experienced the vast worlds of MMORPGs. This game ties with Dragonica on my favourites list and I would love to play it again, but year by year the community dies. Out of the several hundred hours I've poored into this game during my childhood, I've never regretted it one bit. I'm not telling you to try it or waste your time on a game that you won't ever enjoy, but atleast respect this game for what it is or even what it was. If you do try it, I reccommend downloading it from the main client. Seriously though, LISTEN TO THE SOUNDTRACK!

I've played this for a while now and wanted to leave my thoughts. I've only played till tier 9. If you try the game yourself you'll soon figure out the goods about this game.
A bunch of different PvE maps, quite a lot actually, then the skirmish PvP and PvE has some fun maps too, the matchmaking at this point is really balanced as far as I remember it. At tier 7 you can start exploring open space, so there's a lot to see. Also imo shooting, moving and general gameplay is really fun. The core game is great but there's a bunch of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t letting it down.
First of the PvE skirmish/Co-op, player matchmaking seems to be 1-5 | 6-10 but the enemy AI spawns 1-3 | 4-6 | 7-9 | 10-12. If everyone in your team is tier 6 except for 1 guy who is tier 9, every enemy AI will spawn at 10-12 with some tier 8 destroyers. Which means a tier 6 ship can meet a tier 12 which will insta kill him. Even by tier 9 command, which is semi tanky, can get killed under 2 seconds by 1 guard only shooting his lasers. If it wasn't for this, and the fact that it's so easy to change, I'd not think this game mode is bad at all because the maps and game modes are fun imo. This mode has a lot of potential too.
I do play quite some missions PvE, Interesting and fun at first, but it's static without variation (no random spawn location, or variables in what spawns, when or anything at all) and there's a few locations on some maps that makes it too easy. I noticed a quite new map though, it replaces the old level 1 map and moves the old map to level 3. The new map however is way too hard for newbies and should probably be a late map. The rest of the maps I've played are too easy for most part and you can do all maps with only 2 ships. This is because you 2 shot small ships with guns like the singularity one. Every map except the new level 1 map are all exactly as easy to play. No difficulty progression. (I've not played the last maps as I only played with tier 9 as highest.)
Open world: Lots of open space with some rocks, more space rock and some broken buildings, some cool alien stuff, it's alright. What bothers me is that it feels unfinished, 1 area the mobs are really easy, the next you have giant alien ships that shoots giant balls at you but so far it's actually not much harder. Then next map you have the same giant aliens but this time they also have 1 scout. The thing is, the scout has more hp, shield, does more damage, and gives less points. Why tho? I will never know.
PvP + summary: I can't recommend it. It's okay, at first but the more you progress, the less you wanna continue on the same maps over and over. PvP queues are very long compared to the rest so you might not play a lot of it. When it starts a game it's usually only 1-2 players in each team and because of this the rest is filled up with bots, imo it feels way less empty obviously, but it's kinda a bot game. It's a little fun to me, like the master of puppets 1v1, but like the other things, it gets dull after a while. Also seeing how expensive the dlcs are and people complaining about their tier 15's being useless against op stuff I wouldn't recommend anyone to put their money into the game because it's simply too expensive, maybe they start releasing cheaper content making more ppl buy it. Play if you like, but I can't recommend you to try it out because there's a lot of options out there that do a similar thing.

This early access game offers some of the best arcade dogfighting I've experienced, but I'm even more impressed by how remarkably well-balanced the missions are. Missions objectives generally consist of destroying static targets surrounded by defenses like AA guns and SAM sites. In early missions you can dodge or ignore defenses and take out targets directly, but it soon becomes necessary to remove layers of defense before you can attack targets without being blown apart by a hail of missiles. You can return to base to repair your plane or switch to a different plane or loadout, allowing you to specialize for the current phase of the mission, but spawners---carriers in the air and aerodromes on the ground---pose an interesting complication, since you need to balance your capability to destroy the aircraft they're launching and the spawner itself.
There are multiple effective strategies. For dispatching enemy aircraft you can outfit a maneuverable craft with fast, short-range missiles and engage in topsy-turvy dogfights, but with too many foes in the mix you'll inevitably take some hits, and maneuverable planes aren't so durable. Or you can put long-range missiles in a fast interceptor, outrun your enemies, and be the ultimate jouster, but this isn't as expedient as close-in dogfirghting and you might not be able to destroy enemies as fast as a spawner produces them. Or can try to make an all-around fighter that's decent at all three of dogfighting, ranged anti-air, and bombing, and hope you're still nimble enough to win dogfights. Yes, you can switch planes mid-mission, but if you're being pursued by a faster enemy you might not survive the trip back to base. Ground targets can also be taken out multiple ways: bombed from altitude, dive-bombed, or strafed with rockets, guns, and cannons.
It only takes a few hours to unlock almost all the planes and items, giving you a wide variety of loadouts and strategies to experiment with, and 14 hours in I'm still uncovering new strategies for getting to later missions. Excellent work, Fractal Phase.

I love this genre, I've been playing it for 20+ years, and you can trust me when I tell you to avoid this mess of a game.  If you need more than my word on it, read on.
First of all, the Unreal Engine was not built for 2D sidescrolling platforming run-and-gun games; the controls feel floaty and unresponsive and the physics (which only really come into play when you ragdoll on death) are glitchy as all get out.
The level design is uninspired and tedious and boring and repetitive and insipid and samey and dull.
The difficulty can best be described as "Ghouls and Ghosts", in that you will often be one-shot by things before you have time to react or before you can line up a shot due to the locked 8-way fire with no bullet-drop. And then, eventually, you run into the end-of-level boss, which is usually some sort of large factory machinery for some reason (Imagine an autonomous forklift from the year 2100), and the battle is either over in an instant or takes ten tries, with nothing in between.
And if you manage to power your way through this travesty long enough to encounter the enemies with grenade launchers (which is a clone of a powerup that you can acquire), BEWARE, because the hit detection on explosions is insultingly off, to the point where you'll ragdoll across the screen dead because a grenade blew up and the very edge of the smoke particle effect was a solid 5-feet away from you.

I like this game a lot. It's fun and engaging and makes for rewarding--and also punishing--gameplay. The main task is keeping your colonists alive, which can be a serious pain sometimes. The start of the level is critical, and you need to carefully distribute your resources to different buildings right away, otherwise you will find your colonists dying from dehydration, hunger, sleep deprivation or asphyxiation within the first 10 minutes. After several tries and fails, I got the hang of it and managed to expand my base across almost the entire seeded map on one playthrough, with a population somewhere in the many hundreds.
I think the trading system needs a complete overhaul. You should be able to broadcast purchase orders and have them delivered to your base, rather than the "[random] trading ship has docked" system that they have now. I think more food and leisure, and building options would be nice to implement in a future expansion, as well. And I would like to be able to assign sleeping quarters to particular staff, because currently they will sleep wherever the closest bed is when their sleep need reaches critical, which can be far away from where you want them working if you aren't careful in your layout.
Speaking of layouts--there needs to be a more effective way of changing locations of your buildings. Currently the game only allows you to deconstruct one building, and reconstruct another in a different location. This is a VERY long process since first the building needs to be removed, then all the worker's needs need to be met (which in itself takes awhile) until they can begin construction on the new building. And in-between that time they may need to exit the base to retrieve the dropped resources one-by-one to put them in storage and use them in the construction of the new building.
That brings to to one last request: changes to the random map seed.
--I think the maps are really cool, actually. They have the atmosphere and design to them that makes you really feel like you're on another planet. But the multitude of rocks/hills makes constructing a base in the layout that you want extremely difficult. There should be a slider option to adjust the amount of "open terrain" on the map, promoting more growth and development. The terrain shouldn't be flat and devoid of scenery, but it should be slightly customizable. I find myself starting games over and over and over again just to recycle the seed until I find an open-ish map that I can work with. <--This is a nitpicky suggestion but one that would go a long way towards replayability, I think.
Alternatively there could be some kind of terraforming option (possibly even mining protruding rock for metals), thereby flattening an area of terrain.
Despite these suggestions for improvement, don't misunderstand. This is a well polished game which I have enjoyed very much and which I have gotten my money's worth out of so far already, and I see even more replayability in the future. Hopefully updates will continue to come on a regular basis, providing more content and extending that replayability even further.

Planetside is what you’ll google when looking for Planetbase.
Planetbase is a base building game. You land a few people and robots on a hostile planet and get to work building your base. Oxygen generators, Biodomes, Dorms and everything else you might need to survive this harsh environment. Besides the lack of food, water, oxygen and building materials you will be bothered by meteoroids, sand storms, solar flares and later assaults. It’s up to you to create a second home for your people.
Planetbase is a very calming game. I usually don’t use the speed controls in games like these so what could have been a 30 min session turns into a few hours. But I find watching your people move around the base like little ants very enjoyable. There is a good amount of challenge, especially in the beginning trying to keep up with food and lack of energy but as you get the hang of things the game becomes easier and lets make more mistakes or build in less than optimal way.
Being very calm game Planetside is also not very deep. Once you’re over the initial hurdle of establishing a colony there’s little you can to do screw up. There’s also not much point in expanding the base. Neither from the story perspective, of which there is none, nor from objectives. There is a few technologies to acquire by trading and a few milestones to achieve but it all feels a bit weak.
All in all Planetbase is a nice game that fills in that need for a calm game of watching something grow. It fuels my imagination of what if would be like living on a different planet.

In the interest of full disclosure, I got this game during the winter Steam sale for $1.39. To be honest, I think it definitely is worth full price but I am happy that I got this game basically at a steal.
To start off, I love the game's art style. It's got an almost storybook charm to its setting and world that I can't help but fawn over. The cuteness translates over to certain mechanics like making the titular detective draw out what he thinks is happening in his notebook complete with snarky little word bubbles like “I have a stupid nickname” to add character. The voice actors are great and if you're familiar with internet voice actors you might recognize Detective Grimoire's voice actor from the old Trapped series of flash games and the voice actor for Agent Folder from literally anything Arin Hanson has done. The actual mystery is pretty interesting but if you're anything like me, you'll call who did the murder right away. Regardless, I still really liked how suspenseful the story was and even though the actual murder didn't get me the side story does. I'm being intentionally vague here so as to not spoil anybody.
My only real issue is a mechanical one. In the beginning of the game there's a feature where you can switch to “walk mode” and go to different areas. I like the idea because I can examine everything I want without having to worry about clicking on a way out accidentally. However, a little under half way through the game, I had unlocked all the areas and was using the map feature to fast travel from place to place. I think the only times I even clicked on the walk mode button again were misclicks. But it wasn't challenging at all. I'm not saying that in a I'm-smarter-than-you-and-all-other-gamers way. I mean that the puzzles seem like they were made for kids: you match shapes of objects with shapes of holes; you mix blue and yellow liquid to get green liquid; all important words are in a different color font. I loved the animation style and Detective Grimoire, so I'd be willing to give a sequel another shot; but I can't recommend this game to adults. If you're under the age of 13 and enjoy point-and-click adventures: (1) you're awesome and (2) you SHOULD play this game.

It's been established that I like mystery adventure type games. And Detective Grimoire is just that, except maybe geared towards a younger audience. This is a bit different from what I'm accustomed playing because it lacks all the climax and thoughtful moments but who says all games have to be deep. Some can just be good fun. Would I recommend this to someone who enjoys a deep meaningful multi-layered, mind melting journey? Probably not. However, if they have a kid under the age of 14, just to give a grounded figure; I'd say this is one of the child friendly adventure games a kid can play.
I consider this a bit like the Professor Layton games, except very lite on the puzzle aspect. The game even makes a quip about the guy with the tall hat. Story wise you're looking at maybe 2 hours of murder mystery. Your main goal is to uncover as much information as possible by talking to people and finding clues. And while I didn't feel that much invested in the story it wasn't super easy to figure out who did it until nearing the very end. Finding the murderer took actual reading and thinking, which was good. There wasn't so much detail that you'd forget what you had to do.
The side puzzles were simple and sometimes Grimoire would go into what I'll call "create a sentence" mode. These were the main parts I had to really think about what clue I was trying to uncover or put together. In the end though it was a fun little game and as I said very family friendly so I'd definitely recommend it for younger gamers.

A short note: The Witness is not a game about line puzzles at its core, but spoiling what the game is really about would, well, spoil the game. This isn't to say the many line puzzles aren't interesting, each element of the puzzle language adds new constraints that cause you to approach puzzles differently, but once you know, it's clear that they're there to facilitate the true nature of the game, rather than an end unto themselves. This also explains why the game
to take place on its island, rather than just presenting the line puzzles on their own.
The Witness doesn't seem like it should be an exciting game, but it certainly was for me. I found each new element exciting with the possibilities for puzzles it added. I found finding solutions, which range from simple to devious, exciting and satisfying too, especially when I was convinced a puzzle was impossible to solve. And, of course, without spoiling it, something else is amazing if it hasn't been spoiled for you. You might play through all the line puzzles without experiencing it, though, so, oh well.

Cast of wonderfully quirky characters you end up caring about so hard; neat evasion of dystopian cliches to bring us a world of surprising depth and charm, and above all; sweet waifu bartending action.
Seriously, this is too good to be in the Visual Novel category.

As the name suggest, this game involves some bartender action, as you're Jill, a bartender. Jill works in a bar, mixing drinks for customers, listens to their stories, and of course, earns some cash, like an adult.
The gameplay itself is really simple, you listen to each character, make them a drink, and read some more dialog, nothing more, because it doesn't need anything more than that. As Jill said: "Time to mix drinks and change lives". You are the bartender, you make drinks, nothing more(of course you'll chat with customers, but there won't be any dialog to choose, everything's filled for you). Basically, all you have to do is to make a drink for your customers, depending on what they want.
To some people it will get repetitive quickly, yeah, sure, but if you decided to buy it, you are probably buying this game for its story, which is quite beautiful(so far, as I'm still playing it now).
The setting of the story is somewhat pretty, a dystopian city, and you're just a fellow citizen living your live, meeting different strangers every night, and everyone has their own story, and their stories are remarkable, I mean, I'm those who will forget a character's existence fast, but not this time, when a new character appears, I can remember them easily, even if my memory slipped a bit, I can still recall it. And during the interaction between Jill and customers, it's quite real, and it's like you are part of the story, rather than just a bystander, or just some self insert stuff.
Also there're some memes or jokes and stuff in the dialog, well it's kinda funny, it's a plus I think.
Now I wanna talk about Jill specifically. Maybe because I'm assuming the role of her, I like this character so much. However there's more reason behind that. Being the female protagonist, Jill isn't really the usual "cheering" waifu even she can change people's lives with her drinks, she's more like a calm, and with some sarcasm within her. And then I realized she's somewhat like me, like, I can relate to her. If she was real I believe we'd be smoking and drinking together, and sharing stories.
Overall a really really great game. And I just need to play it at 3am, and get myself some alcohol for the full experience.

You are Jill, a bartender. You as a player don't know about Jill and world around you anything, but Jill of course do so you will learn about life in Glitch City from talking with customers but also reading magazines and internet blogs. Talking with guests is a main part of the game. Some of them will become regulars, or even your friends. You will help them with their problems, talking about some random things and serve them drinks of course!
Serving drinks is the only way how you can change dialogues a bit. By serving correct drinks you can unlock different endings and secret lines. And correct doesn't always mean the drink your client wants. You can make some of your customers drunk by mixing more alcohol in the drink. There are many ways of manipulating story by serving drinks, but they are well hidden.
And what is the story about? Well, there are many threads, because every customer have it's own story to tell. You will learn about Alma's family, corporation where almost all of the workers are Corgis, Sei and Stella's friendship or Dorothy's sex toys. You will give advice to them how to solve their problems but in the end, you will need it from them. Characters and world around you are mysterious and well created so you won't be bored reading about them.
Graphics in the game really fit cyberpunk style. They are just pretty, what can I say more about pixel graphics. But a soundtrack... It's just a masterpiece. You can choose from many tracks at juckbox and all of them fit cyberpunk bar perfectly. It's worth buying this game for music only, really.

I usually enjoy hard games. Dark Souls, Super Meat Boy, Shovel Knight. And I grew up with platformers like this on the Genesis but this is bad. Not because it's hard but because its unfair in it's difficulty. There's only one checkpoint every level, and levels can be ten to fifteen minutes long, meaning if you at any point including right at the end, you get sent back to the very start.
Again, I'd like to stress that I'm not adverse to repeating the area until I get it right. I loved that about Dark Souls and Shovel Knight. But in those games, the checkpoints were frequent enough that you never felt like you'd lost too much. Just the sheer length you have to redo is not just irritating, it's tiring. I was just straight up bored after a dozen or so deaths whereas with the previously mentioned games I never felt bored because the goal was always in sight.
The controls also feel sluggish and awkward. The jumpings slow and a challenge in itself to get right. I found sometimes just trying to jump onto a slim platform was harder than anything else. Plus your character moves, turns and fights like he's just dove into a pool of water wearing ten layers of clothing.
There's also some major BS in the level designs. Some jumps are intentionally too big for you to make without using a spear and you won't know until you fall in and lose the fifteen minutes of progress you made. There's also other instant deaths like spikes and traps that you'll mostly die to because the precision platforming is awful.
And enemies just.. don't.. die. You ever see videos of a spider egg opening and suddenly thousands of the f**kers start crawling out. It's like that. After a certain point I just gave up fighting enemies that weren't directly in my way because they respawn every two seconds.
In conclusion, this game is difficult, but not satisfyingly difficult. It's like shoving an entire fizzy drink can inside your♥♥♥♥♥♥ It's kind of cool if you can manage it but afterwards you'll probably just feel like you've been f*cked.

Volgarr the viking is a very challenging (at first), tight action platformer in which you control a viking sent on a mission by his god. There are going to be various enemies as well as obstacles and occasionally boss encounters throughout your journey that are going to make your life a nightmare.
The game's graphics are absolutely great, they make you feel like playing an old school platformer, and overall make for a great atmosphere.
This game is very challenging at first, it requires a lot of trail and error. You die constantly. The game is built around experience, with each death you learn, and move a bit further (well, for the most part, unless you fall like a nub, we all had that happen). The game is exceptionally well made. After you get used to the controls and everything, it all feels great. The game has multiple routes to finishing too, so after you're done, you're not truly done. There are also a few upgrades, that help you on the journey. Such as a helmet, a shield and a sword, which all allow you to get hit more, but are also valuable to keep, as the sword is also a damage upgrade, and the upgraded shield doesn't break. To sum it up, volgar is a very trial and error based, tough as nails platformer game that has a very good concept and is rewarding you for playing well. If you decide to buy it, the spear may not be the only thing you end up throwing though ;).

The whole concept of this game is to colonise a Mars type planet. You have to manage resources really well in order to keep you colony alive. For example you need metal and Bioplastic to build structures like solar panels and bio-domes,(Fancy name for a very large greenhouse.)
The game starts with you playing the very detailed tutorial, taking you through building and other game machanics. Once you know how to play the game, you can start your first base. You can name is whatever you like and then you can choose where to start on that planet. The world starts with a short cinamatic of a lander pod landing on the planet, (which can be annoying as it's unskippable,) then seven astronaughts and two rovers get out of the pod. You start by building an oxygen generator and an airlock. Then you need power so build solar panels and a power collector. If you don't connect them, then the game will remind you, which I find really useful as I'm still sorta new to the game. It will also remind you of what to do in sandstorm etc. You can build mines, refinaries, factories, landing pods, wind turbines. Do I have to say more? This game has loads.
The Upsides:
This game has a lot of gameplay value to it. You can play for hours on end, building and rebuilding bases. After a while you can unlock new planets, with totally different environments to switch up the gameplay a bit. This is awesome as you don't have to get bored looking at tons of sand 24/7. This game is also absolutley beautiful. You can have it on the highest possible setting and have a microwave run it. Like what? I donno about FIGHTCADE but Mame32K, Mame64K and Mame32++ offer way more control customization, ROM customization, tweakable settings and most importantly, offer MORE THEN 6 PLAYERS ONLINE in match. Or 3 vs 3 online (like KOF 14 now has!) + spectators too not to mention online training mode.  The K in Mame32K stands for kaillera and doesn't offer the best multiplayer sync code in the world.  It desyncs can hang and freeze emulator and sound like a broken record till u ctrl+alt+del it, but when it works it's the best thing ever.
Ever.
Forever.
It will never get old as a result.  Donno if FIGHTCADE and GGPO and RomStation.fr have such unique co-op and 6 player online features, but they def have more stable netcode then kaillera.

This Steam edition of the game even has some updated features that make it the definitive version of KOF 2002: a polished presentation, some new music, a few old fighters get fresh moves, some balancing changes, a new fighter is added in, and there are extra game modes to fool around with. I’m pretty impressed with the work that was done to buff this game up for the modern market. ROSE Online is one of those games I wanted to try for a while but never gathered the nerve to - the childish graphics and chibi-like art style were both major factors in chasing me away. The other factor was that no MMO is worth playing for more than a while. This one didn't last nearly as long.
So, what are the good factors?
-Fast levelling...?
-Long draw distance for easy targetting?
Ok, not so many pros. Where does this game go really wrong? Well, upon starting the game up, you are greated by Zidane Tribal from Final Fantasy IX. Hello, Zindane. Didn't expect to see you here. Then again, I didn't really expect to see blatant Chocobo clones in Elsword. These manga/anime MMOs love their plagiarism. What else does this game do wrong? You can place several points into your strength attribute and it will make about a 1-damage difference when you strike. Did I mention you begin using a wooden plank sharpened into a spike? Yeah, mix that with your terrifying pink fairy wings you get as a stardard issue, and you have one hell of a warrior. Why, he's so good, he fights beasts that match equally his stoic stature...jelly beans.
What could top such absurdity? Not too much, but there seems to be a pretty big problem with the enemies having HP pools deeper than the Ocean. You can hit a wasp so many times, you swear it had over a hundred health. You do, what? 10-20 right now? It definitely has more than a hundred...it has hundreds.
Time to do what we came here for! Time for adventure! Time for exploration! Time to take a stroll down the grassy lands of Whateveria where there are some trees, lots of paths and...wow. This IS empty. The first town you enter has a few NPCs. There isn't a thing you can buy. Really. The equipment is too expensive and I got to level 5 or so killing beans n bees and I didn't gain any money. Sure, I could sell a few things, but that's just it - a few things. Enemy drops are very few.
I couldn't find any quests. The first town has some NPCs, sure, and there's a guard who looks like he might have a job for you near a bridge, but no. They say something and the player responds with a short line and walks away. Same with this lone boy who appears to be lost and with a lot of goods. He HAS to have a quest. Maybe a bandit problem. Nah. He says some useless fluff and your character says "Good for you".
Good for you? It's like your character KNOWS how useless these people are and is just annoyed to not be doing anything.
Wait, what's this? A free mount! Kickass! I can go so many places! Maybe a bustling city full of quests!
What's that? A little green worm that looks like he should be in A Bug's Life? Yeah, he's quick and all, but I'm hanging to the ground riding a juicy green bug. I can't even fight while I'm riding. Why would I use this thing? I have pink fairy wings and a wooden plank. I'm a warrior of great respect, not a child!
Ok, I jest. Looks like everyone here is. Not the bear though...he's a bear. What the hell...

This also explains why the game
to take place on its island, rather than just presenting the line puzzles on their own.
The Witness doesn't seem like it should be an exciting game, but it certainly was for me. I found each new element exciting with the possibilities for puzzles it added. I found finding solutions, which range from simple to devious, exciting and satisfying too, especially when I was convinced a puzzle was impossible to solve. As others has said, Danganronpa is a cross between the Zero Escape, and Ace Attorney series, and I'd argue with a bit of a Persona vibe thrown in as well. As these three games are among my favourite series, I had always wanted to play Danganronpa, but lacked a PSP or Vita.
After finally playing the game on it's steam release, I can safely say this is one of the most fun and engrossing games I've ever played.
Technically speaking, it's not a Visual Novel; there is many aspects of gameplay, most noteably during the trials, where you shoot down false statements quite literally. It's pretty fun, though I never found it terribly challenging. Usually I figured out the culprits of the cases before even entering the trial, with a few exceptions, but that may be due to my expertise in Ace Attorney, and not a fault of the game's difficulty itself.
Though this game isn't a visual novel, it does have many elements of one; namely a complicated plot oriented game, with a lot of reading. Seriously, about 90% of this game is reading, which is not a bad thing, but may turn off some players. There is voice acting, though it's not constant, which again may bother some players. It is good voice acting though, including the best stuttering voice actress I've ever heard, odd enough as that praise may seem.
The plot itself is one of the most engrossing I've ever seen; I regularly played this game in eight-nine hour sessions due to a desperation to know the next plot twist, and even then I usually only stopped if I had too. I never felt burned out on this game.
The characters are also very strong, with one or two exceptions. If you're into character development like I am, you'll probably replay the game a few times to befriend characters you haven't before, and even if you're not, you may do it anyway to see how different skills affect trials (tip: get Byakuya and Hifumi's ultimate skills, as they're OP as hell). I also love the main character, Makoto. Some may argue he's flat, but he's such a pure cinnamon roll I can't help it. It's the type of protagonist I adore.
If you're looking at this game at all, I definitely recommend it, since if you came here at all it's probably because you're into Ace Attorney or Zero Escape, and if you're into those, you will definitely like this. It's got a great story, a fantastic ending and morale, top tier characters, and fun mysteries to solve, and a fun and unique way to do it. I definitely see myself replaying this many times in the future.
(Sidenote: I would recommend playing this game before trying the second; while the plot doesn't directly connect as there are different characters, and imo the second is better, it does assume you've already played the first, and the difficulty supports that. It's less a sequel, and more on the lines of a second episode in an episodic game.)

When I first saw this game, I had already purchased another one of the same type (Sol 0) - I believe that's the name. I must admit I am a bit of a sucker when it comes to this types of game (Strategy/Simulation/Build/Management). Even though I thought the other game was just OK with good potential... PlanetBase seemed even more intriguing.
The graphics are quite good, yes, for a game like this one doesn't need much better graphics really. The soundtrack at the begining really gets you into the grove that you are about to go into space and colonise on a far away planet... I was really into everything and letting myself immerse in the experience.
The first 3 games, sadly for me I must admit, I pretty much killed all of my colonists quite fast!
There just seemed no way to be able to keep a balance on the things one needs to build for survival of the small colony you start the game with.
Particularly food! Food was always an issue. It didn't seem like I was ever able to keep enough food being produced (bio-domes took too long to produce enough materials to fill the meal making machines in the canteen).
Also, there seemed no way of really prioritising any of the jobs your 'sims' (I'll call my colonists sims for the sake of ease) have. So a lot of the time they just stand around being 'idle'. Being the masochist I am clearly, I tried to persevere and figure out what I was doing wrong.
Eventually, I was able to develop a colony, enough to have just over 30 sims in it.
But even then, somehow the bit of the map I was in had hardly enough space to build as there is no way to get machines or bots to break through the hills/mountains/whatever you want to call that are all over the place. I understand the purpose that they're needed for the sake of building mines and producing ore but... and a big but... there should be an alternative to this issue!
Anyhow... eventually after much fiddling around with the map, starting a game, seeing what the map is like before starting to build, quit to menu and restart the process all over again,,, I managed to figure out my way to a semi decent sized map with enough space to build a 'decent base'.
Still I really like the graphics.
The music became a tad annoying so pretty much just opted to have it off most of the time and leave the sound effects on. The meteors, the spacecrafts, the lasers, the solar panels moving, etc are pretty cool sound effects that helpt the game immersive potential.
However... There is as much great about this game as there are possibilities to improve it (and needed improvements). It would be great to have a bit more control over what priorities one can/should give to its sims... better control over the different food types, what goes into each meal making machine (for example we should be able to select how much of veggies and meats a particular machine should hold; this would give the option to have properly balanced meals on some machines/canteens and simply fast meals like salad or whatever on others for quick hunger quenching). Also, maybe I am missing out on how it works in the game, but we should be able to assign a work machine or at least a specific dome/area to a specific sim and hopefully this would avoid the fact that since they spend most of their time trabelling around the base the machine works are produced considerably slow for the needs one has sometimes. SO trying to balance those out can get annoyingly challenging (fiddling with colonist percentages, etc) since they'r not quite maazing. They work well I guess if you just really focus on developing one group of sims at a time for whatever one single need one wishes to develop... but that means you're lacking on other areas...
I think it would also make this game a lot more interesting if you had demolition bots or tools to craft the terrain in order to expand your building map.
I could go on and touch on more in depth thoughts and ideas... but I wouldn't want to bore anyone that bothers to read this review any more than I already have by possibly making it this long.
Well... I think it's a good game with potential to be great, with improvements needed for sure. Still quite enjoyable until you sort of get the hang of how to control the small controls available to expand your colony/base.
6/10 for potential that's for sure. Wonder if there are any developments to come that will make the game more enthralling!
So I will recommend the game since there isn't a level of marking this game other than Yay or Nay! As I enjoyed it and wish for more (once the game improves)... I will leave it for others to decide if they Yay or Nay the game after all!

EDIT: Changed my review to negative. As no matter how often i boot up the game now it just leads me to frustration. I always end up being soft-locked into failure due to AI's fault, in this review i stated that gaining some power of influence to the AI would eventually fix the issue but was disregarded to be "Part of the challenge." I disagree with it however.
So Planetbase, first time i have heard about this game is after i found a video on Youtube of someone introducing it. As i saw the gameplay i was totally convinced this is my sort of thing, even tho he only showed the start of it.
So now i bought it and sunk multiple hours in it and i must say, for a non-early access im abit dissapointed.
I wont write a big wall of text so i make it short.
The major problem is the AI of each colonist in the game. Sometimes they take the longest possible Paths or ignore priority of certain functions they have to fulfill. I wouldnt say i didnt find any more problems then this and give it a good rating but the AI is so bad it will kill your entire gameplay experience.
Now for the long part!
How to fix this? Well only the dev can do it, but you and me can find solutions for it and suggest changes. And so i will.
1. "Uh.. What am i doing? Where do i work? Ah i will just idle in the corridor here."
Probably my biggest issue here. While i see its the appeal of the game just to set everything up for your little AI minions to do their own thing with, it does certainly not help the game out. The only priority control you get is for some workplaces and yet-to-be-built domes, even with that its not sufficient of how you can plan on getting enough susitance for your colonists. Building things is always prioritized even tho the same materials are required to build important components like Spare Parts. So Dev, please, Give us a function where we can assign staff to certain room/functions to have them stop wandering all over the place!
2. "I just ate.. well i guess i can go eat some more anyway."
Problem here is that alot of times Colonists would go and consume any resource of time to use a bed or something like that to replenish their lil Bars, even tho these are still in the green. Not only does it waste the food you accumulated. It also prevents them from working efficient, espicially when they have longer walkpaths. To fix this is easy, let them go for what they need only if the status reaches the red or orange area. If those reach 0 they shouldnt just die like that, how about a healthbar or them refusing to work until they got what they want?
3. "Sheesh dude, when i go to work to maintain all those vegies, i must always walk some sort of marathon!"
Noteable issue here is that you cannot easily replace buildings or upgrade their size to create more efficient room, most importantly Biodomes for food. You will end up building like 3 over a large scale of your base which has a siginificant issue with the AI of your botanists. Sometimes one of them does not get required maintenance and sometimes they even ignore the domes they are close to just to work on one far away. Unless you have already a plan on how best to build with said efficienty a fix would be the one i mentioned in issue 1.
4. "Outage again? Damn this electricity system is wonky nowdays.."
While i cant say this is a major issue but its something that needs to be adressed. Often times you will notice outages during the night because (obviously) your solar panels cant give you any energy on it. So you end up building Windmills right? Well, yeah, if you are lucky enough to have wind happening during the night. I fixed this problem by building alot.. a unneccesary lot of Energy storages to make sure i make it through the night, but those ended up taking so many building materials that my gameplay experience was slowed down a bunch. I ended up using windmills only to reduce the loss of power during the night if i didnt have enough resources to keep up with the power-storages. So.. A fix? Well one idea would be is to give the storages more carrying capacity. Or have electricity you created be more efficient (Use less over time.) Of course another source of electricity would help too.
This is more of a review of the games issues, so i will not rate the game, but i definitly recommend to follow it if it still recieves its share of development. I did notice it still recieves updates and i hope my opinion gets recognized, not just for me but for those with the same issues like i have.
The game used to be almost unplayable from AI, but its much better now and I'm happy to see the developers constantly churning out updates.
