(Don't use the lack of playtime recorded as a judgement of my review. I played this game on and off since 2006, long before this game was put on steam and have continued playing it without steam)
This is one of the best games out there in the mmo genre, could be considered the single best mmo when it comes to this type of graphical style, it's been around since  2006 and there are still a ton of people in the game and the developers have consistently added more to the game since then. The game has regular events, like Christmas, saint Patrick's day, World cup to name a few.
The game is supported by a item shop, but realistically you could play the whole game without ever spending any money in it, most of what is sold on the item shop is cosmetic and the things that are not are mostly things that speed up your process in the game, like for example Exp boost. The item shop does sell a few skills, but you do not really have to get these and you won't feel gimped if you don't have them, that is the only thing you could consider needing to spend money on, but it is not required. A great thing about how Rose Online does the item shop however is that everything that is sold in the item shop can be given or resold to other players, so if you really did not want to spend money in the item shop but still wanted an item from the item shop you could easily buy it from another player who is selling it for in game money, be aware though that you probably won't be able to do this early on in the game, because the prices of item shop objects are not cheap.
The game has an amazing crafting system, it may not be in depth as other games and may not feel as satisfying when you craft objects but it's massive. Nearly ever single drop in the game (like 90%) is used as a crafting component, the rest of the things that are not are gear, health/mana pickups, vendor trash or a gift box, which there are different types and contain something in it when you open it, like having a random chance of getting a crafting component out of 5 types, basically it's a dirty crystal and when you open it you find out what color crystal it is and crystals are used to craft objects.
CAUTION, it is not recommended you sell your loot to the first few shops you find, there are a few people in the game that try to take advantage of new players lack of knowledge and will pay you very little for your loot (some people may call them scammers,me included, but they are not really, as a new player you should be cautious of things like this in any game) , it may look like a lot when you only have 200G and a player offers you 2.000G for a object you picked up 7 of, but you will kick yourself when you get to the second city and find out the average price you could have gotten for that item was 40.000G. Do NO sell any of your materials before you get to the second main city in the game called City of Junon Polis. When you get to this city take some time and look around at a bunch of shops, there are many players shops set up here, take your time go around and look at the prices of stuff when you have looked at a good selection of shops, you will have a better idea what stuff is worth and can make a better decision on how much to let things go at.
If you want to craft your own objects, you will have to roll a Dealer, which is the only class that can craft objects. If you do choose to craft objects, do not go and pick up every crafting skill there is as doing so will make your character at killing stuff and thus be very slow at leveling. Crafting skills are part of your normal skills and putting a point into crafting means one less point into a damage dealing ability. Usually just pick one or two crafting discipline, and get a few combat skills and save the rest for your advanced job. Also to help you if you choose to become a crafter CON (concentration) increases your chance at succesfully crafting and objects and SEN (sense) increases your chance of getting extra stats on the crafted object. Carts,Castle Gear and Gems can't have extra stats so, sense is less useful if you want to craft these items
There are 4 basic classes and 8 advanced classes in the game, everyone starts out as a visitor and when you reach level 10 you can choose on of the basic classes, the basic classes each have two main trees, Muse (mage) has a healing tree and a damage tree. Soldier (Warrior) has a 1 handed tree and a 2 handed tree (1 handed is more for tanking and 2 more for dealing damage). Hawker (rogue/assassin) has a Melee tree and a Range Tree (and then melee has two types, Katar (firstweapon) and dual swords). Dealer has an offensive tree and a crafting tree (crafting tree has some offensive abilities but for the most part it's crafting focused). Each of the basic classes has a basic tree, which help them no matter what they side they go, Muse has increased INT, mana  and mana regen. Soldier has increased Strength, increased damage and increased health. Hawker has increased Dex, increased attack power and increased attack speed. Dealer has Increased CON (Con increases their damage also), increased SEN and increased movement speed.
Try to always be in a party, Rose Online rewards you for being in a party, it has this system called Party Level, it starts at and can go all the way to 50. Party level gives you bonus EXP, the higher the party level the higher the bonus EXP is, this rewards people for grouping up. Some people even leave their game on to save their party level when it gets really high and then when they come back to play tomorrow they don't have to rebuild the party level and get increased bonus EXP from the start  You can be in a party and gain exp as long as nobody in the party is more then 20 levels apart from each other. Getting an AOE skill is highly advisable, what many groups do is go to a location on the map where there are a good amount of mobs, have someone pull a group of mobs and that that person brings the group of mobs the the party and then everyone AOE's the enemies down, this way you speed up your leveling by a lot.
Hope this extended review helped you and have fun in Rose Online.

Volgarr is a hit or miss game. It has a lot of issue that leave it somewhere between good and bad. The controls feel...incomplete. Imagine fighting the bosses in megaman but megaman is a lead weight with only melee attacks. Volgarr doesn't have any momentum whatsoever. This is obviously intentional on the developers part but it wasn't ultimately necessary to make the game as "brutally difficult" as they intended. It is a difficult game but not because of good game design. It's difficult because you are essentially given unfair enemy placements and death traps and told to figure out a way. The game sort of ramps and wanes in difficulty with me having the most trouble on the fire level because of said instant death traps. The controls are so clunky that anything but perfection will leave you dead. Enemies have a fair amount of health with most things dying in a single hit and bosses taking around 10-15 hits to kill. Except for the bird boss. For some reason he takes around 20 hits. Even with fire sword, it just felt like he had way too much health. Coupled with a poorly designed room and difficult controls (especially while in the air) the game feels like it should have been tweaked a bit more. The sense of accomplishment you get from beating a boss is great so the game has that going for it but know that it can be prone to crashing when you defeat a boss. I'd heard of it but it only happened to me after defeating the bird boss. If you're looking for a game that is simply difficult, (I'd say this is up there with dark souls in terms of 1st playthrough difficulty) then Volgarr is for you. If you want a game that feels polished then steer clear. The graphics are SNES era 16-bit fair and the music is good but those don't help the game to get above a 6/10 from me.

Volgarr the Viking is an awesome game. It has great graphics, excellent gameplay and a great soundtrack.
There will be minor spoilers for the story:
You play Volgarr, a viking with a mighty sword and an unlimited supply of spears that he can use to attack enemies or use as platforms. Your task is to travel through five worlds (each consisting of two sections) and defeat the bosses to open Fafnir's tower.
Should you be good enough, you can obtain warrior spirits that serve as lives to play the more difficult parts of worlds 2-6.
Depending on what you do, you can earn one out of three endings.
Mark my words though: This game is not for everybody. It has a high difficulty spike.
Playing Volgarr for the first time can be extremely frustrating. I spent 3 hours of my first playthrough in the first two worlds before I got good enough alone. However the more I learned how to control Volgarr and the neat tricks he can do, the easier it got. Now I got all achievements and just completed the game a second time on the Valkyrie path.
I would say that Volgarr is basically Dark Souls the Jump n' Run. Once you have learned the game's tricks, it becomes extremely enjoyable and rewarding.
Try to answer these questions:
Do you like to get challenged by a game?
Do you like to try, try, try again until you finally beat a world?
Do you like to eventually master a hard game and feel like a beast when you played through it a second, third or even fourth and so forth time?
If you can answer all these questions with yes, then you should check out Volgarr.
If you don't like to get constantly killed until you finally mastered a difficult section, then better turn around now and look for something else to play.

Solid, heavy, and brutal.
The controls support the notion that you are a heavy, strong viking. The game is quite difficult and requires mastering the controls in order to succeed. Solid plaforming and combat come together to make this a challenging adventure.
Controls are stiff, but rather than taking away from the player's experience it adds more of a "heavy" and "strong" feeling behind actions, fitting in with the theme of the character and setting. Enemies and levels are designed around these controls so deaths, while frequent and frustrating, are "fair" and lend themselves to helping the player become better through experience.
Enemy movements are subtly varied but tailored around the player's controls, forcing the player to adapt tactics while perfecting his handle on the controls.
I recommend this to fans of hard-core platformers.

It took me about 15 minutes to fall in love with Sky Rogue. This game scratches an itch that many other flight combat sims do not, and allows you to enjoy the thrill of flight and aerial combat without the immense frustration of repeating a difficult failed mission over and over to progress. If you fail, you are simply given a new series of missions, procedurally generated missions with objectives that you must bomb off the face of the earth or shoot out of the sky. Each mission also presents numerous optional objectives which you can destroy for additional credit towards unlocking the next tech, which can be new aircraft, weapons, or utility items like afterburners and IR flares.
This game is rather reminiscent of the sleeper gem Starfighter for 3D0, which had similar graphics and open-world objectives (and many other remarkable features).
Visually the game is appealingly simple, flat vector graphics with striking aircraft designs featuring pleasant details and moving parts that react to your control of the craft, such as a swing-wing interceptor that changes configuration as you accelerate.
The controls are smooth using a gamepad.

A nice, casual point-and-click adventure game with resource management and a decent storyline, Hero of the Kingdom is a nice game that fulfills it's purpose, with low-to-no pressure on the player to get things done fast. It's easy to play, even while distracted. And thus definitely well-suited to a casual player, or someone who wants to play a little something that's not-too-engaging with a little free time.
(TL:DR version and Conclusion at the bottom)
You play as a farm boy with dreams of grandeur, of who's father has left you to take care of the farm while he takes care of some errands in town. One day, while you're out repairing the old lookout tower down the road from the farm, bandits set your father's farm ablaze. Not even raiding it, just raizing the whole thing! Now with no home, you must set out on a quest to find your father, who has not returned, and find out why the bandits destroyed your home.
Throughout your adventure, you find many people in need of your aid. Some who also were hassled by the same bandits who burned your farm to the ground. And soon find that there are much bigger things at work than just the bandits.
The story is engaging enough to encourage playing it through to the end, but simple enough to allow players to take a break if need be, with no pressure or timers.
The interface is barely there, which is nice for those who prefer a minimalistic UI. At each of the four corners of the screen, there are buttons to bring up the actual UI or to serve as a function of their own, of which they tuck themselves out of view when not moused over.
My only real complaint is how cluttered the inventory can get, but.. I figure one easy fix would be, I dunno... Cleaning it out?
... I've got a problem with playing pack rat, yes...
The gameplay is pretty nice and simple. The layout is from a overhead view, and you click on what you want to interact with. Arrows at the edges of the screen indicate that you can move in that direction to another screen. Typically little icons will hover over things that need to be, or can be interacted with.
But, as you progress through the game, there's more things to interact with that aren't highlighted. Hidden objects of a sort, if you will. Of which result in some very nice resources in-game, and achievements if you find a lot of them.
The graphics are nice, sweet, and to the point. They're well done, and it's not often that there's sprites or the like that overly clash with the area. Everything blends well together, and doesn't have severe drops or increase in certain objects' quality, thus looking like they'd logically exist in the same setting.
The music serves it's purpose decently. The music is nice, without being overly repetitive, and matches the settings quite well. But it's also not the kind of music you'll be finding yourself listening to when not playing the game. The sound effects are nice, and also serve to give a idea on what's in the current scene. There's not much of this employed though, sadly. And I do hope that's addressed in the sequel.
- Decent storyline.
- Easy to play casual gameplay.
- Nicely done graphics that don't look out of place.
- Music and sounds that fit the location.
- Good amount of Achievements.
- Minimalistic UI is only there when you need it.
- Fairly short game.
- A bit too casual for those wanting something more from their game experience.
- So... Much... Backtracking...
A simple game to fill a simple need, Hero of the Kingdom is best suited for the casual gamer, and suits them well. The asthetics and gameplay are well done and serve their purpose. The game is seemingly well crafted despite it's simplistic nature, and doesn't seem to suffer from a lack of quality, inciting that the developer put much love in to this game and didn't make it to purely be a cash grab. Which is nice to see.
It's definitely a good game to pick up on sale, which just so happens to be right now as of me writing this. So if the game sounds good to you, it would be a nice thing to pick up for a couple bucks.
Thank you very much for taking your time to read my review.

As others has said, Danganronpa is a cross between the Zero Escape, and Ace Attorney series, and I'd argue with a bit of a Persona vibe thrown in as well. As these three games are among my favourite series, I had always wanted to play Danganronpa, but lacked a PSP or Vita.
After finally playing the game on it's steam release, I can safely say this is one of the most fun and engrossing games I've ever played.
Technically speaking, it's not a Visual Novel; there is many aspects of gameplay, most noteably during the trials, where you shoot down false statements quite literally. It's pretty fun, though I never found it terribly challenging. Usually I figured out the culprits of the cases before even entering the trial, with a few exceptions, but that may be due to my expertise in Ace Attorney, and not a fault of the game's difficulty itself.
Though this game isn't a visual novel, it does have many elements of one; namely a complicated plot oriented game, with a lot of reading. Seriously, about 90% of this game is reading, which is not a bad thing, but may turn off some players. There is voice acting, though it's not constant, which again may bother some players. It is good voice acting though, including the best stuttering voice actress I've ever heard, odd enough as that praise may seem.
The plot itself is one of the most engrossing I've ever seen; I regularly played this game in eight-nine hour sessions due to a desperation to know the next plot twist, and even then I usually only stopped if I had too. I never felt burned out on this game.
The characters are also very strong, with one or two exceptions. If you're into character development like I am, you'll probably replay the game a few times to befriend characters you haven't before, and even if you're not, you may do it anyway to see how different skills affect trials (tip: get Byakuya and Hifumi's ultimate skills, as they're OP as hell). I also love the main character, Makoto. Some may argue he's flat, but he's such a pure cinnamon roll I can't help it. It's the type of protagonist I adore.
If you're looking at this game at all, I definitely recommend it, since if you came here at all it's probably because you're into Ace Attorney or Zero Escape, and if you're into those, you will definitely like this. It's got a great story, a fantastic ending and morale, top tier characters, and fun mysteries to solve, and a fun and unique way to do it. I definitely see myself replaying this many times in the future.
(Sidenote: I would recommend playing this game before trying the second; while the plot doesn't directly connect as there are different characters, and imo the second is better, it does assume you've already played the first, and the difficulty supports that. It's less a sequel, and more on the lines of a second episode in an episodic game.)

Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc is a port of the PSP/PSVita game, and it is beautiful. The voice acting generally breezes over, but it's still good. The character design and motives make sense especially in a bleak, hopeless environment like this, and the cases and trial mechanics hold this giant, adorable teddy bear together, to the point where the seams are nearly invisible.
The stuffing comes in the form of the story. The story is very enigmatic, and unravels slowly throughout each trial, each meeting and every step you take. The main antagonist is never who you were expecting--nothing is. The murderers are never who you expect them to be, and YOU are not what they expected. You can interact with various characters during what is known as FREE TIME, where you aren't investigating and you can build trust with whoever you'd like. Granted, certain characters' will react differently to your actions. You can also provide gifts to characters during FREE TIME, which will also allow you to build trust. Every character is eccentric in their own way, and that's what really makes them fun.
Within my short time playing this, this has become my favorite game of all time. Looking forward to getting the sequel. 10/10

Amazing game.  There isn't really much I can say about the gameplay mechanics, graphics, and sound design that hasn't already been said over and over, so I won't touch on those things.  I played this one through on both Steam, and on the Dreamcast.  The game is smoother on PC, but the DC port is totally playable.  If you do decide to play it on the Dreamcast, please buy it for one of the other platforms.  It's a really amazing game and the devs and publisher deserve to get paid for it.
A common complaint I see is with this game's difficulty.  Personally, I think the difficulty of the gameplay is fair, but I wish there were a few more checkpoints.  Each stage is divided into two section, and each section has a checkpoint at the beginning.  You die, you restart at the beginning of the section.  And to make it worse, the boss for each stage is at the end of the second section.  If you die at the boss, you restart the whole section.   Maybe a checkpoint before a boss would be enough?  That would create a new issue though, since the player then wouldn't be able to fully upgrade their gear through the level after dying to a boss.  It'd have to be an optional checkpoint.  Whatever the case, I'm sure the devs are capable enough to figure out how to make that work.
That is literally my only gripe with the Volgarr the Viking.  I've played it probably 12 hours on the Dreamcast on top of the time I have invested in the game on Steam.  I think it's a solid and fun game, and I love a challenge.  I'm currently working on completing the Valkyrie path, which is essentially a different version of each level with limited lives.  It's basically the hard mode for an already really hard game.  After that, I intend to speedrun it.  I totally got my $10 worth.

Does anyone remember Decent or Forsaken? Games from the early days of 3D graphics and when you had a graphics card you were considered to have a powerful rig. The 6DOF genre came into existance and basically it took the normal strafing from games like Doom and Hexen but then added strafing in all directions. Since the game engines of the time couldn't handle open spaces very well, these early space-sims had you flying around corridors. Oddly enough it worked because it wasn't trying to capture the style of those movies with little ships zipping around amidst two fleets facing off against one another like we had seen in films like Star Wars or Battlestar Galactica.
However, you also had the other kind of space battle seen in Star Trek with large capital ships slowly moving around each other in some kind of space version of the classic galleon vs galleon battles from the naval days of old. These were also very impressive and the size of the vessels themselves really wouldn't have looked right if they were zipping around and barrel-rolling this way and that. But with those large ship to ship battles the aim wasn't to hit the other ship since that was actually very easy, the aim was to hit specific parts of the ship to give you a tactical advantage. Weaken shields on this side/that side, knock out weapons/propulsion. It was more about managing the situation than needing to aim straight and that still made things interesting.
So then, is Star Conflict more Star Wars or Star Trek? Well, not even the developers can decide and this has led to one of the most bizzare results I could have imagined.
You see, unlike games such as Freespace or Strike Suit Zero the controls in SC allow for aiming with the mouse as you pilot the ship around. This is a novel idea but paradoxically it actually means that playing with a HOTAS flight-stick will severely handicap you. But further to this, the fighters and inteceptors handle like frigates with very tiny turning circles even at top speed as long as you're not using afterburners. This means the usual ballet that ensures as pilots in other games adjust their speed and pitch to line up shots is completely lost and the fact that you can mouse-aim removes all of the dog-fighting you'd expect from a space-sim. This control behavior has led to SC players actually not moving around at all. In fact, the best way to play this game is to park your ship behind some cover and peer around it taking shots at someone else. If you attempt to actually engage in a furball with another ship you basically end up in pieces very quickly because once you're at mid-range it is almost impossible for you to miss the other ship as you track it with your cursor while staying completely still.  It's like how you play Counter Strike, only people have been replaced by ships. The speed of the ships is also incredibly slow with the exception of the Inteceptors so evading incoming fire is a waste of time.
The end result in many of these encounters becomes a bunch of ships hiding behind cover and very slowly strafing back and forth - even if they are lighter class ships. It just looks and feels wrong in every way when you see a tiny, sleek and agile looking fighter suspended almost motionless in space while sheepishly taking pot-shots from behind an asteroid.  For the larger class vessels however, this doesn't look or feel unusual but results in some very slow paced and tedious game of peek-a-boo in space.
Star Conflict has almost created some wierd slow paced 6DOF game as a result and I really can't recommand it to anyone looking for a genuinely entertaining space-sim MMO.

After 2001, it's the end of the King of The Fighters ~ NESTS saga. You would be wondering, Is there a new story coming out from Eolith? Well, no, you will be playing the Dream Match game once more, after KOF98. The second dream match is up for you players to have another experience on the fighting arena once more. Behold! King of the Fighters 2002 ~ Challenge to the Ultimate Battle!
This game doesn't rules, but bringing back the past KOF memories.....With New Face Team back, Iori's past team mates Vice and Mature ''revived''. Rugal...... well, I can gurentee you would want to play it. And all characters were stronger now. With moves, and new experience!
This game doesn't have storyline, unfortunately, but it doesn't matter, since you are playing the ''non-story'' KOF game. This game still provides some pack of fun and fighting experience that you've ever imagined. However, your boss, is still the same Omega Rugal, except for now, he's much stronger.
Artwork could use some improvement. But a big great news is Athena became a main ''model'' for this years KOF. Her hair is longer, her cloths is beautiful. and her two fans will be with her during the whole out battle. With a cute introduction pose. She even prettier than KOF99 (sure, she is 10x better than she was in KOF2001). However, the character portraits could give some improvement. Not bad in terms of drawing, but the style doesn't give out the sense of beauty. But more or less it's up to players who decide this. I still prefer the KOF2000 artwork if you ask me.
Gameplay is still the same way as the previous KOF games, you still fight, with power bar which you fight to build it up. And use the Desperation Moves or Super Desperation Moves to do a finishing move to a character, it's the same old way that KOF games that they ever provided. Except that now, Characters gained a Hidden Super Desperation Moves, which you have to activate it when you're low on life. And needed certain command to execute it. Not bad actually.
Some of the old abilities like: Cancel, Autoguard, Backstep Jump, Rolling is back in this game. Surely, mastering the usage of those abilities will help tremendously on your fighting skills throughout the whole game. But those need some time to master it. For experienced KOF players, this never be a trouble for them. But for newbies, mastering them needs some time. Honed with those skills help you playing the versus mode easier, when you want to challenge someone into battle. Connecting Combo moves and end with a finishing move is a KOF players goal. That's what you've to do on it. Since you are more focused on combo's, not the basic Street Fighter II fighting style anymore.
Music is somewhat downgraded. Although it is taken from the previous KOF songs, I still prefer the old theme. It feels like Eolith just take the theme from the previous games and simply rearranged it. But Arcade centers are usually noisy, you won't hear that so clearly. Try to buy the soundtrack if you want to. Voice acting is good. Character voice acting is changed, to much aggressive tone. But sometimes, you'll get annoyed. Have a rest if those bugged you too much.
Loving this game is easy, replay this game is fun, but to master this game still needs your previous KOF experience and skills to play it. It's not easy if you ask me, the CPU's difficulty is tweaked, and your opponent is much smarter, and more difficult.
Overall this game is provided the best gameplay so far, so it says ''Graphic doesn't matter much, gameplay must be fun and attractive.''. I rather Eolith refines the graphic and their artwork. If they do so, I would be definitely mad on this game.......Well, at least I do love Athena this year for now! ^_^

Like other players already mentioned: The Witness is no casual puzzle game.
You awake alone on an beautifull island with no clue what to do or where to go. You start wandering through the landscape and abandoned towns, while stumbling upon some 2-D puzzles. For solving those you won't get any new skill or item. The only thing you'll achieve by solving those is a immense feeling of sadisfaction. Not only did you manage to understand the mechanic of one of the many puzzle-types, but you were also capable of solving them. Some puzzles are, at first, realy frustrating, but sometimes it helps alot to focus on other things/puzzles first bevore facing certain challenges. Do yourself a favor and don't look up the solutions or mechanics, it takes the whole experience away.
Besides the difficult puzzles, the game offers a very colourful landscape. It is, at least for me, very relaxing just to walk around the island with no clear goal in mind. You may even find puzzles, eastereggs or secrets you've missed earlier in the game.
So, for me the game is alot about perspecitve. It challenges you to look at problems in different angles (figuratively and literally). The Witness is one of the greatest games I played in years and I appreciate the developer put into this. Even the feeling of joy is still present and I haven't played the game in like 6 months (or so).
+ beautifull scenery
+ relaxing atmosphere
+ a good bunch of "secrets"
+ difficult puzzles
+/- the ending (kind of anticlimactic. I get the meaning, but still...)
+/- no real story
- the price (37€ is a lot of cash. I love this game, but I would recommend to wait for a sale)
Rating: 10/10

I wish there were a "mixed" option for recommending this game, as I think for a lot of people out there, this is a fantastic game, and it's definitely well made with a lot of love and attention to detail in many respects. I really like puzzles and problem solving, so part of my disappointment with The Witness is that I really thought I would enjoy the game. Myst was one of my favorite games growing up, and I was extremely excited to see a well-reviewed game in the Myst genre surface after far too long.
The problem for me was that The Witness is very much a game about the journey, and not the destination. It turns its head on the genre as it's less a game about solving puzzles within a set of rules, and more about discovering what those rules are. And for the most part, it does that well. Instead of the usual game conventions, rewards for solving hard puzzles weren't any kind of story unlock, more just to give you a harder puzzle. That approach was fun for awhile, but some story unlock would've been appreciated, especially because there is so much mystery and it's such an immersive world that was clearly built for a reason and has a fascinating backstory.
Some of the mechanics also just seem arbitrary, or at the very least, not quite obvious enough. Sometimes perspective puzzles require you to either take a screenshot or jot down on pencil and paper the answer, then transfer it on screen. That seems like lazy game design and worst of all, takes you out of the immersive experience. It's possible I'm mostly tone deaf, as some of the sound puzzles seemed almost impossible to me, despite numerous listens. There's also just the repetitiveness of the "pathfinding" puzzles, which range from challenging (and satisfying) to punitive in their difficulty spikes. It's in these difficulty spikes where I think the core game mechanic of pathfinding lets you down, as it requires you to be much more of a planner than a "hands on" problem solver. In a game like this, I would think it would accommodate multiple approaches, but really there's a right way to approach this game, and a wrong way. Unfortunately for me, I think the way I approach puzzles (trial and error) is strongly discouraged, at times in punitive ways.
The philosophy from the audio/video portions will likely be appreciated by some, and for some come off as the worst kind of douchey-hipster nonsense. Had they been delivered in shorter pieces, I might've fallen into the former. But as rambling as some of them are, I found them more annoying than enjoyable unfortunately.
I don't know, I'm really torn on this. It's a well made game, and while it seems so open and non-confined, I found the game to be far too linear in mechanics and how to approach problem solving. At times it actually made me feel like a lesser thinker because I have a different approach to puzzles than what the game designer prefers. What I'm sure is a really fun journey for some, left me disappointed with the destination.
Am realizing this reads a lot like an apology for not liking this game, which I think it is. I really, really wanted to love The Witness, but in the end, not only was this game not for me, but I genuinely feel lesser for that fact because I feel like I should have loved it, and just didn't.

This feels like a throwback to the days when videogames were about the journey and not the destination; it's not the most action-packed game, but that doesn't mean it doesn't get the heart-racing, a smile forming, or the brain working vigorously.

I don't bring this up as an unrelated ad hominem criticism. This attitude is inherent in The Witness. Which is a problem for me.
I hate to say it, but it seems a very elitist game. There's nothing wrong with that, and it has it's place. I just believe for most people that place will be on that busy post-retirement shelf.
It gets a thumbs up from me, because it is really an incredible piece of art, but I wanted to include my warning that the enjoyment you can get from it can be somewhat restricted, due to the fact it's a slow burner that doesn't feel like it should have to respect your time. This is part of what makes it great and unique, but hugely limits how I would engage with it.
So purchase with caution!

This game is excellent. Lately, I've found myself with an overwhelming desire to blow enemy aircraft out of the gorgeous blue sky at all hours of the day. It's just as easy to get short, bite-sized play sessions out of this game as it is to sit around for an hour trying to progress past day 4. Make no mistake: this game can get difficult. But nothing about it feels completely impossible.
Great:
-Art direction. Beautiful in its low-poly simplicity. And the colors! Gah.
-Progression. If you cause enough destruction before you eat that last SAM, you'll gain tech points that unlock a seemingly random array of upgrades ranging from new planes to weapons to maneuvering addons. Collect them all!
-Handling. There's just enough tension between what you want to do and what the plane will allow that those moments when you slam into a frigate because you didn't pull up in time feel like your fault rather than the game's. In a single word, superb.
-Replayability. Set in a world where the average pilot life expectancy is less than two days, the focus on flight combat and procedurally generated maps keeps the gameplay fresh. You'll play those first few days over and over, but you'll find it just as fun as the AI finds you repulsive and in need of death.
Not so much:
-Music. There is one track that plays during flight. That's it. It's catchy, but it's just the one.
-Control. Mouse is kind of finicky, so I've been going all keyboard. I'd prefer to use my flightstick (Logitech Extreme 3D Pro), but all it can do is control roll and pitch, and the buttons are somehow completely useless. Your experience with a flightstick may differ. Better options for editing joystick/controller inputs will probably come in future updates (I hope).
-Stats. This game should track pilot statistics. After referencing average pilot life expectancy earlier, I want this concept in the game.
Sky Rogue is currently in alpha, so don't expect a fully polished experience. That said, this game is worth your money and your time right now. So buy it already.

This review will be free of story spoilers because really that's what you should be here for, the story.  So far I've played 999 and its sequel and Danganronpa and I'm sitting here writing this waiting on Danganronpa 2 to unlock (5 more hours).
THE STORY
The storytelling is the reason to play any game by Spike Chunsoft.  This isn't just a bit of fluff either, where drops of water in a desert taste sweeter, with the trappings of an epic tale (but still lacking some intangible element).  No.  The developers here have a keen sense for what makes stories compelling and have obviously worked hard to make those guidelines apply within the boundaries specific to the video game as a unique medium.
I used to be in agreement with Roger Ebert who famously once said that video games couldn't be art.  The very nature of storytelling itself is at odds with the inherent nature of gameplay -- one demands that we examine choices taken and the other demands that we have some sembelence of choice ourselves.  This is what made Bioshock so compelling and successful and indeed the only other example of great storytelling in the medium, because the developers understood this tension between traditional storytelling norms and the specific constraints placed on them by the medium they're working in.
THE GAME
If you're in it for the story then great!  The gameplay is fun too, but you should know up front that all the Spike Chunsoft games (or at least the ones I've played) are more like a storybook with a game attached.  If you're afraid that might mean the gameplay is a second thought then don't run off just yet.  The story is absolutely the prime focus here and takes up the lion's share of 'gameplay' time but the game aspect is crucial and, for my part, extremely well developed.
It's not a secret that Danganronpa was developed as a graphical novel first and then gameplay was developed to add to it but, without giving too much away here, the gameplay seems like it was designed with the meaty aspects of the storytelling in mind.  I mean, I don't know, but for the themes that the story was trying to get across I felt the gameplay reinforced those themes in a way that made it more real feeling than simply reading it would (or listening to the voice acting, as it were) and I find it easy to believe that this was every bit intentional.
GAMEPLAY
Practically speaking there are 3 parts of the game:  Story time, exploration/friend making, and investigations/trial.  If you're not listening to the actors or moving between stages you're walking around the school and "making friends" or you're looking for clues and then participating in a trial.  The friendship building sub-game earns you powerups you can use during the trial phase and requires you to find/earn special coins to randomly obtain items that you'll have to figure out which person likes and give it to them at the right time -- overall I didn't like this aspect too much but it's easy enough to look things up online and I found that it didn't venture too deep into spoiler territory; it's forgettable but also interesting to hear the deeper backstories of the different players.
The trial has different phases and mini games.  Some are more or less frivolous but not without purpose; they allow for a pacing that lets the trial build and build to a big climax.  With decent twitch skills on the PC you could easily set both difficulty settings to high; one makes it a little more difficult to click targets (I think it increases reticle drift and the amount of blocking 'blue text' items that appear), the other gives you more options to select between when trying to resolve a question.
THE MOOD
I figure if you still aren't sure if you want the game or not you're not sold on the gameplay (which, again, is really fun but supportive of the story rather than the other way around) and you may need to know what the game feels like.  Some people may find it kind of a spoiler but I figure it's unavoidable if you need to know about the mood, right?
So, -spoiler warning- etc.  Although not really.
The setting of Danganronpa is similar to Battle Royale or The Hunger Games -- a situation that pits young adults/children against one another in a zero sum fight to the death.  The rules for Danganronpa are a more patient, however, and the game plays out more like a series of whodunit cases where the trial determines the perpetrator of a murder.
Thanks to strong character development you'll find yourself with affections for the characters, carefully developed, until they betray you in some way.  The roller coaster of emotions is evocative of Game of Thrones in that it seeks to build you up only to tear you back down again.  Only difference here is that this despair is overtly celebrated and you'll find yourself intrigued with how the game invites you into the cyclical trap of hope and despair exactly as it says it will.
SUMMARY
I really can't recommend this game enough.  There's a bit of 'made for PSP' to the edges of the game world but like most things it's overcome with tremendous style and a real passion behind the project.  You'll be "watching" more than "playing" but the strength of the storytelling is paramount here and the gameplay flows with and (more importantly) reinforces the storytelling.  There are precious few games that are like this, you need to play it to truly understand.

It has been a bit since I last played/read this. I will try to keep anything too close to a spoiler from the review.
It's one of those CYOA novels where the personality stats are more for flavoring the text, some things your character thinks/says will be different depending on their personality. It was actually done fairly well, with your characters view of those around them being fairly interesting to read and to set you up for thinking through justification for their thoughts. This goes along well with good (not great) scene writing.
While their are different paths to explore, there are not many and certain parts of them simply do not seem to change. You can basically be a warrior, a thief, a wizard, and a bard. These can have different story paths that can be fun, but the big events of the game seem largely unchanged other than how your character will skill check something. The description can be a good read, but the choice aspect of it doesn't seem as strong as others in the CYOA genre (such as Mecha Ace, one of my favorite and first CYOA by the same author).
The main problem with the novel, is that it lacks a lot of character development. Your character is essentially the A list, and there are a few B list. All of the others are basically extras. This might not be so bad if the B listers had more character development. Two of them have a decent bit, but even they are more of a few paragraphs of backstory and a few lines  of personality driven action than anything that really makes you care about them. They do not seem as their own people who have value other than telling your character some things to do and a few encouraging words. They are nothing outside of that. Your own character has some good development, though some of the studying and skill building seem to be more for a bigger world than what this CYOA provides.
This CYOA novel is okay, though the time and money might be better spent on others. It feels like the beginning of the building of a world, almost like a demo. A sequal seems hinted at by the way the CYOA is written, but I can't remember it ever being deliberately said. Currently, the novel provides some good reading but the feeling of being cramped and rushed, especially when you decide to stop and try to get a feel of what's around you. It's not the worst, but a sequal or a big rewrite is the only way I can recommend it.

So i was going to the steam store after a little vacation away from my pc with my family, to check out new deals, and this review window popped up for sky rogue, which i bought and played quite a lot of before I left. So, I figured I might as well write the review. Anyways, Sky Rogue is a nice little gem, if it was rather hidden for a while. (And still seems to be, as far as I know, I saw it had been released by looking at the new releases on the mobile steam app, as poorly designed as that app is. Like I said, it might have been on the front page, might not, idk)
On to the review. Sky Rogue is an interesting game, originally a game you could get for free (or pay for, if you liked it, which i think is pretty cool of the devs!) on their website, although i forgot what the site was. They might still have an old version up for free, last I knew they'd stopped releasing updates for free. It is a nice game, with a (imhop) neat art style, reminicsent of some more recent old arcade games that I can think of. The controlls are nice, as long as you have a controller, the keyboard and mouse controlls are ok, but not amazing. There are a few different building types and enemies, although I haven't gotten very far. It is a rogue-like, after all, you get tech points and cash by destroying enemies and buildings, and you can develop new technology using these tech points. Among these things you can unlock are new planes, bombs, homing missiles, guns, engines (which give special abilities like dodging and boost), etc. When you die, you lose some of the weapons you were carrying, but (thankfully) not the different planes. you then can use the money you earned to buy these back for use. It sounds kinda annoying, but it isn't too much of a bother. The missions are varied, whether to destroy a lab, large plane, or giant helicarrier with missiles and drones. there are many weapons, and I especially like using the bombs. There is something... beutifull about passing by a building from several kilometers in the air, and watching your carefully dropped cluster bombs hit their marks directly, as you fly into the distance. anyways, I definitely think this is well worth its cost, and that it is an amazing game.

This game tries to be a fast paced combat flight simulator. The game attempts to provide the player with a large sandbox with several targets and objects to shoot and destroy.
The issue I have is not that it is graphically simplistic (it appears it's only for the aesthetic, and not even for higher frame rates or anything), the issue is not that the game is poorly set out or that menus are atrrocious.
The issue I have is that the game is not fun.
After working the unintuitive camera and targeting system, you line up a shot and blow up enemy jets only to see a 2D explosion and the simple model slowly move down from where it was. The buildings when shot produce a particle effect and are absorbed into the ground at a rate comparible to osmosis.
Then there's what you're doing. You have little idea what's shooting at you, and often it appears as if you're killed by an enemy sneezing at you.
In the game blurb at the top of the store page the last phrase "when you die, you're dead" is a silly tautology that makes little sence. But once you play the game realise that what that means is when you're shot down, your progress is reset and you start all over again.
That fits into the next part, the dificulty curve. Following the tutorial that a 3 year old could probably complete, you're thrown into a mission that has everything set up against you, enemy jets, SAMs, etc. So you have to go thorugh securing air superiority, then dominating the ground, THEN you can go and strafe at the mission dependent target.
More or less, the issue I have is not that this game is in Early Access and that so many parts of what I didn't like would change, my issue is that the core gameplay mechanic was not fun, it was not satisfying and importantly wasn't rewarding enough. This is why I think you probably should be sceptical of this game and really consider if you really want it.

I think the witness is a good puzzle game exclusively. Unlike other games in this genre, it diches aspects of exploration and narrative to put as much emphasis as possible on puzzles, and I think it pays off here.
In the witness, the game teaches you how to solve certain types of puzzles with these special symbols in set areas with each area focusing on a different type of special rule. The game does a good job of explaining these rules to you while working you up to more complex puzzles. However, it IS an open world game, and the benefit of that is that if you are stuck on something, you can go to a different area, and try your luck there.
The benefit of that is that you should never feel like you have any one puzzle that is stopping progression since you can always go somewhere else, and when you come back, you may find that you saw something you didn't see before, which led you to the solution.
One criticism that I see from outsiders or people who never got far with the game is that it's all line puzzles. I can assure you, that is NOT a problem. No matter where you are, it's never as simple as solving these line puzzles to unlock the path/next area. EVERY puzzle area uses the environment and often the player's position and perspective of it. Many aspects such reflections, lighting, shadows, sounds, color, and positioning are all frequently used throughout the games puzzles, and it's not as simple as just drawing a line on a screen from point A to point B with the environment as just some background.
Speaking of the environment, you may notice some...interesting things as you traverse the world. Once you see more of these, you will see the game in a whole new light, which I think speaks to the creativity of the developer in many cases.
If you like to solve hard puzzles, then you will like the witness!

This was a good game when I played it. After a while, I stopped enjoying it. I enjoyed Digimon in the past, but, man, the grind game is real here. Say you found a spot where you can get a Digi-egg drop of your favorite Digimon. Now, spend about 2-3 hours to drop at least 3 of those eggs. Next, if you haven't done so already, grind specific data to hatch the Digi-egg. For the amount of data, it all depends on the egg. As for the time... difficult to gauge, but longer than an hour for around 30 data. After all is said and done, it's time to try to hatch the egg (the most nerve-racking and rage filled portion of this event). With regular egg drops and not those bought from the Cash Shop, you can very well lose the egg on your first attempt of hatching it. If you get the egg to level 3, you're in a decent spot. I say decent because it's the lowest you can hatch your Digimon at, which is most of the time under 100% of its full potential. If you want better than decent, pray to RNGesus that the attempt to level 4 doesn't break your egg. To get your egg into top tier, try your luck at level 5... Actually... just... no... slim to none chance of it actually reaching there... And that's just one thing that grinds my gears. If your Digimon aren't strong enough, you're gonna have a hard time advancing. Even your starting team (minus your starter) are below their full potenial, so doling out a lot of damage is difficult.
To sum up a poor rant, head into the game if you just want a huge grind fest.

A nice game, with some major flaws.
If you have hours and hours to waste to wait for the stupid "AI" to bring your plans to effect then this might be the game for you. Believe me, you will be hooked for hours without end. I like the music, the graphics are cute.
At the moment, however, there is actually nothing you could call an AI as in artificial intelligence. In truth, the tasks you order your population to perform are more or less randomly assigned to the available units, as well as the pathes they walk. You will often witness several of your construction units idling around close to a construction site while the task to build goes to the worst possible choice: some engineer who is on the opposite side of the base and low on nutrition and oxygen.
A regular occurrence is an engineer carrying the last needed material item to a building, then walking away instead of just building it. Another construction unit arrives half a minute later to construct the building but again walks off and leaves the construction of the connection to another unit, probably the engineer that carried the last material to the site in the first place. So it is  a matter of pure luck if building a desperately needed oxygen generator or water extractor takes a minute or five minutes (bringing your base to the brink of extinction).
On top of that the pathing is also just randomly generated. If you got 5 airlocks to leave the base you will often witness your little people chose the worst possible way to move to a target location. Indeed Ive seen people die of lack of oxygen after passing 3 airlocks in a row because the "AI" ordered them to take the detour through the 4th airlock for no good reason at all.
The worst effect of this random number generated instead of intelligent and efficience based task and pathing assignment code is however that all progress gets incredibly slow. All your plans take an eternity to show some effect. And it gets worse with the growing size of the base and the population. Adding a new solar panel to a 100 building base takes much much longer than the same task on a 20 building base. On top of that come the risks of mass starvations and the likes, and the only way to avoid these giving everything more leeway ahead, and this means throwing even more patience and time at the game.
Planetbase is a waiting game by design, you mostly watch and wait, and sometimes react to certain developments and sometimes give out orders according to your general plan. But the stupid "AI" makes the waiting really hard to endure when your base grows larger.
Do I regret the purchase? No! It is quite fun for a while if you like the kind of management and planning game. And it is fun to ponder and discuss about the problems of AI design.
Would I recommend it? Yes and no. If you dont have much time to play video games, then no. If you have plenty of spare time and dont mind to become badly bored a bit prematurely, then yes.

My Review:
"Planetbase" is a management and strategy game where you are tasked with building a self sustaining colony on a hostile planet. The game requires you to balance resources like food, water, oxygen, and electricity. You start the game right after your ship lands and have to start building immediately or your colonist will die. The game can be hard to learn at first especially because there is little room for error in the beginning. The game dose come with a excellent tutorial which I recommend playing first. I personally found this game very fun but, it's not a casual or easy. This game requires patience and thinking, and micromanagement if you don't want to think, don't play this game.
Closing Statement:
Planetbase is a fun, difficult, strategy, and management game where you have to micromanage a colony on a hostile planet, I found it enjoyable but it's not for everyone.
The Verdict:
Buy this game if you like this type of game

Very small and simple, but charming game with relaxing gameplay and beautiful art style. You move from one screen to another, interacting with characters, accomplishing quests and gathering various resources all over the map.
Story is simple and naive, but there lies its charm. Young man, whose farm was burned by bandits, is trying to take revenge on this thugs and find missing father. This story offers no surprises, but develops logically and well designed.
There is open world, you can more or less freely move around the map. On the other hand, the world is very small and it is impossible to get lost here. Quests do not shine with diversity, they just fit into formula "find something somewhere and bring it for someone". There is no variations in dialogues and you can not choose answers of your character, events are completely linear. But, as i said, story is well designed, it is interesting enough to follow the storyline and completing the quests gives you a nice feeling of progress.
There is a lot of quests and sometimes i really missed something like journal where it would be possible to see the list of active quests and their description. On the other hand, as i said, the map is small and you can walk through locations in seconds so, if you forget what people asked you to bring, it is not difficult to find active characters again and re-check what you need to do.
Sometimes, game lacks logic. For example, to kill a boar you need a dagger. You do not have a dagger but have a sword and bow with arrows? Well, then you can not kill the boar, go and find yourself a dagger. Why i can not hunt this poor pig with arrows? Game offers no answer.
Eventually, your character will learn skills to collect pearls, hunt wild animals, gather algae and so on. There is plenty of hidden items that can be collected and sold to merchants - eggs, mushrooms, treasures, crawfish... all this objects are very small and usually are well hidden, so gathering turns into annoying and merciless pixel-hunting. This is bad for eyes for sure! Fortunately, if you do not want to complete all achievements then it is not necessary to seek for hidden objects.
There is no way to lose the game, i just can not invent a situation in which you can get stuck. Abundance of resources means that you will always find something that you can sell and earn some coins. Storyline can be completed in four or five hours but, of course, if you want to collect all the mushrooms, then pixel-hunting can detain you for long. After you had finished storyline, you can continue to play and solve incompleted quests and achievements. But there is no random events, enemies and resources do not respawn, so game offers no replayability.
Anyway, game is very well designed and i can safely recommend it to anyone who seeks for relaxing and casual gameplay. Hidden gem. Very small and inexpensive gem, in fact. But still a gem.

As long time fan of the Point&Click genre, I purchased this game with little to no expectations given it was dirt cheap (less than 2€). And given that I finished it with 100% in under three hours, I'd say it was worth it.
The game is simple is to describe and analyze. It's a cartoon-animated, detective style point & click adventure with a focus on humorous yet dated jokes, puzzles that are way too easy to be worthy of the name and surprisingly good voice acting. There's not combining item+item or item+environment in order to MacGyver your way out of trouble. There's a bit of exploration and dialogue. If you click on all the right places, you'll get a puzzle that will move the story forward. Like I said... Simple.
However, despite the aformentioned features, the creator does a good job in creating a narrative that makes you want to see the game through. The characters are well thought out and the story (even thought predictable at some points) is captivating.
If you're looking for a simple yet entertaining couple of hours to pass time on a plane/trip, or if you'd like an inexpensive gift for your young gamer son/nephew, I recommended it.

After 2001, it's the end of the King of The Fighters ~ NESTS saga. You would be wondering, Is there a new story coming out from Eolith? Well, no, you will be playing the Dream Match game once more, after KOF98. The second dream match is up for you players to have another experience on the fighting arena once more. Behold! King of the Fighters 2002 ~ Challenge to the Ultimate Battle!
This game doesn't rules, but bringing back the past KOF memories.....With New Face Team back, Iori's past team mates Vice and Mature ''revived''. Rugal...... well, I can gurentee you would want to play it. And all characters were stronger now. With moves, and new experience!
This game doesn't have storyline, unfortunately, but it doesn't matter, since you are playing the ''non-story'' KOF game. This game still provides some pack of fun and fighting experience that you've ever imagined. However, your boss, is still the same Omega Rugal, except for now, he's much stronger.
Artwork could use some improvement. But a big great news is Athena became a main ''model'' for this years KOF. Her hair is longer, her cloths is beautiful. and her two fans will be with her during the whole out battle. With a cute introduction pose. She even prettier than KOF99 (sure, she is 10x better than she was in KOF2001). However, the character portraits could give some improvement. Not bad in terms of drawing, but the style doesn't give out the sense of beauty. But more or less it's up to players who decide this. I still prefer the KOF2000 artwork if you ask me.
Gameplay is still the same way as the previous KOF games, you still fight, with power bar which you fight to build it up. And use the Desperation Moves or Super Desperation Moves to do a finishing move to a character, it's the same old way that KOF games that they ever provided. Except that now, Characters gained a Hidden Super Desperation Moves, which you have to activate it when you're low on life. And needed certain command to execute it. Not bad actually.
Some of the old abilities like: Cancel, Autoguard, Backstep Jump, Rolling is back in this game. Surely, mastering the usage of those abilities will help tremendously on your fighting skills throughout the whole game. But those need some time to master it. For experienced KOF players, this never be a trouble for them. But for newbies, mastering them needs some time. Honed with those skills help you playing the versus mode easier, when you want to challenge someone into battle. Connecting Combo moves and end with a finishing move is a KOF players goal. That's what you've to do on it. Since you are more focused on combo's, not the basic Street Fighter II fighting style anymore.
Music is somewhat downgraded. Although it is taken from the previous KOF songs, I still prefer the old theme. It feels like Eolith just take the theme from the previous games and simply rearranged it. But Arcade centers are usually noisy, you won't hear that so clearly. Try to buy the soundtrack if you want to. Voice acting is good. Character voice acting is changed, to much aggressive tone. But sometimes, you'll get annoyed. Have a rest if those bugged you too much.
Loving this game is easy, replay this game is fun, but to master this game still needs your previous KOF experience and skills to play it. It's not easy if you ask me, the CPU's difficulty is tweaked, and your opponent is much smarter, and more difficult.
Overall this game is provided the best gameplay so far, so it says ''Graphic doesn't matter much, gameplay must be fun and attractive.''. I rather Eolith refines the graphic and their artwork. If they do so, I would be definitely mad on this game.......Well, at least I do love Athena this year for now! ^_^
Pros:--
-Good gameplay
-Athena is prettier
-New Abilities and Super powers, worth to try it out
-New gameplay experience
Cons:--
-Artwork needs improvement
-Music
-Difficulty is much higher than before
Overall it has more pros. than cons. But overall it is a nice game. I can't complain much on this. Hop on, It's time to play KOF2002 again. In arcade!~

I played this game when the english language version was in Closed Beta, and on and off sine then. Basically, if you're a Digimon fan, go ahead, try it, if you're not, this is a very ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game.
Objectively speaking, this is one ofn the most generic cookie cutter MMOs I have ever played, it brings absolutely nothing nre to the table and is grindy as all hell. Some like to say it's P2W, but I disagree, you can do everything without paying a single buck, with the drawback of it probably taking you your whole life, as you slowly waste away to dust. Occasionally you'll get a fetch quest (keep in mind 75% of the game is fetch quests) that refuses to let you get the required drops, and you'll be stuck grinding for hours and give up because why waste your time.
As a Digimon fan? It's fun. I coughed up the 10 or so bucks to get my favorite 'mon directly from the cash shop with items to get it to a decent size (the size percentage of your Digimon when it hatches is a permanent stat boost, RNG as ♥♥♥♥ without cash). It's still super grindy but it's a bit more tolerable when you're working towards the goal of evolving the very special computer gremlin you got with your hard earned money. There's a pretty solid guide that speeds things up too. There's a lot of Digimon available, so you're gonna have at least ONE of your favorites in the game for sure. As far as I know, every main digimon from seasons 1-5 of the show are available either through grinding or coughing up the funds. Unfortunetly the Xros Wars/Fusion cast isn't in any version of this game besides the Korean version, and I doubt Global servers will get them anytime soon. There's also a lot of neat areas inspired by the shows, like most of File Island from Digimon Adventure. Korean version also has some Xros Wars/Fusion zones, but again, not in this server yet (if it ever comes).
Outside of gameplay, thought I should mention that there are many non-english speaking players (I play on Lilithmon server), not that it's a bad thing, as it is the Global version of the game, and most team effort content doesn't need you to talk at all, just figure it's something worth pointing out ahead of time to avoid language barrier frustations if you decide you actually WANT to interact with human beings in a a game about fictional computer code creatures.
This game is absolutely horrible but I'll say give it a shot if you're a Digimon fan, at the very least it's great service to fans if you just want to get your favorite Digimon and kill some time, honestly.

First, I have to say I really enjoy this game.  If you like Banished, you will like this.  So I am recommending this.  That assumes you don't mind eventually losing, because you will under current circumstances, and that you are the type of person that does not enjoy the constant battle / zombie scenario.  Mercifully, battles seem to be at a minimum and you don't have to waste your resources on constant weapon production.
Now, there is one issue I will mention that really really annoys me.  I will call it the poor me scenario.  You have these events happening and trading, such as it is, going on, you finally get the items you need to help your people and they do... absolutely nothing.  Example:  They are standing around doing nothing because they are hungry.  Understood.  We trade for food.  There it is.  And they do, you guessed it, nothing.  Oh, except wander around the station - ok then go get food!  Eat!  Don't starve!  Nope, they wander around until they starve.
Suggestions to fix the poor me scenario - allow a rescue mission or perhaps more colonists to show up that will care for these people.  Or, make them smart enough to go. eat. food. no starve.
The other thing I would also like to see would be more planets.
I recommend this game.  It is a fun game and relaxing when I don't want to fight zombies.  This has actually become one of my top 5 favorite games I've played on Steam.

Each planet demands different strategies to survive the unique environments, each with a unique set of extremes.
This game is extremely difficult and unforgiving. You may fail quite a few times before you can get a grasp on how to manage things. Even then it can still be unpredictable at times.

I personally found it entertaining to name my crew after other Sci-Fi crews, and pretend that the characters from those books/movies/television shows were now in this realistic situation. Quite fun to watch, and losses feel more meaningful, at least in my opinion.

Overall it's a fun and challenging game, and should definitely be checked out. Buy it, play it, love it

I bought Völgarr 2 years ago and played for a while, 3 or 4 hours to be exact, never got past the second stage, so I raged quitted pretty hard, the thing is, I didn't hate the game, I hated myself for always making the same mistakes and getting caught in easy to avoid traps, I had just finished playing hotline Miami so I wanted to do everything really fast and reacting at everything as the came, something you should not do when playing Völgarr and here's why:
Völgarr is pretty straight forward, when you start the game there's nothing on the screen but Odin pointing right, and as you walk though a no more than 2 minutes of tutorial to teach you the whole game there's not much challenge when your commands consist of jumping, dodging, attacking and throwing a spear, seems easy right? and to tell you the truth it is, as long as you master these 4 actions you'll finish the game without problem.
And it may sound easy at this point but I assure you I've never played anything harder than this game, maybe because I'm impatient, but it's so easy to mess up, and It's never really something's fault besides your own, enemies can be dispatched easily with one to two hits usually, and if they take more than that I assure you they're really slow and have really easy to read attacks.
The main of the game is the platforming, it is your worse enemy for it cannot be killed, it has to be dealt with, once you jump your arch is set, you do have a second one where you can change the way you're going, but I'd say it's only on the game to make it easier, I don't thing you really need it to go through any platforming.

The little hidden object collectibles are interesting, and I think probably the thing that kept me playing the longest, since they respawn after enough time has passed.
I would like to acknowledge that the music in this is actually pretty fantastic, though. Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc is a murder mystery game with psychological horror elements that intertwines a solid theme, thick atmosphere, interesting characters and an amazing soundtrack to create one of the most compelling and engaging storylines in recent memory.
Players take control of Makoto Naegi. An average high school student who becomes enrolled in a prestigious academy full of exceptional students through sheer luck. All is not as well as it seems however as Makoto and his classmates quickly find themselves locked within the centre of a high school death game with no means of escape. That is unless they can murder one another and get away with it while the remainder of the class try to discover the identity of the killer in order to save themselves from the harsh consequences of getting the suspect wrong under the ever watchful eye of the school's headmaster, Monokuma.
The gameplay of Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc focuses upon the elements of investigation, class trials and the interaction between the characters during the entire progression of the story. During investigations it is up to Makoto and his fellow classmates to try and discover "whodunnit" and escape punishment. This is achieved through a point and click-esque system whereby you will search the school for clues, match statements with classmates and otherwise try to formulate evidence in order to take to the class trial. The class trial is where this evidence is steadily materialised into a clear image of what has transpired through the use of debate with a constant back and forth attitude whereby a lot of the enjoyment of the game comes from. Seeing the incident at hand, having a theory about it, developing the evidence and then creating your case is an immensely satisfying experience which will give you that "I KNEW IT!" feeling time and time again. Makoto can also interact with his fellow classmates during "free time events" during the story whereby he can get to know them better by seeing their viewpoint on things, viewing their own personal backstories, gift them presents and gain skills which can be put to use during the class trials themselves or in daily school life.
Overall you will find many twists and turns throughout the course of the game which will leave you shocked, bewildered and utterly amazed as the plot unfolds. Several mysteries are there to be discovered within this game and it is an extremely entertaining adventure to wrap yourself in if you're a fan of a good storyline. I would recommend this game to anyone who is even a little bit interested in the concepts highlighted within this game as it delivers on them wholeheartedly. I, myself was initially put off by the visual novel-esque style of the game at first but having since played the game I have discovered that this misgiving was entirely unfounded and the game should not be discredited for that fact alone. It stands as an incredible entry point into the visual novel style and is something I wish to see more of in the future.
**** On The Psychological Horror ****
For those who are curious on how much "horror" is within this game and are wondering whether it may put you off of this title, I will talk a bit about it briefly to help you with your decision.
The game contains little to no aspects of gore, you will see no guts and/or organs around the place. Even during the investigations at crime scenes. In addition, all blood is pink to help eliminate the gore factor as much as possible. They're also no jump scares or outright scary scenes which are present solely to get a reaction out of you. You will also not encounter environments which are inherently repulsive or make you want to vomit such as walls covered with blood and/or bodies. All aspects of terror and tension within the game are created via the storyline, the general atmosphere of the game itself and your own imagination. You may find that you are uneasy, "on edge" or maybe even creeped out by simply walking around the academy. This is perfectly natural given the overall theme of the game itself but that is the extent of it. Overall I wouldn't worry about it to much unless this is something that you don't think you can deal with.
I'm addicted. Thanks a lot Danganronpa.

The trials are a similar contradiction-objection! deal. It's filled with a lot of evidence-themed minigames that ends with a fill-in-the-blanks comic strip to replay the events. Combined with its catchy music and ever-present countdown timerit often gives the impression of a hectic, heated debate.

This was the first Choice of Games title I played, so that perhaps makes me a bit biased towards it. Regardless, though, here is my review of it.
Story wise, it's pretty simple. The description really tells you all you need to know - You're a start-up hero in a fantasy world, trying to save a city from an Evil Wizard (TM). The end game is pretty much the same no matter what path you take - Congratulations! You saved the city from the Evil Wizard (TM) and are lauded as a true Hero of Kendrickstone! Not much of a spoiler there, really. In spite of the simplicity, though, it does scratch the "fantasy hero/D&D" itch that no other CoG titles have managed to scratch thus far. The supporting cast, while as cliche as the rest of the game, still manage to be charming in their fantasy tropishness.
Mechanically, it's still not the best of the CoG games, either. Only two morality stats, compared to the sometimes five other CoG games have. The attribute system is something only a few other CoG titles can claim to have, but it is still perhaps the simplest of these attribute systems. However, it is unique in that it has a pretty detailed equipment and economy system, where you can spend money to buy permanent equipment, to gain new abilities and skills (Some of which are necessary for certain ways of completing quests), to gain temporary morale boosts which increase all of your attributes for the following quest, or to gain permanent attribute boosts. Unlike some other CoG games where cash is just sort of a show-stat so that you can delight in how much money your character has (A Wise Use of Time comes to mind), The Hero of Kendrickstone actually requires careful management of your bank account - Do you buy that book to learn wilderness tracking techniques, or do you splurge on a nice room at the inn to keep your character chipper and ready to fight the wild beasts? Do you pay the crime lord's protection fee, reducing the amount of money you have to spend on other things, or do you defy him and wake up with a knife in your bedpost, hurting your morale for the next mission?
tl;dr: Simple but charming plot, with unique equipment and currency mechanics. 8/10

I purchased this game a fair while back when it was on Itch.io, and I'm so happy I did! I enjoy flying games but often I find the really hardcore sims are just too much for me (DCS, Falcon, etc.). As such, it's nice having this more accessible game, but what really impresses me about the design is how it still manages to convey so much of what makes modern air combat interesting in such an easy-to-play package.
There are numerous types of aircraft, all of which handle significantly differently from each other. Add on top of that you can load out the different planes with different weaponry (but you can't overload your airframes maximum payload!).
The game procedurally generates islands for you to conduct your air war, and each island poses a different challenge that can be completed in multiple ways. If your target is a ground structure, do you want to destroy the enemy carrier so you won't be harassed by enemy aircraft and can bomb with impunity? Or do you want try to get a fast plane to dodge enemy fire and zip in-and-out of range before they can catch up?
The developer is very active and responsive, and I'd imagine this game will expand in some very interesting directions. But frankly, even if it doesn't, it's well worth the money for the accessible-yet-deep air combat you'll experience with the game as-is.

This was the first interactive story I've ever bought and oh boy was it worth it. It took me several days of reasonable reading rates to get through a single story-line, and from the choices to be made there are more than a few meaningful replays to be had.

I've played every DoTP on console, and they're all very fun, so I'm not sure 2014 is the best of the series.  But it is a fine iteration.  I like the mixture of new- and old-school cards, and the decks are well-themed with a few new ideas.  Sealed play is a strong addition, leading to some surprising combinations.
FAVORITE DECKS
Avacyn's Glory - Probably the "best" deck in 2014, human/angel racial with great synergy & removal
Bounce and Boon - First DoTP deck that abuses bounce mechanics, very fun when it works
Dodge and Burn - Izzet deck, almost entirely damage/counter spells.
The bad aspects are mostly flaws endemic to the series.  Such as the tedium of unlocking cards.  Why the pointless grind?  Just let me build a deck!  There must be a better way to structure unlocks.
With a fully unlocked deck the optimal card choices are mostly obvious, leading to a lot of similar builds.  Next year I'd like to see a best-of-3 mode with a sideboard you can dip into between games.
