This is my first ever review for a product and for good reason. I remember buying this game for $5 and having it sit around in my library for awhile without touching it. I've always heard good things about the X series and thought to give it a whirl. And when I did... phew.
8/10
Overall, this game is about as solid of an economic simulator that you will ever find. The sheer size of the galaxy with all of the stations, sectors, and ships is truely impressive. The premise of making money is buy-low and sell-high. However, this is a little tedious at first. With only one ship that is a bit dated it can take awhile to get the ball rolling but once you do this game shines. I've only put 40 hours in (taking a break to move on to X3) and I have about 50 ships along with about 15 stations. By carefully placing factories and making a few traders you can easily exploit holes in the in-game economy (which are intentional). As far as an economic simulator this game ranks among the best.
There is a great community behind the X series. If you ever have a question there is always a forum post to consult about figuring it out. Plus people have really gone crazy with modifying the game and there are a ton of add-ons that you can play around with. I haven't just because I wanted a normal playthrough my first time.
Combat isn't exactly the strong point in this game. Don't expect to build up massive fleets of ships like in a RTS until very late in the game. And even then, managing a huge combat fleet can be tedious. The one downfall of the combat system is that you cannot create fleets (at least I don't know how to) and this means you have to individually order all of your ships to move from place to place and attack. Despite this, I would say the combat on 1-on-1 ship battles is quite good. Thanks to a HUD it's a little easier than you would think to blow up or capture a few pirate ships. Overall, if you are looking for a game focused on combat, try elsewhere. Or at least wait until you get a Capital Ship ;)
As far as the technical side of things graphics are not bad for a game this old. The scaling is a little off and you'll wonder why a scout ship isn't the size of an ant next to a carrier trust me. The best visuals are the nebulas by far. Just fly through one and be amazed.
Well the main thing to understand about this game is that it really really really really takes a ton of fortitude. You will not have a massive empire after 20 hours (if someone knows how to get one please let me know?). You will not have billions and billions in the bank after 20 hours. Heck 20 hours was about the point when I started opening up a few factories. This game will be an absolute grind from start to finish simply because there isn't a whole lot of self-automation. Micro-managing a fleet of just 50 ships and like 2 dozen factories is super tedious. So just imagine after I play another 40 hours. So please. UNDERSTAND. This game isn't for the feint of heart. That being said, if you are a hardcore gamer than this game is right up your alley.
The other major flaw is this is somewhat of a sandbox game. Well there are objectives and a story line but they are average in that regard. How you feel about this game is determined by what you want to accomplish. For me, I want to eventually get to a few billion credits and slowly sweep everyone off the map. So I don't mind watching my ships slowly move from place to place and for my bank account to slowly grow.
Absolutely buy this game if you are looking for one of the best economic simulators. Do not buy if you want to blow up everything in sight (at least in the beginning) or if you lack patience.
Cheers!

This is a great starting point for jumping into the X-Universe.  At this point the original X: Beyond the Frontier is pretty old and probably not worth playing to someone new to the franchise.
The storyline for this game isn't that long, or particularly enthralling, but X's real draw is it's sandbox style outlook to economic empire-building in space.  It's a ton of fun if you're into that kind of thing, and the dogfighting can be a blast too.  The dynamic economy is fun to engage with, and it's not very difficult to carve out a niche for yourself and build towards being the galactic mogul you want to be.  It's a complex game, but not intimidatingly so, and once the learning curve is done with it's pretty rewarding.
Don't expect it to be primarily an action game though, and don't expect to be wowed by the plot.  Overall I recommend it because I really enjoy these type of RTS/Sci-Fi games and this is one of the better ones that I've played

Detective Grimoire is a quirky, but simple murder mystery full of charm.
First off, I'd like to say this is the second game in the series I've played. The first is a free flash game, also titled Detective Grimoire, that I played back in 2008. It's made by the same developers, SRB Games.
While the art style has improved the overall gameplay is the same. Talk to suspects, discover clues, wonder who this little girl is and why she is always at your crime scenes. It's simple enough that younger sleuths won't become frustrated, but older gamers are not bored stiff thanks to the atmosphere.
Peculiar suspects, entertaining dialog, and satisfying sound design in both music and voice acting make playing Detective Grimoire an enjoyable experience that doesn't wear out its welcome.
The only mystery left unsolved is who the little girl is?

To all the whiners panning this game: grow up.
Magic 2014 is not perfect, I will be the first to admit that. But the worst thing you can say about this game is that it does not allow for the scope of freedom that is inherant in Magic: The Gathering.
The positives, as in any good game worth your money, far outweigh the negatives. First of all there are many pre-arranged packs of cards which you can use in both the single player campaign and online with other players, and winning games unlocks more cards for each pack. You can play 1v1, or 'Two Headed Giant' mode for 2v2, or Free For All for as many as 4v4. The campaign is straightforward and entertaining (even if I still think 'Clones of Simic' encounter is lame) and teaches even novice Magic players the rudiments of the game.
Sealed Mode, which is obviously the most controversial part of this game, is misunderstood. Many players complain about not being able to trade for cards, or 'reset' their decks to get a mulligan. Guess what? That's the point of Sealed Mode, you have to make the best with what you're given. This teaches deck optimization and conservative thinking, and you can play online knowing every other player did the same, they didn't just pull a trade to arrange some pre-conceived card combo they looked up online from players better than themselves to give themselves an unfair advantage.
Magic 2014 is not only worth your time, but your money. You'd be missing out if you didn't pick it up.

This is a terrific game!  It captures the feel of playing a typical computer RPG, but without any combat difficulties.  My daughter and I play this together, and it's a perfect casual RPG for people who don't enjoy the combat aspects of typical computer RPGs.
The basic mechanism is point and click, with some hidden objects that are reminiscent of Totem Tribe.  The objects are not hidden in artificial scenes, but scattered throughout the landscape.  Actions that you can take will have prerequisites (objects you must have, for example) and you cannot take the action without meeting the prerequisites.
The game is relatively short, but if combat is your least favorite part of typical RPGs, and you hate grinding to gain levels, Hero of the Kingdom is probably for you.

Let's be honest. If you're looking for excitement or action, this is not the game for you. However, if you like casual point-and-click style games with a hidden object element and some minor resource management, this is a very satisfying little time waster. It's a bit akin to playing a facebook RPG except without having to wait for actions to refill.
For me, personally, I really enjoyed it. It satisfied my gamer OCD to see all the little actionable items slowly getting action'ed and fading from the screens, getting through the little checkpoints and "battles" without feeling rushed and thus being able to micromanage resources to their efficiency.
Considering this is considerably cheaper and lasted many times longer than, say, a comparable game from Big Fish, I highly recommend. Especially if you can pick it up on sale.
Also, about an hour of my total playtime was looking for the last f****** couple of mushrooms to get the related achievement. Thankfully, while the game does boot you back to the title screen on completion of the plot, you can still use that save file to continue getting all the achievements, if that's you wish.
Short, but fun game. Plus its very easy to get 100% achievements.

In Hero of the Kingdom you click on exclamation marks to see a checklist of materials, and then you click on the various icons scattered throughout the map to collect those materials, then you click on the exclamation mark to turn-in those materials.  You will repeat this process for the next 3-4 hours until all the exclamation marks are gone.  Then you win the game.
There is no strategy - you simply click what needs to be clicked.  This game is "item management" at its most tedious.
There are no role-playing elements - labelling this game as an RPG is inaccurate, even by the loosest of definitions.
There is no tension - you cannot fail any of the tasks given to you (which, again, is just gathering materials).
There is no story - well, there is, but it's about as generic and shallow as a story can get.
There is no gameplay - unless you're the kind of person who thinks moving rocks from one pile to another counts as a "game".
I did not hate my time with Hero of the Kingdom, but I did not enjoy it either - it simply felt like I turned my brain off for a few hours and gained nothing from it (besides some trading cards).  If that experience appeals to you, by all means buy this game (on sale).  But if you like games with even a modicum of depth to them, you should look elsewhere.

It is a good and fun game. No overdetailed graphics that run at 5 fps and are hard to look at, just very well done, various, solid design which reminds about mods HardQore (for Quake 4), HardQore 2 and Z-Hunter (for Doom 3); smooth 60 fps.
And the spirit of challenging classic 2d games is there, but modernized. In those ones you spend months of retries to complete one game, here you spend minutes of retries to complete one level, so it's nostalgic but not annoying.
And if a level is still too hard for you, you can buy one-time powerups or permanent upgrades for your weapon to make it easier.
The challenge was very fun for me, and interesting to see how far I can go, so I completed all game without any items and upgrades, only maxed out the standard gun before last boss because it seemed to be impossible to complete otherwise.
Replay value is also very enjoyable. It is a pleasure to revisit the game with more skills and better weapons.
It's funny how enemies sometimes fly off the screen. It's another nice homage to old games, modern remake of their enemies' falling through the floor.
Hilarious ending rewarded me with a good laugh.
What i'd like to criticize is that randomization of enemies and powerups didn't seem to work well at times for me. At few occurences it led me to luck-based encounters where I had to replay the level over and over until the amount and type of running enemies happened to be manageable, sometimes I got a medkit at the beginning of the level which was useless due to 100% health.
Overall, it's a really enjoyable nostalgic experience that's worth playing.
Update: it has come to my attention that some players experience a crash on level 2-2. I decided to do a quick test and successfully reproduced the bug. It happens when the flying powerup collides with an enemy, so you simply need to kill him before the powerup appears, and then you'll be able to continue.

And when you think you're finished, in a very self-referential twist the game reveals another layer of itself to complete the story. Striking and distinct audiovisual side perfectly complements the setting and folklore elements, making the game just as beautiful as it is grim and unnerving. Some criticize it for being quite short. While this is true, it doesn't have to be seen as something negative - the game is polished to the point of being virtually perfect, with no unnecessary content to better capture the essence of its meaning. I have absolutely nothing negative to say about it. It left me astounded and reflective. I have a feeling I'll be thinking about it for quite a while.

If there is anything axiomatic about game design (and perhaps design in general), it's that a well-designed piece is deliberate, each of its elements added for a reason and serving a function.
Unfortunately, even this simple rule is broken all too often in the current gaming scene: artists add flashy things because they look pretty and cool; writers create stories that don't necessarily fit gameplay well or aren't needed at all; designers use traditional elements and mechanics without giving them much thought. Obviously, there are exceptions to these sad trends, but you'd  be hard-pressed to find a reasonably complex game where nothing is arbitrary.
is such a game. More than that: it actually goes beyond simply being deliberate. Every element in the game, be it art, sound, animation, etc, doesn't only serve a purpose—it usually has
functions. As the game's designer Jonathan Blow so astutely (if unkindly) put it,
And he doesn't only criticize. He delivers too.
is a puzzle game that has you walk a visually stunning island with several separate areas, each having a bunch of puzzles, secrets, and thought-provoking vistas. What they don't have is any verbal tutorials. Everything you need to learn, including the most obscure puzzle rules, is learned through actually doing it.
Sounds simple enough, but the result is mind-blowing. Figuring out each rule feels like an achievement. The game knows it full well: your reward for being smart is often more puzzles (because no superficial reward can compare to the chance to figure out more stuff). The puzzles are very different too, requiring unexpected approaches and thinking outside the box. Going into further detail would be spoiling the game; let's just say it's very consistent in its theme, so everything you see is there for a reason.
(When grasping at straws and trying to find a flaw in
design, I half-jokingly thought that the only thing that seemed random was that we could see the protagonist's shadow for no apparent reason—having no plot, the game doesn't have to show us that the main character is human at all, so why add the shadow? Well, sure enough—as soon as I thought this, the shadow was used in a puzzle.)
This is a rare and precious thing to say, but I honestly feel that
enriched me. It made me smarter. It tested and massaged my cognitive abilities in all the right ways; even the audio logs scattered across the island (one of the more "flavourful" and less fuctional elements of the game) were genuinely interesting, with smart people talking of smart things in compelling ways.
So if you're a puzzle lover, play this game. If you're in doubt, play this game. If you're a teacher or designer, play this game. Actually, if you're none of those things, I honestly feel like it would do you good to play

I actually just bought the steam version since Gamespy has failed to authenticate my old copy of the game.  I hate DRM.  I probably have more hours in this game than any other, although I may have more time in another franchise, like Elder Scrolls, that's over three games with .  I have just never gotten into X3.  It is prettier, but the mechanics do not work for me.  This is the only game I have ever played that I can set it up and let it go, for days sometimes.  Things happen when I am away, I loose ships, but if I set it up well I can minimize that.  It is also useful to set this up efficiently since you don't want to have to handle a ship under attack somewhere else while you are playing a storyline mission.
This game is a bit dated now.  The graphics could have been better when it was launched, but this game is more about building a space empire than it is about wiz-bang graphics.  You do have to fly and fight some, but you can avoid most fighting and just be an industrialist.  The story is rather short, which is my only real complaint.
This game does take a while to learn, both the economy, and the mechanics of space flight to get the edge you need to succeed.  Many people complain about not having a mouse.  That's like saying you want a spoon to eat spaghetti!  Seriously, the mouse is just not as efficient here.  You need a keyboard to navigate the menus and a joystick to fly.  I chain my commands together so fast now I don't even have time to see what the options are anymore, I've memorized them.  Anyone with a mouse would be much slower navigating the menus.  Take a ship, "C" for command, "1" for navigation, "2" for dock, "enter" to select the current system, arrow down a certain number of times to select the destination, and hit enter to submit the command.  That is five different screens you need to select an option from for this one command.  And you may need to do this ten times in a row.  A mouse does not work with this interface well, but if you wanted to completely redesign the interface I am sure you could make a mouse just as efficient.  X3 has tried it, but it doesn't work for me.

The mysteries are a bit too simple at times and you can see some of the big plot revelations coming from miles away because of very obvious hints and foreshadowing. However, it doesn't take away from the fact that Danganronpa has a very interesting story which will keep you guessing until the very end.
I highly recommend this to any visual novel or mystery fan, or to people that might be interested in trying a visual novel. It's accessible, and the localization is done very well too.

Planetbase is not attempting to 'revolutionize' the genre. It sticks to what works and is fun in a "survival puzzle city/base builder" game.  Older gamers from the 90s may remember Sierra's Outpost game, which Planetbase strongly resembles.  This is a good thing since both games are solid and entertaining.  Younger players who are not familiar with that series can look to Banished for a similar type of game.   The game is very clean and polished.  The UI is wonderfully simple, graphics are current and the difficulty ranges from easy to increasingly difficult as you progress, similar to Banished.  Planetbase doesn't have a storyline or mission beyond surviving and growing your base.  There are some milestones that the player can reach which give a feeling of accomplishment, which is something lacking in Banished.  As I mentioned earlier, the game does get more difficult as your base grows as resource management and logistics become complicated.  Don't be surprised to see careful planning result in starving or asphyxiating your colonists due to a meteor crash! :) Overall, if you are into this type of genre and looking for a solid game to casually spend an afternoon with, choose Planetbase.  Unlike many (most) other games in the strategy market at the moment, this game isn't trying to smother you with nonsense features (that are poorly executed).  Planetbase sticks to what works and have made a game that is worth paying for.  Rate: 7/10

A minimalist, atmospheric, pretty, challenging horror puzzle game.
Year Walk captures the eerie essence of a supernatural Scandinavian forest by night, and really succeeds in the horror aspect. There is a tension that accompanies the cold sounds and bleak environs. I was very impressed by the artistic style of Year Walk. It was minimalist, bleak but also beautiful. The colours aren't vibrant but they needn't be - hell they *shouldn't be*. This is the snowy wilderness of Scandinavia. I expect white, greys, blacks. Purples and reds are also used sparingly and effectively. The puzzles can be difficult, which I find helps the game a lot. It's a bit of a throwback to when games just sort of left you to it, with few or no hints. You're pretty much on your own in Year Walk, and I had to consult a walkthrough a couple of times. Some puzzles require some thought, and I found myself utilising the whole map to complete the puzzles, so no wasted space there at all.
The story is a difficult aspect to critique because I feel the gameplay tells the story itself. So to critique the way I play the game is to critique the story. That being said, there is some backstory, which is told through some basic dialogue at the beginning of the game, and there is an encyclopaedia which accompanies you in the game, which is pretty critical to completing the game - but the information in the (very small) encyclopaedia helps give background also. I find this method of story telling to be quite innovative and also found it really help immerse me in the game. The controls are basic - arrow keys for navigation, mouse for point/click. Can't really go wrong there.
In conclusion, Year Walk is a quirky, beautiful little game. Not particularly long, but it achieves a lot in that short time, particularly in regards to puzzle solving, immersion, horror and artistry.

The thing to understand about Volgarr is that it's less a true platformer, and more a real-time puzzle masquerading as one. Each level consists of a string of little areas with some platforms, enemies, and sometimes environmental hazards. And in each area there is at least one series of actions, that, one you've found it, will allow you to path unscathed 100% of the time. At first, figuring out how to pass each area requires a lot of trial and error. But as you get used to controls, and learn enemy movement and attack patterns, you'll be able to come up with solutions on the fly. This actually makes the alternative "hard" path of the game somewhat easier than the "easy" path, as by the time you attempt to do it, you're much better at the game.

This game feels a bit too unresponsive.  Time to kill is longer than you think with most weapons.

When you pick up a new weapon, the system may automatically switch to that new weapon, which you may or may not prefer.  I was trying to use a certain weapon and get a feel for it, but every time I ran above another weapon or an enemy's corpse, I had to cycle through all the weapons again to get back to the one I wanted.  Tapping the number keys to access a particular weapon seems alright until you realize you need to reach awkwardly with i-dont-know-which finger while still controlling the WASD keys.  It seems like you build up weapon inventory, so scrolling UP to go BACK a weapon slot is strange - it should be scroll DOWN.
The weapon that is most like a sniper rifle feels wonky because the crosshair is a circle with nothing actually showing where the bullet will go in the middle of the circle.  The standard pistol feels ineffective, even when landing multiple headshots. Claiming to 'frag like it's 1999', as per its tagline, Toxikk has a hefty expectation to live up to. The game needs to not only draw inspiration from the golden age of twitch shooters like Quake 3 Arena and Unreal Tournament but to also make something new and relevant for 2017. It needs to remind us why we loved these games in the first place without being a pale imitation of a superior predecessor. Thankfully, Toxikk delivers. The game definitely feels more like a spiritual successor to Unreal Tournament: big, open maps with vehicles, a variety of classic weapon archetypes, and that classic twitch gameplay which nurtures a skillset all its own. While Toxikk doesn't enjoy the same expansive modding community that UT enjoyed, the Steam workshop integration has the potential of extending the life of the game beyond the standard experience. The solo campaign only takes a couple of hours at most but provides a nice introduction into the various game types before you choose to take on Multiplayer. This is where the game really takes you back into that simpler time of FPSs: kill or be killed without the burden of excesses of the modern shooter: no classes to choose from, no pseudo-RPG leveling to unlock weapons, and no microtransactions. If that sounds like a welcome invitation, then wholeheartedly take this trip to the past and fall in love with the FPS all over again.

So... where to start.
DMO is a MMORPG that is...somewhat connected to the well known Digimon franchise.

. But they are usually sold at a price which is not affordable.
So... you can have some fun for free... but the endgame is hardly available to those who play for free - unless ,of course, you cheat.
This is the main reason I am giving this game a negative review. It is ridden by bots and psc (a macro which allows you to attack a digimon before it spawns) users. I'd say that 50% of the servers population are actually bots. So you got a 50/50 chance to talk to a bot when attempting to talk to someone. nice, ain't it?
And the GMs /admins/ devs or whatever they are, are beyond overwhelmed by the situation. There IS a macro protector- which doesn't work in 9  out of 10 cases-or even less. And There IS a report section on the forum, BUT reporting a bot requires you to record it while playing, put it on youtube and post it on the forums..... only to then be ignored by the GMs (ergo, seeing the bot you reported one week ago bot it's way thru the game). Sounds quite frustrating , amirite?
So....
Unless you don't mind farm bots and players that steal your mobs per PSC macro - DO NOT play this game.
Or unless you plan to use a bot yourself....Which will.... most likely go unpunished,...
By the way: The punishment for botting are  a 7 day ban. So... they just come back even if your report got responded to.
A large portion of players are interested in this game mainly because they have memories of Digimon being their favourite thing during their childhood. -And I am no exception- BUT the quests have little to do with the story we used to love so much. Instead we get random quests with no story whatsoever.
So.. not much nostalgia was being had... at least not for me.
But maybe the immense number of Monsters is enough to impress you:
I have to admit that the variety of Digimon and their specific evolutions/ attacks is somewhat impressive. Even tho acquiring them is pretty.... difficult. Because we soon learn that size matters: A successfull hatch can be either 3/5, 4/5, 5/5. The x/5 determines the size of the Digimon.... Bigger= Better. Each x+1/5 requires a succesfull data insertion- IF the insertion fails, there is the possibility that your Digi-egg will break. 3 successful data insertion allows you to hatch a Digimon. But of course you want yours to be strong and big. So you go for 4/5 or 5/5.... And hatching a 5/5 manually... from 0/5 to 5/5... is pretty much impossible.
But you will get 5/5s as you lvl up... you get one for reaching tamer lvl 50 and one for tamer lvl60.... so...there's that. Personally I also got 2 5/5s from a single event.... without much grinding.....
So... even tho a lot of people use the immense RNG involved in hatching aS  a reason to down vote this game.... I gotta say....
And about the variety....- what does it matter if the meta can be counted down to one hand full of Digimon? (oh... and the meta can- of course- only be reached with cash shop items.... pay wall much?)

I'm iffy on M2014 at best. It wasn't what I expected. I expected basically a deck-building toolkit and the ability to play other people online, since I can't afford to go to local tournaments or keep updateing my deck every few months. This is sort-kinda what you get, but it has some severe limitations.
The biggest glareing issue is the fact that you don't seem to have any freedom in building a deck at all. Yes, there are about 30 different varaities of deck that you have (if you buy the gold edition), and more that can be unlocked as you play through singleplayer. But, each of those decks consist of approxamently 45 cards (not counting lands), and 30 "extra" cards that you can swap in or out of your deck to tweak it a bit; you're not allowed to greatly alter how the deck plays, nor build one from scratch. Those 30 "Extra" cards are also unique to each deck and can't be used in different decks, even if they use the same color. So if you wanted to, perhaps, move some mana acceleration from one deck to your prefered deck, or to help speed up a tragically slow deck, tough luck.
This said, whether or not this game would be good for you depends on what you're wanting. If you want free-range to build your deck and test it against other people, you're going to be greatly dissapointed. If you're a new player, unfamiliar with the game and wanting to learn how to play, then this offers a very nice interactive tutorial on how the game runs and what you can expect. If you're an experianced player, you're probably going to be frusterated by how restricted of a card pool you have to work with and how you MUST adhere to a specific archetype.
I'm going to have to vote against it. It has some good points, to be sure, and will probably help alot of newbies get into the game, but the deck-building restrictions break it for me.

My final complaint is not so much with this game in particular, but with Choice of games in general. There is no way to easily go back a page or remake a choice, You have to restart the entire story in order to reread anything or change any choice. It does not take too long to quickly remake your choices and catch up to where you left off, but doing so can be very tedious. A simple back button or save option would go a long way to making these games (Books?) more enjoyable for those of us who like to quickly explore different options and paths.

This game is indeed a work of art. Just about every member of this game's huge 60+ character roster is lethal. Beginners may have a tough time with things like learning whole teams or executing some of the higher damaging combos for certain cast members but the game is generally forgiving due to it's focus on strong pokes, unlike KoF XIII which is centered around big damage from light-confirms. And much like most other KoF games, the focus here is movement options, which can leave players from more footsie-based games (like street fighter) feeling overwhelmed/stiff until they get a grip on how to move and how to counter the options.
The netcode is wonderful (comparable to GGPO in feel but it's actually not rollback based AFAIK)  but don't expect terrific performance on WiFi (fighting games generally hate dropped packets). My only gripe is a lack of matchmaking options and chat.
And last but not least, the presentation of the game itself. The voice acting and music is superb (comparable to the likes of Guilty Gear) and I'd buy an OST CD if it was ever made available. Lots of stages if you care about that sort of thing. One fault I'd like to address here is the lack of color options / custom palletes.
Overall this port of the game is the definitive version of an almost flawless fighting game and I'd say it's an instant buy if you're even remotely interested in the series.

Before reading this, know that I own and have played plenty of fighting games, including Street Fighter, Tekken, DBZX (doesn't really count here) and both Wii and Xbox versions of NSUNS. I don't want to come across as arrogant, but I know what i'm talking bout when it comes to 2D fighters.
REAL REVIEW FOLLOWS
Pros:
+Great soundtracks
+Huge roster with very diverse characters
+Amazing online play
+Nostalgiac pixelated graphics
+Smooth gameplay
+Steam Trading Cards :)
Cons:
-Small number of online players
-No story/career mode (not really a problem with endless, team play and challange)
First of all, the all important graphics. While the pixelated arcade fighter graphics may be a major turn off for some people- and believe me, I initially didn't want to buy a pixelated fighter, however my graphics card would not allow that- it really, REALLY works with the game. You really get the feeling of playing a traditional 2D fighter. Once you start getting into the game, it really doesn't bother you. You want the pixelated graphics. You want the artwork border. And you want it to be hard to tell if a character is half nude or not (helps a lot when a parent comes in the room ;)
Online gameplay is amazingly smooth. If you have a lower end computer, you may experience very minimal lag, otherwise you'll play as if it was you versus the AI. There's actually a setting to limit the amount of frame lag there can possibly be in your match. The only problem is that there aren't too many players online all the time. Try playing later in the day, or grab a friend.
Now for the actual gameplay. KoF 2002 UM's mechanics and responsiveness is golden. Never have i had a game related problem with playing the game, not even online. This means maybe I messed up a combo move, but i've never had the game cause me to mess it up. Every character is balanced and equally powerful in my opinion. Some moves are more powerful than others, some more annoying than others. But that's one of the main components of a fighting game: every character is different and takes a different level of skill to master. There are some characters designed for veteran players- namely May, who has two different play modes in one- and some designed for beginners- namely Bao, who has a very simple moveset.
The actual roster is expansive, much larger than most fighting games including SSF4:AE, with 66 playable characters. About 60 if you discount the Orochis and secret form characters. For younger players, players with protective parents or Muslims (like me), most of the females are actually dressed decently, and I would confidently play as them in front of my parents. Stay away from Angel♥, Mai, Vice, Mature, Blue Mary, Leona, Foxy, Vanessa and Shermie. If you choose Hinako, be aware that she may panty flash you at the beginning of the match.
Just about every other aspect of the game is perfect. This is a great purchase for fighter fans and those looking for an exuse to smash their best friend's face in. If overpriced at all, I would say only by about a cent. Maybe 2 cents. If you really don't want to pay full price, grab it on sale. I got my copy and a friend's for about 6$.

VA-11 Hall-A: Cyberpunk Bartender Action is like taking a peak at what ordinary life could look like in the far future.  Life still has its troubles; people are still complex, flawed, and have secrets; and regardless of what you do or think, the world keeps spinning.  Even if society and technology have evolved to the point of having sentient AI, talking dogs, and nanomachines be a part of the daily routine, some things never change.  It may not be the most glamorous life, or the most hopeful, but we make of it what we can, and we meet people along the way who make a little corner of the world their own just like we do.  VA-11 Hall-A takes place in a world much like ours, and puts us in the shoes of someone much like you or me, to be a part of a story that's fascinating, tragic, mundane, funny, and all too familiar.
The game takes place in the titular bar VA-11 Hall-A (Pronounced Valhalla) where the main character, Jill, is the bartender.    As any normal bartender does, she mixes drinks and enjoys conversations with customers.  You're joined by your co-worker Gillian, a nice guy who nobody knows much about, and your boss Dana, a woman with a quirky personality and more than a few rumors surrounding her about her past exploits. Along the way you meet various customers, all with their own stories to tell and quirks to discover.  From an android sex-worker, to a hacker, to intelligent talking dogs, and even a few Average Joes, the game runs the whole cyberpunk gamut.  There's more to these characters than initial impressions however, and getting to know them feels like the real reward of the game.
The gameplay is minimal as you are recommended to relax and enjoy the dialogue; pallet-cleansing every so often by mixing a drink according to a customer's whims with a very simple and straightforward mixing interface.  Before each shift, you can select from a host of cyberpunk-inspired tracks to add to the jukebox that plays in the background as you go about your business, and they're all very pleasant.  The bulk of the game is spent with the characters though, and slowly developing them into people you probably wouldn't mind being friends with in real life.  The writing is sharp and grounded, and feels about as close to natural speech as text on a screen can.  Crucially as well, none of these presences feel like caricatures despite their initial labels or occupations, and the writing expresses a self-aware attitude that makes sure no character feels like just a plain archetype.  It makes the game a joy to read, and effortlessly invests the player in all of the personalities Jill encounters.
Jill herself as well, is a compelling character that feels very true to life in all of its mundane glory.  Being good at her job and serving the correct drinks puts you in good standing with the bar, and improves your pay so you can afford trinkets and decorations for your apartment during interludes away from work.  During these times, you can look up news or blogs on her phone, expanding upon the intriguing lore in the game and getting incites into the city Jill inhabits.  You can also go to a shop to buy things so Jill won't get distracted at work, but be careful not to spend too much or you could miss your rent or electricity bill.  The game comfortably deals with all facets of everyday life, even if they seem boring or depressing.  The government makes decisions that are unpopular, corporations try to get away with corruption, and the little guy (or in this case girl) has to struggle and take little moments of joy as they come.  It mimics reality and makes the world of VA-11 Hall-A feel relatable despite its more alien aspects, and the story and characters benefit from the touch of realism.
All in all, VA-11 Hall-A feels like a conversation with friends.  In many ways, it puts up a mirror to our own lives, and gives us a way to see a bit deeper and more personally into the human dilemma.  It handles its material with an intimate and mature touch rarely seen in fiction, and when it's making you laugh, or stay up late to experience more of it, or search the internet for other people who played it, or feel empathy for a fictional character, you know you've found something special.

So, a quick review of X2 The Threat.
X Games are a genre unique unto themselves. The game is basically a sandbox universe made up of multiple sectors or solar systems connected by jump gates.
The main objects in the sectors are factories which consume and produce products; and different kinds of space ships flying about doing different tasks; such as freighters collecting or delivering products, military ships defending the sector, pirates doing their business (they don’t bother you too much), and a mysterious enemy called the Khaak (that will bother you relentlessly).
You can choose the kind of role you want to play. Be a pirate hunter, stealing their ships and selling them. Become a pirate yourself if you want. Build a commercial empire with factories in multiple sectors and your own fleet of freighters – and get rich so you can buy the high-end ships and equipment and go and conquer the universe. VA-11 Hall-A: Cyberpunk Bartender Action is like taking a peak at what ordinary life could look like in the far future.  Life still has its troubles; people are still complex, flawed, and have secrets; and regardless of what you do or think, the world keeps spinning.  Even if society and technology have evolved to the point of having sentient AI, talking dogs, and nanomachines be a part of the daily routine, some things never change.  It may not be the most glamorous life, or the most hopeful, but we make of it what we can, and we meet people along the way who make a little corner of the world their own just like we do.  VA-11 Hall-A takes place in a world much like ours, and puts us in the shoes of someone much like you or me, to be a part of a story that's fascinating, tragic, mundane, funny, and all too familiar.
The game takes place in the titular bar VA-11 Hall-A (Pronounced Valhalla) where the main character, Jill, is the bartender.    As any normal bartender does, she mixes drinks and enjoys conversations with customers.  You're joined by your co-worker Gillian, a nice guy who nobody knows much about, and your boss Dana, a woman with a quirky personality and more than a few rumors surrounding her about her past exploits. Along the way you meet various customers, all with their own stories to tell and quirks to discover.  From an android sex-worker, to a hacker, to intelligent talking dogs, and even a few Average Joes, the game runs the whole cyberpunk gamut.  There's more to these characters than initial impressions however, and getting to know them feels like the real reward of the game.
The gameplay is minimal as you are recommended to relax and enjoy the dialogue; pallet-cleansing every so often by mixing a drink according to a customer's whims with a very simple and straightforward mixing interface.  Before each shift, you can select from a host of cyberpunk-inspired tracks to add to the jukebox that plays in the background as you go about your business, and they're all very pleasant.  The bulk of the game is spent with the characters though, and slowly developing them into people you probably wouldn't mind being friends with in real life.  The writing is sharp and grounded, and feels about as close to natural speech as text on a screen can.  Crucially as well, none of these presences feel like caricatures despite their initial labels or occupations, and the writing expresses a self-aware attitude that makes sure no character feels like just a plain archetype.  It makes the game a joy to read, and effortlessly invests the player in all of the personalities Jill encounters.
Jill herself as well, is a compelling character that feels very true to life in all of its mundane glory.  Being good at her job and serving the correct drinks puts you in good standing with the bar, and improves your pay so you can afford trinkets and decorations for your apartment during interludes away from work.  During these times, you can look up news or blogs on her phone, expanding upon the intriguing lore in the game and getting incites into the city Jill inhabits.  You can also go to a shop to buy things so Jill won't get distracted at work, but be careful not to spend too much or you could miss your rent or electricity bill.  The game comfortably deals with all facets of everyday life, even if they seem boring or depressing.  The government makes decisions that are unpopular, corporations try to get away with corruption, and the little guy (or in this case girl) has to struggle and take little moments of joy as they come.  It mimics reality and makes the world of VA-11 Hall-A feel relatable despite its more alien aspects, and the story and characters benefit from the touch of realism.
All in all, VA-11 Hall-A feels like a conversation with friends.  In many ways, it puts up a mirror to our own lives, and gives us a way to see a bit deeper and more personally into the human dilemma.  It handles its material with an intimate and mature touch rarely seen in fiction, and when it's making you laugh, or stay up late to experience more of it, or search the internet for other people who played it, or feel empathy for a fictional character, you know you've found something special.

On the gameplay side, there isn't much depth or though required. If you're hoping for a challenging, bar management experience, this is not the game for you. The game really relies on it's story and characters to drive the game beyond the relatively simple gameplay, and while I firmly believe it succeeds, if you aren't into story driven games, this is probably not for you.

Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc jadi salah satu game paling unik yang pernah saya mainkan. Menggabungkan genre Visual Novel, Misteri, Detektif, Dating Sim, bahkan sedikit FPS kedalamnya, Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc menjadi salah satu game paling seru & menegangkan.
Tidak ada alasan untuk tidak memberi nilai 10 untuk segi cerita. Dibangun dengan sangat matang, cerita Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc benar2 sangat sulit ditebak, asalkan kita belum menonton animenya yang sudah dirilis 2013 silam.
Kita bakal disuguhi kasus yang begitu rumit dan tricky untuk dianalisis. Cuma pada kasus pertama kita diberi petunjuk yang begitu jelas untuk diungkap, namun jangan harap bisa mengungkap kasus kedua hingga terakhir dengan mudah. Semua clue begitu membingungkan hingga "Class Trial" dimulai.
Seperti yang dikatakan sebelumnya, Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc menggabungkan genre Visual Novel, Misteri, Detektif, Dating Sim, bahkan sedikit FPS kedalamnya.
20 menit pertama, kita akan melihat gameplay standar Visual Novel yang linear & membosankan, namun selanjutnya kita bebas untuk bermain layaknya game dating sim (atau lebih mirip social link pada Persona 3 & 4) kita bisa menghabiskan waktu dengan seorang karakter, mendapatkan info personal tentangnya dan mendapatkan skill yang berguna pada "Class Trial". Kita bisa memilih dengan siapa kita menghabiskan waktu. Kita pun juga bebas menjelajah sekolah dengan mode first person.
Seiring progress cerita, kita mendapatkan sebuah kasus misteri pembunuhan & kita wajib mengungkap kasus tersebut. Kita diminta mengumpulkan petunjuk dan kesaksian setiap karakter (layaknya game point & click ala Telltale games) semua petunjuk & kesaksian yang mengarah pada kasus akan menjadi senjata kita sebagai "Truth Bullet".
Selanjutnya diadakan "Class Trial" untuk mengungkap siapa pelaku dibalik kasus tersebut. Semua karakter akan beradu argumen untuk mengungkap setiap aspek misteri dalam kasus melalui nonstop debate. Beberapa karakter akan mengungkapkan argumen lemah dalam debat. Tugas kita cukup menembak argumen lemah yang tidak sesuai dengan "Truth Bullet" yang kita miliki layaknya genre FPS (walaupun sebenarnya yang kita tembak hanyalah kalimat).
Terakhir kita menyusun semua aspek misteri menjadi sebuah satu kesatuan adegan saat terjadinya kasus tersebut. Pelaku  & semua yang dia lakukan terungkap, "Class Trial" selesai & kita akan kembali menjalani kehidupan sehari2 dengan mode dating sim.

I should probably write this to be more coherent.
Danganronpa 1 is a game that I liked and I can't remember why. On a second look, everything about it is terribly awful.
Being a VN, the plot is probably the most important thing and is a good starting point considering it's completely terrible in every way. From the start it's established you play as the blandest man on Earth, a guy who blindly follows trends and is essentially an attempt to make the self insertiest self insert ever. Obviously it's difficult to self insert as a guy who is bland and has absolutely nothing relatable about him, and if you need me to explain why then you're probably either the devs themselves, a basement dweller, or a writer for a FotS anime feautring the same repetitive scenario with harems.
This bland and unrelatable character is set forth to a school because he's really lucky or something along those lines, really this never comes into play aside from a few jokes. You meet a bizzare(ly undeveloped) cast of characters who are most known as:
1. (you)
2. The Detective
3. The Smug One
4-16. the rest
Very few of the characters are directly related to the plot at hand. In the end, when there's only 6 survivors, you could remove 3 of them and the plot wouldn't change one bit. In all, outside of their episodic cases, I think only say 5 were relevant to the overarching plot and weren't just forgotten about right after they played their parts.
But I guess those 5 characters could carry a pretty good plot, right? Nope. The plot is this: All of them get trapped in a school and have to kill eachother to get out. For pretty much the entirety of the plot they make zero progress towards this goal until the end when the mastermind basically lets them discover everything. Along the way you trip over red herrings that you never bothered to consider because they're not all that memorable (i.e. there was a traitor at one point, the 16th student, alter ego dying and coming back as a deus ex machina to save the day).
Really, I can't remember much of the plot in hindsight and I think I got all of the highlights aside from the worst part: the mastermind herself. The mastermind is Junko because the one who died was her body double and the 16th student (way to go). I could do a damned case study on how godawful of a mastermind Junko is and how her character makes no sense. Here's some concise points so I don't get a hernia writing about her.
1. How does she lead the entire world in despair despite having the attention span of a two year old?
2. How does she mastermind a killing game despite having the attention span of a two year old?
3. Her character can be summed up as "teh penguin of d00m" in real-life format.
4. How does she breathe despite being so stupid?
That and more. I forgot the finer points of why I hated her but I think the first point is more than enough to inspire a burning hatred for Junko and everything she stands for. Maybe this was explained in the anime, but I don't want to touch anything danganronpa for a while. In any case, Junko could've been handled in any number of ways other than being a Mary Sue who everyone loves so much to kill themselves for an abstract concept that very few people would want to experience and her brainwashing methods are clearly unmatched since she's able to erase people's memories. For some reason. I guess.
The rest of the characters are as unmemorable as I stated prior. They were really only shining by the light of either their sexual appeal or their talents rather than actually being somebody. It's not 'Star Wars Prequels" tiers of bad characterization but it's still awful. Most of them are killed off to serve as red herrings to the plot or just to move along the plot by opening up other parts of the school.
In fact, that's the worst part of the plot: the overreliance on cheap methods to get a jab in at the audience. You get a partner, then she dies off. There's a traitor, but they never really do anything. Alter Ego gets made, but then dies and comes back only to be a deus ex machina. There's also a 16th student, but they already died ages ago. Genocide Jack is actually one of the students, but they don't do anything other than act really annoying and appeal to the yandere audience. Out of all of these twists that could've -gone- somewhere, they chose to put in a dumb Mary Sue with a stupid motive that sounds like a Homestuck fanfiction character brought to life. And would you believe that people praise this heap for jabbing people like that despite the fact that it's not good writing at all? Basically the only appeal is that you'll /never know what happens next/ even if what happens next is headache inducing, forgettable, or just plain awful.
Really, the plot is probably the biggest of my issues with the game since the plot basically is the game. But it's not a VN (or KN I guess) entirely since the class trials that happen to decide who's the killer are given little minigames throughout. To make a long section short, let me just list down the ones I remember.
1. Endless debate. Students go in circles about something stupid and you have to tell the most stupid one who's the stupidest by tossing a truth bullet at their glowly statement. Makes up the bulk of trials and I guess it wasn't too bad.
2. Hangman's Gambit. Lose all of your health and give up several times because the game wants you to type a word in a very specific way.
3.Closing Argument. Probably the best of the minigames, you sum up the case with your logic and a manga-like closing screen. Also the best showcase of the art which was 'different' at best in other parts.
4. Rhythm game. Somehow worse than Hangman's gambit, you use your fever meter to pray that you can rush the game before you lose all of your health. The best part is when it ends.
The worst part of the trials besides the minigames circles back to the plot again, because apparently you, Kiri "tell em Naegi" giri, and Byakuya "tell em Naegi" whatshisface are the only three competent people in any given trial. If you haven't guessed by now, their competence extends to making your their mouthpiece and being cooler than you at any given moment.
You might ask "gee aren't you being a little silly there? if anyone else was competent then you'd be the stupidest guy there!" but that wasn't the case in 2 where several students were able to make suggestions and you could assist them using evidence. Not to mention the two relevant students from that one didn't use you as a mouthpiece for any other reason than plot significance, instead of doing it because muh logic game.
I'm getting tired of writing this so I'll leave all of the rest of the stuff I hated about this in a numbered list:
1. The music is, for the most part, annoying.
2. The art, as I said earlier, is only 'different'. The effects they use to make it look cooler during the class trials make this game seem like a parody of some sort. (I can almost forgive this since they made it for the Vita originally.)
3. I really, really hate Junko so I'll put this here another time.
4. The fan base is annoying. Basically the nu-Otaku morons who buy and play things because they're Japanese rather than because they're good. If you've ever seen that fat tumblr chick who only has flavor of the year popular garbage on her wall from the post SAO era of animu then you know who I'm talking about.
5. The sequel
6. Your choices don't matter worth a salty damn, all they're good for is useless 'skills'.
7. None of the humor is actually funny.
tl;dr A game that's head is so far up itself in red herrings and tricking the player that they forgot to write a good plot.

An hour or so into the game, I'm given a transporter ship and a mission to ferry some civilians from one sector to another. Accompanying me is my employer's daughter, Saya (who bears an uncanny likeness to Alyx Vance). Just as I'm approaching the last jump gate separating me and my destination, Saya's voice crackles over comms: "...I think we're being followed...I swear I saw a pirate ship." We pass through the gate and my heart sinks. A dozen pirate ships were waiting for me. I hand the controls over to the ship's computer and hop in the aft turret to lay down some desperate cover fire. The intelligent auto-pilot system gracefully and effectively dodges the brightly colored emmisions from the enemies' gamma impulse rays as I fire wildly into space. This is a transport vessel; unequipped for a sustained firefight, and woefully ineffective against a sorty of pirate ships. We aren't going to make it. But then, I remember that I have a ship docked in this sector: an M5 class Argon Discoverer light reconnaissance fighter craft. I call up my shipboard computer and access the ship to ship command console. I order my fighter to fly out into space, then I retake manual control of the transport. This plan might just work. I close the distance between my two craft to about 400 meters, rolling and weaving all the while to avoid the enemy projectiles. Commanding the transporter to dock at the TerraCorp HQ, I eject into space. Saya's voice on comms again: "W-what are you...where are you going? You can't just leave us here!" I ignore it, my plan already seeming foolish enough without her to remind me. I jetpack over to the Discoverer and enter the ship. Payback time. Locking onto the nearest pirate ship, I engage the ship's thrusters and begin pursuit. My M5 has the weakest weapons and shielding available, but I don't care. I have to protect the civilians; I have to protect Saya. The majority of the pirate ships turn to face this new threat. Two still chase the transporter. I throw my ship back and forth, narrowly dodging would-be kill shots, but still sustaining heavy damage. Shields critical. Hull at 43%. This plan was suicide. I lock on to the transport to track its progress. 200 meters out from docking. A few seconds away. With renewed hope, I turn my craft around and fly towards TerraCorp HQ and the transport. I just might pull this off. Suddenly, one of the pirates tailing the transport increases its speed and positions itself between the station and the transport. I'm 2 kilometers out, just out of effective firing range. I can only watch as the pirate ship fires a volley of lasers directly into the cockpit of the transport ship. The transport erupts in flames, spirals out of control. "No," I hear myself utter, "no no no..."  The transport ship careens into the station and explodes, and with it, my passengers. My ship's computer makes an announcement: "Attention, your Argon Express has been destroyed by a pirate Orinoco in sector Home of Light."  Saya, my employer's daughter and my character's potential love interest, dead. The pirates break formation and scatter, their mission accomplished. My M5 is crippled, my S.E.T.A. booster, one of the alpha impulse ray emmiters, and my duplex scanner all destroyed. I haven't the time to mourn, however, as I'm already receiving a message from my other employer: the Argon Secret Service. "Welcome to X2," I think to myself, as I fly my busted ship back to TerraCorp HQ. X2 improves upon Beyond the Frontier in almost every way. You can now fly any ship, leave your ship in a space suit, and trade and command stations remotely. Combat has been heavily refined, the story line improved, graphics modernized, and the universe expanded. This is the one of the few times I've ever seen a sequel outshine its predecessor, and I know that I'll enjoy every second of my journey across the X-universe.

Basically put, most players won't make it to the 3rd checkpoint. This game is so hard, it isn't even fun. Don't spend your money on this. Less then 75% of players complete the first mission on this game. Let's look at some statistics. Only 24.6% of players have even unlocked the achievement for completing the Lizard King Boss Fight. And only 54% of players have earned the achievement "The power of gray-skill" which is where you earn the flaming sword. That is the most commonly earned achievement, and only 50% of players have it. That means 50% of people won't even unlock a single achievement on this game, yet alone complete a single level. Achievements are the best example you can use, because they start being tracked once you actually play the game. If you purchase a game and just let it sit in your library, your achievement stats won't be tracked. So that means, once again, that less then 75% of active players will even beat a single level.

Tip: Take it slow. This is not a game you rush into. Be observant about what's coming up next.
You'll swear that you remember this game from "back in the day" even though it wasn't around when you were a kid. This game is tough, but fair. You will have to memorize where the enemies are, their patterns, and how to defeat them, but not in a way that seems boring, unfair, or cheap. There is a genuine feeling of accomplishment when you figure out how to get through an area. Your deaths (there will be a lot of them) always feel like your fault, and not the fault of the programming. You would have lived if you would have pressed a button just a split second faster, timed a jump a bit better, or remembered to roll at just the right time. The controls are tight and responsive. If you remember the golden age of the Super Nintendo and Sega Genesis rivalry, you'll feel right at home here. It's tough, but rewarding. You might rage quit after failing to get through a section over and over, but you'll eventually come back to try again. I highly recommend trying Volgarr the Viking.
A highlight is that there is no long, drawn out story. You start playing immediately. When you die there is no game over screen, you just start again at the last checkpoint. The ability to get into the gameplay so quickly makes this game perfect for picking up and playing when you have a free moment. There is no fluff between you and the action.
NOTE: You CANNOT steer while jumping. Once you commit to a jump, you have to wait for it to play out. This was not a problem for me, I barely even noticed it, but many people can't adjust to this play style. You have been warned.

So glad to finally play a casual game on PC that isn't a mobile port. I would characterize Hero of the Kingdom as a casual adventure game with some trading elements. There are no reflexes required, you simply need to click around the different maps to collect various items and turn them in to complete tasks. When you complete most tasks you beat the game. Overall you shouldn't expect to play this for more than a couple hours but it is a good use of time where you don't need to stress out. I found the story to be serviceable given the scale of the game.
All actions in the game are ultimately governed by its currency, which is gold. So if you want to do lots of things, such as stock up on supplies, get more hit points or hire more helpers, you need gold. This is where the trading part of the game comes in. There is only a finite number of resources you can gather before you run out, but you can manufacture more money by astutely trading the resources between various NPCs. I found this to be kind of interesting, but ultimately maybe not that constructive as the game actually gives you a good amount of money. I blame it on my RPG hoarding tendencies, but if you sell everything you gather (and you should! there are no missables!) you should only have to do a minimum of trade farming.
Lastly, many people play this game because it is easy to get 100% achievements. Not really my thing, but that could be a reason to play this game as well.

original review below:
This is a port of the XBLA version of the game.
Quite simply, this Steam port is dreadful. The sprite filter options are here but have minimal effect.
As said elsewhere in the review section, there is a distinct "line" around the sprites, hightened even more by the fact that the backgrounds in this port have been forced into hi-rez.
The screen scrolling, as your character moves left and right, suffers from judder, despite constant frame rate.
All this makes your inputs feel laggy.
I have seen others point out these problems in the reviews and they get thumbed down.
Likewise, in the forums, they get accused of not appreciating "pixel art".
The issue is not a lack of love for pixels. The issue here is a bad port.
Missing a bunch of features from the PS2 port, buy only if you played the pirated version of the original port.
"2002"...it uses sprites from 1993, same goes for the gameplay...if you want a retro KoF, go for '98.

I waited a long time for this to be ported to Steam and was excited to get it for 80% off. Though I do recommend it if you have never played it before, I have to say it is a lazy port. If you bought this on Xbox Live, you'll notice the sprites on the 360 version look less pixelated and jagged than the Steam version but if you can get past all that you'll still find KOF02 to be a solid fighting game.

If you're a fan of the older games, and you have someone
to play with, you should get this. Basically, it's the ultimate resource for KoF, and I think this is the best overall roster list you can get right now. You can see the complete roster online, but you're really spoiled for choice with this game!
It also has great controller support. Both my Xbox 360 pad and my SNES pad work perfectly, which isn't all that common for the SNES pad. And of course, keyboard is there for those that want it.
There's not really a story mode though, and this means there's no character interaction beyond the intro to a fight, where some characters might have a unique animation+sound depending on who they meet
. But keep in mind it's all Japanese audio with no subs.
KoF13 has connectivity issues, but in 2002 Ultimate Match
However, you may have to "shop around" players for a decent ping
. I've found anything up to
.
Online play is dependent entirely on ping, so if your opponent is based far away, the game will slow down to keep both players
in sync. This means that you can play with anyone in the world and have an equal chance to win, but far away players result in the game being played in slow motion! The closer you are to them, the faster the gaming experience.
You can see someone's ping before you play with them and cancel out if it's too high, but if you accidentally go ahead, there's no way of quitting without forcing the game to close via Windows!

Okay I want to start off by saying that as much as I wholeheartedly reccomend this game, it IS a horror game. I just finished a puzzle that ended in a really freaky jumpscare, and overall the atmosphere is really creepy and intense. If that's going to really freak you out or if you really can't stand games like that, this isn't the game for you.
Overall my reaction has been wholly positive so far, even if I did just get the pants scared off me. The art is gorgeous, the music is eerie but nice, and the controls are very simple, making for easy-to-learn gameplay. I don't think I'm close to finished quite yet, but between the art and the overall atmosphere of the game, I'm really enjoying playing.
And it's not just a horror game; it's a puzzle game. Puzzles that are original and unique from what I've seen in other games for the most part, and they aren't just random little things; everything seems to be fitting together, puzzles take you through many different areas of the game (thankfully there's a map), and there's an easy-to-use hint system that keeps me from getting frustrated by an 'unsolvable' puzzle. There does seem to be quite a bit of backtracking involved, as where you can move is limited (only side to side, and forwards/backwards only when there is a path), but I feel that that's a minor flaw in an otherwise entirely enjoyable game. I'll definitely be posting my full reaction to the game once I've finished, which will make for a more comprehensive review :)

X2: The Threat is the continuation of the X saga and is, for it's time, the quintessential space game. That is not to say it starts off that great. Most people will quit after a few hours of gameplay and label it a mediocre experience and they'd be right to do so, X2 is not a game that impresses in the beginning, it is a game that requires tremendous investment in time and effort before you start to understand and appreciate the scope of the game.
As the game starts up you're treated to some low quality cut-scene with poorly modeled people trying to cover up their lack of animation, you're then booted into the game with little instruction on how to do anything and a tutorial that is so completely useless at actually teaching you anything it might as well be a deterrent to keep new players from learning the game.
You will spend your first few hours struggling with your flight controls and trying to figure out how trading works stopping every once in a while to curse at the unintuitive HUD and the lazy save game system.
But then, at some point between frustration and throwing your PC out the window you will discover something. This game is awesome once you figure it out. X2 like it's predecessors doesn't want to tell you want to do, it simply wants you to do. Want to be a pirate? Go do it. Want to be a trader? Go do it. Want to be bounty hunter or a mining mogul? Go do it. Change your ship, create a fleet, manage vast networks of trade ships and mining complexes, you are free to do as you please in this vast and open universe.
There is a storyline hidden somewhere out there between the stars. The game starts you off in the classic role as a prisoner getting one last chance at redemption and as you progress through the game a story will unfold, if you want it to. The storyline is entirely optional and most people will probably end up ignoring it most of the time in favor of the open-ended gameplay that is at the core of X2.
The game is quite beautiful as you float between the stars and watch the myriad of anomalies, space stations and ships that make up the various star systems you visit. The character models and the cut-scenes however are of a much lower quality and will often make you dread having to speak to somebody aboard a space station.
All in all X2:The Threat is a great game, if you can get past the insanely steep learning curve.

The trade-fight-build-think motto quite sums it up. The game itself consists of huge universe which is divided into sectors, between which you fly by gates or jump drive. At almost all sectors there are stations at which you can land and buy/sell wares on. A factory produces weapon components which a ray emitter factory need, and will buy energy or ore from you. AI-controlled freight ships fly between those stations, across the whole universe, and search for good trades. The more ammounts of some ware a station needs, the lower the price, and so it dynamically changes and creates a complex, working economy system, which the universe relies on. You attack a ship transporting energy to a station, the station won't receive what it needs in time, it won't be able to produce the required ammounts of products, and it's sales will go down. So all your actions have their consequences and the universe feels "living" because of this, as you see all those ships traveling around you, everywhere in the universe (you should have a decent processor for this btw).
You can also make money by fighting pirates, which fly around and randomly attack other ships. If you destroy their local station, you will significantly reduce the ammount of them, in the specified area. Or if you want, become one of them and smuggle space weed on your own risk.If you choose the trade route, you can build stations and create a huge, prosperating empire. Assign freight ships to them, give them commands to work autonomously, also the same to defense ships. Then you can afford those huge capital ships which you can fly by yourself, from the bridge. The commanding console system gives you a huge power if you learn how to use it, especially if you love automatisation and to see how money quickly flow into your account!
The story is in some parts a bit frustrating and hard. Newbies find it hard to even dock with a station without exploding, or to get any money. But keep in mind that this game needs a lot of time to learn, to fully enjoy it. If you're starting with only a light fighter you can usually only attack the same classes or only one-class higher from you (and not in formation) ships, if you're good enough. I recommend to start by fighting light pirates, trading wares between stations, and do many side missions. But the real fun starts when you build at least 10 factories and get yourself a nice corvette with turrets and go exploring on your own ;)

Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc jadi salah satu game paling unik yang pernah saya mainkan. Menggabungkan genre Visual Novel, Misteri, Detektif, Dating Sim, bahkan sedikit FPS kedalamnya, Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc menjadi salah satu game paling seru & menegangkan.
Tidak ada alasan untuk tidak memberi nilai 10 untuk segi cerita. Dibangun dengan sangat matang, cerita Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc benar2 sangat sulit ditebak, asalkan kita belum menonton animenya yang sudah dirilis 2013 silam.
Kita bakal disuguhi kasus yang begitu rumit dan tricky untuk dianalisis. Cuma pada kasus pertama kita diberi petunjuk yang begitu jelas untuk diungkap, namun jangan harap bisa mengungkap kasus kedua hingga terakhir dengan mudah. Semua clue begitu membingungkan hingga "Class Trial" dimulai.
Seperti yang dikatakan sebelumnya, Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc menggabungkan genre Visual Novel, Misteri, Detektif, Dating Sim, bahkan sedikit FPS kedalamnya.
20 menit pertama, kita akan melihat gameplay standar Visual Novel yang linear & membosankan, namun selanjutnya kita bebas untuk bermain layaknya game dating sim (atau lebih mirip social link pada Persona 3 & 4) kita bisa menghabiskan waktu dengan seorang karakter, mendapatkan info personal tentangnya dan mendapatkan skill yang berguna pada "Class Trial". Kita bisa memilih dengan siapa kita menghabiskan waktu. Kita pun juga bebas menjelajah sekolah dengan mode first person.
Seiring progress cerita, kita mendapatkan sebuah kasus misteri pembunuhan & kita wajib mengungkap kasus tersebut. Kita diminta mengumpulkan petunjuk dan kesaksian setiap karakter (layaknya game point & click ala Telltale games) semua petunjuk & kesaksian yang mengarah pada kasus akan menjadi senjata kita sebagai "Truth Bullet".
Selanjutnya diadakan "Class Trial" untuk mengungkap siapa pelaku dibalik kasus tersebut. Semua karakter akan beradu argumen untuk mengungkap setiap aspek misteri dalam kasus melalui nonstop debate. Beberapa karakter akan mengungkapkan argumen lemah dalam debat. Tugas kita cukup menembak argumen lemah yang tidak sesuai dengan "Truth Bullet" yang kita miliki layaknya genre FPS (walaupun sebenarnya yang kita tembak hanyalah kalimat).
Terakhir kita menyusun semua aspek misteri menjadi sebuah satu kesatuan adegan saat terjadinya kasus tersebut. Pelaku  & semua yang dia lakukan terungkap, "Class Trial" selesai & kita akan kembali menjalani kehidupan sehari2 dengan mode dating sim.
