I should probably write this to be more coherent.
Danganronpa 1 is a game that I liked and I can't remember why. On a second look, everything about it is terribly awful.
Being a VN, the plot is probably the most important thing and is a good starting point considering it's completely terrible in every way. From the start it's established you play as the blandest man on Earth, a guy who blindly follows trends and is essentially an attempt to make the self insertiest self insert ever. Obviously it's difficult to self insert as a guy who is bland and has absolutely nothing relatable about him, and if you need me to explain why then you're probably either the devs themselves, a basement dweller, or a writer for a FotS anime feautring the same repetitive scenario with harems.
This bland and unrelatable character is set forth to a school because he's really lucky or something along those lines, really this never comes into play aside from a few jokes. You meet a bizzare(ly undeveloped) cast of characters who are most known as:
1. (you)
2. The Detective
3. The Smug One
4-16. the rest
Very few of the characters are directly related to the plot at hand. In the end, when there's only 6 survivors, you could remove 3 of them and the plot wouldn't change one bit. In all, outside of their episodic cases, I think only say 5 were relevant to the overarching plot and weren't just forgotten about right after they played their parts.
But I guess those 5 characters could carry a pretty good plot, right? Nope. The plot is this: All of them get trapped in a school and have to kill eachother to get out. For pretty much the entirety of the plot they make zero progress towards this goal until the end when the mastermind basically lets them discover everything. Along the way you trip over red herrings that you never bothered to consider because they're not all that memorable (i.e. there was a traitor at one point, the 16th student, alter ego dying and coming back as a deus ex machina to save the day).
Really, I can't remember much of the plot in hindsight and I think I got all of the highlights aside from the worst part: the mastermind herself. The mastermind is Junko because the one who died was her body double and the 16th student (way to go). I could do a damned case study on how godawful of a mastermind Junko is and how her character makes no sense. Here's some concise points so I don't get a hernia writing about her.
1. How does she lead the entire world in despair despite having the attention span of a two year old?
2. How does she mastermind a killing game despite having the attention span of a two year old?
3. Her character can be summed up as "teh penguin of d00m" in real-life format.
4. How does she breathe despite being so stupid?
That and more. I forgot the finer points of why I hated her but I think the first point is more than enough to inspire a burning hatred for Junko and everything she stands for. Maybe this was explained in the anime, but I don't want to touch anything danganronpa for a while. In any case, Junko could've been handled in any number of ways other than being a Mary Sue who everyone loves so much to kill themselves for an abstract concept that very few people would want to experience and her brainwashing methods are clearly unmatched since she's able to erase people's memories. For some reason. I guess.
The rest of the characters are as unmemorable as I stated prior. They were really only shining by the light of either their sexual appeal or their talents rather than actually being somebody. It's not 'Star Wars Prequels" tiers of bad characterization but it's still awful. Most of them are killed off to serve as red herrings to the plot or just to move along the plot by opening up other parts of the school.
In fact, that's the worst part of the plot: the overreliance on cheap methods to get a jab in at the audience. You get a partner, then she dies off. There's a traitor, but they never really do anything. Alter Ego gets made, but then dies and comes back only to be a deus ex machina. There's also a 16th student, but they already died ages ago. Genocide Jack is actually one of the students, but they don't do anything other than act really annoying and appeal to the yandere audience. Out of all of these twists that could've -gone- somewhere, they chose to put in a dumb Mary Sue with a stupid motive that sounds like a Homestuck fanfiction character brought to life. And would you believe that people praise this heap for jabbing people like that despite the fact that it's not good writing at all? Basically the only appeal is that you'll /never know what happens next/ even if what happens next is headache inducing, forgettable, or just plain awful.
Really, the plot is probably the biggest of my issues with the game since the plot basically is the game. But it's not a VN (or KN I guess) entirely since the class trials that happen to decide who's the killer are given little minigames throughout. To make a long section short, let me just list down the ones I remember.
1. Endless debate. Students go in circles about something stupid and you have to tell the most stupid one who's the stupidest by tossing a truth bullet at their glowly statement. Makes up the bulk of trials and I guess it wasn't too bad.
2. Hangman's Gambit. Lose all of your health and give up several times because the game wants you to type a word in a very specific way.
3.Closing Argument. Probably the best of the minigames, you sum up the case with your logic and a manga-like closing screen. Also the best showcase of the art which was 'different' at best in other parts.
4. Rhythm game. Somehow worse than Hangman's gambit, you use your fever meter to pray that you can rush the game before you lose all of your health. The best part is when it ends.
The worst part of the trials besides the minigames circles back to the plot again, because apparently you, Kiri "tell em Naegi" giri, and Byakuya "tell em Naegi" whatshisface are the only three competent people in any given trial. If you haven't guessed by now, their competence extends to making your their mouthpiece and being cooler than you at any given moment.
You might ask "gee aren't you being a little silly there? if anyone else was competent then you'd be the stupidest guy there!" but that wasn't the case in 2 where several students were able to make suggestions and you could assist them using evidence. Not to mention the two relevant students from that one didn't use you as a mouthpiece for any other reason than plot significance, instead of doing it because muh logic game.
I'm getting tired of writing this so I'll leave all of the rest of the stuff I hated about this in a numbered list:
1. The music is, for the most part, annoying.
2. The art, as I said earlier, is only 'different'. The effects they use to make it look cooler during the class trials make this game seem like a parody of some sort. (I can almost forgive this since they made it for the Vita originally.)
3. I really, really hate Junko so I'll put this here another time.
4. The fan base is annoying. Basically the nu-Otaku morons who buy and play things because they're Japanese rather than because they're good. If you've ever seen that fat tumblr chick who only has flavor of the year popular garbage on her wall from the post SAO era of animu then you know who I'm talking about.
5. The sequel
6. Your choices don't matter worth a salty damn, all they're good for is useless 'skills'.
7. None of the humor is actually funny.
tl;dr A game that's head is so far up itself in red herrings and tricking the player that they forgot to write a good plot.

Has no personality: not good, not terrible.
Is it the worst game ever made? No. Is it as good as Quake 3 Arena? No. First of all, you need a very good computer to run this game, if you put the game at low settings you will get only about 20 fps.
The game is overhyped, is it anything new? No not really, it's basically Unreal Tournament, but with sterile modern graphics. If you like sterile modern graphics, and you like unreal tournament, you may like this game, but you won't go crazy about it.
Now, the problems with this game.
The problems with this game are, the hitboxes are too narrow, making the pistol and bullet guns somewhat useless. The flamethrower is the only good gun, but you can't see anything that you are shooting when you flood the room with fire.
This game has no personality, no character, just the sterile, modern art style with nameless soldiers with no name, or identity, to be slaughtered in a meaningless, repetitive manner. There are no death animations, just ragdoll physics, to imply the most minimum effort possible when designing and creating the characters personalities. Overall, not the worst game ever made, but if you want a game with personality play Quake 3/Quake Live, despite the hype this does not "revolutionize" the fps genre and is actually filled with BS. Or you can play this and be flooded your soul with modern O.M.G. overflowing of modern just vacousness.

*THE VERDICT IS CLEARLY OUTLINED BELOW*
Prepare to bite your tongue and grit your teeth because "Volgarr The Viking" is HARD. Proudly flaunting that "old school" platforming difficulty that so many games go for these days, this game truly nails it. Overall the game is fun. It has some good music, it controls pretty well overall (although I personally would have liked a little more air maneuvarability when jumping), and the gameplay is satisfying. The choice to block with your shield, try to hack an enemy down with your sword (which like the whip in old school "Castlevania" games has a rythm to it and cannot be spammed for rapid damage), knowing whether or not to use an evasive roll or jump and the use of long range spears which can also act as platforms when thrown in to walls make for satisfying combat that tests not only your reflexes, but your know how. The level design, while nothing extrodanarily special is pretty good overall, with a few really cool stages in there (I particularly like the horror themed levels filled with all of the dead vikings). The same can also be said about the game's bosses: pretty good with a couple of stand-outs. My biggest issue with this game, however, is just how difficult it is in conjunction with level length and lack of check-points. You get unlimited lives (Odin be praised), but if you die it's back to the beginning of the level. While these levels aren't incredibly long, these aren't the kinds of levels like in "Super Mario Bros." where you can get through in about a minute or less if you know what your doing, either.  With each death I found myself, almost as if on instinct alone, quickly and precisely getting to where I died, getting past it, dying again, rinse and repeat. Needless to say this could be a bit tiresome from the repetive nature of its difficulty at times and a mid-level checkpoint would work wonders to alleviate this conundrum.
VERDICT
"Volgarr The Viking" is as painfully tough as shoving rusty, flaming nails in your eye sockets, and will surely cause some serious rage, especially since it could really use some mid-level checkpoints to help keep playing the same level you get stuck on  (which in my case was most of the levels; seriously this is HARD) seem less repetitive. However, pretty tight controls, fun combat and platforming, mixed with manly viking tunes make this game a treat to anyone who can handle a truly difficult game that even puts some of its "old school tough" ancestors to shame.

Have you played a game recently and thought to yourself "I don't know why this game has checkpoints or allows you to even save at all!!! It's a good game that's very hard and is fun (sort of for a sitting or two). The controls are a little on the stiff side. You cant steer yourself in the air as you can in a mario game for instance. See the game has checkpoints technically speaking. They cut the level in half into about 10 minute sections. That's not much of a checkpoint. What you do in effect is play the earlier parts of the game to absolute perfect in order to get another chance at something you might be struggling with. Is that hard? Yes it's absolutely hard to spend 10 mins doing things you are flawless at to have another go at the boss. Is it good game design? Uh... well....
No (real) checkpoints, No saves, not even an old time password system for nostalgia. Brutal difficulty that requires and insists upon repetition, perfection, and memorization. Old school hard that makes a man out of ya or antiquated game design that is not a part of most modern games for a reason? You decide. I already have.
One last thing. If you like this game and it's your jam then that's cool and good. It's good at what it does. You should check out Rastan. It's very very similar and I think it might be better so check it out if you like this game.

Fractured Soul is a wonderful 3DS escapee. A platformer built on short levels with a dual-screen dimension shift gimmick that is as disorienting as it is clever and boy does this game take that gimmick through its paces. Every possible iteration of warping between two similar platforming levels gets tried here in these tight, compact levels. The difficulty is brutal, but checkpoints are plentiful. There really is not much keeping you from the end of the game even on the Hardcore difficulty setting... well, apart from always clever, always interesting, always quick platforming. Not a second of your time is wasted (Well, I can't really say that for some of the shmup levels but even then they average out quite good, again, using the gimmick always well. And when they waste time it's just a few seconds here and there.).
The end goal of this game, though, is to go back to each of these stages and replay it until you can get a 5 star ranking, by collecting all the secrets, clearing it under par, and taking no damage. Leaderboards are implemented for those who really want to compete, and the levels do lend themselves well to perfect speedrunning.
However, even if you don't think speedrunning is the bee's knees, the levels themselves are still consistently interesting and fun for a lovely little platformer. Far, far better than the indie schlock you might see elsewhere. (*Cough* 1001 Spikes), nor does the speedrunning feel like a crutch attached to a game that just isn't worthwhile if you aren't speedrunning (*Cough* Mighty Switch Force.). Whatever your tastes are, if you want a clever, tough platformer that does not beat around the bush, you should definitely dig into Fractured Soul.

Having played this game incessantly on the 3DS, I jumped at the chance to own this masterpiece on Steam. As with most things of great value, it takes a little time to fully appreciate Fractured Soul. Initially, the gameplay, while razor sharp, will confound most players. The ability to navigate the levels over both screens is one which will take time to grow, but when it does, playing Fractured Soul is an absolute joy. The innovation behind the dual-screen mechanic is anything but a gimmick. With time, one will realize how carefully and intuitively the levels have been put together. While it may not take players much time to complete the earlier stages (particularly on the more forgiving "normal" difficulty setting), Endgame have done a wonderful job in steadily introducing additional mechanics. Just as you begin to feel comfortable with the shifting mechanic, you will have to deal with, amongst others, strong wind, inverse gravity and heat damage.
Visually, Fractured Soul looks great (the PC version has a smooth 60FPS), and if you are able to take your eyes off the action, you will appreciate some surprisingly varied and beautiful backdrops. While I very much like the aesthetic, and the story is nicely told through text between the levels (fleshed out from the brief text of the 3DS version), Fractured Soul is very much about its gameplay. The game actually develops a very specific skill set, taking the platforming genre, as trite as it sounds, to a new level. There are really two ways in which you can play this game through to the end. The first is by adequately mastering the shifting mechanic in such a way as to simply complete the levels, using as much health and time as necessary. This will probably be enough for the casual gamer, and will still provide a stiff challenge. The second way is by playing the game to the point where you have intuituvely mastered the shifting mechanic and "understand" the levels, and are thereby able to comple them within the par time, picking up all bonus items, without taking damage. To my mind, this is how the game is meant to be played. This is extremely challenging, but because the game is not "cheap" and the levels are built entirely around the effective harnessing of Entity's shifting ability, a combination of attention, care and persistence will eventually pay off. Fractured Soul is a game which at heart is built around the idea of speed running, and achieving five stars, particularly in later levels, is a truly rewarding sensation. I have recently managed to five star all thirty-one levels on the 3DS, and am looking forward to doing the same on this version.
Fractured Soul is a gem of a platformer. Obviously made with passion, it espouses real creativity and intuition without even a hint of pretension. Particularly with the low introductory price, it is a very easy recommendation, but even at full-price it is money well spent. For those who enjoyed the 3DS title as much as I did, it should be a no-brainer. The technical improvements are clear, and through over 100 brilliantly-conceived achievements you will further hone your capabilities and draw even more from this work of art. Fans of tough and true platformers should lose hours on this, and appreciate every second.
EDIT: I will echo another review that in order to appear on Fractured Soul's leaderboards, you must choose "view leaderboards" after selecting the corresponding level.

The game brings a lot to the table for such a simple concept. This isn't your Sim City, where you're just slathering buildings on the board. This requires a lot of planning and tact. Managing Oxygen, Power from Wind and Solar, Food, Medical supplies, Building supplies, and plenty more. It's challenging, and will take a few trys to get a solid base going.
The downside is the AI leaves a lot to be desired. It suffers from the same SpaceBase-DF9 plague of not being able to control them and having them not do the tasks they need to do. Often times I've had Botnists walk out the airlock and loiter outside only to turn around and clog the airlock up again trying to get back in. You have to place one building at a time and wait for it to be built or else they'll get confused and place all the resources and then walk back inside without constructing anything. Often times I've needed spare parts to repair buildings, and while I have the resources to make them, none of the engineers want to use the machine to craft them.
Other than that, the game is perfect for what it is. It will challenge you and maybe even force you to do some pre-planning before building a huge space city.

Hard to begin this review without wanting to spill everything out and start screaming for people to go buy this now. However I will hold back and express my feelings for such a perfect game.
To start, this game is about relaxing. I played it mostly on my sofa with the steam controller and most often I played this at around midnight because the music/vibe this game creates is perfect for a chill night of drink mixing. This isn't a "game" as such but more a visual novel with interactive elements (More than the normal visual novel however) You will talk to a customer and serve a drink when asked. Something I also need to express is how this isn't some diner game where you serve drinks from customer to customer quickly to make more money. The drink making is more a bridge to keep the conversations going while also being a big part of the story. A day has around 4 customers and all have some story or interesting style you just can't predict as they walk through the door. To repeat this isn't random either it's a story so it progresses and the immersion into this cyberpunk world is overwhelmingly good. After a shift you sit at home reading the ♥♥♥♥♥ esc, page at home or read the news sites that all talk about events in the city that could also end up effecting you in the pub work. This concept is so interesting and the characters/story are so intreguing that I found it hard to stop playing the game. The drink making feels great and its fun to be asked to make something, pull the ingredient list out and begin combining and mixing to get the drink made, the customers respond to what you give them and sometimes test you with vague questions "Bitter and girly" Again you feel great searching the list of drinks to find the perfect one for them or even earn some extra money by serving them a drink that costs more but meets the same requirements.
I said this game was perfect and well it pretty much is, my only complaint was the game has a lot of questions that always remain un answered at the end, whether this is to be dlc or maybe a new story in the future is uncertain to me. However this could also be because the game is centred around the main character Jill and her story is important to only herself, the other characters stories remain un answered because it's not important to you. Other than that this game is worth your time and money, sit back, click play, grab a drink and Watch this universe grow around you in this amazing story.

This is a point-n-click adventure game where you, as Detective Grimoire, are tasked with solving the murder of a proprietor of a tourist attraction that's located in a swamp. The game has nice graphics and is well-made on the whole, but I just found it way too simple, the story so-so, and the interface and gameplay aimed too much at children.
+ Mystery to be solved
+ Pretty, vibrant visuals
+ Fully voiced
+ Voice autoplays during conversations, so you can just sit back and let things flow
+ Good music
+ High production values
+ Quite a few trading cards
- Puzzles are way too simple
- Some puzzles are poorly conceived and have nothing to do with the context
- Mainly just talking to other characters
- No object use (i.e. you never have an inventory and never need to use any item)
- Not a "real" adventure game per se (due to the points mentioned above)
- Almost all the clues are pieced together by combining words to form a sentence
- Very kiddish interface
- Story is dull, uninspired, unoriginal and bland
- Conclusion is really boring and anti-climactic
- No satisfaction in solving the mystery
- Game holds your hand throughout and treats you like you're 5 years old
1) Moving objects aside to find what was beneath them. And you are
to do so. DUH.
2) Selecting the correct phrases to form a sentence. E.g. "___ was told to ___ yesterday." And the choices you are given are dead obvious.
3) Putting the correct pairs together.
4) Entering the correct code to open a lock, and the code has
to do with the lock.
5) Choosing the correct image to form a clue. E.g. On a diagram of a person hiding in a tent, you must choose a picture (out of 4 choices) that depicts what made him stay in the tent. All the choices other than the correct answer are completely nonsensical.
6) Putting gears in the correct place to open something.
7) Choosing the correct string in a tangle.
8) Matching the correct shape to the keyhole.
It's not a bad game, but it's definitely not for the discerning old-school adventure gamer looking for at least some creative & challenging adventure game puzzles to solve. Add to that a really
story with no drama or excitement whatsoever, and I say give this a miss.

This game is a very basic and traditional deathmatch shooter, with some slight variations depnding on map and gamemode, and that isn't a bad thing, because this game is intended to be a simple deathmatch shooter. It has the usual core shooter mechanics, weapon types and basic ranking, leveling and customising systems.
The game consists of a solo mode, which is different types of VS bots, and of course MP, all with a lot of customisable game elements, such as a lot of unique maps, and of course gamemodes, including all the classics, FFA, team elimination, and CTF to name a few. There is also somewhat of a competitive mode, but for neither of all gamemodes I found a lot of players, so most of my experience came from playing against mostly bots, with only so many real players joining me. But when an actual game consisting of real people comes together, the game kicks♥♥♥♥♥
Eventhough it seems quite inconsistent sometimes withexplosions or hit detection, it makes up for it in being a true fast paced fps, it even punishes you for camping, and honestly, the Dragoneer is straight up crappy and illogical, but the other weapons make up for it more than enough. Platforming is also included to make the game faster paced, but youll learn about that enough in the tutorial.
What a lot of people might be concerned with is the Full game. Let me tell you, it's purely game content, not gameplay changing. You really get the full experience, more maps, customisation options and an offline option to play against stupidly over- or underpowered bots (pls work on that). If you enjoy the game and have some 15€ around, buy the upgrade and support the game, because it deseves it.
Of course more content is always better, but for what it is and what it is intended to be, Toxikk excels in its promises. Try it out if you like uncomplicated and fast shooters in an older fashion, and maybe even upgrade to get more out of the game.

Personally, I like the Cities games. They're a cross between the odd social strata-juggling of the series' originator, City Life, and the more familiar 'build it and they will come' of the Sim City games, with the emphasis more on the building than the social stuff. That still remains an important core mechanic of the game though, so if you're looking for a city-builder with a bit more emphasis on the link between population and urban growth, Cities XXL is the one to get.
If you've never played any of the Cities games before, this is the place to start, if for no other reason than that it's a technologically much smoother, more stable ride than its predecessors. If you already have a Cities X game, then you'll have to decide for yourself if it's worth the money (there's a discount for previous owners). XXL is currently the best representative of the series, and an excellent alternative to the Maxis games.

Do you enjoy hardcore platforming while slowly mastering the mechnics in the game? Do you love speed running through levels to get those low times!? Do you enjoy unique takes on the tried and true platforming style? Then this game is for you.
As an original 3DS version players, I have to say jumping back into this game felt amazing. I have stated many times on Gamefaqs that this is the best platformer on the 3DS in my opinion. Now let me get to the review. First review ever actually.
_-Gameplay-_
The game on the 3DS version span both screen but on the PC, both screen are on one screen essentially. You switch your character accross both screens, both with their own enemies and platforms as well as obsticles. Your only actions are jump, shoot, and warp on the controller.  It is you job to get that muscle memory working and be able to not get confused by the amount of "warping" you'll be doing. You'll most likely hate the feeling at first but I insist you stick with it and keep attemping level 1 till you get the warping down and feel comfortable with it. I used to speed run this game a lot and trust me, it took a lot of time and patient to get 5 star rankings on ever level.
Added to this version is a 2 player mode where each player takes control of one of the screens. When player one warps, player two now takes control. I haven't tried it with a friend, but it feels it would be fun to butt heads together.
_-Sound-_
The music is generally quiet and helps you concentrate more on the game than the music. The music does sound a lot better than the 3DS version though, but sometimes I do wish the music was a bit louder or a bit more in the "picture" so to speak. It's a minor complaint but it's just my likings.
_-Graphics-_
Graphics have definetly improved and the colors of objects and the general area have improved. This game isn't the grandest display of GRPHIX POWA but it works and looks clean and simple. You can bump the anti-aliasing up to 8x. In the end, gameplay over graphics for this game.
_-Replayability-_
The game has tons of potential for replaying every level if you wish to improve. Every level has a set Par time to beat, crystals (names secrets) scattered all over the levels and a 5 star ranking system. In order to get a 5 star ranking you need to beat the level under par, grab all secrets, and take no damage at all. The game also saves your "any rank" times where you can rush through the level as fast as possible and score a low time as well. As the levels progress, achieveing 5 star ranks will become much harder. There are 25 normals levels ( 2 SHMUP levels, 3 boss fights, and 20 normal levels) and 6 unlockable levels. These unlockable levels will put your skills to the test and unlocked by getting as many stars from the levels (5 star ranking system). The more stars you achieve, the more extra content you get to play. This game also features leaderboards but I seem to be the only person ranked on the game currently so I'm hoping it's online compatable. NOTE: the game now features a "Normal" and "Hardcore" difficulty setting. I have no idea what the difference is but it's there if anyone was curious.
___________________________________
I hope this review pursuades you guys to experience this amazing game and I hope you enjoy it as much as I did back when I got it on the 3DS. I'm still hoping there's a little something extra for us who are double dipping to enjoy but if not, it's cool. Good luck fellow players, I'm going to be shooting for those low times!

Descending through Year Walk is liking having an ice cube put down the back of your shirt, then being pushed into the Artic Ocean. It's chilling and unnerving in a way that messes with your head, transcending its own existence into something that feels tangible; too close for comfort and so well crafted it causes you to second guess your own instincts that this is nothing but fantasy. As I sat staring at "The End" plastered across my screen, I could still feel my quickened pulse as I tried to shake the feeling of being on edge, something no piece of entertainment in any medium has managed in what feels like a very long time.
Year walking is a practice (largely found in Sweden) in which a ritual is performed by the walker through which they are given a glimpse through time at what the future holds. However, it comes at a grave cost, and there is no guarantee the walker will  even make it through alive.
Walking through a forest at midnight, snow blanketing the ground around you, you come face to face with the horrors that befall those that dare to year walk: The Watchers, twisted and greedy spirits, who demand their sacrifice for showing you what is to come. The deeper you get, the more vile and disturbing these encounters become, before you finally enter the church and see your fate.
This is when the game first ends, but it also marks the point at which the game truly begins. Up to this point you've been bustled along through this story with little in the way of explanation or reason. It's artistically brilliant and frightening to be sure, but all the same largely disconnected and without any real purpose, meant to alarm but ultimately lacking any substance. It's not then until you begin to walk again and the curtain is pulled away that the pieces fall into place and the true meaning behind your circumstances become clear. Terrifyingly so.
Year Walk is a master at what it tries to be. It lets nothing on and leaves you wandering in the dark for a good while, which only makes it more unnerving when it finally lays its cards on the table. The expert use of Swedish folklore ties its world and ours together as it attempts to break the forth wall as it weaves together fantasy and psychological horror into a brief but immensely compelling narrative. If you've gotten this far you've likely realized I've said a lot of nothing in all these words, and that's entirely intentional, as to say what makes Year Walk so brilliant would be to completely ruin it the experience. No, this is one walk that you have to take for yourself, though I promise you won't regret it.

Hard to begin this review without wanting to spill everything out and start screaming for people to go buy this now. However I will hold back and express my feelings for such a perfect game.
To start, this game is about relaxing. I played it mostly on my sofa with the steam controller and most often I played this at around midnight because the music/vibe this game creates is perfect for a chill night of drink mixing. This isn't a "game" as such but more a visual novel with interactive elements (More than the normal visual novel however) You will talk to a customer and serve a drink when asked. Something I also need to express is how this isn't some diner game where you serve drinks from customer to customer quickly to make more money. The drink making is more a bridge to keep the conversations going while also being a big part of the story. A day has around 4 customers and all have some story or interesting style you just can't predict as they walk through the door. To repeat this isn't random either it's a story so it progresses and the immersion into this cyberpunk world is overwhelmingly good. After a shift you sit at home reading the ♥♥♥♥♥ esc, page at home or read the news sites that all talk about events in the city that could also end up effecting you in the pub work. This concept is so interesting and the characters/story are so intreguing that I found it hard to stop playing the game. The drink making feels great and its fun to be asked to make something, pull the ingredient list out and begin combining and mixing to get the drink made, the customers respond to what you give them and sometimes test you with vague questions "Bitter and girly" Again you feel great searching the list of drinks to find the perfect one for them or even earn some extra money by serving them a drink that costs more but meets the same requirements.
I said this game was perfect and well it pretty much is, my only complaint was the game has a lot of questions that always remain un answered at the end, whether this is to be dlc or maybe a new story in the future is uncertain to me. However this could also be because the game is centred around the main character Jill and her story is important to only herself, the other characters stories remain un answered because it's not important to you. Other than that this game is worth your time and money, sit back, click play, grab a drink and Watch this universe grow around you in this amazing story.

Hope's Peak Academy is the top tier high school of Japan where every student aspires to go, the students are hand picked by the school categorizing them as the best of their fields, except for your own character Naegi who only got in by chance (like his talent for entry literally is just being lucky). Except when he sets foot into the school he blacks out and finds out he's locked in. Danganronpa is a "whodunnit" murder mystery game set in a high school where students are forced to kill each other under coercion by the headmaster - an evil teddy bear through motives and incentives, without being found out in order to "graduate" and leave the school or be confined within the walls of the school until the day they die. Following the murders, an investigation period is allowed where the other students will have to find evidence to use against the culprit during the class trial, where a debate among the students is held to present evidence who the culprit was. The class trial ends when the culprit is found guilty or otherwise, if so the culprit is executed, otherwise the rest of their "class" is executed and they are allowed to leave.
In terms of the story and the overall concept, I think the game does very well in those departments. It's usually never long between every murder, so the paranoia you may have against your fellow students is ever present. However, the story is actually very linear, resulting in most interactions during trials having only one correct answer and investigation periods never end until you have found every single piece of evidence you were supposed to come across. There are slow days in between every murder of course where nobody has attempted to kill anybody yet, during these days, you are given "free time" to go and talk to your classmates and get to know them better. In addition to just conversing with your classmates, you are allowed to give them gifts which help progress your friendship and earn the rewards such as skill points or skills to use during class trials. These kind of play out like what one would expect from a virtual novel or dating sim (I suppose?), but do not have any effect on the character's disposition towards you outside of these sessions. Either way, you will have to sway your classmates to trust you during the class trials as Naegi is usually the first suspect during any murder for whatever reason.
Your classmates are vastly different from each other as their expertise lies in different fields and thus can present some very interesting (or very annoying) personalities. As per the anime tradition, some of these fall into some typical stereotypes like the fat anime nerd, the japanese biker with the weird pompadour hair (why does this always prevail), the small petite loli girl, including your own character being the soft-spoken protagonist (outside of class trials). Your classmates include a stellar cast of Japanese voice actors such as Megumi Ogata (Shinji Ikari from Evangelion), Akira Ishida (also from Evangelion, Kaworu), Takahiro Sakurai (X from Megaman, Cloud from Final Fantasy), Kappei Yamaguchi (Ranma from Ranma 1/2, Inuyasha), Yoko Hikasa (Mio from K-ON!). the headliner Noboyo Oyama (Doraemon!!!) and others! You won't get to know them all
, but you'll know them well enough through the free time events! (Byakuya Togami is my favorite, arrogant rich boy persona and all, but he's not coddled or ignorant) The game's story does build on the characters and unfortunately most of them won't survive, be prepared to lose favorites and learn to not hate your least favorites so much.
The game allows you to walk in 3D around the school when going from place to place (not in the rooms themselves though), the backgrounds are extremely 2D despite this and may actually not have anything visually aesthetic to look at most of the time. The character models are also purely 2D, so if you were to tilt your camera angle in any direction they would appear like cardboard cutouts. It threw me off a little at first but in the end I paid it no mind. It's an interesting style really, the backgrounds of rooms and such drop in and come together when you enter, like a pop up book unfolding. Character art is good enough, nothing that sticks out very much but nothing that is underwhelming. There is an unlockable gallery that allows you to unlock character art and other art, I assume this is a typical visual novel feature but some of the art is pretty cool. I'm not sure how much emphasis virtual novels place on their music but Danganronpa has an unlockable gallery with music, so I would assume it's proud of its music. No doubt the music is impressive, the game goes on for a pretty long period of time but I didn't get tired of the music at all. During your class trials, the music is a bit more upbeat to emphasize the action part of this game and it does that well enough.
During the class trial sessions, you are presented various mini games that you will have to answer correctly in order to advance to the next stage, most of these are 2D shooting ones where you aim for sentences with inconsistencies or contradictions using your "truth bullets" (evidence). There are multiple sentences that can appear highlighted and you must match your shot to the right one. As I have mentioned since these have only one correct answer and the bullet graphic can only fit so many words, the usage of the bullets and where you shoot them is entirely up to interpretation and can get pretty frustrating especially when you figured out the mystery yourself. During this session, when you are presented your bullets you should read them over again to understand how to use them. Other games you are up against are a game of hangman, a rhythm game involving your argument against your classmate where you will have to follow the tempo of their statements and shoot them down, and a picture puzzle of sorts that summarizes the case all of which include an element of mystery and puzzle which you would still have to solve. The case summary picture puzzle is actually presented with manga art (which looks very good tbh) and presentation, so don't forget to go from right to left! During all of these games, you start out with 5 lives with a skill to add on another 5, answering any of these wrongly result in a loss of a single life, however answering correctly may also restore a portion of your lives back.
Last but not least is the localization, I suppose the text translation over to English is not terrible. There are some things I read in the direction translation by the author of the LP of this game some 3 years back that are apparently completely lost in translation such as references to Japanese culture and lifestyle and honorifics that some of the characters use to refer to others which would be hard to translate into English. But it's not entirely a 4kids butchering of the text, so on that note the game does okay in terms of translation. Though there are some parts that might not seem especially impressive because of the lack of emphasis in the English definitions. Quite bluntly, garbage.  The only crimes are presenting the game as being meaningful in any way and charging money for a product that wouldn't even be worth the time spent playing it for free.
Forget the idea of a world where police have forgotten why they do what they do.  The only connection to that world is in the one-sentence tagline for each of the five "games".  The games themselves are mindless mimicry of art piece drivel, the kind of stuff that you'd get on the lower end of a Junior High English project.
This could still be salvageable if the game play itself had some value, but it doesn't.  The five games are as absent in game play and mechanical design as they are in higher meaning.
The first game, by the store description, says you must "balance collecting citations with an abstract deficit, looking for tiny crimes".  No, just no.  You just trudge your tiny pixel person after any generic other pixel person, clicking your mouse on them to make numbers go up, then pressing the space bar to collect your points.  After 20 seconds, the "game" ends, and your points are added to your deficit. Then the game starts over. Because (Junior High School student idea of) "art".
The second game is about the drudgery of playing capture the flag without an opponent in a harsh environment (more Junior High "art"), which comes down to holding up+right for several seconds (to walk to the flag) then holding up+left for several seconds (to return the flag to your base), then repeating this presumably indefinitely because "art".  Though in practice, you'll probably quit right after returning to base the first time.  There isn't even a police connection in this one.
The third game actually has the basis of a real, potentially decent game.  It doesn't do anything to make it into a real, potentially decent game, but it at least has the basis of one.  The theme here is collecting evidence, but the cops have forgotten why they collect evidence or even what evidence is, so you just pick up everything you cross until you die from falling too far.
The fourth game is about controlling a couple of cops on a raft in a flooded city. As with the second game, there is again no connection with policing (or any message about it) other than the detail that the characters on the raft are cops. You just drift through the city (you have no control of the raft), and click the mouse as you pass piles of garbage (to search them.)
The fifth game doesn't bother to even pretend to be a game anymore.  And yet again, it has absolutely no connection to policing (or some distortion of policing) beyond the playable character presumably being a cop.  Walk your tiny pixel cop around a beach filled with garbage.
Rooftop Cop completely fails at delivering any message or provoking any thought.  It fails to be entertaining.  It doens't even succeed at its theme, as only two of the five games are even about distorted ideas of policing.
Piece of art. Not for everyone.

I personaly very much enjoyed, still enjoy I'll admit, these five mini-games that compose Rooftop Cop. Why for me is simmilar to my enjoyment of the Welcome to Night Vale podcast.
Both, at least to me, represent a subjective puzzle in which the player attempts to solve their lore, history, and story of how those systems(typically made of characters, objects, ideas) function in themselfs plus their interaction with one another- allowing you the player to project and stitch together the narrative: Through the five vignette* games you're given a vague picture where by its narrative evolution depends upon the lenses one analyzes it with.
Perhaps my comparriosn to WtNV sheds off here in that within its own meduim, you are not driving the ship, when unlike  video games there's the epectation for direct and explicit rewards from effort; input then fallows personally impactful output. More so, if being someone who holds the epectation of a fully air-tight complete story [or general dislike for making "narrative hypothesis" and self constructed story connections], that's not what Rooftop Cop provides.
It's a impromptu for you to fill in the gaps of the story; and, that's why I compare it to WtNV becuase that radio-podcast is the same in that both are subjective to your intrpetation, yet in WtNV progresses without imput. I mean beyond playing it and fallowed by listeing to it, WtNV progresses wither or not you've individually given its aspects thought.
Meanwhile with Rooftop Cop because its a video game I can see the un-ideal prospect of its mechanics being more of an obstacle; over that of additional layer for promoting contemplation, at least of the subjective story it evokes in each of us. _Side note, on that subject Idea Channel created a video in relation of 'Mechanics vs Nerrative' linked:

if interested.
Anyways, I enjoy the mechanics for they reminded me of the feeling of being placed in a foreign realm who's operations, traditions, and social norms differ from my own, hence [for me, implying] in order to begin to understand I ought be observant plus alongside employ experiential thought processes, and to extent; I think says upfront that this void of hand-holding, which several games do typically, is done intentionally. Fallowing the analogy just set-up, not every culture is catered, and sometimes there's fun figuing it our for yourself.

An unsettling buzz, a breaking of sunset through the fuzzy scanlines pulsating through the glow of the screen. Right away the title screen for Rooftop Cops is of a metaphysical order and not a concept we can grasp with our own hands. It's a world and a mental state that exists in already crowded and chaotic headspaces, but it is also oddly calming.
Yes, Rooftop Cop is as strange as it sounds, a collection of 5 seemingly unrelated scenarios with different metaphorical consequences accompanied by some incredible soundscapes and ambient shiftings echoing through your ears and exiting through your soul. The games are confusing, they are slow-burning in progression but that only lends itself to the incredibly strange and disjointed narrative presented. It's not something you play for "fun", but as a meditative space for thought.
If you don't like games that cause you to think or contemplate, avoid this. If you prefer having your hand held and all of your thoughts served to you on a silver platter then by all means go play one of the thousands of generic action games already on Steam, but if you're willing to dedicate your headspace to a different train of thought, to a form of art with a bit more meaning than just 'video games' then this is one surreal trip worth taking. Close-minded people need not apply.

This game is horribly, poisonously addictive.
The idea of the game is to click on certain map hotspots that either advance the plot or give you resources. You can then click on different map hotspots to exchange resources for other resources. This is sometimes puzzle-solving but much more often simply deciding which trade would be more valuable in the long run. I did say "map," and I meant it; you're looking at the Kingdom you are the Hero of from an altitude of a few hundred feet.
There's some combat, there are some choices of which path to pursue first, but overall the game is fairly linear and very simple. There's a kind of thin plot involving finding out what happened to your family, but it plays out very slowly. It feels like this was originally a mobile game, and seems especially suited to a touch screen ... though I wouldn't want to read this much text on a screen that size. (Also, there are irritating hidden objects, like mushrooms, scattered around, which are barely visible even on a full-size monitor.)
Although it never actually happened to me, it certainly seems like it's possible to get stuck without the resources you need to continue and without any ability to accomplish anything. So there's an element of resource management. Otherwise, though, this is a decidedly mechanical point-and-click game, distinguished only by the UI's bird's-eye view.

Hero of the Kingdom mixes turn-based fantasy strategy gameplay with tycoon-like resource management on a strictly casual level. What is remarkable about it is the good balance between the gameplay aspects.
Hero of the Kingdom is a resource management strategy game– something that fits well to the portfolio of the Slovakian development team– with a fantasy adventure theme.
The goal is always to gather enough resources to pass the current objective. This requires a careful management of gold (for tools to gather the resources with) and strength (which serves the role of time units). There is no combat or levelling: if you have the resources to pass an obstacle, you automatically do so.
The mechanics are decent, but not perfect: there are exploits to get infinite gold and strength (although slowly), and it is easy to get confused by the variety of required resources by the end.
The story is fairly basic: find abducted relative, find bad sorcerer, kill bad sorcerer. This simplicity works to its advantage though as it lets the game put more focus on the dozens of side quests, giving it a classic RPG feel. Still, most players will likely reach 100% completion status within 4-5 hours, making Hero of the Kingdom a short, but fun game.

When I first watched a trailer for Year Walk, I instantly fell in love with the music and art style.
Then I found that old folklore was thrown into the mix, and was instantly sold.
I didn't know whether or not the game would come through in the end, but I hoped that it would.
And it did.
You're a simple man who wants to know that which many of us wish we could foretell: "Will they always love me?"
If given the chance to see into the future over this matter, myself, I would have done the same thing.
The path is riddled with creatures that desire to impede you, and sating their desires requires some thinking and wandering.
There was never a moment that the art direction and soundtrack did not bring everything together perfectly, and as such I was completely taken into immersion.
This is definitely a horror game, and while I usually can't handle playing this genre being the scaredy cat I am, I managed to finish this. If that shows any indication as to whether or not you should pick it up if you're easily frightened, the answer is yes.
It's a bit on the short side of things, but that works just fine as you need multiple playthroughs in order to reach the true ending.
The story is much deeper than it originally presents itself to be, and I was left speechless at several points.
Year Walk took my expectations and delivered higher than I even anticipated.
I'm in a difficult time in my life right now, and can put myself inside of the protagonist's shoes perfectly. Just reverse the sexes and there you go.
This game gives you a lot to contemplate about your own life and what exactly you are willing to give up for a glimpse of what is to come.
I no longer yearn to see the future, as enticing as the notion seems to be.
At what point do we play into fate's hands or carve our own path?
That decision is yours, just like the decision to play this game.
I can't help you figure out the prior, but the latter is definitely pointing towards trying it out for yourself.

- This game is about 2.5 hours long. By the time I had 100% completetion and all achievements, I still only had 3 of 5 card drops. Had to reinstall the game and let it idle in the background to get the last two cards.
- The "puzzles" are a bit simple, and all (but one) can be solved almost by accident.
- The "internal monologue" minigame feels like a great idea that wasn't fully explored, despite being the only recurring puzzle type. Hopefully, a sequel will expand on this, as it's a refreshingly logical alternative to the "use inventory A on environment B" trial-and-error "puzzle" typical of point-and-click games. It also would have been nice to be able to call up the "thought puzzle" UI at any time to come up with new lines of questioning, rather than only in response to scripted events, with too many "obviously wrong" options to be challenging.
- The "suspicion marks" on suspects have NO bearing on any other aspect of the game, aside from one achievement. I expected them to have some effect on Grimoire's questioning of suspects, but no.
- Despite the above objections, this game is ABSOLUTELY worth buying for $5 or less, and is definitely worth two to three hours of your time.
- Headphones aren't actually necessary, but you will want to be able to hear the fantastic voice acting. Because it's fantastic. Seriously.

Recently I've been really into the old Fatal Fury games from SNK, namely Fatal Fury 2 and Special, which is why i bought KOF XIII not too long ago. While KOF XIII is a great game and is a lot of fun to play, so far KOF 2002 is my favorite of the two. The roster of 2002 is way bigger than in XIII, (there are 66 fighters for you to pick!) i really like the pixelated style of the game and many characters got an overhaul by getting new moves added to their moveset.
The controls are fluent, the special moves are easy to remember and use and i also like the fact that it actually makes a difference if you do a special move with either a light kick or a hard kick, that adds a lot more strategy to the fights.
The netcode of this game is a mixed bag, sometimes the netcode is really good, the game is fluent but other times the game runs really slow and / or choppy, but most of the time it's good. You can also see the ping difference between you and the guy you want to play against in the lobby, so if the ping is too high, you can still leave or kick the guy.
The developers are also very close to the community, they patch the game regulary and the community as a whole is very helpful.
So overall, if you enjoy fighting games with a huge variety of characters and a very high learning curve (and if you are not afraid to get your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you online) get this game. You won't regret it.

Like the King of Fighters '98 UM FE port on Steam, The King of Fighters 2002 UM port has decent netcode. I play with someone about halfway across the US and don't ever have any lag problems regardless of what the ping indicator says. Just making it that far is a struggle for the more poorly coded games, so I would assume it's good enough for continental US. Anyway, now that the most important thing is out of the way...
While 98UM FE feels pretty much like '98 to me, 2002UM feels significantly different than the 2002 I'm used to. Admittedly I've always been more of a '98 person so my playtime on 2002 isn't that high but this version feels much faster and the controls more fluid than I remember. The balance too is definitely better and most of the characters feel improved over the way they were before rather than nerfed (though there are some exceptions!). I still feel like there are some weird hitboxes, but that's not a terribly big deal compared to psycho ball cheese.
The presentation is improved, but there's only so much you can do with the ancient sprites. Whether portraits or menus pretty much everything is redrawn that isn't the actual sprites. There are new stages with cameos of other SNK characters too if you like that, but unfortunately no sort of filter to help alleviate your eyes of the pixels the size of your eyes for the actual sprites themselves.  More importantly though, the game also has an arranged soundtrack with the character themes in it. A pretty good one at that. It's one of the best additions for sure because the music Eolith put in 2002 was absolutely terrible.
'98 may be a bit dated for people who didn't play fighting games before their revival with Street Fighter 4, but I feel this version of 2002 is definitely something that can be appreciated by both newer and older players alike. It's a much better port job than 98UM FE and a fast paced, exciting game. I'm hoping more classic fighters hit Steam soon.

* You don't already own Cities XL and the game is on sale

In the beginning days of video games, your average video game was "just X" where X could be brawling, jumping, shooting stuff, etc. You had a basic gameplay loop, sometimes with a little finesse, and that was it. Story was either non-existent or laughably bad, with characters much the same. If the gameplay hooked you in, you would like the game, and if it didn't, you probably wouldn't like the game. Why? Because the game was "just X." That's typically all it was. The entire game boiled down to doing a very specific thing indefinitely.
As time wore on, extra variables were added. Sometimes, other gameplay elements would be added in, so you could have X, Y, and Z, while non-gameplay variables were added in as well, such as an A, B, and C, where A was plot, B was characters, and C was an amazing sountrack. Games had so much more going on in them; not just multiple gameplay elements, but these other elements, too. Those non-gameplay elements could appeal to players who normally would be bored out of their minds with "just X." I have been swayed into liking some games I never would have liked if not for non-gameplay elements that I enjoyed.
Toki Tori is a game that ignored this form of gaming natural selection, choosing to focus on being a puzzle game with a cute look, and nothing more. For folks who are sold on that - which is a large number of people - the game may very well be enjoyable. However, for people who think the puzzles just look "alright" or "decent," that may not be enough. Story, characters, some non-gameplay element of some sort was needed here to appeal to the crowd that doesn't want "just X" with this game's puzzles being "X." Just look at Portal's GLaDOS dialog for an example of adding something that isn't the gameplay to a puzzle game. That kind of thing wins me over, while Toki Tori was "just X" and did not. I wish I liked it (I paid for it), but I didn't have fun.

Before the age of smartphones, handhelds were the predecessors of bite-sized games meant to be played for minutes between destinations as well as challenges that resulted in player angst from defeat, which resulted in periods for the player to cool off as well as to mull over new solutions that haven’t been explored to overcome a test of skill or of wits. Toki-Tori is in the latter category as a puzzle-platformer/Rube Goldberg game formerly on the Game Boy Color before being remade for the Wii, smartphones and, finally, the “definitive” edition PC.
When I describe this version as “definitive,” I am not saying there are missing features as only the PC version has all the bonus levels, the rewind button and various control methods and level-editor. It’s when you put the history into perspective that the question of whether playing this game on the PC is the intended experience, or is likely to find its intended audience, on a platform with concerns about the first two hours of every game as well as access to the internet to find solutions due to a lack of patience with modern day puzzle games. These concerns as well as the difference of expectations for these types of games from retro handheld and modern smartphone audiences are all the weight of history Toki Tori must overcome on its bird brain.
At its core, the puzzles behind Toki Tori are not meant to be intuitive the farther you delve past the training levels that introduce mechanics and area-themes before the real challenge begins in the hard and bonus levels. Even when it comes to the basic/”easy” levels, the latter half varies specifically how much you grasp the subtitles of your tools but also in how to analyze rationing out the tools you are given for success. This combination is likely to result in player fatigue without frequent breaks.
To say that puzzles behind Toki Tori feel dated is an understatement, and that is both indicative of how modern puzzles have avoided this problem as well as simplified their challenges. In games like Snakebird, the difficulty behind the challenges may be obtuse but most puzzles can be solved in less than a minute when you know what you’re doing. In many other puzzles, the teaching of the puzzles is the real challenge whereas the precise mechanics are never a concern as players are within safe environments (a.k.a. Portal). Toki Tori, however, possesses puzzles that are so elaborate that encourages the player to try all the alternatives before coming up with the one solution that can result in the puzzle taking upwards of two to three minutes on top of the amount of time for level resets. The worst feeling a game like this can create is making you restart the whole level because you used one tool in a spot meant to psyche you out that would be required at the very end.
If you are the more patient type that enjoys spending between 15 to 30 mins on the more difficult challenges, then the satisfaction these crafted levels brings will reward the most diligent of players. These types of people are probably also the type who would enjoy making their own Toki-Goldbird Machines from the Level Editor that would test the limits of a player’s ingenuity. The result is a puzzle-game that is difficult to recommend not because the puzzles fail to be engaging but test the limits of all but the most dedicated in rigorously testing out solutions. (Thankfully, there is a demo available if you are not sure if the game is for you.)
With videos like Mark Brown’s “Game Maker’s Toolkit” gushing in praise about Toki-Tori 2, this is perhaps a cautionary review for people interested in playing Toki-Tori chronologically to understand that just because they are both puzzle games does not make them the same. As someone who tends to have a lot more patience than others, even I found the bonus levels’ difficulty spikes and some of the later stages to test my own limits whereas I enjoyed Toki-Tori 2 as much as possible without guidance. Does this make the first game worse? No, it’s indicative that these two games have differing tastes and that comparing them is like comparing collecting Oranges to utilizing Orange Portals.

Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc is a visual novel style game with elements of the Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney games. I was turned on to Danganronpa after it released on Steam and I saw it was developed by Spike Chunsoft who was also responsible for 999 and Virtue's Last Reward, both of which I'm quite fond of despite their respective flaws. Even though Danganronpa and the Zero Escape games do not share the same writing talent, they do all feature Japanese anime styled characters and have similar-ish themes.
In Danganronpa, you play as Makoto Naegi - an average student who was nevertheless accepted to an elite high school academy that only admits students considered to be the best at what they do. During his first day of school, Makoto blacks out and when he comes to he finds that he is one of several students that are trapped in the high school. All the exit doors have been barred and the windows sealed. The high school is deserted with the exception of the students and a creepy remote-controlled teddy bear who calls himself Monokuma. Monokuma tells the students that the only way to escape the high school is by killing another student without getting caught. As the days go by, various murders eventually take place and it's up to you as Makoto to gather the evidence and solve each crime
After investigating a murder scene and gathering evidence, a "class trial" takes place where the facts of the case are deliberated. Here, you'll often need to catch other students either misstating a fact or outright lying and support your cause with pieces of evidence from the case that contradict what a classmate is saying. This is where Danganronpa is most game-y and most separates itself from being just a pure visual novel. It's also where I feel this game is at its worst. The evidence puzzles seem to usually fall into one of two categories. Either the puzzle is so painfully obvious that it feels unsatisfying to solve or the puzzle is so contrived and obscure that you have to trial and error your way into the game's very specific line of thinking. The latter is particularly frustrating when the game tries to railroad you down one particular line of thinking when other possibilities seemed just as plausible to me. There are also weird rhythm game sections during the class trial that feel weak and forced. I appreciate that the game was trying to break the monotony of just reading text forever, but I often found these sections to be more frustrating than exciting
The strength of Danganronpa lies with its storytelling. It's probably unfair to compare this with the Zero Escape games even if it's the same developer, it's a different writer, but I'm going to do so anyway. I felt Danganronpa had a pretty good cast of well written characters - probably a stronger cast than any of the Zero Escape games. If you like wacky high school anime characters, Danganronpa is your game. But I found the mystery of each murder and the overall mystery of the high school much less compelling than anything written in the Zero Escape games. The Zero Escape games had me on the edge of my seat trying to figure out "whodunnit" and how it was possible and the revelation of those mysteries was always mind-blowing. Danganronpa's murders seemed a little too random and contrived. The revelation of its mysteries was always weird and wacky, but in a way that was often too unbelievable.
Summary
Danganronpa was fairly solid - good enough for me to await the release of its sequel on Steam. But I can't recommend this game without a caveat. It's still probably unfair of me to compare Danganronpa to another game not even in the same series or by the same writer, but I feel these games are similar enough to warrant me doing so: If you haven't played 999, do that first. If you have, then know that Danganronpa sacrifices a focus on a compelling and well thought out mystery in favor of more character focused moments full of anime melodrama and silliness.

A game that teaches you not to fall in love with a character, because they'll probably die.
Joking aside, I've been waiting quite a while for Dangan Ronpa to get transferred over to PC. I'm not much of a person for the PSP, so when I learned this was getting a port, I got pretty excited! It's a game that I've shown interest in, but was too lazy to read scripts for outside of the game because I have a hard time reading something that I know I could have a visual on. (If that makes sense. Basically since I knew DR was a game, I didn't want to read the scripts without pictures/audio, because it didn't feel as great to me.)
I can get why people attack the graphics of the game -- there are often visible white cut-out lines in the game, but I can't say I can attack it at all considering, well, it IS a port from the PSP. That aside, I've always adored the art style of the game. The characters are all very uniquely-designed, and the scenery in general is very nice.
The story is also very well-done, though I wish it were longer (even if the game generally takes around ~20-24 hours to beat in most cases like myself). 2-3 students getting killed per chapter cuts it quick when there's only 15 to start. ( ;) ) You think there is only killing and crime-solving to the story, but it does go a little deeper than that. . .
The ability to interact with characters and more or less form somewhat of a dating sim is pretty nice, too. Getting to know another side to a character is great. Sure love giving away some salt to someone and watching them accept it. Also love interacting with a certain Genocider very casually.
If you're willing to do quite a bit of reading and love mystery stories, I highly recommend Danganronpa to you.

After sinking many hours into this game, I can say with confidence that this is a must-play for puzzle lovers. The atmosphere and aeesthetics of the game are gorgeous, and you will find yourself pushed to your limits, in a good way, in order to make your way through this game.
Do be wary that the puzzles are ALL based on the same structure. More or less, each puzzle is like solving a maze, but with a basic twist. You need to discover the rules of this world on your own. No mandatory tutorials, no hand holding, and no in-game tips. There are certainly areas of the game that can help you learn the puzzle mechanics, but you still have to put the work in on your own.
I don't see this game being for everyone. There will be times where you may need pen or paper, or feel like giving up and looking for the answer online because you just can't figure out a puzzle on your own. However, if you enjoy puzzle games, and want an experience that I would put as the poster-child for "Video Games are art", then you'd be doing yourself a disservice by not playing The Witness.

Detective games are a somewhat tricky nature. Most lie under the hidden object category and try to convince people they're actually about mystery. Others, however, remind people of the fantastic and absurd Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney games, and Detective Grimoire is no different. In fact it's resemblence at a glance is what made me even consider buying this game. However there are a few features that seperate this game and make it a wonderful experience. Very much worth it's price tag.
If it's not going to be a hidden object game, it has to point-and-click. Not that it's bad. I'm a fan of point-and-click. And Grimoire doesn't try too much different. Standard, as far as most of its mechanics go. If you've played Sam and Max, Grim Fandango, or any game in that area, you really won't be caught off guard.
It does at least try new mechanics to invigorate the formula. For starters, every suspect has a profile attached to them with clues relavent to them and you can mark weither or not the information is suspicious. While I never noticed this mechanic to be relavent, it does help with organization quite a bit. Not to mention it makes you feel more like a detective than some random guy with way too much room in his pockets. There are other (and I hesitate to use this) mini-games that really add to the detective experience.
There is one major thing I couldn't get around, though. For movement, it is required that you click the 'move' button every time you want to move to the next area. At first it seems alright, but as I got deeper into the game, it just became an annoyance.
The characters absolutely make this game. Each of them were distinct from eachother and felt very real to me. They all act like they're going about daily life and would greatly prefer to not be interogated by some dork in a trenchcoat. (Also, Arin Hanson voices one of the characters in this. Didn't expect that!) The story itself is filled with intregue the whole way through (as is to be expected. Not much of a mystery game without a mystery). Each character has a shread of both innocence and guilt to them, and sorting out who's clean and who's the culprit is tough and rewarding.
. . . is what I would say if the culprit wasn't painfully obvious. Throughout the entire game you go back and forth between people, getting more information and grilling anyone with holes in their stories. Then near the end of the game, once you talk to everyone, a new character appears. I literally even said to myself "this guy did it, didn't he." It feels like the developers knew the other characters were too morally gray for the player to decide who it was, and added this last character to make sure no one made a wrong choice.
Does this ruin the game? Absolutely not. The story is wonderfully interesting and rewarding. The visuals are delightfully cartoony. The characters are an absolute joy. The game is great.

The first negative review I've written and certainly not something I take much pleasure in.
Chaos Domain as has been mentioned by many reviewers is a return to the age old Contra formula, static 8 directional shooting (much like the sort a classic D-pad was meant for) with awkward platforming, enemies that can shoot you through platforms that are supposed to be solid objects and ridiculously slippy controls without all the fluidity of Contras double jumping, this game is best left on the wayside.
For those of you like me, who don't own a 360 controller and don't necessarily see it as a requirement for games on a PC- don't get me started, the control scheme is a nightmare. I'm left handed and the standard controls are made with a right handed user in mind so you'll need to go through the borish task of arranging them to better suit you. The keyboard controls are poorly responsive and in a twitch shooting game where dozens of enemies might be shooting at you at once this is unacceptable.
Now on to the basics, I played one mission- that's three sections of a map that are broken up to create a single mission- so three 'check points' as it were. The beginning of the game as you might expect has you running to the right- but not able to return to the left (!) to collect missed pick ups or kill enemies and has you repeat this process three times, all while being shot by enemies through floors and walls, ceilings and anything else they seem to teleport their bullets through, which would be forgivable if you didn't get three lives (and one continue on the easier difficulty per check point) and died when you were hit once.
At the end of the first mission I was faced with a boss that is clearly a rip off of the loader from Aliens and other titles in the same franchise where it might well crop up. You are on a conveyor being dragged towards it while it fires either on a platform above it, or down the conveyor you are travelling on. You MUST hit it in the cockpit, meaning you need to be on the upper platform- not an issue, if not for the respawning guy on the platform above, lobbing grenades down at you that have an AOE far larger than is indicated by the explosion shown on screen.
It was at this point I turned the game off, and cursed myself for even bothering to pick it up.
I'm not going to list pros and cons for this, as I can't be bothered to do so. I'll simply offer my honest advice, keep your money, don't waste your time and don't waste a friends time- unless he/she and you are equally brain dead, by forking cash over for this half baked attempt at a classic and realized concept. Your friendship will swiftly end, your irritation will reach maximum levels in record time and your relatives will swiftly disown you if they learn you have this in your library.

I wasn't expecting too much from this game when I started out. There is something very minimalist about the user interface and moving about the world that I quickly found rather appealing, though. The game is very well balanced in how you gain new skills, the things you can find, the quests you can solve, and though not strictly speaking linear, there is a rough order in which things need to be done.
There was something refreshing in how you move through the world not as a fully-fleshed 3D or even 2D character, but by clicking on the buildings, people and items you wish to interact with, clicking on direction arrows on the edges of an area to move instantly to the next one. For adventure games requiring a bit of walking back and forth, and strange as it was to start with, this makes it less boring as many other games as there is no transit time to speak of to get around.
It makes for a nice game in between other more time-consuming games. With a playthrough time of 3-4 hours if you wish to do everything you can, find all you can, craft all you can, hunt all you can - not strictly speaking necessary, but there is something satisfying about making as much money as possible too.
The story is fine, the hidden-object aspect of the game for finding treasure, mushrooms, eggs, etc is nicely done, and even the unconventional combat system, if you can call it that, where you gather the resources you need to win a given battle and return to the location of it with the weapons, manpower and potions needed to overcome the enemy is an interesting and refreshing twist on what you'd expect to see in a game like this.
I think I bought this very cheaply in a bundle, but even at its regular price, I'd still feel I got a few hours of entertaining gameplay's worth for my money, and cheaper than spending a similar time in the cinema, which is how I often calculate entertainment value when it comes to computer games.
