I hate this game... For $20 there are just so many better games out there.
I love tight-controlling, 3rd-person action games. I have played DMC, Bayonetta, GoW, Ninja Gaiden, Nier, Metal Gear Rising: Revengence, Kingdom Hearts, Shiness The Lightning Kingdom, Jedi Power Battles (hey at least the reflect mechanics in power battles were "tight" :P), etc... Twin stick shooters isn't my favorite genre, but I still like those games generally too. My favorite twin stick shooter is Super Stardust HD.
If I love all those games, why don't I like Furi?
Combat ------------------------------------------
This is NOT a deep combat system at all. There are two types of combat: 1 twin stick shooter, and 2 rock-paper-scissors (the close-up melee parts).
1. During the twin stick shooter parts, you fire an EXTREMELY slow gun that does relatively little damage. These sections are all very easy but take a long time due to bosses having large timespans of invulnerability. Plus they are made easier because the bosses constantly throw out health orbs during these sections. Even though they are easy, they can sometimes be unfair at times due to the camera angle. The camera is not stright top-down, making it hard to judge depth, and sometimes the camera will zoom in away from the action. For example, during the "The Scale" boss #4, he will shoot out a large AOE and then teleport. But if he shot the AOE in the lower right of the screen and teleports to the upper left, the camera will move to the upper left and you might not be able to see the incoming AOE attack... As a twin stick shooter, Furi is kinda crappy. Other twin stick shooters like Super Stardust or Geometry Wars have much more to offer than this game.
2. After each twin stick shooter segment, there is a close-up melee fight. Every time you go into these phases, you wait for the boss to initiate an attack and counter it. You either: 1 attack him, 2 block, or 3 dodge the AOE. That is pretty much it... It is rock... paper... scissors... Having a pure rock-paper-scissors gameplay as a core mechanics is bad enough IMO, but the enemies also use the same exact same patterns every time. Thus it is no longer even rock paper scissors. It is just "who can memorized this game's bullcrap?"
Soud ---------------------------------------------
Some of the music is decent, but it gets old really fast listening to the same tune for 5+ minutes fighting one boss.
The sound effects on the other hand are awful. Most of them hurt my ears because they are just digitized scratch noises.
What about the dialogue? The enemies in this game will not shut up!!!! Some of them give the Sonic games a run for their money on how annoying they can be. And even the rabbit side character is annoying as hell. The game is trying to add to the mystery and wonder with the rabbit's dialogue, but instead of making the experience more mysterious and magical, I just noticed the writing was bad... SHUT UP RABBIT AND LET ME GET ON TO THE NEXT BOSS!!!
Rewards for beating bosses ----------------------
So you just beat a boss! Time for a reward! Guess what you get? TWO MINUTES OF WALKING ANIMATION! :P Seriously... wtf were they thinking...? Making me watch my character walk around for +2 minutes? Give me a break. They even add an auto walk feature that turns the walking sections into more-or-less a movie because the controls in the walking sects are soooooooo bad. If you try to control the walking character yourself, you will constantly fight the game as the camera angle changes and you have to release the joystick in order to re-calibrate the joystick to the current camera angle. They were smart enough to add an auto-run feature, BUT WHY CAN'T I JUST SKIP THEM?!?!?! I don't want to see my character walk around... I want to control him and be a bad♥♥♥♥♥..
Graphics ------------------------------------------
For a non-AAA game, the graphics are actually pretty decent. Some of the environemnts are neat IF I COULD ACTUALLY EXPLORE THEM INSTEAD OF JUST WATCH MY CHARACTER WALK THROUGH THEM!!!
They put more effort into the environments in-between boss fights than the boss arenas themselves. The boss arenas are such simple and forgettable locals.
Story/Atmosphere -------------------------------
This game is clearly going for a mysterious, dark, ominous atmosphere, and the story takes a back seat to the atmosphere. However, as mentioned, most of the atmosphere is established by watching your character literally walk around.... I don't give two craps about this game's attempt to build a world/story. It can go screw itself...
Conclusion ---------------------------------------
I obviously don't like this game. If you want a twin stick shooter there are better games out there (Example: Geometry Wars). If you want a 3rd person action game, there are WAY better games out there (Especially the Devil May Cry franchise).

You wake up with 15 other students in a completely sealed school and you're told by a mecha-bear that the only way out is to kill one of your team mate without being caught by the others. At the beginning everyone is of course against the concept but Monokuma will start pressuring everyone with various motives...
This game is split in 2 parts:
-slices of life where you explore the school, become friends with people and try to solve some secrets. Befriending people is done through hanging together, giving presents and it has the benefit to unblock skills that can be used during trial mode.
-trial mode where you first need to investigate the crime scene, collect clues and witnesses accounts. Then comes the trial itself where you try to discover the culprit through several kind of mini games (think Ace Attorney series of games).
When you finish the game, you unblock school mode which take place before the main story.
It's a classical resource management game where you have to collect materials in a given time frame in order to build a Monokuma clone. In parallel you get the chance to befriend everyone and complete their report card which unlock a kind of sim dating mode where you need to visit some places and choose the right dialogue option in order to improve your connection with them. This allow you to know them better and unlock their deepest thoughts via a kind of bullet event.
Overall this game have a distinct graphical (kind of 2.5D) and musical identity, story is captivating and full of cliffhangers. I can only hope that Danganronpa 2 will be available soon so I can re-immerse myself in that world.

I came in this, thinking "Oh, another Choose your Own Adventure game, I have a couple Hours to kill." These words, have never rung so falsley, I have played my fair share of CYOA, and almost all of them, span for only around three hours at most, normally with a second playthrough. But this behemoth, this magnificent behemoth of a game, clocked in at over seventeen hours.
To be honest, I bought this purely because I bought Safe Haven first, and now playing this game, it was well worth the money, all the characters where likable, even Heather and Devlin the two who were made to be unlikable still came across as charming characters with their flaws and it only made the losses of any character that more painful. Even token side characters who you knew were destined to be in the story for at most two chapters still were loveable and if anything because of their shortness the loss of them in the story resounded so much more, with such little development compared to characters like Emma or Heather, it made me feel even more, wanting to know more about them, how they survived, did they want that damn Truck. Each character really feels like just that, a character to love and cherish.
And this is all pulled together through amazing writing, few times did I notice a rehashed line, the only exception with choosing a loudout, though that is to be forgiven since you are experimenting with loudouts quite often, how many times can they describe a fifty foot coil of rope? Not too many times I imagine. But all thsi writing would be wasted on without a good overarching narrative. And did it have one? Yeah.
It is generic, by lord is it generic, but the writing style makes up for it and genericisim is never a bad thing. If done right it can become a great literary tool, something this honestly is. But overall, Ten out of Ten would play again.

It's a very pretty game with some neat puzzles but the real good stuff takes a backseat to the kind of puzzles you'd find in the sunday morning newspaper or puzzle books for the grand majority of the game-- which of course begs the question, why does this need to be a video game? These puzzles *are* handled really well, however. The Witness manages to teach players new mechanics wordlessly-- given the player can actually find the area that teaches each mechanic before they come across an area with it already in play. I managed to come across a later game area within my first ten minutes-- I almost stopped playing the game completely since I thought it *meant* to toss a bunch of new mechanics my way right out the gate. Some sort of map or hint at where to go near the beginning area would have helped a lot. Only a handful of puzzles work around perception, angles, and the like-- I actually enjoyed them-- that's what I came to this game for. Perhaps the story is the saving grace for The Witness? If there was a story, maybe. I get the feeling that the developers wanted players to take some deeper meaning from the game but it just isn't presented very well-- and by that I mean it's only through audio logs of a seemingly random assortment of lectures, writings, quotes, and documentary excerpts that seem to exist soley to give the impression of something deeper. If you want something pretty to explore, this game is fantastic. If you like a game full of longer puzzles back to back, you'll enjoy it. If you want anything else with the puzzles? You're out of luck.

is easily the hardest puzzle game that I have ever played, and I

People who will like this game: fans of Myst, people who like puzzle games
People who will not like this game: anybody expecting an adventure game that is as much adventure as it is puzzle-solving.
First, the good. This game is beautiful. The colors remind me of my first impression of Mirror's Edge. It's visually incredible. The sounds also reflect the environment beautifully. There are also these recordings you can find throughout the game that augment the experience with quotations from philosophers, scientists and theologians, which contributes to the overall atmoshere of the game. The scenery of the island and the landscape itself is also quite interesting and well-crafted.
The game is created to encourage your sense of mystery. What happened to the island? Where did everyone go? What are all of these machines for? The clues you pick up along the way suggest the island folk were pushing toward something deeply mysterious--some sense of the supernatural but deeply scientific.
Unfortunately, the biggest problem with the game is the game play. You start off solving these basic maze-type puzzles. And then you solve more. And then more. In fact, the entire game is a very basic puzzle-solving game with a narrative somewhere in the background. Tired of doing that "start at the beginning and go to the end" type puzzles? Too bad. Getting bored of the "variations on a theme"? Too bad. That's literally the whole game: solve one puzzle to unlock another puzzle, to unlock another one and eventually to get a giant laser to pop up and then go and solve more puzzles.
If you're thinking this will be like adventure games of yore (Syberia, Monkey Island, Indigo Prophecy, Darkfall), be ready for disappointment. You never get any clues from the environment or other persons. There's nothing to tell you what you should be doing, and you're basically left with pure trial-and-error style gaming. This means you are left with three options for advancing alogn the game: one, spend hours trying to figure out how a basic set of puzzles is supposed to work; two, go online and look up walkthroughs for every puzzle type; or three, have a preternatural gift for figuring out puzzles that do not always have obvious rules to them.
The game is designed to imitate Myst: you're on an island by yourself and there's no direct information about what has happened. What it lacks, however, is any variation in the game play or obvious hints for puzzles. It does, however, maintain the frustrating lack of feedback to help you figure out if you're doing things right or not.
Don't get me wrong; it's not an awful game. It works, it's beautiful, and I still find myself drawn to it. However, the monotony of the puzzle solving is enough to hamper my sense of mystery and wonder.

This is probably the nicest review I will ever write for a game I hate. That's because regardless of how I feel about it, Volgarr exists to do one thing, and that is imitate the old hard-as-balls 16-bit platformers of yore. And it does it really, really, really well.
You play Volgarr the Viking, unsurprisingly, risen from his grave by some totally metal deity to kill a whole bunch of everything. He controls like a slightly less-sticky Castlevania protagonist, with no air control unless you double-jump, certain attacks locking him in place, and being launched backwards (usually into pits) every time he gets hit. He does have a bevy of moves like a downward strike, a roll, and some very useful spears to throw that can also form platforms. It feels just like playing a classic SNES side-scroller, and that extends to the graphics and sounds as well. Pixel blood and bones fly as you hack and slash through the game's many varied levels.
IF you can get to them. The make-or-break issue with Volgarr is how much patience you have for punishingly hard platforming. The game uses a very Ghosts 'n' Goblins system where you find bits of armor to bolt on to yourself that then get knocked off a couple pieces at a time by enemies. Your shield is one of those pieces, and if you lose it, certain traps are going to be all but impassable. This is to say nothing of the many bottomless pits and trap enemies waiting just off screen to knock you into them. All of this would be fine, except that the levels are made up of two quite lengthy sections with only a single checkpoint between them. This means any mistakes you make are punished with redoing the last couple minutes of exacting platforming again. And with no checkpoint before bosses, just learning their patterns or performing less than perfectly can force you to replay 5+ minutes of level you've already had to suffer through.
This to me is just straight-up bad design, evidenced by how few games make use of similarly punishing systems now. It is forgiven only because it was the standard for NES classics such as Castlevania and Mega Man, except that even those games had multiple checkpoints per level. It becomes a question of how much of your time a game is allowed to waste when you make a mistake, because doing the same level opening ten times because you can't quite get a boss's pattern down immediately is very much a waste of time. Modern games like Dark Souls have found elegant solutions to this problem, such as allowing you to accumulate resources across attempts. Volgarr makes no provision for that, forcing the same actions over and over until it (hopefully) becomes muscle memory.
I really did hate Volgarr when I started playing it, but after a little more time with it I came to at least appreciate what it represents. When I was a kid, I had the patience to beat my head against Ninja Gaiden II for weeks and weeks until I could finally finish it. I don't have the time or the inclination for that kind of dedicated memorization anymore, but I can see where there might still be space for it. Volgarr is very much not for everyone and smacks of the kind of game that gets recommended by everyone and played by no one, but if you really, truly are looking for that brick wall NES difficulty curve, look no further.

Year Walk introduces you to a whole new world of horrifying supernatural phenomena.
Drawing upon the events of the Swedish tradition of the same name, the protagonist (you) seek to learn the future -- and what better way to do so than to lock yourself in your cottage without food, fire or speaking to anyone for the day to later venture out into the woods at midnight to hallucinate from a combination of starvation and hypothermia?
If somewhat simplistic, the game is steeped in Swedish culture and macabre in design and plot.
There are new creatures to add to your nightmares and several absolutely terrfying moments, rendering the horror tag well deserved. This horror component adds to the overall atmosphere of the game, the main purpose focus being a series of puzzles that you must unlock with your keen senses.
The early stages of the game are frustratingly vague however, the first few moments are spent wandering around uselessly until you realise there is both a map and a hint section. Once you get the hang of it however, Year Walk sucks you in, driving you deeper and deeper into delirium.
While a little short, there is an option to play again and unlock the secrets that bested you the first (or second) time around.
For me it crashed out a few times in the early stages, refusing to load the first time so I was allowed to stare at an empty screen for five minutes, but I won't hold that against it. Year Walk saves automatically which is a definite plus when playing on temperamental computers.
Definitely worth the price. 10/10 would walk again.

Edit: TL;DR: If you're a fan of the series and don't mind that this is more or less exactly the same as Cities XL, then yeah its a nice "update" to buy. If you're not a fan and you're expecting something brand new, stay away.
If you've played Cities XL, then you've played Cities XXL. This shouldn't have been a new game, this feels more like a fix for all the bugs that plagued Cities XL, but instead they introduced it as a brand new game.
Pros:
- Supports Steam Workshop now (YAY!)
- No more memory leak like in Cities XL (that I can tell so far...)
- Game runs a bit smoother than its predecesor.
- Sky box leads to very pretty screenshots of the city.
- New buildings and offers more in terms of environment and countering pollution.
Cons:
- It's still buggy, and still lags when the city population gets too high.
- It feels like it should've been an update to Cities XL.
- A handful of new buildings and fixed bugs doesn't make a new game, not really.
Do I recommend this game based on what I see purely upfront? No, I really shouldn't. However, consider Cities XL and all its bugs. Most of it wasn't fixed with a simple patch because the issue lay with the core engine. Focus Home decided to tackle the engine problems and release the improvements at Cities XXL. As a city-building sim fan at heart, buying this at $20 was like buying really expensive DLC content. Is it worth it at full price? Not really. Why do I recommend this then? Because at the end of the day I still think this is a better game than Simcity.

You wake up with 15 other students in a completely sealed school and you're told by a mecha-bear that the only way out is to kill one of your team mate without being caught by the others. At the beginning everyone is of course against the concept but Monokuma will start pressuring everyone with various motives...
This game is split in 2 parts:
-slices of life where you explore the school, become friends with people and try to solve some secrets. Befriending people is done through hanging together, giving presents and it has the benefit to unblock skills that can be used during trial mode.
-trial mode where you first need to investigate the crime scene, collect clues and witnesses accounts. Then comes the trial itself where you try to discover the culprit through several kind of mini games (think Ace Attorney series of games).
When you finish the game, you unblock school mode which take place before the main story.
It's a classical resource management game where you have to collect materials in a given time frame in order to build a Monokuma clone. In parallel you get the chance to befriend everyone and complete their report card which unlock a kind of sim dating mode where you need to visit some places and choose the right dialogue option in order to improve your connection with them. This allow you to know them better and unlock their deepest thoughts via a kind of bullet event.
Overall this game have a distinct graphical (kind of 2.5D) and musical identity, story is captivating and full of cliffhangers. I can only hope that Danganronpa 2 will be available soon so I can re-immerse myself in that world.

First off, I'd like to start by saying this game has a very beautiful art style as you roam around an island solving puzzles.  This game is for puzzle lovers and puzzle lovers alone.  A story is practically nonexistent (or just so deep in understanding I couldn't comprehend it).  The game does not tell you how to play, but instead teaches you through the puzzles (being easy at first and progressing in difficulty).  Sometimes you may have to come back to a puzzle if it includes an aspect you have not learned yet.  Some people find this frustrating as I have read in other reviews, but personally I enjoyed it.  It is a puzzle game, and part of the puzzle is how to solve it.
You may read other reviews that say the puzzles are too easy or that its the same puzzle over and over.  If they say it is too easy, they most likely did not get that deep in the game.  I think I am quite good at puzzle games for the most part and finished the base game in about 25 hours of gameplay (And I solved all puzzles on my own without any outside help).  With that being said there is so much more to be done, with more puzzles to complete, some hidden within the world itself (I've decided to go back and try to find them).  To give you an idea, for the most part you have to walk up to these monitors which host the puzzles that you must solve.  However, you can find in the world a puzzle within the scenery that can be completed as well.
As I said before, some people believe the puzzles are repetitive.  This is because the puzzles consist of starting at a node on a grid and making your way to the exit.  As the game progresses things will be added to the grid that restrict your movement or require specifics for when you make it to the end.  (I will not state them here if anybody wishes to play and figure them out on their own as intended.)  While the idea is repetitive, the new aspects make you think of solutions that are not so obvious causing one to think outside the box critically.  I enjoyed this.
Next, although I do recommend this game I do not believe it is worth the full $40.  I managed to get it on sale for $12 on humble bundle and would say its worth about $20 max.
Also after you beat the game it will start a new one, but I have been told if you'd like to reload your file (to go back and complete ALL puzzles) then there is a way to reload your old file from the main menu.
Thank you eys for the tip!

First off, I'd like to start by saying this game has a very beautiful art style as you roam around an island solving puzzles.  This game is for puzzle lovers and puzzle lovers alone.  A story is practically nonexistent (or just so deep in understanding I couldn't comprehend it).  The game does not tell you how to play, but instead teaches you through the puzzles (being easy at first and progressing in difficulty).  Sometimes you may have to come back to a puzzle if it includes an aspect you have not learned yet.  Some people find this frustrating as I have read in other reviews, but personally I enjoyed it.  It is a puzzle game, and part of the puzzle is how to solve it.
You may read other reviews that say the puzzles are too easy or that its the same puzzle over and over.  If they say it is too easy, they most likely did not get that deep in the game.  I think I am quite good at puzzle games for the most part and finished the base game in about 25 hours of gameplay (And I solved all puzzles on my own without any outside help).  With that being said there is so much more to be done, with more puzzles to complete, some hidden within the world itself (I've decided to go back and try to find them).  To give you an idea, for the most part you have to walk up to these monitors which host the puzzles that you must solve.  However, you can find in the world a puzzle within the scenery that can be completed as well.
As I said before, some people believe the puzzles are repetitive.  This is because the puzzles consist of starting at a node on a grid and making your way to the exit.  As the game progresses things will be added to the grid that restrict your movement or require specifics for when you make it to the end.  (I will not state them here if anybody wishes to play and figure them out on their own as intended.)  While the idea is repetitive, the new aspects make you think of solutions that are not so obvious causing one to think outside the box critically.  I enjoyed this.
Next, although I do recommend this game I do not believe it is worth the full $40.  I managed to get it on sale for $12 on humble bundle and would say its worth about $20 max.
Also after you beat the game it will start a new one, but I have been told if you'd like to reload your file (to go back and complete ALL puzzles) then there is a way to reload your old file from the main menu.
Thank you eys for the tip!

I honeslty enjoy this game.
It's a very good piece of interactive fiction, and I really enjoy those kinds of games. Some may not, and that's their choice, but personally, I find the classic nature of a good text-adventure to be relaxing and exciting at the same time.
The Pros:
1. The story is actually pretty well written. You get a sense of both who your character is as they develop, along with the supporting characters of the tale.
2. There are a lot of different choices to make, each with it's on rewards aand consequences. This adds a lot to the story as it progresses, but I will touch on this again in the Cons.
3. The game brings a general creeping feeling, as you're playing. You never know what is going to happen around the next corner. Whether you will live or die; make a good or bad choice for a scenario and defines your character in a different light. Things can take a turn for the worst at any second, and it keeps you on your toes.
The Cons:
1. The story itself may be enough to keep you going, but I sometimes felt the narrative was a bit wordy. I feel, in IF anyway, that you should be shorter in sentences, and deliver the majority of the details in quick sentences, rather than long narratives. Another problem that I found was that the writer needs to deliver more of the "show, don't tell" rhetoric that most writers use. Could help in the long run.
2. As I stated above, I would come back to the choices. While there are plenty of choices, some of them have no effect on the story itself. Such as weapon choice at the beginning. Honestly, I found no change in my actions when playing a character with a rifle, or a character with a knife. Just an observation, and probably nit-picky, but I digress.
Overall, this was an exceptional game and I really enjoyed playing it. I definitely recommend it for the text-adventure lovers out there, and any zombie survival fans.

But even the more generic ones were at least interesting in design, visually.
Here they arent really.

Firstly, ignore my playtime, I have completed this game on Furier difficulty before, then bought it on Steam.
Secondly, this game is great.
I will put myself out in the firing line saying this statement: 'I don't like Dark Souls' combat.' It's loot based system and the stamina bar takes away so much skill from the game, making the player farm and literally DO NOTHING to defeat bosses. And that is just not fun. Furi is the exact opposite.
In this game, from the very first level you can do everything. You are given your whole moveset right from the start, you will not unlocks skills, you will not unlock perks, but you will learn. Each boss forces you to perfect a new mechanic: parrying, charge dashing, charge attacks, perfect parrying and so on. Bringing me to my next point:

But this isn't a bad thing, you aren't given tutorial prompts or whatever, you won't realise the training wheels are off until you finish the game, and unlock Furier mode. This mode is the real game. Proof? Just watch the end credits in the Furier mode.  The first playthrough is fun, but you haven't scraped the surface yet.
Propelling you through these many bosses and retries are plenty of things, firstly the small lashings of story you are given, it is not much but by the end of your first playthrough, you will be satisfied, hell, it even has a great twist ending.
Secondly, is the great boss design, each boss here is unique and looks completely different, the two minuites before fights are often spent thinking about the next boss, usually themed with the background too.
Thirdly, the amazing soundtrack. This soundtrack is on the next level. Genuinely amazing. It is the first game in ages where the last boss theme is the BEST THEME, as it should be, a reward and a reason to keep playing, even when it gets tough.
I only have two problems with this game. Firstly is the port, load times can be too long for the game, though they are far far far from bad, my pc is pretty good. (Check my profile for specs.)
Secondly (SPOILER WARNING):
Also, the developers of this game are amazing, if you are stuck on a boss they will actively help you in the steam community, in the best way they can. Great job guys!
Thank you for reading.

I love boss fights and I enjoy difficult games, so a game with nothing but boss fights seems like a slam dunk for me. Unfortunately, these boss fights are *long* and the challenge feels tedious more than exciting.
The first boss in this game has 7 stages, each with multiple waves of attacks. The second boss of this game has 6 stages, and she regenerates her health bar once on each stage (so each stage is double-long). Each stage takes 1-2 minutes to complete if you know what you're doing - and longer if you don't. Furthermore, if you lose 1/3 of your health on a boss, its health for the stage resets *entirely* and you have to repeat the stage.
All in all, you're spending 10-20 minutes on a single run of a single boss fight... and you repeat the entire thing if you die.
I'd much rather each boss be half as long and twice as challenging - I don't want to repeat 5 stages I've already mastered in order to work on the 6th. If that doesn't bother you, feel free to pick up Furi.

I've been wanting to play this game ever since it came out on iPad, but since I didn't have an iPad I had to wait painfully for over a year. Finally it arrives on Mac, and I was not dissapointed. This is an absolutely one-of-a-kind game. I can't even think of a game that is close to it (although of course there many games I've never heard of so take that with a grain of salt).
You are a 19th century Swedish Man who has just been told by the woman he loves that she is going to marry someone else. Desiring a glimpse into the future, you set out on the ancient but dying tradition of a Year Walk: at the stroke of midnight you set out from your house to reach the church, but along the way you encounter numerous mystical creatures and artifacts.
The gameplay consists of puzzle and exploration elements. It is 2D, but you can move forwards or backwards at preset places on your path. The world is not very large but it's still quite easy to get lost, so thankfully the game includes a map. Every puzzle in this game is unique and enjoyable, so the game stays fresh for its three hour or so length. There was only one puzzle I disliked and couldn't beat, because it used sound and I'm completely tone deaf, but thankfully there's a built-in hint system that will guide you through any puzzles you can't solve.
The art style is quite stark - flat and angular and washed out. Yet it is beautiful all the same. The creatures are grotesque or beautiful or both. The snow-covered Swedish woods are haunting and lonely, evoking a sense of foreboding and wonder at the same time. This juxtaposition is not easy to achive and I applaud the developers.
The story is surprisingly deep and moving, which I did not expect. The game deals with the theme of overreaching and trying to change things that are not within our power. Once the game is over, there is in fact a larger story to discover and a true ending to the game that will stick with you for quite some time.
The best part of the game is discovering and interacting with all the spirits you meet along teh way. The encyclopedia that accompanies the game gives background lore on these fantastical spirits that most have never heard of. They are all wonderfully bizzare and fascinating, although I may be a little biased as I am quite into lore and the mystical.
If you want a game that completely sucks you into its unique world, then this is it. I will not forget Year Walk for quite some time.

This was a fun little murder mystery game. As Detective Grimoire, you must gather evidence to discover how and why the murder was committed, and then interrogate people to learn facts about them, which will help you to work out which one is the murderer.
The game is simple to pick up, and fun to play. In particular I enjoyed the "challenge" mechanic, which allows you to quiz each suspect on a key topic and use evidence to get the truth out of them. This mechanic was reminiscent of the Phoenix Wright games for Nintendo DS. The puzzles were very simple, but in a way it was nice to play the game and enjoy the story without getting stuck on complicated puzzles.
The story was fun, and the characters were entertaining and well-acted. My only criticism is that it is a very short game (about 2 hours long), which would be fine as the first episode in a multi-part series, but as a standalone game it does leave you feeling unsatisfied. The game could easily be extended to include more than one case, and hopefully the developers will do so in the future.
The graphics in my opinion were fine, a very simple 2D cartoony style, but I imagine that some people would find the style very ugly and it would put them off the game. I would encourage them to look past the graphics and try to enjoy the game for the story and gameplay. One thing I did notice about the graphics is everything was very large, as if it was a mobile phone game stretched to fill a full-sized screen. This is game is growing on me.. It's a mixed feeling at first because it starts out slow. I still would buy if it was released today though.
I like that the cities are large (not like Simcity), but size isn't everything.. The game needs to be fun. The cities seem to run well so far, the Steam workshop is a very nice feature and will continue to grow, some added buildings, like the bridges/road options, freeways, etc. Zooming in and seeing things in more detail is nice, clicking a car and seeing things from that cars perspective going through the city is nice. I also want to mention that there are some cool building options.. I just noticed I can place certain restaurants, a night club, etc. There are a lot of cool new buildings that you can select and place; this is in addition to the standard ones that develop in zones. These extra buildings are growing on me, and really could help make this game much more enjoyable for me.
There are tutorials in the beginning menu, and I suspect most people have not even looked at them. I am going through some of them now, and they are very nice. There also is a hidden menu on the right that shows more detailed information like traffic areas on the map, satisfaction, etc. If you hover your mouse way to the far right of the sceen the extra options come up; this is in addition the menu options of top of the screen..
As the city gets larger it becomes more of a joy to play.. I am enjoying setting up the transportation system, seeing the city expand, demand change, etc.
Things I don't like include the buildings don't develop like in Simcity which to me is a big deal (at least it was for me when I first started playing), the city progression starts out really slow (demand for goods seems to stay pretty low for a while which I think is where some people lose interest, but it gets a lot funner soon after), and the graphics/buildings aren't all that exciting to me (it is growing on me though like I mentioned in regards to the specialized buildings). Trade/manufacturing chains are to simplistic. .
I'd say if you want a large city builder this could keep you entertained, but shouldn't be the only city builder in your aresenal imo. City Skylines looks like it will be good as well, Simcity was nice from the manufacturing/trading standpoint and it was fun, but small maps. If it were me and I either liked Cities XL but wanted better performance, or you like city builders in general I'd pick this up. I will say that we also live in an 'instant gratification' world, and 1 hour of gameplay isn't going to do it for those people; so expect to see the enjoyment increase as the cities grow.
I will say I haven't developed a 'huge' city yet mostly because it starts out really slow, but I am now enjoying this game and see myself playing this more.

The game itself is not your average point-and-click retro adventure game, even though the graphics might suggest it, but it's more like a... Bartender Simulator game. As weird as it sounds, it's a game where you literally have to serve different customers approaching you at the bar your work in, set in a futuristic environment full of human-like cyborgs and interesting cocktails.
I'm only at the very early stages of the game, but the plus and minuses so far:
+++ Funny dialogues, interactions and banter between yourself (aka the Bartender) and the coworkers/customers more often than not made me giggle a bit.
++ Retro-style graphics with some Manga-like character design.
+++ Very nice retro soundtrack to boot
+ The game looks pretty easy and linear so far, but I don't know if it's going to be the same for the whole experience.

Again, it doesn't bother me because you kind of have to follow the chapter to get into the storytelling of it, but some people may get bothered by it.

That being said, so far I'm having a great time with this game and I would HIGHLY recommend it to anybody who just wants to chill and relax listening to people stepping into your bar, having some laughs and following up a pretty interesting storyline set into a "soft" futuristic environment a-la Ghost in The Shell (without graphic violence and with way more cuteness)

I've been really struggling to decide how I want to rate this game because, although I have played it for around 50 hours, now that I see that there's no amount of practice or strategy that can get past a fatal flaw in the game design itself, I wish I hadn't.
Scroll down to the bottom for the summary, if you like, but I really suggest you read the entire review to get a grasp on my reasoning because, although the game is stable and not completely devoid of merit, it is basically broken, and unfortunately, without someone explaining it beforehand, you'll have to invest a lot of time before you see exactly how.
If you like games where you assign a task, such as building a building or using a machine, and then some guy goes and actually does said task, and the game is essentially this concept multiplied repeatedly, with all the logistics problems left for you to figure out, then you'll like this game, at least for a while. Probably for 5-10 hours or so.
Everything hinges on how you plan your base. This, in essence, is the entirety of the game.
In a way, this is good, as it gives you the feeling that your design choices really matter. Where you place the mine, in association with where you place the ore processor, in association with where you place the semi-conductor making machine, in association with where you place the robot making machine, will define the success or failure of your colony.
You've played games like this before -- everything from the Anno series to Starcraft/Warcraft series of strategy games. Your placement plus automated workers of some kind using the things you place equals the game, more or less. In Planetbase, though, you're never preparing for war (there are "invaders", but they're a joke), and you're never trying to get to the next scenario or goal because there pretty much aren't any of either.
Even this is alright, though, since, for one thing, it's only a $20 game. It is not, however, a "sandbox" game, as it is tagged, unless you consider a severe lack of any real goals to mean sandbox.
Although I wouldn't recommend it, I do feel like most people will get more than $20 worth of gaming simply out of getting to the point to where they can hit all the milestones on the third and final planet. After that, though, there's really not much left to do, and you'll probably be bored of the repitition well before you get to that point (as I was).
No, my major complaint about this game is actually more of a combination of two elements.
First, everything you build is connected to each other. It's either outdoor structures (power and oxygen generation) or indoor structures (domes where your people can do things) and you must build pathways to connect them. Due to terrain, you will often find that the only way to continue building your colony is to either separate your outdoor structures from your indoor structures entirely, meaning one meteorite strike on that connection can instantly spell the end of your colony because, although you can connect the entirety of your colony to all of its power and water generation with one single connection, and one of the first and cheapest structures in the game is the mine, you inexplicably cannot connect parts of your base through any amount of rock.
(Edit: I have been advised in the comments that external connections, which are those built only to power and water generating structures, cannot really be destroyed, and therefore you could build all of those structures away from the base. Although true, this seems almost like an exploit or, at the very least, a very limiting strategy since you could never build any interior structures in that direction as the game won't let you "split your base", as it puts it. It might be a workaround for the above issue, but it's certainly not a solution to the problem. As per the devs (see link in comments), they don't allow that link to be destroyed via meteor strikes because it would make the game "ridiculously hard," indicating that they see segregating all exterior structures as the only viable strategy.)
The other option is to build these external structures alongside your internal structures. This strategy, however, will invariably lead to multiple instances of places where there is only one way to get from one end of the colony to the other because, apparently, the concept of building tunnels over or under hills was never invented in this particular alternate reality.
On its own, this conundrum could be seen as part of the game's strategy. After all, the main premise is that you're building a city out of domes an alien planet, right?
Well, that could work fine if it wasn't for the fact that there is virtually no AI controlling the colonists, and the colonists are a bit like Sims in that they need to eat, sleep, and keep entertained, in addition to doing their jobs and carrying things around, the latter of which can often take up most of a colonist's life, at least until the colony is advanced enough to produce robots to do the carrying for you (which can take a while).
Now mix the extremely limited pathways with the needs of the colonists, who lack the programming to anticipate their own needs in any way, and add the fact that every device that satisfies a need can only be used by one colonist at a time, and, if you're experienced with these types of games, you're already starting to see the big shiny, flashing, glaring flaw in the core design of the game.
If you're not seeing it yet, here's a direct quote from the developer in response to my asking if this was considered part of the intended difficulty of the game, or if the colonists are not supposed to be ignoring their basic needs when they're in the same room as the thing that can provide for those needs:
This means that your colonists are going to spend much of their time walking across the planet to get to a device to fill a need simply because the nearest device was being used right at the second they decided they were hungry, or thirsty, or sleepy. It doesn't matter that the device would be out of use in less than a second. That colonist is going to spend an entire in-game day walking to that other water fountain because he wasn't bright enough to stand in line behind the one guy at the first one. And the developer only sees this as a UI flaw.
You can read more on the forums regarding the complete lack of an actual AI in this game, and how horribly it mixes with the concept of domes and limited pathways but, what it all boils down to is, you end up designing the base around the stupidity of your colonists, which shouldn't be the point at all, but basically defines the game past the first 20-30 colonists.
Once you realize this, you quickly become annoyed with playing a game that doesn't involve much more than compensating for its own bad design.
So, here's the TL;DR
(See comments for any of my replies to the developer responses. Review has been lightly edited in light of some comments and developer response.)

Already I like this game! I think the devs are doing a wonderful job!

As of the writing, I have only played for a very short period of time, but I watched let's plays for many hours before deciding to purchase.

* What is Planetbase?
Planetbase is a gem of a little SCI-FI sim builder game. It is still being actively worked on by the devs (as of DEC 2015) and continues to improve with each new version they release. The movie/book The Martian comes to mind when, from the trailer the key character says, well in order to survive we are going to need to "Science the $#!T out of this!"; yes, that is a fitting quote =)
* What happens at the start | setting?
You set down on the first world type (others may be unlocked via achievenments), a Type D, think Mars and your first colonists step down the ramp and to this new world. From there you have to move quickly to move supplies from your landing ship, in order to get power, water and air generated.  I had more than one colony die off, when first learning the ropes so I suggest you pay close attention to the tutorial. The game is fairly easy to pick up however but difficult to 'master', which is ideal IMHO.
* Controls | UI
Are easy to learn and laid out in a logical fashion. I really liked the fact that if you do not have access to certain functions, EG security controls, then the function key short cut simply will not pop up the menu. F2 through F8 will provide you with various easy access to the information/controls/settings that you need.  The UI itself is clean, no issues; though the sure number of buildings and items you can create may overwhelm just a bit at first.  Trust me you will adjust quickly and be asking for more stuffs! =)
Graphics | Audio
The graphics are very good for this type of game and with consideration that this is an indie game from a small studio. Even when zoomed in people, structures and interiors all look quite good, if not a bit cartoonish (which I rather enjoy). As to the game sound effects, the secruity alerts can be a bit annoying. The sound effects in general however and the music are solid. The music has that perfect blend of sci-fi feel to it, without being over done.
* Would you recommend this game?
I absolutely do recommend this game. Even if you aren't a big sim builder person, this game has a lot to offer. If you are a fan of the genre then you need to get yourself a copy!
Take care and good luck to you!

The Witness could be described as "RHEM lite", in that it's an island of interconnected puzzles that can get rather difficult. I say "lite" because there's only one type (or only one family) of puzzle, and you don't need to keep nearly as many notes.
The puzzles all involve drawing a path through a grid. The details vary, but that's what you'll be doing. A lot. Sometimes you'll need to draw a path that avoids going through broken lines; sometimes you'll need it to make certain shapes; sometimes you'll need to divide the grid into equal-sized regions; but it's always a line through a grid, and that can get repetitive.
The game also doesn't explain the rules of the puzzle, and that's a puzzle in itself: each area of the island has "tutorial" puzzles that help you figure out the rules for this particular type of puzzle. But you might get tripped up: if you split a 2x2 grid into two 1x2 areas, is the rule "divide the grid into sections of size 2"? Is it "divide the grid into two equal-sized sections"? At times, you may have to look back at your earlier solutions to reconsider your assumptions. If you get stuck, there's enough to do that you can go work on something else for a while, then come back to the frustrating puzzle later.
In addition to the main puzzles, there are side puzzles that, again, usually involve tracing lines, though this time not always through a grid. Sometimes they involve tricks of perspective, so you'll spend time walking around and admiring the scenery, so it's a good thing that the island is pretty.

There are some moments where this game shines brilliantly. Moments where you feel incredible for managing to dodge that one attack, weaving in between bullets, parrying the big hit that would've killed you...
But Furi prides itself on being difficult. I'm no stranger to difficult games, and in fact welcome it. But here's the thing: Trial and Error is not difficulty. Memorization is not difficulty. QTEs are not difficulty. These are time wasters.
Precision is one thing, but when you are called on to be precise with an enemy that acts randomly, that's when things fall apart. When I'm parrying a flurry of blows, am I going to parry once, twice, or four times? If I parry one too few times, I get hit. If I parry one too many, I miss my chance.
This need to memorize patterns and split second tells reminds me of the worst parts of fighting games and bad precision platformers. When the absolute optimal path (or something close to it) is the only way forward, all freedom and creativity in how you approach a boss is eradicated.
There's a word for games that demand precision and memorization along a completely set path: they're called Rhythm Games. This game's soundtrack is phenomenal, but I'd much rather be playing it to a beat.

So actualy a bit more like

Most of the gameplay consist of fighting bosses, with the story being hinted in-between fights as you walk around. There really isn't much exploring for those curious to see what's around, though I hear there's a couple hidden dialogue if you do decide to explore, but mainly you can press the dodge button to just auto-walk as a breather between fights.
The fighting is hard and challenging just as a boss game should be, but actualy a bit more forgiving in my opinion. Your movset is pretty limited which makes learning how to move around simple and sweet, so the gameplay is about learning the attack patterns of each boss and reacting accordingly by dodging, parrying, or getting an attack when there's an opening.
As for how it's forgiving, you are not a one hit wonder here, you can take multiple hits and can even recover health by parrying or shooting green projectiles for health drops. The fights consist of phases where if you deplete the boss's health, you go into the next phase and you regain all your health. If you loose all your health, you loose one out of three "lives" and the phase resets. If you loose all lives, the entire battle resets, but if you complete a phase, you regain a life. This system lets you learn and recover from loosing a life, but still makes it dangerous enough that you don't wana get reckless and constantly take hits as you get close to beating a boss.
Overall, it's a really enjoyably challenging game.
On a sidenote, I beat the entire game using a mouse and keyboard, the game recommends you use a controler but I was too lazy to actualy plug one in. I ended up paying for it with several moments where pressing 2 movements keys makes the dodge key not work because keyboards are stupid like that. Was able to get around it by letting go of moving before I dodged, but it did give me several moments where it felt like the controls wern't very responsive. It's entirley playable and beatable using a mouse and keyboard, but yea, just a heads up incase some people decide not to use a controller and think the controls arn't working as they should.

This game was fun, addictive, and... well... like almost every other game thats out there. This games, back when it was good, brought an old concept into new light. When people fought in teams, they fought together as a team. Everyone knew what to do and they would do it in the smartest and, mostly, risk free fashion. People would group together and use each other's abilities to overcome the other team. When someone was in danger of being overtaken 2v1, others would help that person out and push the other team back. Victory felt well desurved and defeat kept you pushing for more. I admit there were problems with the game before, but it was still fun despite. Teamwork was what made the game fun. The game has been change almost completely since then. "change is good," some might say, but with change comes new problems. The game gives people too much power. Strategy isn't what it is anymore. People lack weakness and planning is almost out of the picture. For example: when there was a "tank" that was much more powerful than the rest, the smaller ships would either distract or damage "the tank" so the other ships could destroy "the tank" while its weak. That "tank would deploy counter-measures or bring a few friends along with him to stop these attacks. Most matches now, people will go off on their own or in small squads, and ignore the rest of the team. Now, the problem everyone is talking about: real world cash for ingame money. This game was heading into this direction from the start, but its hit the point of utter annoyance. From over-powered moduals and weapons, to even just wanting to change you name. Sure, if you cram you can get anything without paying for it, but for somethings that would take years. This game was great before, but, like everything I've explained, this has changed. The developers have spent so much time trying to add to the game that they forgot to fix the problems. I wish I could say something good about the game, but with every groundbreaking improvement is an equaly annoying and ruinous problem.

I have been playing Star Conflict for so long...like, before Open Space was actually useful. I decided that it was probably time to finally write a review...especially since there is a bunch of reviews on here with people that are either grinding out hours on there to make a review look worthy, or have literally played the game for so long and then write a crap review about it. Star Conflict I would have to say is mixed up hard. In my honest opinion on the game, it has ups and downs. Some of the reviews are legit on here, others make no sense to me. Lets see what makes up the integrity of Star Conflict and then rate it.
I remember a time when the game was in it's early stages and the dreadnaughts had no even come out. I can't tell if the game has gotten better or worse since then. There are multiple modes in Star Conflict; PvP, PvE, Co-op v AI, and Open Space; on the higher tiers you have Tournament level stuff where high level players can team up against each other or against a huge enemy. PvP is what you expect, You vs. the other team. In PvP, there can be different objectives, my favorite personally being Combat Recon; one ship on each team is randomly chosen to be the commander for their respective teams. Your goal is to destroy the enemy commander and wipe out the rest of the team. After the commander is destroyed, no more respawns are allowed for that team. This diversity in gameplay allows for a lot of different playstyles, which brings me to my next topic.
The vessels and factions in Star Conflict are incredible. From what I've gathered, Empire ships are high fire rate, (relatively) low damage and fast. However, they also have really powerful and really slow sniper ships equipped with a thermal cannon weapon known as a "Disentigrator". Federation ships are basically support type ships that use drones and stuff. Their fighters tend to be really good with escaping enemy grasps and showing up from behind and taking out enemies. Jericho ships are basically go big or go home. Shield tanky vessels that are slow and deliver a punch of built correctly. Their fighters love to just tank damage. Each faction has their own ships and each ship can be of a different class and type. This variety just lets the player play like they want to. I like the giant tanky sniper/full frontal force vessels of Jericho origin (more on that later).
in the gameplay category is how certain things are done. You can manufacture ships (more on that in a moment), but the resources required for some vessels can take months to collect if done correctly and without buy stuff. I will say that
Open space was also a joke until Dreadnaughts came along that required Iridium to manufacture. There was no point to OS until then. Gaijin has gotten really good about it now and added a lot of features.
Also since it's a match based (apart from Open Space) you have to enter a queue (like in war thunder) to get into a match, occasionally, it can be really bad, but on average it's fine and easily overlooked timewise.
Matchmaking can be a jerk sometimes. I'm a rank 9 or 10 (kind of in the middle) mercenary, and I'm continuously paried with rank 15 players if I throw my rank 10 ship into my ship pool. I hate the way that's done but anywhere before rank 10, matchmaking is fine. That's the biggest downfall I think.
Another would be the resourcing you do to manufacture ships. I didn't make this pain in the neck process number one, because it's totally optional. :)
Luckily, the best loot used for ships like Destroyers and Dreadnaughts are obtained through the loot drops at the end of battles. Like I said earlier, resourcing and matchmaking can be bad, but since they finally made OS useful with Destroyers and Dreadnaughts, it's not so bad. The turn out on this one however is that most people don't like the new Destroyers update. I don't know why, I think it's becuase they think it's unbalanced; but here's the thing. if you start out as a new player or stopped playing for a while, all the rank ups you get in a faction literally just hand you the components needed for the destroyer. BOOM. Easy as pie. And all the while you're accrewing the materials, you are earning money, making up for the 3 million credits you need to manufacture one. Dreadnaughts on the other hand require some more explanation.
Dreadnaughts are about 10 fold or more, powerful than a destroyer. These massive battlecruisers are constructed by corporations (mainly corporations that house a group of 10 players, rank 10 or more). Corporations are like factions in the game. These dreadnaughts however take a lot of time to make, but once you do, your corporation can engage in sector combat...another gameplay mode. You can take control of sectors in open space. I think that's insanely cool, but thats just me.
8/10 (Really nice, some textures can be made better, but the attention to detail on the guns (how they move with the cursor and whatnot, is really well done)
6/10 (Can be improved apon still. Grinding out resources isn't my favorite thing to do, but the payout is about 80% worth it after you rank the ship up some.)
9/10 (Well done, each faction has leaders and each leader has their own biography. The stations themselves have lore and pretty much every sector has lore behind it as well. Very well done.)
5/10 (Very grindy, leveling up can be a pain in the neck after like rank 4 or 5, fixed by maxing out the synergy on your owned ships to increasy your fleet strength synergy gain percentage)
7.5/10 (Best competivive F2P game I've ever played)

It is a really short but very interesting game. Based around Norse mythos and Swedish legend, Year Walk has the player go through a series of puzzling tasks to achieve the beyond and catch a glimps into the future. It is not a scary horror game but does have a few jump scares. The art work and music are also very good.

The only thing that bothered me was the short lenght of the game, other than that I'd say its pretty much worth the tiny heart attacks that occur every now and again even when its really nothing especially scary. The art style is pretty simplistic, but it really is beautiful and, to me, it really does help the game pop and settle it in its own, distinctive thing. The puzzles aren't really that difficult if you're used to this type of game (though the musical sequences don't apply to this). There are several bits which can be a bit nerve wrecking (e.g. the safe just outside your cottage) and many of the throphies require you to play the game once or twice again.
All in all it really is a solid, little piece of work which is well worth the money. I don't want to spoil anything, seeing how it really is gratifying when you figure something out on your own. Buy it, play it again and again, lose your mind over (what are essentially) really simple tasks and ease into the unsettling, unnerving atmosphere that will make you jump at your own shadow.

One of the more unique games you'll play. It draws upon Swedish folklore, something that lends an interesting flavor as you explore mythology that may be unfamiliar. The art and music are both gorgeous. Be warned: this game makes you work. I was thrilled to find myself making notes and drawing little sketches to help myself solve puzzles. Don't be deterred, though; hints are available should you want them. The game has horror elements, but, aside from a couple of jump scares, is fairly subtle in its delivery. To get the full story you must play the game twice, though I suspect some may find the secondary story to be disappointing and a little too sci-fi in comparison to the first story. The game is short, maybe an hour for the first playthrough, but it uses its time effectively to show off interesting ideas and beautiful art.

Never too difficult as to need hints, but the puzzles seem more a secondary tool to support discovery of the folklore as presented within the game anyway. This review based solely on the PC/Steam version of the game. Easily recommended.

If you like
playing a really difficult game (and we're talking
difficult), then this is the game for you!
No health bar, cumbersome control, lots of cheap hits, and enemies that can move faster than your character are the name of the game here. It is
difficult, and I have to say that it isn't to the game's credit.
Retro gamers will be reminded of the game
, in that in both games you control a barbarian-type character who attacks with a sword while (mostly) walking to the right. But whereas
is a game that you can learn from,
isn't. This is mostly due to the fact that when you die, you go back to the last checkpoint, and checkpoints in this game are few and far between. Your character starts with a sword for his main attack, a spear for distance attacks and for climbing up walls, and a shield for defense, which can deflect some projectiles and that you lose after taking a single hit. If you're lucky, you can find a treasure chest that will first upgrade your shield (I have no idea what this does because you lose the upgraded shield after one hit -- it doesn't go back to the normal shield, mind you, it just goes away like the regular shield), then upgrade you to a helmet (that will take an additional hit, bringing your hit points up to two, after which you die), and a flaming sword that I presume increases your attacks (I don't know because I lost the flaming sword every single time after I got it on single-hit enemies).
The graphics are pleasant to look at in a 90s arcade sort of way, and the sound is certainly up to par with titles in that vein, but that's about all I can say in its favor.
Now, I'm occasionally up for a side-scrolling platforming challenge: I've beaten
on the SNES, every version of
on every system it was ever made for,
on the Sega Genesis and quite a few of the NES
games. Maybe it's my old age setting in, or maybe I'm just tired of developer B.S., but I'm really starting the hate the kind of cheap, artificial challenge some of these modern platformers are offering by making the game so unforgiving. I've played the game for about two hours, and I've only ever gotten to the second checkpoint (not even the end of the first stage, if there are more stages). Oh yeah, and you have to start the game from the beginning every single time you quit the game and restart, so you'd better get good at those first few areas. I was really looking forward to this game and now I'm just angry that I've purchased it.
If masochism and self-mutilation are your thing, then by all means: Go for it! Anyone who just wants to play a fun, challenging platform game can spend their money on
or any of the dozens of other titles on Steam that are more rewarding, more forgiving, and certainly more fun.

Spoilers
I have done my best to keep this review from spoilers so that readers can enjoy it without regretting reading it. As with food though, there might be some traces of "allergens".
My experience of older games
I grew up playing the Sega Master System, Sega Mega Drive, Super Nintendo (SNES), and Game Boy (first generation). I found it appropriate for me to write my first review on this particular game since it belongs to a genre that I hold very dear. The SNES console is my all time favourite game system.
Graphics
Völgarr truly captures the feeling and aestethics of games of the past! People who have played a game called Rastan seem to recognise elements from that game and while I never played it, based on pictures on Google I see why. The enemies and levels are clearly inspired from that game.
The graphics remind me, however, of another game which I think Völgarr resembles at least as much: ActRaiser II. This game was released on the SNES console and Völgarr's graphics are defenitely 16-bit. The character's poses, movement and moves and also the music and variance in level themes resemble in a way those in ActRaiser II.
One thing that reveals Völgarr is a modern game is the background/the horizon which has been blurred to give a sence of depth. While the purpouse is obvious, I have never seen that in a 16-bit game and would have preferred graphics limited to the style of the time. Sence of depth was very well achieved in the old games too, but one pixel was one pixel and could never be blurred.
Gameplay
This game could easily have been published back in the early 90's. The character moves just like in a viking/swordsman/fantasy themed SNES-game: Relatively slowly, giving a sence of weight (muscles, armor, weapons and muscels). The attack moves are slightly delayed and need to be perfectly timed just like in the old games (if you remember games like Altered Beast you know timing is everything!)
The controls are 2 buttons + arrows / 4 buttons + arrows depending on how you choose to play. if you want one button for each action, you go with 4. I chose to go with 2, which means e.g. that throwing a spear = UP + ACTION.
Let's just lean back for a moment and enjoy the nostalgia...
Right, let's continue!
One of the main themes the developers advertise in the game trailer is dying. All of us who played NES, SNES, Game Boy, Sega Master System or Sega Mega Drive games know what it feels like to fail over and over and over again. It was so frustrating, yet addictive. You HAD to beat that level and you HAD to figure out what series of moves and attacks the boss had in order to beat him/her. Völgarr captures this beautifully! Just getting through the first level/world and beat the boss feels like conquering the world! (The developers of Völgarr have been kind though - back in the days you had often limited lives, limited "Continues", and sometimes no checkpoints at all!)
After a while, when you decide to play the game all over again, you suddenly realise how good you've gotten at this game. You're wielding your sword and throwing spears as if you were born doing so. That moment made me smile - it really brings back memories...
My thoughts (who am I kidding - you know what I'm gonna say!)
I LOVE THIS GAME and anyone who grew up with or has ever happened to fall in love with 16-bit games in particular will too! I began this review feeling quite sophisticated but after writing this and realising how much I really like this game, I end up feeling like a kid on saturday morning - waiting for my best friend to come over for a sleepover with snacks and video games all night!
I really have to try to fix my SNES console (showing black sreen of death)...
Fun, hard as #%@!, but fun.

I get this game is made for the prupose of being a challenging but rewarding game. And if you love that stuff you may like this game. It has a lot going for it but has two big problems:
- Jump control is too uncompromising
- The amount of tedious work you have to do over again when you die - i.e. lack of checkpoints.
I've played games with infrequent checkpoints and its normally more enjoyable because you don't feel like you are trudging through the same stuff you have already perfected just to get to the harder stuff. There is some sense of variety that keeps it interesting every time you die (Dark Souls or Hitman games if you are trying to stay stealthy).
The jumping to me seems like it is designed to screw you over more often than help you. I'd prefer good control of my character with harder obstacles rather than feel like I can't make use of this guy because the controls are so rigid.
Despite all that though it's honestly worth a couple bucks to try because if the jumping doesn't bother you and you are a masochist, you'll probably find a lot of value in the game.

A very charming point-and-click 'mystery' game.
Over the course of the game you learn about nine potential suspects (including the deceased) and meet a few helpful characters besides.  The dialogue is succinct, humorous and well voice-acted -- I loved every voice in the game.  The jokes are well-timed and the characters do not miss a boat.  Beat.
The detective (Grimoire) keeps ample notes on objects, places, and items (with only the occasional misspelling), so that you do not spend time trying to find out about something you already know.  Characters also (helpfully!) remember what you have asked them about -- greying out those choices so you do not find yourself repeating the same questions over and over.  (Of course you CAN ask those questions again if you wish).
There are a few exceedingly simple puzzles scattered throughout the game.  I do not think they add much, but they also do not detract much.
The mystery itself is ho-hum, but the journey of exploring and talking to the loveable cast of characters makes this game worth a look.  I found myself smiling and laughing as I played, and I do not regret the purchase.  Great for an evening's entertainment.

To me, adventure games are like french fries.
I enjoy the anticipation of french fries. I like their smell, I like how they look, and I even enjoy eating the first few french fries. However after eating first few fries, they sit like an iron weight in my stomach and I start feeling sick. Then I remember "Oh yes. This is why I shouldn't buy french fries. I should remember never to buy them again." I buy a lot of french fries.
I also enjoy the anticipation of adventure games. The videos tease an interesting plot, cool artwork, funny dialogue, or a tantalizing mystery and I can't resist. However, after playing one for a few minutes, I remember why I hate them. Most of the gameplay consists of searching for something to click on, watching unskippable cutscenes, or waiting for characters to walk... and I remind myself never to buy one again. I buy a lot of adventure games.
...and this is the first one I've enjoyed playing. The high points for me are what's not there:
- You will never need to watch a character walk.
- All the cutscenes are skippable and most are repeatable if you miss something.
- Movement is instant. Click on the map location you want and your character is instantly there.
All the puzzles are trivially easy, and the gameplay itself mainly consists of dialog trees. You click on all the dialog options in order while the game tells you its story. This is a good thing, though. A game like this is all about the story, and difficult puzzles just interrupt the storytelling.
If you'd just like to be told a story and you hate the gameplay in traditional point-and-click adventures, this is the adventure game for you.

Replayability - 0/5, honestly. It's a pretty short game, all achievements are available in one go-through. There is a "To be continued", so it might be possible to want to refresh on the story.
Price point: I purchased this for $1.74 on the Winter Sale. I do believe it's worth it's $6.99 price. The game left me with chuckles, a want to play more. A short game; I would have loved for it to be a bit longer, however I enjoyed it a lot! The game's soundtrack was wonderful and there was plenty of ambiance within the game itself. The artwork was splendid and I loved the style, it really matched the humor of the characters. The jokes were also my cup of tea. The animation was fluid and added to the style of the game. It got a bit repetitive as you're clicking around looking for clues, and so I wish there was a way to turn off the voiceover, though there might have been and I just missed it. The interface for the suspect profiles is a bit tedious to work around, but I thought it was very cute. The voice acting was rather fitting of all of the characters and I really enjoyed hearing it whenever they weren't repeating lines. The timing was perfect, and was fitting of a detective game, leading you to be suspicious of certain things people say. I did think that the culprit was easy to figure out, and I felt like the game could have made it a bit more difficult, thus also lengthening it. All in all, I thought it was a good game, and definitely worth a buy.
PROS:
+ Cute art style
+ Fluid animations
+ Subtle Humor
+ Ambiance/Good timing
+ Soundtrack
+ Voiceovers were really cute and well done
+ Boggy merch
+ Side puzzles
+ Grimoire's notebook
CONS:

- Easy/not very challenging
- Lines get repetitive
- Voiceover is sometimes annoying
- Lots of random clicking
Tl;dr Short, easy, quirky, and cute

VA-11 Hall-A is a good visual novel with great characters and a terrible drink mixing minigame. The characters all discuss very real problems (from parental pressure to poverty to AI rights) and establish their individual personalities while rarely feeling like they are just complaining, though they are, considering that these talks are at a bar.
The plot is mediocre until the final Act 3 and just has characters coming in sporadically, which only works because the characters are established well. The drink mixing was fun at first, but became tedious by the middle of Act 1 because it's boring, pops in 3-4 times a conversation, and you have to drag the drinks to the blender instead of just clicking them. You can hover the mouse on the line between the drink and the blender and click them in, but it's really annoying. Still, at least it does influence the character interactions uniquely in a way no other visual novel can replicate (with the getting drunk part).
Overall, I'd give this game a 7/10, and would recommend it situationally.

This game is colorful and simply lovely to look at from a visual standpoint. You walk around a pretty area finding television screens with puzzles you have to draw a line through, and it's far more complicated than you might imagine. When the game does a good job of conveying how a particular type of puzzle works, it does a really good job, and when it does a poor job of conveying it, I found myself bored and annoyed at length. Wandering around looking for puzzles you can figure out is okay for a while, but eventually it simply became tedious. A severe deficiency in music made my time with the game even less enjoyable.
From my time with the game, there did not appear to be a story, though you will find audio logs on occasion. Don't expect BioShock or System Shock quality plot and character background, however. Instead, you will be greeted with audio of some of the most pretentious existential rambling I've ever heard in a video game, and it's not story- or character-related dialog, either. It's pretentious dialog for the sake of sounding smart/artistic.
One might think I simply hate puzzle games, but the Portal games and Anti-Chamber were quite fun and memorable for me. Puzzles can be fun, but these rarely entertained me like those did on a regular basis. The scenery is the only overall positive for me, and even that wasn't worth my time with the game. You may enjoy it, but I simply could not find anything to merit continuing.

Don't be fooled by the tags. This is probably not the type of experience you usually hope for with first person puzzle games. This is a first-person setting for many, many 2D line drawing puzzles. The gameplay consists of solving these puzzles and mostly aimless wandering to find the next line drawing puzzle that you actually know the rules for. Once that realization set in, I became less interested in "exploring" to figure out those rules. I've always considered this method of extending gameplay to be cheap or lazy. Had the path been a little bit more intuitive, I probably would have stuck with it long enough to see the story, but I couldn't muster up the interest. If I did more research, I would have avoided paying even the 12 bucks for the bundle this came in. The environment is pretty in it's own stylized way, but I'd rather it be used for an actual game. Huge disappointment for me, but I guess some people dig it.
