Surprisingly addictive game. If, like me, you like the logistics of building bases in RTS games but don't necessarily enjoy the horribly nuanced combat mechanics these games bring, you will enjoy planetbase.
There is, however, one horribly annoying aspect of this game, which is amost game breaking. The colonists' AI  is TERRIBLE. Nevermind the fact that their pathfinding iss so bad that they often build connections in a way that gets them stuck without an airlock (which, in a real base, would be fixed by simply having a rudimentary ladder that goes over the connection), or the fact that even with the priority set to high, engineers only man the telescope stations about a third of the time which, given that the telescopes control the anti-meteor lasers, is often deadly (another thing that, in a real base, would be easily fixed using some roster system).
What really ticks me off is how 10 boxes of medical supplies were just left on the floor of the spaceport to rot. The same thing happened with 20 boxes of bioplastics from a recycled structure. Or when a trading ship was left for over an hour waiting for ONE box of spare parts (which I had over 50 boxes of in storage), blocking the spaceport for the duration of that time.
This would be fixed if the devs gave us the ability to give specific commands to individual colonists.
Despite this, I have more fun in this game than I do in much more expensive titles, therefore I still recommend it.

Where do I start. I nearly gave up on this game after my first catastrophic disaster wiped my base. Basically I had a small food shortage, and some of the crew started dying. But for some reason only my biologists died (who are the only guys who can grow food) turning a small mistake into complete failure. It didn't make sense to me - surely in a food crisis the biologists would be the power brokers, and the guys you would feed first?
I gave up on the game for a few days, but then decided to go back to it, loading from my last good save point (which is my first important point - save often!). I narrowly avoided the previous food shortage and carried on. Have been enjoying the game ever since.
Some of the negative reviews are a little unfair on the game. Someone said there's nothing to do after hitting 250 people - well, try building a base on the next hardest planet (I bet that was the easiest planet). It's a rogue-like game, so the point is that the game will eventually beat you, unless (at the highest level) you are very, very good and have invested many hours into it. If you beat it on the hardest planet, then congratulations - you got your moneys worth. Other players are obviously struggling with understanding what is going on when things go against them, which is fair enough and could be helped by some UI changes.
Pros:
- The game runs well, looks great and has little to no bugs (perhaps except for the RNG issue I had with my biologists).
- The game is nicely challenging, making you carefully consider what you build next as resources are very scarce, and you may need something else to be built first to avoid disaster.
- A nice combination of intense, but relaxing gameplay. Can play for hours at a time and always have something to do.
Cons:
- The UI should be more helpful, especially for new players. The grid status (power, water, O2) should be always visible, and you shouldn't have to swap between some UIs (like daylight hours/wind, and resource levels - they should be separate panels, and visible all the time). Would avoid a lot of rookie (and frustrating) mistakes this way.
- NPC AI is a little frustrating sometimes. Would be nice to have some level of control (or suggestion) over them. Many, many situations where they build a structure, but not the connection (despite all the resources being there). This isn't a deal breaker, but more an annoyance as you see it all the time.
- Wind Turbines are next to useless, as wind is so unreliable and fickle. Simpler to invest in solar and masses of power storage, and always have way more stored than you can use overnight. Need a way to make wind more usable.
Overall a nice game with a lot of promise. If you like dynamic, resource management style games, then this could be for you.

This is a tentatively positive review.  I love the idea and execution of this game.  It's great at the start and kept me playing for a good few hours while I honed my skills.
However the more I played the more broken the game started to feel.  There are some issues with the AI and a few aspects of game play that badly need to be re-balanced.
For example, setting priority on buildings doesn't seem to do much, even when most other buildings are disabled.  Even when I have heaps of engineers, I can't get them to go where they are needed using building priority.
I also had people starving to death when there were vegetables, meat and meals available, and spare seats in the canteen.  What's up with that?  And if the biologists starve first, the whole base collapses.  No one else can pick food from the biodomes.
It's frustrating to watch a base fail when you have all the raw materials and labour required to succeed but can't seem to (even indirectly) direct activity.
This is a good game, but I think there is still work to be done.
If you liked games like Caesar 3, then you will like this.  In my opinion, if the balance issues are sorted, this has the potential to be as much of a classic.

Tl;dr: Its a bullet hell game with a walking character and a dodge + parry mechanic with melee only parts.
The excellent soundtrack alone is worth the asking price, unfortunately it doesnt come included with the game. Cool visuals for an indie title.
The gameplay does get a bit repetetive, the game is fairly short (3 hours to get to the 2nd to last boss on normal) and some of the gameplay mechanics are plain bad.
My main gripes with the game are the controls which neither work particularly well on pad nor on mouse and keyboard. I found myself switching between the 2 but never getting comfortable with either.
A number of people had issues with the fact that attack and dodge inputs are on button release not push (to enable "charging"). I personally did not have problems with that.
Quick time events in a 2017 Indie title... was that really necessairy? ♥♥♥♥ that...
The other big thing is the parry mechanic. The characters are too small to see animations very well, so the game introduces a white flashing light that is supposed to tell you when an attack is coming. The issue is that this white flashing light is INCONSISTENT. I.e. the time it takes after the flashing light to appear until the boss attacks VARIES depending on boss and attack chain. THIS LEAVES NO OTHER OPTION THAN TO MEMORIZE THE TIMINGS FOR PARRIES BY TRIAL AND ERROR. THIS IS ESPECIALLY AN ISSUE ON LATER BOSSES WHICH VARY MORE IN THEIR TIMINGS.
This issue and the annoying stealth boss led me to eventually quit the game.
I did quite enjoy it up until that point and it gave me that adrenaline rush feeling that difficult extended boss fights offer.
Buy it when its cheap! The game itself is not worth 20 Euro.

I'll admit it: I'm downright terrible at puzzle games. I have never once gotten through one without extensive help from walkthroughs. Then why do I love them so much? I realized the answer after finishing Year Walk. I adore the stories. I delight in the synergy of art and music and immersion. And this game delivers.
Year Walk is a haunting trip through Swedish folklore. At times it is peaceful, if lonely, as you wander across the snow. At other times it is incredibly unsettling, such as when you must carry squirming bundles through the woods or the few jump scares. The reigning atmosphere of the game is one of uncertainty, unease, and foreboding; It is a fitting tone for a foolhardy quest to break Nature's laws and peer into the future.
The controls are simple enough. There are no save or load buttons, as this will automatically be done while leaving or entering the game. A pen and some paper will help with some of the puzzles, as will reading the included information about the various spirits. The hint feature was wonderfully done (there was only one clue that failed to enlighten me), which I am ever so grateful for.
Your journey will be a fairly brief one, but the experience will linger long afterwards. I always sit in a stupor through the credits after a good movie, still caught by world I've just witnessed. After your Year Walk, you just might feel the same.

I highly recommend Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc to anyone who: *Enjoys Pheonix Wright, *Enjoys Persona, *Enjoys character development through conversation, *Enjoys Visual Novels, *Enjoys Murder Mystery, *Enjoys new kinds of music and art, *Enjoys quirky, lovable characters, or *Enjoys the satisfaction of something solved. Danganronpa is a beautiful, brilliant game. With a colourful cast and an intense story that compliment eachother wonderfully, you will love at least a few of the characters and enjoy the investigation and class trials in the game. (The comic relief is actually really funny, if not relying on certain characters.) Looking at negative reviews for the game, the people writing them are writing them because, *They experienced some glitches, (I had 0 glitches, on day 2 of release.) *They don't like some of the characters that are still around, *They simply apparently can't handle all the text, (It is a visual novel... It even has a fast-forward feature.) or *They were upset that the game had a linear story that your dialogue choices doesn't change. As you can see, there aren't very many good reasons to dislike a game here. And there aren't many reasons to dislike Danganronpa. Advice going into the game would have to be, *Don't give up on liking certain characters - If there's somebody that seems annoying, DO THE EVENTS WITH THEM! You may end up loving them, *Don't expect the game to be extremely hard. You'll most likely mess up a few times, maybe a couple retries, but using trial and error you will get the correct answer, *Don't assume anything that the game doesn't tell you. Inspect what you can, even if not in Investigation Mode. Don't be afraid to open up the Transcript and go back and see exactly what that one character said. Sometimes things that seem pointless are really important. (Also, if you don't like to see your faves die, stick around till the end and then check the main menu on your save ;))
TL:DR: Danganronpa is an amazing game, and I would recommend getting it to pretty much anyone reading this.

Danganronpa is an engaging VN style thriller, wherein you have to solve mysteries to save the protaganist and his friends from death. It is well-written, engaging and the character development is neat. Some twists are unpredictable, while others are easy to anticipate beforehand. I have got immense satisfaction from playing and completing this game.
Pros:
-Cool Story
-Neat character development
-Does not look too shabby for what is essentially a PSP game
Cons:
-Some fourth wall breaking stuff, that simply seems out of place
-Tedious gameplay. It would have been much better served with Phoenix Wright or Devil's Attorney style dialog based combat, instead of rhythm games, timing based point and click games, etc.
-Some hit detection issues with the aforementioned timing-based point and click games.
-Framerate chugs in certain areas of the game for me (Intel i74710HQ, 16 GB RAM, Nvidia GTX 850M with 4 GB of RAM)
-Mid-trial game glitch, wherein the video stops playing but the audio keeps going, requires a restart to correct. I would recommend saving often. Particularly egregious in Chp 5 and Chp 6 class trials.
Overall while the list of cons seems too long, I would admit that except for the gameplay part, most of it is nitpicking and maybe an issue with my setup. None of the bugs encountered are game breaking
I am not a fan of VN adventure games like Telltale's games, Life is Strange, etc. Haven't played any of those games to completion, but somehow this title stuck a chord with me and I thoroughly enjoyed it.

So there's a great, great amount of detail that cannot be discussed due to spoilers.
With that out of the way, let me tell you: I don't play these kinds of games. I play FPS, RTS, Turn Based, Action, Strategy, everything BUT this genre. I have spied these types of games many, many times and thought they looked HORRIBLE. I mean, it has no REAL gameplay mechanics, right?
You'd be correct: The 'game' is more a series of mini-games, reminiscent of DDR, light-gun games, and a mini-game straight out of Phoenix Wright. You expect to hear OBJECTION! at any moment!
However, that's not the attraction to this game. It's only there to engage you in the moment. The real attraction?
It is one of the
storylines I've ever encountered. I was ENRAPTURED and could not pull myself away. I play a lot of engaging action games, and those hadn't gotten my adrenaline pumping like this does. The twists, turns, and dead ends in the storyline are amazing and keep you rooted to your chair the entire time. The last trial absolutely takes no prisoners and drops all pretense. The voice acting is solid (despite what people may say), the character art is pretty and demonstrates their emotions.
You feel for the characters, sympathize and empathize with them. You find yourself becoming sad at the prospect of a friend dying or a friend being executed for murder. You may be surprised at the reaction of kicking someone's logical butt in an argument and seeing a previously stoic, stuck up pretty boy (lookin' at you Byakuya) suddenly lose his composure at the prospect of not thinking of something a 'lowly peasant' like the main character could.
All in all, I would say get this game if you enjoy a compelling storyline, a whodunnit, and a challenge for your brain.
The only detractor I can think of is sometimes the statements are somewhat illogical although as frustrating as this may get, it does not really detract from the game. If this becomes too annoying, just get a strategy guide. I skipped the last chapter due to this and still found myself staying up through the night just to finish it to find the ending (and boy did it blow my socks off!)

Only MAJOR complaint I have:
I wish this game had higher replay value. The only reason to replay it is to uncover each characters story and with the Steam version, the bonus game requires extra tokens you can only get in the original storyline replay.
Different culprits each time would definitely keep me playing it.

Sadly, I didn't had a chance to play original Toki Tori game on GameBoy Color, so I can't compare how good this remake is. Toki Tori is puzzle game with elements of platformer. Maybe it doesn't look exciting on screenshots but trust me, once you will start to play and get into beating each of many puzzles it starts to get really fun. There are many puzzle games which with progress gets boring but it's not a case with Toki Tori. Each of world is really different to play and demand from you something else! Every world starts easy, to learn you new mechanics, and then goes hard to even superhard - to be honest I had some trouble with few of puzzles and that means Toki Tori pass the test on enjoyability as puzzle game. As hard, I don't mean not being able to progress at all but stuff like mistakes made on earlier stage of level which would result in missing some items to finish it at all. Option to move time back is great, so you don't need to restart game when something goes wrong also, you don't start all over again once you will get touched by monsters or fell into pit/spikes/lava/something else. Even tho graphics aren't really outstanding, and music is decent at most, Toki Tori isn't any less fun because of that.

The
were a bit too sparkly for me. They didn't fit the rest of the game, being more suited for a children's game, with a cartoony look. Regardless, they're otherwise functional.
The
is open, I believe, but it was well chosen. There isn't much to say about it. It's pretty simple, fantasy-like background music, but it did its job of getting you into the game's atmosphere.
There were a few
issues I've had, but I've later found out that most of them could have been avoided, with a bit more explanation. Basically, everything requires 2 clicks --
. First, you click the objective or object you want to collect, and then there's some feedback, and a box appears with a "V" for you to click, to continue. This last step, in my opinion, was completely unnecessary. Also, the box appears in the object's place, so you'll often have to "backtrack" with the mouse, if you were ready to leave the screen, or something.
This is avoided by pressing SpaceBar when the box appears. That way, you can just press it and the box will go away, so it partially solves the problem -- this, however, was
, in the game.
Overall, there are just lots of unnecessary clicks, in a game that's all about clicking. I believe that the visual and audio feedback was sufficient, but I may be wrong.
As I've mentioned, the story is completely cliché. Your farm burns, and you go on a quest to save your father and be an hero. Then, you find that there's a bigger evil on the world, and you want to eliminate it. That's about it.
There's isn't any real idea to be trasmitted by it, no interesting characters, nothing whatsoever. Bottom-line:
.
The
also felt very amateur, in general. The game just feels like it could be written by a middle-schooler. It's not awful, but there's nothing, at any point, that will surprise you or even amuse you. The phrasing is very simple, with not character having any personality... Meh. You can easily skip it and you won't miss anything.
It's hard to separate this from the mechanics. This game is a
, and it's almost all structure, and no mechanics.
Basically, you have a character whose main attribute is stamina. You lose stamina with every meaningful action, and you'll have to sleep on a camp to recover it. There are many camps spread around the map, requiring different resources for you to use them. Some are town inns, which require money, others will simply require different types of food.
Then, you'll also visit several towns that specialize in different things. There's alchemy, fishing, hunting, etc. Each requires different tools, which the townsfolk sell you. In those towns, there are also side-quests, that give you money, honor, and resources.
Honor is basically used for you to unlock certain quests, that require you to be more trust-worthy.
Despite the existence of several different occupations, they're all the same. Once you have a tool and skill (that you get from a quest), the maps will now have a new icon over the resource that you can gather. Then, you click it and there you go.
There's no crafting per se. There are some vendors that give you a potions for herbs though, for example.
Each action will require tools/resources, and stamina. Some of them also require Hunters, Repair-men, Soldiers, etc. You can buy these (as if mercenary) to help you.
As you can tell, the
is about getting resource X and either selling or trading it for resource Y, so that you can do the next quest.
In every map, there are items spread around, but that are very small and often blend with the background. These are mostly optional, but they can also be useful. These include Mushrooms, Eggs, Lost Crates, etc. These won't be unlocked from the start, you'll unlock them progressively, when following the main quest.

The maps tells you nothing useful, but let's you fast travel to every location. So, instead of having to waste 2 minutes and 15 clicks, you'll waste 10 seconds and 2 clicks.
This is fine, and I think it helps the game substancially. However, it could have been much better. Has different areas have different vendors and quests, it would have been useful to have those marked on the map. Perhaps a little quest description and the person who gave it to you, the main vendors, etc. You can very easily get lost, since you take to memorize everything.
Everytime you gather a resource, hunt, etc. you'll lose stamina, and also have a chance to break your tools. If that happens, you'll have to go buy another. Eventually, I just bought every tool twice to avoid backtracking. However, it's very cumbersome, in general. Especially with the later tasks, everything may cost up to half of your stamina. So, you'll travel, do 2 minor things, and have to go back and get more stamina.
I think it's mostly unnecessary, how you constantly have to go back and forward...
The tutorial is very typical of mobile games. You have to click this very specific icon, or else you can't advance. This goes on for a while. While the game opens up
, it's also holding you hand.
If I had focused only on the story line, it would have bored me to death, probably. It's like the game tells you its story through instructions. "Do this. Now, do that. Good, now get that to achieve this! No, no that-- this! Here! This shiny button!" ... It's very, very restrictive. The sidequests help a bit.
Regardless, it's never an adventure of your own.
This is the trick about this game. There's an achievement for every meaningless task. It's annoying and patronizing. However, it's one of those psychological tricks that keeps you invested. Everything feels like progress. Also, every field will disappear after being gathered "x" times, so there will come a point when you've literally completed the game. And I think that's the strangely compelling thing about this game!
It keeps you going for far longer than I'd have guessed. The game has nothing interesting about it, but it still grabs your attention, for those 3 hours!
I would
recommend this game, in most circumstances. It's very bland, and has nothing interesting about it. However, it's still compelling. Besides, it provides a good formula. If you can integrate a
story, and some mechanics into it, perhaps a great game can be made!
. For what it is, it's good!

Zombie Exodus is a text based game putting you in the middle of a zombie apocalyse. Now, I, as well as many others, steer clear of text based games due to them not being as fun as other games, however I was genuinely surprised by how well this game was done. The decisions in this rival those in Telltale's The Walking Dead, and you really do have to make hard decisions. Unlike Telltale's The Walking Dead, this game has 9 possible endings, many character's survival relies solely on your decisions, and your decisions REALLY DO MATTER.
The game starts off quite slow, but quickly builds up to life in a world full of zombies, bandits, and other dangers coming from every angle.
I rate this game at 9/10, and the reasons it doesn't get 10/10 are listed below:
1. A couple of plot points don't get resolved (depending on which ending you get). Some pretty major things happen towards the end of the game, and depending on your choices, you may or may not find out what happens/happened. I know it counts towards the realism, but when someone betrays you, and you never find out who, or when someone stays behind, and you never find out if they live or not, it kinda feels like the loose ends needed wrapping up.
2. A lot of the decisions come down to "Pick the smart option". This is something I like. However there is one point where the writer trades in the "Zombie survival" element for an Indiana Jones-style action sequence.
3. The epilogue is kinda rushed and forced. I got an ending with 9 survivors, and then the game wrapped up with 5 pages set 5 years later telling me how each of them died randomly, and gave a lot of information that wasn't needed. It's kinda like if you watched the first 5 seasons of The Walking Dead, and then had everything past that summarised in 10 pages at the end of the season 5 finale. I would've much rather had a sequel, or DLC (which is something I don't say often).
All in all, this game was highly enjoyable, and I'd definitely recommend it to anyone who enjoys Zombie stories, or interactive story and character driven games.

When I first saw the trailer for this game, I was immediately sold. The stylistic art design, the intense and epic looking boss battles, and the absolutely beautiful music by Carpenter Brut - who is one of my favorite music artists - sold me on the game. However, I was saddened by the fact that it was on PS4. Well, to my surprise, I found it on Steam a little over a year later.
So was my hype worth it? For the most part, yes!
-Story: As soon as you begin the game you are thrust into a simple but effective combat system surrounded by a mysterious and intriguing world. Everything in the world makes you want to know more about what's going on and why the characters are all doing what they're doing. By the end of the game, I was left not just feeling emotion for the story but also satisfaction. The story is not completely straightforward so you have to pay attention to every line and little details to fully grasp what's happening and I really appreciated being fairly challenged to decipher the story as I was being challenged in the gameplay.
-Gameplay: While the game doesn't explain exactly what you're supposed to do during each fight, I never truly felt that the game was being unfair to me. I saw a couple of reviews saying that the game was hard in the wrong way, which I completely disagree with. When you encounter a new boss, you don't know exactly the extent of their abilities or mechanics so you will have to experiment as the fight goes along in order to figure out how to beat them. I absolutely LOVED this. Sure, it felt bad getting beaten every now and then by the crazy amounts of mechanics surrounding a boss but every time I failed, I went back in and tried new strategies until I figured out the best way to defeat them. Aside from about 4 of the bosses, I was able to beat the rest within 2 or 3 tries and it took me about a total of 6 hours to beat the game. Your average casual gamer will probably struggle quite a bit to get through some parts of the game but as long as they are open to trying new strategies and analyzing the boss fight, they will undoubtedly get through the game. Fast reaction time and thinking on your feet will be required.
-Additional Thoughts: Despite absolutely loving this game, I will say that I was left wishing there had been some additional encounters with maybe against some minions or puzzles to solve while walking through each of the awesome prison stages. They were so cool I wish I could have done more in them including maybe explore and find collectibles.
So Furi is definitely a fun and pretty challenging game. While I wouldn't say it's one of the hardest or most content filled games I have played, it did present a fun challenge to get through and a simple but fascinating story with some genuinely sad moments. It was definitely worth the price. I look forward to returning to it a little bit later to beat it in the Furier difficulty now that I have it unlocked and I do so hope there is a sequel later on or at least a spiritual successor because I loved the style and I loved the boss fights!

Detective Grimoire is a point-and-click mystery game where you attempt to solve a murder and meet a myriad of fun and unique characters along the way. The game balances humor and murder suprisingly well and on occasion breaks the fourth wall to give a nod to the game that came before (Detective Grimoire first appeared within a free flash game online) and the games that will (hopefully) come after this one. The art style is beautiful and the voice acting and soundtrack help liven up an already vibrant world.  Though the game itself is short, it still packs a solid punch and leaves you wanting more.

This is truly a unique experience. It captures the folly of man and the horrible thing he does to try and give himself comfort. It captures the evil lurking within us all, and the secrets of life, and lays them down in woven layers to be slowly unravelled, but along with it, your life. This captures the dark nature of pagan rituals and the dire consequences of trifling with spirits.
The game provides several hours of play, and is deeply captivating for it's subliminal use of imagery to remind the Year Walker what is really happening. All this imagery is deeply rooted in folklore, philosophy, and ancient religions. The soundscape is eerie, and grows more haunting as the Year Walk progresses. The world itself takes on a sinister appearance, and all the while you get the feeling of hostility. A feeling that these spirits do not approve, and they do not want to to be there.
My words can not do the game justice, however. This game is truly unique, and definately worth the money if you like deep storylines that need no narrative.

As said by many others, it used to be good, but not any more. It's another game where all the devs care about now is making money, not the game, and certainly not its players. Don't download it, and definitely don't spend money on it, just avoid it.
Some fifteen, to twenty years ago online games were a niche thing, devs didn't make them expecting to make mountains of money, they were just in it to make games, and with all being pay to play games, they focused on making them their own brand of fun, so people that liked it would keep paying for subscriptions. Then the free to play (F2P) model became a thing, and over time more F2P PC games adopted the more abusive F2P model that used to just be the kind of thing seen in browser, and mobile games, where your only real options to get ahead in time was to no life the game, or spend money, lots of money. Now more, and more online games just seem like they're only there to make money, and nothing else, fun be damned. In fact, they'll purposely put in things that are frustrating, just so they can say "look, you can alleviate your frustration with the cash shop."
That's what has happened here. In the early days they defended paid premium ships as just things that were a different variant of the ships you can get without spending money, as they provided no real game play advantage, which was largely true then, other things to spend money on were cosmetics, and modest boosters to gains. Now decision after decision seems to have no other reasoning other than to milk as much money as they can from players too easily parted with their money. Short on the parts needed to make that new super powerful item/ship since they just increased the volume of materials you need multiple times over, without increasing in-game material rate of accusation, or are about to remove that ship from production? No problem, you can now buy those materials in their cash shop, through random boxes, even materials to make in-game items you can gain in no other way, that's right, such things can basically be called cash shop equipment like weapons. Want to grind it instead, well maybe, but if that is possible you may need to spend hours a day for months, and you likely need to fly fully levelled ships, so all that XP you're getting is wasted, unless you're willing to spend real money to transfer the excess XP to other ships. They will make new items, and classes of powerful ships after a short release event timed exclusives not available again for a period of months just to create more demand for them during the release event, and get people to spend up to several hundred dollars US to get
ship before they're gone.
All this can come at the expense of balance, and game play since they're removing the ability of other players to get said items, providing the whales with an advantage. The game feels like it's losing players too, causing them to keep making increasingly desperate (and unpopular) changes to their matchmaker rules so rounds can start more easily, since most of the game needs other players for you to even play. The part that doesn't need other players (open space) just gets ignored, and gutted to make other parts "better," with nothing but the promise of some all important fix all update that has been delayed for months. Although, if that update is as effective as their recent module upgrade update, then it will just make things grindier, and all around worse. What it comes down to is that any company willing to hurt their game, and their players to make money, doesn't deserve your money, or time, just don't bother.

I was really disappointed by this game. At first, I really liked the graphical pixel design as well as the soundtrack, mainly because it's very minimalistic but does not feel like some 8 Bit peeptone concert. Plus it is a game about a Viking, which I personally really enjoy hence there are not many Viking-themed games out there.
BUT! The game is not just horrendously hard, it's unfair. Where games like Dark Souls give you enough time to explore and try some moves etc. here you have almost constantly enemies spawning from everywhere and you cannot see them because you range of view is quite small, therefore you often cannot react fast enough. Addicionally the feeling of the jumping mechanic is really outdated for a 2D sidescroller, meaning once you jumped you cannot change your direction exept you do a double jump. But even jumping onto a little block in your way will be pretty difficult because you jump to far. It's supposed to be like this because it used to be this way in the classical 2D sidescrolling era. But it doesn't make it automaticly a good thing. For me it just feels clunky, difficult to control and overall outdated.
The problem with the difficulty is that you simply have to memorize where and when enemys spawn and when to jump. When I want to play a game, difficult or not, I do NOT want to memorize everything! I just want the opporturnity to play through with my skill, not because I know that I have to jump in 3,4 seconds.
Too bad this game equals difficult with unfairness, at least in my opinion. I get it, there are many gamers who want an expierience like in the classic 80's NES-era platformers, but in my opinion this just doesn't fit today as it did back in the day. Retro gaming in general can be very good and a lot of fun but memorizing whole levels is just a sign for bad leveldesign. It always has at least to be possible to play the game through all by your skill. Due to the design choices overall the game feels kinda dated.
Hence this game really doesn't cost much I still recommend to try it out for yourself and probably you will like it better than me.

TL;DR at first: It's Phoenix Wright meets Battle Royale with quirky art direction and fantastic music. It's p. damn good!
Got introduced to this game when Onenronen started the quite legendary thread on Something Awful where he translated the game for his screenshot LP. At the time it was literally the only way to experience the game in any translated form and it did gain quite a huge cult following, thanks to Tumblr's involvement etc, and this eventually attracted Spike Chunsoft's attention and they eventually decided to release the game in the west.
Now, few years later, I'm getting to play this game on Steam and having first hand experience with this small web phenomenon that I was checking up multiple times a week for many, many months... And the game's tight. Definetly recommend using the japanese audio instead of the english one, as the english one's pretty damn cheesy, and you will miss some quite notable voice actors - for example Shinji's VA from NGE is voicing the protagonist in this game, and the old lady who voices Doraemon does actually do VA work for Monokuma, that's quite a fresh and unexcepted from her, really fitting though!
Playing on controller, it might look or control a bit clunky at first, considering this was originally a PSP game, but other than that it works fine. Only had one crash and that was due to too much alt tabbing for matter of hours and it eventually didn't like that.
But yeah. Very fresh 'n quirky art direction (jeesh the cutscenes in this game!), music is fantastic and while the characterisation is bit tropey at times, the writing saves a lot and this game packs quite a bunch of twists and mystery for you to untangle 'n experience.
I'd say give it a shot definetly if you dig murder mysteries and visual novels. I do like this, but I'm a sucker for these sorta games anyhow.

Hero of the Kingdom isn't a very involved or "deep" title, but the entire time I played it I had no desire to stop. It isn't a long title, and there isn't a tremendous amount of replay value, but it is definitely worth a play through at least once.
The game is a point-and-click adventure that follows the story of a farm boy on what starts as a rescue mission and ends as a world saving quest. Through the entire thing you'll gather resources, hunt, fight and trade, all with simple mouse clicks. There are no mini-games to complete for any of the activities, and the game play is simplistic overall. That said, it is still enjoyable.
If you're looking for a quick, narrative-based game. Hero of the Kingdom gets the job done.

This could be in part because the screen would go white whenever I went fullscreen but it's mainly because the border and drink ingredients menu take up so much of the screen that I can barely tell you what the bar I was working at looks like. It's cool that the hud is supposed be the hud the character sees but that doesn't help me get immersed in the world. If you really want to see the story just look at a playthrough on youtube. I'll preface this by saying that I tend to enjoy most games I play. All the same, however, I binged this game for two days. Most games don't go that way for me.
To start with, the game is as the game says when you first start it up; "best enjoyed comfortable". It's a fun, low-effort (on the player's part) where you serve some drinks and listen to some characters tell you various things, whether it's their life story, events going on in the game world, their worries, fears, happy times, whatever.
Now, admittedly, that may not sound so fun. However, I can say that I found it to be incredibly fun and funny as well. The dialogue is well written and is chock full of humor (even if a lot of it is somewhat low-brow or "toilet humor", which I'll admit I have a soft spot for sometimes). The characters are all interesting, even if you only meet them two or three times. Many of the regulars you meet four or five times in the game are great, but even characters that you seem like you're meant to dislike come off really well at the end.
The gameplay is incredibly basic puzzle solving (for lack of a better term at the moment), as well as a bit of pattern recognition when it comes to getting certain charcters' endings, but the game really isn't about the gameplay. It's about the characters and dialogue, primarily, and that's what this game does incredibly well. Even the main character is a compelling character despite the fact that you spend most of your time listening to other characters.
Finally, the music is top notch. Just about every song on the soundtrack either serves a purpose and does it well, or is just incredibly catchy. I thought it was so good that I gladly bought the whole soundtrack.
To sum this review up: if you enjoy good writing and good characters and enjoy laidback (almost mindless) gameplay, VA-11 HALL-A is the game you're looking for.

First off:
This game has the best title screen and title screen music in existence.
I DO NOT RECOMMEND this game if you are expecting a Visual Novel with 75% reading and 25% gameplay (Ace Attorney Series, Nonary games).
I RECOMMEND this game if you don't mind a decent story that is 99% reading and 1% gameplay. I expected the former (75/25 ratio story/gameplay).
I am setting the game to Recommended status simply because, for what the game is and achieves, it's good. It however is not to my liking....at all. As a story driven gamer, this title barely falls short.
Sound/Music: 10/10 - Amazing, especially the music. Great job.
Gameplay: N/A - You make and serve drinks. Sometimes you have to guess the right drink based on wording given by the client or by remembering a clue in a previous part of the game. There isn't much else here. This is the 1% gameplay.
Story: 6/10 - Here's where I gripe. First off, the writing in this game is fantastic. It's hilarious. Awesome. Now... The story in and of itself as a whole bored me to death. I found myself reading through texts and conversations so fast that it was like I was cramming for a college history test the next day (that I failed). The problem lies in that there is little to no conflict in the overall story. It comes together as just an ordinary person in daily life slugging their way through just to get by. This would be fine, but nothing really "grabs" you beyond that. You are waiting and expecting something to, but it never does.
Overall: 7/10 - This was of course my personal experience. I say again, that for other gamers that are story driven, I do recommend you give this one a try. Please take a look at the overall consensus for the title. It may just be your holy grail story you've been looking for.

I think the reason so many people have mixed opinions on
is because they expect something from it other than very hard puzzles, and Thekla (the dev) have brutally compressed this game into only hard puzzles and nice views.  In my opinion, those puzzles are mostly really interesting, instructive, and the good kind of difficult, but you might not think so, and the difference between liking this game, and not liking this game is more about brain-shape than good-taste geniuses vs. bad taste dummies.
Let me explain more about game design, and where I struggled so you know what you might be in for: In Braid, Thekla's lead developer's last game, you could hop around and murder rabbits while you chewed on each piece of the hard puzzles, while in
you can:
> Look at the puzzle
> Try to solve the puzzle
> Look at the beautifully designed world while feeling intense anxiety about puzzles
> List ends, solve the puzzle already dummy.
It's easy to take the simplicity as pressure.  As somebody who played Zelda, I felt like the game expected me to solve the puzzles faster than it actually did, so the game became much more fun as I decided to just lean into the puzzles.  Another stumbling block, for me, was explicit fail states, which is to say,
will tell you you did the puzzle wrong, and often punish you for it (this prevents you from mechanically brute-forcing puzzles, and
wants to help you do hard things wit your brain instead of easy things wit your fingers) which hurts, it can feel like the game doesn't like you.  The trick is understanding that you are alone with the puzzles, and you have to try to be like a zen master, and really struggle for a while with some of them.  If the idea of that makes you sad, then you're not hardcore enough for this game, and you should probably only play minecraft...
you tiny baby.
I came to an existential crisis that everyone I have talked with about the game has come to: "
."  because parts of this game are unpleasent to get through depending on how the pressure you feel to achieve lines up (ha) with your ability to solve very hard puzzles.
The tonic for this problem is either to defeat the anxiety of "I have to get to the next thing" by leaning into the problem, switching tasks, or looking that♥♥♥♥♥♥up in a guide, if you must.  Be careful about looking that♥♥♥♥♥♥up in a guide, because that will quickly wreck the game for you if you do too much of it, but I definitely looked some of that♥♥♥♥♥♥up in a guide, feel good about all of it, and advocate your right to look that♥♥♥♥♥♥up in a guide.  The standard I'd reccomend is: "Do I want to learn what this puzzle is trying to teach me" and if you don't, then it will not make you happy to solve the puzzle.  If you feel like you need to move on to another puzzle, or never play the game again, move on to another puzzle, one way or another.  Skip things that you find boring, not things that you find difficult, and you'll feel good about the game.
A note on accesibility: it's often remarked in negative reviews that vision, or hearing impaired can't play this game.  You can beat the game without doing those sections, which are the shortest, arguably most-skippable, denying you one achievement and the least interesting 5% of the game.

The game resets all your progress upon completion!
In a weirdly twisted understanding of the New Game+ concept, all that you keep when starting a new game is your real-life understanding of how the puzzles work. So, make screenshots!
While it may be true that it never really says "New Game+" anywhere, the way the game teases more content via inaccessible areas that you can see but not reach imo kinda implies that this still is a New Game+ of some sort.
That's the thing: technically, you *can* reach those "inaccessible" areas already on your first playthru. The only thing blocking that path are hard puzzles and yet undiscovered secret exploratory ways. – *If only* the game didn't decide to be an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and reset everything without warning.
I'm usually against most forms of spoilers but this is something that I feel everyone who wants to reach the end should know. Because having to redo a hard puzzle;   a puzzle you already wrapped your head around for hours, if not days;   a puzzle that you've already solved before;   but this time you have to do it *while being angry* – it's frustrating, it's torture, it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ttery deluxe. It is bad design.
Now, as for the actual game: Lovely! Memorable! Wonderful! A contrast that may be hard to believe. Aside from a few elements that simply aren't for me (like the nature of the puzzles during the "Peer Gynt run"), I like the overall design very much – which is, I would consider, a well-crafted combination of abstract puzzle solving and mellow exploration.
And "The Witness" is definitely a gem for explorers. For one, the island has several beautiful vistas (even on the lowest settings) which is one of the reasons to examine every possible corner. But the more time you spend on the island, the more you're going to discover how many things are hidden in plain sight. The secrecy is so dense! "Collectible" audio clips presenting philosophical quotes about science are just one of many treasures that you can find. Personally, even 72+ hours in I was still discovering new things.
The puzzles themselves are easy at first, obviously – but once you leave (what I call) the fort, you gain access to the majority of the island at once. Therefore, you might be overwhelmed by the options and the sudden spike in difficulty as you possibly encounter a few confusing puzzles with foreign new mechanics. Rest assured, however, that for every mechanic there is a respectful, non-textual, no-hand-holding, non-immersion-breaking, learn-while-you-play, in-game tutorial *somewhere* on this island. And that, my friend, is good design.
"The Witness" might not be a game for everyone but enjoyed it immensely.

Video Blogger Story Public Service Announcement
Update Version: Initial Release
Disclosure: This game copy was bought by the reviewer.
AVOID THIS GAME!
I had my suspicion of the game quality as soon as I noticed the red flags in the trailer provided. I decided it would be best to confirm the warnings now and hopefully save a few people money. With the recent success of YouTuber Life, the obvious competition they claim inspired them to go into Early Access, I knew clones would appear just as relevant clones appeared for DayZ and Five Nights At Freddys. While I understand games will be similar, the staggering void in regards to content left me concerned.
The ultimate goal of the game is to become the top "video blogger" and dethrone clear spoofs of  well known Youtubers (such as Markiplier which is pictured using the famous mustache). You start with 500 dollars and begin buying games with one or two letters differences from the games being spoofed. This would be fine had the developer not used actual logos (DOTA symbol is sideways) and used images of official art (LoL character art for example is water smeared, but easily discernible) for video icons. You select a game to review and the equipment before waiting for the review to finish. Slender man for some reason appears and the video ends with you gaining subscribers and likes.
You can upgrade your equipment and games, but you don't do much else. The main objective for subscribers is achieved by setting up a Let's Play and then doing nothing as it finishes. You also need to rest in order to review, which is done by waiting. Outside of this, there is absolutely nothing to do. This is more of a sitting simulator with no real interaction. The amount of images used for video icons that are of other properties is staggering, so maybe spend the downtime linking how many Google Maps photographs were used.
Bugs are plentiful as well, including a game breaking one that made it impossible to earn money. Icons wouldn't react, sliders don't respond and some windows became stuck. This game feels, plays and looks rushed outside the character himself that at least looks decent. I am further investigating this game for any possible issues, but for now I strongly urge to avoid it all together.

This game is just fantastic.
The player character has just as much arsenal as the bosses; all attacks are useful in some ways and it's up to you to figure out the best strategy; aside from the tutorial boss there is no "one-way to do it" approach in any fight, so you are free to explore every tactic. The combat is so quick and the controls are so responsive that sometimes when I got into the flow, my brain couldn't keep up with what was going and I had to rely purely on muscle memory to react. The camera works very well, maybe aside from some bullet hell phases, but it's something one can get used to.
Between each fight there is some lore exposition for a boss you're about to fight next. No fighting there; you just walk (or auto-walk) and listen to the guy that knows everything. It was a good idea to do it this way, because the adrenaline levels get pretty high during each fight and these sections give you some time for much needed rest.
Music. It's majestic. Each track is very different from one another and each creates a different atmosphere for the fight. The title screen itself gives you all the feels you need.
Give Furi a try. If you don't like what you see in the tutorial boss, you can always refund. But bloody hell, please do not miss out on this game.

So after giving up on Ryse two days ago, I give up on Furi soon after it.  And while the action is the same the end results are completely different.
Ryse was a very dull repetitive game that end up being both dull and repetitive.
Furi on the other hand is a vibrant colorful, fighter which has a non evolving combat style (in fact there's no upgrades) but yet is shockingly good.
The entire game is built around 9 boss fights, where you walk between locations (exceedingly long walks, but luckily there's an auto walk, though if you need an auto walk how not doing the vistas instead?)  and then have incredibly excellent fights against colorful and different bosses.
Imagine if you just fought against the bosses of Bayonetta, or Devil May Cry.  This game does that, it doesn't have the craziest bosses, but it does have some excellent fights.
So why should I give it up?  Well there's really two problems with Furi, and neither make it a bad game, though I do take issue with one.
The first issue is simply that Furi is hard.  Not just "Oh this is difficult" But at the Dark Souls area of "hard" the first boss is relatively simple, the second boss is difficult, and the third boss is considered one of the hardest in the game (and he is).   I really hate that third boss.  He's what beat me down.
And the thing is the game makes some allowances.  If you die, you only restart the current "phase" and each boss has a different amount.  The Third boss (called The Line) has long phases and none of them are impossible.  But boy they will beat you down.  In fact I have a feeling every boss in this game will beat you down until you learn the fight.
Problem is I just can't get The Line down, much like I just can't beat certain bosses in the Souls games.   I've tried and I've tried and I just can't perfect parry, I just can't dodge every attack, and I eventually get whittled down, and yet I get up.
Eventually though I stayed down, and it wasn't "I hate this game".  But rather I'm not very good at it.  Maybe I'll attempt it again, even talking about this boss makes me say "That's not where this story ends" but for all I know, that might be the farthest I get.  Shameful but I accept that, and in fact respect that.
But that leads to my second problem with this game.  There's two difficulties at the beginning of the game (with a third locked off).  The normal difficulty is hard.  The easier difficulty is supposed to be a little easier but still challenging.  Problem is the easy difficult removes achievements and kind of insults you when you select it.  The insult is annoying but the achievements make me feel that my time beating the game isn't worthy of being considered.  Now listen, it's ok to not give me all achievements, there's difficulty achievements in games all the time.   But if I do X I deserve to get the achievement for X.   Reward the player for enjoying the game THEIR WAY not only in the way you deem it acceptable.  I honestly feel like the game grudgingly put the easy mode in and I just can't bring myself to walk down that path.
So after slamming against that wall for 2-3 hours I finally said I have to put it down.  I couldn't let myself take the easy path but there wasn't another option so I went off and played Super Hot.  Like I said I MIGHT return but I think that's unlikely.
Yet I recommend the game, with the caveat that you need to be the type of player who likes Dark Souls, who likes that super hard fight and wants to try to be the best, because this is a game that will demand a great deal out of you, but every fight even each phase is quite an accomplishment.

On a scale from 1 to 10 this game is an 11, and it'd give itself a 12.
Jokes aside, Furi is a very memorable experience and one of the best games I've ever played. If you're looking for ultra-stylish, challenging and rewarding action game with intriguing story and high replay value, you will enjoy it.

I enjoyed this game. It is challenging to get the colony going. I had to restart multiple times due to faillures of one sort or another. The A.I. isn't as bad as some people are making it out to be, once you figure out why things happen the way they do. Basically, you want to add redundant colonists as soon as possible and grow only as quickly as you need to--too  quickly and you won't have enough manpower to run the place. If you only have one engineer for example, and something unfortunate happens to him you're in for trouble.
$20 is maybe a bit steep for the amount of content there is. It kept me occupied for a few evenings but that might be the last for me.  Some of the buildings could use more variety of furniture. The dorm only has one fixture to add--the bunkbed--it would be nice if I could add plants or entertainment systems. The cabin is almost the same but it's a different kind of bed--a single--supposedly more comfy.  Its really only a 2D game because you can't build on anything other than the plains. Hills are just obstacles that you have to build around.
I'm recommending it because it fills a genre hole that I haven't really seen before (a city-builder type of game in hostile environments) and I do think its more fun than Project Aura, but it seems to me like its almost an early access game, because I feel they still need to add more features to it to make it worth $20.
The intruders are a bit lame. Random visitors just start shooting up the place and hopefully you have armed guards to fight back. I'm also not sure about these boulders constantly falling from the sky. Micrometeorites would probably be easier to understand. A better variety of random events could improve the game, too.
I find there are a lot of city builder games where you get to the point where you have pretty much everything the game has to offer in your sim and then you start to wonder, what can I do next? In this game it might happen a bit sooner than the others.
Just as bad as all of the negative reviews say sadly :(.

If you enjoy grinding then you may enjoy this game. That said, everyone else shouldn't even bother. I like digimon, and I was excited about the prospect of being able to obtain and use my favorite one's in this game. The subpar graphics and lackluster combat wasn't much of a deterrent in the face of my nostalgia. The rng mechanics however, made it impossible to enjoy. In the 8 hours I played, I never even left the first area. I grinded a digimon I liked to get a very low drop chance egg that I could hatch for use on my team. Then I grinded the necessary items to hatch the egg. Then, after numerous failures, the egg broke. After breaking several more eggs I realized that the chances of success are abysmally low. Eggs are basically duds for anyone without godlike rng or far too much time on their hands. This means everyone else has to pay money in the cash shop just to get anything other than the starting digimon. I really wanted to like this game, but when the game keeps setting you up to fail in one of its (imo) most important feature, it's just not worth it.

This is one of those games that feels like crack. When I look up and it's 5:00 am and I have to be to work in 3 hours, you know you have a winner.
But..... This is one of those times I wish Steam had a middle option between yes and no on the recommendation. This game has so much potential. It has given me one of the best resource managment simulator experiences of my life, and yet manages to fall very very short in longevity.
I love how fragile your ecosystem is, and how easily one small mistake can snowball and wipe out your entire colony, even if it is massive and once rather stable. The game forces you to be really careful and wise when you expand. The rewards from succeeding where you once failed are among the best in gaming memory for me. And the rewarding feeling of mastering a planet and developing a stable colony that can service a dozen ships and hundreds of visiters is incredibly satisphying.
But once you've conqured 3 planets, the game is done. The foundation is fantastic, but there is absolutely no content. It's so frustrating. Rarely is a game so well balanced, and yet so darn short.
This game could use 4 things, 1. a map editor or more planets 2. a more diverse set of challenges 3. deeper data menues that give you the ability to follow your names conolists and get a better sense of their lives. 4. more fluf.... more content, more entertainment options, more items, etc.... the game is solid, it just needs a lot more depth.
So expect to find a really good game, that feels unfinnished.

This game is horrible. Nothing different from MtG 2012 or 2013. Which I was okay with.
All I wanted was the ability to build my own decks with the new "Sealed Deck" Gametype and duel the computer. Maybe let the computer play one of my own decks. That would be cool, too.
But that wasn't happening. You can only play "Sealed Deck" twice until you have to buy new slots for your custom decks. No deleting decks allowed. After you draw your boosters, those boosters are locked to your acccount, and you can't shake them or Re-draft (Start from scratch). You have to buy more slots from WoTC. This is a money grab, plain and simple.
When I dug into it, I found out their reasoning was for "Online Play", they didn't want people to sit around and re-roll decks to get the perfect combination and head to the top of the Online Ladder, so they locked cards in place. But then they let you re-roll decks anyway, however you have to "Buy Slots". Which means, people will still be doing the same thing -- sitting around and re-rolling decks to get the perfect cards. The only difference? They have to shell out three bucks everytime they do it, now. So, we can clearly see why they put this mechanism into place.
Which is the dumbest part. I suck at programming, but I know a monkey could seperate online from offline play and let me reroll my sealed decks, even if its just against the computer. But, they opt not to. Because they want your money.
I'm not joking when I say I beat the Single Player campaign within an afternoon (3 hours), and when I found out I couldn't Re-Roll decks, I uninstalled this application and rebooted MTG 2012. It's a more solid / balanced game with more fun decks, and Planechase is Worlds Better than the current iteration of Sealed Deck.
Try again, Wizards. Nobody wants to play a MtG game where they are paywalled for building decks. That is what this game is about. Building decks and taking them apart. Why are you preventing us from doing what the very foundation of this game is about? That's like telling a Kenyan Runner he has to complete the 400m dash, but you hack his legs off and charge him if he wants to use them. What is the sense in that?

I have played all of the iterations of the "Magic: Dotp" series and I have to say this is another great addition to the series. The new drafting mode is an interesting and refreshing style of play that has been well waited for. One of the less exciting changes to the game is the make over that has been done to the HUD. Oddly they have chose to go for a lighter and brighter theme as opposed to the darker more metallic version of the previous entry. It isn't a bad choice but the bright blue is a bit distracting. Another aspect of the game that is a favorite of mine is the DLC decks that come every once in a while, this time around they are all pretty good, but personally I don't find them as interesting and unique as previous DLC decks. Overall the game is really fun especially if you can play with a few friends, a definite buy if you liked the last one or want to get prepped for DOTP 2015.

I have enjoyed the previous installments of DotP.  They all added a new game type, mechanic, twist, and the decks were varied and interesting.  Chandra's deck in the previous installment could literally be played with no creatures...Jace's mill deck was surprisingly fun, and the demons of Liliana's were brutal and made for some interesting happenings.
What I have played of this, and of the 5-6 decks I have played...each deck is LITERALLY the exact same.  Well...not exact, but they all follow a basic premise...mana ramp, play big creature, win with big creature.  Even the non-green (the color best known for mana-ramping) followed this pattern.  Whichever side dropped the bombshell first, won.  And the time I've played, only one deck acheived this on a consistent basis for you.  The AI pretty much cheats it's way to beating your face in.
The campaign itself only unlocks a handful of decks.  In order to unlock the myriad of others, you have to play a "revenge" mode, where you re-fight all the people you fought...with better versions of their decks.  And then, you encounter and unlock the other missing 10341 decks you didn't get before.  So much grind, such hassle.  Or, you know, the alternative exists...pay them real money to eliminate the grind...which also destroys much of the (non-existent) fun of facing new decks with what you have and winning.
This was the first DotP I did NOT enjoy in any sense.  I gave up on the campaign after losing repeatedly with the two decks I had at my disposal.  Eventually, i did succeed and tried other decks, only to find that I couldn't win ANY matches without using one specific deck, period.  And I play MtG on a quite frequent basis.
Bottom line, ignore this one...by 2013 instead.  Not quite as smooth, but far more fun, with far more versatility in the decks.

An alright "retro styled" platformer; but a very poor imitation of an arcade classic.
I'll put it this way: RASTAN, a coin guzzling monster of an arcade machine made in 1987, a game which this one desperately wants to copy, is far more forgiving, fair and balanced than Volgarr. The absurdity of that staggers me. I cannot think of a worse example of nonsensically exaggerated "Nintendo Hard" difficulty - a recent idea which is purely the product of people's dim memory of the past and laziness.
You can't blame this game's poor design choices on anything but the creators' inability to recognize and recreate the good aspects of something they sought to imitate. It's not "oldschool" to have ridiculously long stretches between checkpoints or rely on poor placement of annoying enemies to challenge the player, it's just plain bad. Try harder next time, guys.
On the positive side, the graphics and animation are fairly pleasing (if inconsistent) and combat is generally satisfying. I honestly want to praise this game just for aspiring to be like Rastan (which was long overdue for a proper tribute); but the more I play it, the more it infuriates me. Just get one of the many excellent Taito arcade collections instead.

Pros:
+ Gameplay is distinctive enough to make it "not just another VN", entertaining and it makes you think.
+ Decent runtime of about 18-20 hours, with more gameplay possible if you participate in the bonus mode unlocked on completion of the game.
+ Very interesting characters who I wanted to know a lot about.
+ While I don't like the direction the ending went, the story itself is very enjoyable and engaging.
+ Music is very nice, as is the artwork and stylistic choices.
Cons:
- Story is great, but ending is a bit... lacking? A lot of the explanation is practically handed to you, and it's honestly kind of weak and vague.
- Would recommend doing it on hard mode to get the best experience -- I played on what was "normal" and honestly it probably wasn't much harder than easy.
- I honestly wish there was a greater amount of free time to figure out everyone's "secrets" and "motivations".
Overall:
I'm not typically huge on Visual Novel anime games and whatnot, but I had a lot of fun with this title and enjoyed it immensely. It kept me on the edge of my seat, and despite being relatively easy (compared to, say, a Phoenix Wright game or something), I still found myself having a moment or two where I had to sit and think, or work harder than normal.
I would recommend the game to anyone who is into the sort of gameplay VNs provide. It's very interesting and I'm still desperately waiting for the second one to be ported to PC.

Do you like dark murder mysteries?  Weird visual novels with lots of distinct characters?  EXTREMELY Japanese nonsense?  This is right up your alley.
I had given up hope on seeing this game, since I do not have a Vita, and seeing it pop up on Steam was an extremely pleasant surprise.
This game has a very compelling plot that keeps you on a hook to see what on earth is going on at every point.  You are constantly suspicious of everything, while desperately needing to figure out who is lying, why, and just what exactly even happened.
The music is great, and really enhances the mood, especially during the courtroom scenes.
The game is oozing with that great style some Japanese games especially seem to have, and the anime aesthetic is well-drawn and a lot of fun.
If you dig visual novels with some great flair, and love mysteries, shell out for this one!  You'll plow through it straight through, and won't want to stop.

This game is very hard, and made me feel bad a few times, but I'm having a great time, and I reccomend downloading it, and returning it if you don't like it.  By hour 1.5 you will have experienced the basic loop of the game in it's entirety.
I think the reason so many people have mixed opinions on
is because they expect something from it other than very hard puzzles, and Thekla (the dev) have brutally compressed this game into only hard puzzles and nice views.  In my opinion, those puzzles are mostly really interesting, instructive, and the good kind of difficult, but you might not think so, and the difference between liking this game, and not liking this game is more about brain-shape than good-taste geniuses vs. bad taste dummies.
Let me explain more about game design, and where I struggled so you know what you might be in for: In Braid, Thekla's lead developer's last game, you could hop around and murder rabbits while you chewed on each piece of the hard puzzles, while in
you can:
> Look at the puzzle
> Try to solve the puzzle
> Look at the beautifully designed world while feeling intense anxiety about puzzles
> List ends, solve the puzzle already dummy.
It's easy to take the simplicity as pressure.  As somebody who played Zelda, I felt like the game expected me to solve the puzzles faster than it actually did, so the game became much more fun as I decided to just lean into the puzzles.  Another stumbling block, for me, was explicit fail states, which is to say,
will tell you you did the puzzle wrong, and often punish you for it (this prevents you from mechanically brute-forcing puzzles, and
wants to help you do hard things wit your brain instead of easy things wit your fingers) which hurts, it can feel like the game doesn't like you.  The trick is understanding that you are alone with the puzzles, and you have to try to be like a zen master, and really struggle for a while with some of them.  If the idea of that makes you sad, then you're not hardcore enough for this game, and you should probably only play minecraft...
you tiny baby.
I came to an existential crisis that everyone I have talked with about the game has come to: "
."  because parts of this game are unpleasent to get through depending on how the pressure you feel to achieve lines up (ha) with your ability to solve very hard puzzles.
The tonic for this problem is either to defeat the anxiety of "I have to get to the next thing" by leaning into the problem, switching tasks, or looking that♥♥♥♥♥♥up in a guide, if you must.  Be careful about looking that♥♥♥♥♥♥up in a guide, because that will quickly wreck the game for you if you do too much of it, but I definitely looked some of that♥♥♥♥♥♥up in a guide, feel good about all of it, and advocate your right to look that♥♥♥♥♥♥up in a guide.  The standard I'd reccomend is: "Do I want to learn what this puzzle is trying to teach me" and if you don't, then it will not make you happy to solve the puzzle.  If you feel like you need to move on to another puzzle, or never play the game again, move on to another puzzle, one way or another.  Skip things that you find boring, not things that you find difficult, and you'll feel good about the game.
A note on accesibility: it's often remarked in negative reviews that vision, or hearing impaired can't play this game.  You can beat the game without doing those sections, which are the shortest, arguably most-skippable, denying you one achievement and the least interesting 5% of the game.

The game resets all your progress upon completion!
In a weirdly twisted understanding of the New Game+ concept, all that you keep when starting a new game is your real-life understanding of how the puzzles work. So, make screenshots!
While it may be true that it never really says "New Game+" anywhere, the way the game teases more content via inaccessible areas that you can see but not reach imo kinda implies that this still is a New Game+ of some sort.
That's the thing: technically, you *can* reach those "inaccessible" areas already on your first playthru. The only thing blocking that path are hard puzzles and yet undiscovered secret exploratory ways. – *If only* the game didn't decide to be an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and reset everything without warning.
I'm usually against most forms of spoilers but this is something that I feel everyone who wants to reach the end should know. Because having to redo a hard puzzle;   a puzzle you already wrapped your head around for hours, if not days;   a puzzle that you've already solved before;   but this time you have to do it *while being angry* – it's frustrating, it's torture, it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ttery deluxe. It is bad design.
Now, as for the actual game: Lovely! Memorable! Wonderful! A contrast that may be hard to believe. Aside from a few elements that simply aren't for me (like the nature of the puzzles during the "Peer Gynt run"), I like the overall design very much – which is, I would consider, a well-crafted combination of abstract puzzle solving and mellow exploration.
And "The Witness" is definitely a gem for explorers. For one, the island has several beautiful vistas (even on the lowest settings) which is one of the reasons to examine every possible corner. But the more time you spend on the island, the more you're going to discover how many things are hidden in plain sight. The secrecy is so dense! "Collectible" audio clips presenting philosophical quotes about science are just one of many treasures that you can find. Personally, even 72+ hours in I was still discovering new things.
The puzzles themselves are easy at first, obviously – but once you leave (what I call) the fort, you gain access to the majority of the island at once. Therefore, you might be overwhelmed by the options and the sudden spike in difficulty as you possibly encounter a few confusing puzzles with foreign new mechanics. Rest assured, however, that for every mechanic there is a respectful, non-textual, no-hand-holding, non-immersion-breaking, learn-while-you-play, in-game tutorial *somewhere* on this island. And that, my friend, is good design.
"The Witness" might not be a game for everyone but enjoyed it immensely.

As said by many others, it used to be good, but not any more. It's another game where all the devs care about now is making money, not the game, and certainly not its players. Don't download it, and definitely don't spend money on it, just avoid it.
Some fifteen, to twenty years ago online games were a niche thing, devs didn't make them expecting to make mountains of money, they were just in it to make games, and with all being pay to play games, they focused on making them their own brand of fun, so people that liked it would keep paying for subscriptions. Then the free to play (F2P) model became a thing, and over time more F2P PC games adopted the more abusive F2P model that used to just be the kind of thing seen in browser, and mobile games, where your only real options to get ahead in time was to no life the game, or spend money, lots of money. Now more, and more online games just seem like they're only there to make money, and nothing else, fun be damned. In fact, they'll purposely put in things that are frustrating, just so they can say "look, you can alleviate your frustration with the cash shop."
That's what has happened here. In the early days they defended paid premium ships as just things that were a different variant of the ships you can get without spending money, as they provided no real game play advantage, which was largely true then, other things to spend money on were cosmetics, and modest boosters to gains. Now decision after decision seems to have no other reasoning other than to milk as much money as they can from players too easily parted with their money. Short on the parts needed to make that new super powerful item/ship since they just increased the volume of materials you need multiple times over, without increasing in-game material rate of accusation, or are about to remove that ship from production? No problem, you can now buy those materials in their cash shop, through random boxes, even materials to make in-game items you can gain in no other way, that's right, such things can basically be called cash shop equipment like weapons. Want to grind it instead, well maybe, but if that is possible you may need to spend hours a day for months, and you likely need to fly fully levelled ships, so all that XP you're getting is wasted, unless you're willing to spend real money to transfer the excess XP to other ships. They will make new items, and classes of powerful ships after a short release event timed exclusives not available again for a period of months just to create more demand for them during the release event, and get people to spend up to several hundred dollars US to get
ship before they're gone.
All this can come at the expense of balance, and game play since they're removing the ability of other players to get said items, providing the whales with an advantage. The game feels like it's losing players too, causing them to keep making increasingly desperate (and unpopular) changes to their matchmaker rules so rounds can start more easily, since most of the game needs other players for you to even play. The part that doesn't need other players (open space) just gets ignored, and gutted to make other parts "better," with nothing but the promise of some all important fix all update that has been delayed for months. Although, if that update is as effective as their recent module upgrade update, then it will just make things grindier, and all around worse. What it comes down to is that any company willing to hurt their game, and their players to make money, doesn't deserve your money, or time, just don't bother.

First off:
This game has the best title screen and title screen music in existence.
I DO NOT RECOMMEND this game if you are expecting a Visual Novel with 75% reading and 25% gameplay (Ace Attorney Series, Nonary games).
I RECOMMEND this game if you don't mind a decent story that is 99% reading and 1% gameplay. I expected the former (75/25 ratio story/gameplay).
I am setting the game to Recommended status simply because, for what the game is and achieves, it's good. It however is not to my liking....at all. As a story driven gamer, this title barely falls short.
Sound/Music: 10/10 - Amazing, especially the music. Great job.
Gameplay: N/A - You make and serve drinks. Sometimes you have to guess the right drink based on wording given by the client or by remembering a clue in a previous part of the game. There isn't much else here. This is the 1% gameplay.
Story: 6/10 - Here's where I gripe. First off, the writing in this game is fantastic. It's hilarious. Awesome. Now... The story in and of itself as a whole bored me to death. I found myself reading through texts and conversations so fast that it was like I was cramming for a college history test the next day (that I failed). The problem lies in that there is little to no conflict in the overall story. It comes together as just an ordinary person in daily life slugging their way through just to get by. This would be fine, but nothing really "grabs" you beyond that. You are waiting and expecting something to, but it never does.
Overall: 7/10 - This was of course my personal experience. I say again, that for other gamers that are story driven, I do recommend you give this one a try. Please take a look at the overall consensus for the title. It may just be your holy grail story you've been looking for.

I will play more and see if this crops up again. If it does, it is game breaking enough to garner a negative review. I already get a little ticked about how the game interprets clicks as it is, I can't put up with lost activated abilities.

A decent buy if you're already a Magic player, don't bother if you're not, at least don't buy it at full price,because there are many better choices among card games now, and for free. It also still lacks proper deck building, proper balancing and a real campaign mode.
I still say "Yes" because Magic remains the best TCG ever made.
